s: Kryptos, Keys and the CIA Campus
t:
An aside for anyone keeping up – I have been treating this research as largely exploratory in nature, following the associations where they lead and basing conclusions on them rather than fixing on a particular hypothesis because artistic themes don’t enjoy the same provability that encryption and decryption do. That said.

It’s all fine to have this theory of hidden themes and keywords such as PURPLE, WINGS, CAESAREAN and RAY, but an equally important and missing link is the CIA itself. This made me wonder if the puzzle at play isn’t associative in nature, describing a location, an area, or an exhibit.  So I took those keys and  looked around (virtually), starting with the obvious CIA seal  with its eagle and compassrose..

This is located in the OHB (Original Headquarters Building. Curious as to the actual color of the seal, since it’s depicted in black, deep blue and purple elsewhere, I found it…. It’s black. But looking at the images, I noticed something else…. There’s a bunch of columns by it. In some images, these columns are black, in others purple, depending on the amount of light. A relationship between Kryptos themes, K1 and a specific location between the areas of the entire Kryptos Exhibit which ranges from the Morse on one side of the building to the Sculpture and beyond on the other.  The seal is on the floor before the columns.

This would seem to be the association There you have purple columns, rays (the compass rose) and caesarean (cardinal directions, of caesarean or Roman origin). The eagle’s head has no wings, but the building does, eastern and western.

On November 3, 1959, Eisenhower testified to the value of war and peace time intelligence gathering while laying the cornerstone to the OHB.

On November 3, 1990, Sanborn dedicated the Kryptos Sculpture to intelligence gathering at the NHB.

Moreover, I *believe* (cannot seem to confirm anywhere) there is a plaque at this location from the Eisenhower administration where a cornerstone ceremony was performed for the OHB. (Also unclear is the actual location of the cornerstone. The north-eastern corner?)

Conclusion? This could lead off on a separate trail that seems more K4 oriented. More to the point, specifically in looking at K4 is the arrangement of words on the CIA Seal, two phrases in opposite directions from different points around the rim as on the Lotus/Alabaster  Chalice with it’s inscription to the North Wind.

Conclusion 2: It may be required to look at K1 to K3 in a different way, mapping out a circle with "T" as the central position, either on that same 24 character arrangement that I'm using, or another shift.

~ James

s: The keyword HYDRA and its significance
t:
The word Hydra is obviously important, imo, derived from the DYAHR letters.  The cyrillic projector used a similar hidden keyword, Medusa, that led to it being decrypted.

I think the reason that the DYHAR characters are arranged like they are is to simply just give a hint that it is a transposition cipher that is involved.  However, that still leaves us with the keyword of HYDRA.

Adding to its importance, on Jim Sanborn's site, he has a video a work of art he created, called (wait for it...) Hydra, using CO2 and it's directly listed above Kryptos.

I did some searching on the word Hydra, and there was a cryptographic network that used to exist at somewhere called Camp X and it was called the Hydra Network.   It used a machine called the "telekrypton" machine to send and receive messages via some type of system that seems to involve morse code and one time pads of some sort, from what I believe after glancing over it.   This might be worth looking in to....

s: The keyword HYDRA and its significance
t:
My issue with this assumption is the implication that Sanborn could only include this hint if those letters existed somewhere.

What would Sanborn have done if K3 didn't have the letters of HYDRA in some order?  Or, worse, if the ciphertexts of K1-K3 happened to contain no transposals with which he could send along this message?

For primarily this reason, I'm hesitant to place importance on the letters in particular.  My belief (or, maybe more accurately, my hope) is that no matter what the letters happened to be, he could have raised the characters in the 4th, 5th, and 7th positions of the panel (or 2nd, 3rd, and 5th positions of some demarcated five-character block) and still sent along the same message.

s: The keyword HYDRA and its significance
t:
Hey man. I described in detail how easy this was. You'll have to search the archive.

Sanborn did this more than once as well. He did it on the Zola restaurant pieces, moving words to the top left corner via transposition. And he did it using the same passage.

It's super easy when you have a 1,000+ character passage and you get to pick and choose which words to include and what the width is. Even easier when you start modifying the verbs to move a letter one to the left or right.

Jim

s: Kryptos - The Keys and the CIA
t:
Making sense of all the information gathered with practical application.

"In part of the code that's been deciphered, I refer to an act that took place when I was at the agency and a location that's on the grounds of the agency." ~ Jim Sanborn

K1 – "Between subtle shading and absence of light lies the nuance of illusion."

 The Location - Square black columns give the illusion of turning to a cloudy and eventually vivid purple under raking light: This is the entrance to the Old Headquarters Building where the CIA Seal is found, the upper level.

K2 – "It was totally invisible. How is that possible? They used the earth’s -magnetic field.."

The Location + Act - An entire lower level exists beneath the four visible levels above with their columnar windows, one that extends outward beneath the central Kryptos exhibit courtyard and is not immediately visible in most of the restricted photographic views available at the time of JS’s construction. That’s obviously changed with policy since, with an obstructed aerial view and a fairly nice side view of this level available now. That’s illusionary in itself, an optical trick of the electro magnetic spectrum to hide things from view.

JS might not have immediately known about it with his limited access, but since they were renovating and allowed him to design the entire courtyard, it would no doubt have become obvious to him. Hidden before and hidden after, though no great secret by most deductions. That act was the creation of Kryptos Exhibit,

K3 – "Slowly desperately slowly the remains of the passage debris… was removed… Can you see anything? Q"

The Act, particularly of discovery. What would he have seen by looking? Perhaps the same as was to be found in the basement of the Q Building at the OSS in Foggy Bottom before the move, that being the remains of a Message Center.  The OHB had pneumatic tubes, and they’ve either been replaced or added to since then.

Conclusion:

K4 – November 3 of 1959  and November 3 of 1990 are matched dates in which Eisenhower and Sanborn  set the copper-plated cornerstones of the northeast OHB and the northwest NHB respectively, locations on a diagonal ray from each other. As is King Tut’s tomb, Eisenhower’s cornerstone is a time capsule bearing various documents, as is Kryptos of covert surveillance history, apocryphal and cryptic.

~ James

s: A stab at a new code
t:
I've been reading the book "Quest for the Golden Hare" by Bamber Gascoigne (1983) recently. It's about the book Masquerade, how the puzzle was devised, the people who wrote to the author, and the solution. Long out of print, but I love some of the quotes from it ... because the themes are uncannily similar to Kryptos.

"Masquerade" was published on 20 September 1979, and the hint was in the Sunday Times on 21 December 1980. It was the hint that brought the book to the attention of the people who solved the riddle (Mike Barker and John Rousseau) and they'd solved it by November 1981. The heart of the puzzle ("Close by Ampthill") had been devised in February 1977.

I would have to agree with you about wishing the creator of Kryptos would put equal effort into creating a clue.

[page 2-3 ... Bamber Gascoigne was the only other person in the world who knew how the puzzle worked and where the hare was buried]

Letters to me were invariably a last resort. Some came from bystanders, desperate because members of their family had changed before their eyes into unapproachable fanatics or were spending the housekeeping money on apparently insane journeys in quest of the treasure. Others were from the Masqueraders themselves, begging for a single word of encouragement to show that they were at least on the right track. I invariably wrote back saying that in my view the puzzle was far too difficult and advising them to give it up.

...

Kit had explained to me the basis of his puzzle, but even with that privileged information I was unable to make it work out. The cause of my growing uneasiness was the thought that if it was in fact impossibly difficult, then I was the only person in the world in a position to form that opinion. Kit considered it very possible, even perhaps dangerously easy, because he had invented it. The publishers considered it possible because Kit had told them it was. But if my hunch was right, and if people all over the world were beating out their brains and emptying their pockets in pursuit of the unattainable, what should I do? Insert a notice in The Times to the effect that Masquerade was insoluble? I would not have been popular in 30 Bedford Square [home of Jonathan Cape]. Yet clearly the one passenger who believes that a train is hurtling off the rails has an obligation sooner or later to pull the communication cord. So it was pleasant indeed when, in spite of my forebodings, the train pulled neatly into the station.

[page 141-142 ... this one is quite like the 38, 77, first 11 letters of K1 as a key for K4 idea. Perhaps this could have been a gentle way to explain to people who thought that was significant how contrived it sounded]

... But Neil [Parrack] also wanted the almost professional advice of his friend Tony Bennett, who works in intelligence at the Government Communications Headquarters in Cheltenham, an establishment lately much in the news. Tony brought his family over at midday and soon proved himself as good as his reputation. He noticed on the map that a pylon was marked near Needlehole, and the sign for a pylon is an X in a square. Clearly this X was to mark the spot for the solution of Masquerade, itself an anagram of Made Square. It was all beginning to fit, and soon Tony had discovered even more exciting confirmation. Taking the numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 from the Penny-Pockets square, and using the numbers in the same squares on the final page of the book, he came up with a sequence 10 46 4 7 5. By adding the 4 and the 6, he turned this into 10 10 4 7 5. He now told the astonished army of Parracks and Bennetts to turn back to the zodiac page, the one which had put them on to Gemini. He used his sequences of numbers to count through the letters on that page, starting at the end and going anti-clockwise. The last letter is G: 10 back from that gave E: another 10 came to M: 4 more
to I: 7 to N: and the final 5 to I. Gemini again! It was indeed an astonishing coincidence. Numbers and letters intended for totally different purposes by Kit had quite logically turned up the very word already identified by the Parracks as the master clue. Moreover of all the twelve signs of the zodiac on that page, one only is partially obscured. The elbow of the sun man conceals half the sign of Gemini. The full symbol is II - two Is
or two Eyes - so only one I is showing, and one Eye means Needlehole.
...

[page 201-202]
... such was the fertile ground in which so many meaningless coincidences were discovered. That said, I have to confess finally to two Masquerade coincidences so improbable that even my own dispassionate explaining away of such oddities reels a little from the blow. They are in the two areas which I have described as being most suspect - number patterns and anagrams - but they do somewhat astonish even the professionally sceptical.

The number pattern involves Kit's own initials. In using the Dürer magic square in the Penny-Pockets picture, he had to leave out one number to create a necessary space. He omitted the number 7 merely because it is the number most frequently singled out as special. This gave him an equivalent blank space in his final square of numbers (in the sand on the last page) and this seemed a natural place to sign his own initials. KW, which he had included somewhere in each painting. Beneath that final picture he had written `A Culmination', and it was later pointed out to him that his initials did culminate a number pattern quite unintended by Kit. In the Dürer square every quarter of numbers adds up to 34, so Kit's omission of 7 was apt in that 34 can be seen as 3 + 4, making 7. Equally apt was his insertion of his own initials in the other blank square, for K is the eleventh letter of the alphabet and W is the twenty-third. So KW = 11 + 23 = 34. But 34, as 3 + 4, brings us back to 7 which can also be expressed as 1 + 1 + 2 + 3. These digits provide 11 and 23, giving K and W in the alphabet, or Kit's initials, which is where we came in. A surprising culmination indeed.

That number pattern is surprisingly neat, but most of us have no way of judging how surprising such neatness may be in the field of arithmetic. More immediately striking is the mysterious matter of the anagrams. Several Masqueraders noticed that Kit Williams is an anagram of `I will mask it', a fact of which Kit himself had been unaware but which caused him considerable amusement when it was pointed out. ... [finally, the man who found the physical hare, Dugald Thompson, had the pseudonym Ken Thomas, which is an anagram of "the mask on"; he'd called himself Ken and the publisher Tom Maschler had suggested Thomas]

---In [courriel], <[courriel]> wrote :

Another great example, and Rob will back me up on this one, is from the book Masquerade by Kit Williams.  His puzzle was amazingly designed, but also very difficult, so difficult that after 20 years he put an equal amount of effort into a clue (something I wish Sanborn would do) to bring it to a solution:

Here's the link to the wiki for that book for those interested.

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masquerade_(book)

This was the hint eventually released by the author.

Jim

s: A stab at a new code
t:
Hi Jim,

Masquerade is something that I looked at with interest back in 2010.  Having set my own cryptographic puzzles in the intervening years, there is definitely an iteration stage where if you're lucky you can spot some of these unintended consequences and then tweak the scheme a bit to make the most out of them, but yes with so many degrees of freedom I agree that almost anything is possible.
I'm writing up the final paper on the Antikythera connection at present, so I'll add a side note that takes an educated guess at which 'coincidences' were exploited during the top and tailing of the piece.

Mark Brady notes that 'FOCUSED LIGHT BEA(N)S' has been acknowledged as a genuine solver for K1, which I would concur with having arrived by a different route that only concentrated on the constituent letters of FOCUSED.

I think in time this 'FOCUSED LIGHT BEA(N)S clue will turn out to be a classic case in point of how puzzle makers can exploit the kind of 'coincidences' that your raising here as I suspect this was inspired by a genuine coincidence that was spotted in K3 during early iterations.

I'll hopefully have the new paper out by the new year in a new format that people can slice and dice to aid their own research, but this very point about mathematical 'coincidences' may be something that we return to as a resulting philosophical question.  In the absence of having any strong methods of discriminating the intended from the coincidental we're left dead in the water to some degree, so all attempts at Kryptos are effectively a leap of faith.

If Jim and Ed ever read these message boards then please don't release any more clues, but please do leave some memoirs for posterity that detail the 'coincidences' that you never accounted for, as I bet there are some fascinating ones!

Have a great Christmas!
Matt

It occurred to me that this occupies most of the left rim of the Kryptos plaintext, and that a metaphor to the Tut Lotus Chalice from the tomb  and CIA Seal might exist, a set of null ciphers encircling Kryptos separated by null at the end and the beginning. The result, starting from K1 left, and then rimming K2 right is a series of null ciphered words as I see them:

Yellow and pale as ripened corn

Xanth, is of course, another word for yellow.

s: The abscissa of the coords only has two factors, both prime numbers; this seems VERY odd...
t:
Modern cryptography is based on the fact that you can take two prime numbers and multiply them, and multiplication is a very simple feat for a computer.  However, the reverse is a very hard problem, taking a given number, and factoring it to find the sole prime factors from a large number.

Take the abscissa, 38 degrees, 57 minutes, 6.5 seconds (385765) and factor it.  You end up with only two factors (not including 1 and itself), both of which are prime numbers: 5 and 77153.  (I really like the 77 at the start of the larger number there, which is first part of the ordinate of the given coordinates...almost as if that validates that you are on the right track).

If K4 has something to do with this, it completely explains why the coordinates given are slightly off and not directly on top of the statue.  A prime number was needed that could be multiplied by another prime number and get coordinates that almost exactly matched the statue’s location.

This method above is doing exactly what the text essentially says was done: it used the earth's magnetic field to transmit the information.  And we are using the abscissa of the coordinates, here, to do so.

It even makes sense with the whole aspect of how it was expected for it to take "years" for it to be solved.  Let me elaborate... Factorization of large numbers in the late 80s and into the early 90s maybe wasn't at a point yet where it was feasible for a computer to brute force K4 if it was encrypted using one of these methods, which is why both Ed Scheidt and Sanborn both stated that they expected it to take years to solve and it would take time to solve, basically. Computers had to get better, in the event it was to a point where brute force was needed to solve it.

Some other interesting facts:
-K3 has a prime number of characters, 337.
-K4 has a prime number of characters, 97.
-Each line of K4 (after OBKR) even is a prime number of characters long, 31.

I think the lowered D and H from DYAHR signifies a Diffie-Hellman key exchange, which is sometimes simply just referred to as DH.

I have a lot more to say about this, and DH key exchange just lets you basically agree on a public key while each individual has a private key.   I can post more tomorrow…but the fact that the abscissa has only two factors, of which are both prime is VERY suspicious to me.

One other thing I will say, I was messing around with an online RSA tool, using the factors I got above of 5 and 77153 for “p” and “q.”   I ended up with a “K” value of 308309 by following the RSA algorithm with the tool.  The next step in the tool finds the factors of this number.  The only two factors of this number are 44087 and 7.

So….Look at that, I started off with the abscissa coordinates of 385765, and I end up with the numbers in the ordinate part of the coordinates (44087 and 7 which make up 77 degrees 08 minutes and 44 seconds).

What are the chances of everything I just posted being merely just a coincidence?

s: The abscissa of the coords only has two factors, both prime numbers; this seems VERY odd...
t:
Look, everything at this point clearly is pointing me towards this being something based off of the Diffie-Hellman key exchange in a way to start the process.

Here are some quotes from Sanborn that I found online:

"He said/implied that he had built in some dead-ends to throw some people off the track."

"He said that part of the code was designed to be solved with multiple keys -- a code where different keys could be given to different people, but they'd all still be able to solve it."

 RSA can very easily be done via pencil and paper (especially with smaller numbers).

I used a few tools that try to perform different types of attacks on RSA and noticed something very interesting when using the numbers 5 and 77153 I described above.  Look at the example private and public key I was able to get:

Notice the "ww" very close to the start, and I like the "Ed" at the end, heh.

-----BEGIN PUBLIC KEY-----

MBwwDQYJKoZIhvcNAQEBBQADCwAwCAIDBeLlAgEd

-----END PUBLIC KEY-----

Using the above public key, the same program ended up outputting the following private key:

-----BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY-----
MCECAQACAwXi5QIBHQICfLUCAQUCAwEtYQIBAQICfLUCAQI=

-----END RSA PRIVATE KEY-----

If read backwards, the repeating "IQ" from the end of the string REALLY intrigues me.  It repeats 5 times.  Note, that's base64, so the ending = is just a padding character, essentially a null.

I'm not saying these keys are correct, but we really should look into the Diffie-Hellman key exchange system and associated algorithms used around the late 80s and early 90s.   The quotes from above along with other quotes I've read really have me leading down this path here.

Modern cryptography is based on the fact that you can take two prime numbers and multiply them, and multiplication is a very simple feat for a computer.  However, the reverse is a very hard problem, taking a given number, and factoring it to find the sole prime factors from a large number.

Take the abscissa, 38 degrees, 57 minutes, 6.5 seconds (385765) and factor it.  You end up with only two factors (not including 1 and itself), both of which are prime numbers: 5 and 77153.  (I really like the 77 at the start of the larger number there, which is first part of the ordinate of the given coordinates...almost as if that validates that you are on the right track).

If K4 has something to do with this, it completely explains why the coordinates given are slightly off and not directly on top of the statue.  A prime number was needed that could be multiplied by another prime number and get coordinates that almost exactly matched the statue’s location.

This method above is doing exactly what the text essentially says was done: it used the earth's magnetic field to transmit the information.  And we are using the abscissa of the coordinates, here, to do so.

It even makes sense with the whole aspect of how it was expected for it to take "years" for it to be solved.  Let me elaborate... Factorization of large numbers in the late 80s and into the early 90s maybe wasn't at a point yet where it was feasible for a computer to brute force K4 if it was encrypted using one of these methods, which is why both Ed Scheidt and Sanborn both stated that they expected it to take years to solve and it would take time to solve, basically. Computers had to get better, in the event it was to a point where brute force was needed to solve it.

Some other interesting facts:
-K3 has a prime number of characters, 337.
-K4 has a prime number of characters, 97.
-Each line of K4 (after OBKR) even is a prime number of characters long, 31.

I think the lowered D and H from DYAHR signifies a Diffie-Hellman key exchange, which is sometimes simply just referred to as DH.

I have a lot more to say about this, and DH key exchange just lets you basically agree on a public key while each individual has a private key.   I can post more tomorrow…but the fact that the abscissa has only two factors, of which are both prime is VERY suspicious to me.

One other thing I will say, I was messing around with an online RSA tool, using the factors I got above of 5 and 77153 for “p” and “q.”   I ended up with a “K” value of 308309 by following the RSA algorithm with the tool.  The next step in the tool finds the factors of this number.  The only two factors of this number are 44087 and 7.

So….Look at that, I started off with the abscissa coordinates of 385765, and I end up with the numbers in the ordinate part of the coordinates (44087 and 7 which make up 77 degrees 08 minutes and 44 seconds).

What are the chances of everything I just posted being merely just a coincidence?

s: The abscissa of the coords only has two factors, both prime numbers; this seems VERY odd...
t:
Bboylen2, a couple factors (no pun intended), the first of which you may be unaware of.
Sanborn is a mathphobe, so an RSA or similar public key/private key-based system is
definitely not in his wheelhouse.

“This method above is doing exactly what the text essentially says was done: it
used the earth's magnetic field to transmit the information.  And we are using the
abscissa of the coordinates, here, to do so.”

The analogy isn’t quite perfect since geographic coordinates have nothing to do
with the earth’s magnetic field, and in fact longitude is an entirely arbitrary construct
based solely on historical convention (and its origin hasn't always been Greenwich).

"Some other interesting facts: -K3 has a prime number of characters, 337."

True: if you count the question mark. And if you want to solve K3 using modular
arithmetic, you'll need that prime number for the modulus. However, as we all
know, K3 can more rapidly be solved by a conjugate pair of pads and 90-degree
rotations -- almost certainly how Sanborn created it (since he prefers visual
systems).

I suspect the fact that K4's length happens to be a prime number is incidental,
and not relevant to its encryption methodology. After all, a message of random
length <= 100 characters has a 1 in 4 chance of being a prime number.  --Rob

s: Using "O" or "N" as the alphabet key to decrypt K1 instead of "KRYPTOS" both reveal "Q" at position 1 and "YES" as the last 3 characters
t:
Can you see anything Q?

Use the link below rumkin keyed Vignere below, then click the link to insert K1.  Change the alphabet key of KRYPTOS to either O or N, then look at the deciphered text.

rumkin com

I'll also just post here the results for you for each, in case you don't want to check, yourself:

O x PALIMPSEST

QLHXBTGGZMLWLKEPSFGTPJEEETPINQFI
LGFABSYIAULKHXUNZLFILGFYTTZKYES

N x PALIMPSEST

QLHXBTGGZMLWLKEPSFGTPJERETPVOQFI
LGFABSYIAULKHXUOZLFILGFYTTZKYES

It is very interesting that K1 is 63 characters and the K4 clue started at character 64.  The first character of K4 CT is 'O' and obviously the 64th character is 'N'.  Even more interesting to me, these are the ONLY two characters where you end up with the word "YES" at the end like this, if you try to decrypt K1 with those letters.

Also, note the additional L's surrounding the Q, both above, and below it.  Could this be the source of the extra L on the line starting with N?

The main reason I even tried this was based off of looking at the Antipodes sculpture having K4 first, followed by a space, and then K1.  That, combined with the keyword of PALIMPSEST, it led me to believe there's more to the K1 text than meets the eye.  Additionally, Sanborn has stated very clearly that he chose the words VERY carefully for K1.

Take this hypothetical example of a potential way to solve K4: using characters, one by one, try to decode K1 with it.  Then, using some algorithm of some type, a SPECIFIC letter is chosen from the remaining text, and removed.  Keep doing this over and over, and eventually you will run out of characters and have to start over (at position 64).

Now, I have no clue what the algorithm would be and am NOT proposing the above is the way to do this, only an example of one of the many possibilities, and we should consider them all.

But what are the odds that the word "YES" happens to show up at the end of K1 like this, with Q at the start, and ONLY for those two letters, and at the repeated periodicity in K4 of the 63 letters that K1 consists of?   Statistically speaking, the odds of the word YES just appearing from 3 random letters, assuming randomness here, would be (1/26)^3, or 0.00568957669%.

The odds get even more remote if you factor in the Q, along with the fact that this occurs for only the two letters that would be in position "1" if you repeat every 63 character in K4 (character 1 of O and character 64 of N).

This all fits with the keyword itself, PALIMPSEST.  K1 is literally a palimpsest if something like this was done.  This also would be some form of stego, in a sense, depending on how the algorithm works, where there is text hidden within other text.

Using this method would allow K4 to be solved without first solving K1-K3, and Sanborn has said this is possible that you can solve K4 without first decrypting K1-K3, but not for K5.

We have always just assumed that KRYPTOS was the alphabet key for the system, but what if there is a different true key or multiple keys?

Two last funny facts.  If you try inserting K2 using the link above, and then try to use the alphabet key of Q, with the passphrase PALIMPSEST also on K2, the last 2 characters are "NO" and the word "HUMOUR" (likely a coincidence, but funny still, nonetheless) can literally be seen on the second line.  ;)

I think it is very obvious at this point that K1's ciphertext and K4's ciphertext are somehow connected.  Not only from this finding, but also from Scott's breakthrough of finding BERLIN at position 64 in K4 with (77+38*position)%97 and using EMUFPHZLRFA, but this finding, as well.  Perhaps this finding is nothing more than a validation of the connection between K1 and K4 or perhaps the algorithm actually used somehow overlaps one another such that what he found is a side effect of something we do using a method such as what I'm proposing here.

s: Kyptos: OSS & CIA - Something More Basic
t:
I’ve made a lot of to-do about the various underlying thematic keys that I believe are present in the Kryptos sculpture, but after further examining the transformation/transition of the wartime OSS Foggy Bottom site to the "new" peacetime CIA Langley site in Nov 3, 1959, there’s some interesting similarities that crop up between the plaintext and clues in Kryptos to the original site. I'm not abandoning the original premise, but it seems to me there's some more overt links here.

K1 – "Between subtle shading and the absence of light lies the nuance of illusion."

On the burgundy-purple roof of the East Building (the one bisected laterally) there is an octagonal dome structure with what appears to be described as a Diocletian window on each face.  This allows for an interesting light play very similar to a sun-dial, a shadow rotating around the dome like a gnomon.

K2 – "they used the earth’s magnetic field" "transmitted underground to an unknown location"

In addition to the Message Center below the East Building, there was a radio and engineering section below the South Building, iirc, that used a classified (at the time)  electro magnetic Very High Frequency system known as "Joan-Eleanor" to send messages securely. Underground and virtually invisible in a landscape that, like Langley, doesn’t give many clues to what lies below the topography. The path, of course, is much like the one laid out on the Langley Campus between Kryptos and the Survey Marker.

K3 – "Details of the room  emerged from the mist" "Can you see anything? Q"

Foggy Bottom was literally named for the heavy mist coverage.

If one were to enter  the domed structure from below and look out one of the eight windows to the south/southwest corner  of the campus, they would see Building M and Building Q, temporary structures.

K4 – "Berlin Clock"

The 24-sided World Peace Clock in Berlin rotates in similar fashion, but more literally on its rotunda, rather than in lightplay.

Clues

IQLUSION – NUANCE OF I QLU

The South Building is shaped like an "I".

UNDER GRUUND

The locations are under ground, or as the Germans might say, "ground" aka the initial setting…. or in this case site.

Conclusion? The Kryptos sculpture might be a rough map of the OSS campus on the ciphertext side.

~ James

s: The abscissa of the coords only has two factors, both prime numbers; this seems VERY odd...
t:
I would encourage you to continue looking at asymmetric cryptography, but to widen your perspective.  As Rob Matson noted, Sanborn has called himself an "anathemath", so math-heavy algorithms such as Diffie-Hellman and RSA are extremely unlikely.  Yet some of the mathematical principles underlying these systems can be implemented in non-mathy ways, so it's definitely worth thinking about such approaches.

Consider this.  Even something as simple as a "skip" transposition (as rumkin.com calls it), falls in the category of asymmetric crypto.  The skip value for decrypting K3 is 192.  The corresponding skip value for encryption is 251.

One doesn't have to understand the concept of the modular multiplicative inverse* and its role in public key cryptography to implement such encryption and decryption.  It can be done with columnar rotation transpositions, as Ed taught Jim how to do.

* 192 and 251 are modular multiplicative inverses, modulo 337

Tracy Cobbs

s: The keyword HYDRA and its significance
t:
Sure, fine.  But then this is wholly unsatisfying.  It means that this encryption method can only be used in contexts where there is other text alongside it that can be manipulated and used to transmit whatever "DYAHR" is meant to tell the recipient.

How does this work with the billboard in Moscow?  Would such a billboard require some other text conveniently nearby (or, presumably, also on the billboard) in which some letters can be anagrammed, partitioned off, and vertically adjusted, DYAHR-style?

I'm uncomfortable with that kind of impurity (requiring some public secondary text in order for an encryption method to work), but also acknowledge, I suppose, that it could be what we're dealing with.  It would just be unfortunate given the assertions of things like repeatability and the billboard.

Raised letters have to have something to do with it. Its either that and/or the dual alphabets (A-Z & K-Z) on the tableau side. It’s all I see in plain sight that could be useful.

s: The keyword HYDRA and its significance
t:
I'm not debating whether one can do what you're saying (in practice, anyway; any good crypto system needs to address theoretical situations where doing what you outlined just happens to be impossible, but fine).

I'm just saying that I would be super disappointed if K4--"the apex of the pyramid" of a captivating cryptographic structure--used an encryption method that requires secondary text to transmit information. That would really dampen its elegance and hinder its usefulness. The method is said to be repeatable, but with just a little imagination, you can see scenarios where such a requirement is quite a burden.

I think this is fairly compelling. Nice observations!

s: The keyword HYDRA and its significance
t:
What Ed said, was that the precise method for K4 couldn't be re-used but the concept could, don't forget that or misquote it.

He's also said explicitly what you're denying to be necessary, that he transmitted all the information the agent needed on the sculpture. Further, he went on to say that the agent and he would know the system, but not necessarily the key, so the agent would need to be able to walk up to that sculpture 15 years later, or see the text of Kryptos on a Billboard in Moscow and know exactly what to do with it. Nothing I've suggested is out of line with that concept.

I can't figure out which of the two things you're hung up on, the masking technique or the encryption method. If the raised letters (which can be arbitrary) signal a key for how to use the masking method for the agent, then I assume you have no issues?

You seem to be hung up on using "HYDRA" as a keyword. But why? He didn't transmit the keywords for K1 or K2 and they theorhetically able to be solved by "the agent". And we've talked about the the fact that the agent would either have had access to those keywords, recovered them via crib dragging the Morse Code.

You don't need access to a secondary text to create a keyword, but it's a clever way to give you access to one part of the puzzle that you need, Max. On the Cyrillic Projector, he straight up gave out the keyword - MEDUSA, then substituted it (via a method I've been using in masking technique trials) and enciphered a phonetically spelled/misspelled piece of plaintext. Now, you could solve that sculpture without knowing MEDUSA (and it was), but it was difficult.

I'm suggesting for this flavor, it's just a slight twist on that. That the masking technique wasn't a phonetic masking this time, yet instead a dynamic substitution of each plaintext letter for another letter governed by a system we already know Ed taught Jim, and that Jim has used more than once. After that I'm proposing he encrypted it with "HYDRA". Because decrypting with HYDRA would still yield a plaintext with an IC at or near ~3.6 this would be a necessary assumption to remove a degree of freedom.

Otherwise, these things are unsolvable. He could have just as easily done what he did on the Cyrillic Projector and cram the word "HYDRA" into the plaintext of K4 in a different font, but perhaps, just perhaps, as an artist, he saw he could also make it "appear" in K3 via text he already had access to. You've taken a chicken and egg approach here where you're certain he needed to do that, but it could just be that he wanted to do it that way.

The things Sanborn controlled were plaintexts, keywords, raised letters and the Tableau he published.

Jim

The more I think about it, the more compelling this looks.

Warning: this turned out to be quite long!  Apologies.  I'm happy to answer any questions or clarify anything written below.

To summarize what Brett wrote: in K2, we have the keyword ABSCISSA and coordinates in the plaintext.  The abscissa of those coordinates, when concatenated, is a product of two primes, as required by RSA and other DH algorithms.

This indeed gets a bit mathy and will not sit well with those who feel strongly that Sanborn wouldn't go this way.  All of the following can be cross-referenced on the RSA page on Wikipedia.

Determining the Keys

Down this route, n = 385765 would be the key modulus, with prime factorization p = 77153 and q = 5.  [1]

We calculate λ(385765) = lcm(λ(77153), λ(5)) = lcm(77152, 4) = 77152.

Next, we need to choose a public key exponent, which is any number between 1 and 77152 that is co-prime to 77152.  Interestingly, 77152 = 2^5 x 2411.  [2]

This means that we have lots of options for a public key exponent, including any odd number from 3 to 2409 and any odd number from 2413 to 77151 that isn't divisible by 2411.  Quite a few options, but a trivial number for a computer.  Call this public key exponent e.  [3]

Once we have our public key exponent, we determine a private key exponent—call it d—by solving ed ≡ 1 (mod 77152).

At this point, we have our keys.  The public key is the pair (e, 385765), and the private key is the pair (d, 385765).

Key Selection Example

As an example, let's say we choose e = 3.  This is co-prime to 77152, because 77152 is not divisible by 3.

Then we calculate the associated d: a number such that 3d ≡ 1 (mod 77152).  In other words, d is a number such that when you multiply it by 3 and divide it by 77152, you get a remainder of 1.

You can solve for d fairly easily (e.g. using the Extended Euclidean Algorithm or an online solver); in this case, you get d = 51435.

Encryption and Decryption

To encrypt a message, it needs to be in the form of a number.  This is a bit of a roadblock; how might Sanborn have converted the BERLINCLOCK plaintext into a number to which this algorithm can be applied?  [4]

Anyway, given this message in number form—call it m—encryption into a ciphertext in number form—call it c—is straightforward:

c ≡ m ^ e (mod 385765)

Only owners of the private key can decrypt c back into m, as follows:

m ≡ c ^ d (mod 385765)

Summary

Again, yes—this looks really mathy.  But these instructions can easily be explained to anyone, including people who aren't super into math, pretty simply.  You don't need to know the details; you can be given a set of instructions—"do all this stuff on your calculator"—and make this work without much trouble.  I believe it to be within the realm of possibility that Scheidt gave Sanborn a crash course in this algorithm and left him to do what he wanted from there.

This isn't a smoking gun, by any means, but I am inclined to believe that the keyword and coordinates in K2, along with the suitable nature of the numbers they yield (i.e. n = 385765 and λ(385765) = 77152) makes this an avenue worth pursuing.

The biggest problem, to me, is the issue outlined in note [4] below.

Notes

[1] Typically, you want p and q to both be somewhat large.  The use of q = 5 is potentially worrisome.

[2] This prime factorization is, I think, another compelling data point supporting this approach!  Indeed, it is noted in the Wikipedia page linked above:

"... it is recommended that (p − 1) and (q − 1) have only very small common factors, if any besides the necessary 2."

An easy way for Sanborn to ensure that this is the case is to have one of p or q be small with few factors; this could justify a choice of q = 5.

[3] In keeping with (2), we might assume that Sanborn would choose a smaller value for e, like 3, despite it being less secure.  Also of note: in practice, good values for e are numbers one greater than powers of two.

[4] Another wrinkle here is that such a number must be smaller than our key modulus value, 385765.  That is way too small for the plaintext of K4, and this, to me, is the biggest hurdle with this entire idea.

You can split a ciphertext into smaller chunks and encrypt them in sequence, but this is considered insecure.

Another possibility is that something aside from the plaintext is encrypted this way—another key, maybe—and then this is used to decrypt K4.  (This is commonly done nowadays; RSA is often used to encrypt a key for AES, another encryption method.)

Some material to share to provide insight into some of my posts.

Pure speculation of course that the prototype is the "original matrix" that Sanborn referred to, but this is an attempt to make sense of the changes that occur between the prototype and the finished sculpture based on objective distinctions. I believe the end-results are not just a clue in and of themselves, but that there may be clues in the transformative process.

 I've also added notes regarding the corrupted copies as it helps me keep things straight.

Prototype (Sanborn’s screen, as viewed on Wired)

~ Kryptos CT & Tableau in natural state, no reflection

~ Clean, justified lettering on all sides, both halves

~ No L outlying.

~ DY A HR may not be present.

~ No arc’ed void below x-axis

~ Clipped corners on upper and lower inner tableau

Finished Sculpture  (CIA sculpture)

~ Kryptos CT & Tableau are reflected against each other

~ Serrated CT text and tableau text on lower half of y-axis, upper half is justified text.

~ Central L outlying.

~ DY A HR is present.

~ Arc’ed  void to immediate right below x-axis

~ No clipped corners

Common-use Copies (online)

~ Natural, unreflected state

~ Serrated CT text, clean tableau

~ L as an outlier on the right hand side of Tableau

~ DY A HR messy but present

~ No arc’ed void below abscissa

~ Random usage of clipped corners

James

t:
Hi Jim -- even a very crackable (i.e. small p and q) RSA system is going to be quite awkward

when it comes to determining a numerical equivalent to the plain text message (necessarily

a sequence of integers, each less than the modulus). A triplet of plaintext letters could be encoded

by a number from 0-17575, but four letters would span 0-456975 -- greater than his

modulus. So fine, you break up K4 into 33 3-letter chunks. The trouble is after encryption,

you will end up with new integers that 96% of the time will not be in the range 0-17575.

How will you unambiguously convert those back into ciphertext letters?  It is essentially

the same problem encountered when performing 5-bit operations on single letters A-Z

encoded as 0-25, and occasionally ending up with values from 26-31.  --Rob

t:
I'm happy to provide an example.  Yes, this post is also long, but I'm going over every step in detail (and, well, I like this kind of thing).  If we were to skip the explanation of it all, the actual process could be written out in simple steps that anyone could follow.

---

Before we begin, I'd like to say that the contention that I will not be able to provide an example is unhelpful at best.  The only effect it really has is to antagonize.

I'm aiming to help build our community's body of data, and so even if I couldn't demonstrate an example, it wouldn't render this approach completely without merit.  There is value in getting people thinking about it.  Maybe something tangentially related sparks something in someone else; that is the worth of every single idea put forth in this group.

Discussing this, however wild one may think it is, is in line with the belief that we should (especially at this point!) attempt to properly explore every little lead we have.

So here we go!

Plaintext and Keys

Consider the plaintext:

FOCUSINGONESENERGYONMOREPOSITIVEANDRESPECTFULINTERACTIONSWILLFOSTERAMOREACTIVEANDENGAGEDCOMMUNITY

We will use the following keys, selected in the example in my previous post:

Public key: (3, 385765)

Private key: (51435, 385765)

Generating Encryptable Numbers

The main piece that I left as an open question in note [4] in my last post is how to convert a plaintext into numbers that can be encrypted using this method.

We will use one of the suggested approaches: splitting the plaintext into chunks small enough to work with. [1]

Our modulus is 385765.  In binary, this is 1011110001011100101, which has a bit length of 19.  For this example, we'll accordingly encrypt 19 bits at a time [2].  In cases where this results in a number larger than our modulus, we can flip a bit to make this not the case. [3]

To convert our plaintext into bits, we'll convert each character to a number from 0 to 25 and then convert these numbers to binary.  We can then lop off 19-bit chunks, convert to decimal, and calculate the corresponding ciphertext chunks as described in my previous post.

We will encrypt and decrypt the first chunk; the rest will be similar, but with different values.  While it wouldn't take very long—maybe an hour or two—to encrypt the entire thing, this will be sufficient to concretely demonstrate the method.

Converting the Plaintext to a Number

Beginning of Plaintext: F O C U

Beginning of Plaintext in Decimal: 05 14 02 20

Beginning of Plaintext in Binary: 00101 01110 00010 10100

First 19-bit Plaintext Chunk: 0010101110000101010

First 19-bit Plaintext Chunk in Decimal: 89130

Encrypting the Numeric Plaintext

Our message m for this chunk is 89130.

Our formula for obtaining the ciphertext is:

c ≡ m ^ e (mod 385765)

Substituting our values:

c ≡ 89130 ^ 3 (mod 385765)

Taking the value satisfying this equation that falls in 0 <= c < 385765, we get:

c = 216885

We've got our numeric ciphertext!

Converting a Number to Ciphertext

Then, to some actual ciphertext letters, we work backwards.

First Ciphertext Chunk in Decimal: 216885

First 19-bit Ciphertext Chunk in Binary: 0110100111100110101 (one zero is prepended to pad to 19 bits)

Beginning of Ciphertext in Binary: 01101 00111 10011 0101...

Beginning of Ciphertext in Decimal: 13 07 19 [10 or 11, depending on next chunk]

Beginning of Ciphertext: N H T [K or L, depending on next chunk]

And so our ciphertext begins NHTK or NHTL.  We would proceed with encrypting each chunk of 19 bits in the exact same way.

Decryption

Decryption follows the same process, but with the private exponent 51435 instead of the public exponent 3.

Yeah, that's huge, but that's our problem, not Sanborn's!  Thankfully, there are straightforward methods to deal with large exponents in these kinds of calculations.  The first result of a Google search for "modular exponentiation calculator" takes you here, where this can be done quickly and easily.

We convert the first 19 bits of the ciphertext to a number.

Beginning of Ciphertext: N H T [K or L]

Beginning of Ciphertext in Decimal: 13 07 19 [10 or 11]

Beginning of Ciphertext in Binary: 01101 00111 10011 0101...

First 19-bit Ciphertext Chunk in Binary: 0110100111100110101

First Ciphertext Chunk in Decimal: 216885

Then we decrypt using the formula and the calculator linked above:

m ≡ c ^ d (mod 385765)

m ≡ 216885 ^ 51435 (mod 385765)

m = 89130

This was the exact plaintext number we started with.  The math works!  For completeness:

First Plaintext Chunk in Decimal: 89130

First 19-bit Plaintext Chunk in Binary: 0010101110000101010

Beginning of Plaintext in Binary: 00101 01110 00010 1010...

Beginning of Plaintext in Decimal: 05 14 02 [20 or 21, depending on next chunk]

Beginning of Plaintext: F O C [U or V, depending on next chunk]

And so our plaintext begins FOCU or FOCV.  We would proceed with decrypting each chunk of 19 bits in the exact same way.

Conclusion

Yes, it's possible, and it's not especially difficult.  It's exceedingly unlikely that this is the exact method Sanborn used, but if RSA is involved, then some elements here could be relevant.

He may have chosen a different public key (which would also change the corresponding private key), he may have used a different method to partition the plaintext, and he even simply be using the method to encrypt something else (which is typically what RSA is actually used for: encrypting keys to use in other systems).

There's a lot to explore here.  I don't claim that this is necessarily the path; all I'm really saying is that I agree with Brett that the nature of the number 385765 (which is, again, the abscissa of the coordinates given in K2) and its suitability for small-scale RSA really is interesting.

Notes

[1] Just want to re-emphasize the point in note [4] from the previous post: this method is not especially secure.  However, (1) this is just for demonstration, (2) there are various methods to remedy the issues, and (3) well, this sculpture was created in 1990, and many of these insecurities were exposed after then.

[2] We could consider taking 20 bits at a time, which is essentially four-letter chunks and therefore maybe a bit neater.  We run a much greater risk of getting messages larger than our modulus, but we can just flip a bit or two to remedy this. [3]

[3] This'll introduce some fuzziness/masking, which may be desirable anyway!

Imagination leads to degrees of freedom, which quickly render almost anything impossible.

Not to mention your disappointment doesn’t really change the fact set.

Some consider the degrees of freedom imagination is unmanageable due to its unlimited nature but it's worthwhile to consider that when trying to divine meaning from art, there are restrictive means to do so, and that there are practical applications for determining intent. One of these is PALIMPSEST aka pentimento, those things which are seen when viewed at an angle on a work --  brush strokes and processes and other artistic techniques that become visible in raking light. There is also comparing the kryptos prototype and the kryptos sculpture analyze what the artist may have been trying to convey in the changes that he made to the original.

Additionally, a shift in perspective means that DY A HR could be seen as a key idea rather than a key word. Some might find it of interest to examine Sanborn's 2009 video exhibit "HYDRA" which displays two rays of light intersecting through a block of dry ice creating a hydra'esque visual effect that is similar to a compass rose.

James

s: Circling Back To Sanborn on The Cyrillic Projector
t:
This one is my dead horse to beat. And while I'm sure it mostly falls on deaf ears, it's one of the few first hand accounts from Sanborn about his artwork and how he has chosen his keys. I'd encourage everyone to read (it's from message #828 here):

"Sanborn:  Yes.  Within a year of doing the CIA commission, I did an exhibition at the Corcoran Gallery, in 1992, called "Covert Obsolescence", which consisted of "The Code Room" and "The Listening Post".  From the titles you can see I was dealing with espionage in light of the Cold War.  I saw the work of the agency as still reflecting a Cold War mentality, where the KGB versus the CIA was the big topic.  But from about 1990 to today the topic has shifted tremendously  So now it's the CIA and Moussad versus Islamic radicals, et cetera.  The Corcoran installation had some references to Greek mythology.  There was a freestanding cylinder in the center of the room that was totally perforated with encoded text.  Half of the cylinder was perforated text dealing with CIA operations.  The other half of the cylinder dealt with KGB operations.  The two existed side by side.  A pinpoint light inside the cylinder projected these encoded texts, including the word Medusa, which was embedded in the texts, over the inside of the gallery, so that they covered every inch of its surface.  It created an effect where the Medusa's gaze, represented by these bright texts, fell over one's body as one walked through the room.  There was a petrified tree in the room, a tree that had turned into stone.  I felt as if the projected light was a visible ray that was as toxic as the information on that cylinder.  It was a transformation from a text written to a text projected to a text that became toxic when it touched your body."

And on why/how he came to choose MEDUSA (from message #202):

"Metaphor has always been important to me. Petrified trees and fossils were once moving, growing, and living, but have been somehow transfixed, turned to stone.  In this way, the inclusion of those elements in The Code Room allude to the transfixing gaze of Medusa.  The word Medusa is hidden as a key in one of the decoding charts.  I chose Medusa partly because the last three letters of her name -- U.S.A. -- are also the initials for our country, and because the story of Medusa references the invisible quality of the gaze and its ability to transfix the viewer, to 'turn them to stone'."

It makes me wonder if Sanborn chose to highlight "YAR" as "RAY" when projected with a light source from back to front. Not in the physical sense, but in that those three letters when projected would spell RAY on whatever the fell on. Anyway, I still feel like between the pool of water, the previous connections to Greek Mythology and "DYAHR" anagramming to HYDRA that it is in fact a key to the Vigenere layer of the encryption. And he very well could have chosen HYDRA and it's angrammed form with RAY in order because he liked what it conveyed artistically.

Okay, my dead horse beating is over. I'll go back to brainstorming how the masking technique could have worked, in silence. Take care group :)

Jim

s: Circling Back To Sanborn on The Cyrillic Projector
t:
All of this is good information because it gives insight into how the artist thinks (which is

probably quite different from how most cryptanalysts’ thought processes operate). Over

the weekend I started to dip my toe back into the Kryptos pool after a several year

hiatus, and tried to imagine a simple masking technique that was visual, could be

easily derived from the sculpture (without decoding any of the prior sections), and was

non-repeating over at least the length of K4. The simplest I came up with was to

utilize the offset DYAHR as a two-rail kernel, and apply that directly to the top two

lines of the tableau half of the sculpture. Since the kernel’s width is 5, it is coprime

with the alphabets’ lengths, and therefore the keystream pattern will not repeat for

130 letters – more than sufficient for K4. Specifically, the key starts:

ARYDTFSAICKEFNHPJLSNUUVXXZKRCP…

So, what happens when you apply this keystream to K4?  It certainly has an effect on

the “flatness” of K4 – it causes a bit of a peak at period 11 (coincidentally, the same

length as our BERLINCLOCK crib):

OKRXDKELOXE

KJNKYUEJTPJ

QTQUGUZCCHN

ZJUNGBGYLFI

OATPRCSLNJF

ATULREVBBDJ

LRHLABBOKJB

RZJYSXOYSEO

TTUYSEIJU

There are repeats in every column except for column 9, with multiple repeats in

columns 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and 8 (including a triplet of T’s in column 2). The polyalphabetic

IoC works out to around 5.7%. Compare this with K4, which has no IoC greater than

4.4% at any period up through 20.

Alas, the known plaintext for positions 64-74 does not correspond to an English-

looking keyword (nor does applying this “key” beyond positions 64-74 yield

new plaintext):

Ciphertext:  BDJLRHLABBO

Plaintext:   BERLINCLOCK

Derived key: KZIKFUBJPZO

Jim is more an expert than I on the statistical relevance of a 5.7% “hit” when applying

a pseudo-random keystream to K4. My gut tells me that it’s probably not that rare,

but at least the method was derived entirely from elements of the sculpture.

--Rob

s: Circling Back To Sanborn on The Cyrillic Projector
t:
Hah, that dead horse now has a fan. I wasn't aware there was a horse's corpse, of course. That makes a whole lot of sense in context of Kryptos, the reflections and how I've been approaching the Kryptos Prototype vs the Sculpture.

Bearing in mind that the prototype has no reflection, the RAYs (visual effect on tableau, also notable on the CT side of the prototype), you could visualize the transformation this way: Asterisk is the axis point, the horizontal dashes are the abscissa, the vertical lines are the y-axis. forward/backward slashes represent RAYS:

1. Prototype. All rays align.

  /    |     /

--    *   --

/      |    /

2. Sculpture @ CIA. Rays reflect to the right.
/    |   \

--    *   --

/   |   \

 3. Sculpture reflection in pool. As above, so below.
\      |     /

--    *   --

/      |      \

You now have a metaphor for a mythological HYDRA, even better reflected in Jim's dry-ice HYDRA exhibit. Rays radiating outward from the central body in the cardinal and sub-cardinal directions, focused light rays indicating what is hidden.

James

s: Circling Back To Sanborn on The Cyrillic Projector
t:
Good to see you dipping a toe back in, Rob.

I've had two or three distinct ways at looking at this problem.

From a cryptanalysts view, I can see why you'd first want to decipher with a masking keystream and then look for IC spikes, and I do include this as one of my variations (encrypt then mask after).

I do still strongly lean toward mask, then encrypt. The reason is simply because there are so many degrees of freedom on the masking technique that in order for the crib to have been useful, I think you have to be able to decrypt with the Vigenere keyword first (I'm still only pursuing Vigenere as the classical layer). leaving you with something to look for.

When I make this assumption and decrypt with HYDRA, I'm left with:

LSJKH LVUFA AIXOX PGYAR CDAKI
SMNKF ZXVOX JUQNZ YMVOT FWIVK
JHJJH VGWVB ODXMU IQQPE EDNZJ
ZBJXL JHZCB ZXEGH NNRZY NZ

This leaves:  MUIQQPEEDNZ

to correspond with BERLINCLOCK.

Anyway, I've been focused on trying to find a logical algorithm (not necessarily a keystream) that changes BERLINCLOCK into MUIQQPEEDNZ with my primary focus being something like a slide ruler:

https://www.cryptomuseum.com/crypto/aristo/index.htm

or a cipher wheel like the Confederate Cipher Wheel.

https://www.cryptomuseum.com/crypto/usa/ccd/index.htm

Anything that you can adjust after making a substitution according to some pattern is of interest to me. I've been drawn to the cipher wheel because of Sanborn's interest in compasses and the loadstone pulling it off North along with his use of magnetism to pull things out of alignment in his exhibits.

Those are my musings. Bottom line is if it's masking an encryption, the masking technique takes it to an IoC below 3.8 and that has to be dynamic and pseudo-random in nature. And must be only pseudo-random to be recoverable in this analog space.

Jim

There are a number of threads talking about HYDRA and RAYS at present, so thought I'd chip in with where the my research has taken me this last year as its extremely relevant to this topic.

I'm writing this up at the minute, but the major revelation for me has been the discovery of the final planetary dial analogue for the Antikythera mechanism (please read my earlier papers on this if you're at a loss as to what I'm talking about).
This particular discovery was arrived at by looking at the tangent relationship formed between 3 and 31, which resolves to an angle of about 5.5 degrees.  This angle represents the approximate offset of the moon from the plane of the ecliptic and is the very reason for why we have eclipse cycles in the first place.  I'd already noted this at the close of  the paper, 'The Machine', but early in 2018 I happened across a completely separate derivation that I'd never noticed.

Tucked away in the corners of K4 is an anagram of the word KRYPTOS that spans 31 columns and 3 rows.
When I overlaid this derivation over my own, which was TU (TAN) CAR (MOON) something incredible happened that you can repeat for yourselves tonight.
Draw a line (or ray) from the U to the R in:

U
T
V.......................... CAR

And then draw another  line (or ray) from  R to the T in:
                              KR
                              SO
T............................PY

These two rays intersect directly under the letters SOL.

From there it just gets better.  One ray clips the edge of STTR in K3 before hitting ?OBKR in K4.  The other ray clips KLUDI in K4.

Once you put the D back in place of the ? to create DOBKR you get the following results (2 are anagrammed) using a simple caesarian shift.

STTR -> NOOM at 21
OKBDR -> EARTH at 10

LUDKI -> VENUS at 16

There are a number of things that excite me about this result.  The first is that this model of a ray hitting an Earth that is about to be eclipsed by the moon is about as much verification as you can get that you might be on to something. The second is that VENUS makes repeated conjunction patterns with the SUN that trace out a pentagonal relationship.  No other planetary orbits give rise to anything quite as beautifully mathematically and yes the coordinate relationship once again allows us to perform this calculation on the machine.

A crumb also gets thrown out as a result of the visual clues that would appear to set us on a potential path towards a viable decryption scheme.  The way the paths interact shows a stepped pattern over 3 rows and 31 columns.  You'll remember from 'The Machine' that it was shown that the string UNYYCKB was thought to be significant as when 'encrypted' using OKBRUOX  it gave the string KRYPTOS.  Revisiting that original research in the light of these new clues I reasoned that for each block of 3 rows over 31 columns that 7 letters were being selected each time, before the process then moved down another row.  If this process is repeated over 14 steps then we end up with our 98 letters.  I am of course missing out the role of row shifts over a field of 31, but I shall leave that for the write up!

What questions does this raise if this is right?  If the artist has managed to put a mini solar system into K4 then what encryption schemes does it leave available that would allow him the degrees of freedom to still generate something meaningful from the overall message.  The row scheme mechanism hinted at above would only be possible if he had some direction over the row shifts applicable for each step, but that's a lot of numbers to supply from somewhere, so I'm currently looking at the role of the misspelled cardinal point anagrams in the plain text as a potential guide instead.

More than anything I hope this particular post can build something of a bridge between the crypt-analysts and the more artistically inclined as the sculpture as a whole would appear to be describing the most beautiful thing we all hold in common, which is the sky we all look up at every evening!

Have a great evening!
Matt

s: Flushing out the nature and values of the K4 keys
t:
I thought there might be a bit more traffic on the back of the last posts, so I'll kick start the attack on K4 armed with the knowledge gained so far (all this can be found in my existing papers btw)

First 3 rows of K1+ K2 are functionally linked.  The NORTH and SOUTH pole clues appear to be instructions for the order in which to read the letters, i.e. Left to Right or Right to Left.

A left shift of 13 on Row 1 of K1 causes the row to start with a U.
Row 2 of K1 is left unchanged (although due to the spacing of the Y's there is the option to shift to an alternate set of Y's that fit the same pattern.
A right shift of 13 on Row1 of K2 cause the row to start with a K.

I've uploaded a copy of what this looks like in the tool I wrote to work through the rows in batches of 3.

You'll notice that the plain text spells out STEEPLE where PL and extraneous E are read backwards (see the NORTH and SOUTH pole clues in the paper for an explanation).

Now that we suspect we have a D at the front of OBKR, we can see that we have a new 7 letter key which is GKRYPTO (making use of the extraneous P that fits the PUNY clue in K3, (again you'll need to read the existing paper to get a handle on that, but its from the TINY BREACH clue in K3)).

The symmetry between the top and bottom panel text formatting suggests that DOBKR may well be a key or allusion to something 5 bit in nature (perhaps a checksum).  It would also suggest that the corresponding symmetrical 6.5 blocks of the coordinate scheme in row two of K2 (see paper for full scheme) contain initial settings for 6 rows followed by another 5 bit key.  In other words it looks like the first 3 lines of the sculpture and the last 3 lines of the sculpture may well be somehow linked.in a scheme of some sort.  As mentioned before, my suspicion is that we move a row down each time with new settings in the top left panel.

From what I've read of the history, people have been looking at similar possibilities from day 1, so if anyone can remind me of the schemes that went nowhere on this front from memory then I'd be much obliged.

Kind regards,
Matt

Good catch on the numbers adding up to 64. I've often wondered if K4 was split into 2 sections, such as ~64 characters and another ~33 characters (or 48/49), as the beginning and end seem to have somewhat different characteristics (though 97 characters is not much to get useful data from). K1 is 63 characters long, and 64 is an interesting number (2^8, or an 8x8 square). And BERLIN starts at position 64 (not 65, though, from what I can tell). It would be sneaky to give us a clue that covers 2 different encoding systems. Also interesting is that while Sanborn had to use the numbers from the coordinates (they are the actual coordinates of the CIA headquarters), he did add the "POINT FIVE" in there. There was a reason; it could just be that he thought it sounded better. Or maybe he added it as a distraction. Or he could have added it to get those numbers to add up to 64, or insert another digit. I played around a bit more yesterday with this, but didn't get anywhere. One possibility I looked at is that the first 64 characters of K4 have 11 words, with lengths of 3, 8, 5, 7, 6, 5, 7, 7, 8, 4, and 4 characters long. Note, too, that K3 has the words "TRANSMITTED" and "UNDERGUUND" next to each other, both 11 letters long. -Scott

s: Circling Back To Sanborn on The Cyrillic Projector
t:
A quick online search for the mythical hydra leads to the following page:

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lernaean_Hydra

There are a few different things on this page that sparked my interest, assuming that HYDRA has something to do with K4 or other parts of Kryptos.

- "In the canonical Hydra myth, the monster is killed by Heracles (Hercules) as the second of his Twelve Labors."  Since Heracles / Hercules defeated the mythical hydra, could that same name hold similar power to defeat this hydra?  Perhaps uses as a keyword in masking or encryption?

- "The hydra possessed many heads, the exact number of which varies according to the source. Later versions of the Hydra story add a regeneration feature to the monster: for every head chopped off, the Hydra would regrow two heads."  Could this regeneration feature provide a clue as to a potential masking technique, something where a value is doubled, or incremented by one, several times along the way?

- There's also the idea that all of the heads of the hydra had to be vanquished before the beast itself died; the idea that K1, K2, K3, and K4 (each a "head" of their own) all have to be solved before the true nature of Kryptos is known, and the Kryptos puzzle itself "defeated," may provide a sort of metaphorical analogy.

There's also a link to the constellation Hydra, but I think that may be stretching it a bit to have to look for a significant / logical / meaningful relationship between the constellation and Kryptos.

Apologies if these concepts have been presented or rehashed previously; I wasn't able to easily scan back through the years of prior messages and conversations.

At the end of the day, though, I'm with Jim - if we can't recreate a solution with pencil and paper and what is plainly given on the sculpture itself, we're probably overthinking it.

You can take it one step further.........

3+8+5+7+6+5=34 which is the columnar position of the raised "A" in the 42X8 solution of K3,

7+7+8+4+4=30 which is the columnar position of the raised "R" in the 42X8 solution of K3.

Dan

t:
I wouldn't write off Hydra as a constellation clue (it's also an island off the coast of Greece like Antikythera btw!) as there is a very specific aspect of the way 'the machine' works that may well rule it back in.  The 360 characters that are traversed in the layer two scheme represent 4 minutes of time each.  The Earth spins on its axis every 23 hours 56 minutes, with the last 4 minutes only seeming to occur as a result of our motion round the sun.  As a result the constellations (such as Hydra in the plane of the ecliptic) appear to move backwards 4 minutes each day, which gives rise to the Suns apparent motion through the zodiac.

In 'The Machine' this can be achieved by shifting the characters in the calendar group west by one block every time we hit 359 characters/block in our transition through the coordinate blocks for degrees and minutes.

For the purposes of visual display I write my programs to do everything in situ on the sculpture, but for the ease of explanation I might additionally create some circular abstractions that put the 360 characters into a circle and light up in order to explain this particular concept better .

This is just another example of something cool that you can explain using the sculpture text on a 33x28 grid and it may not necessarily be connected to the decryption of K4, but it's definitely something possible within the parameters of the design.

Run the numbers and give it a go.  I've tidied up my personal folders under 'Matz Machine Paradigm' to separate K4 related clues from 'Machine' related research this week btw.

Have a great day!
Matt

While the point of exploratory research is to see where it leads you, CS Lewis’s "Transposition" was an informational  head-butt that I did not even come close to intuiting.

T = TRANS

"T IS…" is a set of null ciphers I found while examining the plaintext grid based in rows of 24.

TRANSPORTATION – T IS AST BALLOON (K1, first letter of each word)

TRANSLUSCENT – T IS FLOWING ROBES (K2, grid fringe)

TRANSCENDANT – T IS HROHNL (K3, grid fringe)

The combined clues with their shared key of "trans" appear to describe one of the Miracles CS lewis spoke of in his sermon, Miracles, that being the Transfiguration of Christ.

"…the vertical ascent like a balloon, the local Heaven, the decorated chair to the right of the Father’s throne…" C.S. Lewis, Miracles

FR (first recorded) ISTANBUL WATCHTOWER SESTOS XANTH F.L..B.L. (left fringe of K1 and right fringe of K1 through K4. This format is a mimickry of the inscription on the first "Wondrous Thing" found in King Tut’s tomb…. The Lotus Chalice.

Refers to the artwork of "Last Watch of Hero" depicting the tragic Greek romance of the virgin Hero and Leander. This is framed as an opposite to a play that CS Lewis mentions in his Transposition sermon, referred to as "The Virgin Martyr" the tragic Christian romance of the virgin Dorothea of Caeserea  under the anti-Christian reign of the Diocletian.

//TRANSFIGURATION  - – Painting by Alexander Ivanov = T IS YOUR POSITION?

This particular painting is a depiction of the Transfiguration from the Synoptic Gospels (now found in a set of four famous palimpsests). If you analyze it, you’ll find that the RAYS radiating outward from Christ form an abscissa, and have carefully aligned diagonal angles as one might find in 0362514 coordinates.

TRANSPOSITION

"…If you are to write a language with twenty-two vowel sounds in an alphabet with only five vowel characters, then you must be allowed to give each of those five characters more than one value…" Transposition, CS Lewis

"….The most familiar example of all (transposition from richer to poorer medium) is the art of drawing. The problem here is to represent a three-dimensional world on a flat sheet of paper…." Transposition, CS Lewis

Points of interest: CS Lewis may have been an influence on Andrei Sakharov, which is an interesting contrast as Sakharov was a pacifist, and Lewis was not.

The Y in YAR is a digamma. Two gamma rays. There are 28 lines in each of the two quadrants on each side - this means there is a 28 character alphabet - the period = X (and others) and most importantly the COMMA. Go through K4 and find all of the double letters; those are all MM. Before and after those are ACO and after are AA - making all of them state ACOMMAA, which is one of Herbert’s sculptures - A,A in Houston. The DIG at the bottom does not follow the acommaa structure - it is DIGAMMA.the Greek symbol for gamma is Y. It is spoken as a W. So WW is YY which actually becomes EE which becomes I as evidenced by the EE in BETWEEN our first word -  which is then also Berlin. The next word is SUBTLE. But that’s too many letters for CLOCK so we remove the B from subtle because it is silent (the subtle nuance - which is also the hook in the period) and get subtle. Which becomes CLOCK. The next word SHADING is scrambled to spell DASHING as in the dashes in the Morse code.

The Morse code:

VIRTUALLY INVISIBLE - as a comma is when compared to a period.

DIG ET AL INTERPRET AT I - means
DIGAMMA AT THE I (the I before the Q in Iqlusion becomes a Y but it is pronounced as a “W”.

Gamma is also a Ray in the invisible electromagnetic field spectrum.

SHADOW FORCES - a comma in a sentence can be used to ‘foreshadow’ in writing, or it can be used to speak of the past: LUCID MEMORY

s: Can anyone transpose the ciphertext in some manner in order to get dYAhR to line up to spell HYDRA in order?
t:
This quick idea I had doesn't have to only be K3 alone, but could also include a combination of K3+K4 combined, or even K1-K4 combined.

What if it's as simple as transposing (even transposing a few times like K3's solution) the entire contents of the ciphertext of K1-K4 such that HYDRA is correctly spelled out in order, and then by tracking the position of where each character in K4 ends up, maybe the plaintext is simply the next character after that character from K4?  (Or the character before it, above it, etc)  Obviously this is just one example of a possible way this could have been done.

Just thinking out loud here.  Not sure if anyone has thought of trying to attempt this yet.  The letters and the way they are oriented look to my like its basically telling you to transpose...now, obviously, that could just be a hint for K3 itself.  Or, what if it's more?  Why hasn't anyone tried to find a way to line up the letters via multiple transpositions to try to see if its possible to get those letters to spell out HYDRA in order?

I really don't think it's a coincidence that this word is featured as a Sanborn piece with a video on his website immediately above Kryptos, and that combined with the fact that he also used a keyword of MEDUSA in the Cyrillic projector that was obvious in a similar fashion to how dYAhR/HYDRA is.   I think this word is important and we should explore it more.
