s: Quagmire III BERLINCLOCK matching + masking thoughts
t:
We must remember that Mr. Jim Sanborn is an artist first and foremost. He not a cryptoanalyst, nor a cryptographer (Mr. Ed Scheidt would be one) so it our effort will continued to be foiled if we keep assuming the plain text is actually grammatically correct English.

Simply put, the questions we are asking is WHAT kind of cipher(s) did Jim use, rather than WHY he would choose "cipher(s)" and then HOW the problem should be approached in the totality of Kryptos. The Quagmire III substitution cipher utilizes direct symmetry like classical Vigenere substitution, and utilizes the principle of indirect symmetry (as described in Friedman's paper below) for the pencil and paper decryption for K1. That is, the distance/shifts in the tableau are inherently preserved in Quagmire III. For example, KRYPTOSABC, the shift from K to A is 6 characters and its distance will always be preserved in the plaintext and ciphertext. For K2, while it also uses direct and indirect symmetry, it introduces the skill of frequency counting and the inherent rise to IC (invented by Friedman). The combination of symmetry and frequency counting will allow for the pencil and paper decryption of K2.

You can read his paper on: The Principles of Indirect Symmetry and Position in Secondary Alphabets and Their Application in the Solution of Polyalphabetic Substitution Ciphers
https://www.nsa.gov/Portals/70/documents/news-features/declassified-documents/friedman-documents/publications/FOLDER_226/41760669079979.pdf

For K3, I have yet to see anyone manage to recover the original intended keys. This might lead to vital clues for the K4 decryption. In regards to masking, it would be best to assume masking is not equivalent a substitution or transposition, but an irreversible step either by the deletion of the character or irreversible change to another symbol (i.e *****). If this were the case, the phrase "COPY THAT." could be masked to "KPTATX" and brute force dictionary attacks would probably miss such plaintext anyways.

Re:  The Aenid and the ciphers a good source is:

https://toebes.com/Flynns/Flynns-19260424.htm

I believe Antipodes might be an integral piece worthy of intense scrutiny. Jim installed Kryptos on the CIA grounds, fully aware that It would be inaccessible physically by the general public. Antipodes on the other hand is fully accessible by the general public. Let's say possibly that Antipodes is giving the 'people' a level playing field. I'm guessing most of y'all know the differences between Antipodes and Kryptos.

Something kind of 'hit home' about it and that is if we integrate the first word of K1 - 'Between'; which seems a fairly integral and important word in these works; what is Antipodes and the Hirshhorn museum 'between'? It is almost equidistantly between The US Capitol Building and the Washington Monument. It gets a little confusing here as the tomb was moved around a few times. One interesting fact was that at the Mt. Interestingly after the damage from the lightning they installed copper as part of a lightning protection system.

There are a few other interesting facts that seem to play into the narrative of Kryptos/Antipodes that you can find on Wikipedia. In Ed's perspective, Kryptos can also represent a homage to William F. Friedman and his contribution of Military Cryptanalysis (Parts I-IV). The techniques of symmetry (direct & indirect), transposition matrix reconstruction, and asymmetrical cryptograms (K4) are all present in Kryptos.

If a Quagmire III substitution is used with the Vigenerie modified tableau of KRYPTOSABC...then working backwards the 1:1 relationship of NYPVTT MZFPK to BERLIN CLOCK relationship could be encoded/decoded with ELYOIE CBAQK instead of PALIMPSEST/ABSCISSA for K1 and K2. This would imply that K4 could have a key length of 97 characters and ELOYIE begins at the 64th key character. Assuming the key is self-contained in Kryptos, then it could either be hidden in:

1. K1-K3 ciphertext
2. Vigenerie modified tableau
3. K4 itself

Circling back to Ed Scheidt's cryptic "Moscow Billboard" thought experiment (and hint), it could be thought of an exercise in the deployment of ciphertext and the related keys/tableaus. With combination substitution-transposition systems, question lies in whether the decryption should be substitution first or transposition first?

A. Substitution (decryption) then transposition - minimum of TWO keys/tableaus would need to be deployed to the operative
B. Transposition then substitution - one SPECIAL case scenario with ONE key only (see below)

K1 and K2 both used the tableaus (upper for K1 and lower for K2..both stenographically laid out) and Jim left stenographic clues to the recovery of the keys. K3 seemed to have various methods/keys involved, but I prefer the method of the late Gary Warzin on his K3 key recovery. In regards to the special case, the special case scenario is when the ciphertext is also the key when transposed. The transposed ciphertext would then be used to decrypt itself through the standard Vigenere tabula recta, XOR, Vernam, OTP, Running Key (all same decryption methods). If this were the case, the key would then be MUYKLGORNA instead of ELYOIE CBAQK for the BERLIN CLOCK CRIB. The approach would be then constructing a transposition method (the algorithm) to decrypt K4. This might be the reason for the PALIMPSEST/ABSCISSA keywords referring to the Vigenerie Tableau that has been conveniently been modified (previously Tabula Recta) since IT'S AS SIMPLE AS ABC.

Just for extra fun, let's just make the K4 transposition matrix asymmetrical, do unorthodox double "shifted" columnar transpositions , AND mask/conceal the plaintext so that letter frequency counting won't work. To summarize, K4 is just a substitution decryption, AND the key recovery (K4 transposition portion) must be done by analog means.

At the time, Western Union charged "by the word" so the question arose of how much to charge to send an enciphered message:  is it a single "word" of 100 letters, or 100 words of 1 letter, or something in between.  It was decided that the average word in English was 5 letters in length, so telegrams were sent in 5 letter groups and charged accordingly.
Doug

s: William F. Friedman NSA Collection - Jim's possible primary sources of research
t:
The Friedman Lectures on Cryptology - https://archive.org/details/41785109082412
Lecture I - Background on cryptography (kryptos - Greek for hidden)
Lecture II - History of cryptography (Cryptography and cryptanalysis), Egyptians and the Rosetta stone (Kryptos figuratively represents a Rosetta stone)
Lecture III - Cryptography in the American Revolution, Rosetta Stone decryption and reference to Archimedes eureka moment
Lecture IV - Civil War cryptography, USMTC (columnar transposition), Confederate (Vigenere square with repeating key)
Lecture V - Western Union Telegraphic Code, transposition ciphers, Army field codes
Lecture VI - World War I to end of World War II, Cipher machines M-138, Jefferson/M-94
----
From an artistic perspective, Kryptos can be considered both a homage to William Friedman's work and a historical timeline to cryptography as a whole. If Mr. Sanborn chooses a 100% American approach as an artist, then all inputs must be of American origin (i.e Paul Revere 110 copper). This should also imply that the cryptological methods of Kryptos is American origin AND specifically K4 is of American origin.

Military Cryptanalysis Part IV - William F. Friedman - https://archive.org/details/41761079080022
Section VIII - Combined Substitution-Transposition Systems - Paragraph 36(b) Other types of combined substitution-transposition systems (Page 94-96):
A few remarks may be made in regard to the order in which the two processes, substitution and transposition, are employed m a combined system. It is clear that when the substitution is monoalphabetic it is immaterial, so far as cryptographic security is concerned, whether substitution is followed by transposition or vice versa, because the equivalent of each plaintext letter remains fixed regardless of the order in which the plain-text letters appear in the plain text. However, if the substitution is polyalphabetic in character it is better that the transposition process precedes the substitution process, and that the number of alphabets employed be different from the number of elements in the transposition key, if columnar transposition is the case. The best situation, from a cryptographic security standpoint is when the two key lengths (substitution and transposition) have no common factor. If the two keys are of the same length the letters in each column are enciphered by the same cipher alphabet and thus the cryptogram would contain a certain number of sections of approximately equal length, composed of letters falling in the same cipher alphabet.
----
Even Friedman advises of an encryption of substitution THEN transposition. The K4 decryption steps would be the inverse as transposition THEN substitution (K4 plaintext masked/concealed for bonus Scheidt step). In short, K4 will require the recovery of the transposition algorithm which is embedded on Kryptos just like K1 (cipher-alphabet + keylength upper tableau lines A-K), K2 (cipher-alphabet + keylength lower tableau lines O-W) and K3 (en dYA | hRohn for 5-bit binary 24 and 8) have stenographic clues to provide the key length. Anyone with a mini-kryptos model can spot the simplified stenography on the right margin of the tableau for K1 & K2. The pencil and paper method would just require running the tableau through the "shifts" and using direct/indirect symmetry.

ELYOIE CBAQK would be in the Quagmire III style of the tableau as KRYPTOSABC...Z. This may be Jim Sanborn's original intent, but we're only guessing here. To date there are no stenographic clues for K4 relating to the tableau. For K1 & K2 there are stenographic clues to utilize the tableau for decryption.

MUYKLG KORNA would use the tabula recta ABCEFG...Z - if PALIMPSEST/ABSCISSA refer to the tableau (and K4), then the original tableau without the horizontal abscissa is simply a tabula recta allowing for any use of Vernam, XOR, one-time pad, Vigenerie, or running key cipher. This would allow for a single key recovery if K4 is just the decryption key, but scrambled (transposed) in some unorthodox manner.

During 2015 Ed Scheidt's workshop (43:33), he clearly said "this is not a one time system" and then with the magic of misdirecting hand gestures he immediately qualified it with "...in the sense that it the difficulty would be forever"

Hi Ross. Great to hear from you!

I took a look at something Elonka said about the 6 pairs of letters in a 7 (or 8) column version of the K4 passage that she shared on a video on Youtube. I looked not just to the 6 horizontal pairs she pointed out, but also to the total of 15 pairs of letters that were horizontal, vertical, or diagonal. It didn't seem to be random, in any way. I wanted to know if this represented something visual. I started by taking the text, as it sits in K4, and turning it into varying numbers of columns. I didn't see anything special when doing this.

Then I decided to use the cipher table on the right side of the artpiece (kryptos passkey) to convert the K4 passage, while I kept the ?. I saw the 31 columns represented in the cipher table on Kryptos and decided to make this converted text into columns from 1 to 31. These were then my jigsaw pieces. I colored in all of the contiguous double, triple, ... letters. The first thing that seemed to pop out was a "7." From there, I began to put this together and could see the potential of 12, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, and 7 coming out of the puzzle. Those numbers could be in the positions you would expect on a clock. Just a quick point of clarification.  KRYPTOS is a tribute to CIA, not to NSA.  KRYPTOS highlights agent communication, which uses cryptography but adds some quirks as Ed had described:  the ability to reconnect with an agent after many years, the use of signals (put it on a billboard, which means something to the agent) etc.

The agent, as Ed described, is not sophisticated when it comes to cryptography;  he/she needs something dirt simple to use.

An example might be sending something in morse code (everybody sees it, as if it were on a billboard) and the agent knows what to do with it.
For example, if the encryption used QUAG with 4 alphabets, where each letter was encrypted using 1 of the 4 alphabets, the agent would have to send the sequence of alphabets he used (which he may not be able to do);  alternatively the agent's control could provide the sequence and send it as a series of 1/0 dih/dah morse code elements.  Either way, both communicants have the sequence which can then be used to encrypt, and subsequently recover, the message.

While this would be consistent with what we see (unexplained morse code, a KRYPTOS tableau with 4 columns to the right, etc.), I have no evidence that this is in fact what Ed did.

Another aspect of agent communication that Ed described is the use of duress codes, so that a recipient would know if the agent was compromised and forced to send a message.  This could be done as take a 91 letter message, encrypt it, insert a 6 letter authenticator ("berlin"), and reencrypt the resultant 97 letter composite message.  While he talked about duress codes, he did not say whether K4 incorporated one.

Again, I have no evidence for how K4 was actually prepared, but I'm fairly confident this was done as an example of agent communication and will have some of the quirks that Ed described.

KRYPTOS is a tribute to CIA (running agents) and not to NSA (traditional cryptography with securely distributed keys, etc.).  (Trust me, CIA is not going to pay for a tribute to NSA!)

I believe the emphasis here is not on the cryptography (coming up with a super secret algorithm that nobody has ever seen), but rather on the application of cryptography to agent communication (e.g., using something simple like QUAG but with a twist, that is "good enough" for infrequent use for small messages)

Just my opinion, for what it's worth.

Generally speaking, it will come down to the interpretation of masking. There are two schools of thought on masking:

1. Reversible masking - when characters/words can be substituted for another related secret meaning (i.e. meeting at 3PM would be "See you for tea"). A 1:1 mapping of plaintext and ciphertext is not required.
2. Irreversible masking  - when characters/words are removed, but still maintain the meaning (i.e. CUFORT or C U FOR T). A 1:1 mapping of plaintext and ciphertext can still be established.

In terms of K4, I would say the latter of irreversible masking is used on the plaintext of K4 to make it nearly impossible to brute force. The reason why Mr. Ed Scheidt is flabbergasted at the question (watch on YouTube), is that if K4 is irreversibly masked, it can ONLY be applied to the plaintext and not the ciphertext. Ed goes on to defer because it might steer us in the wrong direction if misinterpreted.

I believe where we are getting stuck is that Kryptos is an analog puzzle and must be solved using analog means. This does not mean we cannot use computers, but things have been done to eliminate the computational advantage through transposition and masking. For transposition, it is an unorthodox asymmetrical transposition that cannot be easily programmed AND for masking, the plaintext is concealed so that it would be near impossible to brute force. The result is that there will be an analog component of a person who has to perform the transposition and be able to read the masked plaintext (computers won't be able to read it).

I have been thinking about the quantity of characters on K4, and I have been looking into potential aspects of padding and/or truncation. I feel there is the possibility of a truncated K4. However, one angle that I'm pursuing is that instead of viewing K4 as having 97 letters, I am looking at it as a combination of 97 letters and placeholders combined. One example, there are an odd quantity of double letters when read left to right.

I am looking at different possibilities, including that the double letters indicate the start and end of padded lettering, added to confuse the cryptoanalysis; the last set of double letters not having an end set, and being open. As a result, all of the double letters, as well as, those character spaces between the sets of horizontally read double letters are just placeholders!!

I'm evaluating the possibility that remaining non placeholders get pulled from K4, analyzed, then returned into their transposed positions on K4, around the stationary placeholders.

Another clue that I am evaluating is the Pre-K clue of ETRANSEWJ. Remember, that this was garbled text at the end of that solved section, and was, I believe, meant as a key clue for K4. The reason I believe it was a clue for K4, was because we have been told by JS that we do NOT need parts K1, K2 and/or K3 to solve K4. By expressly eliminating these sections, he left the door open to the possibility of including other sections.

Previously, in another entry, I had brought up the idea of truncating K4 using ETRANSEWJ, rearranged as JETANSWER, then interpreting that as AIRFORCE1. By using a 1, instead of "ONE" allows me to maintain the correct character count to build a proper matrix. However, by using the "1", I am able to truncate K4 by an entire column of letters. Of course it's important to track the positions of the moved letters of the "1" column, because they will be placeholders, when reassembled into the 97 positions of K4.

Another thought I had regarding ETRANSEWJ, was that it could also be rearranged as TRAJENEWS, TRAJE NEWS.
TRAJE is indicative of the number 4 in Chaldean Numerology. Chaldean Numerology being considered a more accurate number system than Pythagorean Numerology. When the numerology charts are compared for both of the 2 systems, I began to realize that one could create an arbitrary-looking cipher text if the Chaldean Numerology system was used instead of the Pythagorean Numerology system, as the letters are not fully sequential. Therefore, any base 8 (Chaldean) or base 9 (Pythagorean) numerology system would offer more confusion if run together (especially, if there is a numerical substitution at some point, based upon 2 distinct alphabets).

And, then one other point that I had thought about was whether there were any clues on the original K4. My thinking is that I'm only looking for 2 distinct differences in the actual K4 at Langley. Specifically, when closely scrutinizing the actual K4, does one get the idea that, despite workmanship, are there 2 distinct formats to create K4. It could be the radius of the cut corners of the letters where different axes of a letter come together; creating a "block" letter set and a "rounded" letter set. Or, does one letter in the actual K4 appear out of place? Because, it may NOT be a single letter that is out of place, but it may represent a shift of an entire row (or, column) that shifts. For example, there are 4 rows to K4. Generally, 3 rows correctly spaced would indicate a pattern (the 4th row, if slightly more spaced vertically would indicate a pattern shift!). Can someone, at Langley, measure the spacing between JS's scribe marks? I am speculating that there may be 2 distinct letter spacing criteria. Obviously, these subtle clues would be too difficult to recognize from any photograph. The point that I am trying to make is that I want to determine if there are 2 distinct alphabets being used to mask the text. Perhaps, the combination of Chaldean and Pythagorean Numerology systems, etc.

Finally, bringing this full circle, it has been my thought process that K4 incorporates a One Time Pad. There is a very specific note, laid out in block lettering, on JS's webpage that is the correct length of K4. Because of the number 4, and a colon (:), it can throw you off, a bit. However, this note is available for everyone to see (just like a billboard on the side of the road). When I laid the 97 characters of K4 underneath this note, and applied a Mod-26 to the letters, I got "berlinclock" at the correct space locations, which convinces me that I am on the right track. It's just a matter of finding the correct letters to apply the Mod-26 to, to arrive at the solution for K4!!

*But, keep in mind, if there is truncation, or padding, then some of the letters of K4 might remain exactly as they are!! The actual message could very well be less than 97 characters in length, but the overall solved K4 will incorporate the message AND the placeholders, and be the true 97 characters with the clue EXACTLY where it should be, just like JS has indicated!!!

Could someone provide me with some feedback? Thanks in advance.

Interesting take on the Archimedes Palimpsest, whose relationship with Kryptos seems intentionally hinted at in the exhibit. There’s several items like it throughout the study of the sculpture’s text, plain and cipher, and when I say “like it” I mean in context of certain Lost Works, specifically referring to the Palimpsest, Tut’s Tomb, Aeneid (integral to my own study) and the Urania World Peace Clock in Berlin – and of course Kryptos itself.

The Archimedes Palimpsest was *rediscovered* lost among other texts by a historian named Heiberg, and assembled as it is now.

Tut’s Tomb is reported formerly lost primarily because the entrance had been covered by debris from building another tomb nearby.

The Aeneid, like Max Brod’s Kafka works, was intended by Virgil to be burned because of its unfinished state and some problems Virgil had with what he had written. By decree of Caesar, some edits were made, and it was retained anyway.

 The Urania World Clock was a replacement for the pre-WWII Wettersaule clock which was destroyed along with much of Alexanderplatz. I don’t know if the original is retained.

Kryptos itself was built during a period of transition – Sanborn didn’t just design the sculpture, but the exhibition grounds in the central area, and one can note the changes to the landscape, and guess at what originals may have changed. There is the pulped-documents as well, that he used in the Spy Restaurant exhibit.

Some thoughts to consider.

As I'm sure you're aware, part of what makes the OTP impossible to solve is having 2, or more, unknowns and 1 known. However, by giving us this clue, JS has given us 2 knowns, and we're left to try and figure out the 1 unknown.

By giving us the secret message for spaces 64 to 74, and my assumption of the Key, we're left with simply solving for the unknown Plain Text, which will ultimately find itself at spaces 64 to 74 AFTER the successful completion of whatever steps need to be completed to get that character string to those spaces, in the proper order. Think of it as a "cheat", whereby you can check your work. Should you arrive at a solution, all you have to do is verify that letters have been properly arranged at spaces 64 to 74. Now, regarding the backfill of the "berlinclock" clue to arrive at the unique solution for the jumbled Plain Text:

Some facts & assumptions must be made to determine the unique solution.

(1) The "berlinclock" clue's characters must fit in the same spaces at the same location of the original Plain Text "NYPVTTMZFPK", as per JS.

(2) You have to assume, for the purpose of this exercise, that the Special Note on JS's website (described above) presents characteristics, which are conducive to a potential solution for K4. And, [b] there has to be a logical explanation why the size & font of the characters used on this string of words was chosen to highlight this Special Note, when other important data could have also been added, (ie. $50 cost to respond to KRYPTOS inquiries, or address to send inquiries to, etc.).

(3) You must suspend your disbelief about the size of a potential solution's Key size when using a 97 character OTP Key, instead of a small Key used in repetition.

Once you have mentally gotten past the size of the Key, you must lay out the intermediate Cipher Text (the OTP Key). Next, you align the "berlinclock" clue at the exact spaces the of where "NYPVTTMZFPK" resided (spaces 64 to 74).

You must assign the Mod-26 number to each character in both the message (berlinclock; 1, 4,     17,     11,     8,     13,     2,     11,     14,     2, 10) and the Cipher Text (IONTOTHEREM; 8,    14,    13,    19,    14, 19,     7, 4    , 17    , 4    , 12)

Then, you're just solving for the equivalent non Mod-26 number. Two knowns and one unknown, using Mod-26. Actually, you will get a Mod-26 number. But, you make it a non Mod-26 Letter, upon conversion to the Plain Text. For example, A non Mod-26 = 1; A Mod-26 = 0.

* It's important to remember that because it is a One Time Pad (OTP), there can ONLY BE ONE UNIQUE SOLUTION!! You're solving for the Plain Text, which should be in spaces 64 to 74, after all of the other operations have been completed (ie. any substitutions, transpositions, etc.).

The technique of seriation has been mentioned only twice in this group before - in the groups.io numbering, since Yahoo Groups will close soon (2013, Mike Brophy, #15086, below) and 2017 (Geoffrey Caveney, #19358).

It is used to add a transposition step to a polygraphic cipher and increase the difficulty. It combines the main two types of cipher - transposition and substitution.

Scheidt stated in 2015 that “[he] would consider [K4 encryption] [to be] more than one stage”.

Seriation is usually used with Playfair, but it can be applied to other polygraphic ciphers.

The ACA guidelines for Playfair and Seriated Playfair can be found at

http://www.cryptogram.org/downloads/aca.info/ciphers/Playfair.pdf
http://www.cryptogram.org/downloads/aca.info/ciphers/SeriatedPlayfair.pdf

These are both based off the description in Gaines (1939) “ELCY” which was expanded in Bowers (1959).

As an example, take this 5x5 Polybius square and combine I and J in one cell. You could consider this to be a "matrix" that Sanborn keeps talking about.

GMNET
DPXHI
ZRBYU
LCOKA
VWFQS

Seriate the K4 ciphertext at width 24. Incidentally, the Berlin Clock has 24 lights and is a 24-hour clock, and works modulo 5, like a 5x5 Polybius square.

Although the clock can theoretically represent hours from 00 to 24 (25 hours), the minute after 23:59 is 00:00 on the actual Berlin Clock. So you could say there is one hour that you never "see".

Also, 24 is the lowest width value where you don't get any doubled letters in the seriated K4 ciphertext. If you are doing "standard" Playfair, you won't see any doubles in the ciphertext. Or you could change the rules to allow them, e.g. in Kahn's "The Codebreakers" p593 in a story about JFK in WW2 they just put doubles through unenciphered.

Here is the seriated ciphertext starting with OBKR … the first 96 letters. We can also get a similar answer starting with ?OBKR.
Again, this is a different kind of “matrix”.

OBKRUOXOGHULBSOLIFBBWFLR
VQQPRNGKSSOTWTQSJQSSEKZZ
WATJKLUDIAWINFBNYPVTTMZF
PKWGDKZXTJCDIGKUHUAUEKCA

Here one digram (BS) occurs twice in row 1/2 (near the right hand side).

Now decipher NYPVTT MZFPK using the above square as follows. Use the ACA Playfair rules as in the ACA link above, but flip the two letter output. Otherwise, you won't be able to have K decipher to K. This is probably the simplest change to the Playfair rules that would "work".

First column is the CT, second column is deciphered.

NU BT
YH EH
PU RI
VA LS
TU IS
TE NE
MK CE
ZC LR
FA OS

WP MC
AK OK

Now using seriated Playfair (variant) instead of normal Playfair, we can certainly say "NYPVTT MZFPK" corresponds, in order and in the right places, with "BERLIN CLOCK" in the output.

With a seriated polygraphic cipher, there's no ambiguity about whether the crib correspondence is "one-to-one" as there might be if it was ordinary polygraphic "many-to-many" encryption.

Output

FFKMZFNOVQAGFSFVHFFFMODU
LYYPYBDCTIBARAKAHWUUQQZZ
MOSTHOUPSTRIXNOBERLINCLO
CKMDLAYITUCHTVYTHISSEERS

Writing it out in one line

FFKMZFNOVQAGFSFVHFFFMODULYYPYBDCTIBARAKAHWUUQQZZMOSTHOUPSTRIXNOBERLINCLOCKMDLAYITUCHTVYTHISSEERS

You can see "BARAKA", "THISSEERS", "MODUL", etc, but it's not very convincing English text for non-deranged people. And that rule change may be a bit contrived, although the same thing happens in one step of the "Doppelkastenschlussel" (below). Would you really be thinking of this change before the "CLOCK" clue of 2014?!

To try to get better English plaintext, you could try some or all of ...

    •    permute the letters in the Polybius square. Or you could manually guide them to be more like KRYPTOS or an English word in some order
    •    combine/omit different letters. Maybe U/V instead of I/J, or combine Q/U based on K1,2 PT misspellings
    •    change the seriation width. At some widths, you'll get doubles
    •    change the dimensions of the Polybius square - e.g. use a 6x4 (combine I/J _and_ U/V, or drop out J and Z since they're never used in the K1,2,3 PT) or a 9x3 rectangle (add "?")
    •    try to guess some more plaintext, and force that in the output
    •    use a different polygraphic cipher for the seriation
    •    start modifying the ciphertext arbitrarily e.g. drop a letter out somewhere so the length of the new CT is 96, divisible by 24. Gary Warzin used to suggest it. Risky!
    •    lose your mind and start seeing patterns where there are none! People do this with K4 and the Zodiac cipher Z340 all the time - believe and achieve!

It's been pointed out here by three people independently (Tim Kirchner 2003, Ed Hannon 2010, and Geoffrey LaTurner 2016) that seriating the K4 CT at width 21 gives you many repeated digrams e.g. check Ed Hannon's post history since 2010. But then with a seriated digraphic cipher at this width, you'd have the problem that the T in the adjacent repeated ZT digrams has to decipher to both the I and N in BERLIN. How could that happen?

This observation about width 21, to my mind, is the most significant one I've seen about K4. Another is the KR, SO, YP down the K4 CT RHS, which would seem to be a hint towards a digraphic cipher.

There are also things in the other parts that don't seem to be coincidences (e.g. "OSS BATTALLION" is an anagram of the K1 PT initials, and IDBYROWS/LAYERTWO in K2 PT). For a long time I thought that second one was a hint towards Trifid, but that led nowhere.

Something that doesn't seem to have been mentioned in the group yet is that seriating the K4 CT at width 7, you'll have I and J missing in alternate rows. This could be evidence for a system with 5x5 Polybius square(s) with I and J combined. It's also aesthetic - seven pairs of rows of width seven, the same number of letters in the word "KRYPTOS".

Some other digraphic ciphers you could try with seriation for K4 are

    •    Hill cipher (but Sanborn has said he’s an “anathemath”)
    •    Other Playfair variants, like Wheatstone's original method in his 1854 paper - again, check Kahn p199, though the method is not explained in the book text; he has a 3x9 matrix there too, which might account for the extra "?" making K4 98 characters (Scheidt in Wired 2005 said K4 was 98 _characters_ rather than 97 _letters_)
    •    Two-square (left/right and top/bottom variants, pairs in the same row/column go through in plain or transposed, or with Playfair-like rules)
    •    Four-square (a couple of people e.g. Bill Briere in 2009 have linked it to the structure of the sculpture itself, an “obvious hint” in “plain view”. Although with four mixed squares it would be probably be impossible)
    •    the "Doppelkastenschlussel" cipher Germans used in WW2, mentioned by Mike Brophy here in 2013; with the final CT written out horizontally ("by rows"), as in the Charles David paper (1994). Other versions were described pre-Kryptos in two 1987 papers by Currer-Briggs and Schick, but with the final CT written out by pairs. It has also been called "double Playfair" (probably first publicly by Bertrand in 1972/73, then in SRH-124 in 1981, but Schick wrote that he never heard it called that), double box, double key, double cassette, double casket, double stop, non-indicator cipher, NS 42, Nachrichtenschluessel, and Truppenschluessel. “It was not some minor system — it was the major German field cipher for the whole darn war.” So was BERLIN a hint towards that?

Polybius square based systems fit well with the 2011 Scheidt quote relayed by Ed Hannon: "K4 cryptography is similar to what would be provided agents or pilots in case of capture." You could even argue that a system using just one Polybius square would be more likely in that case.

The more Polybius squares you use, the fewer variants there are. By the time you get to four-square, I think there's only two sensible variants depending on how you arrange the CT output. Whereas for Playfair, there are many variants (check MilCryp and Gaines). Gaines mentions a variant by W. W. (heh!) Rouse-Ball where letters in the same row go down and letters in the same column go right.

With the last cipher here, the DoKa, you can certainly get BERLIN CLOCK at the right place. The David article about it has several parts reminiscent of Kryptos, with the seriation width 21, the repeated KKs in an example, and best of all he states "What is your position?" (from Kryptos Morse, "wie lage" in German) was a great crib!

It would be very difficult to solve, though, I think, at this length. And the squares in WW2 were random, not keyword based. But because the unicity distance of the cipher is only around 45 letters, it might fit the "expected to be solved eventually" nature of K4. There might be some trick to solve these ciphers more easily I don't know about.

The late Richard Gay on his website kryptos-cia.com (still available through archive.org) suggested K4 could be based on Playfair or double Playfair with a "super-encryption additive" of some kind.

The underlying cipher for the seriation doesn't have to be digraphic. It could be trigraphic - both of these systems uses just one Polybius square.

    •    The "trigraph cipher with a short key for hand use" of Kruskal (1985) (an American invention). This can have a geometric ciphering method using RAYs, like Sanborn's 2005 statement that "K4 is geometrically tougher", allows a 5x5 or 3x9 Polybius square, and is related to the Hill cipher - if you think the HILL down the sculpture RHS is significant
    •    Trifair (an ACA invention by ZENITH, 1983)

The Kruskal cipher seems to be very hard at this length. One problem is placing the crib.

Military Cryptanalysis Part IV – Transposition and Fractionating Systems by William F. Friedman
Section III – Incompletely-Filled Rectangles
Paragraph 12(a):
In the system designated keyed columnar transposition the feature which differentiates an incompletely-filled rectangle from one that is completely filled is a very simple one from the cryptographic point of view The bottom row of the rectangle in the former case merely lacks one or more letters, a feature which only very slightly complicates the system in practical operation; But the consequences of this simple difference between the two types are, from the cryptanalytic point of view, quite profound, and the cryptanalytic effect of this small change in cryptographic procedure is seemingly all out of proportion with the simplicity of the difference.

Section VIII – Combined Substitution-Transposition Systems
Paragraph 35(e):
Of course, if it should happen that the substitution process involves known alphabets, the cryptanalyst can remove the effects of the substitutive process before proceeding to eliminate the transposition, even if in the encipherment the substitution came first. For example, if a standard cipher alphabet were employed for the substitution the unilateral frequency distribution would give indications thereof and the cipher letters could immediately be converted to the normal plain-text equivalents. The latter may then be studied as though mere transposition had been applied. But if unknown mixed cipher alphabets were employed, this initial step can not be accomplished and a solution must usually wait upon the removal of the transposition before the substitution can be attacked. The latter may be very difficult or impossible where a good transposition method is used; where simple columnar transposition is used the removal of the transposition can be effected if the message is long enough.

s: Wondrous Patterns: The K4 Mushroom Cloud Over Berlin
t:
Ref: “Morse Stones as Visual Markers”

    A while back, after pursuing research into the AST Balloon acrostic clue from K1, I applied the clue to a grid formation of K4 resembling a hot-air balloon or a wing of a Titan satellite. This had spectacular results – each corner referenced back to the Morse stones – LUCID in each corner, a T shape referencing T is your Position and digiteal interpretatu , and so on, topped off with a neat “AST” diagonal stripe. Visual markers, it seemed, but I wasn’t able to do anything with it. You can see the grid I made of it in the post titled above.

  Pursuing the cryptoanalytic cribs from K1 and K2, the “Inker of Light”, I came up with a painter named JMW Turner, whose body of paintings bore a shockingly large pattern of relevance not just to my research, but to the K3 plaintext, as well as other elements and ending in a painting called “The Parting of Hero and Leander” Useful, but no apparent application at the time, and backburnered with the Balloon Grid.

    My most recent research was the discovery of a simple +6/1/-6 rotation key that results in a lot of anagrammable text in K4 that is one of the hallmarks of columnar transposition. Fussing around with it a lot, but the patterns revealed don’t make sense in a plain blocky grid. But attaching the key, the grid, and the artwork together does something different...

  It throws up a visual association – the “balloon” grid can be viewed also as a Mushroom Cloud, like that of an atomic explosion, a visual key prevalent in much of JMW Turner’s worker, where the nuance of his “light” painting styles involve the sun peeking through a cloud cover, a ray of sun striking the surface of water  in an inverted “T”. Much like the waves of Kryptos’s sculpture.

  While the Berlin Wall connects with many people due to the other Kryptos clue, it’s slightly out of place time-wise, and there’s a more significant event that would be recent to Sanborn – the Alexanderplatz demonstration at the Berlin Peace Clock. This was when the wall started to fall and the doomsday clock  started to turn back on nuclear war. I’ll eave the CIA’s involvement to others to research, but they are among many who played a role.

  What this leaves now is the start of a 6/1/6 pattern on a mushroom cloud in K4 that begins to make sense – the grid is up on groups.io if anyone is interested.

Speculation: The pattern of the 6/1/6 key may show how to properly translate ciphertext

s: Friedman comments on cryptographic solutions & K3 key recovery
t:
Friedman's Lectures on Cryptology - Lecture I: Introduction

Now there can be no logical reason, point, or purpose in taking the time and trouble to encipher anything unless it is expected that some other person is to decipher the cipher some time in the future. This means that there must exist some very direct, clear-cut and unambiguous relationship between the enciphering and deciphering operations. Just what such a relationship involves will be dealt with later, but at this moment all that it is necessary to say is that in enciphering there must be rules that govern or control the operations, that these rules must admit of no uncertainty or ambiguity, and that they must be susceptible of being applied with undeviating precision, since otherwise it will be difficult or perhaps impossible for the decipherer to obtain the correct answer when he reverses the processes or steps followed in the encipherment. This may be a good place to point out that a valid or authentic cryptanalytic solution cannot be considered as being merely what the cryptanalyst thinks or says he thinks the cryptogram means, nor does the solution represent an opinion of the cryptanalyst.

Solutions are valid only insofar as they are objective and susceptible of demonstration or proof employing scientifically acceptable methods or procedures. It should hardly be necessary to indicate that the validity of the results achieved by cryptanalytic studies of authentic cryptograms rests upon the same sure and well established scientific foundations, and is reached by the same sort of logic as are the discoveries, results, or "answers" achieved by any other scientific studies, namely: observation, hypothesis, deduction, induction, and confirmatory experiment. Implied in what I have just said is the tacitly understood and now rarely explicitly stated assumption that two or more, equally competent and, if necessary, specially qualified investigators, each working independently upon the same material, will achieve identical or practically identical results....

But now to return to the main theme, the place mathematics occupies in cryptology, let me say that just as the solution of mathematical problems leaves no room for the exercise of divination or other mysterious mental or psychic powers, so a valid solution to a cryptogram must leave no room for the exercise of such powers. In cryptologic science there is one and only one valid solution to a cryptogram, just as there is but one correct solution or "solution set" to any problem in mathematics. But perhaps I've already dwelt on this point too long; in any case, we'll come back to it later, when we come to look at certain types of what we may call pseudo-ciphers.
---------
Circling back on K1-K3, while we did recover the keys of PALIMPSEST and ABSCISSA, does anyone know how the K3 keys (8/24 or 42/14 per Sanborn K3 encryption matrix sheets) were recovered?

Originally I had hypothesized that the K3 "endYAhRohn" was phonetic reference to dYAble columahR transpOHsitioN but it turns out to be:

DYaHble Roh (double row "transposition") "H" (8th letter) & "N" (14th letter) for dYAhRo-h-n. Combined with PALIMPSEST, it provides the encryption matrices of 8 rows x 42 columns then 90 degree rotation (palimpsest text is scrapped off and then rotated 90 degrees to be overwritten), 14 row x 24 column, and then another 90 degree rotation.

If this K3 stenographic technique is used on K4, then the most likely candidate will be at QQ PRNGKS SO where the P baseline is slightly raised (like K3 dYAhR) to refer to a pseudo random number generated key stream (PRNGKS), implying that the key for K4 is literally a transformed K4! The difficulty will be to determine the transposition route to produce MUYKLGKORNA or ELYOIECBAQK (BERLINCLOCK) at positions 64-74 of K4. We have no idea if Mr. Sanborn used the standard alphabet or Kryptos alphabet for the substitution. but if PALIMPSEST and ABSCISSA combine to PSITSASSIMPLEASABC then it might refer to a standard alphabet.

I have seen it.

And then I did not see it.

It’s an ILLUSION, which appears when you are walking past a printed copy of the Kryptos panels taped to a wall, HOWEVER, you can see it if you look at it!

You only see it if you are walking past it, but you are looking straight ahead.

I think that the receptive cones (rods?) in the far outside corners of our eyeballs are responsible for this visualization.

You can see for yourself how this works by looking at a spot in front of you, while you gradually move your hand forward, from behind your head, until you see it.

Of course, when you see it, your eye(s) glance that way, as a reaction, formed early in life.

But if you have someone put there hand in that exact place, where you noticed your hand moving forward, and they and you are very still, and you open your eyes and look ahead, you will not see the object.

Those “far corner” receptors only notice a object in that field of vision, if the object is moving.

Or if the person is moving and the “object” or “image” is stationary.

But let me be clear about this.

The image of George Washington is definitely in the Kryptos.

And as Mr. Sanborn has told us, you can solve the puzzle completely, without looking at the actual panels. He has stated that we can print up the four panels on sheets of paper and solve it.

So I hope that someone with greater knowledge of the other aspects of Kryptos will be able to discern whether the presence of the image of George Washington in the puzzle has significance.

s: I believe K4 is actually 121 different characters instead of 97, using an alphabet of 28 characters.
t:
When Sanborn was cutting out the sculpture with the jigsaw, there are 6 letters that are unique in that they required two separate templates to cut the letter out, otherwise you would have a hole in the center of the letter.  For example, if you just cut out the letter "O", it would look like a circular hole.  Thus, he had to separate it out into two parts, like ( ) for "O".

The 6 characters that seem to follow this pattern are: B, D, O, P, Q, R

If you take the ciphertext of K4 and then split it out such that those characters are considered 2 instead of a single character, you end up with K4 ciphertext being 121 characters long.   That's an interesting number since it is 11 squared, for one, which just makes it a fun number and easy to arrange into a grid made of the prime number 11 squared.

I wrote a script that was very basic if anyone wants to see what such ciphertext would look like, but I had to choose special characters for each of the new characters, and here's the mapping for those (these could be anything, but here's what I used so you can understand the ciphertext I'll paste):

Since the last time when Sanborn was questioned as to whether the one to one mapping of K4 was the same as how K1 was, and he deflected and wouldn't say for sure this time, this is a possible line or avenue of approach we can consider.  Also, this is something I think an artist would do, especially when they spend 2.5 years cutting out these letters by hand, they are going to notice how they are actually having to cut out 121 separate things instead of just 97.

I don't think we should read too much into the actual context of the plantext yet.  It doesn't make any sense to have to look into a specific clock in Germany when we would have had no way to know that without the hint.   Just because he intended it to refer to that, it doesn't mean that is necessary to actually solve K4.  It instead may be relevant to K5.

On the topic of K5, I think it will be something along the lines of replacing specific words with other words from the document.   For example, there are two locations mentioned in the deciphered text (if you include Berlin).  The other is Langley.   I think K4 will end up being a series of keywords that we then have to map to other words from the plaintext to find the true meaning.   Thus, Berlin would be replaced with Langley, Clock would be replaced with something else, etc, and you'd end up with the solution to K5.

Building on Scott Perry's observation, it looks like the 97 letter K4 is composed of three pieces:
63 encrypted letters, 6 letter BERLIN, 28 encrypted letters
This 97 letter sequence is Vig encrypted using the first 11 letters of the tablet (1st cipher letters of K1) EMUFPHZLRFA, followed by a transposition.
Let's assume that's the masking step.
Now the question is what was used to produce the 2 blocks of ciphertext letters.

63 could be 9 rows of 7 letters
28 is 4 rows of 7

Way back when, I seem to recall there was some discussion about the statistics of the first part of the message not matching those of the latter half.

Maybe we have a rule that a Vig key is only to be used for up to 63 letters, then changed.

Or maybe we have a 9 x 7 grid as part of the encryption process.
For the 2nd block, we would fill the grid with 28 letters and 37 pad characters.
You could then do a Transpose, substitute, inverse_transpose and discard the last 35 letters and you'd still be able to decrypt it.

Another possibility, which I don't think is correct, is that there's a 63 letter One Time Pad.
The two blocks could be in depth.
This would highlight the VENONA work, but that wasn't a CIA program.
Since CIA commissioned the art work, I'd expect the KRYPTOS project to highlight CIA uses of cryptography.

(Yes, I'm discounting what Jim said about 1:1 which we assumed ruled out transposition, etc.
It's hard to believe there isn't some form of transposition involved, since K1,K2,K3 teach the use of substitution and transposition, and the Scott Perry analysis is somewhat compelling.
For now, I don't care whether Jim didn't understand or was being deliberately deceptive.
I just want to look at actual message statistics and see where that takes us.)

Just a theory that there are 2 separately encrypted blocks in use -- anybody have any statistical evidence that would support or refute this?
If so, we have a 63 letter message with no crib, and a 28 letter message beginning with CLOCK.

Doug

cryptosystems applied on top of each other. Such as, for example, a
polyalphabetic substitution on top of a transposition (using K1-K3 as
motivation).

The strong hint that individual ciphertext letters decode to individual
plaintext letters in sequence seems to suggest that this specific idea is
wrong, in that there's no transposition of the ciphertext going on. K4
could, of course, involve transposition of something else; it could be a
Quagmire III with a very complex key schedule, for example.

But there's one simple idea that I want to explore here: What if K4 were
two cryptosystems interleaved?

That is, suppose you had two ciphers where one letter encodes one letter,
and a common sequence of bits. You could use those bits to decide which
cipher to use for which letter.

Here's an example. Suppose we encode the text "BETWEENSUBTLESHADING" with
Quagmire III using two different keys. Picking some keys at random,
encoding with NORTHEAST as the key gives:

RJORZVKFZRCMIQZHJNFM

and encoding with BERLINCLOCK as the key gives:

JVOHKTYWKLTZVAOVPXDM

Now let's also suppose that we have a common bit string,
say, 11100111010101110011. If you see a 0, use the first key, and if you
see a 1, use the second key:

JVORZTYWZLCZIAOVJNDM

As we know, the index of coincidence measures similarity to an expected
natural language in a way that is statistically unchanged if you apply a
monoalphabetic substitution, a text-independent transposition, or a random
sample.

So here's the question: Are there ways to divide the letters of K4 into two
subsets, each of which individually has an IC close to that of English?

The answer to that, remarkably, is yes. There are quite a few of them. Here
are three examples:

0100100010111001111100101000111000000010110010000101011110011011001000010000100001011001011110000
0101101010111101111101010111101011010101011100010010001011010110000110111000000110101101011100001
0111001011001000011111010110111100001010100011101000100101100111100000011111011100010110000011011

Each of these splits K4 into two subsets, each of which has an IC of 6.2%
or higher.

But there's a catch.

It turns out that you can almost always do this trick. I generated a few
random strings of length 97, and it turns out, yes, you can find a string
for all of them that will give you ICs close to English. Just to prove it,
here's a bit string that will do it for K1, which we know was not generated
this way:

0101100001110001110001010111110001110110100000010001011110000110111011110011000111111011110000111011

I haven't sketched out a proof, but it seems reasonable if you know a bit
of information theory. Remember, the IC of English is around double that of
random text, so inventing one bit of information per letter should do it.

So while this is probably nothing, it may be worth thinking about. If this
were how K4 was encrypted, what else would you expect to see which
distinguishes it from randomness?

Unsurprisingly, so far I haven't found a pattern in any of these bit
strings. I know, "digital interpretation". But digital interpretation of
what?

Morse code is unlikely, because Morse is an entropy code. In any English
(or French!) text, there's roughly double the number of dits as there are
dahs, because a dit takes half the time to transmit as a dah. All of these
strings have close to equal numbers of 0's and 1's; certainly nothing like
a 2:1 ratio.

Converting text to binary, like ASCII or Baudot code, isn't out of the
question. Or even taking a sequence of letters and using their odd/even
place in the alphabet. I haven't noticed anything yet, but bear in mind
that, once again, if you used English text to do this, you would not get a
1:1 ratio of 0's and 1's.

Enjoy.

Andrew Bromage

s: The latest clue & my prior K4 analysis
t:
In May, 2013, I came up with a way of getting BERLIN (the first clue) in the correct position. To me, it was very elegant: it used Vigenere (like K1/K2), with transposition (like K3), using a keyword taken from first characters of the Kryptos ciphertext. I shared my results here.

The keyword was the first 11 characters of the K1 ciphertext, the transposition starting at the 77th letter of K4 and taking every 38th letter. The 38 and 77 are from the coordinates in the K3 plaintext.

The problem, of course, is that the rest was "alphabet soup" (otherwise Kryptos would have been solved in 2013). Still, I felt this was statistically very improbable (not every agreed, though).

As soon as the 3rd clue came out (NORTHEAST), I plugged it into my program. Nothing. But then I tried just NORTH. NORTH had a match with ENDYAHROHNLSRHEOCP -- the first 18 characters of the bottom half of the Kryptos sculpture. That really jumped out at me. But the transposition is starting at 73 and taking every 74th character (seemingly random numbers). And shorter words are more likely to match than longer words.

So I then decided to look back at the 2nd clue (CLOCK) -- and found something I missed before: one of the hits was LZHPFU -- which is in EMUFPHZLRFA backwards. However, the transposition was every 50th character starting at position 64.

As reference, taking a dictionary of 98,000 words of 6 or more letters, about 5% have a "hit" with the Kryptos ciphertext using this method (3 match "ENDYA...", 9 match "EMUF..."). Just over 0.01% match the beginning of of the K1 or K3 ciphertext.

From what I can tell, it would be extremely difficult to create a cipher that would work in this way with the different values for transposition (I.E.  every 38th letter for BERLIN, every 74th character for NORTH and every 50th character for CLOCK). Perhaps with K4 having 97 characters (a prime number) it could be possible?

For now, I'm not planning to do further research into this. But given what appears to at least be an eerie coincidence, I wanted to share with the group.
                             -Scott

Rob, I tend to agree with you.

This seems to be a classic elucidation problem:
1.  Did we ask a clear unambiguous question
2.  Did Ed/Jim understand the question
3.  Did they intend to respond directly
4.  Did they convey their answer clearly and unambigously
5.  Did we understand their answer

We asked about 1:1 (CT in position 64 equates to PT in position 64) and didn't define our terms;  Ed probably understood, and Jim may not have.  Ed deferred to Jim, who gave a somewhat ambiguous answer, ending with BERLIN is at pt position 64.

The answers were ambiguous and rambling;  it is easy for each of us to read into it what we wanted to hear and come up with multiple answers.

We asked Ed about whether the masking step was applied before or after encryption;  we didn't ask the prior question of "is there an explicit masking step".  This was after Ed said "in K4 we masked the statistics...".  When asked the before/after question Ed's answer was "interesting question..." and left it at that with no answer.

I can only tell you I "believe" transposition is involved, but this is not based on anything definitive that Ed/Jim explicitly said (or explicitly ruled out).  My belief is based on 2 things:
a.  I view K1, K2, K3 as "agent training" exercises as Ed taught Jim the methods of substitution and transposition;  makes sense that K4 would combine these.
b.  I view Scott Perry's analysis as compelling:  transpose using specific numbers we were given, and vig decrypt using K1 ct as a key -- makes sense as a masking step.

Further,
c.  My GUESS is that there are 2 blocks of (up to 63) letters that are separately encrypted, with a plaintext BERLIN inserted between them before the masking step.  I believe that's what Scott recovered.
d.  Arguing against Scott's analysis is the fact that Ed taught Jim how to do transposition with rotating grids, and I don't see a way to implement the masking transposition with a grid.  Maybe Ed taught him I showed you how to do a simple transposition using grids, now here's a more general method....  (pure speculation).
e.  I don't find Scott's second analysis very compelling (take the unmasked 97 letters and subject them to another SP transformation using vig key CRYPTO and an unrecognized  transposition key to come up with the 5 letter crib CLOCK.  To believe this requires me to believe that the crypto is chained, encrypting one word at a time, AND that he's going backwards by words (CLOCK encrypted before BERLIN) and that he ends with the the word at 64 (presumably starting the who process with whatever word precedes BERLIN and working backwards).  He either need to have a whole bunch of keys (vig phrases and transposition number pairs) or some way to generate these on the fly, or perhaps use a couple alternately.  The process would be prone to error  (decrypt a "word" surrounded by random letters which could end up with bigger "words" by sheer coincidence).

Doug

s: Reconfiguring my Ideas based upon new clue
t:
Having scrapped my 97 Letter OTP theory, I have doubled down on my idea that the clues to solving K4 lie in the Pre-K and Morse Code (K0) sections of Sanborn's work, and not just on the metal statue, based upon my reevaluation; having the new clue (NORTHEAST). See the following.

Some things that I've noticed. As I have mentioned in the past, it was my understanding that per JS, K4 could be solved without using hints from K1, K2 and K3. That said, the Pre-K and Morse Code (K0) sections do offer up tantalizing clues.

First, I believe JS offered a "breadcrumb trail" to help solve K4 using clues in the Pre-K and K0 sections. As he said, K1 to K3 are NOT needed to solve K4.

1) The gibberish at the end of Pre-K (ETRANSEWJ) is what I had originally thought was, in of itself, a key. However, I have come to recognize it as the place to pick up the breadcrumb trail. Upon shifting ETRANSEWJ forwards AND backwards, I think I have revealed clues, which help reveal the nature of the masking technique and details to help with the transposition in play.

a) When shifted forward 8 sequences ETRANSEWJ becomes: MBZIVAMER

b) And, when shifted in reverse 16 sequences ETRANSEWJ
becomes: ODBKXCOGT

*Now, these 2 sets of shifts are important (Yes, I could have gone Forward 8 + 2, or Reverse 16 - 2. But, I display as separate directions, because anyone who discovered 1 without the other could have reasonably been expected to stop at the first, without proceeding to discover the second.).

Regarding MBZIVAMER: From a cryptography perspective, this hint speaks volumes, especially, when combined with my analysis of the Morse Code regarding a 2 matrix solution.

MBZIVAMER = MBZ IV AMER = Must Be Zero Initialization Vector AMER. I believe "AMER" will need to be added to the Key (when it is found). I feel the same Key is used for a 2 matrix solution (see below). Therefore, the Key will be required to solve the first matrix, and the Key+ AMER (KeyAMER, if you will) will be required to solve the second matrix. Therefore, the dual matrix design involving the same key + an Initialization vector is used to mask a frequency distribution analysis.

Regarding ODBKXCOGT: The fact that some of these letters correspond (in order) to the beginning of K4's letters cannot be pure coincidence. OBKR to O(D)BK(XCOGT); I need to investigate if AMER (the Initialization vector) is added to the cyphertext at the beginning of K4. OBKR = AMER? I don't know yet.

MBZIVAMER is informative with details, while the ODBKXCOGT provides a more geographic scope. The fact that JS chose to provide an intermediate key (of sorts) was because he felt both pieces of information were critical to solving K4. Therefore, ETRANSEWJ is where the breadcrumb trail is picked up.

2) Knowing there is an Initialization vector involved means there needs to be more than one section to K4. I have discovered more breadcrumbs in the form of the extra e's in the Morse Code. These extra letters are not meant to be distracting filler. They develop a pattern, as follows:

First, I counted the "e's". However, I decided to count the separations between groups as colons between the groups of "e's" as hard stops. Therefore, starting from the left, and counting the "e's", I arranged the counts as follows:

2, 1:6 (ex. Line 1: 2e's, 1e : (hard stop) 6e's)
3:      (this line added to count between :&:)
2,2:5 (and, so on.)
3:1
0:1
0
0

Quantities of "e's" added together in between hard stops.

2e's + 1e : 6e's + 3e's :
2e's + 2e's : 5e's + 3e's :
1e + 0e :
1e + 0e + 0e

Rewritten as:

3e's : 9e's
4e's : 8e's
1e's : 1e's

Rewritten as:

3:9
4:8
1:1

Rewritten as:
39
48
11

It is my belief that these represent the size of 2 matrices + the size of the Key, when the Initialization vector is added. (Initially, I was working with KRYPTOS and KRYPTOSAMER as Keys, but got sidetracked. So, I will have to return to those at a later date.)

Also of interest are the locations of the clues from JS. NORTHEAST begins at space 26, and BERLINCLOCK ends at space 74. 74 minus 26 equals 48. 48 is the size of 1 of the 2 matrices required to solve K4, per the e's in K0.

The word KRYPTOS is evident in the letters of K4. KRYPTOS (7 letters) + AMER (4 letters) = KRYPTOSAMER (11 letters). <-- the 11 from the "e's".

Therefore, it's possible that the 48 letter Matrix runs between spaces 26 and 74 (if that's JS' reasoning behind the locations of the clues. And, the 39 letter Matrix being supplied with letters from spaces 1 to 25 and 75 to 97. Again, it is an avenue of investigation for me.

Ehen

I've always assumed that the four P's and C's in the margin of his notes stand for Plaintext and Ciphertext.  Since there are four sets of them, that would indicate four keywords are needed to decode.

If you take K2 ciphertext starting from the 121st character:

H    R    R    Y    I    Z    E    T
K    Z    E    M    V    D    U    F
K    S    J    H    K    F    W    H

Then using my decryption program, I found that if you put in K2 ciphertext in positions and perform a Quagmire III Decryption with KRYPTOSABC on K4 with the partial keys:
26 through 34: 122-125-100-143-194-124-106-137-177 you get NORTHEAST and
64 through 74: 104-149-204-193-176-183-114-112-212-148-129 you get BERLINCLOCK exactly!!! To get 20 of 20 hits using K2 ciphertext is statistically significant!

Based on the statistical requirements, it is very possible that Scott Perry's method can be improved by taking characters 121 through 218 of K2 and then perform a non-linear skip decrypt!

s: The latest clue & my prior K4 analysis
t:
Something to consider in concert with Ted's idea of a word picture, perhaps something like a virtual tangram: In my study of the patterns of cryptographic and plaintext on the sculpture and how the four K sections related to each other, I've noted certain patterns that seem to stand out. Part of one of them you've noted here is EMU - a three letter pattern at the beginning of K1 that reverses itself near the end of K2. In fact, there's a very strong candidate for these as the 97 letters of K4.

EMU/UME-26. The 26 letters after the UME in the last line of K2 CT.
YRD/WET-13. The 13 letters between this formation in K1 & K2 CT
TEW/DRY-38. The 38 letters between this formation in K3 CT.
HROHNL-6. Found after the DYAHR CT in K3.
PRNGATIHN-9. The first instance of PRNG found in K3 CT.
NYPVT-5: The first instance of NYPVT found in the K3 PT under shift on a 24 row PT grid.

Total: 97

My analysis method involved looking at the classical cryptoanalytic attacks used to decipher K1 and K2 and treating those attacks as clues in themselves, since Sanborn expected that the first three sections would be solved quickly. "Classical cryptoanalytic attacks" refers to the recurring VJYQT ciphertext string in K1 and the recurring GWHKK string in K2, NCEOF and SIBLE respectively. Took it a step further and used the Cs and Ps as a hint to 24-row grid. I was able to do a lot with all of that, that I won't rehash here, but putting it all together in a fashion that works with K4 is a puzzle in itself.

Intentional patterns in both the CT and PT. as I see them, circling around the idea of cribbed text recurring and repeating from one section to another.

s: The latest clue & my prior K4 analysis
t:
"My only concern with this is that we have been told that K4 can be solved without K1-K3. If you are shuffling the letters and looking for substrings from K1-K3 then that is going against that advice. It is not unusual to find small words when deciphering a random string of letter with random strings of letter.
Chris"

Not to worry, I think, as it has now been taken about as far as it can be:  Scott & Nick have found all the words that we know are a) in K4 PT at all, and b) located in a position certain.  To be sure, if we tried all possible strings from the first three sections, forward & back, all lengths, &c., as secondary Vig keys, we'd find all kinds of words, even some big ones, but we would have no way to know that they were actually K4 PT, and as long as they didn't "step on" known PT positions, we'd have no way to know where to place them if we did think them really likely.  (JAIL remains as a dubious possible PT, since it comes up in the same sequence as BERLIN, thus IF we decide it's PT, we know WHERE it must be positioned, as it's hooked rigidly to the properly positioned BERLIN, so to speak, and where that places it, it doesn't overlap any known PT.)  The sequences, BTW for those who might be confused, aren't shuffled, they're unchanged initial sequences from each of the first three sections.  But there probably isn't much point in finding more words in this manner, tho if somebody found an unchanged string from K1-3 that put JIMSANBORN in K4 88-97, I'd buy it.

What remains from this is to look at 3 sets of:   K-Section-Origin / String Length & Direction / Skip Interval / Start Point, and see if  anybody can find patterns that would tell us what other such sets ought to look like.  If this does have anything to do with how the addressee is supposed to decode the thing, it seems it would have to be a methodical algorithm - surely Bob isn't expected to memorize a random jumble of lengths, intervals & points to extract each of Alice's words.

If the effort were not disproportionate, it would be kind of fun to keep doing this until some where and how we could make out "Mary Magdalene".  They've had plenty of fun at our expense, I'd enjoy teasing J.S. with that.     >:)

-Carl

Another hint that I am thinking about regarding my 4 letter Initialization Vector idea is when connecting the incorrect cyphertext letters of K1, K2 and K3 by striking a line (vector) connecting the "K-Q-L" from the misspelled letters in K1, K2 and K3 (on the statue), the vector points roughly to "UOXO".

REMEMBER, JS SAID (and, I paraphrase here) THAT THE MISSPELLED LETTERS WERE DELIBERATE. IT'S NOT WHAT THEY ARE, BUT THEIR ORIENTATION OR POSITIONING.

This is especially important because it ignores the "OBKR" (the first 4 letters of K4). Remember, the clues I found on the Pre-K (MBZIVAMER and ODBKXCOGT)? Somehow there is a relationship here. If JS is trying to elucidate the actual beginning of K4 minus the Initialization Vector (OBKR = AMER), then OBKR is the Initialization Vector that allows one Key (key for 1st Matrix; key + Initialization Vector for the 2nd Matrix) to be used on the 2 Separate Matrices (see my discovery from the "e" count in the Morse Code!! 39 Letter Matrix and 48 Letter Matrix). Normally, the Initialization Vector is placed at the beginning (or, the end) of the passage requiring it. Therefore, by pointing to the "UOXO" and excluding the "OBKR", I believe JS is showing us that "OBKR" is the Initialization Vector, it's 4 letters in length, it is separate from K4, and that K4 without the Initialization Vector begins at "UOXO", not "OBKR" as was previously thought by everyone!!

Even if I am off by a letter, or so, on  "K-Q-L", any Vector created by connecting letters in the vicinity will get you down to that general area. The point being, that the "OBKR" is ignored!!

Sorry, if it sounds like I'm repeating myself on some of my points, but I think you get the picture.

Eben

Well I was trying to find a connection between using these K3 P and C lines that I shown in this file. The only part that makes no sense is if JS says K1-K3 solving is not needed, then having this 42x8 solved K3 chart with P and C in the amrgin means nothing. But why would he have had such a chart with P and C on it. Anyway, I want to show what I have found as a possible connection of using K4 CT to decode K4 using K3 and binary masking.

So basically in the file I shown, I shown groups of four characters going downward in K3 PT lines. xBER LINC LOCK is the ones I'll focus on for what I am showing.

LOCK is the most interesting one to use because there is only the one K. So, below the four letters of PT lines LOCK (lines 1,3,5,7) on the k3 chart, is cipher letters. EEHE respectively on lines 2,4,6,8. So the K4 letters for LOCK is ZFPK. So, I went back to my chart I have for doing binary masking of letters (using BAUDOT binary code for each letter) and performing an XOR (Exclusive OR) mask. I started with the last letter first and the masking K against E produced "Z", then when one letter back and got P against H and got X, and continued until I saw WXZ and that stood out as the order of the letters on the vigenere side of Kryptos alphabet. However the next letter going back was "C", so possible a particular square was used to layer K4 over the the vigenere chart that wrapped back to C. I continued and sure enough the next letter was B then A then S...so forth. I back masked the letters to have:

KRYPxOSABCWZX (the only letter that didn't translate was the t in KRYPTOS it was an X).

NOTE KR is two letters before BERLIN and that translated to LABERLINCLOCK (...L "a berlin clock"?)
However I hit a dead end after this, and still trying to see the NORTHEAST part against this method.

But basically, if JS started with Plain text  "(LA) BERLIN CLOCK" and used the k3 to lines on the 42x8 PC chart (one line at a time downward), and came up with cipher text using the letter below each PT.  you would get XAIMHBRNGEEHE then take this and XOR the binary code against it against KRYPxOSABCWZX you get FBNYPVTTMZFPK

Could this be luck or coincidence? maybe, since I haven't gotten anything legible past this yet. The problem is there are multiple PT letters (for example if your CT to check K3 is "E" you could have 3 or 4 PT letters to choose from. but the fact that it worked for the system I did above is interesting.

It shows a double masking of K4 CT to PT.

Hi! I am hoping the group will use the possible keyword/keywords to solve K4 and let’s see what we can come up with. I believe it is the right invisible interpretation JS was talking about. By the way, hidden info in K4 is just a part of the whole riddle, that means 60% or more is just out there ready for interpretation.

First of all, I want to mention that I'm new to all this, and have only lately gotten kind of up to speed with what needs to be done to solve K4 (minus the hocus pocus fantasy of underlying meanings - sorry about that stuff. I really was clueless. Pun intended. LOL). Second, in my explanation, I hope to uncover areas to revisit, should the end result seem somewhat contrived. And, finally, by following a narrative, it allows me to cut through the myriad of manually created attempts at solving K4 using the myopic view of a giant spreadsheet afforded me on my smartphone. Anyway...

From a subtle hint that I picked up (it may have been a radio talkshow interview with JS), he mentioned the 96 or 97 letters of K4.

Here's the thing, 97 letters is a prime number (I think, I'm pretty sure. LOL). But, 96 ÷ 4 = 24. The remainder was 1, so I dropped the last R in K4, as it didn't play into my attempting a Rail-Fence solution.

The Rail-Fence needed to be modified. I shifted the top line that began with OBKR to the right 3 places. At that point, via a zig zag, OBKR became the Code group ODBK (from rows 1 & 4), which happens to be the first 4 letters of the shifted ETRANSEWJ clue, ODBKXCOGT. It became much easier when I removed rows 2 & 3, and closed the gap between rows 1 & 4.

Next, I scanned the working rows to see how I could obtain the XCOGT. Moving to the right 5 letters (both rows - from the B & K) I noticed that, via a zig zag, XCO came together. The "G" from the second Code group could not be used in it's present position. Therefore, just after the "OC" of XCO, I (modified) the Rail-Fence by flipping the rows after "OC". By doing this, the zig zag Code group XCOG was complete.

Having 2 complete 4-letter Code groups, I figured the remaining "T" was to be used to denote where the next pattern began. It turns out that the Code group development began on the Top row and moved down and to the right. Therefore, to move back up and to the right, the "T" had to be on the bottom row. The new starting point "T" was indeed located on the bottom row. It was 5 letters to the right of the initial starting point "O", then down to the bottom row's letter (right between the 2 Code groups).

I removed the formulated Code groups, pushed the remaining letters back together, and continued to the next 2 Code groups. When rows 1 & 4 were exhausted of letters I moved rows 2 & 3 into position to continue the Rail-Fence. Row 2 became the new top row, and Row 3 became the new bottom row. (*As I was modifying the Rail-Fence, I never paid attention to the removed rows, as I flipped the working rows. Thus, if the second half of the solved puzzle makes no sense whatsoever, I will revisit this potential mistake!!).

Using up the remaining letters, and maintaining empty spaces at the end, I was able to remove another 6 letters (3 Z's, O, F, R). This seemed to make sense because I just removed 3 Z's. I mean, how often does "Z" get used in any message having only 97 letters? Not much. Therefore, these 6 plus the remaining "R" meant that K4 was potentially padded with 7 extra letters (*Another area to revisit if I made any mistakes!!). However, the removal of these 7 letters created the opportunity to do a series of Transpositions, because of the space provided.

I began a vertical (columnar?) transposition due to the available spaces at the lower right hand side of the matrix. This created available space at the upper left hand side of the matrix. Therefore, I did another transposition. But, this time I did a horizontal (row-wise?) transposition, which created another series of openings at the lower right hand side of the matrix. I repeated this series until i got what I thought was an "SOS" and an "RQ" in the matrix. (*This would appear to another area to revisit, should my results seem dubious - In Engineering, there a concept known as tolerance stack. I may be guilty of this, but at least I know where I will revisit.)

At this point, using a LOP chart found on the internet, I began using a trial and error approach using various clue words that I found in the Morse code, and the word KRYPTOS, etc. What led me to realize that I was onto something, was when 3-letter reversing patterns began to emerge, which coincided with logical words (and, purposely misspelled words) in phrase format.

Another important part of this, is that it appears that the conversion from cyphertext to plaintext, using the LOP chart, begins at lower left most letter, moves up 12 letters, then begins a new line just to the right of the first line (underneath, if it was horizontal). However, the new line uses an entirely DIFFERENT Key word (3 letters, reversing, back and forth). Line 3, uses another reversing 3 (possibly 4 letters). I have only completed 3 lines, so far.

Using a the shifted clue from the Pre-K(K0) of ETRANSEWJ, that became MBZIVAMER (AME):
copybyccqnef
AMEEMAAMEEMA

Using KRYPTOS (TOS)
oknbwavubees
SOTTOSSOTTOS

from "T is your position" (TIS or SITS):
pnorthwashfu
SSITSSTISSIT

Here, "north" is indeed at 26 to 30. While the rest of the message may appear to be incoherent to some (I don't know if words were misspelled and/or abbreviations were used as a way to further confuse someone trying to solve it using computer program), it does seem to follow some logical sequence. That said, I am well aware that going back and revisiting areas that I drew attention to may improve my result. It got me looking at K4 a little more. There are irregularities in the
distribution of letters in the first half versus the second half. Here is
k4 where all but the letter showing in a given line has been masked with
"." and the vertical bars surround the center letter. Other letters not
shown show up in both halved of the k4.

.............S..................SS.....S..SS....|.|................................................
O....O.O......O...................O.............|.|................................................
................................................|.|A.......A................................A....A.
.........................QQ...........Q..Q......|.|................................................
................................................|.|......D....................D......D.............
................................................|.|.................................C...........C..

To mask the true characters one may
1) substitution of one plaintext character with one ciphertext character, a
1-to-1 mapping
2) change each position in the plaintext by a value determined by that
position, e.g. the value added at position "i" might be a mathematical
function of position "i" or it might be the value of a character in a "key"
that is controlling the values

We already know that if there is a mapping and no transposition then it's
not 1:1 since NO and ST of NORTHEAST all map to Q (and the first T maps to
R while the 2nd maps to Q).

If there is a transpostion, doesn't it seem unlikely that you would end up
with all of a few characters only in half of the string?

Here's a 3rd way to mask a letter: replace all occurrences of it in a
certain *region *of the string with a letter that hasn't been used in the
plaintext *and *replace all other occurrences of it elsewhere with another
unused character. If you picked the first and second half of the string to
do this to the letter E -- replacing it with J in the first half of the
string and Z in the second half of the string, you will have split the
frequency of the most common letter in half.

Could something like this be at play in k4?

Chris
