s: Why Alexanderplatz World Clock is a likely candidate for BERLINCLOCK
t:
I uploaded a file to Jonah's folder. It's a photo collage explaining why I think the NORTHEAST clue comports with the idea that the Alexanderplatz WORLD CLOCK is the Berlin Clock referred to in K4.

*Washington and Berlin are both on the clock
*They are separated by 6 segments; 6 hours.
*I included an earth night & day map to show "subtle shading" - that refers to sunlight.
*6 hours is 25% (1/4) of a clock.

For those of you that are able to look for patterns in every "nth"
character to look for patterns, have you considered the following
possibilities?

For a prime number of items (like 97) there are at least 4 common ways that
I think someone might pick every nth value. For specificity say there are 7
elements and we wish to take every third.

One variety is to imagine that you are picking chairs from which a member
will be selected.
If the chairs are in a line you can go to the end and then restart from the
next occupied chair at the beginning or you can continue the count as you
return to the beginning (which is equivalent to imagining that you are
counting chairs that are in a circle). Call these two methods
chair-line-skip and chair-circle-skip. The

Another variety is to imagine that you are selecting people that are
standing in a line and after you pick them they leave the line. The people,
too, may be arranged in a line or in a circle. Call these queue-line-skip
and queue-circle-skip. (Note: linear_char_skip is equivalent to a
write-by-rows and read by columns and card dealing when cards are dealt and
flipped over as they are layed down into piles and then brought back into
one pile again by placing the last pile on top of the one before it, then
placing those two on the one that came before, etc... until all are in one
pile which is then turned over.)

For each of these there is an issue about how to begin. Again, for 7 people
taking every third, do you skip, skip, pick or pick, skip, skip. Using the
pick, skip, skip method here are the result for 7 items picking every third

chair-line-skip   [0, 3, 6, 1, 4, 2, 5]
chair-circle-skip [0, 3, 6, 2, 5, 1, 4]
queue-line-skip   [0, 3, 6, 1, 5, 2, 4]
queue-circle-skip [0, 3, 6, 4, 2, 5, 1]

The start of each is the same but then they are different in latter part of
the sequence. Are results ever the same?
yes:
- for the chair skips, the line or circle arrangement is the same when you
pick every 1, 2 or 4 (i.e. when the remainder of division of 7 by the skip
value is 1 less than the skip value, e.g. 7 divided by 4 is 1 remainder 3
and 3 is 1 less than 4).
- for the queue skips, the line and circle arrangement give the same
results only if you take every 1 or every 6th.

When there are 97 characters the same reasoning holds: chair-like counting
is only the same for a line or circle arrangement when picking every 1, 2,
7, 14, or 49th chair; queue-like counting will always be different unless
not skipping (or skipping by 96). For taking every 6th element from 97, the
first 17 characters picked are the same for each method but the ordering
differs after that.

If skipping were used by JS and he was writing characters on a grid I would
guess that he would use queue-based striking-off of characters since it is
easier to count the ones that haven't been crossed off at each stage. And I
would guess that he would use circle-based counting because you would have
to look ahead to see that there were characters not yet crossed off and you
would have to count them anyway to know if there were enough. So if you
counted them and there weren't enough I would guess that he would keep
counting as he returned to the beginning. But using the column transpose
(write-in-rows-read-by-columns), i.e., the chair-line skip, is perhaps
cleaner. But based on one guess of how he did k3, none of these methods
would have been used: he prefers to write into a matrix and then turn the
paper and read out from left to right, top to bottom. This is equivalent to
write-by-row, read-by-column-from-the-bottom, e.g. for 7 elements

1 2 3 4 5 6 7

write row by row in 3 columns

1 2 3
4 5 6
7

rotate left (counter clockwise)

3 6
2 5
1 4 7

read rows

3 6 2 5 1 4 7

if the intial matrix were rotated to the right instead of the left, this
just reverses the result to give 7 4 1 2 5 6 3

Do we have any evidence to suggest one type of transposition over the
other? If transposition is not involved, how do we explain the odd key
needed to decode the k4 into the known plaintext?

Chris

I haven't yet given much thought to the double letters nor to the preponderance of infrequent letters like Z, J, K, etc. The double letters may or may not stand for some non alpha characters. The double letters and unusual letters might be for padding out the transposition matrix. Or maybe not.

There may be multiple ciphers. Plain Vigenere for the first few characters that someone discovered using the key TOKEN, and something else for the rest. This would also make sense given K1, K2, and K3.

I also feel that K4 may be 98 characters including the ?, and the ? may be the additional mystery letter that makes the bit of Vigenere work.

Is this plausible? If we were given a clue that placed BERLINCLOCK past 82
characters then this encoding would not be plausible since those trailing

Assuming similar statistics in terms of inflation, there would be about 8

everything past that would be an artifact of the encoding

So what has been revealed makes this plausible. Does it match any clues?

1. this involves masking: the distribution is changed significantly when
regrouping the letters in sets of 3: there is a one-to-many encoding where
a given plaintext character may end up as several different cipher text
letters

2. there is, in a sense, a truth in saying the the revealed clues match (in
position) with the given k4; it would not be possible to say this with the
last dozen or so letters which are an artifact of the inflation

encodes to a given 3-element triplet whereas Morse code produces variable
length coordinates which are then taken in groups of 3.

6. There is no fancy math or anything more complicated than looking up
codes and perhaps doing some column transpositions

Another possibility in steganography is that letters of words used to construct the key are sprinkled throughout K4.

Excluding letters in the known crib locations, there are many words that can be extracted from the remaining letters in order. Here are some combinations of such words that together can be extracted:

GHOST DANCE [i.e. there is a G followed by H followed by O followed by S, etc... in order (but not necessarily contiguously) in k4 letters.]
UBOAT CIGAR
KGB SOLILOQUIZE

These words can be used to construct a key. I suspect that since we know that the key that unlocks the given cribs does not look like a word. So to construct a key we could use one word to encrypt the other and then use that to encrypt the original plaintext.

So to encrypt THEMESSAGE with UBOAT CIGAR encrypt UBOAT with CIGAR (using Vigenere with the KRYPTOSABC) to give TWMHO; then use that to encrypt THEMESSAGE -> BEPSJDPZRJ. Now sprinkle the characters of the 2 keywords into the text  ubBEoPaStJcDiPgZarRJ (and have fun doing so, even spelling other words inside like 'PAST and DIP).

The final keyword TWMHO would not work to unlock the phrase as a whole, only segments that happened to be in the right position as when the key was applied. e.g. using TWMHO to decipher UBBEOPASTJCDIPGZARRJ gives LEJWKZDHJEOGWIBUDCGE which doesn't reveal much.

Didn't JS say that you wouldn't be able to read (all?) of K4 when it was decrypted or was he implying that you could read it but it would be a riddle of sorts?

Anyway, this really has the palimpsest idea since the two layers would be visible at the same time. What clues do we have that could help to tease the two layers apart? And what clues do we have that could suggest how the one layer was used to encode the other?

I suspect portions of k4 -- or especially reversed k4 -- that look like words contain letters of the words that were used to make the key; it's just too fun to not put them where they would make words appear in the cipher. :-)

Chris

It's a creative idea. It's called "Fractionated Morse" and is one of the ACA cipher types.
And frankly it's great to see someone looking at actual crypto techniques.

Two points

(1) If you look at Bion's "ACA Reference Statistics" web page, you'll see the IC mean and standard deviation for
FracMorse is 47 and 2.

The IC of the 97 characters of K4 is around 36 (divided by 10,000). So if the SD is really 2.0 it's more than five standard deviations below the mean.

If the IC is really normally distributed, that's more than "one in a million" - you'll have to do some encryption simulations to see how rare it actually is.

You could argue the key was chosen to flatten the IC right out - after all, there's 26! possible keys, way more than a million,
but you should probably look at some of the other stats too to see if they're in line with FM.

(2) The Sanborn talk at the Hirshhorn Museum of 2005 made it sound like a letter for letter decryption. Relevant part "same number of letters and characters as what's on the screen". i.e. it means 97 or 98.  (Here is the quote, below:)

“Now as far as people cracking it is concerned, there is some very fine line that separates really great cryptographers from totally insane people.  And so, you have no idea, over the last fifteen years, how many “cracks“ of the code I have gotten, be it email or documents.  Basically, the code is a series of passages and sentences with a finite number of characters like English characters— Roman Characters, and so if you decode it, the decode will be the same number of letters and characters as what’s on the screen.  The final section that hasn’t been decoded yet is approximately one hundred characters.  If I say it’s any more specific than that, then I’m giving you guys a clue, but I’m not gonna do that.  So it’s approximately a hundred characters.  And so, basically, if somebody cracks that— that code, when you read it, it will be a Eureka! moment when it’s cracked, and it will be approximately a hundred characters long.”

James Sanborn
Hirshhorn Museum, Washington DC
September 23, 2005 at 12:30 pm

s: Clarifying what is meant by mistakes and typos
t:
There seems to be confusion and disagreement about the semantic distinction between actual and deliberate mistakes.

There are typos and misspellings which were intentional, and then there are errors which were oversights either in the design of Kryptos, or in the production (cutting of it).

I want to clearly, clear up, distinguish between them. Calling them typos/mistakes/mispellings when they were planned as such makes it confusing and difficult to talk about an actual "oops"; unforced error.

Which of these from K1-K3 is the latter? In other words which of these typos/mistakes/mispellings is genuinely an "oh no, that isn't supposed to be there?"

And if K4 has any of them, shouldn't JS tell us *now* that "the 3rd from last position should be a O not a C" if that was the case?

(Mod.:  Actually no one among us has any knowledge of this classification other than those which JS has already stated.  You can certainly desire to define them all into correct classes and expect that JS will reveal all of the non-intentional changes from plan, but don't hold your breath.)

s: Clarifying what is meant by mistakes and typos
t:
There's two items in what you seem to be angling at, and that's intentional "error" vs items Jim didn't intend to put in there.

The only actual "mistake", aka unintended error, noted by Jim so far is the problems with the XLAYERTWO sequence.

The "misspellings" on the other hand, depend on how you look at them, but their presence is intentional - those being IQLUSION, UNDERGRUUND and DESPARATLY.

I use quote marks around the word misspellings, because it is my belief that they can be taken not just at face value as misspellings, but also as wordplay intended to shift the meaning of the sentences they are in. IQLUSION, for example is I-QLUS-I-ON.... EYE CLUES. EYE ON. Noting of course that spaces in a deciphered text are at the interpretation of any reader.

In this context, the reading shifts to:
"Between subtle shading and the absence of light lies the nuance of eye clues. Eye on it was totally invisible. How's that possible?"

The same can be done with the rest.

s: Clarifying what is meant by mistakes and typos
t:

K1 : in Antipodes there is still the K that translates in Q, but Jim said it was an error.

I think that we can say these things without any doubt.

Scott Perry came up with an astonishing result that the word BERLIN results in the correct place if you take the 97 letter K4, decrypt using the first 11 letters of K1 as the key (EMUFPHZLRFA), and the transpose using start 76, step 38 (where I label the first location as 0).

That would say the corresponding encryption process is to transpose the plaintext using the inverse transpose (start 95, step 23) followed by the encryption using EMUFPHZLRFA.
Scott's decrypt is close, but not exact.

That leads me to think we may have a 97 letter running key derived from "something on a billboard" which might be a transposition of the K1/K2/K3 ciphertext.
(A running key is just a long key, where each letter is used once.  An example is something called a "one time" pad, where the running key is written down and printed on pages of a pad.  An example of a "two time" pad is VENONA, but that's a different story.)

Also, there's been some debate as to whether he may have applied a transposition before or after doing the substitution.  Scott assumed he did the transposition first, although the norm is to do the substitution first (that's the basis for SP substitution/permutation networks used in algorithms like DES).

If K4 uses a running key, and uses a 95/23 transposition to encrypt, then the running key is either of the form
-------------------------VTPVLIKQH-----------------------------MZULFRISMMT-----------------------
or, substitution follows the transposition,
---F----------L-----S---U------Q---P-T---R---M------I---V-M---L------H---V-----I---Z------K---T-M

Does anybody recognize either string?

Also, because the first clue was the word BERLIN starting at 63 (the 64th letter of K4), it's possible that he's using a worksheet of 63 letters at a time;  he just read off the first word from his page 2 worksheet.  If so, he may be using a grid of 63 letters as a running key.  (The same 63 letter page is not used for block 1 and block 2 if substitution follows transposition;  haven't checked the case for Transposing first).

Note that K1 is 63 letters, so it's possible K1 is used as the basis for forming a 63 letter running key.

Just a thought.

To highlight what may seem obvious to some, historic methods in some regions included making cylinders and casting light through them.

In regards to section 3, it has been noted that once you transpose into 7 columns. The solution follows a pattern nicknamed the stairway to heaven.

However, it should be noted that there are other techniques that result in similar results including the Scrytale.

I would recommend looking into some of the older and less techniques. It would be a shame if they were forgotten.

That said, there's a degree of pleasure in seeing a puzzle stand this long and it would be a shame to spoil it.

Instead of relying on your "gut feel", it's better to do a simulation. With a few lines of R, I can see for random 9 letter strings, the mean of the sum of the 1 bits is 20.8 and the standard dev is 2.6.

So your 22 and your 20 are very common values for the sums of the bits.

library(timma)
rep1 <- replicate(1e6,sum(dec2bin(sample(26,9,replace=T),5)))
cxx <- 0
for (i in 1:1e7)
{
  s1 <- sample(rep1,1)
  s2 <- sample(rep1,1)
  if (s1==s2) cxx <- cxx+1
}

After 10 million simulations with random 9-letter strings, you get sumOfOneBits(randomString1) = sumOfOneBits(randomString2) about 1 in 9 times.
So it is not significant at all. If you try nine different things, you'll probably find something like that.
I think you will find the same results but you should start with 00000.

I think this is part of the learning experience - you can try to code it in whatever language you know. I chose R because you can do everything in a few lines.
You might be more familiar with Python or C, or you can start learning one. These are all good programming exercises.

Mark Siegal in The Magazine wrote "Kryptos has motivated me to do more enthusiastic programming than almost anything else in my life."

You can unravel my code from the inside out, so start by seeing what sample(26,9,replace=T) does, and so on. You can just modify my code.

If you don't use simulations or statistics, you're just running off feelings, which isn't really satisfactory.

It is also a good exercise to explain clearly (to yourself and others) why this idea that gets bandied around sometimes about coming up with an algorithm along the lines of "start at character 77 of K4, skip to every 38th character, and use the first 11 letters of the K1 ciphertext as a key and get BERLIN in the right place of the output" isn't really a valid approach. To read about that just search for "skip 38 77" in the search box here.

There are hazards on the other side, too - first identifying a pattern, and then saying "that can't be a coincidence" can lead you down the path of Bible Codes madness.

If you want to know more, I'd really recommend the book "The Improbability Principle: Why Coincidences, Miracles, and Rare Events Happen Every Day" by David J. Hand; he is one of the gods of statistics.

t:
Hi FoxG (Laura?) and welcome to the Kryptos group. Having grown up in Northern Virginia, and also
having attended Montessori school as a child next door to the CIA in Langley (part of McLean), I
can attest that the CIA certainly had no control over the naming of the community, which dates
back to the 18th century and Langley Hall in Shropshire, England. And I think it's doubtful that
DCI Allen Dulles chose today's site of CIA headquarters (it had been at Foggy Bottom on E Street
when it was the OSS, along with many scattered buildings around D.C.) because of the name.
He liked the location for a number of reasons, not least of which was its easy accessibility by its
employees who lived in surrounding Washington, Maryland and Virginia, but probably primarily
because it was (and still is) pretty secluded, being almost completely surrounded by parks and
government-owned land. That seclusion simplifies the problem of maintaining security. It was
a big land parcel, too, allowing for future expansion.

As far as the author that Jim Sanborn considered involving, I think Thomas Harris is probably
unlikely. Many think it may have been Dan Brown, but that's not much more than speculation.
I don't think Jim has ever named the author, nor do I think he has excluded any of the names

s: Baudot (ITA1 & ITA2) Code + Masking Technique + Relevance to Kryptos
t:
I'm pretty sure that someone in this forum already had the correct idea, but we didn't dive deep into it to get the solution.
We should be ashamed of not having been able to find Kryptos's solution even though we have significant technological advantage compared to 30 years ago.

On Wikipedia I’ve found a document of CCITT Recommendation which was published 1988 implying that during the 90s (when Kryptos was published) it was relevant. I looked up the inventor of the first means of digital communication (Baudot code) whose name is Émile Baudot. Reading through the Wikipedia article reveals that "In 1926 the International Telegraph Communications Advisory Committee of the International Telecommunication Union met in Berlin and immortalized Baudot by designating the baud - shortened from his name - as the unit of telegraph transmission speed.“ By using the Baudot Code in Kryptos, Jim Sanborn may have had the intention of „immortalizing“ Baudot as well.

I wanted to look into this a bit more.

A = 00000, B = 00001, C = 00010, D = 00011, E = 00100, F = 00101, G = 00110, H = 00111, I  = 01000, J = 01000, K = 01001, L = 01010, M = 01011, N = 01100 , O = 01101, P = 01110, Q = 01111, R = 10000, S = 10001, T = 10010, U = 10011, V = 10011, W = 10100, X = 10101, Y = 10110, Z = 10111

The plain alphabet is represented via the Baudot (ITA-2) letter mappings.
The key is represented via inverted Baudot (ITA-1).
The cipher alphabet is represented by the standard alphabet given in 5-bit binary as above.

Let's apply it to QQPRNGKSS (NORTHEAST):

Baudot (ITA-2) of QQPRN
Key in Baudot (ITA-1), but inverted, so 10111 becomes 01000 = Y
NORTH in 5 Bit Binary (normal alphabet)

10111-10111-10110-01010-01100-11010-01111-00101-00101 (QQPRNGKSS)
                                  XOR (00 = 0, 01=1,10=1,11=0)
11011-11010-00110-11000-01011-11110-01111-10100-10111 (inverted YUKOSAPFC)

results in

01100-01101-10000-10010-00111-00100-00000-10001-10010 (NORTHEAST)

Let's apply the same to NYPVTTMZFPK:

01100-10110-01110-10011-10010-10010-01011-10111-00101-01110-01001 (NYPVTTMZFPK)
                                  XOR (00 = 0, 01=1,10=1,11=0)
01101-10010-11110-11001-11010-11110-01001-11101-01000-01100-00000 (XCAIUAWEVZP)

results in

00001-00100-10000-01010-01000-01100-00010-01010-01101-00010-01001(BERLINCLOCK)

Now we only need to find out how to get the key.

I looked at the double letters and noticed that the distance between those letters looks quite suspicious.

Let's look at the double letters:
Q -> U (distance: 4)
Q -> Y (distance: 8)
P -> K (distance: 5)
P -> Z (distance: 10)
P -> A (distance: 15)
S -> F (distance: 13)
S -> C (distance: 16)
N -> S (distance: 5)
N -> X (distance: 10)
T -> W (distance: 3)
T -> A (distance: 6 or 19)

Before I wanted to post this I just checked in groups.io and even Elonka Dunkin made a comment about the Baudot Code back then in 2011
(see https://groups.io/g/KRYPTOS/message/12743)

which makes me believe even more that this could really be the way.

(Mod:  Don't forget Gray Code as a possible focus...)

It has always bothered me that Jim chose cribs at seemingly random spots -- the question in my mind was Why these particular spots.

BERLIN follows the first 63 letters.
CLOCK follows the first 69 letters.

K1 happens to be 63 letters in length.
I originally thought that maybe the K4 message is encrypted in blocks of 63, using some arrangement of K1 as the (running) key.

Scott Perry showed that K4 could have been produced by first transposing (start 95, step 23) followed by substitution using the first 11 letters of K1 as the key.
If you decrypt K4 by first undoing the substitution, followed by the inverse transposition (start 76, step 38) you get BERLIN at the proper place.

This also works if you do the substitution BEFORE the transposition.
Vig Encrypt BERLIN at 63 with the key MUFZLR, then transpose with start 95, step 23. The decryption step is transpose with start 76,step 38, followed by Vig Decrypt with MUFZLR.

If you write K1 out in 5 rows and use the middle 3, you get MUFZLR

E H ...
M Z
U L
F R
P F

But this doesn't extend into being able to decrypt the letters that follow to get CLOCK;  there seems to be a boundary after 69 letters.

What if:  the plaintext is divided into strips of 23 letters.
A different substitution key is used for each strip.

The whole thing, after substitution,  is then subjected to a 95,23 transposition.
(The strip length 23 and skip length 23 is somewhat interesting if he's using grids to perform these operations).
The receiver applies the inverse transposition 76,38 to K4, and then decrypts the individual strips.

We don't yet have a "Scott Perry analysis" of the new crib NORTHEAST to see what Vig key might be used, and relate it back to K1, etc.

The 6 characters we have, MUFZLR,  is not enough to say that he's using the middle rows of K1 blocked by 5.
It could also be there's a binary mask applied to K1:  01110 0111x ..... which selects the letters from K1 to form MUFZLR.
The mask could come from the morse code, for instance.

But, just a general comment:  BERLIN CLOCK may have been encrypted using 2 different keys, and thus the 11 letter BERLINCLOCK is not a proper crib for a single encrytion key.

Just food for thought, as we all self isolate and spend our idle moments on this!

Doug

s: Iron curtain, Morse code and Microprocessor
t:
Hi Group,

Based on Jim Sanborn’s interview with CBC radio last Nov. 24,2014 after releasing the “Berlin” clue, the fall of Berlin wall was in his mind when he was building Kryptos.

The Kryptos sculpture could be the “Iron Curtain”, the other name of Berlin wall.
The happy side or the vantage point of the Kryptos sculpture where the three elements ( quartz, granite and bubbling pool) are,  is the Western block and the other side which is kind of sad side of the copper screen is the Eastern block.
(This portion is taken from Wikipedia:The wall was built to keep the country's people in. But the Soviets and East German government said it was to keep capitalism out. They said that West Germany refused to recognize East Germany as an independent country because they wanted to take over North-East Germany just like Hitler took over Poland)
During those times, often the Eastern block countries operate using a numbers station, also known as a one-way voice link (OWVL), is a special type of unusual radio broadcast, generally on the Short Wave (SW) radio bands, reading out incomprehensible lists of (spoken) numbers or morse coded messages. In most cases, such stations carry OTP/OTT encrypted messages being broadcast by Eastern or Western block countries aimed at their secret agents operating undercover.
Supposing the Western block was the one sending the intelligent message at their agents in Eastern block, the agents were instructed to listen to specific SW frequencies at fixed days and times, often using a commercially available SW-receiver, from brands like Sony, Panasonic and Grundig. After the message is decoded, the agent will deliver a returning hand-written message using a dead letter box or a concealment device like pen or stone.
I suspect that the granite bench with an interesting feature behind the Kryptos sculpture is the “dead letter box”and something buried in it.

Back to the morse code of the Kryptos, the “e’s”or dots may be used to convey a continuous wave transmission. During transmission, when an error is detected, the message with an error usually with 3-character error is being resent using RQ(from ARQ or Moore Code, read info about ARQ-E and ARQ-M)meaning request repeat together with the code with an error. The other name of RQ is Signal Roman One or designated as “1” as what I had read from Wikipedia.
I suspect that SOS, T is your position and Digetal Interpretatu had character errors during transmission. I have an idea that the messages on Morse code were clues on using a microprocessor. SOS could be SSO( System Status Output), T is your position could be ( TIME is your position,RQ( Request Repeat), SF from Shadow Forces( S flag), IDIV from Virtually invisible and Digetal Interpretatu( Signed Divide) and ALU from Lucid Memory( Arithmetic Logic Unit). Also,  please read info about INTEL 8088 and the maskable interrupts.
These are just my observations, hoping they can help the group.

Best,

Jezail

Hello Everyone,

The first three letters of K3’s ciphetext END could be a clue referring to Endianess.

In computing, endianness refers to the order of bytes (or sometimes bits) within a binary representation of a number. It can also be used more generally to refer to the internal ordering of any representation, such as the digits in a numeral system or the sections of a date.

In its most common usage, endianness indicates the ordering of bytes within a multi-byte number. A big-endian ordering places the most significant byte first and the least significant byte last, while a little-endian ordering does the opposite. ( source from Wikipedia)

Also, in Gulliver’s Travels written by Jonathan Swift, there was an interesting story of the Big Endian and the Little Indian about the right way how to break the boiled egg.
Traditionally, Lilliputians broke boiled eggs on the larger end; a few generations ago, an Emperor of Lilliput, the Present Emperor's great-grandfather, had decreed that all eggs be broken on the smaller end after his son cut himself breaking the egg on the larger end. The differences between Big-Endians (those who broke their eggs at the larger end) and Little-Endians had given rise to "six rebellions ... wherein one Emperor lost his life, and another his crown". The Lilliputian religion says an egg should be broken on the convenient end, which is now interpreted by the Lilliputians as the smaller end. The Big-Endians gained favour in Blefuscu. The Big-Endian/Little-Endian controversy reflects, in a much simplified form, British quarrels over religion. Less than 200 years previously, England had been a Catholic (Big-Endian) country; but a series of reforms beginning in the 1530s under King Henry VIII (reigned 1509–1547), Edward VI (1547–1553), and Queen Elizabeth I (1558–1603) had converted most of the country to Protestantism (Little-Endianism), in the episcopalian form of the Church of England. At the same time, revolution and reform in Scotland (1560) had also converted that country to Presbyterian Protestantism, which led to fresh difficulties when England and Scotland were united under one ruler, JAMES I (1603–1625).

Jezail

Hi,

thanks for your reply.

Using your method I get the same values.

I also realized that a part of my method had a flaw (and is therefore wrong).
For example

11000 (Y)
   xor
11100
   is
00100 (E)

I wrote that we invert the key 11100 which gets us 00011, but 00011 does not exist in ITA.
That number 00011 exists in Gray-Code, but there's another problem.
For example

01111 (P)
  xor
01101
  is
01011 (C)

We invert the key 01101, which gets us 10010. That number does exist in Gray-Code, but it doesn't make sense as it's at the 28th position and we're only working with 26 positions (letter A - Z).

I also thought of trying that with 8 bit binary numbers, like Jeffery Donauhue did, meaning

01001110 (N)
    xor
00001100
      is
01000010 (B)

but we can exclude that method as well because 00001100 does not exist in 8 bit binary.

What might work out would be "shifting", i.e. something like this:

10111 (Q in ITA2)
   xor
11011 (shift Q by 1 to RIGHT)
   is
01100 (N)

etc. (some pattern)

I'll experiment a bit by looking for shifts depending on the position of the letters, hamming distance etc.

June 9, 2005 - NPR Mary Louise Kelly

KELLY: Part four is so hard because it's short...In the first three, Scheidt says you could rely on the fact that in English some letters occur more frequently than others.

Mr. ED SCHEIDT (Former Chief CIA Cryptographer): For instance, if you could determine that--the number of E's vs. the number of Z's in the English language, then you would have some insight into the potential words that they made up, because there are more E's in the English language than there are Z's.

KELLY: But Scheidt says in part four he deliberately masked that advantage...

From the three statements above:
1. K1-K3 has a CT:PT relationship with English language and letters
2. Cryptanalysis techniques such as IC or frequency analysis can be used on the ciphertext without knowing the actual plaintext
3. The advantage of cryptanalysis could be used for K1-K3, but has been deliberately masked for K4.

Therefore if the cryptanalysis advantage is masked then there are two main masking types:
1. Single step irreversible plaintext masking using jargon or acronyms instead of proper English words
2. Multi-step reversible ciphertext masking involving the deviation of a direct CT:PT relationship with multiple ciphers involving at least 1 subsitution (transposition does not change overall letter frequencies but may alter IC)

Since Ed has confirmed that K4 is a multi-step cipher, then it would very likely be a reversible mask that can be executed with pencil and paper and it should be dealt with first.

I don't post comments here much anymore, because this venue has become such
a wasteland. However, it's important to call out this "Kryptos Fee System"
nonsense.

It's about time this group stopped promoting and using Sanborn's tacky and
embarrassing solution-verification service. It's almost unbelievable that
people have been sending him money for this, but many apparently have. This
system preys on certain types of people who, for whatever reason, are
vulnerable to this sort of approach. No serious cryptanalyst would ever
send Sanborn a dime to verify a solution attempt. When K-4 is solved, it
will be solved, whether or not Sanborn is paid to verify it. The rest of us
can verify it just as well at no cost.

If you know that you have solved K-4, simply post the solution, the method,
and the keys here or anywhere else online to timestamp it. That's it. It's
free. You've solved it for all to see.

Those who claim solutions that have no method and keys are mistaken about
how this stuff works. Hundreds of these so-called solutions have been
proposed over the years.

If you've really solved it, then everyone else will be able to get the same
result by using the cryptographic systems and keys that you used. (And no,
the arbitrary construction of a one-time pad to produce a desired result is
not a solution.) If you claim a solution that isn't really a solution, then
the rest of us will let you know that we were unable to duplicate your
results.

If your work is not repeatable by anyone else, then you're fooling
yourself. If you're asking Sanborn if your attempt is correct, then you're
doubting your own work. When the correct solution is produced, there will
be no need to wonder if it's right.

Bill Briere

Hi Bill -- I would agree that the quality of posts here is not what it was a decade ago. These days, I
see mostly ad hoc approaches that bear no resemblance to cryptanalysis.

I would not be so hard on Sanborn for setting up his solution "verification" system -- I believe it
was primarily an attempt to deter individuals from filling his Inbox with inanity. Unfortunately,
he probably set the price too low, as it doesn't appear to be much of a deterrent.

As you pointed out, we don't need Jim to confirm a solution, any more than we needed him for
K1-K3. The correct solution will be self-evident -- even without the crosschecks of BERLINCLOCK
and NORTHEAST.

I wish we had an unambiguous answer to the question of whether K4 is positionally 1-to-1
like K1 and K2 (e.g. CT N --> PT B, CT Y --> PT E, etc.), and unlike K3. If it is, that still wouldn't
rule out transposition (e.g. for a polyalphabetic substitution cipher, the key could be
transposed/scrambled), but it would greatly thin the field of candidate cryptosystems.

--Rob

The basic Kryptos tableau is a symmetric 26x26 matrix with the KRYPTOSABC... alphabet written across row 0 and down column 0.

To encrypt, you can go across row 0 to find the column with the plaintext letter, and down column 0 to find the row with the key letter, and the ciphertext is at the junction of the selected row & column.

They could have used a standard autokey method:  use a prior C (CTAK), K (KAK), or P(PTAK) letter as the current key.
I used the BERLIN, CLOCK, NORTHEAST cribs to rule these out.

When we consider the extra 4 columns, these can be used to select a row, which can be used to fashion another variant of autokey cipher:
CTAK:  go down column 27..30 to find previous ciphertext (with lag n, typically a small number such as 1, i.e., use ciphertext 3 to encrypt plaintext 4).
If column 0 holds the Key, then the row selected by the previous ciphertext is the key to encrypt the current plaintext.

for KAK, go down column 27..30 to find the previous key, and that row selects the current key
for PTAK, go down column 27..30 to find previous plaintext, and that row selects the current key

I assumed the 4 extra columns were either a standard A..Z or KRYPTOSABC alphabet, shifted to spell a word in row 0 (KRYP in the sculpture).
Again, I used the cribs to rule these out.

(As an aside, I repeated these tests with both the K4 ciphertext and a transposed (start 76, skip 38) ciphertext to correspond to Scott Perry's analysis).

Since the 26x26 tableau is symmetric, you can swap rows/columns:  you can go down column 0 to find the plaintext and across row 0 to find the key.
But, if column 0 represents the plaintext, the (lookup prior P/C/K) 4 extra columns gets more complicated since the rows (selected by cols 27..30) represent the plaintext;  I'm not sure how I'd use the extra 4 columns to build an autokey structure.

Any ideas?

Doug

s: Doorways - not a solution but an idea.
t:
Kryptos - The Early Years on CNN
"There are lots of doors to go through to get to the meaning of the code. And umm... everytime you enter... were to enter one doorway you might.. you know in the distance see another doorway and you go through that doorway and then you go through another doorway. and it unfolds as it's deciphered."

I had seen this before and was interested but never really made much of it. However a couple of weeks ago that changed. After watching this I remembered seeing folds marked in the K3/4 images extracted from the PBS Nova ScienceNOW video and I think another one. In the images it was noted that there were folds and I was able to see them for myself even in the 240p video. It also noted a symbol in the bottom right hand corner and they didn't know what to make of it and I didn't really either. I thought maybe it was a cube that was drawn quickly. But seeing it right after watching this made me think I saw it as an open door/doorway. There were 3 such markings noted and I was able to see part of one which almost seemed to be intentionally covered up by his thumb. I haven't been able to see a clear image of the scribble for myself.

So my theory is that K4 is encrypted multiple times by using 3 or more "one-time pads" created by the text of the cipher. I wanted to bring this to the community because I don't think I would be able to do it. I don't have the computer skills to be able to try different variations all at once.

So the portions with doorways marked on these images were:
K3 & K4 - this image had a fold 6 letters from the left and 7 letters from the right. and was marked TOP #4
K3 - PT written out in 8 even rows. with alternating rows marked P/C
K3 - same as above but the last 11 characters on each row are separated by a fold (this is possibly a second page because of the length)

As for deciphering it I wouldn't know where to begin. My guess would be with Vigenére but it could be anything. It could even change by layer. The unfolding and the folds could be that only certain portions were encrypted at a time. For example if the K3/K4 is the "TOP" maybe only the middle section is decrypted once at this point and then one or both sides are unfolded and all of k4 is decrypted in the next layer. This would make it so that parts of the message are encrypted more times than others. The middle or sides could also have been used to encrypt there opposites, for example the folded edges could have been used to encrypt the center more or vice versa. Maybe even as a digraph.

The image that has K3 PT written out in 8 rows has P & C alternately written down the margin. This could be the the first row is considered PT and the second row CT. By having a PT and CT a Key could be derived which would be written out in 4 rows. As I mentioned above there is a fold and possibly a second page attached because of the length and this portion has another doorway symbol. The width of the unfolded portion is 31 characters long. Using that portion this would then make 4 rows of 31 characters. There is also another potential fold marked on this page.

I do not know how many doorways there might but in the quote he mentioned 3 doorways before saying it unfolds as it is deciphered. I do not know which order they might be in, maybe K2 is the second doorway it was encrypted with (layer two)? Maybe each section was used.

Something else to note is that the K3 documents are numbered which to me suggests the order of steps that was used to encrypt K3. It could be that each step of it is a doorway, I have not seen symbols on them though. Where K3 is written out in 8 rows there is the number 1. Where K3 is written out in the 24X14 grid after a rotation it is marked with the number 2. I have not seen a number 3 but it would simply be the rotation of 2 which also had "end" written in the correct direction after a rotation. There might not be a 3 because maybe The TOP 4 is referencing K4 or maybe it is simply plate 4. Also if I am not mistaken the folds on the K3/4 document line up with the Q in K1 and the unraised H in YAHR. With the Q I do believe he said something along the lines of it is not so important what it is but where it is. This to me would suggest it serves as some kind of a marker.

Thank you for your time. I hope everything I wrote made sense.

I suspect that the "deciphering" process refers to K1 to K3, that being the normal process of deciphering these that tends to get skipped over in exploration. If you start by approaching them using the classic attacks of looking for repeating ciphertext, it seems to me that a series of puzzles that could easily be considered "doorways" opens - the initial SIBLE/DYAHR clues, coupled with the rest of the repeating text - the null cipher found in K1, K2 and encircling the entire kryptos grid, and the Morse Stone callback clues that go with them.

Q if treated as a question is very important, because if it's meant to invoke Kryptos and its exhibit, the question is what *you* as the viewer can see, and it's something that exists in the stones - the Hidden vs the Visible in (WHA) T IS YOUR POSITION. Maybe T is indeed your position, but what exactly is your position and how is it partially concealed or more to the point - totally invisible vs virtually invisible?

A reminder, perhaps, to not just see it as text, but to look for answers to the questions it asks.

s: Wondrous Patterns: Dante's Tears, QQPRNGKSS and the K/E/Y
t:
Dante’s Tears, QQ-PRNG-KSS and K/E/y
This is the application of multiple theories regarding K4, as placed on a 10 row, 9 column grid (7 columns on the top row). Note that the NORTHEAST string from Jim’s clue fits evenly on a full row of its own.

Theory 1:
K/E/Y and +6/1/-6 Alphanumeric Binary
1.    Every row will either use the alpha K/E/Y or numeric 6/1/6 encryption.
2.    In K/E/Y, E = the initial plaintext, while K and Y represent ciphertext relative to that absolute value of that position in a 26 letter alphabet, with a binary choice.   If your PT is O, you can choose either 2 or -24 to encrypt to the CT letter Q. This option is more effective for pattern analysis of known clues.
3.    +6/1/-6 is the numerical equivalent of K/E/Y – K and Y are + and – 6 to E respectively.

Theory 2:
That each row represents a Bolgia or “ditch” from Dante’s Inferno, Circle 8, Canto XVIII  and the cipher is based on the “characters” in those ditches. For our purposes,  we are looking at Canto XX – the ditch of the Sorcerors, those who tell the future. They walk backwards with their heads twisted around on their shoulders, blinded by their own tears, and Dante is so moved that he weeps as well.
This row is specifically QQ-PRNG-KSS which has been noted before as resembling a pair of weeping eyes, while the PRNG is a recurring kiss/crib in K3 and K4.

Application:
Because of this curious set of synchronicities, I’ve chosen to analyze the alpha and numeric transitions between NORTHEAST AND QQPRNGKSS
N + 3/-23 = Q
O +2/-24 = Q
R +24/-2 = P
T +24/-2 = R
H +6/-20 = N
E  +2/-24 = G
A +10/-16 = K
S + 0/0=  S
T -1/+25 = S

Looking at these as a binary, I observed this pattern and made my selection based on it.
(-23) (+2) / (+24) (-2) /  (-20) (+2) / (+10) (0) (-1) = NORTHEAST
These have been separated to represent single “characters”, all palindromic and all possessing virtual “heads” that are backwards to the rest of them.

Conclusion: Determining whether there is a rule for using K/E/Y or 6/1/6 would be helpful.

s: thoughts on approach (are we looking at this all wrong)
t:
If we look at this in terms of doorways, and consider the entrance to K4 to be the first door we are trying to enter, it seems to me that an analysis of K4 requires the use of tools given in K1 through K3, which Sanborn, in a Wired article, stated exist in the form of clues.  He also he expected K1-k3 to be solved quickly, and K4 to be much more difficult. Additionally, one might also note that the exhibit is titled “Intelligence Gathering” which expands it beyond mere cryptanalysis and solution.

By the time we reach K4, we have a series of decryptions that we can go back and subject to analysis.  How did we get to where we are?  People can solve it with what they have now, but the process to getting there is set in classic Keyed Vigenere methods of crypto analytic attacks. The most discussed part of that seems to be frequency analysis, and interestingly enough Step 1 seems to get little attention or dismissed.

Step 1 involves looking for repeating strings of text to be used for further analysis. In K1, that is VJYQT (NCEOF) and in K2 that is GWHKK (SIBLE). Those are the two most notable for size, though there’s also a number of smaller paired strings. The question is what meaning they have beyond immediate face value. SIBLE is a common word component, but since Sanborn carefully chose his words, like cribs and other repeating text, it should be considered significant. We see it in the Marker stones  (VIRTUALLY INVISIBLE) and in the plaintext (TOTALLY INVISIBLE) and (POSSIBLE) are all SIBLEs. It also occurs in K3 with a simple rotation and in slightly adjusted form. If we

DYAHR rot+1 VIRTUAL-LY-IN-VI -SIBLE or TOTAL-LY-IN-VI-SIBLE = SZBLE ->  SIBLE
DYAHR = SIBLE

SIBLE certainly looks like a big clue. Doorway #1 unlocked?

In Historical terms, we'd be jumping from Vigenere over a whole generation of rotor machines to something modern like DES.

DES uses a Feistel structure:  divide the message to be encrypted into two halves.  At each round, pass one half unchanged;  use that half to derive a key which is then used to encrypt the other half.  Swap halves and repeat for each round.

It's easy to envision a paper and pencil method for encrypting using this structure.

Others have shown that the 97 letter K4 could consist of two 46 letter pieces (using the W in the ciphertext as separators).
Surprisingly, the letter distributions of the two 46 letter pieces are identical (exactly 1 letter in each half occurs 5 times, etc.).

DES also uses an SP network to generate the random number (running key) which is used to encrypt each half:  each round subjects the passed half word to a substitution (implemented as S boxes) and a permutation (transposition) which are the fundamental operations Ed taught Jim via K1 thru K3.

Best of luck with your analysis.
Doug

Jim Sanborn did the K4 encryption while driving cross-country (with petrified wood) from I think Arizona back to VA.
I just don't see Jim performing DES encryption -- certainly not while driving. "I am a person who has zero mathematical
ability, took tutoring for algorithms in high school." It's going to be a visual system like K1-K3 were. Yes, all the prior
ciphers had mathematical equivalents, but Jim constructed them using visual, matrix-based layouts.

It is trivial to create an unsolvable 97-character cipher. What's hard is making it ~just barely~ solvable. The jury is
still out as to which box K4 falls in.  --Rob

I certainly don't see this as actual DES, with S Boxes and bit manipulations.

What I could envision is a simple pencil & paper scheme using a Feistel structure:  split the message into 2 halves, and alternately use one half to generate the key for substitution of the other half.

I'm not saying I think he did that;  I'm only saying that a paper & pencil scheme could be designed using a Feistel approach.

Doug

t:
Hi Everyone,

I just wanted to disclose some information that I've being keeping close to my chest (Until now).
I arrived at the conclusion mentioned in the subject line, by first considering the idea that K4 was encrypted by a running key. I had considered the idea of using a numerical key / OTP (Digital interpretation), several years ago. The idea of using the value of Pi, which is an infinite series was among many that I tried. I considered other potential keys such as root 2 etc. For example PI = 3.1415926...could be split into pairs 31, 41, 59, 26.
Then you would encrypt by just taking 31 Modulo 26 ( = +5) to Caesar shift the first character by +5, 41 Mod 26 (= +15) for the second and so on.
This idea bore little fruit, and so I abandoned the idea several years ago. However upon reading about the most recent clue, I noted that NE = 45 degrees, the sine of which is Root 2/2 = 0.70710678118... or expressed in radians is 0.785398... Both nice infinite series! And that got me thinking again about the compass glyph and the coordinates mentioned in K2. At this point I had an epiphany... Most of the decrypted texts and clues mentioned in the past by Sanborn suddenly began making sense.

This is what they said to me:

K2:
IT WAS TOTALLY INVISIBLE HOWS THAT POSSIBLE? = A euphemism for it (a message) was concealed by encryption.

THEY USED THE EARTHS MAGNETIC FIELD = There is only really one way to "use the earths magnetic field" and that's in conjunction with a compass. This is a hint that compass bearings are important in concealing the message.

THE INFORMATION WAS GATHERED AND TRANSMITTED UNDERGRUUND TO AN UNKNOWN LOCATION = There exists a currently unknown but important underground location.

DOES LANGLEY KNOW ABOUT THIS ? THEY SHOULD ITS BURIED OUT THERE SOMEWHERE X WHO KNOWS THE EXACT LOCATION ? = We are STILL talking about a specific underground location here. We really need to find it.

ONLY WW THIS WAS HIS LAST MESSAGE X THIRTY EIGHT DEGREES FIFTY SEVEN MINUTES SIX POINT FIVE SECONDS NORTH SEVENTY SEVEN DEGREES EIGHT MINUTES FORTY FOUR SECONDS WEST = The phrase emphasises the importance of GPS coordinates. This is an example of the format required to announce the location of the underground location (when you find it), using the location of Kryptos as an example: I.e. GPS coordinates of the form Degrees, Arcminutes and Arcseconds to one decimal place. When we identify the underground location, we should take heed of the "EXACT LOCATION" specified and record it in the format prescribed in WW's example message.

K3:
SLOWLY DESPARATLY SLOWLY THE REMAINS OF PASSAGE DEBRIS THAT ENCUMBERED THE LOWER PART OF THE DOORWAY WAS REMOVED WITH TREMBLING HANDS I MADE A TINY BREACH IN THE UPPER LEFT HAND CORNER AND THEN WIDENING THE HOLE A LITTLE I INSERTED THE CANDLE AND PEERED IN THE HOT AIR ESCAPING FROM THE CHAMBER CAUSED THE FLAME TO FLICKER BUT PRESENTLY DETAILS OF THE ROOM WITHIN EMERGED FROM THE MIST X CAN YOU SEE ANYTHING Q ? = Well done! You cracked K3! Here you go. This is the Underground location mentioned in K2 that you needed. It's Tutankhamun's tomb! Don't forget (from K2) that you need the exact coordinates of the underground location! So you need to take the coordinates of the location of Tutankhamun's tomb (Also known as KV62): These are found to be LAT: 25° 44' 15.2" N, Long: 32° 36' 3.1" E. Now you know the exact position of the unknown underground location!

Morse Code Message: T IS YOUR POSITION = Tut is the position you need. Just to reiterate, we are indeed talking about the location of Tutankhamun.

Morse Code Message: DIGITAL INTERPRETATION = The keys are numerical, the encryption scheme involves numerical operations. The encryption keys employed are the coordinates values!

"Hidden in plain sight", "A billboard in Moscow" = You could conceivably display a well known landmark on a poster in Moscow as a means of broadcasting the key.
For example if you had a photograph of a glamorous model drinking a branded beer, framed by the checkpoint Charlie guard box (in Berlin), on a poster; then you could secretly but openly pass a numerical key (I.e. CC's GPS coordinate). Alternatively, the GPS location of the billboard itself could be the prearranged key.
A key could be exchanged in this manner, "in plain sight". Who would ever guess that the GPS coordinate of a point on Earth is the message being conveyed, or that the coordinate is an encryption key?

I now believe that the keys employed to encrypt K4 are the GPS coordinate pair  LAT: 25° 44' 15.2" N, Long: 32° 36' 3.1" E that locate Tut's tomb.

The issue with this idea, is that there are still many possible encryption schema that could employ the coordinate values. For example, you could convert both values to radians and thus get a pair of infinite sequences. You could also find Sine of each. Do you take the integer part, or discard it? Do you interpolate each value into a single key stream? Etc. etc. This is why I decided to share this idea. I simply can't test every possible scheme that I can imagine. I will however test as many as I can think of.

Anyway, this is my interpretation of the decrypted messages and clues. I'd be interested in any feedback.

Regards,

Paraic.

Did Ed/Jim ever say/imply that there's no key for K4, e.g., that the method is the key?

One could split K4 into 2 halves, using one half to compute a running key for the other half.
If there's no keyword, the running key could be a permutation/transposition of the half that gets passed thru to the next round.
(If there us a keyword, the running key could be substitution of the half that gets passed through).

In both cases, the running key would then be used to encrypt or transform (probably vig substitute) the other half.

I haven't played with this to say there's any evidence for/against this method;  I'm merely saying this is one possible pen & paper approach that "could" have been used (one of thousands!).

Doug

s: Trifid cipher and features of Kryptos and K4
t:
Just brainstorming here...

Has there been discussion on this board about the trifid cipher? It involves arraying the alphabet into three 3x3 grids, called Layers. It's curious in this regard that "LAYER TWO" appears at the end of K2. Typically the extra (27th) space in the last grid is filled by a symbol such as a period or a plus sign, but it's possible that one could just repeat the first letter of the keyed alphabet as the 27th letter. I note that "K", the first letter of KRYPTOS and thus the first letter of the KRYPTOS-keyed alphabet, occurs 8 times in the ciphertext of K4, the most of any letter (no other letter occurs more than 6 times), and very close to double the number of expected occurrences of a single letter. (This method would create a small amount of ambiguity in the deciphering process, in which the receiver would have to test both positions of K each place it occurs to decipher the message. The ambiguity could be minimized if, for example, the two K's in the trifid grid were placed in the same Row and Column of two different Layers, so that only one of its three coordinates would be ambiguous.) Note that "ID BY ROWS" and "LAYER TWO" can both be related to the format of a trifid cipher grid. They are not clues to help one solve K4, but they may perhaps be clues to use the K4 trifid cipher grid to solve the additional riddle after K4 is solved.

The trifid is neither a substitution nor a transposition cipher, so it is distinct from the methods of K1-K3. It's also a pretty darn difficult cipher to decrypt. Its 3-dimensional layout may have appealed to a visual artist such as Jim Sanborn, and the simple numerical coordinates involved in the encryption process could be conceptualized visually as Layers, Rows, and Columns, so there's not too much complicated math involved for Jim. By the way, "PALIMPSEST" could be interpreted as Layers on top of each other, as in the trifid cipher grid, and "ABSCISSA" is the horizontal or x-coordinate of a point, also one of the three coordinates of each box in a trifid cipher grid.

The question is, how hard is it to decipher even an ordinary trifid cipher with only 97 characters? And how much extra "masking" of the plaintext could Jim and Ed have done on top of this, without making it impossible to solve?

Again, this is all just brainstorming. No one will know for sure what the actual encryption method of K4 was, until someone has deciphered it. Just offering my two cents and hopefully some food for thought here...

Geoffrey

That is the essence of cryptoanalysis, after all, and not all patterns boil down to numbers as the Kasiski Test proves.  I’m working from a conceptual form of cryptographic index of coincidence, that is looking at specific strings of text that repeat either in the Stones or in the CT/PT.

Concrete, confirmable and repeatable results?  Absolutely. A 24-column of flattened Plaintext starting from K1 and ending at K3 will yield a series of meaningful null ciphers on the left and right margins of Kryptos. Null ciphers are a most ancient form of concealment cipher, a simple form of steganography.

My conclusions based on those results are subject to interpretation.

Masking means that something was done to keep the usual cryptanalysis tools such as frequency analysis etc from being used. It also means that using a dictionary attack to find a key using the given cribs is unlikely to be successful.

My sense given the techniques used in K1-3 is that there were two or more paper and pencil field ciphers used. But there are a lot of those.

s: "ID BY ROWS" and extra "L" row in tableau as Polybius square
t:
One of the most evident possible clues in Kryptos is the extra "L" at the end of the first row of the bottom right quadrant. It is so visually jarring and out of place with the evenly lined up row lengths in the rest of the Vigenère tableau, that it cannot be an accident and must have some meaning. Also, I believe it's a feature that Jim and Ed have *not* denied that it could play a role in solving K4.

I notice that this extra L follows the letters "IJ". It so happens that I/J are the two letters most commonly combined into a single box of a 5x5 Polybius square, to allow the 26-letter alphabet to fit into the 25-box 5x5 square. If one then simply begins with I/J and fills out a 5x5 Polybius square by reading this row of the tableau backward, from right to left, the first row will be I/J H G F E, and the second row will begin with D. It is curious that in this case, "I D" are the letters that begin the first two rows of this Polybius square.

Now of course these "I D rows" and the phrase in K2 "ID BY ROWS" may well be a pure coincidence, as is every such observation that does not happen to be related to the actual solution of K4. But I thought it was worth mentioning.

Geoffrey

s: K3 is Instructions; Clear The Debris for Layer Two
t:
Just throwing this thought out there... we know there's something about
"layer two" but there has been little discussion about actually,
physically, layering the Kryptos panels atop one another. I'd like to
hypothesize how this method may look:

1)  Layer the K3/K4 Panel on top of the K1/K2 panel.

"THE REMAINS OF PASSAGE DEBRIS THAT ENCUMBERED THE LOWER PART OF
THE DOORWAY WAS REMOVED"

2) K3 instructs one to clear the debris under the doorway. So do it, remove
the debris... that's the 97 characters. They're dust. No wonder why this
"K4" has gone unsolved. We now have the "layer two" characters revealed,
showing through from the first panel.

"I MADE A TINY BREACH IN THE UPPER LEFT HAND CORNER AND THEN WIDENING THE
HOLE A LITTLE I INSERTED THE CANDLE AND PEERED IN THE HOT AIR ESCAPING FROM
THE CHAMBER"

3)  K3 instructs one to make a breach in the upper left hand corner and
widen it. This is ambiguous, since we don't know the orientation for "top
left" w/ a number of backwards and upside-down clues in Kryptos. I suspect
we have to mirror the K1/K2 panel, revealing FUME as the first four
characters. If that is correct, the width of the hole we have to make is 4
characters.

The reveal of FUME may be evidence that the solver oriented the grids
correctly since the absolute first thing you see is "hot air escaping".

4) Using clues like the intentional misspellings, I'd be willing to bet we
can punch more holes in the top layer to reveal certain characters on the
layer underneath.. like a cardan or grid.

Layer 1, meet Layer 2.

Any thoughts?
Hey Mark, nice work! Did you try it out on the rest of the K4?

s: how to square 1-to-1 matching with "turning" and "flipping" comments
t:
I've been reading up on developments in K4 over the past couple years, in particular Elonka Dunin's notes on her conversations with Jim Sanborn and Ed Scheidt last year. I know Sanborn's comments in that discussion were considered confusing by many people, in light of previous comments by Jim and Ed. I especially thought it was a shame that Jim Melichar, one of the very best folks on this board, seems to have given up on K4 in response to Sanborn's comments last year, which he felt pointed toward a hopelessly unsolvable cipher.

I'm very sympathetic to Jim M.'s reaction, and I agree that some of Sanborn's comments over the years seem confusing when they are all taken together. But I also try to keep in mind that it was really Ed who designed the encryption methods, not Sanborn, and Ed knew the difference between a very difficult challenge and a hopelessly impossible challenge. (I wish it was Ed answering a lot of our questions about the K4 cipher, instead of Jim!)

It seems to me that the greatest difficulty in Sanborn's comments last year was his hemming and hawing about the previous statement that in the cribs, the plaintext maps 1-to-1 to the ciphertext (i.e., B=N, E=Y, R=P, L=V, I=T, N=T) and his new statement about all the work he had to do to encrypt K4, including "turning" and "flipping" and "running it through the washing machine". That sounds like a description of a transposition cipher method, such as that of K3, in which case the 26th to 34th and 64th to 74th plaintext letters would not be directly related to the 26th to 34th and 64th to 74th ciphertext letters at all. It is understandable that Jim M. and others may see these statements by Sanborn as completely contradicting each other.

In this post I want to suggest an interpretation that may reconcile the seemingly contradictory statements:

Perhaps the "turning and flipping" comments describe a transposition method used in the *creation of the key for the masking step* --
but then the main encryption step is a 1-to-1 substitution cipher method, or at least not a transposition that removes all connection between the nth plaintext letter and the nth ciphertext letter.

Yes, that seems to involve a great degree of difficulty in finding the key for the masking step. Combined with an also difficult main encryption step, it may seem that this would create a hopelessly unsolvable cipher for just 97 characters.

However, if the transposition methods to create the key for the masking step are similar to the methods employed to encrypt K3, and if the main encryption step is similar to the encryption method for K1 and K2, perhaps the whole thing together could still be considered an extremely difficult but still fair and potentially solvable challenge.

As an example of what I mean and have in mind about the key for the masking step, consider for example the idea of taking some block of ciphertext from K1-K3 and performing some sort of transposition methods on it. Then the resulting transposed text could be used as the key for the masking step. Sanborn would have had to do a lot of "turning" and "flipping" in that process, but it wouldn't have broken the 1-to-1 connection between the K4 plaintext and final ciphertext. It only would have affected the *key* for the masking step.

To illustrate what I have in mind, and possibly as a challenge to talented cryptographers on this board, here is a 97-letter "key" that I created, using ciphertext from K1-K3 and transposition methods to encrypt it:

MFRDB NCXWT UNRRE TRHJI FCTAG
LITIH FERAP VIMEF QADGE ITFFH
KREXR GETDR NADAC AZDIL KVEAE
NVZEO LBENR RLODD YAJEF NE

Notes:
The original block of ciphertext was *not* simply 97 consecutive characters from somewhere in K1-K3.
There is no substitution involved in my method, only transpositions.
The 5-letter blocks are by convention, and do not necessarily indicate any period-5 method in any step.
However, I did choose to use DYAHR, Y-A-R, and Jim & Ed's comments about it as part of my transposition methods.
Note that since this method only takes visible text and uses it only to create a key for a masking step --
it does not have to be reversible or recoverable in principle in its own right.
That is, the intended recipient would never have to take the above key and decrypt it into the original order of the block of ciphertext.
The recipient would simply have to know where to look to find the right block of original ciphertext --
and know the method to *create* the above key, the same way that the original encryption did.
Thus, to solve my challenge, you have to "think like the encryptor", rather than purely working backwards from the above key and using only decryption methods.

Well, surely that is too many hints, somebody must be able to figure it out now!

Geoffrey

s: how to square 1-to-1 matching with "turning" and "flipping" comments
t:
Hi Geoffrey: I think you've pretty accurately captured Jim M.'s exasperation with Sanborn's possible walking-back
of the original 1:1 comment (or potentially worse, the seeming lack of understanding of what is meant by it),
leading to Jim M.'s subsequent throwing in of the towel. I think the straw on the camel's back was Sanborn's
additional remark that the raised letters in K3 (dYAhR) had nothing to do with the encryption of K4. (I'm not
100% sure of my memory here, but I believe that is an accurate recollection).

Since Jim M. (and I) had spent considerable time on masking approaches that might be implied by that YAR
kernel, I feel like the removal of that crib from the toolbox was a fatal blow to Jim's interest. We were back
to having no clue whether transposition was or was not involved, coupled with elimination of the YAR
curiosity as any sort of sculpture clue.

Yes, we considered that the cipher could still be 1:1 if the just key is transposed and not the PT or CT, but
dictionary attacks would likely have turned up the solution by now if the key was a modest-length scrambled
English word, given that we have 20 crib letters to work with.

As an aside, I'm not sure we even know that Ed's masking is a distinct, separate step from otherwise classical
encryption, or if it is the encryption method itself that ends up masking the tell-tale English letter frequencies
that are obvious in simple transposition, or leak through in polyalphabetic substitution.

We know as an artist -- and by example in K1-K3 and the Cyrillic Cylinder -- that Sanborn likes visual encryption
methods (Vigenere matrix, and the likely double rotated matrices he used for K3). We also suspect that he
would dislike a purely mathematical system such as RSA. Ed would know this, and would focus on systems
that could be easily carried out by the artist, and yet yield strong encryption. From inspection, we know that
K4 is neither strictly transposition nor strictly polyalphabetic substitution (at least with a reasonable keyword
length). Unfortunately, that leaves a vast number of systems he could have used. This is why we were hoping
to get an accurate answer to the 1:1 question: either a yes or no would help thin the field of candidates.
Even if he didn't want to give that as a clue, it would have been better to just say so rather than leave us in
the Schrodinger's Box limbo we now find ourselves. Personally I lean toward transposition being involved --
and not just key transposition.  --Rob

s: how to square 1-to-1 matching with "turning" and "flipping" comments
t:
Hi Rob: Thank you for the reply and for the interesting and helpful summary of the state of affairs. I appreciate it.

A few comments: Even though the raised Y-A-R letters may not be involved in the encryption of K4, that doesn't mean DYAHR / HYDRA itself wasn't involved. Those are two different things. The raised letters create one possible transposition of the letters of HYDRA; the string DYAHR is a different transposition of the letters of HYDRA. And HYDRA as a keyword at some step is still in play.

Regarding the comment about a dictionary attack on a modest-length scrambled English word if just the key is transposed: I see many layers and possibilities to unpack and consider here. There may be two different keys involved, one for the masking step, if it is indeed a separate step, and one for the main encryption step. Even if the main encryption step is just Vigenere/Quagmire III with a keyword, transposed or not, a dictionary attack wouldn't necessarily reveal the solution if it couldn't figure out the initial masking step.

The initial masking step may be based on the use of some ciphertext from K1-K3 as a key, possibly even combined with the positioning of some letters in the Vigenere tableau. Any such key based on K1-K3 ciphertext or on tableau letters will not be found by a dictionary attack. I consider that the use of K1-K3 ciphertext in the encryption process may be likely, given that Ed has said things like "I used some steganography in K4." I do recall an old post of yours that mentioned an examination of 97-letter blocks of K1-K3 ciphertext in various arrangements. This is the kind of idea that I have in mind. But keep in mind that it's also possible that the process used some block of ciphertext that did not consist of consecutive letters of the K1-K3 ct, but which used some other geometric arrangement of some part of the text.

One more comment about dictionary attacks: I can think of many ways that a thematic keyword might *not* be a "dictionary" word. I believe I used BRANDENBURGGATE as one example in a post a few years ago. A two-word proper name, not in a "dictionary attack" database, but a valid and thematic keyword rather than a meaningless random jumble of letters. Here's another example I thought of recently: HYDRATRITON. Hydra and Triton were the code names of the first two Enigma U-boat ciphers. Notably, "Medusa" was the third such cipher. I think HYDRATRITON would be perfectly thematic; the DYAHR string would give a clue in the right direction but wouldn't give the whole keyword away. Since it is two words put together, a "dictionary attack" wouldn't necessarily find it. I rather think that Ed would lean in this direction: He surely knew all about computer-based dictionary attacks, he wanted to create a challenge that they couldn't easily break, and he designed a keyword to rather reward creative ideas outside the dictionary. Of course that doesn't mean any of my particular ideas is right, but it's the type of keyword construction I think we should consider for K4.

I agree with the comment about Sanborn and visual encryption methods. Any possible solution would likely require the identification of a primarily visual way to perform the encryption, rather than a purely mathematical process.

I still doubt wholesale transposition of the PT/CT itself in K4. Digraphic substitution I think is in play, but not something like K3. Sanborn just put too much emphasis in his BERLIN CLOCK clues that BERLIN is related to NYPVTT and CLOCK is related to MZFPK. In all of his clues, he has always included the corresponding ciphertext string along with the plaintext crib as part of the clue. If a K3 style transposition method was involved, I don't think he would have done that. He could have said "the 64th through 69th letters of the message are BERLIN", without emphasizing or even mentioning the NYPVTT string of ct. But he has always mentioned and included those ciphertext strings in his clues.

I am still hopeful that the whole process may involve a cleverly hidden masking step key (perhaps a whole 97-letter running key) somewhere among the visible text of the Kryptos panels, followed by Vigenere / Quagmire III with a relevant thematic keyword. By the way, for the Quagmire step, I would consider not only the KRYPTOS-keyed tableau, but also the alphabetical order top row and left column of the tableau on the right-hand side panels. Using the alphabetical row for the plaintext and the alphabetical column for the key letter, but using the KRYPTOS-keyed interior grid of the tableau for the ciphertext, would create an interesting twist that is still easy to perform visually simply by using the tableau right there on the sculpture. The challenge is this: It's hard to do any kind of brute force search on both the unknown masking step key *and* the main step keyword at the same time. It seems to me you have to guess ideas about one or the other, and see if any kind of interesting or identifiable pattern shows up as a result as a possibility to be the key of the other step, rather than a meaningless jumble of letters.

Final thought: Has anyone found a good reason why the Vigenere tableau on the sculpture is extended to have the four extra columns on the right that simply repeat the 2nd through 5th columns? They don't seem to add any necessary information in terms of using the tableau to encrypt and decrypt. They simply serve to match the typical row lengths of the K1-K4 ciphertext side. I do wonder if they serve some purpose in the masking step, likely in combination with K1-K3 ciphertext in corresponding positions.

Geoffrey

s: A argument for the third class of cipher
t:
I’ve noticed that speculation on cipher types in the forum tends to fall into a hard binary between Substitution and Transposition, so I want to talk a little about the third type. What I refer to, of course is  the Concealment Cipher, something that seems to have limited direct discussion in the forum unless there’s some terminology I’m unfamiliar with. I have absolutely no idea how widely Helen Fouche Gaines is read as her book on Cryptanalysis was written in 1939, but in reading her explanation of this form of cipher, it seems to me that a Concealment Cipher is highlight compatible a form of masking, since it doesn't heap ciphertext on ciphertext, and that the use of the word Masking to describe this cipher type is a good way to avoid giving something away immediately by opening up a category that people typically wouldn’t consider.

     The nice thing about Concealment Ciphers is that they seem to be simpler in general, and are the sort of thing someone might want to use for clues on text they expect to be solved quickly rather than the chosen system (for K4) itself. Given that one must design their chosen plaintext  first, it’s seems as if it should be basic to apply  a bunch of null ciphers or grille into the plaintext to create your special plaintext, and apply other ciphers to your result. Not necessarily K4 itself, but the means of getting there. Nor are these plaintext clues “required” if one were to stumble on the proper decryption method without them.

$0.02

t:
Hi Rob,
Frustrating, isn't it, that we haven't been able to get a straight answer out of them.
At one point Jim says it's 1:1, but later backtracks on that.
Ed says he "did something to mask" the english letter statistics;  we didn't ask if there was an explicit masking step, but assumed there was and asked only if the masking was applied before/after the encryption;  his answer was "interesting question" and moved on.

So where does that leave us:  a single cipher text message with a couple of cribs.  Not much to work with.

In a sense, K1..K4 could show an evolution of cryptography from substitution to transposition to ???
(Did K2 merely repeat the same technique as K1 -- was anything evolutionary added?)
Maybe the era of rotor machines, where a long running key is generated from rotors.
Maybe a running key produced by scrambling "something on a billboard" such as the morse messages, or perhaps a section of ciphertext from k1..k3.
Maybe a combination of Substitution and Permutation(Transposition) such as SP networks a la DES, with or without a Feistel structure.

A running key would be consistent with 1:1 if in fact the encryption process is 1:1, but who knows.

The observation that using 'W' as a separator leads to two alternating segments of 46 letters, each with identical letter distribution, is interesting, but could be coincidental.

We assume that the message is encrypted and we need to decrypt it;  the sender could have applied the decryption to the plaintext, and the recipient would encrypt it to recover it.

Maybe K1 is a 63 letter "one time pad";  transpose it one for letters 1..63;  transpose it again for page 2 letters 64..97.  (At one point I thought they might be highlighting Venona, using the same 63 letter pad for each block of 63 plain letters, but block 1 doesn't appear to be in depth with block 2).

So.many.possibilities.

Doug

s: A argument for the third class of cipher
t:
A concealment cipher is more commonly called a null cipher today, and I see the idea mentioned on this board. In general it can be seen as one form of steganography, which can appear in many forms. I certainly agree that some type of this method is very much in play in some step of the K4 encryption, especially for a key for the initial masking step. Ed Scheidt even said once, "I used some stego [steganography] in K4." It could be a grille, but it could also simply be some kind of geometrical or logical pattern within the letters on the four panels of the Kryptos sculpture. Given comments by Jim & Ed like "the answer to K4 is hidden in plain sight", I lean more toward a clever but logical or geometrical pattern within the letters, rather than a complicated grille with an obscure pattern.

Geoffrey
