s: evidence against digraphic ciphers in NORTHEAST and BERLINCLOCK and their ciphertext
t:
I think it's just as important to share evidence *against* certain possible encryption methods for K4, as it is to share ideas and evidence in favor of certain possible methods.

I was just looking at the digraphs (2-letter pairs) in K4. Now a digraphic cipher would *already* be very difficult to break with standard cryptanalytic methods and only 97 letters of ciphertext to work with, which only yield 48 digraphs. The most common English digraphs only occur about 2% of the time, and most are much less frequent, so 48 digraphs provide very little material to work with, even in an ordinary digraphic cipher. So there can't be *too much* additional encryption in this case, or it would quickly become hopelessly impossible to solve.

I note that if the expected word "THE" occurs before "BERLIN CLOCK", then NORTHEAST gives a repeating digraph: either TH in 29th-30th and 61st-62nd positions, or HE in 30th-31st and 62nd-63rd positions. However, the respective ciphertext digraphs in those positions are not the same: RN and NF in the first case, and NG and FB in the second case. So we may conclude that if THE is correct before BERLIN CLOCK, then K4 cannot be an ordinary digraphic cipher.

Moreover, even if for example a four-square cipher grid is rotated 90 degrees to encrypt each letter in turn -- I believe Jim Melichar mentioned this idea once, and it is a very good and thematic idea that would suit Sanborn's preference for visual encryption methods -- the whole four-square grid would still repeat its orientation every 4 digraphs, or every 8 letters. And in this case the 29th-30th and 61st-62nd positions would still be expected to repeat, as would the 30th-31st and 62nd-63rd positions, since they are 32 letters apart, which is a multiple of 8. Therefore, if "THE" is correct before BERLIN CLOCK, we may rule out any digraphic cipher method that repeats the same encryption matrix every 4 digraphs, such as the four-square 90-degree rotation idea.

Geoffrey

s: how to square 1-to-1 matching with "turning" and "flipping" comments
t:
Hi Doug,
I am under the impression that Ed earlier implied the masking step was applied before the main encryption step. Phrases like "masking the English language" imply masking the plaintext, which would be applied before encryption, not after.

K2 repeated the same technique as K1. It seems to me the main challenge there was simply to figure out that the first panel contained two separate messages with two different keywords. Once that is determined, the method is the same. It's interesting that K2 must have been much easier in practice than K1, since the K2 text is so much longer but its keyword is actually shorter. K1 is only 63 letters with a 10-letter keyword, although the repeated letters in PALIMPSEST help.

Never forget that Jim Sanborn wouldn't have performed complicated mathematics to do the encryption. So it's hard to imagine rotor machines or SP networks or Feistel structures. Also, the Morse messages are basically out of play, since Jim & Ed have always stated that the information on the Kryptos sculpture's four panels alone is enough to solve K4.

I'm glad you mentioned the W separator idea. It's interesting that none of Sanborn's crib clues include a ciphertext W, leaving the idea in play. (Whereas the crib clues have now shown there seems to be nothing special about the double letters or about PRNG.) However, assuming each segment between the W's is a coherent portion of the message in its own right, the crib clues do place some restrictions on the possibilities: The 5th such segment would be [INFB] BERLIN CLOCK. The most logical word by far to precede BERLIN is "THE", but this is at odds with exactly four letters before BERLIN in this segment between W's. The 2nd segment between W's would be [FLRV] NORTHEAST [OT]. This is also a small and restricted number of letters before and especially after NORTHEAST, if one wants to pursue the W separator hypothesis.

Geoffrey

t:
Thanks much. This sounds to me like when the ciphertext is finally decoded back to the original plaintext, BERLIN will start at character position 64. It is pretty clear from the dictionary attacks that some have done that BERLIN doesn’t start at position 64 of the ciphertext. What if K4 was done using the K3 technique followed by the K1/2 technique?

“We spent quite a bit of time asking Jim about the correlation between the plaintext BERLIN and the ciphertext such as NYPVTT. Specifically, we were trying to find out if there was a 1:1 relationship from NYPVTT to BERLIN, or there was some other step, the masking technique. Jim was confused when we mentioned masking technique, evidently it's something that Ed said that Jim didn't understand. Jim said that yes the ciphertext and plaintext were connected, but when I tried to explain what exactly we were asking, like that in K1 EMUFPH is exactly BETWEE, but in K3 ENDYAH does not map exactly to SLOWLY, Jim backed off and said he would only commit to the fact that K4 is exactly 97 characters long, and that BERLIN is plaintext that starts at exactly the 64th character, but he wouldn't go further than that.“

Thank you Manny.

I agree that Zygalski sheets have a number of curious features that seem to be possibly relevant to some clues in Kryptos: abscissa like you mention, also palimpsest for layering sheets on top of each other, "subtle shading and the absence of light" for seeing letters through the perforated holes, and "a tiny breach in the upper left hand corner and then widening the hole a little" for the perforated holes. I even notice the top of a Zygalski sheet has three raised holes representing I suppose the starting positions of the three Enigma machine rotors, and their raised position somewhat resembles that of Y-A-R in Kryptos.

However...I understand that Zygalski sheets were specifically designed to decrypt the Enigma machine and its particular rotor design, the interrelation of how the three rotors moved, etc. The usefulness of the sheets, I understand, is directly connected to the technical mechanical operation of that particular rotor machine.

I simply don't believe that Jim Sanborn & Ed Scheidt built an Enigma machine to perform the K4 encryption. That's the only way Sanborn could or would have done an Enigma encryption -- he wouldn't have had the mathematical skills or interest to work out the mathematical equivalent without using an actual Enigma machine itself. So I think this possibility is off the table.

About your 3-letter blocks and key rotations: This would imply that the underlying plaintext was identical in those 3-letter blocks, wouldn't it? Otherwise the resemblance of the other two identical ciphertext letters would just be coincidental anyway. I don't believe there was likely more than 1 repeated 3-letter block in the 97-letter text of K4, so I don't think this approach will get us very far.

If you are saying the 3-letter blocks are just keys themselves...well you would have to explain the method by which the key blocks and the ciphertext of K4 could be the same thing. There are two quotes, neither of which is unambiguous:

In the Wired interview, Ed is quoted as saying

You can get insight into the sculpture through that technique because the English language is still visible through the code.  [But with] this other technique, I disguise that. He thus refers to the encryption method as a "technique" which better removes english language statistics than the techniques used for K1/2/3.

The second quote is from the meting at Ed's house, in which we tried to get him to elaborate on his use of the word "mask" as a verb:  we didn't ask if there was a distinct masking "step" so he didn't answer this;  we assumed there was a "step" and asked if it was performed pre or post encryption, which elicited the coy "interesting question" non-response.

When Jim was asked a similar question, he expressed confusion;  that would be consistent with there being no separate "step" and we asked if he applied the "step" before or after.

As far as I know, neither Ed nor Jim ever used the word "step" except perhaps when he was repeating back our questions.

When we listened to Ed's initial discussion about masking the effects of English, before we got into a discussion of "step", I had the impression he was talking about something like autokey or running key, i.e., something embedded in the encryption technique itself, or possibly a combination of techniques from K1/2/3 e.g., combine substitution and transposition,  IF Jim's initial answer about 1:1 were valid (before he retracted it) that would seem to rule out single transposition (although something line Trans/Sub/Inverse_Trans might be viable).

With the cribs, we can rule out autokey (kak, ctak, or ptak) using single prior letters as the current key (e.g., use K[i-3] for K[i], or CT[i-5] for K[i], etc.).

That seems to leave a running key, possibly computed from "something on a billboard".

I also don't know what to make of the 4 extra columns on the tableau, plus 1 letter, for a total of 105 letters.  105 happens to be the product of 21 (consonants) and 5 (vowels), i.e., the number of digraphs consisting of one vowel and one consonant, so maybe some kind of encoding of a letter into a digraph of one vowel and one consonant, but that would seem to imply K4 would only have 48 or so letters which doesn't match what we were told about the crib positions.

Doug

s: An argument for the Acrostic Concealment cipher
t:
Building on the concept of steganographic concealment ciphers aka null ciphers, I’d like to focus on a specific type – the Acrostic.  Dating all the way back to ancient oracles, like many concealment ciphers, they’re among the most ancient type.  They have excellent potential for clues, since they are concealed in plaintext and do not involve substitution or transposition, and thus are not subject to those classical methods of cryptanalysis. I’ll take that a step further not just speculating but stating that they exist throughout K1-K3. I can’t take credit for this idea – I believe it was initially raised by Com NAV in a discussion involving the first letter of every word in K1. I’ve taken it much further, but that is where it begins. This re-introduces some previous items I've posted, but with important revisions that start to clarify the T position.

K1 - BSSATAOLLTNOI
T IS AST BALLOON. An AST Balloon is a hot air balloon, and for reasons I won't get at here, is a perfect fit for the Morse Stones and K3.  It builds on the theme, clarifying that your position is not only T, but something about it invokes the hot air balloon.

I’ve referenced my AcroAen excel file before, but since the grid isn’t well-labeled, I’ll offer the results here. What the grid is – based on Jim’s handwritten notes, the Kryptos flattened prototype, ID BY ROWS and other clues, I determined that the best method of flattening to find more acrostics would be a grid of 24 columns.

Results:
K2 Rows – T IS SE RING OF BOWL
K3 Rows – T IS OVER HROHNL ID
K1-K3 Remaining Left and Right Rows:
F.R.  ISTANBUL / WATCHTOWER / SESTOS / XANTH / F.L.B.L.

The K1 and K2 acrostics  would appear to refer to Tut’s Cup, the first “Wondrous Thing” found in the tomb, and probably the southeastern border of K3/K4 as well.
The other two refer to the ciphertext at the beginning of K3 and a highly specific  painting titled The Last Watch of Hero, by Frederic Leighton Baron Leighton.  Note that if you look up the painting most of the images cut off the bottom half of the painting that includes Leander’s rubble-strewn corpse and plaque.

"
NSA's declassified AXIS SIGINT in WWII, Vol II, Notes on German High Level Cryptography and Cryptanalysis contains some interesting crypto related info. The Lorenz SZ-42c cipher teleprinter with synchronisation, named SK-44 and SK-45, would generate and send a continuous pseudo-random five-bit stream. The receiver mixed its identical stream, by XOR-ing, with the incoming stream, resulting in nothing to print, since (K ⊕ K) = 0. When sending a message, the plain teleprinter message was mixed into the stream. The receiver mixed, as usual, the received signal with its own stream, which results in canceling out the stream and the original plain message being printed instantly, since (K ⊕ M) ⊕ K = M.

An eavesdropper would not know if or when the random stream contained an actual message or how long it was, thus effectively preventing traffic analysis. The U.S. Army Security Agency (ASA) suggested that analysis of the continuous mostly non-message-carrying pseudo-random stream, generated by the  SZ-42c, might compromise the machine's secret key settings. This would enable them to predict the stream and decipher all message that follow. The principle of continuous random stream was nevertheless brilliant and used in the 1950s on the more advanced U.S. KWR-37 JASON and KWT-37 Fleet Broadcast crypto system.
"

Bringing this thread back because I like the insights and ideas presented by Richard Bean in this post.

Yes, I think seriation of a digraphic cipher is a natural option to consider. It even defeats standard frequency analysis of common bigrams such as TH, HE, ER, RE, etc. The only thing one can really look for is any two frequent individual letters that happen to coincide in the seriated digraphic letter pair.

The observation about the 6 repeated bigrams in K4 when the message is seriated at period 21 is quite interesting, I agree. 21 is a multiple of 7 and was the period of the World War II German army field cipher that American cryptanalysts broke -- a brutal *double encrypted* horizontal two-square cipher with randomly filled squares! -- as described in the interesting article mentioned in Richard's post. However, as Richard mentions, the decrypting of the adjacent repeated ZT digrams to xI and xN (in BERLIN) is a big problem with this hypothesis.

The only solution to this problem seems to be some additional layer of encryption, which raises the question of how a seriated digraphic cipher with another encryption step on top of that could possibly be solvable for 97-98 characters. If periodically alternating methods of digraphic encryption were used for each digraph, no regular periodic alternation would match the distances of the 6 repeated bigrams, since the 6 pairs are separated from each other by 1, 6, 8, 13, 17, and 22 bigrams respectively. Therefore, I can't find any logical explanation for the 6 repeated bigrams with period-21 seriation other than chalking it up to an unusual coincidence.

I'm still interested in this general approach though.

Geoffrey

s: A argument for the third class of cipher
t:
How does one decide? By creating a Krypto-graphic artist's take on what cryptanalysts would be familiar with as an "index of coincidence", that is instead of ciphertext that is most meaningful being repeated, plaintext that follows the same concept, with a very clear ruleset. Part and parcel of Sanborn's claims that someone not gifted with numerical skills could conceivably crack the code.

So, the ruleset:

1. That preceding clues support the anagram/acrostic
2. That the acrostics/anagrams relate directly to revealed plaintext.
3. That the anagram/acrostic possess a direct relationship to the ciphertext.

Ideally such an index should also be able to correlate with the Geographic Kryptos exhibit as well, and can be framed not just to build on the preceding clues, but lead to others. Mine was created with that relationship in mind and passes all those standards.

Bear in mind, the theme of Kryptos is "intelligence gathering" which is In line with what cryptanalysis is about, not the act of simply solving a cipher.

A couple more observations about seriation, K4, and Sanborn's crib clues:

Period-7 and period-5 would both be quite thematic for K4. Period-7 because the 98 characters (including the ? character) divide neatly into 7 blocks of 14 letters each, which can then be seriated so that the letters are paired into bigrams and encrypted in the pattern 1st-8th, 2nd-9th, etc. Multiples of 7 and 14 also feature in both steps of the K3 transposition encryption which arranged the 336 letters in a 42x8 array and then a 14x24 array. And of course KRYPTOS itself is 7 letters. Period-5 is also thematic with the length of the DYAHR/HYDRA block.

I note that the placement of Sanborn's crib clues within K4 happen to occur so as to provide the minimal possible number of complete 2-letter bigram pairs if the K4 text is seriated into period-7 or period-5 blocks beginning with the ? character. In NORTHEAST, NO is the end of the second 7x2 block, and RTHEAST is the first half of the third 7x2 block. But the placement yields no complete bigram cribs with this seriation. Likewise, in BERLINCLOCK, BERLIN is the last 6 letters of the fifth 7x2 block, and CLOCK is the first 5 letters of the sixth 7x2 block. Again no complete bigram cribs are provided by this arrangement. Only 4 out of 14 possible placements of an 11-letter block do this, and only 6 out of 14 possible placement of a 9-letter block do this, so this complete lack of period-7 seriated bigram cribs would only happen by chance 10% of the time.

Likewise, even seriation into perod-5 blocks starting with the ? character provides the absolute minimal possible number of complete bigram cribs in Sanborn's clues: The 11-letter block BERLINCLOCK must provide at least 1 such bigram, and indeed it provides only exactly one, BN -> NT at the end of the seventh 5x2 block. NORTHEAST is located so that NORT is the end of the third 5x2 block, and HEAST is the first half of the fourth 5x2 block: no complete bigram cribs at all! Only 2 out of 10 possible placements of an 11-letter block yield only one complete bigram this way, and only 2 out of 10 possible placements of a 9-letter block yield no complete bigrams. So this minimal number of period-5 seriated bigram cribs would only happen by chance 4% of the time.

Geoffrey

s: how Sanborn could have made Scheidt's cipher unsolvable
t:
I recall one old Sanborn quote where he said something along the lines of this: "I took Ed's method and added something to it, so even he couldn't solve it." Now maybe Sanborn didn't really mean this, but it's a concern. Ed has stated that K4 is a "fair challenge", and talks about K4 as if he knows the whole thing. But the two of them refused a request to re-check the K4 encryption during the visit of Elonka Dunin and others last year.

Add to that Sanborn's comments last year about the difficulty of encrypting K4, "turning and flipping" and "running it through the washing machine", and I can imagine the following plausible scenario:

Let's say for argument's sake that the basic encryption method is the four-square cipher. Let's say that the message is seriated into blocks of a certain length, so that the bigrams to be encrypted in the four-square are not adjacent letters. (See the discussion in the "Seriation" thread.) All of this is fair game. Very difficult to decrypt, but fair game for sure. By itself, this is probably not novel enough to be the unique K4 encryption method.

Now let's say the novelty of the K4 encryption method is to rotate the four-square grid during the encryption process. This has a geometric elegance to it that could have appealed to an artist like Sanborn, and would not require mathematical skills to perform the encryption. I recall that Jim Melichar and I thought of this idea independently before, and perhaps others have as well. It is also consistent with the "turning and flipping" comment. "Flipping" fits even better if some of the bigrams were encrypted in the opposite of the usual direction of four-square encryption. These rotations and reversals provide 8 distinct ways to encrypt each bigram in the four-square grid.

Now this is quite novel and elegant, but also getting extraordinarily difficult for a 97-98 character cipher message: Seriation + four-square cipher + rotation/reflection of the four-square grid.

Alas, we can add one more thing: doing a *double* four-square encryption of each bigram. That is, take a bigram, encrypt it in four-square, and then take that and encrypt it *again* in four-square to produce the final ciphertext bigram. This is actually not an entirely new concept: It was done with a horizontal two-square cipher in the World War II German army field cipher called "Doppelkastenschlussel" ("double-box-key"). This double two-square encryption was also combined with period-21 seriation of the message in this German cipher. Nevertheless, American cryptanalysts managed to break the cipher, as described in the Charles David paper in 1994 that is also discussed in the "Seriation" thread.

Thus, seriation + double four-square encryption actually has a thematic precedent in this German "Doppelkastenschlussel" cipher broken by American cryptanalysts. The rotation/reflection of the four-square grid would be the novel element that Scheidt & Sanborn added to the encryption method. Again, this is all quite elegant, but is there any reasonable hope of solving it from a single 97-98 character message? (In the war, the cryptanalysts had multiple messages with typical repeated common phrases to work with. One such phrase was "Wie lage?", which means "Where is your position?" !)

Finally, here is my additional concern: It would have been rather easy for Sanborn himself to "extend" this encryption method, by not stopping at a double encryption, but going on to do a triple, quadruple, or as many multiple four-square encryptions of each single bigram as he pleased. He may have combined this method with rotation/reflection of the four-square grid, just to perform the encryption of a single bigram: Do a four-square encryption, rotate the grid and encrypt again, rotate again and encrypt again, as many times as he liked, just to produce a single ciphertext bigram. Once he had the rotate + multiple encryption method, he wouldn't have needed any particular additional cryptographic or mathematical skill to extend the method as much and as far as he liked. Since Sanborn is not a cryptographer or cryptanalyst himself, he may not even have realized that he was taking an already *almost impossible* method to solve that Ed gave him, and then gone and made it *completely impossible* to solve with the extra four-square encryption and rotation steps.

Once again, the entire method could still be quite thematic and geometric and elegant, especially if it was quadruple rotated and encrypted four-square of each bigram. But any hope of solving a cipher with such an encryption method is another story. One would almost have to guess the four-square grid they used, and even then it's an awful lot of work to test all the possible seriation periods and all the possible ways to rotate, reflect, and encrypt each bigram four times each, as well as rotating the starting position of the four-square grid to begin the process for each bigram. Again, this method is perfectly elegant to describe, but virtually completely impossible to solve.

So yeah, that's my concern about what happened, based on some of Sanborn's comments.

Geoffrey

Thanks for your comments. I did look quite a bit at all those ideas I wrote about and couldn't find anything yet.

It's almost an "aesthetic" argument - I see the length of the ciphertext is 98 characters, which is 7 rows of a seriated digraphic cipher with width 7.

I still think the number of repeated digraphs at width 21 is a key observation, or indicated something which is not a coincidence...

For Trifid, I think I've gone over it fairly thoroughly, personally, but don't let that dissuade you. I could have missed something obvious. I think that's a lesson for me from the IRA cipher and Thouless cipher experience. The last time people tried to solve those, the tools were not as good as they are now ...

I used to wonder if "...ID BY ROWS" meant "TRIFID BY ROWS" (text missing from the start, like "T IS YOUR POSITION", confirmed by Sanborn to be "WHAT ...").

To answer the question "how much Trifid ciphertext do you need to find the plaintext without a crib", it's in the same ballpark as, say, Playfair. The unicity distance of Playfair is 22-27 letters - 25! different keys, assuming you have I/J combined. With Trifid you have 27! different keys, plus a period.

If you have 97/98 letters/characters, and 20 known plaintext letters, then it almost uniquely determines the key and the period. You could use "simulated annealing" to solve it at that length, without a crib - it's been described by Michael J. Cowan (ANCHISES) in The Cryptogram.

For more detailed description of unicity distance, there's an old article by Cipher Deavours in Cryptologia (1977) and a similar shorter version on James Lyons' (fellow Brisbanite) Practical Cryptography website.

It also might be fun to use code like Bion's trifid crib dragger to see what periods, if any, work with the known plaintext/ciphertext.

My opinion is that anything like that goes as long as the true plaintext is reasonably recognizable. The decryption could yield "masked plaintext" that you need to "wash up" to get the real plaintext. Several intentional misspellings are a possibility. (But at the same time we should be careful not to over-interpret failed decrypts that have some random PT fragments in them. I think one will clearly see the difference when one hits the correct decrypt, even in the presence of inserted errors.)

However, I would expect such intentional obfuscations to hide the English statistics, for example NQRTHXAST for NORTHEAST.

t:
I have always taken that bit about Jim changing something to mean that Jim changed the PT, just a little, and somewhere where he was sure it couldn't hurt.  I really don't think Jim would have wanted to risk messing this project up, and I'm sure Ed must have emphasized to him that in cryptography one little mistake in the wrong place can wreck the whole thing, and urged him to come back and check with him if Jim had any doubts whatever about technical feasibility or solubility.  That's what Ed was there for.  Let's check that quote anyway - my recollection is that Jim said Ed doesn't know what K4 says, not that Ed couldn't solve it.  (I believe Ed has said he isn't trying to, or hadn't tried.)

The quotes & hints are simply not all consistent.  At the Ed's-house meeting Ed said he showed or taught Jim a half dozen methods, give or take, and told him that he (Jim) had what he needed, now go do it.  I can't, and I don't think anyone else here can, believe that that was the end of Ed's input,  and also  that Jim Sanborn is something that any ordinary person would consider an anamath, I don't care if he was tutored in math in high school.  For someone who supposedly wouldn't know the difference between 19^2 and 192 and 19+2, he sure is good at making little operatюnal puns on such.  By 1981 he had made a sculpture, North By Northwest , and it seems likely he knew then that NNE = AZ 337½°, and is congruent to 697½°.  Until he met Ed Scheidt and planned out Kryptos he wouldn't have known that  Err. 2 QUAD1 + (H YAHR  • Length K4 )  =  1 • ☉°  + Length K3 , that is, 115+(6•97)=360+337=697, but he had the numbers brewing in his mind.  337° is also congruent to 1057, 1417, 1777, 2137 (& of course an infinity of other numbers), much of which looks like numbers we've seen in connection with Kryptos .  Maybe he's an anamath fascinated by math - anyway, my point is that the hints and statements might be interesting, but aren't to be relied on.

This is supposed to be like a message for Our Man In Moscow to figure out for himself, from itself , presumably without spending weeks of time and massive quantities of paper.  He doesn't have people communicating hints to him (else why bother with the message?), and it won't have been written using methods that any decent clerk in Russian cryptanalysis is going to be familiar with.  Bearing KISS in mind, it should not be a whole lot of layers & transformations, but the few should be novel, and indicated by salient points of the sculpture.  We can't guarantee there wasn't [a] mistake[s], but I think the odds are high that we just haven't hit on the method.

My $.02,

s: partial atbash as a masking step
t:
Just a thought that came up as I was working on some ideas about K4...

A very simple but possibly quite effective initial masking step would be to begin with a *partial* encryption of the plaintext in a super-simple elementary cipher like atbash (reverse alphabet A=Z, B=Y, etc.) or ROT13. By itself such a cipher is trivial and meaningless, but if it is applied only partially to the plaintext, in a not too obviously predictable pattern, and then the main encryption step is applied, that could actually add quite a lot of difficulty to the cryptanalytic effort needed to break it. For example, an X could mark where the atbash parts begin and end, and then there is no repeated or regular pattern to the plaintext and atbash parts of the message. Just a thought.

Geoffrey

s: A argument for the third class of cipher
t:
There’s a greater question that exists in balance of cryptanalysis using anagramming techniques that are incorporated into columnar transposition as well.

Consider this.

Kryptos has 869 characters of plaintext and 869 characters of ciphertext. Taking a random sampling of four paragraphs of the same amount of plaintext with added encryption from any book from the Bible to Harry Potter and flattening it into 24 columns, what are the odds:
1.    The first and last rows will form nothing but legible, anagrammable words, a proper acrostic cipher?
2.    That these rows can be divided into smaller anagrammable phrases  by paragraph.
3.    That these anagrammed words and phrases will relate to both the cipher and plaintext.
4.    That these words and phrases form consistent theme with each other and a non-book source
5.    That the acrostic ciphers can correlate to a nearby geographical location
6.    That anagrammed words will also reference another highly specific related item.
7.    That the results will include ALL of the previous qualifiers, not just one or two.

What are the odds of all of that being an accidental result?

I understand that with any anagram there is room for error and interpretation and one has to be very wary of forcing results. However, I also understand that for anagramming to be considered a proper classical cryptanalytic attack on a columnar transposition cipher, there has to be an index of coincidence that takes it beyond mere “interpretation” into an item that was intended to be found and used.

M. Ferguson,

s: trial partial decryption of K4 with thematic 2-square, period-7 seriation, rotation of 2-squares
t:
The following is far from a complete decryption of K4, but I have discovered enough interesting material that I consider it to be worth sharing here.

The basic cryptographic method is vertical two-square, but with the important strengthening that letters in the same column are not left as transparent identical PT and CT, but rather they are shifted one letter down and swapped. This is actually similar to the WW II German "Doppelkastenschlussel" horizontal two-square cipher, in which letters in the same row are shifted one letter to the left and swapped.
Also, like the German "DoKa" cipher, there is double encryption: each bigram is encrypted in two-square, and the resulting bigram is encrypted in two-square again to produce the final CT. The original twist in the method I propose here is that *the bottom square is rotated 90 degrees clockwise* in between the first and second two-square encryptions of each bigram.
Another feature of the method that I propose is that in the usual case where the two letters are not in the same column, each letter encrypts *vertically* to the letter in its own *column* in the row of the other letter.
Thus in each step, the encrypted letter is found in the opposite square from the original letter. But in the second two-square encryption step of each bigram, one locates the "middle step bigram" letters back in their opposite squares again to perform the second encryption. Example: If A(top sq)B(bottom sq) encrypts to Y(bottom sq)Z(top sq), then after rotating the bottom square 90 degrees clockwise, one finds Y in the *top square* and Z in the *bottom square*, and then performs the second two-square encryption step on them.

My most important discovery, I believe, is a simple but I believe novel idea for how to use the K1-K3 ciphertext to fill out the two-square grids. It is actually very simple: For the top square, fill the Polybius square with letters *in the order in which they first appear in the K1-K2 ciphertext*. This produces the following Polybius square:

E M U F P
H Z L R A
X Y S D I/J
K N G V Q
T B W C O

For the bottom square, fill the Polybius square with letters *in the order in which they first appear in the K3 ciphertext* -- but ignore EN at the start and begin with DYAHR. If one wishes, one may relate this idea to "a tiny breach in the upper left hand corner." Of course it is well known that DYAHR is set apart from the neighboring letters with extra spacing, and it is natural for it to be the top row of a Polybius square. Several quotes from Mr. Sanborn are important hints on how K4 is encoded:

1) A Washington Post article on 14 January 1990 quoted Mr. Sanborn, "The secret phrase will be cut into the plate.  Anyone who knows a coding system called the Vigenère Tableau, invented in 1586 by French diplomat Blaise de Vigenère will be able to decipher one-half of the phrase.  The other half will be encoded in a modern system created for the project by an expert cryptographer”.

2) It’s hiding in plain sight.

3) It’s as simple as “abc”.

4) The techniques of the first three parts, which some people have broken, (used) frequency counting and other techniques that are similar to that. You can get insight into the sculpture through that technique because the English language is still visible through the code. (But with) this other technique (in the fourth part), I disguise that. So ... you need to solve the technique first and then go for the puzzle."

5) Wired: “Are all four of the processes known processes? There aren't any that aren't known, right?”
Sheidt: “The masking technique may not be known."

So what is this novel “modern system”, “technique”, “process”.  I submit it is indeed hiding in “plain sight” on the half of the sculpture that displays the Vigenère Tableau.  There is an Extended Tableau which could be described as an unknown technique.  Use the standard “abc” alphabet at the top edge of the Extended Tableau to represent the plain text (PT).  The repeated kryptos alphabet matrix contains the cipher text (CT).  The standard alphabet running down the left side of the tableau contains the keyword letters.  The Extended Tableau may be used in an analogous technique to the encoding and decoding technique as the Vigenère Tableau.

I submit the encoding method for K4 could use two keywords with a different tableau for each keyword.

When you stack the quotes like that, it does raise a possibility that there's no key at all (i..e, encryption) but "merely" some masking technique, i.e., that the technique IS the key.

I believe that may be consistent with everything Ed/Jim has said over the years.

Ed did talk about a scenario in which we have a sleeper agent, and after several years we need to contact him;  we don't want him to have to remember a password/key after several years, but he might be able to remember a "technique" for how to take a scrambled message and decode it using "information on  a billboard" (or maybe the scrambled message itself is text somewhere on the billboard).

Ed always used the word "mask" as a verb (e.g., "I masked the English statistics") or adjective (masking technique).  When he used the phrase "masking technique" he never coupled it with a separate "encryption technique".  He never used the phrase "masking step" to describe K4 (WE asked him if the masking was done before or after the encryption, and he ducked with a "that's an interesting question" response;  if there isn't a separate "step" that would be an appropriate answer).

The contract for the Kryptos statue was let in 1988, and it was dedicated 2 years later.  So what simple, but modern crypto techniques existed in 1988?  Something relatively simple to implement by hand.  Perhaps something based on RC4, although that was proprietary/licensed at the time.    Perhaps something based on a Feistel structure (as used in DES).  If all I want is "scrambling" or "masking" we don't need a key;  we just need  a technique that scrambles the text.  Maybe the first couple of letters is used to seed some algorithm which then proceeds to unmask the remainder of the message.

Prior to the DES/RC4 era, shift registers were often used.  Instead of a binary shaft register, possibly a 4 or 5 or ... 7 or 8  or whatever length word is used, shifted one character to the left at each step, with prior masked characters fed into the vacated rightmost position.  That could generate a running key used to "encrypt" the message.  I'll  have to go google shift register cryptology.  But I do seem to remember various "privacy" systems that were sold commercially in the 1970-1980 timefrarme that masked text or voice and did not use a key.

You may be right that different tableaus are used (e.g., one with the normal ABC alphabet and one with the KRYPTOS alphabet);  others have suggested two tableau being used in an alternating or otherwise repeating fashion.  Or something making use of the 105 letters on the right side (I was playing with some ways of mapping text to digraphs containing one consonant and one vowel;  there are 105 such digraphs 21 x 5).

So.Many.Possibilities.

Doug

s: Cryptanalysis: a study of ciphers and their solution, Helen Fouche Gaines (1939)
t:
I tend to go on about this author obliquely, so I figured I should get this out of my system and give her actual book a well-deserved mention. I’m not endorsing this for any special Kryptos related reason, merely as excellent extra-curricular reading.

Gaines was a member of the American Cryptogram Association who is responsible for creating the first “elementary” book on codes and ciphers referenced above and her work is apparently respected enough to have gotten her book a place in the public NSA archives.

To be honest, this book is probably below the expertise level of any more or most experienced cryptographers of the Kryptos forum, but is an excellent read for any novices or amateurs. Particular selling points:
1.    Educates on  the difference between code and cipher
2.    Makes the  idea of stacking one cipher on top of another more comprehensible
3.    Provides actual education on the third form of cipher (Concealment)  that gets very little mention in the substitution vs transposition debates.
4.    Numerous examples and working study.
5.    Special bonus  - references an uncredited unsolved cipher on page 217 that has some strange similarities to K1 in general and K4 in specific. That’s not to suggest any sort of certain relationship. At this point, I consider WW NU Q a funny coincidence at best.

Given the age of the material, you should find it easily available through libraries, online booksellers or pdfs. Enjoy!

s: Stranger coincidences, Kryptos and the Gaines Cipher
t:
The latter refers to the unsolved and uncredited cipher in the Gaines cryptanalysis handbook.  I first noted a sequence "WWNUQ" as being a funny coincidence, but my brain wasn't able to let the odd little similarities go and I wondered if it was possible to build an index of coincidence. Strangely, the whole thing matches up heavily with chunks of K2 - if deliberate, that's on Jim's part since Gaines has long since passed on. My index involved matching bigrams/trigrams from (mostly K2) with the Gaines Cipher and while the bigrams are easier to dismiss, the correlation between the trigrams and the misspelled text & Vigenere attack sequences (CT repetitions) was really odd, like pointers or signals.

Result:

K1/K2 CT    EMU x 2        trigram on first and reversed on last lines of K1/K2
K2 CT    IYC        ??
K2 CT    GGW        signals misspelling 2            and vigenere        last letter in sequence of three, line two
K1 CT    VJY(QT)        signals first misspelling            and vigenere
K2 CT    GKF        signals vigenere attack
K2 CT    DQ x4        signals vigenere attack
K2 CT    QC x 2        signals misspelling 2             and vigenere
K2 CT    UF x 4        ??
K4 CT    VQ        sets off the QQPRNGKSS sequence

Unsolved Cipher Bigrams
DO, GW, QL, GG, VQ, PV, NU, NI, XR

The bigrams are odd as well - each correlates to the misspellings and cryptanalytic attacks in K1 and K2, as well as special mention for the "Ds & Os" from the handwritten notes. XR is the only one that doesn't seem to have an immediate explanation.

Thoughts: It may be some kind of specialized cipher based on the Gaines handbook, or perhaps Sanborn did something weird like cobbling chunks together into a single code.

s: Stranger coincidences, Kryptos and the Gaines Cipher
t:
I’ve gone on at length about the T IS HROHNL/Hero and Leander discovery in the plaintext acrostic cipher, as well as the geometric shapes and reversals relating to Tut’s Tomb. So finding items that directly relate to them in Gaines  Cryptanalyst Handbook has officially piqued my interest -

Overview: At the time Gaines wrote this book in 1939, it was intended to be a sort of elementary primer on the subject as there were none currently.  She had the advantage of working directly with the American Cryptogram Association as a member. One of the features of their membership appears to be that, like the internet of today, they all had their own pseudonyms. Gaines was known as PICCOLA. Many of these cryptographers submitted puzzles to the book, and are credited under their pseudonyms.
When I saw  cross-over between the Unsolved Gaines Cipher and K4, I did some more digging to see if there were other strange coincidences. Page 97 and 217 had immediate results.

Page 97 provides a cipher by LEE ANDER, and the result decrypts to “Devout kaik-beclad hadji”.

The HROHNL story is set in Turkish pre-Istanbul, and the “kaik” hadji apparently refers to the headdress worn by Turkish Muslims on pilgrimage – that headdress is passing similar to the headdress of Tut, and “kaik” appears to refer to the unique rims on old Turkish boats by that name, a shape also resembling the arc’ed lines.

Page 217 is a cipher by CACHE, and the result refers to a real or imaginary plot where a man was found drowned with this code in his pocket.  The cross-over again, this time reversed.
“Cache” was a question posed by Carter while still determining the nature of Tut’s tomb…. Was it actually a tomb or simply a royal cache? It’s a cheap and easy free-association, while the other part is better.

Drowning, of course, is how Leander dies in the HROHNL story.
The path my thoughts are taking on this is that these are Markers like the Morse Stones – designed to draw direct links to this book, though it’s unclear whether it’s the book itself or the Unsolved Cipher that is the answer to K4.

But it seems to emphasize the importance of that geometric shape.
ABSCISSA + 0362514 keys – a flat line intersecting with a northeast bound diagonal line (Cartesian coordinates).
King Tut’s mask – rimmed by abscissa-diagonal lines
Parting of Hero and Leander – a painting featuring this abscissa/diagonal
Kaik boat rims – rimmed by a single abscissa-diagonal line

The presence of reversals suggests that there might be paired shapes.

Conclusion: Some sort of Turning Grille in the former of that abscissa-diagonal?

While looking at the clues "northeast" at spaces 26 to 34 and "berlinclock" at NYPVTTMZFPK, I began thinking about the possibility of the transposition being a Route Cipher, with the the double letters serving to guide movements about K4. However, I realized that many of the overlays of the letters on K4 don't show the actual structure with how the letters were cut into the structure. Is there picture with a legible view of the structure and the proper character cut outs that I could view?

My thinking is that there are 2 (X)'s and they have the same number of letters as the "northeast" clue. ("XOURKDKZX" on K4 has the same number of letters as "northeast") It's possible that the X's serve as distinct points, rather than breaks between words. Just a hunch, that's all.

Also, I believe the puzzle could possibly be broken down into 2 Routes (a forward Route and a backwards Route from the end). However, this 2 Route idea is based upon erroneous overlays of letters onto the structure.

I feel that the extra E's in the Morse code could play a role in the vectors. So far, I have this idea:

The E count is 2,1,6,3,2,2,5,3,1,1. I broke the count into 2 parts, separated by the common 2. In other words, (2)1,6,3,2 & (2)5,3,1,1

Next, I stacked them:

(2)1,6,3,2
(2)5,3,1,1

I arbitrarily decided that you can move to any touching adjacent number. In other words, you could go from 1 to 5, or 6, or 3. But, you can't go from 1 to 1, or 1 to 2. The (2)'s don't count; they just break up the path assignments.

Also, the shifted ETRANSEWJ resulting in ODBKXCOGT give clues as to a start position OBK (the beginning of K4). I'm also looking at some relevance between the X as a break, and a relationship to the E count. For example:

ODBKXCOGT as ODBK  X  COGT

(2) 1,6,3,2 [&] ODBK [or] COGT
(2) 5,3,1,1 [&] COGT [or] ODBK

And, also:
(D)OBK - (OBK are 3 letters found together)
(C)XOG - (XOG are 3 letters found together)
(D)(C) - (DC are found together as CD when read left to right. However, if the Route starts at the bottom from the presumed end of K4 then DC would be CD as you travel along the Route from right to left.

So far, that's where I'm at with regards to the transposition aspect. Obviously, there would be a substitution (if my idea that "XOURKDKZX" = "northeast"). If a key is required, I have also given thought to the "OURKDKZ" from between the X's.

I'm just in the process of reanalyzing my approach with a fresh perspective, based upon hints that I feel still may be relevant.

If anyone could point me in the direction of a good source on Route ciphers, that would be appreciated.

Thanks,

Eben

Okay, while looking into this further, I may be confusing Route cipher with the Rail-Fence. However, the Rail Fence cipher is normally diagonal in nature.

Is there a type of cipher that uses a path (like the Rail Fence), EXCEPT, it follows a vertical and horizontal path? Obviously, it would require a substitution step afterwards, as I'll only get gibberish for output. And, I'm trying to look at this using the clues with the idea that I could figure out the path if I didn't have the clues JS already gave (based upon clues found in the solution to the Morse Code, etc).

Or, does it not work that way? I'm just trying different things. So, if it's not really a method, then please stop me before i waste anymore time on this!! :-) lol

Thanks,

Eben

Scheidt also founded a company, Tecsec, which had a patent, 5369702. A quote from that is ...

"Multi-level security is achieved because encrypted objects may be nested within other objects which are also encrypted, possibly within other objects, resulting in multiple layers of encryption."

This fits in thematically with the "layers" and "onion" concepts Sanborn and Scheidt have talked about, and also the "more than one stage" quote of Scheidt from 2015 about K4.

IP lawyers might be interested in reading about the long-running case around "multi-level encryption" by Scott Graham from June 2019. In the end Adobe didn't have to pay any damages.

Hi Drew, thanks for the update. Some of the still frames of the YouTube video do indeed show the stenography on the tabletop Kryptos model, but the WIRED 2014 has the best angle for K4 stenographic hint to date (reverse side). The K4 approach is concealed within K1-K3 through stenographic means and analog key recovery on both the tableau and cipher panels. Prior to the 2020 NORTHEAST clue, a two layer cipher could be employed, but the new hint will require three layers to be decrypted. The first and third decryption layers are substitutions concealed in K1 and K4, and the second layer is a transposition route or algorithm to assemble the K4 public key. Kryptos can be completely solved by pencil and paper, but correctly identifying the route in 97! possibilities (previously 26 x 97!) through Sanborn's hints has been a struggle.

s: Kryptos, Gaines, and funny little coincidences
t:
I know  some group members already knew about it. I was already using the handbook to enhance my own understanding of Cryptanalysis, and didn’t realize that was there I stumbled across …. Klaus’s? blog I think, where it had already been noted for similarities to Kryptos. Note that this cipher isn’t “new” in any sense of the word – it was found and presented by Gaines in 1939 among many other contributions to the book. She died in 1940. I don’t know how much diversity there is in puzzle-solving in the group – it’s focused on Kryptos, and the other big one of interest with the million dollar chest was already solved/ended.

The ciphers in the book are submissions by members of the AGA at that time – there was collaborative work and the cipher was submitted without credit or detail. It’s noted as unsolved, though it may be that this is only in context of 1939 and someone or someones like Ed  Scheidt solved it already. All other ciphers were credited to their authors and included solutions. I presume it was treated as a minor mystery on which readers were intended to try their cryptanalytic skills. Gaines, like Sanborn, is favorable to amateurs in the way of discovery.

There’s nothing particularly crafty suggested – the book was written to be a first of its kind, an elementary educational tool  in general Cryptanalysis and learning how to attack an unknown ciphers, and Gaines indicated she hadn't solved that cipher.

The manual is excellent on its own merits and runs down all three cipher types, concealment, substitution and transposition. I know columnar transposition and Vigenere are specifically discussed.

One of the downfalls of my interest in the Gaines cipher relationship to K4, is the lack of any previous link between Gaines and Kryptos, so I started going over some familiar territory by running alphabet permutations on her name. Intriguingly, I saw a pattern in K3 that matched up, and aligned her name against that text permutation with some fun results.  The permutation is INE/MRI

HMGFM FEUHEE CDMRIP
HELEN FOUCHE GAINES

H    M.1    G.2    F.3    M.4    F    E+    U    H.5    E+    E    C+    D.6    M.-1    R.7    I    P.-2

H    E.6    L.-1    E+    N.1    F    O.-2    U    C+    H.2    E    G.3    A    I.5    N.4    E+    S.7

Unfortunately, it doesn't bring over colors, so you'll notice several things.

1. H, F, U and E align perfectly.
2. Everything with a number after it has a positive/negative caesarian shift of 1.
3. Letters with a + after them are matches, but not aligned.
4. The outlier that undermines the matches is I/A

This matches earlier discoveries with caesarian shifts and anagramming but is short a letter, so I'm left to question: cloud-gazing or something more concrete? Hmmm.

s: #Kryptos - idea for encryption algorithm - Part I
t:
Hi,

I would like to share some information about *#Kryptos *that I haven`t seen anywhere yet, and I strongly believe will *lead someone to final solution* (as always):)

First one that I wanted to share is connected to the idea that Mr. Sanborn could easily *deceive us* and make decryption a bit more difficult, even without the knowledge of any advanced math or crypto algorithms by himself.

*The idea is following (in pseudo-code):*
|Input:
1) zeros_and_ones: string of 0 and 1
2) plain_text: plain text to encrypt
2) key: key
3) basic_algorithm: selected cryptography algorithm which uses key. algorithm has two methods:
3.1) basic_algorithm.encrypt(position, letter, key)
3.2) basic_algorithm.decrypt(position, letter, key)|

*The idea for new_algorithm is following:*

|new_algorithm.encrypt(zeros_and_ones, position, plain_text, key):
letter = plain_text[position]
if (zeros_and_ones[position] == 0):
return basic_algorithm.encrypt(position, letter, key)
else:
return basic_algorithm.decrypt(position, letter, key)|

*similar approach to decryption:*

|new_algorithm.decrypt(zeros_and_ones, position, encrypted_text, key):
letter = encrypted_text[position]
if (zeros_and_ones[position] == 1):
return basic_algorithm.encrypt(position, letter, key)
else:
return basic_algorithm.decrypt(position, letter, key)|

To sum up in one sentence: it says that in order to produce encrypted letter you either must encrypt it or decrypt – which approach to use is based on the zeros_and_ones string

Why did I write about this idea?
If you get the top rows from morse code:
|E DIGETAL EEE
T IS YOUR
EE VIRTUALLY E
EE SHADOW EE
LUCID EEE|

remove the debris (Es)
|DIGETAL
T IS YOUR
VIRTUALLY
SHADOW
LUCID|

correct the mistake (DIGETAL -> DIGITAL) and you have exactly 97 zeros and ones (dashes and dots in morse code).
This leads us to Part II (soon).

Greg.

There appears to be two ciphers from the pictures. One is the celestial stream headliner, and the other is the morse/braille hybrid dispersed through the rest of the car. The first clue appears to be the RR on the headrest, indicating two lengths (short/long), three tracks (top/middle/bottom), and two states (silver/green). The long bars appear to be middle only and the top and bottom are for short bars. It would be possible that "R" is represented by a silver long bar, then a green & silver short bar, followed by a green long bar. Thus, two RR's can be seen on the headrest.

A third state "missing" in addition to the silver/green (now missing/silver/green) can be found on the cipher around the Spirit of Ecstasy ornament. Unfortunately the "R" identified is nowhere to be found. The closest shape is at the 11 o'clock position of the ornament (YouTube official video 0:58), but appears to be missing the correct green/silver order despite the long-doubleshort-long shape. It may be possible that the ciphertext could decode to WRATH or KRYPTOS given the sheer length of the cipher. As for the headliner, there are large lights and smaller lights, but does not seem to match the concept art for a cipher. Perhaps it is just the Rolls-Royce production timeline with the original Wrath produced in 1938 with the three bar "Rolls-Royce cipher" overlay.

t:
There is a word hidden in the already transcribed ciphertext, formed from the differences between the mis-spellings and their replacements.

In the transcription, the mis-spelled characters are QOA and the corrections are LOE. Put the two together and you get an anagram of the word LAQUEO.

Now this word is particularly interesting, not only because it has many meanings. I've discussed some of them before but in re-iteration they are:

Laqueo (Spanish):
- Lacquer. A type of varnish applied to wood
- First person singular present indicative form of Laquear
Laquear (English): (plural laquears) (architecture) A lacunar.
Lacunar (medicine) Of or pertaining to a lacuna
Lacuna (plural lacunae or lacunas)
- A small opening; a small pit or depression; a small blank space; a gap or vacancy; a hiatus.
- An absent part, especially in a book or other piece of writing, often referring to an ancient manuscript or similar such.
- (microscopy) A space visible between cells, allowing free passage of light.
- (linguistics) A language gap, which occurs when there is no direct translation in the target language for a lexical term found in the source language.

There is one other translation that I missed from my original discovery and that is probably its most poignant.

When translated from Latin, it means "A trap"

I do not think you are wrong about the binary. It is a binary solution however I do think you're wrong about the location. Why do I think this?
I'll give you 3 binary patterns. These are the patterns which solve letters 26-34 and 64-75 (the ones I can confirm).

They are, in order:

1: MMZZZMMMMZMZZZZMZZZM
2: ZMZZZMMMZZMZZMZMZMMM
3: MZZZZZZZMZZZZMZZZMMZ

The pattern the morse produces on the other hand is: MZZZZZZZZZMZZMMMMMZM which doesn't fit. For those interested, the relevant binary for NORTHEAST BERLINCLOCK is (I think, without referring to my notes) the 2nd in the list.

I've explained how I produced the binary for the first iteration here: https://groups.io/g/KRYPTOS/topic/75267491#21510 and will explain the rest once I've proven or dis-proven the method. For the record, I have something that is missing perhaps 2 or 3 rules and a sorting method. Of the characters I can prove I'm missing 4 but have no complete way (yet) to sort them into their correct ciphers. The answer, as far as I can see, is based on binary.

Don't fall into traps. Cryptography is all about mis-direction, getting you to look in the wrong place for information. You have all you need right in front of you.

BTW, I could be completely wrong. Take nothing for granted.

s: Regarding vertical letter pairs in K4 matching the "ALWH" alphabet
t:
I happened to read an old thread and I felt I just want to throw something in.

This is in reply to Bill Briere's posts #18646 and #18645 in 2017 in thread 'Yet another K3 "solution": A Fixed Grille', which also contains talk about the so-called ALWH alphabet, and that is the topic here. The posts are quoted below for reference.

I guess I should relate this to some original thread by Ed H., but it did not turn up in a simple search for "ALWH".
I'm writing a new subject line in this reply post, although unclear whether this increases or decreases confusion.

The throw-something-in reply is:

In the quoted posts it is remarked that in width 21, these alphabetic vertical letter pairs occur in forward direction between rows 1 and 2 and likewise rows 3 and 4, while backwards between in rows 2 and 3, and likewise between rows 4 and 5 if a shift is introduced. (If not, then there is one three-letter forward hit across rows 3 and 4 and 5.)

Want I want to add here, most likely repeating an age-old thought, is that this would be consistent with an alternating progressing key that is 21 chars long. In rows 2 and 4, the key progresses one step in the cipher alphabet. In row 3 it is one step back (to same as row 1). In this model, the observed pairs correspond to plaintext repeats that are aligned in width 21. (When I say plaintext it could also be some intermediate ciphertext, the output of a previous step. With "pt" I simply mean the result of decrypting the ct with a key.)

Speaking against this model is that it does not seem to agree with the cribs. In order to reconcile that, you would need to apply the proposed model in some columns only, and something else in other columns.

I also would like to comment on the alphabet. I think (correct me if I am wrong) the normal way to scramble an alphabet with keyed columnar transposition is to write the plain alphabet in rows of a specified width = the length of the key, then read out the columns in keyed order to get the mixed alphabet. The transformation to the ALWH alphabet does the exact inverse of this. It has also been pointed out, correctly, that the result isn't exactly the same as a modular transposition: step 11 (mod 26). But it is piece-wise step-11; a mathematical consequence of the length of the alphabet and the properties of the word KRYPTOS=0362514, which when rearranged in plain-alphabetic order is exactly a step -2 (mod 7).

Hi, my name's Scott Pearson.  Not really much of a crypto person, but I have a bit of a fondness for trying to solve  clues.  Former correctional officer and application dev/server admin.  Trying to be semi-retired.

I am curious about a potential relationship between the second passage and two of the clues given by Sanborn, "Berlin" and "clock".  I did a quick but not thorough search of the group messages and didn't find anything related.

Passage 2 states, in part, "ONLY WW THIS WAS HIS LAST MESSAGE"

If WW refers to William Webster, former director of the CIA, then his last message would be his resignation letter, would it not? Curiously, William Webster retired the same year as the Berlin Wall was physically destroyed (taken down and its pieces distributed).  Also, there is the Berlin Peace Clock, which was unveiled in Berlin the same evening as the Berlin Wall was opened November 9, 1989.  The inscription on the Berlin Peace Clock reads as follows, "Time bursts all walls asunder".

(Mod.  There are several copies of this in the Files section.  Search in Files for "peace clock" to access them.)

So we have a perhaps spurious connection between William Webster, Berlin, and clock, but I wonder if it might not lead to finding a key for passage 4?

Thoughts?

Scott

Martin, I'm still not sure exactly what you did in each step - I think your explanation is still incomplete - but what it comes down to is odd number  -> ... -> 13, even number -> ... -> 26.

I will number the lines C1, C2, ..., C24 (last one). I will stick to mathematical (mod 26) so 26=0 and 26-x=0-x=-x.

C1 = original cipher
C2 = -2*C1
C3 = -C2 = 2*C1
C4 = C2 - C1 = -3*C1
C5 = -C4 = 3*C1
C6 = C1 - C4 = C1 + C5 = 4*C1
C7 = -C6 = -4*C1
etc (a pattern is emerging, although the sign just changed here)...
...
C24 = 13*C1

Now, y = 13*x (mod 26) has the property y=0 if x even, and y=13 if x odd.
That would be the mathematical explanation.

Sidenote: A perhaps more typical numbering of the letters is A=0 B=1 ... Z=25. Here it is instead A=1 B=2 ... Y=25 Z=26=0.

I do not see what you mean when you say there are "exactly 3 binary patterns".

I think the numbering system for the alphabet is really not important. I use 1 based because if I think about what is the 1st letter of the alphabet I think A. I never think "What is the 0th letter of the alphabet". A 0 based alphabet would invert the binary and the binary is important but I think it would be aesthetic rather than a practical.

I wouldn't get caught up in "You should be using this, not that", it serves no purpose mathematically to the model other than making it slightly harder when moving between paper calculations and programmatic calculations and vice versa.

I did explain all the steps required to get that table but what I didn't say is that this is part of a much larger algorithm that is holding a lot of ground in deciphering k4. That bit is not important to the question I asked originally.

The "3 binary patterns" eludes to this algorithm. There are others, I just didn't explain how to find them. Actually, this is not important to the cipher either. What is important is that table I posted in my first message.

I also said there are two patterns in the table, the binary which at the time I couldn't understand the relevance of, and the second pattern.

I will say this. I can prove that it is possible to find "NORTHEAST" and "BERLIN CLOCK" using nothing more than the 97 characters of ciphertext for K4.

The only reason I've not got more of the cipher is there is a complex set of rules that need to be followed and I have not found all of them yet. It's also highly volatile. Changing 1 rule even by as little as +1 has a huge impact on the cipher.

As an example, changing the rule that creates the second C in clock may move the whole cipher from '[N, O, R, T, H, E, A, S, T][B, E, R, L, I, N, C, L, O, C, K]'  to '[M, O, R, T, H, E, P, S, A][B, X, R, L, I, D, P, L, O, A, H]' or '[N, O, L, T, T, E, A, S, T][H, X, L, L, I, D, C, L, I, A, K]'.

In fact to correct the C from the A you find at first, you have to activate an inverse rule to a previous one, otherwise you end up with '[B, E, R, L, I, N, C, L, O, A, K]' which might fit in with the theme of spies but I'm yet to find a dagger here and am pretty sure isn't intentional.

To give some clarity on this, which may offer insight on why this cipher has stood the test of time, I have a method now which, based only on the 97 characters finds:

- 2 grids
- 6 alphabets

Additionally there are two sets of rules, one of which governs which character in which grid to choose,

With alternating replacements on specific characters, you then find 8 possible squares to choose from, within which you will find a character from one of 4 possible ciphers.

A second set of rules then governs which algorithm to choose to convert 4 ciphers into a single cipher
It is then a simple subtraction to reveal the plaintext.

So far from set 1 I have found 4 primary rules (I think this is a complete set) and 5 secondary rules (I think there are 16 in total)
From set 2 I have confirmed 6 primary rules and found 11 secondary rules, of which I have confirmed only 3 or 4, with there being indications towards there being potentially 16 or 20 (I can't say this for sure because I simply do not know).

If what I think I've found is correct, it's quite amazing what has been achieved here. 97 characters doesn't just hide 1 key, it hides 4. Doesn't just contain 1 or two alphabets like a normal cipher might but contains 6 and it embeds 2 binary patterns out of the 6 required. It's both insanely complex and stupidly simple.

OK, clarity again. There are actually 4 binary patterns. 3 are the ones I have mentioned above, the 4th is as simple as "position in ciphertext % 2" - this one is important as it serves as a starting point for something else.

So where I'm at now is working through the cipher from the beginning looking for the rules which are missing in both sets. Once I've found them all I'll post the method (unless someone beats me to it)

If the method holds, I may also have most of the first 26 characters of the cipher.

s: Kryptos - A method to a solution
t:
So I think I've dropped a few hints now that I have a potential solution to the K4 cipher

Please be aware this is a long post.

I want to make it clear that this is an incomplete method. I have not finished working on the rules but
can provide to the group the method and associated code that supports the method.

The method uses nothing other than the 97 characters of the K4 ciphertext.

Before I begin, a little background.

I came to K4 in 2014 shortly after the word CLOCK was revealed. Since then, I've worked on it on and
off for the intervening 6 years, taking a 2yr hiatus following a move from the UK to Spain before
returning to the cipher in March this year.

When I returned to the cipher, I was not aware immediately of a new clue, I think it took a few weeks
before I realised. After that, my pace has accellerated because I had additional information to confirm
the method with.

This method is nothing I have not previously referenced. In fact I touched upon it briefly in two
(very badly written) papers I published to this group here: https://groups.io/g/KRYPTOS/files/Personal%20Folders/Martin%20Proffitts%20Findings

The method is a continuation of these findings but please bear with me, I'm terrible at explaining.

Firstly let me explain how I came to this method.

I never liked the idea that another cipher might be part of this. I see so many references to "have you tried this
cipher" or "What about this cipher over here" and they always bothered me. They didn't hold water with me and if it
were that simple, the cipher wouldn't have held for the best part of 30 years.

What did intrigue me was the Berlin Clock. I even implemented this in code to see if there was a solution there.
There wasn't but it was a cool experiment.

The idea I liked was the concept that the key was encrypted with the cipher. This felt right and tied in to so many
things I'd come to find out about K4.

This thought process led me to start looking in the spaces between the ciphertext and the revealed plaintext. What
lies there.

I'm not going to explain all the interim steps I took, there were a lot, I deleted more code than I felt I wrote,
probably killed a few trees too.

To look at the spaces between the ciphertext and known plaintext I came up with two methods: `distancefrom` and
`distanceto`. This is Python3 code
for those interested.

distancefrom is defined as:

def distancefrom(self, x, y):
    a = self.a2i(x)
    b = self.a2i(y)

    c = ((26 - a) - b)
    return self.i2a(c % 26)

and distanceto is:

def distanceto(self, x, y):
    """
    Addition vector moving through Z

    :param: char x The starting character
    :param: char y The character to calculate the distance to

    :return char
    """
    a = self.a2i(x)
    b = self.a2i(y)
    c = (26 - a) + b
    return self.i2a(c % 26)

For those interested, a2i returns the current characters index in a list and i2a does the inverse (using a A=1 based
alphabet)

Into each of these I fed in both the known ciphertext characters and their known plaintext

these are:

QQPRNGKSS NYPVTT MZFPK
NORTHEAST BERLIN CLOCK

Now, if we run 'distanceto' over these we get:

00 QQPRNGKSSNYPVTTMZFPK NORTHEASTBERLINCLOCK WXBBTXPZANFBPOTPLIMZ
01 NORTHEASTBERLINCLOCK WXBBTXPZANFBPOTPLIMZ IIJHLSOGGLAJDFFMZTJO
02 WXBBTXPZANFBPOTPLIMZ IIJHLSOGGLAJDFFMZTJO LKHFRUYGFXUHNQLWNKWO
03 IIJHLSOGGLAJDFFMZTJO LKHFRUYGFXUHNQLWNKWO CBXXFBJZYLTXJKFJNQMZ
04 LKHFRUYGFXUHNQLWNKWO CBXXFBJZYLTXJKFJNQMZ QQPRNGKSSNYPVTTMZFPK
05 CBXXFBJZYLTXJKFJNQMZ QQPRNGKSSNYPVTTMZFPK NORTHEASTBERLINCLOCK

whereby if we run distancefrom over these we get:

00 QQPRNGKSSNYPVTTMZFPK NORTHEASTBERLINCLOCK UTRNDNNNMJVRRWRJNEGD
01 NORTHEASTBERLINCLOCK UTRNDNNNMJVRRWRJNEGD QQPRNGKSSNYPVTTMZFPK
02 UTRNDNNNMJVRRWRJNEGD QQPRNGKSSNYPVTTMZFPK NORTHEASTBERLINCLOCK
03 QQPRNGKSSNYPVTTMZFPK NORTHEASTBERLINCLOCK UTRNDNNNMJVRRWRJNEGD
04 NORTHEASTBERLINCLOCK UTRNDNNNMJVRRWRJNEGD QQPRNGKSSNYPVTTMZFPK
05 UTRNDNNNMJVRRWRJNEGD QQPRNGKSSNYPVTTMZFPK NORTHEASTBERLINCLOCK

distancefrom only gives the original cipher, the plaintext and one other cipher. This caught my interest. Why? Because
it means that there is a path from cipher C to plaintext P.

We can confirm this by looking at the inverse (UTRNDNNNMJVRRWRJNEGD to QQPRNGKSSNYPVTTMZFPK) but what about if we
switch the algorithm to `distanceto`

`distanceto('QQPRNGKSSNYPVTTMZFPK','UTRNDNNNMJVRRWRJNEGD')`

00 QQPRNGKSSNYPVTTMZFPK UTRNDNNNMJVRRWRJNEGD DCBVPGCUTVWBVCXWNYQS
01 UTRNDNNNMJVRRWRJNEGD DCBVPGCUTVWBVCXWNYQS IIJHLSOGGLAJDFFMZTJO
02 DCBVPGCUTVWBVCXWNYQS IIJHLSOGGLAJDFFMZTJO EFHLVLLLMPDHHCHPLUSV
03 IIJHLSOGGLAJDFFMZTJO EFHLVLLLMPDHHCHPLUSV VWXDJSWEFDCXDWBCLAIG
04 EFHLVLLLMPDHHCHPLUSV VWXDJSWEFDCXDWBCLAIG QQPRNGKSSNYPVTTMZFPK
05 VWXDJSWEFDCXDWBCLAIG QQPRNGKSSNYPVTTMZFPK UTRNDNNNMJVRRWRJNEGD

So this is interesting. In both the first and last runs we find IIJHLSOGGLAJDFFMZTJO

What is this?

If we run 'distanceto between the original ciphertext and this new pattern, we find another pattern RRTPXLDNNXBTHLLZZNTD
but if we run 'distancefrom' we find 'ZZZZZZZZZZZZZZZZZZZZ'. The new pattern of RRTPXLDNNXBTHLLZZNTD is the only thing
that appears when running QQPRNGKSSNYPVTTMZFPK and RRTPXLDNNXBTHLLZZNTD therefore we can probably surmise that this is M.

This is the first real hint at a pattern I've ever seen with this cipher. I see a lot of "Oh I've seen this random
thing" or "Have you tried looking here" but how many are actually looking at the cipher itself rather than the
surroundings?

The next step is to look between QQPRNGKSSNYPVTTMZFPK and IIJHLSOGGLAJDFFMZTJO. We know there is an RRTPXLDNNXBTHLLZZNTD
there, probably halfway, but what about the rest?

To do this, I wrote a new method which calculated that.

def distance_calculator(self, start, end):
    while self.cache_locked:
        sleep(0.1)

    if not self.cache['calculator']:
        self.cache_locked = True
        distances = [
            (start, self.polarity(start)),
            (end, self.polarity(end)),
        ]
        completed = []
        for pos in range(26):
            for item in combinations([d[0] for d in distances], 2):
                if item in completed:
                    continue
                c = item[0]
                s = item[1]
                for i in range(6):
                    z = ''
                    for j in range(len(c)):
                        z += self.distanceto(c[j], s[j])

                    e = self.polarity(z)
                    if (z, e) not in distances:
                        distances.append((z, e))
                        p = ' '.join([str(self.a2i(t)).zfill(2) for t in z])
                    c = s
                    s = z

                completed.append(item)
            pos += 1

        self.cache['calculator'] = distances
        self.cache_locked = False
    return self.cache['calculator']

Ignore the references to `self` this is from a class method, I'll provide the actual code for this class as part of the
wider solution later.

What this code does is run 26 iterations of the cipher using the `distanceto` method, capturing the output from each,
swapping cipher with intermediate and intermediate with result each iteration.;

This gives an expansion of the table I referenced here https://groups.io/g/KRYPTOS/message/21505

Next, split this into two tables.

The first table is all rows which contain only characters where the index is divisable by 2. That is characters
b, d, f, h, j, l, n, p, r, t, v, x, z

The second set contains all the remaining rows. This will be a mixture of odd and even characters.

Next, remove all duplicate columns from this table and sort the columns by the values of the first row numerically

This gives a 13x12 table for the even rows and a 26x13 table for the mixed rows.
Add a row of all Z's to the evens to make it 13x13. You only have even numbers, you will find nothing but Zs here.

Next we need to construct the column headers for the even table. We can infer that the header for the mixed table is now
the standard alphabet but the evens is a little more tricky.

With the mixed table, If you removed the duplicate columns programatically, you'd have ended up with a 26x12 table which
still contained duplicate columns. That's because the header doesn't change. What you see here is an alphabet running:

FSLYERKX...

Each of these characters is a pair (FS), (LY), (ER)... Each pair is 13 characters apart. Each pair of pairs is 6
characters apart (e.g. F to L = 6)

We have the first alphabet.

I found the rest by trial and error but they are, for the evens table, [14, 6, 6, 12]. This order is important. If you
break it, the tables work but you will not find the same results.

The mixed table runs the standard alphabet across the top and the reverse alphabet across the bottom. The sides, I
believe, are the same.

Now if you try and plot a grid on this, you're quickly going to run into problems on M and Z. These map to each other
so we need replacements.

As I worked the grid, I realised that K and V also poised challenges but K appears twice and in one instance, it didn't.

How did I discover this?

What I realised is that one or more of the cells maps to the "intermediate" ciphers of

UTRNDNNNMJVRRWRJNEGD DCBVPGCUTVWBVCXWNYQS
EFHLVLLLMPDHHCHPLUSV VWXDJSWEFDCXDWBCLAIG

I also worked out that UTRN... and EFHL... are synonymous with each other through Z. So are D and V.

Now, we have 6 ciphers total of which 4 are relevant and we need only the first.

Now for the next challenge, and this is where the rules come in.

Plotting a grid on both of the tables will provide either 1 or two characters which will be from 1 or two of the ciphers

As I think I've explained previously, I call the Z mapping the 'lacuna'.

Where two characters are shown, it's either from a single cipher and its associated lacuna, OR from both ciphers OR
from both lacunas. I've not seen any instance where you get one cipher and a different lacuna (E.g you never seem to
get UTRND... and VWXD... paired together on the tables)

You may also find a character from the original cipher QQPRNG... or its counterpart IIJHLS... Here, you may find
the same letter repeated across the tables (two ciphers or two lacunas) or you may find one cipher and one lacuna.

Now we get to the rules.

The rules for choosing the right square are complex. Not only that, you have to sort that square into the right cipher
and from there you need to choose the right algorithm to decipher it.

I must make it clear, I have not finished this work but this ties directly to Mengenlerhuer and to my mind, it's
genius.

Each character starts off in a False position and alternates polarity. Therefore, if you have 4 Q's in the cipher, each
one will be False, True, False, True.

You have two tables in the cipher. I labelled these False and True in the code with Evens being True (made sense, Even
is positive in boolean). The table is selected by first modulating the index on 2, then adding rules to determine if it
is still True. Think of this like a light turning on on the Berlin Clock - it's either on, or its off.

There are other rules too, all of which are governed by using a combination of the appearance of the Cipher character,
or the Lacuna character, or both along with a number of binary choices:

- Is the index of the character in the overall cipher a 1 or a 0 when mod 2 (Think of the seconds light on the Berlin Clock)
- Is the character odd or even numbered
- Has this character been seen before? If so, what is its current polarity?

I think there are also rules based on:

- index % 5 (Every 5 minutes/5 hours the row on the Berlin clock changes)
- index % 15 (Every 15 minutes, the second row is red)

I'm not 100% sure on these last two but they hold water for now and there may be others (30 minutes, 60 minutes? but I
think not)

I have used this method to successfully decipher both NORTHEAST and BERLINCLOCK and you can find an associated Python3
notebook uploaded at https://groups.io/g/KRYPTOS/files/Personal%20Folders/Martin%20Proffitts%20Findings/k4.ipynb
This is a Jupyter notebook for Python 3.7.5 or later and you'll need iPython, Jupyter, Pandas, ipyevents and widgetsnbextension
installed to run it successfully. If you don't know what I'm talking about, this may not be a solution for you at this time. You
*can* do this with paper and pencil but it is very, very hard.

The notebook, when executed runs a "navigable" table at the bottom which displays both tables, the parameters
for the current character, all positions reachable from the current auto-selected cell and the positions reachable from
all other intersections (this is a recent addition to help me work out the rules). You use the cursor keys to navigate
it. BTW, up and down are buggy as hell. wrote this in about 2 seconds and never bothered to look at it properly. I'll
reply to this with a Github link later. That version might have the issue resolved.

It's not perfect, it's very much a work in progress. I'll put a version on GitHub tomorrow for anyone who wants to
contribute back. I tend to be proud of my code but not of my PoC and this is very much a PoC.
