Hi. I think it's high time I introduce myself as we are supposed to. My name is Anders Hallström, I'm Swedish, and I work as a software engineer in the field of robotics.

I heard about Kryptos a number of years ago, before the BERLIN clue appeared. Of course I unsuccessfully tried to solve it, and since then I have been following the development "from a distance" you could say. I joined this group only a few months ago, mostly reading and trying to get up to speed but I also dared to make a few posts. I was hoping to be able to present myself with a sidenote "By the way, I solved it". No, it didn't happen. So here I am.

What I am missing the most here is a sort of FAQ summarizing what solution techniques for K4 have been tried and (more or less) dismissed. I realize this is a major work to put together, as one would have to keep it brief and to the point without stepping too much on people's toes, without misquoting people etc. Yet one would need to specify some operating conditions too. For example, it is often said that we have run this and that large dictionary search for K4 keywords. Against which alphabet(s)? What were the plaintext criteria that would make the search algorithm report a hit? Since it has been stated that K4 was designed to defeat computerized attacks, I am reluctant to accept computer searches as conclusive evidence that some method was not used in K4. That was a sidenote to illustrate the need for stating operating conditions.

Another thing I am missing, equally hard to put together, is a concentrate of the various quotes by Jim Sanborn and Ed Scheidt. Of interest is the literal quotes as well as how those were interpreted by the experienced group members that have met the creators and discussed the issues with them. To the extent there is any reasonable consensus on that.

Yes, we may all search the database and read for ourselves. Only that's doing research and that's also hard work. When several people are doing this research independently, it is duplication of research work. (True, sometimes this is a good thing as it adds plurality.) If these resources could contribute to stopping some newbies from diving into old rabbit-holes and reporting old findings again and again, it could perhaps be worth spending some work on.

Finally, I would very much like to take the opportunity to throw some paraphrase-poetry at you.

t:
So as I try and untangle the "mess" that are the rules governing this attempt at a solution, I am poised with a question.

Is there more than one message hidden in the 97 characters?

The reason I ask this is many characters in the cipher carry more than one copy of the letters you try to hit. As an example, the N of northeast can be hit from:

a) Table 1, bottom left, algorithm 4
b) Table 2, top left, algorithm 2

This places ambiguity onto the cipher offering multiple ways to actually find what you're looking for, but gives rise by doing so to other sentences to appear.

This is where I find it a little confusing and highly ambiguous.

The first few words could read "OH GOSH WW", or they could read "WHEN HE" or they could read "ALL IS", or my favourite nightmare right now being "OH GOSH I WENT DO TRY ????? HUONG Q NORTHEAST" Which sounds like total garbage until you discover there is a Vietnamese restaurant called Huong Que  on Wiener Straße which happens to be 26 minutes drive west south west of Kurfürstendamm, the original location of the Berlin Clock.

OK so I'm not suggesting that this is a message about a Vietnamese restaurant in any way at all but in all honesty, has there ever been any indication that this is only a single message that is exactly 97 characters long? Or is it maybe multiple messages, or a single message that spans a multiplication of 97?

s: 2009 Interview, 96x9 Flattened PT Grid and NORTHEAST
t:
Based on a conceptual thread I was following, I tried flattening out the entire PT of Kryptos into a 96 Rows by 9 Columns Grid, and unexpectedly got a flattened rectangle for the entire thing. That was a neat twist, though not as fun as coupling it with Elonka’s release yesterday.

Before getting into that, immediate analysis  results:
NORTHEAST scores its own entire row. Not that meaningful by itself, but K2 aligns the word NORTH with it perfectly. There’s also some interesting apparently 2-cell shift going on with not only the misspellings in K1, but PT NYOUS (NYPVT)  in K3 and NYPVT in K4. Notably, that’s also the HELEN FOUCHE GAINES area and the NYPVT corresponds to CT MEHNLE (oddly similar to Mengenlehreuhr.

It’s looking at this point like it might be worthwhile to take a page from Jim’s handwwritten notes and compare the PT against the CT.

Then there’s this, from the 2009 interview from Elonka:

“So I made up two sets: one where I divided into threes, and one where I divided it into two sets.”
~~ 96 divides neatly by 2, 3 and 9.

“"How am I going to do this so that they can read and understand that I haven't written something that's subversive to the point it's going to be removed? Yet, they'll be able to understand—so they'll understand enough, but they won't remember it."
~~ This would suggest either a message with typical code talk double-speak or perhaps a mix of CT and PT that would be overwhelming enough not to retain thanks to a 1600+ character count. Bigrams or Trigrams possibly, but that's pretty recognizable, and hard to read when you've got a couple folks who are supposed to make sure your text isn't subversive.

It's not complete, I'm sure, and details are best left to a reading of the interview.

1.    In high school, JS was unable to do mathematics and accepted tutoring to improve his grades, but does have skill in geometry. Noted for past comments about being an “anathemath”, pun on words suggesting bad at math.
2.    Further education focused on medieval art history and archaeology.
3.    Extensive travel, specifying English cathedrals and Germany in pursuit of Romanesque art. Also notes Egypt and Greece.
4.    Was writing a book (2009) about Kryptos.

8.    Actually got to see and interact with all the items Howard Carter found before they moved to other museums.
9.    Can utilize shadows in such a way that they are indisginguishable from a painting on a wall.
10.    JS worked on the CT for roughly 9 months while the company built the tableau.
11.    When establishing his relationship with Ed Scheidt, which oddly appears to have only been 2 or 3 meetings, according to JS, Ed gave him a “primer on ancient encoding systems” and gave him systems that didn’t necessarily require math, and could be altered.
12.    Ed told him about “matrix codes(?)” – indicating these were the parts (K-K3) already cracked. K4 is a coding system that can be modified in a myriad ways so even Ed can’t understand them.
13.    An account of the “Crying Figure” meeting at Dept of Historical Intel, aka 3 people, one with a photographic memory, who was removed for that. Excellent details on this.
14.    An account of the politics surrounding Kryptos.
15.    Mention of daily neutron x-rays when entering and leaving.
16.    The missing truck story.
17.    Stolen pulp story
18.    Elonka Dunin meeting story.

21.    Kryptos was WW’s hardest to keep secret.
22.    The pool under Kryptos is supposed to spin wildly.
23.    Kryptos was an inspiration for the Atomic Time project.

Actual story,  paraphrased from the 2009 Oral History.

JS had it specified in his contract that the CIA had to know what the message said, and in order to fulfill this, they asked him to give it to the Department of Historical Intelligence. To my understanding, that’s the CIA equivalent of their library on site, hence a small staff of three in a small room.
JS wanted to do this in a way that they could read it, understand that it wasn’t subversive or anything bad, but not be able to remember it later. To do this, he took what he refers to as the English Text ( presume he means plaintext, but is explaining this to a non-Kryptos fan) – He took that script, cut it into strips by sentence. After rearranging them, he glued them to pieces of paper. Because he was anticipating possibly having to remove someone, he made two sets pieces of paper – one set to be divided among three people, the other set to be divided among two. If more than one had phographic memory, he was out of luck.

It probably shouldn’t be surprising that the CIA recruited had a librarian with photographic memory.
He started by lying and telling them he needed them to remember of it, asking if any of them had photographic memory. That person was identified and removed, with an apology. The remaining two people were described as the director and his female assistant or analyst.
He gave the remaining two the correct set and let them review .

Let us keep in mind at this point that CIA is all about its security, classified status, and Jim seems (through reading) kind of naïve and is playing games. Whatever was in that script was something serious enough that this analyst or whatever recognized how serious the responsibility she was given from it, and had serious issues with it. Describes shaking, and leaving the room in tears.
Now, that’s an odd reaction, but it sounds like a panic attack and panic attacks and humiliation aren’t that uncommon.

The DHI told him they could not accept responsibility for it.  No surprise, due to Jim playing games. Figure out something else.

William Webster took care of it.

 I will note that this isn’t the only example of Jim showing poor judgment in this interview based on his take on CIA politics and gamesmanship. The story makes sense if you factor in an unreliable narrator with very human foibles.

Another source of the Department of Historical Intelligence is from the September 23, 2005 Hirshorn Museum talk:

"While I did the code, I made my presentation. I put my model out there. Everybody really liked the idea and really liked the model, and was really concerned about what it was going to say — the agency people. And so I was sorta rouged to do that. I was rouged to say, “Okay, this is what it says.” You know, hey, no problem, because what is a mysterious sculpture when there’s no mystery left? And so, basically, what I did was the CIA decided, okay, what we will do is we will have the secret of the Kryptos Sculpture entrusted by the Department of Historical Intelligence. Now this Department of Historical Intelligence back in 1989 when I was dealing with this was a very small room with no windows and three people inside it. So what I did, basically, was I knew that there were three people in there. There were three people I had to give the code to, so  basically, I divided the coded section. I cut it up into strips, and I reassembled them into three pages. And I can give one page to each of these people, but when each of these people read it, they wouldn’t get the whole picture because they only got a certain section of it that was pieced together. But they would get the gist that I hadn’t done something say, pornographic, or, you know, something that was— would reflect very badly on the agency. They’d get the gist.

So I walked into the room, and the first question I asked of these three people, I said, “Listen, I really want to entrust this secret to whoever can keep a secret really well.” And two of the people pointed to one of the other people, and they said, “She’s got an institutional memory. She remembers every single thing she reads.” Right? So basically I said, “Okay, would you please leave.” So, because I didn’t want anybody to remember what they read. So I also put it into two pages just in case one of these people was the Savant and was gonna figure out the code from what I gave them, so basically I gave two pieces— I gave pieces of paper to each of the two people remaining in the room, and they started reading it. And one of the individuals became very agitated and became basically hysterical, and could not handle it and had to leave the room. And the bottom line was that these two people realized that what if I tricked them? What if they read this code and then forever or whatever a century that sculpture sits in the middle of the agency insulting the agency, their jobs would be at stake, and it was too much pressure for them. So they denied— they refused to keep the code."

s: Kryptos - A method to a solution
t:
A few days ago I made a submission on Kryptos that seemed viable.

It was wrong. Wrong but viable. It met all the hallmarks of being valid,
e.g. had NORTHEAST and BERLINCLOCK in the correct locations, it was
readable although the language was a little choppy and more importantly, it
could be read to carry meaning.

I wasn't sure about the message not because of the text but the rules used
to create it were more complex than I anticipated but I submitted it anyway
because, well you never know until you try.

The message I came up with drew a fairly neat rectangle over Berlin that
placed both Berlin train station and Checkpoint Charlie within the geometry
composed of:

Northwest: Mengenlehruer
Southeast: Huong Que Vietnamese restaurant of which there are two, one on
Berhgmanstrasse and another on Weiner strasse.
Northeast: Eisenbrucke
Southwest: La Belle nightclub, the 1986 bombing of which killed two
American soldiers and led to Reagan ordering air raids on Tripoli.

I still think there is validity in the method I used for this message
however the method relies on a set of rules and the rules I wrote were
wrong.

Where does that leave me? We've now reached summer, I've shut my server
down to protect it from the heat, I've some intense work commitments
heading up for a few weeks, after which I'm sure the cipher will still be
here, sleeping, waiting, more annoying than my 3 month old kitten at
bedtime or my dog when she wants to swim in the sea and isn't allowed on
the beach. I also need time to reflect. The last few weeks have been a
burden of discovery and I'm tired.

There's another pattern hidden on that sculpture somewhere. That pattern
tells us how the rules should be written.

Lastly, in Jims reply to me he specifically used the phrase "shot -in -the-
dark". This got me thinking. Firstly, the phrase is not hyphenated.
Secondly, if you're using hyphens you do not need spaces. Finally, terms
related to darkness and light come up a lot in this cipher.

“Still, Sanborn is keen to point out that those not gifted with mathematical skills are as much capable of cracking the code as those with advanced numerical minds. I'm what I call an anathemath," he said. "As an artist you can come up with myriad coding systems." ~ Jim Sanborn, 2010 CNN interview

The first sentence speaks for itself, even with a made up word like anathemath, but there’s a clear punster's element there – anathema-math. A subject (math) someone violently dislikes. That said, there are simpler classic coding systems for someone in that field, which still leaves things very open.

The 2010 interview is really old news, but the 2009 interview sheds a LOT of light with some key points:

1.    Jim was a failure at math in high school and required constant tutoring.
2.    The Kryptos CT was developed over a period of only nine months.
3.    Jim had a project manager, but that person was not Ed Scheidt.
4.    Jim only met with Ed two or three times.
5.    Jim describes the codes used in K1 – K3 as “matrix codes,”  already cracked. K4 is not.
6.    Jim received an unspecified “primer of ancient encoding systems”
7.    Jim devised the plaintext on a car trip, and Ed’s role comes in later.
8.    Ed gave him ideas for contemporary systems that did necessarily depend on mathematics as a pre-requisite. That’s not to say they’re excluded, of course…

There’s only so much one person can teach another person, master cryptographer or not, in a couple sessions, especially when someone is as mathematically challenged as Jim indicates. My take away from all of this is that K4 is probably far simpler than people make it out to be and elaborate mathematical theories are likely flying high over a bar that is much lower.

s: Delve into John Conway’s GAME OF LIFE/ Glider Gun to solve K4.
t:
Hi Group,

I believe that the Berlin clock which we should be delving into is Alexanderplatz World Clock or the turret clock. It has a back story about the British mathematician John Horton Conway who devised GAME OF LIFE, a cellular automaton. Gosper’s slider gun by Ralph William Gosper Jr. is an American Mathematician.
He became intensely interested in the Game of Life shortly after John Horton Conway had proposed it. Conway conjectured the existence of infinitely growing patterns, and offered a reward for an example. Gosper was the first to find such a pattern, the glider gun, and won the prize of $50. Gosper was also the originator of the Hashlife algorithm that can speed up the computation of Life patterns by many orders of magnitude.

The Conway base 13 function is a function created by British mathematician John H. Conway as a counterexample to the converse of the intermediate value theorem. In other words, it is a function that satisfies a particular intermediate-value property—on any interval (a, b), the function f takes every value between f(a) and f(b)—but is not continuous.

Purpose    Edit

The Conway base 13 function was created as part of a "produce" activity: in this case, the challenge was to produce a simple-to-understand function which takes on every real value in every interval, that is, it is an everywhere surjective function[1]. It is thus discontinuous at every point.

Sketch of definition    Edit

Every real number x can be represented in base 13 in a unique canonical way; such representations use the digits 0–9 plus three additional symbols, say {A, B, C}. For example, the number 54349589 has a base-13 representation B34C128.
If instead of {A, B, C}, we judiciously choose the symbols {+, −, .}, something interesting happens: some numbers in base 13 will have representations that look like well-formed decimals in base 10: for example, the number 54349589 has a base-13 representation of −34.128. Of course, most numbers won't be intelligible in this way; for example, the number 3629265 has the base-13 representation 9+0−−7.
Conway's base-13 function takes in a real number x and considers its base-13 representation as a sequence of symbols {0, 1, ..., 9, +, −, .}. If from some position onward, the representation looks like a well-formed decimal number r, then f(x) = r. Otherwise, f(x) = 0. (Well-formed means that it starts with a + or − symbol, contains exactly one decimal-point symbol, and otherwise contains only the digits 0–9). For example, if a number x has the representation 8++2.19+0−−7+3.141592653..., then f(x) = +3.141592653....(wikipedia)

s: Is Kryptos meant to be a code breaking exercise? Or are there really hints embedded which provide code keys?
t:
I imagine most, who first come onto this trek, assume (as did I) that contained somewhere in Sanborn's Langley work are the keys/instructions needed to decipher the encoded messages, whether explicitly revealed or implied via clever clues.  But, I am unaware of their being any solid evidence, regarding the first three messages, that proves that hypothesis.  Is it the general consensus, of those who've spent time on this subject, that there are no key codes to be found (explicit, or otherwise) for the final passage, as Sanborn intended for this to be an entirely code breaking exercise?

One can find all manner of possible hints/clues when working backwards, once a key word and/or encoding process is known.  But, when you then run the postulated scenario forward, its plausibility tends to disintegrate.  For instance, (as I'm sure many have) I looked at anagrams of ABSCISSA, the longest of which is cassias, the plural genus of a flowering plant. But, Cassius (one letter off) is the name of a political assassin, a Roman senator, who along with Brutus, led the plot to assassinate Julius Caesar.  With already having determined that Dallas is the only significant locale along a trajectory extending from the stone compass pointer, and with Sanborn having just turned 18 years old at the time of the JFK assassination, the abscissa/cassius possibility didn't seem so far fetched. There is also the connection with the Vigenere matrix itself, which has at its heart Caesar Ciphers.

More coincidence, I made note of the 'missing' letters in the first three Sanborn messages. The first L in 'illusion' was gone, replaced by the Q.  The O in 'underground' was missing, replaced by a U.  And the last E in 'desparately' was gone, but replaced with nothing.  So, I got LEO . . . low earth orbit . . . law enforcement officer; could be all over the board, but what if there was something being implied by the missing letters.   And then, I realized that 'desparately' had two letters missing.  There was another E missing, as the first A should have been an E.  Thus, there was L,E,O, and E, or perhaps LEE O.  You can see where that could lead . . . would there be a missing H in the last passage?  Could Lord Carnarvon have said "Do you see anything, H?" (for Howard, but replaced by the Q)

In truth, with only 26 letters in our alphabet and all of them finding a prominent role in just about any subject matter of interest, coincidences are going to be frequent.

The same may be said for physical context.  Is it a coincidence that the alignment used for the courtyard stones has a trajectory that runs into the Smithsonian museum complex (and Hirshhorn Museum), where Sanborn 'purportedly' has (or perhaps had) a piece entitled 'Invisible Forces' (1985); this according to Sanborn's website.  Curiously though, the Hirshhorn seems to no longer have that piece, nor may never had it.  This 'Invisible Forces' is not to be confused with two other Sanborn works with the same name, one in Arlington, Va, and one in Houston.

I followed the trajectory of the stone's alignment for the very purpose of seeing if they were intended to provide a hint, used for decoding Kryptos.  With some other hint (in this case 'Invisible Forces' on the front stones) providing the spot along that trajectory, putting us at the Hirshhorn.  My logic didn't seem entirely whacko, once I found 'Palimpsest' (1989) by Ann Hamilton, owned by the Hirshhorn.  There is a wrench in the logic, it wasn't acquired by the Hirshhorn until much later, having been first exhibited in New York City.

Humor certainly does have its place in this endeavor, as when I did an anagram search on PALIMPSEST, the two longest results returned were 'simplest' and 'misspelt'.  One characterization of the Caesar cyphers is that they are among the 'simplest' encryption methods; and we well understand how 'misspelt' fits into this game.

Going back to the earlier reference of running things forward, it is difficult to believe that (as humorously coincidental as they may be) Sanborn could have expected, in 1989/90, anyone to (precisely enough) ascertain the trajectory of an alignment of stones, or to reasonably think of one particular famous assassin in history and then to scramble his name to find a useful key word.

Another observation made, was that the trajectory made by the front entrance stones goes straight to the White House, or likely more precisely, the West Wing (yet another WW) . . . yet another seeming clue.  But could Sanborn have positioned the stones in both the front and the courtyard so precisely, even if it were his intention to incorporate their trajectories into his maze of clues?  It certainly is possible, had he used the services of a professional surveyor.

The trajectories created by the stone alignments probably have no part to play in this message game; if anything, perhaps they are a mere nod to the Zero Mile post at the northern side of the Ellipse, once proposed as a geographical reference point for the United States.

While the stone's alignments may be red herrings, the explicit compass pointer must serve a purpose.  It seems such a big coincidence that it points to Dallas, more specifically, Dealey Plaza.  And yet there is another interpretation for why the pointer is positioned as it is; though likely just another coincidence.

The compass is positioned correctly, that is, its markers are in alignment with actual north/south/east/west.  With the pointer not pointing North, Sanborn is either illustrating the power of lodestones, or simply using the lodestone as a symbolic means for positioning the pointer as part of a clue to the overall message or as instructions for deciphering the Kryptos code.

What if the compass is fronting/masking . . . for a clock?  With the N representing 12 o'clock on a clock face, the pointer then, each end separately or together, can imply varying times.  Those numbers in one way or another could be used as instructions for deciphering, especially if transposition was utilized.   The pointer's head, if viewed as both the hour and minute hand would indicate 8:42 (or 20:42).  Recall that the third passage used transposition and a 8x42 matrix; which also provides the number of letters (336) in the message.  For a second matrix, one would only need to know one number.  The other half of the compass pointer could be read as 2:12, or 14:12.  The other transposition matrix was 14x24.

So, is the compass (placed at the heart of the CIA) intended to raise the widely held (especially in 1989/90) suspicion of a political assassination plot (ala that of Brutus and Cassius), or is it a cleverly disguised means for providing the numerical keys for deciphering the third passage?

Spoiler alert:

The 5th part of book Muko ends with words: “The key to the fourth part seems to be xxxxxxxx.”.

I will spoil it a bit more in a second.

Since the beginning lots of us – kryptos geeks – probably assumed that THIS is the word, the key to solving K4. Unfortunately I haven`t seen any proof that would give us a slight hope that it really is the key and how it could be used.

The series of Muko books (Legends of Aivirai) were created because I wanted to help anyone to find the final solution and put it in decrypted, publicly available form.
I wanted the K4 to be left in a state where anyone (with just a minor knowledge about simple ciphers) will be able to move it forward.

The key:
To the point. Last sentence in the book is:
“The key to the fourth part seems to be KRYPTOS.”

Introduction:

Now part for more interested readers, geeks like me who spent a lot of time on K4.
Everything started with a message for which hash was put in book 1 – “Muko and the Secret”. The 2nd message from at the end of the book (with hashes) begins with:

BEGIN
The first key to solution seems to be the word:
KRYPTOS
(…)

This keyword combined with clues gives us something interesting.
With BERLIN clue – it could be an incident
With CLOCK clue – it could be a coincidence
With NE clue – it seems to be a pattern

All three clues and the keyword show the same characteristics.
The calculations behind the pattern also shows some additional insight about the methods used as masking and encryption.

Simple definition needed:

What is the pattern and the crack in Kryptos K4?
If we get a random key and a random not-so-easy-cipher than the average distance between decrypted and encrypted letter on a specific position should be something around 6,5.
why?
dist(A, A) = 0,
dist(A, B) = dist(A, Z) = 1,
dist(A, C) = dist(A, Y) = 2,
…
dist(A, N) = 13 = dist(B, O) = …

average distance between A and all letters in alphabet is (0 + 1 + 2 + 3 + … + 12 + 13 + 12 + 11 + … + 1) / 26 = 6,5
The same calculations work for all other letters.

Calculations for K1, K2, K3:

Now average distances in Kryptos between decrypted and encrypted texts are:
Part 1: around 6,7
Part 2: around 8,9
Part 3: around 6,7
Seem to be close to 6,5

if we split letters of decrypted messages to two sets:

* IS_KR={KRYPTOS}

* IS_NOT_KR={ABCDEFGHIJLMNQUVWXZ}

and calculate distances separately, then the distances are:
Part 1 for (IS_NOT_KR vs IS_KR) = (7,1 vs 5,5) – similar (7,1/5,5 = 1,29)
Part 2 for (IS_NOT_KR vs IS_KR) = (8,3 vs 9,8) – similar (8,3/9,8 = 0,84)
Part 3 for (IS_NOT_KR vs IS_KR) = (6,4 vs 7,4) – similar (6,4/7,4 = 0,86)
everything behaves as it should behave in a correct cipher.

Calculations for clues:

Now lets take a look into clues BERLIN, CLOCK and NORTHEAST

BERLIN clue for (IS_NOT_KR vs IS_KR) = (9 vs 2) – incident (9/2 = 4,5)
CLOCK clue for (IS_NOT_KR vs IS_KR) = (11,6 vs 4,5) – coincidence (11,6/4,5 = 2,6)
NORTHEAST clue for (IS_NOT_KR vs IS_KR) = (5,25 vs 1,4) – pattern (5,25/1,4 = 3,75)
These are much larger values than they should be for a random word as a keyword.

Of course there are other words for which we could find larger quotient, but THIS word is the name of the scuplture!

What is more – like I`ve written – this gives a lot of insight about the methods used as masking and encryption.
Let`s think. Why KRYPTOS letters encrypt to other “near” letters?

Greg

I've just taken a look at the picture that Sukhwant Singh says that he got from Jim Sanborn, showing EASTNORTHEAST.

I believe this is real.

The file I examined was a .png file. Unfortunately .png files have almost no metadata (unlike .jpg and .pdf which often include lots of forensic clues).

However, the layout is nearly identical to the .pdf that Jim Sanborn supplied the New York Times in 2010 (https://groups.io/g/KRYPTOS/files/Personal%20Folders/Gillogly/KryptosTable2.pdf). It looks like Jim took a pdf/image *similar* to the one he released in 2010 (it's different: it uses a different font/spacing and color), then added "CLOCK" to it (presumably he didn't have one with "BERLINCLOCK" accessible), and added EASTNORTHEAST in red.

I would find it extremely unlikely that someone other than Jim Sanborn created this (you'd have to be pretty creative to create your own chart similar to the 2010 one (but not actually copying it), include BERLIN but not CLOCK, then resize it, and add both CLOCK and NORTHEAST in a different font).

The only question in my mind is whether Jim might have released this to be deceptive. But what gain would there be to deceive a single (or several) Kryptos people paying him money for his thoughts? And he would run a big risk of losing credibility if he was caught intentionally sending fake cribs.

I'm guessing he planned on releasing EASTNORTHEAST as the last clue, had the clue ready to go, but changed his mind at the last minute and only released NORTHEAST. And accidentally sent this out.
                   -Scott

In Sukhwant's spirit of sharing our information and thoughts with the group, I want to get the ball rolling on the possible significance and clues that EASTNORTHEAST may provide:

First of all, this tells us that a very precisely refined compass direction is part of K4. One might possibly say "Go northeast" as part of a direction in ordinary conversation, but one would hardly specify "Go east-northeast" in ordinary circumstances. A very precise set of compass directions must be involved.

It is worth noting some of the possible mathematical significance of EASTNORTHEAST. It is 67.5 degrees horizontal from due north. Since we also know the K4 message involves a clock, it may be worth noting that the hour hand of a traditional analog clock would be pointing exactly to east-northeast at the time of 2:15. The minute hand would be pointing exactly to east-northeast at 11 minutes and 15 seconds past each hour. Of course the Berlin clocks that we suspect the K4 message refers to do not tell time in this traditional way.

The name of the traditional wind point associated with east-northeast by Mediterranean sailors in the Middle Ages is Greco-Levante.

s: East-northeast air corridor in Berlin Airlift
t:
I have discovered that east-northeast was the compass direction of the air corridor that American planes flew into Tempelhof Airport during the Berlin Airlift in 1948-1949. See highlighted (***) excerpt of the passage below:

<http://www.culturaldiplomacy.org/academy/index.php?en_tar_the-berlin-airlift>

"The U.S. action had the name "Operation Vittles," while the British one was called "Operation Plainfare”.
On June 24th 1948, Brigadier General Joseph Smith was appointed as the Task Force Commander of the Berlin Airlift.  Then operation Vittles was launched by General Clay on June 25th.  The very next day thirty-two C-47 planes set off for Berlin, each hauling 80 tons of cargo that comprised of milk, flour and medical supplies.
The British operation commenced on the 28th of June. It was believed that the airlift would last for a maximum of three weeks.  By the start of July, the system was really starting to come into force.  Further C-54 planes were arriving in number and ***the American aircraft flew east-northeast into Tempelhof Airport along one of the three air corridors***, then returned due west flying out on another of the corridors.  After the planes reached the British Zone, they turned south to return to their bases."

Geoffrey

s: Kurfürstendamm runs east-northeast on way to Berlin Clock original location
t:
Another possible connection of EASTNORTHEAST to BERLIN CLOCK:

The famous avenue Kurfürstendamm, which has been called "the Champs-Elysées of Berlin", along which the best-known "Berlin Clock" was originally located from 1975 to 1995 (so it was still there at the time of Kryptos), runs in an east-northeast direction toward the Tiergarten park and the city center. The Berlin Clock at the intersection of Uhlandstraße was toward the end of the avenue in this direction, so it would have been natural to proceed along Kurfürstendamm in an east-northeast direction for a substantial distance on one's way to the Berlin Clock.

Geoffrey

Well, despite Jim Sanborn's claimed aversion to math, that didn't stop him from including a very precise numerical coordinate location in the K2 plaintext message.

I don't think anyone wants to downplay the significance of EAST appearing twice now, and not far apart from each other at that. However, I think it's already clear by now that the encryption method of K4 must have been sufficiently complex that EAST-->FLRV at positions 22-25 is almost certainly unrelated to EAST-->GKSS at positions 31-34. They are 9 characters apart, so yes, this information tells us that the K4 encryption method presumably does not use a period of 3 or 9 as a key part of the method. But in any bigraphic cipher (encrypting two letters at a time as a block) the fact that the first EAST begins at an even-numbered character and the second EAST begins at an odd-numbered character would make the encryption of the two EAST's completely unrelated to each other: one would be encrypted as EA+ST; the other would be broken up into xE+AS+Tx. Likewise, if the period 7 is key to the encryption method -- length of KRYPTOS, and 97 characters plus the ? is 98, which is 7x7x2 -- then the two EAST's would fall in different places in the division of the text into 7-letter periods.

Geoffrey

This idea is inspired by a couple posts by John Manuel (#21432 and #21440) in June with an idea about a triangular array of rows with increasing odd-numbered lengths: 1,3,5,7,9,11,13,15,17,17 for a total of 98 if we include the ? at the beginning (?) of K4.
Back in June I was playing around with variations on this idea, but I believe I may have never posted it here, at first because I thought it was so good I wanted to keep it to myself so I could use it to solve K4 myself (LOL) and then probably because other things came up and I set aside Kryptos for a while.
So in Sukhwant's spirit of sharing our knowledge, I will share my idea here now:

Arrange the ? + 97 characters of K4 in an array that begins with a row of 13 characters (? + the first 12 letters of K4), and proceed with *decreasing* odd-numbered lengths in every following row.
We will get an array of 13,11,9,7,5,3,1. Arrange them so that they are *centered* in each row:

xxxxxxxxxxxxx
  xxxxxxxxxxx
    xxxxxxxxx
      xxxxxxx
        xxxxx
          xxx
            x

This is a total of 49 characters, the ? + the first 48 letters of K4.

Now if we simply invert this process, and basically turn this shape upside-down, we can arrange the remaining 49 letters of K4 in the same way, creating the following array in the shape of an hourglass:

xxxxxxxxxxxxx
  xxxxxxxxxxx
    xxxxxxxxx
      xxxxxxx
        xxxxx
          xxx
            x
            x
          xxx
        xxxxx
      xxxxxxx
    xxxxxxxxx
  xxxxxxxxxxx
xxxxxxxxxxxxx

This is exactly the 97 letters of K4 plus the ? at the beginning.

By the way, only a number that is exactly 2 times a square number can produce this shape.
98 = 49*2
And of course 49 = 7^2 (7*7)

Perhaps there is some cryptographic process based on the location of each character in its row and column in the distinctive array above.

Geoffrey

s: Bifid cipher with stego-based changing period
t:
I know some of the more experienced cryptanalysts in this group (Rob M., Jim M. back in the day, perhaps others) have done a lot of work looking into the Bifid cipher and related ciphers. Here is a possible twist on the Bifid cipher that I wonder if anyone has investigated before:
In addition to the Polybius square used, the other key step in the Bifid encryption / decryption process is the period length which the text blocks are broken up into before the critical fractionating step. As I understand it, a key step in the cryptanalysis of a Bifid cipher is to determine the period length used.
But what if a cryptographer designed a Bifid cipher with a period length that CHANGES repeatedly throughout the message, perhaps with the period length changing with every text block?
Steganography could possibly be used to deliver the pattern of changing period lengths to the message recipient. In the case of Kryptos, for example, could the varying lengths of each row of ciphertext in K1-K4 possibly communicate the period length of each text block of the Bifid cipher?
Such a cryptographic method would defeat any typical cryptanalytic attack on a Bifid cipher that is based on the assumption that the same period length, whatever it may be, is used throughout the same encrypted message. You can use a cryptanalysis program to check every possible period length of a Bifid cipher, and still fail to decrypt a message if the period length is changing continuously throughout it.
All in all, I think such a method would fall within "fair game" difficulty: a Bifid cipher with a twist that's based on steganography visible in Kryptos.
It would also represent a particular combination that would present great difficulties for any one type of typical approach to cryptanalysis: The Bifid cipher itself is almost impossible to decrypt "by hand", so it tends to attract the attention of cryptanalysts with sophisticated computer programs. But this twist with a stego-based changing period would defeat pretty much all known cryptanalytic programmed attacks on Bifids. Thus, the computer-program cryptanalysts and the creative work-by-hand cryptanalysts would have to collaborate and work together to have a better chance of cracking such a cipher.
Just my two cents, as always.
-Geoffrey

s: Bifid cipher with stego-based changing period
t:
As a follow-up to this idea, I note that if one takes the line lengths of every complete line of K1-K3 (not counting the line on which K4 begins), these lengths modulo 27 -- that is, the number of characters more than 27 that each line has -- add up to exactly 97, the number of letters in K4.
So the K1-K3 line lengths modulo 27 would be a simple steganographic way to indicate the varying period lengths of each text block of K4 if it is a Bifid or similar cipher:
5, 4, 4, 3, 4, 5, 4, 4, 5, 4, 3, 4, 4, 4,5, 3, 4, 3, 5, 3, 5, 4, 6, 2
Actually I can refute the very simplest application of this sequence of Bifid period lengths to K4, because it would result in the sixth text block of period 5 in positions 21-25 being xEAST -> WFLRV and then the eighth text block of period 4 in positions 30-33 being HEAS -> NGKS. But in a Bifid cipher, in both of these blocks the first coordinates of the third+fourth plaintext letters AS would determine the block's second ciphertext letter, which should therefore be identical in these two blocks. But they are not: it is F in the first block and G in the second.
This is an example where the new clue EASTNORTHEAST is actually helpful in refuting a particular specific version of an idea about the K4 encryption process!
But naturally we can still apply this idea in other ways, for example by applying the above sequence in reverse order as the series of changing period lengths of each text block of K4: 2, 6, 4, 5, 3, 5, 3, 4, 3, 5, etc. In this case the sixth text block would still have period 5 in positions 21-25, xEAST -> WFLRV, but now the eighth text block would have period 5 in positions 29-33 and be THEAS -> RNGKS. Here there are no expected necessarily identical ciphertext letters in the Bifid encryption of these two text blocks.
-Geoffrey

s: test cipher: Bifid with variable period lengths
t:
In another post I proposed the idea of a Bifid cipher with the added twist of variable period lengths of text blocks for fractionation that change unpredictably throughout the message, unless you know the basis for the pattern of period lengths. In the case of K4 I propose steganography on Kryptos could very well be the key to this sequence of period lengths, but in principle there are other ways to do this too without making the pattern of period lengths too simple or regular. In other words, the goal is the appearance of a pseudo-random variation in the period lengths from one text block to the next.

For anyone who wants to test their ability to adapt their Bifid cipher solving cryptanalytical computer programs to account for such variable period lengths, I have created a fairly simple example of a ciphertext based on such an encryption method. I will say this much: the variation in the period lengths of the text blocks is pseudo-random, but it is also designed for relative ease of use on the part of the intended recipient who has to decrypt the message. (I believe that excessively long period lengths of text blocks lend themselves to the risk of error on the part of the intended recipient in performing the decryption.)

Hi Sukhwant: yes, several of us have assumed that the most obvious thing about the sculpture as a whole is its
serpentine (S) shape. This hint is possibly further emphasized by the fact that the one letter shared by all
three keywords is S:

KRYPTOS: 1 S
PALIMPSEST: 2 S's
ABSCISSA: 3 S's

Furthermore, the two "errors" in the first panel also involve the letter S:

PT:  I *Q* LUSION
Key: P *S* ESTPAL
CT:  M *K* YRDMFD

Jim erroneously spelled PALIMPSEST "PALIMPCEST" in his decoding sheets, which is why the first L of
ILLUSION got encrypted to a K instead of a W.

In K2, the cause of the error is not 100% clear, but it again occurs for key letter S:

PT:  UNDERGR *U* UND
Key: CISSAAB *S* CIS
CT: TBJLBQC *R* TBJ

On Jim's encoding sheets he has ciphertext "E," which would have been correct for the "O" of underground.
Perhaps he inadvertently reversed the roles of the CT and key: if he started at the top with plaintext O and read
down the column until he found key letter S, that would yield an R. (In other words, the Beaufort cipher.)

Of course, it could just be coincidence that the two spelling errors in K1/K2 involve a key letter S: after all,
with two S's in PALIMPSEST and three in ABSCISSA, there was a 3 in 40 chance that single letter errors
would both involve an S.

Finally, there is the conspicuously kerned DYAHR in K3, which can anagram to HYDRA -- the many-headed
serpent of Greek mythology. The letter S is a simple graphical representation of a snake, and even the
sound of the letter mimics a snake's hiss.  --Rob

And the missing CT "S" which is needed for the creation of XLAYERTWO.

I suppose there are some convoluted ways to do so, with "AT LEAST" or with LEAST ending one sentence and NORTHEAST OF ... beginning a separate sentence. The code can relatively be easily be tuned to run different period lengths for different segments of ciphertext, however the challenge becomes that the smaller the sub-ciphertext portions, the harder it is to extrapolate out the probability that the solve (crack) is correct. Like you, I would love to hear someday just how the puzzle was developed.  Which concepts were implemented first?  Why were the specific blocks of plaintext chosen?  What was meant by [insert cryptic phrase here]?  Why was [S-shape / four-panel layout / petrified wood / etc.] used as part of the artistic presentation? Still, it's nice to see that the latest little trickle of information has reignited the community with some additional fervor - here's to hoping that collective efforts will lead to a solution sooner rather than later.

CLARIFICATION: just to be a little more clear, I don't believe that Kryptos is unsolvable! Why would I be hanging around here hungrily chasing little bits of information if I thought all of it was for naught? I LOVE this sculpture. I LOVE puzzles and mysteries. Like Ms. Dunin said, I enjoy finding order in chaos. Perhaps "flawed" was an inappropriate word, maybe "inelegant" would have been better.

Now, forgive me if this has been discussed before, but I'm new and I haven't had a chance to review all the archives yet. Has anyone thought about the RQ in K0 referring to Radio Quiet? The United States Radio Quiet Zone in West Virginia is home to 2 interesting installations: the National Radio Astronomy Observatory and Sugar Grove. I think, arguably of course, that they might be a nice way of linking the radio communication theme of K0 with the first part of K2.

When radio astronomy was first developed, it was as if astronomical objects that we didn't know existed suddenly became "visible" in the dark skies. Reminds me of the first lines of K2 - It was totally invisible...There's a nice quote on the National Radio Astronomy Observatory website: Radio telescopes can see the invisible and hidden activities across the Universe and are the tools for solving some of the greatest mysteries of our Cosmos.

Sugar Grove on the other hand is an NSA installation responsible for intercepting all international communications over the Eastern part of the United Stated. It was originally the site of a radio telescope used to intercept Soviet radio signals. I think the actual listening post was constructed inside a mountain on the site. Made me think of the part of K2 referring to underground transmissions and whether Langley knew about it (it's NSA not CIA). Very weak but I'll still going to mention it - since we're all hung up on directionality right now with our newest east-north-east tidbit - Sugar Grove is south-west of Langley, meaning that Langley is north-east of Sugar Grove.

Anyway, there's tons of info on the web about radio astronomy and Sugar Grove. Might not help in any manner for solving K4, but I though it a nice kind of thematic interpretation. Morse Code - radio communications - radio waves - magnetism - mapping the skies  - the thrill of discovery - Hydra constellation - underground transmissions - buried inside a mountain - information gathering - the NSA versus the CIA....you get the idea...

Cheers,

Sarah

s: Extreme rare distribution in K4 as period-49 Playfair with DYAHR key
t:
Long ago in this group, in April 2006 (!!), Jason DeSeve mentioned in message #4405 that if we take the ? + the 97 letters of K4 and simply split the message in half, with the first 49 characters in the top row and the last 49 characters in the bottom row, then there are no double letters among the 49 character pairs. He suggested that this may point to a Playfair cipher.

I stumbled upon this fact in my own research the other day and thought the same thing. The "Seriated Playfair" is a known type of classical cipher, although not nearly as well-known as the simple Playfair. Splitting up K4 into two blocks of 49 would be the maximum possible period of such a seriated Playfair for this message. The probability of no double letters occurring by chance in 48 pairs (not counting the one with the "?") from a 5x5 square with an I/J box would be about 0.14. This is not decisive statistical evidence on its own, but it is a curious unusual occurrence. The hypothesis is that a period-49 seriated Playfair could be the final encryption step of K4. Naturally it would not be the only encryption step.

I had the idea that perhaps the K4 encryption process may be a combination of two seriated Playfair steps, *with different periods* and possibly with different keyed 5x5 Polybius squares. If so, the 5x5 square in the second step might possibly be related to "LAYER TWO" and "ID BY ROWS".

So I played around with trial decryptions of K4 as a period-49 seriated Playfair cipher in this way, trying various thematic keyed 5x5 squares. I wasn't looking for meaningful text or the plaintext as the result yet, but I was looking for a text *with no double letters when seriated into period-7 blocks of pairs*. (That is, pair up characters 1-7 with 8-14, pair up 15-21 with 22-28, and so on.) Such a text could possibly have been the result of a period-7 seriated Playfair as the first encryption step.

It is curious in this regard that even after the latest clue EASTNORTHEAST, all the crib plaintext clue locations have been chosen so that no complete letter pair is revealed by EASTNORTHEAST or by BERLINCLOCK when K4 is arranged in period-7 blocks of pairs as I describe. It is also interesting that the newest clue, the first EAST, is the first clue to provide any complete letter pairs in the period-49 arrangement: EAST and LOCK are paired in this way.

Trial decryptions with KRYPTOS-keyed squares, plain alphabetical squares, and a HYDRA-keyed square for the period-49 Playfair did not produce texts without double letters when re-divided into period-7 blocks of pairs.

But when I did a trial decryption of K4 as a period-49 seriated Playfair *with a DYAHR-keyed 5x5 Polybius square*, it did produce a text with no double letters when arranged in period-7 blocks of pairs.

Here is the text that results from the decryption of K4 as a period-49 seriated Playfair with a DYAHR-keyed 5x5 Polybius square. I have arranged it in period-7 blocks of pairs:

(If this comes out scrambled on your screen, the first line is the top row of all period-7 blocks, and the second line is the bottom row of all blocks.
So the top line is characters 1-7, 15-21, 29-35, etc., and the bottom line is characters 8-14, 22-28, 36-42, etc.)

?QGIYWI     OTKKCGG     OYGFNOP     LOQCCWT     HBRXBME     LXETCQE     UNENWXO
UIEAOKG    XGMYPLT       IOZPOMB      ?DONNIO       FIAOXOO      YNTZPMF     WXFLYRZ

Checking the locations of the plaintext clues EASTNORTHEAST and (THE)BERLINCLOCK, I find that no letter encrypts to itself in the text above, which is another feature of Playfair.

The combined probability of the K4 ciphertext with no double letters when split into period-49, the text above with no double letters when divided into period-7 blocks of pairs, and no letter from any of the clues (plus THE before BERLINCLOCK) encrypting to itself in the text above, I calculate as (0.96)^48 * (0.96)^47 * (0.96)^27 = 0.00687..., or about a 1 in 145 chance.

But none of this is the "extreme rare distribution" that I am referring to in the subject line of this post.

The most extraordinary occurrence in the text above is the letter distribution. One would expect a random distribution as a result of a trial decryption of K4 as a period-49 Playfair with a DYAHR-keyed 5x5 square. For the most part, this is what we get, with no letter occurring more than 6 times, EXCEPT THAT THE LETTER "O" OCCURS 13 -- THIRTEEN -- TIMES in the text above!!

The probability of one letter out of 25 in a 5x5 square occurring 13 times out of 96 letters is calculated to be *** 0.0000915, or about a 1 in 10,932 chance! ***

Combining this probability with the other probabilities above, we get a total probability of 0.000000629, or about a 1 in 1,590,000 chance of occurring by coincidence.

I have not yet been able to decrypt the text above as a period-7 seriated Playfair, and I am still thinking about the significance of the letter "O" occurring more than twice as often as any other letter in the "intermediate step" text above. One idea I have is a bizarre kind of Polybius square where the letter O appears *twice* in the square, and perhaps both I/J and U/V share a box each. ("V" does not occur in the intermediate step text above.) Also, I cannot help but notice and mention the fact that "S" is the other letter that does not occur in the intermediate step text! I realize that including the same letter twice in a Polybius square creates the risk of all sorts of problems of ambiguity both in the encryption and in the decryption, so this issue must be resolved in order to justify this hypothesis. Ordinarily it would not be my preferred hypothesis, but I am simply trying to make sense of a text encrypted by Playfair with 13 O's and no more than 6 of any other letter.

I welcome any ideas about how we may proceed with further decryption of my intermediate step text, if indeed I am on the right track with my decryption of the final encryption step as a period-49 seriated Playfair with a DYAHR-keyed Polybius square.

Geoffrey

Sideways

This is a series of roughly remembered exercises from a group event way back in the day. Childish, yes, but designed to promote creative and analytic thinking, I suspect.

INDEMNITY
INDEMNITY
Double Indemnity

      BRIDGE
WTARTUEBRLS
Bridge Over Troubled Waters

GRAIMAGEVEN
Graven Image

Consider that if one wanted to set clues, a great way to go about it would be to apply simplified cryptograms like these that can be easily overlooked by a master cryptanalyst, much like hiding plaintext in plain sight, as it were. Apply that thinking to Kryptos...

DYAHR/YAR
Mixed Array

TOTALLYINVISIBLE
TOTAL-LY-IN-VI-SIBLE

VIRTUALLYINVISIBLE
VIRTUAL-LY-IN-VI-SIBLE

It occurred to me when I free-associated that from another poster that an ARRAY is exactly what Kryptos is, though I rarely use the word in that proper context.

ARRAY - An arrangement of objects, pictures, or numbers (or letters) in columns and rows is called an array

Things I know about mixing up the Kryptos Array from my personal examination:
~ Flattening the entire plaintext into rows of 24 creates a massive acrostic and reveals the alignment of BERLIN pt and NYPVT ct in K3.
~ Shaping K4 like an AST BALLOON from the K1 basic acrostic turns the Morse Stones into a set of visual markers.
~ Aligning the entire Kryptos plaintext into flattened rows of nine results in the alignment of the words NORTH and EAST within K4 and from K2 to K4.

Conclusion: These clues are meant to nudge people towards thinking about those “shifts” in columns and rows, and the cribs provide clues to unmasking and solving K4.

Now that I have had a bit to actually look into this idea, I have a few
thoughts.

A few variants on this idea.  K3 was encrypted by rotating the plaintext
twice clockwise and with the second step, copying the text into a different
dimension matrix.  (For those curious about this method, write out the
plaintext in a 42x8 matrix, rotate 90deg clockwise, copy the now rows into
a 14x24 matrix (compare this step to Jim's paper and you will see that it
matches and that the paper is labeled '2') and finally, rotate 90deg again
and you get the ciphertext.)

What is one's natural inclination when one comes across an hourglass?  To

s: K4 as period-49 Playfair DYAHR-key then period-7 Playfair UFPHZ-key produces interesting text
t:
As I posted earlier, I had a number of reasons to consider the idea that the final encryption step of K4 was a period-49 (the 98 characters split in half and paired) Playfair cipher using a DYAHR-keyed 5x5 Polybius square. Please see my previous post for the interesting details. I also have a few Excel files illustrating steps of this process in my folder, for those who may be interested to check them out in a more clearly readable graphic format with grids.

One striking detail to add since I wrote that post, is that not only does the intermediate step text after the period-49 Playfair DYAHR-key decrypt have the extraordinary 13 O's in an otherwise normal letter frequency distribution, but moreover 10 of those O's occur among the 41 letters (and one "?") in the middle of the message in positions 29-70 (out of 98)! These will be the middle three period-7 blocks of pairs in the next decryption step (previous encryption step), and they begin with RTHEAST and end with BERLIN. The letter frequency distribution of this block of 41 letters is so striking that it is worth showing in full:

Letter frequency: O 10, B 3, I 3, N 3, F 2, P 2, M 2, C 2, X 2, Y 1, G 1, Z 1, L 1, Q 1, W 1, T 1, D 1, H 1, R 1, E 1, A 1, K 0, S 0, U 0, V 0, (J 0)

The probability of the letter O occurring 10 times in a 41-letter block as a chance coincidence is about 1 in 301,500. In combination with the probabilities of the absence of double letters in multiple steps and arrangements of the text as discussed in my previous post, the combined probability of all these occurrences happening as a chance coincidence is about 1 in 44,000,000 (1 in 44 million).

Oh, there is one more remarkable thing to mention about this extremely rare high frequency occurrence of O in this text: In the entire K1-K2 ciphertext on the first panel of Kryptos, there are only THREE ciphertext O's among the 432 letters!! The probability of such an extreme low frequency of a particular letter by chance coincidence is only about 1 in 26,726! I strongly suspect this was not an accident, and it may be related to the extreme high frequency of the letter O in the text resulting from decrypting K4 as a period-49 Playfair cipher with the DYAHR-keyed square.

If one combines the low probability of no double letters in the period-49 K4 ciphertext, no double letters in the period-7 arrangement of the text after period-49 Playfair decryption with the DYAHR-keyed square, no exact matches of the latter text with the clues EASTNORTHEAST and (THE)BERLINCLOCK, 10 occurrences of the letter O in the middle 41 letters of this text, and the occurrence of the letter O only 3 times in the entire K1-K2 ciphertext, the probability of all of these things occurring by mere chance coincidence is a whopping 1 in 1.175 TRILLION chance. That is well above the range of a "7-sigma" occurrence.

(By the way, the entire letter frequency distribution of the K1-K2 ciphertext is a topic well worthy of further and deeper investigation: E and F occur 31 times each, Q 29 times, D 28 times, G and U 24 times; on the other hand, O occurs only 3 times, S only 6 times, C 7 times, B, I, and W 8 times, X 9 times. These are all striking deviations in a ciphertext that is supposed to be designed to flatten the letter frequency distribution and in which the average letter frequency is expected to be 16-17.)

==============

Now I would like to describe my idea for the next decryption step of K4, or the next-to-last encryption step: a period-7 seriated Playfair cipher with a different keyed 5x5 Polybius square this time -- my idea is that the key is UFPHZ.

UFPHZ are the 3rd through 7th letters of the K1 ciphertext at the top of the first panel of Kryptos. This is a thematic key because the location of UFPHZ matches the location of DYAHR at the beginning of K3 in the second panel. It is also curious that "EM" occurs before UFPHZ, while "EN" occurs before DYAHR.

The combination of using a UFPHZ-keyed square for the first Playfair step, and then a DYAHR-keyed square for the second Playfair step, is quite thematic for Kryptos: If one imagines the first panel written on top of the second panel, one can think of DYAHR as the "palimpsest" written under UFPHZ. One can also think of UFPHZ as "layer one" and DYAHR as "LAYER TWO".

UFPHZ is also a good Polybius square key because it is unexpected, seemingly random, not a dictionary word, and it contains a U and a Z to mix up the end of the alphabet in the square, but in a different way than the Y in KRYPTOS and DYAHR.

So, after decrypting the K4 cipher first with a period-49 Playfair cipher with the DYAHR-keyed square, and then decrypting the resulting text again with a period-7 Playfair with the UFPHZ-keyed square, I find that the result is a rather interesting text:

?OMGVQG?KABSCMRNIMPMAVALWWKNIVMUSSFBSUFNIC?ROAAVV
?BNQQKNPFNVDIBUBDRVSSMTAYPSBXRYUWKZPRBRVRSTTZGXLF

Although the Index of Coincidence (IC) is still at 1.14, not as high as plaintext which is typically in the 1.50 to 2.00 range, still there is an aspect of the letter frequency distribution that is quite striking: the seven most frequent letters are S, V (8 each), R, B (7 each), M, A, N (6 each). Thus these seven letters constitute a total of 48 out of the 94 letters (not "?") in this text.

Again, this is an extremely rare occurrence in random text: the probability of 7 out of the 25 letters in the 5x5 square accounting for 48 out of 94 letters in a text by chance coincidence is about 1 in 789,000. (Just for fun: When we combine this probability with the others combined above to produce a 1 in 1.175 trillion chance, the result is a probability that is almost 1 in a QUINTILLION.)

It is still not a simple matter to decrypt the text above. It cannot be a direct simple substitution from the K4 plaintext, because the letters of the clues we know are not consistent with that. It cannot be a simple transposition: for example, E and H are entirely absent from the text. So there is still some challenging step left to decrypt. I suppose one may think of it as the initial masking step in the encryption method of K4.

But to me, because of the seven high-frequency letters in the text above, there is something about it that just seems more "attackable" than the original K4 cipher text that we have been struggling with for decades. If we can decrypt the above text into a plaintext message that includes the clues EASTNORTHEAST and BERLINCLOCK that we already know, then the period-7 and period-49 seriated Playfair cipher steps with the UFPHZ-keyed and DYAHR-keyed squares respectively, as I have described in this post and my previous one, will complete the decryption of K4.

I must admit, I was tempted to keep this latest step and the text above to myself, in order to try to finish solving the whole thing by myself. But I feel like that is against the spirit of this group, as we are devoted to a collaborative effort to decrypt and decipher K4. In the spirit of Sukhwant Singh's disclosure of the EASTNORTHEAST clue to the group recently, I likewise disclose my progress in my own work when I feel like I have made significant progress. I hope that others in this group have some good ideas about how to finish the decryption of the text above, to get us all the way back to the original K4 plaintext that we are all looking for.

Geoffrey

Rohan,

My natural inclination is to treat it as a sort of columnar transposition: Permutation 2 begins with the far left side of the hourglass, so first only the first character of the top row and the first character of the bottom row. Then proceed to the second column from the left, which has two characters at the top and two at the bottom. And proceed likewise all the way across the hourglass, from column to column.

In other words, enter the letters horizontally across the rows of the hourglass in Permutation 1, but enter the letters vertically down the columns of the hourglass in Permutation 2. The point is that the vertical columns have large gaps, making the pattern irregular and hard to figure out or detect if you don't know the intended pattern or design.

This process combines geometric elegance if you know the pattern, with the property of total irregularity if you don't know the pattern.

Geoffrey

I am not saying you collapse the extra L.  I am saying you collapse J/L in
the Polybius square (if bifid or some other cipher that requires a Polybius
square was used).

Regarding the interesting discussion of the "extra 'L'" row of the Vigenere tableau:

One may perhaps interpret it as related to the superfluous 'J' in the typical 5x5 Polybius square, where J is usually merged into the same box with 'I'. If we look at the right hand side of the whole Vigenere tableau, because of the extra 'L', J is the only letter that does not occur as the last letter of any row. So just going up and down the right hand side of the tableau and taking the last letter of each row, we could get a typical 5x5 Polybius square "without J" (that is, with I/J in one box).

Alternatively, the extra 'L' could be interpreted as a signal to pay extra attention to this row of the tableau. For example, it is possible that one step (perhaps the masking step?) of the encryption method of K4 could involve a Vigenere encryption where one does not use the KRYPTOS-keyed row at the top beginning with K to input the plaintext letter, but rather one uses the "extra 'L'" row to do so.

Geoffrey

s: K4 as period-49 Playfair DYAHR-key then period-7 Playfair UFPHZ-key produces interesting text
t:
I try not to make too many additional comments on my own posts; I realize that the material in the posts may seem overwhelming to some people already.

But I can't help but point out the following connection between my idea of DYAHR and UFPHZ keyed Playfair squares and a famous feature of the K1-K3 messages:

In the DYAHR-keyed Playfair square, L is directly above Q (in the middle column, 3rd and 4th rows) and O is directly above U (1st column, 4th and 5th rows).
This means that L->Q and O->U are both standard Playfair cipher vertical encryptions, when the two letters in a pair are located in the same column.
Thus, the misspellings IQLUSION and UNDERGRUUND could possibly be references to both the DYAHR-keyed square and the Playfair encryption method.

Further, in the UFPHZ-keyed square, E->A is a standard Playfair horizontal encryption when two letters are in the same row, since E in the last column of the 2nd row wraps around to A in the first column of the 2nd row.
Thus, the misspelling DESPARATLY could possibly be a reference to Playfair encryption in the UFPHZ-keyed square. (To be fair, E->A could occur in any Playfair square with the row ABCDE, and L->Q also occurs in the standard alphabetical Polybius square, although it is not standard to use that for Playfair! But O->U is not a vertical Playfair encryption in a standard square; it is distinctively connected to the DYAHR-keyed square.)

Geoffrey

I find this discussion refreshing because it reflects my thoughts. If there is an intended and logical workflow to solve all of Kryptos, not by "brute force" cryptanalysis but by systematically recovering the methods and keys from clues, then noone has found it, or at least it is far from settled how to do it. (As mentioned, several after-the-fact suggestions have been proposed for K1-K3, but most/all are unlikely to work in the forward direction when you do not already know the answer.)

I'm increasingly worried that K4 is in practice unsolvable because it was made too complicated, using several layers, each layer using a method that is known but it is unknown to us which method it is, and with at least one unique twist added somewhere according to Ed Scheidt. We need hints to start the decryption correctly, and if it is multi-stage we badly need some means of confirmation along the way that we are moving in the right direction. Jim Sanborn has said (I believe this was also in a private email conversation that was leaked to the group later) that when K4 is finally solved, it will be an all-at-once decrypt similar to parts 1 to 3. This would mean no incremental plaintext recovery and potentially no intermediate reassurance until you manage to do all steps right and hit the complete solution.

I'm also a little worried that K4 was intentionally made unsolvable - there actually is no plaintext - and Jim and Ed have only been playing us ever since. I do not like to think this. I like to think that they are good people that would not do a thing like that. However, if a sculpture is illustrating the history of cryptography, a hoax cipher could be a part of it.

I'm also thinking, after 30 years it would be reasonable to do a timeout event and say OK, you failed to solve it in reasonable time, now the challenge is closed and here is the solution. I'm comparing to the Merlin Mystery, a visual code-breaking challenge by Jonathan Gunson, a prize challenge published as a book that was released globally. This challenge had a time limit, about two years. Nobody managed to solve it, despite crowd efforts similar to the Kryptos effort. The prize was never won, but the solution was published. It showed that there indeed was a reasonably logical solution that nobody had been ingenious enough to uncover.

Finally, I'm wondering whether the CIA director has opened the envelope given to the agency by Jim, and what it says. Does the successor of WW know? Would it be possible for this group to approach the CIA about sharing such information?

t:
Very interesting. I do feel however, that it is already too complicated with at least three major steps from CT to PT: seriated Playfair, seriated Playfair again, unknown final decryption step.

A suggestion: What if you skip the de-seriation steps?
What you have done is: seriation to period-49, Playfair DYAHR-keyed, de-seriation, re-seriation to period-7, Playfair UFPHZ-keyed, de-seriation.
What is the result of this: seriation to period-49, Playfair DYAHR-keyed, *skip* de-seriation, re-seriation to period-7, Playfair keyed with UFPHZ or something else, and again no de-seriation.

If the latter scheme is used, and if it is supposed to produce plaintext (no additional final layer), then the cribs will reveal a few letter pairs. So you could say it is a little easier to crack. I don't mind that, because on the whole, it is very difficult anyway.

s: Bifid cipher with stego-based changing period
t:
Hi. I have also done some analysis of Bifid as encryption method for K4, and it seems unlikely to be the (only) method.

I have concluded that given the known cribs, it is impossible to decrypt the given CT to the given PT using Bifid with a static period of 11 or less.
It has to do with the fact that N occurs in both BERLIN and NORTHEAST and in CT, so does R; L occurs twice in BERLINCLOCK, Q occurs twice in the relevant CT (QQPRNGK), etc.
This creates chains of relations between letters (actually letter coordinates), making it impossible to create a square that fulfills all conditions.

I wonder if there is any static period that allows creation of a Polybius square for Bifid without contradictions, for transforming CT to PT.

And for varying period lengths, it will be a challenge to analyse it in the same way as I did for static periods, but I consider it unlikely that it will work unless inconveniently long periods are used.

Still, it is possible that Bifid is used in combination with some additional step or some other twist that makes it work.

On Sat, Aug 29, 2020 at 4:54 PM Anders Hallström <
[courriel]> wrote:

The 24 letters of plaintext that Sanborn has given us aren't really
"clues" or "hints," even though Sanborn and many of the rest of us often
refer to them that way. A clue would be something like: "The name of a
German city appears in the plaintext" or "the 22nd and 23rd letters are
both vowels." Sanborn has given us dozens (hundreds?) of "clues" or "hints"
over the years.

The 24 letters, though, are what we cryptanalysts refer to as "known
plaintext." They're not clues or hints suggesting what might be. They
aren't even potential cribs, because we don't have to wonder where they
land. They're just straightforward chunks of the solution handed to us.

With a quarter of the plaintext now given to us and none of the remaining
ciphertext cracked, some have questioned if K-4 is even legitimate or
solvable. Most of us in the group would attest to there being good evidence
of the presence of cryptographic structure throughout the ciphertext, or,
at least to the fact that there are features that appear to be nonrandom.
We may not all agree on which features are significant, but we've all seen
hints of "something" lurking under the surface of this thing. Everyone
knows about the five doubles that line up vertically at a width of 7, for
example, but there's a lot more going on inside this thing.

I find it convenient to lay the cryptogram out as 21-letter strings. (Ed
Hannon and others have spoken at length about their reasons for doing the
same.) This layout is often displayed in Scrabble tiles on my kitchen
table. (You'll need 8 English-language game sets to pull this off, since
there's only one K per set.) I usually find it helpful to leave off the
fifth line, which may or may not contain an anomaly; it'll probably sort
itself out in the end. Look closely and see if any more of the architecture
pops out at you. On the rare occasions when I *do *include the fifth line,
I always add a space in position 85, which seems to "correct" for something
(a missing character, or a by-product of reaching the end of the fourth
turn on a grille, or a Sanborn mistake, or whatever), like this:

*O B K R U O X  O G H U L B S  O L I F B B WF L R V Q Q P  R N G K S S
O  T W T Q S J QS S E K Z Z W  A T J K L U D  I A W I N F BN Y P V T T
M  Z F P K W G D  K Z X T J C D* I G K U H U  A U E K C A R*

As Sarah said, this puzzle is "inelegant" in some ways. Some of its
features and some of the clues Sanborn has given us are definitely flawed.
But this puzzle cleans up well, despite the warts, if you take some of the
stuff with a grain of salt and highlight other things that seem to be more
relevant to the science of cryptanalysis.

Bill Briere

s: K4 as period-49 Playfair DYAHR-key then period-7 Playfair UFPHZ-key produces interesting text
t:
Thank you for the feedback Anders. I appreciate it very much.

It's interesting that you explicitly point out the step of "de-seriation" before "re-seriation" in between the two seriated Playfair steps that I propose. And your idea to skip "de-seriation" and just "re-seriate" the text from the order it was in after the prior step is worth looking at.

But the reason I still prefer the idea with "de-seriation" after each Playfair decryption step, is that Sanborn has always expressed a strong sense about the position of each plaintext and ciphertext letter in the K4 clues that he has given. Of course since I'm pursuing a digraphic cipher idea, I don't think it literally has to be a 1-to-1 decryption from each ciphertext letter to its "corresponding" plaintext letter. But I also don't think the encryption and decryption method involves a significant amount of moving letters out of their places. "De-seriation" after each Playfair encryption/decryption step is a way to "put each letter back in its proper place" in the message, before moving on to the next step. I think that is the way Sanborn sees the message, both as plaintext and as ciphertext, so I don't think he left letters "out of their proper places" for too long throughout all the encryption steps. That's why I think Sanborn would have instinctively performed the de-seriation step before/after each seriated Playfair step, so I prefer to pursue the same idea in my decryption efforts. Too much seriation and re-seriation, without de-seriation steps in between, gets complicated to keep track of, and it starts to resemble a transposition cipher in the amount of letters changing places that's going on. That is not my sense of what is going on in K4, based on the way Sanborn has presented his clues, with the ciphertext, plaintext, and their positions all closely linked.

Of course each of us should follow up on our own preferred ideas! If you pursue this idea with no de-seriation more deeply than I do, and it turns out to be right, then you will be the one who successfully decrypts K4! We shall see.

I think at this point it is still in the realm of a "fair challenge". Scheidt and Sanborn can reasonably argue, it shouldn't be impossible for a talented cryptanalyst to think of taking all 98 characters, starting with "?", putting the first half on the top row and the second half on the bottom row, seeing there are no double letters, and pursuing a period-49 Playfair decryption step. DYAHR is fairly clearly marked on the Kryptos sculpture, it calls attention to itself as a possible key for something, so it wouldn't be considered absurdly impossible to think of that as the key for the square for a Playfair step either. So far, so logical, it seems to me. Then when one sees that this period-49 seriated Playfair decryption with the DYAHR-keyed square produces a text that has no double letters when de-seriated (all letters put back in their original order) and re-seriated in period-7 blocks of pairs, it seems natural to consider another seriated Playfair step with period-7. Again, all of this still seems like "fair game" to me, a "reasonable challenge", not easy but not impossible to think of all these things.

The first big leap I feel like I am taking is with the choice of the UFPHZ key for the second Playfair decryption step. That is a leap, much more so than the previous steps I have described. But it does seem logical and consistent enough to me. I am keeping open the possibility that I am right about everything else up to this point, but wrong about the UFPHZ key. One can't be sure about this yet. But I haven't found a more clearly logical and thematic key for the second Playfair decryption step either. Of course it could be anything. But we want to find something logical and thematic in Kryptos.

If you or anyone else has a better idea about the second Playfair decryption key, please share your ideas with us! I mean unless you can use it to solve K4 instantly, then go for it, and tell us that too :)

I wouldn't even rule out *two more* additional steps after the two seriated Playfair decryption steps, *as long as they are logical and thematic and in the spirit of the whole Kryptos sculpture*. I would rather solve two Playfairs and two more logical thematic steps, rather than two Playfairs and one more step that is not logical and thematic. It is the logical process connected to the themes of Kryptos that is the main thing, not the number of steps itself.

Ok, enough for now, just my two cents about all of this.

Geoffrey
