s: grand idea: K+L+EM+EN, two Vigeneres + two Playfairs
t:
I hesitated to write and post this, because there is still a part of me that wants to do the whole thing myself. But I remain inspired by the collaborative ethos of this group as exemplified by Sukhwant's sharing of the new EASTNORTHEAST clue. So I want to share the following grand idea of mine with everyone in this group:

As you may have seen, I wrote two big long posts the past couple of days, describing my idea about a "period-49 seriated Playfair" decryption step with a DYAHR-keyed square and then a period-7 seriated Playfair decryption step with a UFPHZ-keyed square. DYAHR is the well-known letter string after "EN" at the beginning of the K3 ciphertext (bottom left panel of Kryptos); UFPHZ is the letter string in the same place at the beginning of the K1 ciphertext (top left panel of Kryptos), after "EM".

Interested cryptanalysts and cryptographers can find all the details of my ideas, research, and analysis about these two seriated Playfair steps with different periods and different keyed squares, in my previous posts "Extreme rare distribution in K4 period-49 Playfair with DYAHR key" (message #21859) and "K4 as period-49 Playfair DYAHR-key then period-7 Playfair UFPHZ-key produces interesting text" (message #21867).

Decrypting the K4 ciphertext through these two seriated Playfair steps produces the following text:

?OMGVQG?KABSCMRNIMPMAVALWWKNIVMUSSFBSUFNIC?ROAAVV
?BNQQKNPFNVDIBUBDRVSSMTAYPSBXRYUWKZPRBRVRSTTZGXLF

Here is my grand idea: The keys of the two Playfair squares above, DYAHR and UFPHZ, occur after "EN" and "EM" at the beginning of each panel of the Kryptos ciphertext. Next we may continue the alphabetical order in reverse, *from EN and EM to L and K*.

"L" of course is the famous extra letter at the end of the first row of the bottom right panel of Kryptos, the beginning of the second half of the Vigenere tableau on the right side of the sculpture. "K" is for Kryptos, the key of the Vigenere alphabet in the tableau that was used for the encryption of K1 and K2. Setting aside the simple ABC alphabetical grid markers across the top row and down the left column, "K" is the beginning of the Vigenere tableau itself in the top right panel of Kryptos.

Wouldn't it be logical and thematic, if the encryption method for K4 is to begin with a Vigenere step using the top KRYPTOS-keyed row of the tableau, then to do another Vigenere step, but this time using the "extra-L" first row of the bottom right panel -- and then to complete the encryption with the two seriated Playfair steps that I have proposed, with keys that follow "EM" and "EN" at the beginning of the top left and bottom left panels?

This method would proceed in order from "K" to "L" to "(E)M" to (E)N", and from the top right to the bottom right to the top left to the bottom left panels of Kryptos, using key information at the top or beginning of each panel.

I note that when I say "a Vigenere step", I mean using the Vigenere tableau. For the cryptographically inclined folks, the actual encryption methods may be Vigenere or Beaufort or "variant Beaufort" (reversed Vigenere) or possibly reversed Beaufort. Further, rather than the KRYPTOS-keyed alphabetical column on the left side of the tableau, the encryption method may use either the ABC-alphabetical column on the left side *or the column on the right side of the tableau*. The latter method would give an actual cryptographic significance to the extra four columns on the right hand side of the tableau. I also wonder if the very top ABC-alphabetical row may play a cryptographic role somehow, although this may detract from the "K" aspect of the first step of the K+L+M+N theme.

Ok, there you have it, my grand idea for the encryption / decryption method of K4. After all, it begins with K and has 4 steps, you can't get any more of a "K4" theme than that!

I think I've already completed the decryption of the "EM"+"EN" two Playfair steps. Now we just need to finish the decryption of the "K"+"L" two Vigenere/Beaufort steps.

Geoffrey

Inspired by the new EAST crib, I went back to one of my favorite theories
and started playing around with it.  In so doing, I think I've come up with
a plausible encryption method that is:
* artistic
* straightforward if you know what you're doing
* produces something which looks to my inexperienced eye to have the same
statistically similar to K4
* keeps a 1:1 plaintext-to-ciphertext mapping
* is based on a standard encryption method
* and - most relevantly - would be *accidentally *very resistant to
decryption.

I don't have a clue how to try and work backwards to the keywords from the
cribs using this, but I'm hoping that by throwing it out here, someone with
more experience than me can do it.  (Or can definitively shoot it down as a
possibility - I'd be good with that, too.)

Step 1: Take a phrase of the proper length (92 characters for this - the
other 5 will be added later). Remove spaces (but remember where the word
breaks are)
 SANBORNCREATEDKRYPTOSFORTHECIAANDDESPITEBERLINCLOCKANDEASTNORTHEASTITHASNOTBEENSOLVEDCANITBE

Step 2: Break it up into six shorter strings (ideally on word breaks) such
that 1, 3, and 5 have the same total length as 2, 4, and 6.  Stack the
sets.  (Six is arbitrary, as long as it's even.  Chosen to match K4 split
on 'W')
 Step 3: Treat each vertical pair as a digraph for Four Square (ignoring
spaces).  I choose Four Square here because the Kryptos sculpture has four
blocks of text, two "plain" and two encrypted, but any similar
digraph-based cipher could work.
 (keys KRYPTOS and YAR, W as the excluded letter).

Step 4: Put the strings back in their original order, and join them with
the excluded letter (W).  This boosts the length to 97.
 ITFTFNFPIKPMPTGIXNNGNWGIQOHRBFRCICCBNPGNCWYTLHOGTGHYDPGTRRNMWMLOSFABQPESFYNWFDMPTRHWQLMTBCBCMESCB

By interlacing words like this, even a normal Foursquare decryption with
the correct keywords would produce gibberish, so it's quite possible that
someone has correctly figured them out in the past but didn't realize it.
 PUKXKRMRRKENAYKNUSSJQOKNVPMEHIEBTAIERTKSGOAXTHIFDJKEMPKYCBTOTLQRHGICXPOQKCQOKHRSCELOYKPYJDJDQIJBJY

The artistry comes from choosing the right phrase such that it conveys a
meaning and breaks up into the correct-length strings along word
boundaries, from using the sculpture itself as a hint, and from whatever
method we're supposed to derive the keywords.  It also involves visual
transforms that are perfectly clear and easy to a person who knows what to
do, but would not be conducive to any kind of standard brute-force or
computer-driven decryption techniques.

So - is this plausible?  Can anyone build on this?

You say you get SIBLE from a +1 Caesar shift of DYAHR. Well, with one exception that you did not comment: Y is shifted all the way to L.
  D Y A H R
+1 13 1 1 1
  E L B  I S   => anagram =>  SIBLE
With a clean +1 you would get SIBZE.

2.
A +2 Ceasar shift is also interesting. Making an exception using +1 for the H, we get:
  D Y A H R
+2 2 2 1 2
  F A C  I T
with the raised letters spelling ACT.
Another one of those gazillion coincidences...

3.
But already without shift, DYAHR and YAR have several "striking" connections to other parts of Kryptos. Many have been pointed out, and I have some that I have not posted yet (I cannot decide if it is worthy of posting or just silly and/or old news).
OK, examples: (Sorry, these are not DYAHR shifts so off-topic again!)
3.0. Not mentioning RAY and all its interpretations. Nor HYDRA. Nor HARDY. Nor RHYAD whatever that is.
3.1. YAR appearing in the lower right corner of K4.
3.2. Numbering the letters after the KRYPTOSABC alphabet, starting with 1, we get 11 3 8 15 2. YA=38 coincides with the number of degrees north in K2. Incidentally, the famous partial decrypt that gives "BERLINPEEK", takes an 11-letter key from the start of K1, and then modular transposition with step 38. This sure looks like a decent clue for that (well, after the fact). How to interpret 15 and 2 is unclear. (Obviously I have tried variations of using a 15-letter key and step 2...)
3.3. Considering the line endings in K4, "..KR" and "...YP", the matching tableau lines with these endings are labeled Y and A, respectively.
3.4. Considering the last 5 columns of K4, there are KRYP(T)OS letters, ABC, an odd N, and in column -5 bottom-up there is "EFG?". You might argue there are missing letters (T), D and H, coinciding with the non-raised letters in DYAHR. (If you add the first column to this alphabet soup you fill in the missing T, and add UV....)

Throughout my time studying and building theories relating to Kryptos, I’ve always envisioned Sanborn creating the Kryptos codes under the guiding hand of  Ed Scheidt, being educated in a master’s craft much like a student in a classroom.

From it, we leaned that Sanborn had an uninvolved project leader who was not Scheidt, and that his work with Scheidt was limited to the gift of a primer and whatever time they had together in a few  sessions- three? Four? Half dozen?  As a novice myself, I’d say that probably still puts him well below the level of most of the actual skilled cryptanalysts/cryptographers in this forum.

The point?

As an observer, I note that while this may change for someone with skills, the amateur can control their plaintext far better than their ciphertext. This would mean that the most sophistication in placing intentional clues is going to come from the PT limiting CT to items like DY A HR.

Again, the point?

HYDRA arRAYS. There’s a HYDRA-like relationship between PT and CT – With many ciphers, no matter how much you may change the arrays (columns/rows) the body is the same). The same holds true of bodies of ciphertext. Examples:

Primary Array – K3 treats L and S in key positions as WW KNOWS Morsified ciphertext.

AST BALLOON Array – If I shape K4 CT  like an aerostat balloon, LUCID and a giant T appear in key positions – the corners and the gondala / car / rack.

TUT Array – If I flatten the entirety of K1-K4 PT in rows of 24, a mixed Acrostic cipher can be found in the beginning and ending columns, an effect similar to King Tut’s Wishing Cup.

Other items are found in different arrays, and choosing which relies on the Morse Stones. The Plaintext helps, but is not necessary.

Conclusion: There is something like a “SOLUTION Array” which Sanborn might refer to as an “Original Matrix”

The copy of Jim's K1 worksheet shows the final PT "n" on its own row, in order to call attention to it.   Now "n" is equivalent to 14 & "c", as in palimp c est" to 3 (standard alph.).  Thence we conclude that as 14+3=17≅Q, the PT "Q" is to be replaced by PT "nc", giving "i nc lusion".   Adam is clearly on the right track, as there is little which he has not included in his theory.   Besides, "Between subtle shading and the absence of light, lies the nuance of inclusion" sounds so upbeat, and All-American, and downright melting-potly inclusive , just the sort of thing the CIA wanted the sculpture to be.

As ever,
Carl Ellis

I’ve been thinking about the misspelled words in K1, K2 and K3.  Based on this pattern, there is going to be another misspelled word in K4.
I believe the letters that are switched/missing can be arranged into the following order:
E_ EQUAL_ O

If this arrangement is correct, I can deduce two things.
First, the misspelled word in K4 will include an “S”.
Second, the O is most likely to be treated as a Zero.

For instance, if the misspelled word includes a C instead of an S, the following would be true:

My next step to solving K5 would be to find the intersection of E and C on the KRYPTOS Vigenere panels and treat that as the new starting point for the Abscissa and Ordinate axises.

Based on this line of thinking I am concerned that the E-A-S-T clue we just received for K4 (and that JS chose not to provide back in January) may include the misspelling and that would explain why he changed his mind about releasing it originally.

a slik abscissa out of a sow's YAhR:

1.  Arrange the ordinal values of YAhR by the year of the geodetic marker followed by what's left, so:  (AhYR)5-6-4-7
     (incidentally, 1/6 the K3 text length followed by the ratio thereof for the repeat interval, i.e., 4/7)

2.  Add 3 to each digit (because we're working that 1/6 back toward a whole 1.  Or because this is K3, or because JIM has 3 letters, or because good stuff comes in threes.)

3.  Translate your resulting string of 8-9-7-10 via the KRYPTOS alphabet (ABSC)

4.  Find the word in your dictionary which is exactly double this length (our 1/6 is now restored by 3 & 2 to a full-size K3 text length), i.e. 8 letters long.

    Voilà, K1 message key.   A possibility at least?

    Carl Ellis

s: The new hint is not only EAST but also 97
t: Not sure if it matters, but east-northeast of the (original) location of the Berlin Clock is the museum that houses perhaps the second best known treasure from Egypt (after the Tut Mask) - is the Bust of Nefertiti.

For what it's worth, an observation about the alternative ending of K2 that I have not seen reported. So I felt I should mention it for the sake of complete information.

Sidenote: It's hard to search messages for these things, but a search for HEATZIDBYROWS gives nothing. Searching for the classic IDBYROWS obviously gives many hits but I don't think the search engine incudes words longer than what you search for. (For example, 'eastnortheast' is not a search hit if you only search for 'northeast'.) Consequently, I confirmed that a search for 'DBYROWS' gives nothing.

Suppose you accept Sanborn's claim that a mistake was made in K2 and the intended and correct CT includes the missing "S", and it decrypts to "...WESTXLAYERTWO".
I personally prefer this state of affairs because I think it's a much better puzzle if we are given "Layer two" as the direct clue, it clearly tells us to go looking for whatever that is.
So given that this is the correct CT, then shifting the keyword one position actually gives the alternative ending "...HEATZIDBYROWS".

There are several interpretations: HEAT, EAT, AT; most likely "AT Z ID BY ROWS" (or "ROW S").

...or it's still just good old "ID BY ROWS" (if we should only look at the 8 chars following "WESTX"), ...or it is all just coincidential extra plaintext with no intended bearing at all -- only WW knows. Or rather, only JS knows.

Here is another observation that I ought to report for what it's worth.

Take the famous coordinates from K2 pt: 38, 57, 6.5; 77, 8, 44
Remove all punctuation and view it only as a string of single digits: 3 8 5 7 6 5 7 7 8 4 4
Translate to letters using KRYPTOSABC with K=1 etc: YATSOTSSAPP
Read backwards: PPASSTOSTAY
"(P) PASS TO STAY".

(Alternate numbering with K=0 etc gives PBOASOAABTT, and I can't make anything much out of that. I'm poor at anagrams...)
(Normal alphabet, A=1: CHEGFEGGHDD)
(Normal alphabet, A=0: DIFHGFHHIEE)

That's all folks.

The other thing I don't recall seeing remarked on is the interpretations when the beginning of K3 CT is joined to the K2 PT(s):  "ID BY ROWS END" & "LAYER TWO END".  As we have reason to be well aware, Kryptos is full of anomalies which must often be coincidences, but "END" occurring where it does stretches my skepticism.

Carl

Hello to everyone in the group.

My name is Florent Guépin, and I'm a cryptographic student in France.
I wanted to share here some of my though that I had for quite a long time from now.

First of all, we are all aware of the famous 'X Can you see anything Q ?'. For what is worth, this is the only occurence of X and Q in the whole K3 part. When we have a look at the original text, it's like parts with X and Q were ommited intentionally. So, I digged. And I came with the following:

As a starting point, the 'Q'. The mispell of 'palimpsest' with a 'C' is quite ... obvious for someone working on it. As a result, this error count. we have 'iqlusion' instead of 'illusion' -> Q in place of L. Then, one row comes with an extra 'L' in the alphabetic part. Let's take the row for our alphabet.

Next, the 'X'. If you look at K2, and you're taking all 'X' from the PT, and their correspondance in the CT, you obtain the work 'astatos'. On a first sight, this is totally random. BUT : 1 'astatos' is greek, it means fickle in english. (reminder : kryptos is also greek, and means hidden). 2 no manipulation are needed, this is straightforward. Big coincidence. 3 If you don't have the last 's', the word becomes 'astato' meaning unstable, and this become a false clue.

So far, we used clues from K1,K2,K3, not necessarly needed for K4; but definitly helpfull. Also, we have what looks like another Q3 Vigenere. However, this did not hit the PT.

So I worked around : I coded a brut force Q3Vigenere, looking at all the possible english words. I obtained hits for east, north, berlin and clock using different keys, but all with the fickle-alphabet. Results : if east had several hits, only 1 hit for north, berlin and clock. By looking at probability, this is normal to have several htis for east, but only 1 for others are worth telling.

I believe it to be something good to share with the group, it used several clues from all parts, it wasn't difficult enough to be impossible, and it's logic. I believe that so many coincidence is rare, not impossible, but rare. So, digging into some masks before this encryption, or after, might be the solution. Possible use of transposition ?

Also, I noticed that noone, to the best of my knowledge, has mentionned the 'astatos' or 'fickle' clue before.

Hope it helped, or gave some thought.

FG

s: Kryptos: From the Cradle to the Grave
t:
Treasures, and their relationship to Kryptos.

Tut’s Death Mask

Layer 1 CT – Death Mask forehead patterning (ABSCISSA+DIAGONAL) found in the combination of the reflected Tableau with the Kryptos CT.
Layer 2 – PT – K3 deciphers to a heavily modified text on the discovery of Tut’s Tomb.

Lotus Chalice/Alabaster Chalice

Layer 1 CT – Appears to be a wordplay using the Morse Code Ruleset on DY A HR and DIGETAL INTERPRET A-T U, creating an throne name. This is overcomplicated however, requiring the misspelling clue of Undergruund and the greek interpretation of an Upsilon (Y) as a U, and stacks badly on top of the existing and far simpler SIBLE clues. PT is clearly the shorter way with better clues.
Layer 2 PT – K1-K4 Acrostic encircles the flattened plaintext with interruptions much like the patterning of the text encircling the top of Tut’s Chalice.

This patterning, I believe, is not terribly different from the Atbash cipher – Two sentences run in opposite directions from the central ankh on the rim of the cup.

“May your ka live, may you spend millions of years, you, who love Thebes, sitting with your face to the north wind, your eyes beholding happiness”

The elongated Throne Name runs opposite.

Bust of Nefertiti

Layer 1 CT –  Shadow pattern of the Eye on the back of Kryptos matches that of the bust, though it is unclear as to whether it is the “blind” right eye or the normal left eye.  Perhaps nuance suggests both. See also SIBYL/SIBLE strings. Reference to a “BUST KWOTE” may be part of a similar acrostic in K4 CT.
Layer 2 PT – Bust perfectly symmetrical and signals the flattening of the disrupted symmetry in K3-K4

Conclusion: The implied "Wondrous Things" in K3 is in itself a reference to set of clues found within Tut’s Tomb in the form of its treasures, treasures Sanborn had the great fortune to examine directly.

Further clues to the method and mask for K4 may be found in further examination or other treasures.

Speculation: The recurrence of “Cribs” contrasting with the Tomb and the peculiar fusion of Egyptian/Greek culture at the time may hint at a “Cradle to the Grave” theme.

Hello,

A quick introduction: My name is A.J. Jacobs, and I’m a non-fiction author
(my most well-known book is ‘The Year of Living Biblically’).

My next book will be published next year, and the topic is my love of
puzzles. It will be a cultural history of puzzles combined with my
experience trying to solve some of my favorite puzzles. I have chapters on
several different types of puzzles (crosswords, logic, mechanical puzzles,
etc.)

I have a chapter devoted to codes and ciphers. And, of course, Kryptos
plays a large part in that chapter. I love Kryptos and the community that
has formed in the quest to crack it.

For the cipher chapter, I had the pleasure of interviewing Elonka Dunin
several weeks ago. Then, a few days ago, I emailed Jim Sanborn and asked to
interview him for the book. To my surprise and delight, he said yes.

I spoke to Jim for about an hour. I found him charming, smart, interesting
and forthcoming. Well, forthcoming on some things. He didn’t tell me the
answer to K4 or K4, of course.

But he did talk about the process of creating Kryptos, the recent clue, and
several other topics.

The interview was on the record, so I feel comfortable sharing with the
Kryptos community the highlights of what he said. I don’t think Jim will
have any objection to me sharing what I learned. (Though I do feel
reluctant to paste the entire transcript, since I didn’t ask his permission
to do so).

I’m sharing the parts that I hope might help the community crack Kryptos.
Many of these have already been covered in other interviews. But I’m
hopeful there are a few new nuggets or nuances that are new. Some of you
will surely know better than me what is new. (I tried to read everything I
could before the interview, but I’m sure I missed things)

Jim made it clear to me that he granted me an interview because I am
writing a book, not because I am a solver. He stressed that he really does
NOT like being asked questions by solvers (not counting on formal
occasions, such as the occasional meals hosted by Elonka). In general, Jim
said his only communication will be a ‘yes’ or ‘no’ to proposed complete
solutions of K4 (not to partial solutions).

So please don’t see my interview as evidence that Jim is willing to talk or
answer questions in general. I feel I got very lucky.

Also, I am a writer, not a cryptanalyst. I’m decent at crossword puzzles,
but I’m no expert at decoding ciphers. I’ve spent several hours working on
K4, but haven’t made any headway.

I have gone over the main points of the interview with Elonka, and got her
opinion on what would be most helpful. So that is what I'm presenting.

I hope you find them interesting and even illuminating. And I’m sorry if I
missed crucial questions or opportunities. I did the best I could!

Happy to answer any questions to the best of my ability.

Last point before the highlights:

I am scheduled to visit Kryptos in person as soon as Covid allows. If you
have anything you’d like me to look for or ask about, please let me know.

Thank you!!

(Excerpts from the interview are in Files/Personal Folder/AJ Jacobs)
--
A.J. Jacobs

ajjacobs.com
@ajjacobs

If LeCarre was the actual writer, I'm guessing the time spent was as a consultation to separate fact from fiction and get a feel for what he wanted to convey in his Kryptos piece as an artist. While we've probably all got a rough view of what it's like to be a spy, there's a big difference between field work and megalomaniacal plots to overthrow the world or disrupting globe-spanning terrorist cells or what have you.

The gut response might be that he'd gotten that from Scheidt with the cryptography insights, but looking at Sanborn's 2009 Oral History, it doesn't seem they spent that much time together.

Thanks for doing the interview. I think I've read almost everything available from the media now published on the sculpture and I'm not often surprised by new quotes.

I think what you got was versions of what Sanborn said before, perhaps rhyming not repeating. The new part was about the thinking around releasing EAST NORTH EAST in parts.

I think to get the full picture, it'd be best to interview Ed Scheidt as well.

You have quotes in the interview like: Sanborn wanted to "make it as difficult as possible" and he hoped "the [K4 code] would outlive him".

This would seem to imply Sanborn doesn't want K4 solved, or doesn't care.

But the consistently stated intention of Scheidt in many interviews has been that it would be difficult, but solvable within 5, 7, or 10 years. This is really _quite different_ to what Sanborn said.

Right from the start (January 1990) the media articles stated "The secret phrase has been inscribed using two codes - one invented in 1586 by Blaise de Vigenere, a French diplomat, and the other devised by an unidentified cryptographer especially for the sculpture.".

In 1991, Scheidt said he didn't know what the sculpture said; later in 2015, he said he'd gone back and checked K1-3 but not K4.

Would-be solvers are starting to realize that with so much plaintext released and nobody seemingly closer to a solution

(a) it seems more likely that Sanborn could release the whole plaintext without the method becoming any clearer;
(b) the encryption method must be quite complex if knowing 25% of the plaintext doesn't appear to help;
(c) the timeline is absolutely defying the Scheidt expressed intention particularly with so many "hints"

And following on from (c), computer power, networks, storage, and algorithms for solving classical ciphers have improved massively in the last 30 years.

So given all those, plus the continued attention of many crypto experts I've been in touch with, plus the Scheidt expressed intention, we seriously wonder if there's been a mistake in K4 encryption.
Or if Sanborn has "accidentally" made solution impossible by cooking up a new system that can't be solved at this length of cipher. (This is the theory of one of the best contributors here, Jim Melichar).

We see accidental mistakes in the other sections (IQLUSION based on accidentally misspelling the PALIMPSEST keyword once, UNDERGRUUND fixed on another "version" of Kryptos, Antipodes).

Scheidt said in 2005 he was "confident" the encryption had been done correctly; does he still think that?

Because given computer power now, if anybody had guessed the method, the search would be done in an instant...

And was Scheidt's intention that the encryption method could be derived from statistical properties of the K4 ciphertext? This is the working assumption.

(I understand he often deflects that kind of very specific question by saying it's a "Jim question")

People spend time on this because of the reputation of Scheidt. Not Sanborn.

Thanks again

This would explain the half-blind combined visible and shifted+1 near the end of K3 (NY-OUS=NY-PVT)

Conclusion: The system Sanborn devised under Scheidt's guidance may allow for more flexibility in CT than would normally be available to an utter novice.

I just finished reading the historical novel Voices Under Berlin by T.H.E. Hill which describes the CIA tunnel operation to tape Russian communication cables.  It's a good read -- highly recommended.

CIA built a warehouse and dug a tunnel down and across the border to the cables.  This was a major feat in tunnel building technology.

Seems to correspond to K2

"It" was totally invisible (concealed by the warehouse)

How was "that" possible (tunneling up to the cables)
They used the earth's magnetic field (to work entirely underground, dig a tunnel, and come up precisely where the cables were located)

Information was transmitted underground (via the tunnel) to an unknown (to the Russians) location.

From a CIA report on the project, "no one had ever tunneled 1,476 feet under clandestine conditions with the expectation of hitting a target two inches in diameter and 27 inches below a main German/Soviet highway."

In the novel, a faulty tap causes communication noise, which was then investigated by the Russians.  Communication cables are contained in pressurized sheaths, such that a cable break results in a hissing sound that can be located.  When the Russians dug up the faulty cable, they fell 13 feet down into the chamber at the tap end of the tunnel.

Seems to correspond to K3's "hot air escaping the chanber..."

The CIA report refers to workmen discovering the chamber and making a tiny hole to breach the chamber, and then widening the hole to inspect the chamber contents.

If K2 refers to the construction, and K3 the compromise, of the CIA tunnel under Berlin, what might K4 refer to as what happened next?  Maybe the subsequent discovery of the tunnel shaft after the initial discovery of the chamber room at the cable tap site.  The tunnel runs eastward from the warehouse in the American sector into the Soviet sector;  does anyone know:  does the tunnel run east northeast?

There are numerous references to clocks in the novel, that Berlin seemed to have a public clock on every street corner, etc.  Also references to clock merchants, clock repairmen, clock craftsmen etc.

In the CIA report, the discovery of the tap was initially ascribed to bad luck.  However, subsequent analysis revealed that the operation had been compromised by a mole, George Blake.

Not sure how to interpret K1 -- maybe something along the lines of is spying legal:  it's not black and white, but 1,000 shades of gray.

While I appreciate the shout, and I've been gone a long, long time, with today being the day I randomly decided to show up again, some of the best contributors here were all well before my time spent toiling on various encryption methods.

One-off systems do become fast unsolvable, especially when there is an unknown pattern or transposition. My contention has always been (and shall remain), that if you want to make something solvable there are some pretty strict criteria that need to be in place. Those are the things I think Ed Scheidt thought about, but that Jim Sanborn did/does not.

Making something unsolvable is trivial, especially at ~100 characters. I still point to Chaocipher, and it's relative simply encryption method, plethora of both plain and ciphertext and it took the release of how the system works for anyone to really solve the challenge ciphers after about 100 years.

Unless Jim is more forthcoming about how it works, I don't think K4 can be solved. I think it's cool to brainstorm how _you_ or _someone_ might do something similar, but I think trying to match the creative side of Jim's brain and guess what he did is a pretty open-ended endeavor. It's why I always want to believe what Ed said, that an op could show up and not have to remember anything, because it's all self-contained at the sculpture. But it's looking less and less like Ed had any impact on how K4 was designed.

Take for example, any classical encryption method. Encrypt your plaintext. Then send it through some patterned based transposition (that you don't share with anyone), and finally cap it off with just using a simple cipher wheel to make a final substitution to completely flatten the distribution, rotating said wheel one click after each substitution. You'd have a completely unsolvable ciphertext. With no clues to which classical method was used, no clues to what pattern transposition was used and only left to guess if the cipher wheel idea was the actual method for flattening the distribution you'd never solve it.

Jim

Jim M.,

Good to see you again. Several others of us also popped back in here (and
in other groups), just recently, when EAST came out. Your timing is good,
because we all need a reminder, from someone like you, of how bad K-4 might
really be.

We've picked up pretty much where we left off a year and a half ago, back
in early March of 2019, when Sanborn provided us with his discouraging "I
ran it through a washing machine" explanation.

The possible outcomes now, as then, seem to be:

1. It's encrypted in a cryptographically sound, communications-usable,
"difficult but fair game" cipher.

2a. It's NOT encrypted in a cryptographically sound, communications-usable,
"difficult but fair game" cipher--and therefore is not reversible, except
by going back in time and seeing what kind of random activity he used as
his so-called system.

2b. It's NOT encrypted in a cryptographically sound, communications-usable,
"difficult but fair game" cipher--BUT we might still be able to detect,
generally, some features of what he *meant *to do or *should *have done,
even if a full solution is impossible.

Of course, Outcome #1 would be the most satisfying.

And Outcome #2a could be the sorry case without us ever even knowing that
that's what it is.

But Outcome #2b could give a certain small amount of satisfaction, if the
forensics lead to a *convincing *reconstruction of what Sanborn did. In
other words, if the majority of his process can be identified, and if it
can be proved that his steps are not a valid (decryptable/reversible)
encryption system, then we could declare as cryptanalysts that our job is
done. For another effort that's sort of like that, look at how some
productive analysis can be done on B-1 and B-3 of the Beale papers, which
contain no legitimate plaintext (or ciphertext, of course) and yet show
evidence of a pool of pseudorandom letters that their creator drew from. As
in real life, a cryptanalyst's job is not necessarily to *solve *a
cryptogram; it's to *analyze *it and to report on the findings. In some
cases that means identifying it as either not containing a message (e.g.,
dummy text to waste the enemy's time) or as being otherwise unsolvable
(e.g., OTP, hopeless garble, small message fragment, etc.). That would be
the tiniest of consolation, but at least there'd be some closure.

Bill Briere

Bill, good to hear from you as well.

I think my main point is that the narrative around Kryptos needs to change, and Jim Sanborn needs to hear it. At this point ego and pride are getting in the way of actually getting an answer to "is this a fair challenge?" His working assumption is there is a group of 3,000 people plus many others all over the world, pouring over his "clues" trying to decipher K4. That we're all in awe of his genius and are just hoping to unravel exactly what he did.

That may have been true 10-20 years ago, but now, now we're all pretty damn aware of just what happened. Jim went rogue and created something that has layered encryption steps and cannot be solved. Making it worse yet is that Ed gave him instruction on how to erase the English language statistics, which is the only thing we actually "know" from looking at the ciphertext that is K4.

I have no doubt that Ed sat with Jim while Jim chose the systems to be used for all four parts of Kryptos, because Ed alluded to that. What I no longer believe is that a "fair challenge" was created, because Jim has zero understanding of the impact of laying systems. None at all. Maybe less than none if that's possible. To him, it's just mixing up some letters and making some substitutions and "someone smarter than me will come along and surely be able to solve it". That's just simply not how it works.

From Ed's own mouth just a few short years ago:

"I mentioned earlier and I had mentioned in public that there is a masking technique applied so that, uh, the English language wouldn't be that readable"

"I'd say this is a multi-stage encryption"

"Some things that you should have seen is the impact of some kind of math function on the English language, uh, and now, because the tools you had been using or would be using are tools that's based on the periodicity of letters and things like that in existing codes and so there's a mask of some type that now you don't have that as your initial tool. [I've] got to remember your process as well as what you're trying to do. Uh, and most folks the process is let me see how many vowels I have and the weighting of Es and things like that and that will give you some insight. Now added to that is, uh, the math associated with the cryptography in the sense of substitution, transposition."

"The other intent was well is there a way to make the challenge so that the first step is not that and now that gets to be hard, and that's what you all are facing."

"You have been put into the posture of re-creating without having prior knowledge."

We have to flip the narrative on this entire thing. Put the onus back on Jim to prove that what he created is not unsolvable and an utter waste of anyone's time. Teach him why doing even 2-3 very simple things yields something unsolvable. Especially if you leave the author to his own devices around one-off transpositions. Jim wouldn't continue to check solutions and release plaintext if he didn't want some of the spotlight that goes with this and some part of him didn't WANT to see it solved.

At the end of the day, there aren't any direct clues as to which substitution sysytem/systems are in play, the masking technique has been purposely obfuscated and may be a one-off creation from Scheidt, and we have no idea if transposition also entered the mix as an additional layer. All of that makes this unsolvable and an unfair challenge.

Jim

s: Two forgotten hints from John Schwartz (1999) Washington Post article
t:
Thank you John for your lovely Washington Post article "Cracking the Code of a CIA Sculpture" (John Schwartz, 1999)! There were two hints that really stood out.

[Labor of Love]
Some were working from photographs, but Sanborn had placed the stones around the sculpture strategically, so that a photo could not capture all of the elements. Transcriptions of the letters had begun floating around the Internet, but most of them did not fully show the slight misalignment of some letters along the matrix, which might figure in unlocking the secrets.

[Close to a Breakthrough]
Stein told friends about his partial success, and they suggested that he conduct a briefing. Stein agreed, and prepared quite a few viewgraphs, even though he expected perhaps 30 people to show up. In fact, once word got out that the puzzle had been largely cracked, the event had to be moved to an auditorium; some 250 people showed up. "Ed came up to me after the briefing," Stein recalls, "and said 'the solution is correct, but you didn't do it in the way I intended you to do it."

The first [Labor of Love] provides evidence of stenography in K4 with strategic stones and combined with the second part [Close to a Breakthrough], the misalignment of letters along the matrix likely refers to the K1-K3 key recovery as Scheidt's original intention.

Bill, this is outcome #1b It's encrypted in a cryptographically sound, communications-usable, "difficult but fair game" TRIPLE-LAYERED CLASSICAL cipher. Layer one and three have already been removed, so once LAYERTWO has been solved, K4 can be decrypted. Also, with the EAST hint, the ABCDEFG standard alphabet cannot be used, but KRYPTOSABC is still a valid alphabet.

I think that if you take what Sanborn said here at face value, it explains a lot about why the classical methods no longer apply in K4.

" And he also gave me some ideas for contemporary coding systems, more sophisticated systems, systems that didn't necessarily depend on mathematics. That was one of my prerequisites. So he told me about matrix codes and things like that. These are the parts of Kryptos that have already been cracked. So I can discuss them. But he told me about coding systems that I could then modify in a myriad of ways. So that even he would not know what it says. Okay? So that was very seductive to me. And so I took those things."

Basically, all classical systems are out the door, and this system involves modifiable codes which makes them not necessarily "new" but unique to the creator. Because of that quirk or peccadillo, however you choose to view it, it means that it becomes necessary to rely on a simplified sense of Fair Play from the creator, which means adhering to his theme of Intelligence Gathering and finding preloaded clues (as one agent might to another if they chose to indulge in this exercise )that have been laid down in the CT, the PT or both. I believe that it can be done either way and that there's a ridiculously hard way and a somewhat.... easier way.

And you'd be absolutely right in guessing I'm thinking that while it might indulge the "agent communications" puzzle, it would be completely ridiculous in real life field work. But he is an artist, not an agent.

s: Thinking Through The Solution Space, Masking Before/After Encryption
t:
As I said in another message today, I've been gone a long time, with not many thoughts on Kryptos. Though I had done a little thinking, mostly out of fun rather than pursuing an actual solution to K4.

Here are some things I came up with, none of which are interesting at all in terms of solving K4, in case you want to check out now.

Every single classical substitution method is still in play. All of them. Vigenere, Playfair, Bifid, Foursquare, etc. None can ostensibly be ruled out by anything we know. Which brings me to my next brainstorm/thought.

Masking the English characteristics, and whether you'd mask before enrcypting verus after encryption.  Well that really depends on what your classical encryption method does, doesn't it?

If my encryption method leaves only 25 of 26 English letters in the ciphertext, such as the Polybius square encryption methods, then I'd want to apply my masking technique AFTER the encryption, because that would allow for all 26 letters to come into play for the final ciphertext. If I applied it first, and then applied the Polybius square method that would leave the analyst with some idea of what was in play.

Conversely, if my encryption method is something like Vigenere, I could apply my distribution flattening masking technique before or after, it would make no difference. Both outcomes would be similar.

For the periodic ciphers, perhaps part of masking of the English language statistics is removing the periodicity. Using transposition to diffuse the structure of the classical encryption method. Again, that could be applied prior to encryption, or after, having the same effect.

The only thing we really know for "certain" is that some kind of dynamic substitution was used to provide the 3.6 IC we see in K4. You just aren't going to achieve that any other way. What that was, I guess could be anything.

Whether or not transposition was used in tandem with this substitution is a complete and utter unknown. I'd contend that without some pointed comments from the creator of the challenge (Jim Sanborn), if there's a transposition in play and no clue to what it is you're poking around in a 9.6^151 solution space for just the transposition with no real way of limiting it past that.

Not even the best computer on the planet that Jim Sanborn can dream up can do anything with that, and that's before putting an unknown substitution on top of it.

A similar and interesting system, based on a known sequence of numbers, such as PI , E, fibbonnacci.  Mr. Parkhe's example below:

---------------------

"How-do-I-perform-encryption-and-decryption-using-fibonacci-series"
Kishor Parkhe
---

Source Message is: abcd

Password is: xyz

Steps in the Encryption Algorithm

1. The source message is reversed i.e abcd is written as dcba.

2. The password is appended i.e the cipher text becomes dcbaxyz.

3. The Fibonacci series, up to the length of the password is generated. In our case, the password length is 3, so the first three Fibonacci terms viz. 1, 1, 2 are generated. Start the Fibonacci series from 1 instead of 0.

4. Every element in odd position in the cipher text is forwarded by the current Fibonacci term, i.e. in the first iteration all odd indexed elements would be advanced by 1, in the second iteration by 1, in the third iteration by 2 and so on. Once 'z' is reached, we wrap around i.e. if we forward 'z' or 'Z' by 1 the output would be 'a' or 'A'.   Similarly, every element in even position in the cipher text is reversed by the current Fibonacci term, i.e. in the first iteration all even elements would be reversed by 1, in the next iteration by 1, in the next by 2 and so on. Once 'a' is reached, wrap around i.e. if we reverse 'a' or 'A' by 1 the output would be 'z' or 'Z'.

5. So, in our case the Encryption iteration for the cipher text 'dcbaxyz' would be,

* ebczyxa when the current fibonacci term is 1

* fadyzwb when the current fibonacci term is 1

* hyfwbud when the current fibonacci term is 2

6. So, our resultant encrypted string would be 'hyfwbud'.

Decryption operation is the reverse of encryption operation. For e.g. if encrypted text is 'hyfwbud', and password is xyz, then the decryption steps are as below:

* Password length is 3, hence number of Fibonacci terms are 3 viz. 1, 1, 2

* First iteration on encrypted text when the current fibonacci term is 1 will be gzexavc

* Second iteration on gzexavc when the current fibonacci term is 1 will be fadyzwb

* Third iteration on fadyzwb when the current fibonacci term is 2 will be dcbaxyz

* If L is the password length, 3 in this case, then extract last L characters from ciphertext i.e. dcbaxyz and match it with password provided in input.

* If password matches, reverse the remaining text which will be the original clear text i.e. abcd

* If password does not match, then clear text cannot be obtained. See output specifications for more details

Your task would be encrypt or decrypt a given list of strings based on two inputs, viz. file name and password. The file referred to by the file name consists of the clear text strings to be encrypted or ciphertext to be decrypted, respectively.

Jim M.,

Hi Jim,

K4 is encoded using classical ciphers of both substitution and transposition in three unique steps, so it really an individual cipher.

The only necessary hints and assumptions required:
1. Classical ciphers are used (i.e. substitution and transpositions)
2. A 1:1 CT:PT relationship is TRUE
3. K4 is 97 letters
4. (2010) BERLIN crib - reveals at least 1 substitution required (LAYERTHREE)
5. (2014) CLOCK crib - reveals at least 1 transposition required (LAYERTWO)
6. (2020) NORTH crib - reveals at least 1 masking layer (LAYERONE)
7. (2020) EAST crib - rules out the standard alphabet (KRYPTOSABC still valid)

Well, actually, likely the exact opposite.

This account isn't any different than what Ed Scheidt told us 5 years ago. He said he sat down with Sanborn, taught him less than 10 systems for encryption and gave him ways to modify them. Ways to modify classical encryption methods. He also gave him a tool to remove the English language statistics, which we can see Jim also applied.

Take the railfence transposition for example. You could "teach" Sanborn that the first letter is down, the second letter is up and repeat the pattern. Great, one system of transposition down. But you could give him away to modify/personalize it by saying "you know, you don't have to do up/down/up/down/up/down and it could be any number of rails not just two, it could be 18, and the pattern could be anything you want".

You could teach him Playfair and say, "but hey, you don't have to just use the square in the same position, you could rotate the square 90 degrees each time, this will change the outcome. Or you could rotate it backwards once, then forward two times, then backwards again".

You could teach him about "matrix codes" as he loves to refer to them, which are anything Jim can write on graph paper apparently. You can then teach him to write things in vertically instead of horizontally, and vice versa, or that he could write it in diagonally. All of those things would be modifications to existing systems.

And that's the problem here, if everything under the sun is in play, there's no way to reasonably find the answer. Jim seems to have eliminated everything from the courtyard, everything from prior plaintext and everything unqiue from the sculpture (raise letters, extra L, etc etc), so what that tells me is that there are no clues and we're just supposed to guess. Because Jim probably thinks that's how these things get solved, because he has no frame of reference to understand that's not how it works.

Jim

I have pondered the idea of 3 layers of encryption. I had thought about what if it had something to with the way each of the previous sections was encrypted. This obviously led to a dead end because K1 and K2 both used Vigenere (substitution). But upon reading this again I thought about it some more and not just the cipher that was used, but what was done with the text.

**This is not just my final conclusion but my train of thought as I was going through this. Sorry if it throws anyone off or confuses. But I just wanted to include everything incase something I say sparks an idea for someone else like these recent messages have for me. - Also note I use polybius square as an example of a matrix

My first thought was about the end of K2 and how a letter had to be added in order for it to be read properly. But since K4 CT and PT are both 97 letters one or more would have to be ignored or removed in order for others to be added. This led me back to K1 with "the absence of light" this could be represented by the letter C which occurs twice in K4. However even if this was the case it shouldn't necessarily make the entire message unreadable only the text before, after, or letters that were not di/tri graphed with those.

As it so happens though I can never seem to only think of part of K1. Anytime I think about "the absence of light" I always also think back to "subtle shading" and vice versa. This then led me back to the idea of 3 layer encryption. Subtle shading (substitution) possibly subtle meaning simple, maybe even as a shift across the alphabet (like Caesar) or an atbash. Absence of light could be tied in, or it could be nothing. If it is tied in it could be C is moved or removed from either of those methods. It could also be removed from a 5x5 Polybius or 2square. I also pondered the idea of removing C from the key like how X was omitted from K2 and see if it produced a different result (this came out gibberish in different ways but maybe could be encrypted itself or a key- both unlikely.) I also thought about removing C from abscissa or using the letters at C of abscissa to find letters but never proceeded with it.

So then if K1 represents substitution and K3 represents transposition (maybe the text suggests something more) what kind of encryption is K2? Well the first thing again goes back to the removed letter. However even though that is still on the table it seems more like it was just left as a clue to suggest this multilayered encryption. So I looked through and read K2 again and again trying to find anything that is suggestive of a cipher. First obvious thing would be Morse code since the message is like a transmission, the letters could be converted to Morse and then with K3 transposed and put back together. The problem with this theoretically would be that they don't go back together in a way that produces letters, which is something I encountered when playing with ITA 1&2. So what else could be done with it. Well the garbled Morse from the courtyard could be used as an XOR but if the courtyard is ruled out then would the agent from the future have received these Morse messages? So I nixed that idea as well. Read over it some more times and started thinking about the text itself again, what about this section makes it unique. Well it has the X's as the 'stop' for each message, this could be used as a grille. But then I had another idea based on the X's. They separate/split-up the message - Fractionation - popped into my head. It could have been fractionated using something like a Polybius square or several other methods and this could again allow for "the absence of light" to be applied. The only problem with this idea I have encountered so far is that all 26 letters appear in K4. So if this is the method then either the fractionating cipher has all 26 letters, possibly even just allowing C to be combined with another letter in the Polybius square and be used or any other combo of squares like I/J. The other possibility is a letter has been modified so that all 26 are visible and during deciphering would then produce an error/spelling mistake.

So if I were to look at it as a 3 layer encryption it would be:
K1 - Substitution
K2 - Fractionation
K3 - Transposition

K3 could be more complex though, I haven't really put much thought into it in terms of this message because transposition just fits. But the other 2 techniques I derived from the PT, not the method in which they were encrypted. There has been lots of talk in the past about widening the breach and removing debris and inserting a candle. So there is quite a bit to be considered with K3 and its possible methods or type of cipher.

Regarding this something to note is that Jim has said that he used a bit of steganography. This could be something related to this, it could be related to K5 or it could even just simply be the signing of the sculpture/art piece with the raised letters YA R matching IJ M on the Vig tableau.

A couple of closing notes regarding the 3 layers of encryption I proposed is that they could be done in either order, with the only known clue being "layer two" in K2. Also the Fractionation and Substitution could be done together as one cipher and this then be a 2 layered encryption. Lastly something I just though of is that the fractionation could be considered periodicity when considering which cipher.

This all fits with the idea of this section being a "modern" cipher for the time. It doesn't necessarily mean it was done by machine or a block cipher, but it could simply be referring to it being superenciphered by means of both substitution and transposition.

(Replying to the quoted post from another thread.)

The described system strikes me as really, really weak.

- If you know or guess that this system is in play, all a cryptanalyst needs to do is run the decryption algorithm iteratively, layer by layer, until the reversed plaintext appears. It will happen sooner or later for one number in the Fibonacci series.

- Every odd character will be Caesar shifted by the same amount. Every even character by another amount. It comes down to a bi-alphabetic cipher with regular periodicity 2. Any medium-long text can easily be broken with a Vigenére assumption. The "Vig key" will be 2 letters long and pseudo random, determined by the length of the Fibonacci series, the only free variable in the system.

- The reversal step does not add any complexity as every letter is independently encrypted. (Does not depend on neighboring letters.)

Amongst the multitude of "Masquerade" hunters, only the team of Barker and
Rousseau recognized the true clues and interpreted them correctly.

Is Kryptos a fair challenge? If it was meant to be a pure cryptanalysis
problem, then decades of technical effort would seem to answer with a very
loud "No".

But if it was designed to require some of the "human element" that Ed
Scheidt has mentioned to see and then properly interpret the clues, the
majority of cryppies would still say "No" -- but Barker and Rousseau might
disagree with them.

Bamber Gascoigne (witness to the burial of the golden hare) wrote a nice
piece on the dark side:
"Tens of thousands of letters from Masqueraders have convinced me that the
human mind has an equal capacity for pattern-matching and self-deception.
While some addicts were busy cooking the riddle, others were more
single-mindedly continuing their own pursuit of the hare quite regardless
of the news that it had been found. Their own theories had come to seem so
convincing that no exterior evidence could refute them. These most
determined of Masqueraders may grudgingly have accepted that a hare of some
sort was dug up at Ampthill, but they believed there would be another hare,
or a better solution, awaiting them at their favourite spot. Kit would
expect them to continue undismayed by the much publicised diversion at
Ampthill and would be looking forward to the day when he would greet them
as the real discoverers of the real puzzle of *Masquerade*. Optimistic
expeditions were still setting out, with shovels and maps, throughout the
summer of 1982."

t:
All good things to remember Dan. I still point to how Kil Williams decided to move things forward. It didn't ruin anything. Even if his challenge was just a pure steganographic challenge rather than encryption, I can see the parallels for a cryptanalysis challenge. I've completed some stego challenges like that as well, so it's not that I lack appreciation for interpreting clues or stepping outside the cryptanalyst role.

Being that this is a cryptographic challenge, that we previously thought was meant to be solved, there should be some hint to the methodology used to encrypt it. I get it, it's not an analysis problem, I think I've made it clear that I understand that much.

However, if you remove the prior passages, the courtyard and the oddities on the sculpture itself, there's really not much left to get you to:

A) What algorithm (for lack of a better word, because even visual things end up being an algorithm) was used to flatten the English character distribution?
B) What else, if anything (substition and/or transposition) was used?

Where do you go hunt? What do you even do with that? Ed has said that you have to first have a hypothesis for how he hid the English language characteristics. That's the crux of the problem. He's taken away your starting position. I like that as a challenge. After you have a hypothesis for that, you'd be hoping that you could recognize the rest of the problem in the familiar way.

I'm barely okay with if we're supposed to guess the masking technique. That's fine if we are, but in a true puzzle there would probably be some clues embedded or lateral thinking involved. Given that it's an analog system, it's a pretty limited set of things, though probably still too open ended for even 3,000 people to guess at. Maybe not, but I don't see anyone even trying to solve the first step of the problem. We mostly gloss over that part because it's inconvenient.

What I'm worried about, is that even after guessing that, that Jim may have layered systems, leaving no way to recognize it. A truly blind approach. I think it's a fair concern given that Jim has no understanding of cryptography which has become more and more apparent as he continues to release plaintext. I think it's a fair ask for him to explain the general idea of what he did to Ed and have the two of them determine if it's actually solvable.

I think the worry from Jim is that if he does that, Ed tells him "oh yeah, you shouldn't have done that" and the legacy is tarnished. Whereas if he refuses to look at it and subject it to review it will still garner attention. I can appreciate that.

Jim

Hi Dan: I've frequently used Bamber's quote to describe what's going on with Forrest Fenn's "Thrill of the Chase." Exactly
the same psychology at work, and perhaps even more so following Fenn's death only 3 months after the treasure was
found.

With Kryptos, I see a lot of complex or convoluted ideas thrown out that if in any way resembled what Jim Sanborn
actually did with K4, then we would have no chance whatsoever of solving it.

My fear is that Jim carried out a masking step first on the plaintext, then performed substitution, and that those two
operations are not commutative. I hold out some hope that they ~are~ commutative, in which case it wouldn't matter
if you unmasked first or last when decrypting.   --Rob

s: Is The Masking Technique Also On Ed's Mini Kryptos?
t:
Geoffrey made a great point in his reply to me which triggered a thought. Sometimes you do have other works to draw from to try and get a glimpse into what could have been done.

I think, as a group, we've really overlooked an opportunity with the "Pre-K" sculpture as Jew-Lee and Bill Briere have dubbed it.

It very much looks like a proof of concept for Ed from Jim so that he can be assured he could execute everything they talked about.

The interesting part is that we seem to have discarded, glossed over, whatever you want to call it, at the end of that cipher.

Despite the fact that Jim cobbled together a miniature "proof of concept" for Kryptos, complete with a "remove a letter to throw off the end of the cipher" like he did in K2, we seem to have put little effort into figuring out "ETRANSEWJ".

CODESMAYBEDIVIDEDINTUTWODIFFERENTCLASSESNAMELYSUBSTITUTIONALANDTRANSPOSITIONALTYPESTHETRANSPOSITIONALBEINGTHEHARDESTTODECHPHERWHTHOUTTHEKEYETRANSEWJ
TIJVMSRSHVXOMCJVXOENAKQUUCLWYXVHZTFGJMKJHGDYRPMASMZZNAKCUEURRHJKLGEMVFMOKCUEURKSVVMZYYZIUTJJUJCZZITRFHVCTXNNVBGIXKJNZFXKTBVYYXNBZYIAKNNVEKPYZIUTJJYCA

I'm making the assumption that the last bit of that plaintext should have read "ETRANSPOS". Maybe it's a leap, but without leaps we don't really gain anything. The last three letters are garbled, but no readable English is gained through any phase shifting or using the GIRASOL alphabet. I'd like to bring attention to this again.

Jim Sanborn permuted the start of his keyword for this piece. He used the initials "GRU" for the Russian intelligence agency, but started by encrypting with the R to make the repeated keyword R-U-G.

Ending the piece with "ETRANEWJ" doesn't make a lot of sense, but ending with "ETRANPOS" fits with what he was doing with the key. If the original plaintext was "ETRANSPOS" which would be like what he did with "GRU", then you could make the assumption there are a few possibilities for what happened.

1. POS was encrypted with the key letters "RUG" and should have been "JUJ". "JUJ" was then put through a post-encryption masking step and output "YCA".
2. POS was put through a pre-encryption masking step and output "EWJ". "EWJ" was then encrypted with the key letters "RUG" and output "YCA".
3. You assume it was all a nasty mistake and he lost his mind for the last three characters
4. He padded out the plaintext with "ETRANEWJ" just for fun

Just figured I'd try to stimulate some thinking around this. If there's a logical, consistent and complete way of getting from JUJ -> YCA or POS -> EWJ we might gain some insight into the masking step for K4.

Jim

Thanks for the interesting ideas, Jim. It surely can't hurt to try this one!

I have nothing brilliant to make those connections from POS -> EWJ or JUJ -> YCA, but I'll throw out one observation and see if you or others can improve upon it or come up with something better:

I'm just looking back at the previous ciphertext of this message, which presumably is considered "fair game" to use in a masking step for the last three letters, in the same way that the K1-K3 ciphertext would be fair game to use in a masking step for K4.

Finding the first P in the ciphertext, going forward 12 letters in the ciphertext we find E.

Finding the second O in the ciphertext, going forward 10 letters in the ciphertext we find W.

Finding the third S in the ciphertext, going forward 14 letters in the ciphertext we find J.
Also from the third S in the ciphertext, going backward 12 letters in the ciphertext we find J.
(And from the fourth and last S in the ciphertext, going forward either 12 or 14 letters in the ciphertext we also find J.)

I've seen so many false leads and patterns and coincidences in the investigation of K4 that I'm no longer wildly excited to find this roughly or potentially pattern-like system to get from POS -> EWJ. It's just a random observation that may or may not mean anything or have any significance whatsoever. But since you asked for ideas, I thought I'd mention it.

Geoffrey

t: Pre-K could conceivably be the Kryptos portion of Jim Sanborn's macquette for the 1988 CIA National Endowment for the Arts panel. I wouldn't look too much into Pre-K for the masking technique, but the shifted plaintext was carried over into K2. So far nobody can justify the missing 'S' in [S]WJLLAETG at the end of K2 beyond the empty matrix spaces of K1+K2 and palindrome when padded to 33 characters.
I have also thought about Pi as a running key, especially since it starts 31, and there's a lot of 31 popping up.

For reference, Elonka’s source: https://www.aaa.si.edu/collections/interviews/oral-history-interview-jim-sanborn-15700#transcript

IMO and ICYMI: The 2009 Sanborn  interview aka Oral History of Herbert James Sanborn  Elonka submitted  back in July changes or should change how people perceive the deceptively hard-to-solve nature of K4. I believe that there is an unfortunate 30 year build of reputation on K4 that is built not on any great skill of the creator, Jim Sanborn, but on the perceived influence of Ed Scheidt, the master who helped him. The 2009 interview clarified a lot of things because it’s about detailing Sanborn’’s life history in the art world. I’m aiming to shift some of that perception here, not because I dislike Sanborn, but because when you view things from a correct and accurate angle, details change. Speculation dies.

Consider this a reduction of Sanborn, and by default, K4.

1.    Interview – He was a failure at mathematics in high school and required a tutor.

Jim is an “ANATHEMATH”. No, this is not a real word. It’s a pun indicating that math is an anathema to him and that he hates it because he is bad at it.

2.    Interview – Sanborn devised the plaintext on a drive to buy the petrified tree. Not K4.

“And then I wrote the plain text. [01:20:00] I went to Arizona, [inaudible] and bought a petrified tree. On the way back, I devised the plain text, what I was going to write for the plain text.”

3.    Interview – They only met two or three times.

“We met two or three times. And that's what I based the whole thing on.”
No, Sanborn didn’t spend months upon months learning at the knee of the master. The master gave him an unnamed primer and because of phone evesdropping concerns met secretly. That means he probably made sure that the items in K1-K3 were properly encrypted and that Sanborn’s “known plaintext” drops were intact.

5.    Interview – The systems Scheidt offered Sanborn were simple enough for Sanborn to use, but for Scheidt to not know what it says.

Consider the implications. Scheidt knew what he was doing.

“But he told me about coding systems that I could then modify in a myriad of ways. So that even he would not know what it says. Okay? So that was very seductive to me. And so I took those things.”

7.    Interview – Sanborn refers to K1-K3 as “matrix codes.” K4 is not one.

“So he told me about matrix codes and things like that. These are the parts of Kryptos that have already been cracked.”

Gaines Cryptanalysis – There are three code types: Transposition, Substitution, Concealment.

9.    Interview – Scheidt gave Sanborn a “primer on ancient encoding systems”

This was probably Gaines Cryptanalysis, a primer on cryptanalysis that is supposedly the first of its kind and reputable enough to be kept in the NSA library.

10.    Interview – Sanborn considers Howard Carters notebooks one of his favorite texts.

More importantly he has specifically been Greece, and then Egypt, even more specifically saw all the stuff that Howard Carter found in Tut’s tomb at the Egyptian museum in 1977.

$0.02 and a Point? A very skilled cryptographer used an unskilled novice to either intentionally or unintentionally fool a lot of cryptographers at his own level. Add 30 years of interviews where said novice is trying desperately not to give away a game he has no appreciable skill in against people using said interviews to dig for clues and you can see where a whole lot of bad disinformation comes in.

s: Thinking Through The Solution Space, Masking Before/After Encryption
t:
Jim - A computer seems unlikely to figure it out if Scheidt pulled a fast one and instead of Substitution or Transposition, nudged Sanborn to the third type of cipher - Concealment. If one does it the ridiculously hard way, that puts the clues in the CT, and if they do it the easier and intended way, it puts the clues in the PT. Best practices says use both.

I think that over 30 years people have gotten bound up in certain logic trees, not the least of which I mentioned in the binary choice of ciphers I above. There are three, not two, but I suspect that skilled cryptographers and cryptanalysts are more comfortable with the Sub/Trans binary.

 Sanborn has stated in a previous Wired article that clues were placed. I "know" that those clues are there because I've demonstrably shown at least one of them. I'd say that Sanborn went for an artistic interpretation/definition of the concept of "known plaintext" that has a blast radius instead of precision, and utilized that concept to place his clues.

No magic, just a recognition that Sanborn isn't the cryptological rocket scientist or even skilled trainee he's being given credit for in placing his clues.

Dan, are there actual clues though?

Kit Williams set everything up, and although it was stego, it was all there at release to find the hidden messages. He set forth a challenge, with well thought out checks. I love those kind of puzzles. Solved something kind of similar in 2015. In fact, there's another iteration of that particular "code" coming out if anyone is interested in trying it. Just have to follow @TheGinterCode on Twitter. It's related to a Topps baseball card set release (used to be annually) and while it hasn't run since 2015, it's making a comeback right now. You guys might find it fun.

Anyway, the point is, Sanborn doesn't need to be cagey anymore. If there are clues/hints in the previous plaintext to solving the fourth part, just say so. But at this point he's basically eliminated everything. I know you'll argue back at me, Dan, that "need" and "helpful" are two different things, but when you're dealing with an unknown home-brewed one-off system complete with a unknown masking-technique, and you ARE stating there is encryption, not just stego/concealment going on, you're going to _NEED_ clues. They aren't just helpful, they are necessary. If they are necessary and included, just come out and say so.

My entire posture on this thing is because Sanborn seems lost at times, wavering between decades of "sure there's stuff to help you" to now "nah, you don't need anything else".

If Kit Williams said "well, technically you could get the message off the first page without ever looking at the rest of the work" that would be true, but have REALLY long odds. Something I'd never spend time on.

We've had 30 years to play with the Sanborn passages, as if they were Kit Williams-esque double entendres. SUBTLE SHADING = NUANCE. ABSENCE OF LIGHT = DARKNESS. Sure, let's roll with that stuff, "BETWEEN NUANCE AND DARKNESS IS THE NUANCE OF ILLUSION"? Hmmm, Not seeing much there to go on. Stuff like that. I've played that stuff out. And nothing there looks to point to algorithmic things if you eliminate the prior plain/ciphertext, which we need to solve an encrypted passage.

And yes, maybe I'm not the 1 in 10,000 person who can see it, but this thing will only lose more eyeballs as it ages. It would be nice to get a push like Kit Williams delivered (after only a few years) with Masquerade rather than plaintext releases.

I'm sure the solution IS super creative. I'm just worried it's all in Jim's head rather than laid out for someone to find. Wouldn't it be great if he reinvigorated things with "Hey, yeah, the compass rose and shape of Kryptos and the prior plaintext is all describing  exactly what I did, you just need to piece it together?" I'd kill for those words, because I don't think it's implied anymore.

Jim

s: What If Transposition Is the Only Method Saborn Used On K4
t:
This is what happens when you leave me with my thoughts on Kryptos for a couple days and challenge me here with salient points on what is and is not possible.

Free you mind for a minute.

Obviously substitution was used on K4. It's what flattened the English language frequency distribution. My title is based on a technicality. What if Transposition is the only Method _SANBORN_ "contributed" to K4.

But what if Scheidt's masking technique was the only substitution used? Think about it though. There's nothing like Vigenere's Tableau pointing us to an actual historical substitution method and Jim Sanborn seems to only have used words like "patterns", "flip", "rotate" and "mirror" with regard to what he cooked up in K4. Transpositions are the great individualistic component.

So what if it's just Scheidt's method of dynamic substitution, which wouldn't be cryptographically secure on it's own plus one (or more *shudder*) transposition step from Sanborn.

Take for example this ciphertext:

JYXUG XAVPU NGRRO KYCLE BIHSK
UEKRB ATEZH WIGDO INKZS MUKED
MWYQS UCZDM INSJX UDJIT OWFGU
EMHCQ UOOYP ZGFTY RUGAF XK

It's solely masked plaintext with transposition. Now, I'd still have no idea how to solve it (if I were you in this scenario) because I don't know how you (I) masked it. However, you have two avenues to advance.

If I had first masked, then transposed, you'd need to have the key to the transposition delivered to you, yes? Agreed? Then you could unmask it and it would be readable.

Or, if I transposed it first, then masked it, you would need to unmask it, see that it had a plaintext IC (confirming you did that correctly), but would still need to figure out how I transposed it (like K3).

Jim

What if the extra L is not an L but an angle, like a direction.

That line has to be a major clue, and it's what I look at the most.

As JS said in that latest interview, filling in the gaps is going to get easier as more and more clues are revealed.

Take east northeast, for example.

Likely: ...is located east northeast of...
Possible: ...go east northeast, and...
Not likely: ....cheese east northeast banana bread

Why would anyone just want to guess the plaintext?

The payoff is in discovering how it was encrypted.

I mean if it was a typical crypto problem then extending a crib is useful. In this scenario, not so much.

I agree, I was just saying that the "most possible" words either side may help, for example, someone who may be on the brink of discovery. They may see a pattern. I'm probably not explaining this right. :)

I'm not one for randomly filling in plaintext with nonsense. Don't worry.

Given Sanborn's past themed work involving the Coriolis effect, I imagine
the water pool is a symbol for a cryptographic step that involves one or
more strings of letters rotating clockwise, with an alternative row(s) spun
counter-clockwise. We know Sanborn's other artworks contain hints to
Kryptos, but we haven't found the connection to the Coriolis effect in
Kryptos quite yet. This is evident by the reflecting pool with waters
intended to be flowing in opposite directions, per past interviews.

I'd like to present some potential theories about how the coriolis effect
could have been implemented in Kryptos.

*Option 1: Every Other Row shifts X spaces left or X spaces right until a
keyword is displayed horizontally in Kryptos*
*Option 2: Every Other Row shifts +X or -X alphabet positions via Caesar

K1, K2, and K3 have their keys and alphabets completed concealed steganographically. It is most prominent in the 2006 Kryptos tabletop model for "Alias" commissioned by J.J. Abrahams, 2009 WIRED transcript image and the CIA Kryptos itself. The usage of IC was not even required for K1 through K3.

Suppose the triple superencipherment would be performed as:

A) PLAINTEXT encryption via KRYPTOSABC substitution with a 97 letter pseudorandom key
B) Put the pseudorandom key through a washing machine (patent pending block transposition) and then line up the 97 letter string
C) Perform a monoalphabetic substitution mask on the 97 string
D) Write the 97 letter string as K4 ciphertext on Kryptos

Then the decryption would involve:
A) Remove the monoalphabetic substitution mask via K1 concealment
B) Reverse the transposition via K2 and K3 shared secrets to produce K4-Key
C) Reverse the substitution via KRYPTOSABC alphabet to maintain the 1:1 relationship

Again, the entire crux of the problem is solving the transposition. With the masking layer the keyspace was originally 26x97!, now it's 73! or lower.

t: For the masking as you propose, it’s only a mask if it flattens the distribution. I.e. if you just replace all As with Zs etc, you haven’t changed the distributions, you’ve just change the letters for it. But that doesn’t hide the statistics. So you need some method to map A-Z to A-Z but in a mostly pseudo random way. Only way I can think of so far is to use the entire tablet or the table lookup and K4 (or its PT) becomes the lookup coordinates. For example, and this isn’t correct but just an example, if you started in the top left of the tablet with K1 and counted off 15 spaces and choose that letter (for the O in K4), then counted off two more and used that letter (for the B in the second position of K4), etc. This type of method would change the distribution and look pseudo random. But there’s no proof he did anything like that (or any proof in general unfortunately), so we are stuck grasping at straws.

Concerning this, I think we should stay away from looking for ambiental
clues on the grounds and around the sculpture itself, because it is
distracting everybody. Sanborn decisively said and repeated a couple of
times in his interviews that ONE DOES NOT HAVE TO BE ON THE GROUNDS IN
ORDER TO SOLVE K4. It means that AL THE CLUES WE NEED ARE IN K1-K3.

There seems to be a strong ongoing thread around the fairness of the cipher at present.  I would hope I'm on safe ground by suggesting that when Jim had to hand over the solution to William Webster one of the reasons the CIA had to be given foreknowledge of the answer was to make sure that such a challenge wouldn't compromise the agencies mission.  If an artist brought an unsolvable puzzle into the realm of your countries brightest young minds, then you might as well have let a computer virus loose in-house.  This assumption does of course have a flip side in which it could of course be designed to tie up every other foreign intelligence agency instead, but ultimately I believe, its both solvable and intellectually satisfying to all those that might eventually find their way through the large number of cryptic clues that come as part and parcel of parts K1-3.  I'm not sure where an argument on 'fairness' progresses us to.  If a clue is given by Jim about the nature of the K4 concealment then that would surely devalue the efforts of any genuine solves even further than the current plain text releases.  There seems to be an element of psychological 'transference' here in that we are somehow trying to make our own failings Jim Sanborn's failings instead.  That to my mind is a pretty good definition of 'unfair'.  Ultimately, he didn't ask us to come and solve this, we all came of our own accord.  We might have to wind back from our Bayesian world view that success in other cipher challenges somehow increases our chances of completing this one.    Reading the biography of his work and experiences prior to Kryptos its blindingly obvious that he's both an artist and an educator, not a sadist.
