Personally, I read the "push into this square" comment as simply a description of the transposition cipher methods used in K3. At the end of the previous paragraph of Scheidt's interview with AJ (also quoted by Jezail recently), Ed emphasizes the connection between a transposition cipher method and "the square":

It's sort of like looking at a puzzle and you're defining the parameters of the puzzle in the sense of the square, and then now you have the square and you're going to transpose the characters or the letters that are in the square to something that's a secret."
I take this as a description of his method for K3, just as the mention of substitution was a description of his method for K1-K2. And then the little comment "So my secret is push into this square. So that was another step", I take that as Ed wrapping up his discussion of his K3 method. And then he begins his obscure reference to his K4 method when he says, "And then the last step which has been good for 30 years,...." Based on the context of his descriptions, I interpret his references to different "steps" as the different methods he used on K1-2, K3, and K4, not all of them as steps he necessarily used in K4.

separately and are never affected by any of the transposition steps--they
go straight to plaintext, once the homophonic substitution is removed. (And

a summary/mantra/motto/closer. It isn't (yet) clear whether those three

when exactly he stuck them into the puzzle.

I have no idea why "the team" settled on such an awkward word order in
their final analysis.

This is just a post to brainstorm and ask about ideas that perhaps other folks have already thought of or tried. Morse Code is obviously a possible relevant topic for Kryptos and for Jim Sanborn. It came up recently in my research in the following way:
I mentioned here a few months ago that I tried a decryption step on the K4 ciphertext by splitting the message in half (including the initial "?") and pairing up the letters as bigrams: ?+49th letter, 1st+50th letters, ..., through the 48th+97th letters. Then I did a Playfair cipher decryption on these bigrams, using a 5x5 Polybius square with DYAHR as the key (top row) and the rest of the letters entered in alphabetical order horizontally across the rows in the normal way, with I/J sharing a square.
The amazing thing about the resulting string of letters that this decryption step produced is that the letter O occurs 13 times among the 96 letters (the bigram with the "?" cannot be decrypted). Statistically, it is extraordinarily unlikely for a single letter to occur 13 times in 96 letters by random chance. Moreover, the letter S just happens to be absent from the 96 letters entirely. No letter other than O occurs more than 6 times, and the rest of the letters are distributed just as we would expect from random text. What it looks like to me, is a random text (like K4) but where all the S's have been changed to O's.
This is where Morse Code occurs to me: S and O are probably the two best known Morse Code letters of all, due to their use in the SOS signal: dot dot dot, dash dash dash, dot dot dot. The pattern I find makes me wonder if the masking step itself uses some kind of transformation of the Morse Code representations of the letters.
I figure people must have tried a lot of ideas related to Morse Code already, so I'm just curious what folks can share about what some such possible methods might be. Thanks for sharing any thoughts or ideas that you may have or that you may be familiar with.
-Geoffrey

---

12/19/2020

I have a follow-up in this line of investigation that I think is worth sharing:
Beyond just the preponderance of O's and lack of S's that I get from the Playfair step, when the entire text is written in Morse code, there is a general preponderance of dashes and a striking lack of dots. If we arrange the I's and J's from the shared I/J square in the same order as the I's and J's in the K4 ciphertext, we get 169 dashes and only 124 dots from this text:
?QGIYWJUJEAOKGOTKKCGGXGMYPLTOYGFNOPIOZPOMBLOQCCWT
?DONNIOHBRXBMEFJAOXOOLXETCQEYNTZPMFUNENWXOWXFLYRZ
It is notable to me that the seven *least* frequent letters in this text are predominantly "dot-heavy" in Morse code: zero S's (3 dots), zero V's (3 dots, 1 dash), 1 H (4 dots), 1 D (1 dash, 2 dots), 2 U's (2 dots, 1 dash), 2 R's (dot dash dot), 2 A's (dot dash).
Typical English plaintext written in Morse code has about 60.5% dots and 39.5% dashes. Typical random text written in Morse code has about 53.7% dots and 46.3% dashes. (Indeed, the 24 letters of Sanborn's crib clues so far match these proportions for plaintext, and the K4 ciphertext matches these proportions for random text.) But the text I got above has only 42.3% dots and 57.7% dashes. For such proportions to arise from random text by chance would be even much more improbable than for plaintext dot/dash proportions to arise from random text. (The odds of 169 dashes and 124 dots occurring by random chance is about 1 in 40,850.) On the other hand, if this text is the result of a deliberate swapping of all dots for dashes and dashes for dots, then the proportions are much more plausible.
Moreover, it is possible that approx. 46 dots/dashes in this text are "nulls", since 97 letters of typical English plaintext requires about 46 fewer dots/dashes than this text has. If the final 46 dots/dashes of this text are discarded, the resulting text has 146 dashes and 101 dots, which is 59.1% dashes and 40.9% dots. This is getting quite close to the proportions of plaintext with all the dots changed to dashes and dashes changes to dots.

There are two elements necessary to read Morse code as English letters: the string of dots and dashes, and the letter breaks to know where one Morse code letter ends and another begins. So far, my text above is still like random text in terms of the Morse code lengths of its letters, the number of dots/dashes in each letter. 97 letters of English plaintext would be expected to have about 21 letters with 1 dot/dash, 24 letters with 2 dots/dashes, 31 letters with 3 dots/dashes, and 21 letters with 4 dots/dashes. In random text short lengths are rarer and long lengths are more frequent: 7 with 1 dot/dash, 15 with 2 dots/dashes, 30 with 3 dots/dashes, and 45 with 4 dots/dashes.
However, the following regular logical process converts my text above into Morse code letter lengths much more like English plaintext: Take each group of 14 letters in the text and add each Morse code letter length to the line length (number of letters) of each line of the K3-K4 panel of the Kryptos sculpture, modulo 4. Conveniently, the frequent line length 31, which is 3 modulo 4, converts many random text Morse letter lengths with 3 or 4 dots/dashes into more typical plaintext Morse letter lengths with 2 or 3 dots/dashes. As a result of this process, I get a new string of Morse letter lengths: 21 with 1 dot/dash, 27 with 2 dots/dashes, 27 with 3 dots/dashes, 21 with 4 dots/dashes. This is strikingly close to typical plaintext proportions.
Now, by changing all dots to dashes and dashes to dots in my text above, and by redividing the string of dots and dashes with new letter breaks based on the new string of Morse letter lengths described above, I get the following text:
?INUCEXIEMENIMSUIEBERRAUUWSBDNANMEHTHTGNTSXTDIJEEDHSETTIVINNYHEUTSAWNISAOKXMEWKNUSEWSHYPDNDNTEDRIO
This text is very much like English plaintext in many ways: It has an Index of Coincidence of 6.30, or 1.64 times the typical 3.85 IC of random text. This is well within the typical IC range of English plaintext for this length of message. The 97-letter text has 13 E’s, 11 N’s, 9 I’s, 8 T’s, and 8 S’s. It has no Q’s or Z’s.
Of course this is not the solution of K4 yet. But as a result of a strictly regular logical process based on the Playfair cipher, "DYAHR", Morse code, and the line lengths of the K3-K4 panel, the resulting text above looks a lot more like English plaintext than anything else I've seen produced from K4 by a logical process.

12/21/2020

I think it is fair that I should report obstacles and setbacks in my investigation of my ideas, rather than only sharing the promising or successful results.

There is a problematic issue with my Morse Code cipher idea as I have presented it here: Although the K3-K4 line lengths did a good job of turning the Morse letter lengths of my text into plaintext-like proportions, I find that it is much more difficult to use this method to systematically convert plaintext into more random text-like proportions of Morse letter lengths. The main issue is that random text has very few letters with 1 dot/dash in Morse -- just E and T -- and very many letters with 4 dots/dashes in Morse -- 12 letters that make up almost half of random text but only about 22% of typical plaintext. Getting any regular system to convert the more balanced proportions of plaintext letters with 1, 2, 3, and 4 dots/dashes into the very unbalanced proportions of random text, with only 7-8% of letters with 1 dot/dash and 46% of letters with 4 dots/dashes appears to be a very difficult thing to do.

I do have a new idea for a Morse code masking method that could resolve this issue, but I must admit that it calls into question the relevance of my results presented above, since those results are significant for their preponderance of dashes over dots, and my new idea is designed to keep both dot/dash proportions and Morse letter lengths more consistent for both plaintext and random text, and the best way I have found to do so keeps the total number of dots and dashes very close to 50-50.

Anyway, here is the idea for a consistent and usable Morse code cipher/masking step: There are four 4-dot/dash sequences that are not used for English letters in Morse code. They are used for the umlauted vowels ä, ö, ü, and the consonant š in European languages, but we don't need them for English. If we use these four 4-dot/dash sequences to represent E, T, A, and N in Morse code, in place of their typical 1- and 2-dot/dash codes, then it actually produces a very balanced system where both plaintext and random text have very similar proportions of dots and dashes (both 50-50) and proportions of 2-, 3-, and 4-dot/dash letters: 8-9% of letters have 2-dots/dashes (I and M), 31-32% of letters have 3-dots/dashes, and 59-61% of letters have 4-dots/dashes, in both plaintext and random text. In the best such system I have found, E = dot dot dash dash, T = dash dash dash dash, A = dot dash dot dash, and N = dash dash dash dot.

With such a system, the Morse letter lengths 2, 3, 4 as well as the dot/dash strings can be shifted in systematic ways to mask or encipher plaintext as random text.

Hi all,

Sanborn has mentioned that more than one clock should be considered. Mengenlehreuhr has rightly been closely examined, and I do think that one is important. However, another potential clock to consider is a shadow clock found in the Egyptian Museum of Berlin. Here is some potential evidence to support it:
-The clock is significant, because it is the oldest surviving shadow clock (shadows can connect to K0 and K1)
-The clock is in Berlin (Sanborn clue for K4), and is related to Egypt (K3 connection). I believe that the sundial actually originates from Tut's (K3) grandfather.
-The item is a clock (Sanborn clue for K4)
-The L-shaped sundial closely approximates the shape of K1 shown in Sanborn's notes (an L turned ninety degrees clockwise)
-To use the sundial, you place it one direction until midday and then turn it 180 degrees--that fits with the arrows on Sanborn's K1 notes showing left to right, and then changing to right to left.
-The sundial was originally thought to have a central "T" shaped beam that would sit atop it, which is consistent with "T is your position." That beam has since been questioned, but only after creation of Kryptos ( I uploaded a file called Shadow.PDF to my Personal Folder, which has a more detailed explanation of the shadow clock).

-The spacing between the marks on the sundial for telling time are 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. Doubled (i.e., 2, 4, 6, 8, 10), that yields 30, which is one away from the important number of 31 that Sanborn utilizes for his matrices. If K1 is the clock, then the gnomon (the piece that sticks up from the clock) could be the first column, which would result in 31 exactly. Another famous shadow clock had spacing of 3, 6, 9, 12, which also sums to 30.

Some speculation: I suspect that K1 is the key which you have to cut from the rest of the document (abscissa), and then move through the document like a decoder, likely using set theory--as with Mengenlehreuhr--to determine when to move to the next line or sheet. You may have to actually turn K1 180 degrees at the end of a line, or at a fold. The combination of the K1 code and the K2/K3 code could yield text to decode K4. I am obviously not sure on the details. I also suspect, with less confidence, that the number of words in the plain text of K2 is somehow involved, because if you separate by the x's, then the word count yields "7, 6, 11, 5, 7, 5, 7, 20(?), 2." A little addition: 7+6+11 = 24, and 5+7+5+7 = 24. That could be significant because Sanborn's folds often shorten the line from 31 to 24, which is also obviously the number of hours in a day.

-Alister

The "Decipher Puzzle" paper is still on Alan Sherman's website, an amusing read. (Google does index the postscript file, but the browsers I use don't usually have PS viewers integrated.)

The puzzle was a book cipher, like the Beale ciphers, Thouless's "life after death" test, or Simon Singh's "Code Book" problem #5. It's possible problem #5 was the most difficult of the 10 "Code Book" problems.

The eight original clues were

"1. The key is in the public domain - you have easy access to it.
2. 3,19.
3. The first place to start may not be the first.
4. A cube is a clue if you are geometrically inclined.
5. 300 is closer to 'A' than 'Z'.
6. One source will do but what will you do with it?
7. Some numbers are repeated but do not be fooled.
8. If you knew it began with 'C', would it help you?"

(my comment: these clues seem pretty useless for finding the book - I would have taken "public domain" to mean "out of copyright")

The puzzle ($12 each) started in 1983 sometime, and the solution was in a safe-deposit box which was to be opened if no one solved the puzzle by 30 June 1989. Everyone who submitted a correct solution by 1 March 1984 split the $100,000.

"Holland's decision to put the ciphertext on a puzzle was clever - even if the contestant cannot discover the plaintext, he can almost certainly put together the jigsaw puzzle which lets him feel as if he has made significant progress."

"As for the key-extraction strategy, we reasoned that it was probably something that could be easily carried out by hand without the use of a computer - many people would consider it unfair to require contestants to use a computer."

Relevant paras for Kryptos like challenges ...

"We speculate that Holland intentionally designed the puzzle to be controlled by the clues. Doing so would accomplish the following three objectives. First: by forcing each contestant to solve the puzzle by guessing the keytext, Holland can control the difficulty of the puzzle by judiciously choosing the clues. To maximize public interest in this and future puzzles: the puzzle should be solvable yet the puzzle must not be too easy nor too hard.  A puzzle that is too easy would be solved too soon: thereby reducing sales; a puzzle that is too hard might discourage contestants from buying future puzzles. Second: Holland can ensure that the puzzle will eventually be solved by giving away sufficiently many additional clues. Third: by forcing contestants to guess the keytext, lay people and mathematicians are put on a roughly equal footing."

The creator Holland started releasing clues - first of all saying the keytext was a "popular novel" written by one of twenty-one specified authors, then eliminating two authors from the list each month - but the only one that was any use was the very last clue in February 1985, after which 36 people solved it in March 1985. (i.e. all of those people depended on that clue - reminds of "Masquerade", but there only 2 people understood the clue)

"When no one solved the puzzle by February 28, 1985, Holland announced that the key was a sequence of "first letters" from Cosmos [by Carl Sagan] chapter 6." (beginning "first ages of the world...", first letters of all words, treating hyphenated words as single words and deleting all numerals, abbreviations, footnotes and figure captions. "Cosmos" is certainly popular, but it is not a novel!!)

"Holland explained that he designed the clues to have multiple levels (heh!) of interpretation and to challenge people to think more deeply; for most clues the "obvious" interpretation is incorrect. For example, clue 5 means that codenumber 300 is closer to 'A' than 'Z' not in alphabetical order but in the sense that codenumber 300 represents a vowel rather than a consonant. Clue 4, which mentions a cube, refers to chapter 6 since a cube has 6 sides. Holland said that he had used the world 'novel' in the spirit of the clues to mean both 'book' and "new and unusual." The picture of a cube in Cosmos, chapter 10 and the references to the country Holland in chapter 6 were simply coincidences."

"Holland also said that he was surprised the puzzle was not solved within the first year." (now that sounds familiar)

"There are many lessons to be learned from our experience. One of the obvious lessons is "Read instructions carefully!" But beyond this obvious lesson: we would like to reflect on a number of points.

First: throughout our cryptanalysis we found ourselves caught in the following dilemma: how can we tell how close we are to the solution? Although the windowing technique detects some near misses: and although interpretations of the clues provide some confirmation: for the most part it was virtually impossible to know whether or not we were near solving the puzzle. This made it difficult for us to decide how much time to dedicate to the puzzle."

Second: the computer's facility for doing tedious calculations is a double-edged resource. On the one hand: the computer was a tremendous aid in calculations such as trying all possible starting positions in a keytext. On the other hand: the computer posed a danger in inviting us immediately to follow the straightforward approach rather than to think about a possibly more effective clever approach. For example: to check a candidate key  the straightforward approach is to use it to decipher the entire ciphertext and to check the resulting candidate plaintext for English. But if the entire candidate plaintext is checked for English, poor results are obtained because this checking procedure is too sensitive to errors in the keytext. Someone solving the puzzle by hand would almost certainly check a candidate keytext without generating the entire key and without deciphering the entire ciphertext. By virtue of  his  limited  computational powers: the hand-solver is practically forced to use a superior method that detects when part of a candidate key is correct! We do not wish to imply that straightforward methods are necessarily bad; nor do we wish to imply that computers cannot perform clever feats. We simply point out that computers can make it convenient for their users not to think deeply.

Third: we found ourselves more interested in the process of our solution than in the solution itself. For example: we preferred to spend our time analyzing our test for English or adding features to our cryptanalysis engine rather than to run our engine on candidate keytexts. This situation contributed to our missing the deadline.

Cryptanalysis is a complex activity involving probability, statistics, algorithms, computer systems, software and hardware engineering, and general problem solving. We hope the reader can learn from and enjoy our experiences in this fascinating area."

I will write about analog and digital communication systems. Analog systems are based on using an analogy between the original and transmitted information. For example in an audio system, the sound reaches the microphone as air pressure variations, the microphone delivers to the amplifier or following stages as a signal, a voltage that varies as closely as possible with those pressure variations that reached the microphone. In a similar way that pressure can vary in a range between 0 and a certain maximum value, voltage varies in a range between 0 and a certain maximum value. There is a continuity, there are infinite values ​​between 0 and the maximum in which both the sound and the voltage that represents it can vary. In summary, there is an analogy and a continuity between the original sound signal, and the voltage signal to transmit, in this example.

In digital systems, on the other hand, a point is reached where the information is digitized, that is, it is converted into numbers. The variation range is divided into N levels, for example 256 different levels. With a certain frequency samples are taken, the signal is measured, for example 128,000 samples per second. And each of those samples is compared to the 256 levels in our example and an approximation is made to the closest level. In this way, a flow of numbers is obtained, 128,000 numbers per second whose value varies between 0 and 255. That flow of numbers can be transmitted as 0s and 1s if the binary or base 2 system is used, but in general other more efficient systems, with more symbols, are used. There is no continuity, neither in time, nothing is known about the signal between two samples, nor between levels, there is no 233.42 level, it is 233 or 234. Digital systems are designed by choosing the number of samples per second and the number of levels considering the quality of communication and the volume of information to be transmitted.

With these criteria I suppose that the clocks that have continuity in their information, the solar ones, the water ones, the mechanical needles (to a certain extent), we would consider them analog. Clocks that do not have continuity, that can take a finite number of values, those of LED screens, electronics, lights, numbers, we would consider them digital.

There is a phrase from Ed that always intrigued me: "In analog systems as used in Kryptos, the KEY is the algorithm" I understand the message is: do not look for a key, look for the algorithm. And I am working on finding the correct algorithm. But I don't understand what he means when he qualifies Kryptos as an analog system. In Kryptos there are a finite number of possible values, 26 or 27 characters if we include the question mark "?" and 3 more if we include the point, the dash and the space of the Morse code. I would classify it as a digital system with 26, 27 or 30 possible values. What does Ed mean when he defines Kryptos as an analog system?

Jose Luis

t:
Dear colleagues,

IIRC, Sandborn was explicit that he wants Kryptos solved in his lifetime, and that’s why he said he has been releasing the cribs.

I think perhaps he’s afraid that even the encrypted K5 will remain hidden forever if K4 remains secret.  It seems clear that he wants to share the secret, but he wants it discovered cryptanalytically.

Sorry to be an armchair programmer here; the Vigenere has two keys, KRYPTOS and either ABCISSA, PALMPSEST, or ???

(PALIMPSEST has repeated characters, making it an interesting key.)

Perhaps the pair of keys to K4 use a different keyword than KRYPTOS.

I suspect searching for two keywords is likely to be intractable; how long does a single keyword search take?  Square that.

In addition, one or both keywords might be misspelled, somewhat thwarting a dictionary attack.  Repeated letters may either be retained or removed.

Someone (Sanborn?) directed attention to “the algorithm.”  Perhaps there is a clue somewhere that indicates a different technique than Vigenere.  Still, so many eyes have looked, and even the force of large numbers has not succeeded.

I believe that Sanborn drastically underestimated the effort required to cryptanalyze K4. Hence the cribs.  Perhaps his “masking” is too good for his purpose: a breakable cipher.  But that’s defeatist; all we can do is keep trying, and have fun.

.mike

t:
Hi Mike,

Had not yet read your post when I replied to Lars (?) regarding double dictionary attack, which is exactly what you brought up in your message. I posted my solver to the group many years ago -- it's called fastquag. You'll be amused to know I wrote it in FORTRAN. ;-)  To answer your question about how long it takes, a single keyword search takes less than a second. A full search takes a few hours (depending on the # of characters in the ciphertext you want to use for scoring). You have a choice of decoding using Quagmire I, II or III (with Beaufort, Variant and Vigenere options), and you can do English digraph scoring or IoC match to English letter frequencies, German, or just index of coincidence (to cover the case of simple substitution still remaining AFTER solving with Quagmire).

You can find fastquag in a zip archive in my personal folder in the Files area of our group:

https://kryptos.groups.io/g/main/files/Personal%20Folders/Matson

The zip file contains a ReadMe doc, the executable, my dictionary file (human readable text file), a corresponding Vig mixed alphabet file, and text files containing the K1 and K2 ciphertext (which you can use to quickly test the program). (Not sure why I didn't also include a text file for the K4 ciphertext!)

The ZIP archive is encrypted -- the password is KRYPTOS (all upper case).  --Rob

Rohan Muscat is another good programmer in this group who helped me explore some ideas, including some Vigenere steps, last year. One thing I recall that we also accounted for in his program is the following: the possibility that either the input or output or both might map to or from the plain alphabetical top row or far left column of the Vigenere tableau that is on the Kryptos sculpture. This is not the same thing as a "simple plain alphabetical" Vigenere cipher, because the rows inside the tableau are still written in the KRYPTOS-keyed alphabet order. Another possibility to account for is the possibility that the output might map to the far *right hand* side column of the Vigenere tableau on the Kryptos sculpture, which would give some actual significance to the otherwise apparently meaningless extra four columns on the right side of the tableau that repeat the content of the second to fifth columns on the left side. (The far right hand column, reading from the top down, is DPTOSABC, etc.) We considered all of these possibilities for the Vigenere, Beaufort, and Variant options that Rob mentions in his message and also accounts for in his programs.

Geoffrey

Hi Duane -- it certainly isn't JUST polyalphabetic substitution, or the solution would have been found decades ago. But Vig/Quagmire could still be part of it. Ed has said that whatever method he used to foil the usual cryptanalytic approaches (e.g. frequency counting, English language statistics) may not have been previously known in the '90s:

Ed: "The masking technique may not be [a known technique]... That's part of the puzzle I told [Jim] I would keep secret."

The impression I've always had from Ed's remarks is that K4 is a multi-step problem -- his technique + something more traditional -- and that without figuring out the former, the latter is rendered unsolvable.  --Rob

Rob - He said as much in that interview back in November 17, 2020. The details he gave are extremely enlightening.

Copy of that in AJ's Personal file at   EdScheidtKryptosTranscript.pdf

It's especially helpful that AJ came in without a lot of background knowledge and preconceptions. The whole "what did Ed Scheidt actually help with" is cleared away because he deliberately stayed ignorant, and it's heavily implied that there's a PT/CT puzzle that's acting as what we typically refer to as "the masking step"

At the beginning of the year Government Attic published the NSA manual "Military Cryptanalytics Part III" by Lambros D. Callimahos (October 1977).

The FOIA request date was July 2012 ... and it had been the subject of FOI requests since the early 1990s.

https://www.governmentattic.org/39docs/NSAmilitaryCryptalyticsPt3_1977.pdf (25 MB PDF)

It is still quite a bit redacted, but Chapter XI "Principles of cryptodiagnosis" would be useful for people trying to understand the phenomena seen in K4.

First step: manipulating the data

"In all of one's endeavors, the successful cryptanalyst's precept should be kept foremost in mind: "Try the simplest thing first." It is surprising how often this admonishment is disregarded, to the later chagrin of the cryptosinner."

Second step: recognizing the phenomena

Reading through the posts in this group, I can't emphasize the following quote enough...

"After finding a phenomenon - or what is thought to be a phenomenon - an evaluation should follow. It's not enough to say "I think the doublets are high." How many are there? Count them. And, even more important, how many doublets are expected at random in a sample of this size?"

The STETHOSCOPE program presents a variety of fundamental information about a single message:

a. the uniliteral frequency distribution, the monographic IC, and its sigmage
b. the overall digraphic IC, as well as the digraphic ICs on cut A and cut B, and their sigmages
c. the overall trigraphic IC, and the trigraphic ICs on cuts A, B, and C and their sigmages
d. the local roughness (in terms of the observed and expected number of hits, and sigmage), when the message is offset against itself at offsets of 1 to 33
e. width tests, giving average columnar ICs and sigmages of the message if it were written out on widths from 2 to 51
f. the observed and expected number of tetragraphic and pentagraphic repetitions, and their ICs and sigmages
g. a listing of polygraphic repetitions of length 4 or longer
h. if desired, the same categories of statistical information on the delta stream

(here sigmage is the number of standard deviations away from the mean)

Third step: interpreting the phenomena

There is also a reference to I. J. Good "Standard Reagents and Diagnostician's Dictionary", National Security Agency, 1966 ... Good was one of the original Bletchley Park cryptanalysts.
I wonder how long that would take to release...

t:
I took notice of three words in the cipher text of K1, "REV" (reverse),
"USD" (dollar), "FIVJ" (five).

I looked at the back of the five dollar bill and noted some interesting
things.

1. There is a striking resemblance between the Lincoln Memorial and the
"fives" digit of the Berlin Clock. There are 11 spaces, with Lincoln
sitting directly in the middle, and the 3rd from the left and right spaces
are also taken up by decorative items on smaller pillars in the front of
the steps. This correlates with how, on the Berlin Clock, every fifteen
minutes gets a different color light to help you read it faster. (most
likely I'm just reading into a 5 minutes - 5 dollars connection here... )

2. It's "hidden in plain sight" but there are 26 (a useful number, perhaps)
states inscribed along the top edge of the memorial. You need a magnifying
glass to see them. There are more states than 26 on the memorial, but only
26 are visible from this perspective.

Neither of these things have proven particularly useful to me yet, but I
thought I'd share anyway. I looked for other currency that you could
stack/arrange in a Berlin Clock configuration, but couldn't find one. And
plus it comes back to, I wouldn't have thought of that clock unless JS gave
that clue anyway.

I also looked for other ways to get to Abraham Lincoln in the sculpture,
and saw the row with the extra L on the Vigenere side, also ends in an A on
the cipher side, so "AL"... but thats not necessarily a clue. Also, in K1,
the "nuance of illusion" with some creative rearrangement might hint at the
"uncle of Illinois" (uncle Abe)... but again, I'm just confirming what I
was already looking for.

That's all from me for today! Maybe that sparks something for somebody :)

Jamie

My understanding is that, the alphabet in the columns would come out as a by-product of a standard vig attack.

Here’s how I think the vig attack works:
1. Guess at the length of the key, *
2. Arrange the ciphertext in rows of that length.
3. Look down the columns and apply a monoalphabetic cipher attack to each column.
    a. check the letter frequency,
    b. deduce the key.

* You can get clues to the length of the key by the distances between repeated digraphs.

Other members have automated this process, and done brute-force searches with no joy.  (I believe they used a dictionary search, not a full search.)

Other members might correct this.

—-

Including the question mark, K4 fills two 7x7 panels.  Layer two?

I’m fascinated by the periodic double letters.  I can’t imagine they’re a coincidence.

.mike

t:
My comment on Mike's post about the "Vig attack", with my reflections added:

I am not a crypto professional or even expert, but I think your method outline is correct. I want to point out that the way you state it, is very general, and it will work for many classes of polyalphabetic ciphers, from the simplest Vigenere to more sophisticated ones, but the higher the sophistication, the more amount of ciphertext is needed to give you enough statistics to be able to reconstruct the alphabets, the shifts, and the plaintext.

I think of it as roughly five classes of sophistication: (ignorig the hundreds of variants which would blur this categorization)
1. Periodic repetition of a keyword. Plain Vigenere with plain alphabet, shifted according to the periodically repeating letters of the keyword. (The difficulty increases with a longer keyword.)
2. Same as 1, but the alphabet is "mixed" according to a second keyword. This is the "Quagmire III" used in K1 and K2. If the alphabet is known (or easily guessed as in Kryptos), solution is as easy as type 1. Otherwise you need more data in order to reconstruct the unknown alphabet.
3. Same as 2, but the alphabet is "totally mixed", not based on a keyword (or the keword is as long as the alphabet).
4. Same as 2 or 3, but the alphabets are mixed independently of each other, one is not a shift of another one. You have to solve for all the alphabets independently.
5. Same as any previous class, but there is no periodic repetition of a keyword (the encryption key is as long as the text). This is "running key".

Your general outline would, in principle, work for all these classes, but would require increasing amount of CT and labor.

I would say class 1, and 2 where the alphabet can be guessed or some plaintext can be guessed, are reasonable to solve with "pencil and paper". The others are too much labor.

The dictionary attacks that other group members have performed, I think would cover classes 1 and 2. If the system is not keyword based, or if the keywords are non-standard and not in the dictionaries, it will not fall for such an attack. Also, if there is an additional masking stage or technique involved, you may hit the correct keys for the polyalpha decryption but you still won't get plaintext, you may not even get something with plaintext statistics that the computer can recognize, so it wouldn't be flagged as a possible solution.

And in reply to Aapjansen's question in the first post in the topic: Yes, you are right in thinking that an unknown cipher alphabet makes the solution much more complicated. It corresponds to class 1 vs class 2 in my list.

t:
I think it's good that this thread is recapitulating (the correct word?) what has been done in the group previously regarding brute force searching for Vig keys.
It is good for new members to have it mentioned (as searching through 20 years of messages is no easy task), and it is perhaps also a good refresher for old members.

So I read the posts here about what Rob and Geoffrey and Rohan have done, and surely other members have done similar work.

If I may take it one step further than that: Have members of the group tried brute-forcing for a possible combination of Vigenere-ish and transposition? Let me, for the sake of the following example, keep it simple and limit the search space to modular transposition. K4 is 97 chars, with almost that many possible modular transpositions. One should consider the two possibilities that encryption was vig+trans, or trans+vig (not commutative). This yields roughly 200 variations. If a double-keyword dictionary search takes a couple of hours (according to Rob), then the combined search that includes all modular transpositions would take 200 couples of hours, I would call it a couple of months then.

I do not think this work would solve K4, but it would settle that K4 is *not* simply that combination.

I'm curious to know more about how far the group members have taken the brute-force searches of this kind. Please accept my apologies if this is asking for repetition of old news, but as I said I think some recap is good.

(I am aware of the discussions about "1-1" in other topics, that may or may not rule out this kind of encryption scheme...)

s: Brute force entering every key for vigenere decryption
t:
The problem is there are simply too many degrees of freedom at this point.

As pointed out in this thread, the tableau itself was the clue for solving
K1+K2.  Without it, it would be much more difficult since you're probably
figure out it's polyalphabetic, but potentially not that it uses multiple
keywords.

And K3 really was just multiple transposition, which was sort of clear
because of the IC matched english text.

With K4, not only do we not know the 'masking' that Ed keeps alluding to,
but we also have no idea how it's potentially encrypted. That means the
possibilities are essentially infinite. To unravel a big ball of knotted
yarn, you have to find the first strand.  With K1, K2 and K3 there were
strands to tug on, but with K4 there so far isn't really anything to go off
of.  I think that's why interest has gradually dissipated over the last few
years.  A mystery is only fun when there are clues that potentially lead to
other clues. People have been chipping away at K4 for decades with
literally nothing to show for it, so there's just nothing to indicate that
any direction is the correct one.  It doesn't help (in my mind) that Jim
made the mistake in K2 with the ID BY ROWS, since now we aren't sure what's
deliberately a mistake, or just a mistake that Jim hasn't noticed yet (for
example the misspelling in K1 that seems to simply be a misspelling of the
keyword in that one location).

I'd personally feel way better if Jim and Ed would sit down and review all
the progress to date, and ensure that K4 can actually be decrypted.  But
for whatever reason Jim doesn't seem to want to do that.  I passively watch
these threads these days, but without some illumination or step in a new
direction from someone new, I literally have no idea how to proceed (or
rather, I have way too many ideas, none of which have any evidence that
they could be correct).

--
Duane Storey

t:
In regards to having nothing to show for the decades of chipping away at K4, I do believe I may have made some progress. A few months ago I created the QLU post and outlined how you could derive the key 'ELYOIEC' using both layers of the tableau included in Kryptos and the three keys (ABSCISSA, PALIMPSEST and KRYPTOS). I am no cryptanalyst, but, to me, what I discovered is no coincidence and it has always stood in agreeance with a lot of the subtle clues that have been given over the years via interviews and locations of existing plaintext. For instance, I think the IDBYROWS error was not an error. I think it was a hint that K4 might involve diagonal keys, since LAYERTWO appears when you shift the ciphertext over to the right by one character or just match each cipher character up diagonally with each key character in ABSCISSA. I definitely think the iqlusion error was on purpose and I detail my reasoning for why that it is in the supporting "K4 Partial Decryption Algorithms" Word document that I uploaded to my personal folder. I also believe that the importance of the error in K2 lies in the solution charts given by Sanborn. In K1, he writes illusion with PALIMPCEST being the keyword, but in K2 he writes ABSCISSA and underground correctly while putting the misspelling in the ciphertext. Another important clue: "digetal interpretati". I understand this as being good enough reason to delve into what differences there are between analog and digital encoding systems. An epiphany that I had the other day about Kryptos is one that might fall in line with statements made about the methods being used in K4 being "analog" and not "digital" ones. The question I asked myself was "what if some algorithm is spitting out a character and the cipher characters are used to relate that character to the plaintext?" For instance, in one part of my QLU post, I describe an algorithm in which finding the intersection (yes, I am aware that this is just the encryption of one character using the other as a key) of two diagonal key characters (using the inner tableau) reveals "LINC" in BERLIN CLOCK. What if the algorithm that spits out characters is just the intersection of the two diagonal key characters at that location and the cipher text is used as some sort of steering mechanism that points that character to the plaintext? Would this qualify as an analog encoding system? I am not sure, but something tells me that I am on the right track. Some clarification on a few things by Sanborn and Scheidt would be nice, but I am still appreciative of the interest in cryptography that Kryptos has given me and am content with never solving it or being totally wrong because I don't think I would have ever shown as much interest in the subject without it. Every time I get "LINC" or "BER" to appear using my algorithms, I am able to muster up more drive to try different solutions separate from or in addition to those methods. Another coincidence that I think is on purpose: AMQ, APL and BSU only appear twice in all of K4 and just so happen to appear where "berlinclock" and "eastnortheast". Another question I have started to ask myself is whether or not digital compasses can/should really be defined as "digital".

Anyways, I hope I have given you (and anyone else reading this) more motivation to work on Kryptos and not give up on it.

-Velocidev

I think it would probably help if people started implementing their own restrictions in order to remove Degrees of Freedom. We've been given a lot of information, and two of the best new sources are the 2009 Oral History of Jim Sanborn that Elonka unearthed and AJ's recent interview with Ed Scheidt.

1. The Oral History - the best part of this is it's a top-down comprehensive look at Jim as an artist over his lifetime. Kryptos is an aspect, not a focus. He goes into a great deal of detail about Kryptos however, part of which I feel completely removes the whole Vigenere degrees of freedom. It makes it clearer what Ed's role was as well.

2. Ed Scheidt's interview - It makes it clear that Ed knows very little and that lack of knowledge is deliberate, and his help on solving K4 as a code would be useless. It does however, put a great deal of insight into K4 being put together. Not as a code, but as a puzzle. I would hope that the distinction between code and puzzle is clear enough despite the overlap.

3. Continued clues that are intended for a puzzle rather than a code aren't as helpful as we might think.

I'd say that the moral of the story these two new known factors is key in on that distinction. A puzzle may incorporate code, but there are clues to study right on the sculpture. PT and CT. That's a huge restriction.

all know how hard this is, and we are all sort of doing this for fun.  That
said often when I read the documents on the site that people post, I feel
like I'm reading some ancient numerology text or looking at that scene in A
Beautiful Mind where he's in his office and there are strings of yarn all

Notes on analog vs. digital after some deep thought:

Analog devices - less accurate, harder to interpret, but easier to implement.
Digital devices - more accurate, easier to interpret, but harder to implement.

Digital devices rule out the possibility of interpreting or arguing their reading.

Examples:
Analog clocks are easier to implement than digital clocks, but harder to read.
Analog speedometers can be thought of the same way.
Digital compasses offer more accuracy, but I wouldn’t say that they are any easier to read than analog compasses.

Similarly, one could assume that analog messages work in the sender’s favor, not the receiver. This could mean cryptanalyst’s usual efforts would be some of the last to result in any exploitation of the methods used in K4.

Consensus:
The cipher text might as well be irrelevant to the exploitation of the methods used. They should be thought of as just a bunch of blank spaces at the bottom of the sculpture. That makes everything about the preceding messages very important. The disadvantage of not knowing the internals of a digital system must mean that the internals of an analog system are visible the entire time and that the disadvantage lies in the interpretation of the message being sent. You need to speak the receiver’s language in order to interpret the message.

Other thoughts:
Even though there are coordinates given in K2 and they lead to a place near the sculpture, could it be that after applying some alteration to where “true north” is, you would end up somewhere else? The lodestone and engraved compass on the same grounds as the sculpture could reveal this alternate location.

Hidden forces and shadow forces are comparable to ‘total’ invisibility and ‘virtual’ invisibility. One is in plain sight and the other is totally invisible, but both have an effect.

It might be possible to solve K4 without having solved K1 and K2 first, but it might be that having solved them first could make things a bit easier. As an example, the last four letters in K1, Row 1, have FIVJ. There are multiple inferences here, one of them being to change the J to E.Additionally, the last five letters in K2, Row 1, have QJNCE. This is a Cue to look at how J influences NCE in ABSENCE and NUANCE, words arrived at after having solved K1. When you replace the J in each of the VYJQT instances with E, K1 PT changes to: BETWEEN SUBTLE SHADING AND THE ABSENT EOF LIGHT LIES THE NUANT EOF IQLUSION. The meaning of this modified sentence is vastly different from the original, and I won't go into it here. The point is that K1 PT is referred to by the clue in K2.

PaulK

I have a potential solution to K4 but I need to double check with the group that my method works!
Step 1/ Create Baudot cipher letters for ABC and D in a list four times ( number doesn’t matter it just makes it easier to move them), eg ABCDABCDABCD thus creating five strips ie
A XX...
B X..XX
C .XXX.
D X..X.
and repeat. Cut these strips into five so that they can be used as a type of slide cipher. Make sure you number them!
Step 2/ Let’s use N/B  from NYPVTT/BERLIN as an example. Using the semaphore flags as a guide (really important that I stress this is only a guide) find the letter we want to decrypt. In this case it’s the letter N. This shows two flags in two diagonals. Line up the bits so that you can can create the letter N in Baudot code ie ..XX. using the right hand flag as the ciphertext letter. After moving the bits around the letter B can be formed along with a few other letters depending on which bits are used.
Step 3/ Move onto the next letter Y. Look up Y flag in semaphore. Using the right hand flag for the ciphertex move the strips to create the letter Y ie X.X.X Read off the diagonal and you should be able to find the letter E.
Step 4/ Keep working each ciphertext letter according to to flags ( please note that if flags directly up or down I read them horizontally either left to right or right to left, interesting property of Baudot means that it can be read either forwards or backwards)
Step 5/ My working theory is that Scheidt gave Sanborn a crib sheet so that he could pick the plain text letter and then choose a ciphertext letter he wanted, knowing that each letter in the list can be formed using the flags as a guide. The system can be used to encrypt or decrypt depending on which flags use.

Yes, these are the dog days, Fortunatus:
The heather lies limp and dead
On the mountain, the baltering torrent
Shrunk to a soodling thread;
Rusty the spears of the legion, unshaven its captain,
Vacant the scholar’s brain
Under his great hat,
Drug though She may, the Sybil utters
A gush of table-chat.

And you yourself with a head-cold and upset stomach,
Lying in bed till noon,
Your bills unpaid, your much advertised
Epic not yet begun,
Are a sufferer too. All day, you tell us, you wish
Some earthquake would astonish,
Or the wind of the Comforter’s wing
Unlock the prisons and translate
The slipshod gathering.

And last night, you say, you dreamed of that bright blue morning,
The hawthorn hedges in bloom,
When, serene in their ivory vessels,
The three wise Maries come,
Sossing through seamless waters, piloted in
By sea-horse and fluent dolphin:
Ah! how the cannons roar,
How jocular the bells as They
Indulge the peccant shore.

It is natural to hope and pious, of course, to believe
That all in the end shall be well,
But first of all, remember,
So the Sacred Books foretell,
The rotten fruit shall be shaken. Would your hope make sense
If today were that moment of silence,
Before it break and drown,
When the insurrected eagre hangs
Over the sleeping town?

How will you look and what will you do when the basalt
Tombs of the sorcerers shatter
And their guardian megalopods
Come after you pitter-patter?
How will you answer when from their qualming spring
The immortal nymphs fly shrieking,
And out of the open sky
The pantocratic riddle breaks –
‘Who are you and why?’

For when in a carol under the apple-trees
The reborn featly dance,
There will also, Fortunatus,
Be those who refused their chance,
Now pottering shades, querulous beside the salt-pits,
And mawkish in their wits,
To whom these dull dog-days
Between event seemed crowned with olive
And golden with self-praise.

W.H.Auden

Following up on my comment the other day, but now with another example ...
We know the 97-letter ciphertext; and we have Michelle's entire key and a
description of her method; and yet we still have to wonder what the
plaintext is. That's because Michelle's results, whatever they may be, will
not match yours or anyone else's. If all 3,000 members of this group took
the ciphertext and applied this key and this method, we could come up with
3,000 different "solutions." Using this key and method, "OBKR" could
decrypt to "that," "hope," "pray," "Laos," "orts," or a zillion other
random things.

In other words, two people, given the ciphertext, this key, and this
method, will not independently produce the same plaintext in a million
years. That's how we know that this isn't correct.

Bill Briere

s: Help with potential solution to K4
t:
If you sacrifice rarely-used letters, such as “Q,” “X,” and “Z,” you can use a pair of CT letters for a PT letter.

The encryptor has to choose, but they know the PT.

The decryptor has no choice.  Each letter of a paired PT letter maps to only one CT letter.

The K4 CT uses all the available letters.   Something is changing the letter frequencies.  Vigenere does that, but it’s been exhaustively applied.  K1 and K2 were solved early on.

Vigenere is a 1:1 cipher.  Perhaps we’re looking for a cipher that is not 1:1.

(If you use some of the CT letters to double up on a PT letter, and you want one of those “used” PT letters back, just misspell the PT word.  Sanborn misspelled PT a lot.  He even misspelled the CT once or twice.)

.mike

Sanborn’s original matrices for Section III, using the decryption steps:

- Write into 24C by 14R
- Turn left 90 degrees
- Write into 8C by 42R
- Turn left 90 degrees

The starting and ending row count is 8, 14 for encryption and 14, 8 for decryption.

These numbers can be derived by summing digits in the given longitude. It is ambiguous whether the 8 comes from minutes or seconds.

Turns for decryption are left, or to the West.

Section II has a strong horizontal sensibility. Abscissa, X, longitude, W(est) W(est), “double U”. So there is a strong sense that the transposition code is given in the longitude. Which might imply that the latitude (northerly) is the code for any remaining transposition.

With the added ambiguity that XLAYERTWO could imply that the last matrix height comes from multiplication rather than addition of digits.

Bob signals the decryption codes to Alice because that is what she needs to know next; but he may intend her to work out the encryption side herself I’d she is to need that for SECTION IV (and I think she does).

EASTNORTHEAST could be a cheeky clue (too late to do any good, for a blind solver), if Section IV involves using encryption (with East turns) and the northerly set of numbers as the matrix guide.

s: Help with potential solution to K4
t:
You've created a list of legal mappings of plain to cipher and vice versa.
We have a crib EASTNORTHEAST for ct FLRVQQPRNGKSS.

Your list of mappings doesn't allow one to decrypt the ciphertext N into the H of Northeast.  So this doesn't work with the cribs we've been given.

Your lists defines 276 of the 26x26=676 possible mappings as legal.
So you'd have 276 mappings to work with on a 97 letter plaintext.

You have, on average, about 10-11 possible plaintext letters for each ciphertext letter -- if this were to be used, you'd need a way to couple the decoding map with a rule to tell the recipient which specific mapping to use at each letter.

I haven't looked at this closer, because I don't understand how you produced your legal maps:  the words "semaphore" and "flag" are not defined, so I'm not sure what you're doing with the Baudot representations of the letters.  Of a set of 32 5-bit Baudot numbers, 26 are letters and 6 are not;  that's likely the underlying basis for which are legitimate letter to letter mappings.  With your shifting strips and looking for patterns, 26/32 of 5 bit patterns will be legitimate letters and 6/32 will not.

But with all the degrees of freedom, I think you've come up with a form of homophonic cipher that approximates a one time pad;  without rules for using your map, almost all plaintexts are possible form the ciphertext message.

s: Proposed method - Book Cipher, Transposition, Substitution (I have a candidate key)
t:
Greetings, all. New member, with hopefully some progress towards solving Kryptos.

Proposed method:
- Book cipher, transposed into a pseudorandom string (in my proposal, this will include a one-way process!)
- Polyalphabetic substitution, using the derived string as a strong key, along with the provided Kryptos tabula recta

This is similar in some ways to the Vernam Vigenere idea, which was a forerunner to the one-time pad and which still has some relevance in modern digital cipher methods, especially stream ciphers. Encryption and decryption are straightforward substitution processes and fully reversible. The key is a complex pseudorandom string of characters; creation of the key must be repeatable but need not be reversible. A one-way algorithm works just fine (for everyone but Eve, but her feelings are not our concern).

Quick analysis of the revealed plaintext, worked backwards into a substitution key, gives sequences RDUMRIYWOYNKY and ELYOIECBAQK. A full third of these characters are vowels, which - for this sample size - leads to a quick rule of thumb analysis of “jumbled English.”

That suggests a known text passage - at least, known to Bob and discoverable by Alice - that has been mixed through transposition.

I hypothesize that the known text is from a book cipher - and I have a strong candidate!

THE PINS REMOVED THE LID WAS RAISED. THE PENULTIMATE SCENE WAS DISCLOSED - A VERY NEATLY WRAPPED MUMMY OF THE YOUNG KING, WITH GOLDEN MASK OF SAD BUT TRANQUIL EXPRESSION, [SYMBOLIZING OSIRIS.]

Howard Carter diary entry of 28-October-1925.

Guides and cues:

- Answers the question from K3. While it took a further three years from discovery of the tomb, Carter did eventually find the most wonderful thing in Tut’s tomb - the iconic burial mask.
- PINS aligns with the raised letters at the beginning of Section III. (Like the tumblers of a lock!)
- THE PINS...YOUNG KING is 97 characters, so this passage might have come up during Alice’s search for a book cipher, even if she originally thought she was looking for a running key.
- The X and Q from the end of Section III serve to locate the end of the passage, or at the very least that we should go at least that far. Section III’s CAN YOU SEE ANYTHING is 17 characters and may suggest we need to go that much farther to finish the sentence.
- OSIRIS completes a thematic layout for all of Kryptos: SCROLL, CROSS, TOMB, RESURRECTION
- A mask is a nice solution to Section I’s merging of the ideas of ILLUSION and OCCLUSION
- Towards the end of the passage, the linen wrappings of the mummy are described as “longitudinal and transverse,” suggesting the geolocation theme of Section II.
- Two days prior, on 26-Oct, Carter’s entry has a remarkable 7 X’s, matching the corrected Section II.
- All our required letters from the revealed plaintext are here, including the 4 Y’s, Q, and 2 K’s.

Obvious problems and thoughts:
- Working out the transposition is the toughest part of the solve. I’ve actually been stuck here for close to nine months.
- Both variants are longer than 97 characters, so an elimination strategy is required at some point during the transposition. The first variant (ending EXPRESSION) is 137 characters, and the second variant adds 17 characters for 154. Alternately, the key may continue as far as REALIZE THE PAST, which adds some B, C, and Y to the mix but uses a lot more graph paper.
- The source key itself hints at an elimination strategy - remove the pins and raise the lid.
- Most of my guesswork has centered on finding matrices where I can visualize removing PINS (which may be the columns denoted by the raised letters) and also lifting a LID (probably the top row or rows of the final matrix).
- Another way to get to 97 is to write the final transposition into 57+57+40 (using the 154 character source), and then eliminate one of the longer lines. We also have the idea of 57 in the geographic coordinates in the Section II solve.
- I recommend looking online for the “neatly filled matrix” solutions to Section III, as I feel strongly that the transposition idea is essentially the same for Section IV but with the added difficulty of partially filled matrices and the need to work out an elimination strategy.
- The intended solve for Section III is: Write C1 into 24C x 14R. Turn left 90. Write C2 into 8C by 42R. Turn left 90.
- This may loosely connect to the numbers given in the geographic coordinates from Section II. And we may be intended to use those same numbers, or the unused numbers, in our matrices for Section IV.

So that’s where I am at right now. I think Bob was vacationing in Berlin without his one-time pad and he needed to get a message to his friend Alice at headquarters. He concocted a bespoke one-time key by relying on Alice’s fantastic library skills to find the correct starting key from her library. He also gave her the tools to work out his substitution strategy and his transposition strategy. Find the key, turn it, use it to unlock the message.

Eve’s job is a monster if she’s trying to work this out without access to the source key. Too many asymmetries for her to really deal with effectively.

And I’m not assuming this is absolutely correct. But it feels a whole lot more correct than most of the other thoughts I have had - it actually feels really close. Just need to get a B, C, and Q to converge somehow, which still eludes me.

=G

t:
I agree with Ross, I would say the obvious Occam's Razor explanation is that Q represents the question mark at the end of the last sentence of K3. If you look at the graphic of the EASTNORTHEAST clue that Jim Sanborn sent to Sukhwant and others, notice that the actual "?" is included at the beginning as part of K4. The correct solution method of K3 requires that the "?" NOT be included in order to perform the transposition steps correctly. So it is not redundant to have "Q" for the question mark at the end of K3, and then the actual "?" with some other meaning at the beginning of K4.

It also seems to me that Jim wanted to include the letters X and Q in the text of K3. The only letter of the alphabet not present in K3 is Z. As an example of how this could be used, if one wanted to fill a 5x5 Polybius square with the letters placed in the order in which they first appear in the K3 ciphertext, one could do so consistently and without any ambiguity since only Z is missing and it can be placed at the end. If Q and Z were both missing, there could be potential ambiguity about the order in which to place them in the Polybius square in such a method.

s: Is Columnar Transpostion combined with Vigenere Solvable?
t:
Hi there,

The struggle to solve K4 is mostly cause by the ciphertext not giving many clues, which keeps us guessing for the method of encryption.
The only way to get closer to the right method is by crossing wrong methods of the list, and this can be done in several ways.

The first and most obvious way is by analyzing the ciphertext for phenomenons that are expected to show up when using a specific encryption method.
This way we ruled out simple substitution, any kind of transposition cipher (on its own), and probably many more.

This still leaves us with a large number of possible encryption methods, and even a combination of multiple methods may be used.
So we need another way to cross methods of the list.

The second way, which is not nearly as easy, is to come up with a reliable solving method for a encryption method. In many cases this will be a computer program that has proven to be able to beat a certain number of randomly created ciphers with a specific encryption method.

I've been wondering if a combination of columnar transposition and vigenere might be the used method for K4, but i'm not at a point where i can solve a cipher like this on my computer.

So i've created the following ciphertext:
TUHIJNSIYDMYNQYEWKIOIUXUKTYGXVHOLULNNNMVILWWFPDZZIQBBMKWTDLLUBIHUKSQXGZINCFBVUTVZVMFUHGBRGFSZIVJQUZZ

This is a 97 character plaintext, that i've put through a columnar transposition first. And after that i've encrypted the resulting text using vigenere.
I used the KRYPTOSABCDEFGHIJLMNQUVWXZ alphabet, and two random picked words from a dictionary to encrypt this.
Also the plaintext has EASTNORTHEAST and BERLINCLOCK on positions 22-34 and 64-74.

I realize that my ciphertext is longer than 97 characters because the columnar transposition needed padding (that's what happens when you pick the keyword at random). But for the way of solving this that should not be a problem I think.

Does anyone have a good idea about how to go at this? Brute forcing it will take around 1,2234*10^11 combinations of keywords, so probably not a good idea.

t:
K4 analyzes similar to autokey or running key. It isn’t either of those as traditionally implemented, but that’s how the frequency analysis works out. It’s a mostly even letter distribution, but with a small tail on the ends. The NSA solver team identified this back in the early 90s before abandoning further solve attempts.

The frequency analysis for both methods should be similar: a nearly uniform letter distribution in the CT, but with a bit of a peak at one or two higher frequency letters. K4 has 8 K’s which is twice the expected frequency for a random distribution.

But if K4 is not autokey or running key, what leads to that frequency analysis? We don’t get English words when we back out substitution with the Kryptos tableaux. But what we do get is interesting: 8 of 24 letters are vowels. (That isn’t the case with a standard tabula recta - you get 4 of 24 vowels with the standard alphabet). And as a Scrabble player, I don’t mind the consonants I’m getting. We’re missing S and T, and we have some extra Y’s. But I don’t hate it the way I would hate X, V, J, Z all showing up.

8/24 vowels, for this sample size, is a good match for English letter frequencies. 4/24 vowels is a good match for random distribution - but that doesn’t shed light on K as the highest frequency letter.

But this does: look at K’s intersections in the Kryptos tableaux. I/E, O/U, A/N. Three combos with high frequency letters. It would be very difficult to line up two rows of normal English frequency text, and not have those combos appearing at a generally high frequency compared to other combos. And all of those combos result in K in the ciphertext.

Analysis: the letter frequency of the ciphertext is consistent with having English letter frequencies in both the plaintext and the key. The recovered key and the analysis of the highest-frequency letter, K, suggest that substitution is Vigenere style using the Kryptos tableaux.

But - and this is a critical methodology note - the recovered key isn’t legible as English. It has English letter frequencies, but it is not ordered as English.

My hypothesis: The key is jumbled English, created by transposing some English text into a pseudorandom string of characters. This pseudorandom string was then used as a strong, non-repeating key for a final substitution via the Kryptos tableaux.

This is similar in some ways to how modern stream ciphers work. Some apparently random string of characters is created to be used as a substitution key. As long as the method for producing the pseudorandom key remains undiscovered, the end product is essentially as secure as a one-time pad. (With points off in this one instance, because the key is not completely random - it still has the feel of English letter frequencies, and further points off if - as I think - the method for creating the final key is embedded in the solved portions of Kryptos. That’s bad security, but good puzzle design, so I’m inclined to give it a pass.

So in short, I think the analysis leads to:
  *  Some English language source key text, likely from a book cipher
  *  This source text is transposed similar to K3, with some portion forming a strong key for the final step
  *  Final substitution step using the Kryptos tableaux, similar to K1-K2.

This method would fit with my early understanding of Kryptos as a distress cipher. How could you rig up a reasonably secure cipher using very basic and known building blocks, and then encode your method instructions in a way that hopefully only your intended audience is clever enough to work out.

In my first thread on this board, I further hypothesized a book passage that I am increasingly convinced is the original source of the key - Howard Carter’s field diary entry of 28 October 1925*, describing the opening of the innermost casket containing Tutankhamun’s mummy and iconic golden burial mask - and my current solve attempts are based on finding the correct transposition of that text into a suitable 97-character randomized key.

*This was nearly three years after the tomb itself was opened, and as far as I know Carter didn’t write a book detailing this part of the excavation. But surely “his mummy!” is the smart fifth grader’s answer to the question posed by K3, even if it wasn’t the immediate answer given at the time.

Final note: the thread title references Columnar Transport as the means of transposition, but this was not Sanborn’s method. K3 was enciphered via route transposition - in by rows, out by columns. Dead simple to operate on paper - much simpler even than columnar transport.

t:
This is a great analysis - thanks for sharing.  Really insightful.

I tried looking at the letter distribution previously too and was working
out ways on how to get a similar distribution.

What I found is that if you took the letter/frequency distribution for
english and combined it with one or more shifted versions in english, you
could get a similar distribution.

That is if you look at the letter distribution here:
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Letter_frequency

You'll often notice that for the letters that are used frequently, the ones
next to them are used infrequently. So if you shift it, even by one or two
letters, and combine it, you'll drastically flatten the resulting
distribution.

Your comment about the K's is a good one, since many of the letters in
'KRYPTOS' have local peaks in the frequency distribution (K, S, T are the
most common letters in K4).

Taking all of this together, I was sort of wondering if K4 was a
combination of two ciphers, both utilizing the KRYPTOS alphabets but with
different keywords.  One potential way to do this would be to split K4 into
two plain texts and encode each of them separately, then put them back
together.  In practical terms, this is similar to having a scrambled key
like you mentioned, but the key would involve the interleaving of two
different "normal" keys (i.e. CHAINSAW and BAT) in a non repeating way.

For example if the DYAHR was a key to the interleaving (I'm not saying it
is, just saying this is one example), then it's 01101 in terms of the
interleaving.

So, using CHAINSAW and BAT

CHAIN SAWCH AINSA WCHAI NSAWC
BATBA TBATB ATBAT BATBA TBATB
01101 01101 01101 01101 01101

And the interleaving 01101, where 0 is the bottom word and 1 is the top
word, you'd get something like this

BHABN TAWTH AINAA BCHBI TSATC

Which looks like complete gibberish, but is actually two completely normal,
interleaved keys that would effective scramble the IC.

In my example, if you used CHAINSAW and BAT, then the encoding would repeat
at 8x3 = 24 characters.  But if it was coupled with a 5 bit interleaving
like that, then I imagine that pushes it up to 5x24 = 120 characters.
Which essentially makes it look like a one-time pad since it's longer than
K4.

D.

--
Duane Storey

Following up on Rob's replies to Aapjansen's cipher challenge, I agree that an 11-letter keyword for the second step (Vigenere / Quagmire III with the KRYPTOS-keyed alphabet as in the tableau on the sculpture) appears to make sense. For example, in the ciphertext, the letter I appears in the 8th, 19th, 41st, and 63rd positions -- a high rate of coincidence, as this means 4 of the 9 letters encrypted with the 8th letter of an 11-letter keyword would be the same letter. Further in this vein, the letter I also appears in the 50th, 72nd, and 94th positions, so 3 of the 9 letters encrypted with the 6th letter of an 11-letter keyword would be the same letter. Also, the letter Z appears in the 49th, 71st, and 93rd positions, so 3 of the 9 letters encrypted with the 5th letter of an 11-letter keyword would be the same letter. Likewise, the letter H appears in the 31st, 64th, and 86th positions, so 3 of the 9 letters encrypted with the 9th letter of an 11-letter keyword would be the same letter. Such letter coincidences may contribute to the relatively high index of coincidence that Rob finds in his 11-letter keyword.

Further, experimenting with some common ending sequences of 11-letter words, I find that the ending sequence -ITATE works strikingly well to decrypt Aapjansen's ciphertext into intermediate text that looks a lot like scrambled (transposed) English plaintext. With such a keyword, I would be the key letter for the 7th, 18th, etc. positions, T for the 8th, 19th, etc., A for the 9th, 20th, etc., T for the 10th, 21st, etc., and E for the 11th, 22nd, etc. positions. Using the KRYPTOS-keyed alphabet on the sculpture tableau and these key letters, the 45 letters of Aapjansen's ciphertext that occur in these positions decrypt to the following letters:

leusa
eexed
cmars
aednf
otrhi
neali
toote
wlacw
afglh

Like Rob, I haven't found the "k" that we need in "clock" in the plaintext yet. Also the "b" in "berlin" has not appeared yet, although there are still 55 more plaintext letters to decrypt. But everything else in "eastnortheast" and "berlinclock" appears to be present already in this possible fragment of the scrambled plaintext, even both "c's" in "clock".

Thus, I am going to guess that Rob's 11-letter keyword ends in -ITATE. (I also note the presence of one "x" but the absence of "q" and "z".) Hopefully, we are on the right track for Aapjansen's Vigenere / Quagmire step keyword itself.

Geoffrey

s: Is Columnar Transpostion combined with Vigenere Solvable?
t:
Thanks Bill. Of course the solution process was a joint effort with Rob's and Anders' analysis and comments providing great assistance, along with Aapjansen's clarifications.

The biggest takeaway for me is the fact that the Index of Coincidence of the plaintext 97-letter message itself, without the XXX at the end, was only 5.48% or 1.42 (42% greater than typical average random text). And it does not appear to me that Aapjansen even did anything deliberate in particular to reduce the IC of the message. If he had thrown in (another) "X", a "Q", and a couple misspellings, as Sanborn did in K1-K3, the IC could have been even lower. This should be a lesson for us: We cannot necessarily expect a very high IC even in the final plaintext of K4. Aapjansen's plaintext reads like a perfectly normal, natural English message to me, and yet it only has an IC of 5.48%. It just so happens that N, O, T, R don't occur with great frequency in this particular message, while L, C, H, G are more frequent than usual. In a 97-letter message, this is enough to suppress the IC quite a bit without any extremely unnatural distortions of the English plaintext. Given this result, I would not be surprised if the IC of the K4 plaintext could be as low as 5.20% (1.35) or even 5.00% (1.30), with just a few of Sanborn's typical dummy letters and misspellings sprinkled in the text.

Geoffrey

s: end of "Pre-Kryptos" message: logical process to get POS from YCA
t:
Jim M. and others have posted here previously about the mysterious ending of the last word of Sanborn's "Pre-Kryptos" sculpture message: The ciphertext YZIUTJYCA deciphers as ETRANSEWJ, but most logically it should be ETRANSPOS, the word TRANSPOSE with the last letter shifted to the beginning. As far as I know from Jim M.'s post and others, no one has yet found a logical process to produce POS as the last three plaintext letters from YCA.

The decryption process of the Pre-Kryptos message uses the plain alphabetical, classical "tabula recta" Vigenere tableau. Sanborn included this tableau on his Pre-Kryptos sculpture model. But he also put another Vigenere tableau on the Pre-Kryptos sculpture model, using an alphabet keyed with the keyword GIRASOL. The Pre-Kryptos cipher message itself does not appear to use this GIRASOL-keyed alphabet in the encryption process, and I am not sure if it is used anywhere else in Sanborn's Kryptos-related or other cryptographic works.

Here is what I have found: YCA can indeed decrypt to POS if we use the GIRASOL-keyed alphabet Vigenere tableau and the key letters BAZ.

The key letters BAZ can be seen as part of a backward alphabet key: A is the end of the backward alphabet, and then the key returns to Z, the beginning of the backward alphabet.

Of course, as with any such logical process applied to only three letters, there is a 1 in 26*26 = 676 chance that this is just a coincidence. But three letters are all we have to work with in this particular mysterious unexplained piece of message at the end of Pre-Kryptos.

The new encryption method found here is the use of the backward alphabet as a sort of 26-letter pseudo-running key for a Vigenere Quagmire III cipher with a keyed alphabet tableau. I note that such a 26-letter key would be extremely difficult to identify for a 97-letter message such as K4, since each key letter is only used a maximum of 4 times. I doubt very much statistical information could be gleaned from a standard cryptanalytic attack on such a cipher.

Also, the shift from the plain alphabet tableau to the GIRASOL-keyed alphabet tableau suggests to me that according to this logic, such a method for K4 would likely *not* use the same KRYPTOS-keyed alphabet tableau. We would have to figure out the keyword used to key a different alphabet for the tableau.

Geoffrey
