s: CipherChallenge 2: Vigenere, followed by Columnar Transposition
t:
Thanks Aapjansen. We appreciate the challenges!

First thought: The 98 character final ciphertext length strongly suggests to me that the columnar transposition keyword is 7 letters long. It could also be 14 letters long, but a randomly chosen dictionary keyword is vastly more likely to be 7 letters than 14 letters. So that is the first guess I would make in a cryptanalytic attack on this cipher challenge.

Geoffrey

---

An additional observation: If my guess is right that the columnar transposition keyword is 7 letters long, then it can actually be proven that it follows that the Vigenere (Quagmire III) keyword is NOT 9 letters long, as follows:

In EASTNORTHEAST, the repeated EAST strings are 9 letters apart. If the Vig keyword were 9 letters long, EAST would decrypt to exactly the same 4 letters in each place.

If the transposition keyword is 7 letters, then we can find each group of 7 letters (1st-7th, 8th-14th, etc.) in the ciphertext, although we do not know the internal order of each group of 7 letters. But we know that the 22nd-28th letters, in some unknown order, are TMXYZOH, and the 29th-35th letters, in some unknown order, are NKNAKKZ.

We know the 22nd-28th plaintext letters are EASTNOR, and we know the 29th-34th plaintext letters are THEAST. If EAST decrypted to the same 4 letters in each place, those 4 letters would be present somewhere in each of the 7-letter ciphertext groups specified above. But only 1 ciphertext letter is present in both groups, Z. Therefore, the Vig step keyword cannot be 9 letters long.

At least we can thus reduce the computational load of a two-step dictionary attack on this cipher: We can restrict the transposition step dictionary search to 7-letter words, and we can begin by focusing the Vigenere step dictionary search on 8, 10, 11, and 12 letter words, which I consider the most plausible likely keyword lengths for the message encryptor to use, having eliminated a 9-letter keyword.

Geoffrey

---

More subtly, we can also prove that if the transposition step keyword is 7 letters, then the Vigenere step keyword is NOT 8 letters either, in the following way:

If the Vig step keyword were 8 letters, then the 24th, 32nd, 64th, and 72nd letters would all be encrypted with the same keyword letter. Those letters in the plaintext cribs we have are S (24th), A (32nd), B (64th), and O (72nd). It just so happens that those four letters are the 7th, 8th, 9th, and 6th letters, respectively, in the KRYPTOS-keyed alphabet. Therefore, their respective ciphertext letters should be in the same relative order somewhere in the KRYPTOS-keyed alphabet.

It's useful to focus on the group of 29th-35th ciphertext letters, NKNAKKZ (if the transposition step keyword is indeed 7 letters), because it only has 4 distinct different letters in it, reducing the possible options. Thus, the 32nd plaintext letter A must encrypt to one of the four possible ciphertext letters N, K, A, or Z.

If this A encrypts to N, then the 72nd PT letter O would have to encrypt to L. But there is no L in the 71st-77th CT letter group, if the transposition step keyword is 7 letters.
If this A encrypts to K, then the 64th PT letter B would have to encrypt to R. But there is no R in the 64th-70th CT letter group, if the transposition step keyword is 7 letters.
If this A encrypts to A, then the 24th PT letter S would have to encrypt to S. But there is no S in the 21st-28th CT letter group, if the transposition step keyword is 7 letters.
If this A encrypts to Z, then the 64th PT letter B would have to encrypt to K. But there is no K in the 64th-70th CT letter group, if the transposition step keyword is 7 letters.

Therefore, there is no possible encryption with an 8-letter Vigenere step keyword, if the transposition step keyword is indeed 7 letters.

Geoffrey

---

Here is Aapjansen's plaintext message:

IF YOU JOURNEY FROM THERE EASTNORTHEAST AT SOME POINT YOU SHALL ENCOUNTER A BERLIN CLOCK THIS MEANS YOU HAVE ARRIVED O

The keyword for the first Vigenere / Quagmire III step is the 11-letter word UNRECLINING

This gives the following intermediate step ciphertext:

DOPJTAQHJFXWOYJRUPTJTXYZOTHMNAKKNZKOLHCKVQBSZUSSIOVDSTSTXVTGYJKWTHFBQQKVXNNAYREFMYWLXDAQLTBFDSETZX

Then a columnar transposition with a 7-letter keyword rearranges this intermediate ciphertext into Aapjansen's final ciphertext of the challenge cipher:

TWTTNKSTYBNYLTQYTMKQITKQYLBXDHJXNOBOXWKRXFOJRYALSVVTVEDDPFUZKHZDTHXFASJXPOKCUSGFNMQEAOJHZVSSJQAWTZ

Geoffrey Caveney

---

Here is how I cracked Aapjansen's challenge cipher:

In assuming a 7-letter keyword for the transposition step, when I came to examining the possibility of an 11-letter keyword for the Vigenere step, I focused on the following six letters in the plaintext crib clues:

EA (22nd and 23rd letters)
ST (33rd and 34th letters)
RL (66th and 67th letters)

E,S,R should all be encrypted with the same letter of an 11-letter keyword, as should A,T,L.

Again, if the 7-letter keyword for the transposition step is correct, then the 22nd-28th letters of the intermediate step ciphertext are TMXYZOH, the 29th-35th letters are NKNAKKZ, and the 64th-70th letters are BQWTHFQ, each in some unknown order.

Using the KRYPTOS-keyed alphabet, the only possible consistent encryptions of E,S,R and A,T,L with the same keyword letters into ciphertext letters that appear in the above groups of letters are the following:

E>X, S>N, R>H
and
A>Y, T>Z, L>F

And here I checked and found that these six ciphertext letters XY, NZ, and HF appear in *six different columns* in the columnar transposition with a 7-letter keyword! This is exactly what we are looking for, because the 22nd, 23rd, 33rd, 34th, 66th, and 67th letters should indeed be in six different columns in a 7-column transposition of the text.

Based on this observation, there is a unique columnar transposition order that places each of these six ciphertext letters into its correct place: 3 4 5 6 1 7 2. (For example, the keyword FISSATE in Aapjansen's dictionary file would produce such a columnar transposition order.)

At this point, it was a simple matter to decrypt the columnar transposition step into the original letter order of the plaintext and intermediate step ciphertext. Then it is simple to run this intermediate step ciphertext through an online Vigenere cipher decryption program, specifying the KRYPTOS-keyed alphabet and an 11-letter keyword. At this point, such a program easily finds the keyword UNRECLINING and the correct original plaintext message.

Geoffrey

Thank you Bill and Aapjansen.

Honestly the biggest help was the fact that several of us had just worked on your previous challenge cipher with the steps in the reverse order. I know we expected the second one to be harder, but just the fact that we had worked through the first one and discussed it step by step was a very good preparation for me to tackle the second one. So even though technically I solved the second one on my own, I benefited greatly from everyone's contributions in the discussion, analysis, and work on the first cipher.

In terms of the technical details of how certain clues helped in the solution process: #1, just knowing in general what the encryption steps were, and their order, reduces the size of the possible solution space enormously. #2, knowing that the Vigenere step uses the KRYPTOS-keyed alphabet reduces the load on the solver enormously. Then, getting into more particular details, I actually don't think the plaintext length itself was a critical piece of knowledge. Rather, the huge help was that we knew your transposition step keyword had to be a factor of 98. Knowing that, it didn't really matter if the plaintext length itself was 97, 98, 96, 95, or anything else. The fact that you made all the columns the same length in the transposition, and we effectively knew this, was the big clue. Columnar transpositions can also be done with unequal column lengths, and then any length of the keyword is in play and must be considered and tested. Finally, the sheer amount of crib clues that we have, 24 of the 97 plaintext letters, is what enabled me to perform the critical key steps in the decryption. But to be fair, we have this for K4 as well!

s: A new method and brute-force solution
t:
Sukhwant,

Thanks for describing your method. Many solution claims show up here
without any explanation whatsoever of how they came to be.

It looks like you've used an overly flexible arrangement to arrive at what
still doesn't read like plaintext. Both of those features (overly flexible
and not reading like plaintext) raise red flags immediately. The fact that
you had "8 solutions for each character" to work with doesn't lend any
credence to the outcome. And "using brute force" is somewhat vague in this
context. If you were to explain your method to someone else--without
revealing your plaintext--that other person would almost certainly not come
up with anything resembling your result.

Parsing this out, your result might read something like this: "?GNIK
[KING?] A LINE ID BY AND END IN EAST NORTHEAST LIES AT ALE OF WAR AND PEACE
FAINTLY BERLIN CLOCK FLASHING A FEW X AGE SIGN WOR[KING]."

So, no, this isn't the solution. That doesn't mean that I know what the
solution is. It just means that when we see the correct method, keys, and
plaintext, there will be no need to wonder if it's right.

I know you already know this, Sukhwant, but for anyone that hasn't heard it
yet, there are several professional/retired/expert/qualified cryptanalysts
in this group who are willing to check proposed solutions, for free. Anyone
who wants this service can simply post their proposed solution here, along
with a description of the method/system/keys/algorithms or whatever was
used, and ask for verification. It pains me so much to see people sending
money to Sanborn to "verify solutions" (despite your lucky break in
receiving "EAST"). If the work can be scientifically repeated by someone
else, then it's correct. Sanborn doesn't need to be paid to verify it.
There have been hundreds of claimed solutions to K-4 over the years, in
this group and elsewhere. None of them has been correct. But when the
correct solution is found, it will be obvious.

s: K2-K4 Patterns, TBJ’s beginning and UND
t:
Theory: Examining Jim’s non-Kryptos Decryptions for Caesarian shifts involving simple letter/number switching may show a pattern. To this end, I employ an analytic tool called KEY in a less sloppy fashion then the previous post.

KEY is a tool based on each known Plaintext/Ciphertext combination having a known pair of Caesarian shifts, one positive and one negative, depending on the direction one moves in the alphabet when shifting.  B to N has a KEY value of +12 over -14. Both numbers may  also have letter values based on an elementary A=1, B=2  simplified alphabet cipher. Thus B to N may  also have a value of L over N.

With that in mind, we start at TBJ.
TBJ is a recurring three letter ciphertext sequence in K2 that, along with other repeating sequences,  can be used to solve Vigenere under a Kasiski test. It’s helpful for this reason, and even more so for the fact that TBJ = UND… the letters in UND-ergru-UND. So it’s kinda special. So what?

Here’s where I perform a KEY analysis of NORTHEAST and BERLIN.

NORTHEAST
3/23  2/24 2/24 2/24 6/20 2/24 10/16 0/0 1/25   or
c  b   b   b  f  B J .  a
w  x  x   x  T  x p .  z

BERLIN
12/24 6/20 2/24 10/16 11/15 6/20
l   f    B    J    k    f
n   T   x   p  o   t

Note the TBJ alignments and digitally interpret them as lines …. Following the theme of Tut’s tomb, that’s the line patterns on Tut’s headdress….. that’s also the the short and long hands on a clock…. And it’s an easterly line that heads northeast mirrored in a reversed position.  There’s a pattern in that.

There’s also more. TBJ ends at the 32nd letter in NORTHEAST.
TBJ begins at the second letter in BERLIN and the B = 64.

Conclusion: Pieces of a system drawing on the misspelled clues.

s: Scheidt interview comment - reference to BASIC programming language?
t:
In the interview with Ed Scheidt last fall, I recall his comment about the masking step transforming the K4 message text into a "different language", and he also made the cryptic comment that the language was "known then, secret now". It occurs to me, I wonder if this could be a reference to the old once-popular BASIC computer programming language? Indeed, I remember well how it was wildly popular among personal computer users in the 1970s and 1980s, so it still would have been quite "topical" when Kryptos was designed in the late 1980s. But regular BASIC fell out of use quickly in the 1990s, and is now considered an outdated relic as a programming language today.

I also observe that the K2 keyword "ABSCISSA" contains the letters of "BASIC" as its first 5 letters. There is a well-known possible clue that together, "PALIMPSEST" and "ABSCISSA" can be anagrammed to form the statement, "PS: It's as simple as ABC". The word BASIC itself would also match this theme of "simple".

Does anyone have ideas for how concepts from the old BASIC computer programming language might possibly be used to perform a masking step on the letters of a message?

Geoffrey

t:
What confuses me is that using "pen and paper" to decrypt k4 is recommended over writing code (or using cryptanalysis) that traverses various substitutions (and then transpositions on those substitutions) and tries to find English words in them or at least checks the letter distribution to see if you could form BERLINCLOCK and EASTNORTHEAST. That would seem to suggest the use of steganography. Even though k4 is probably not meant to be solved by a cryptanalyst, I think it is important to know how one goes about "masking" the language used in a cipher and verifying its soundness. I am not a cryptanalyst, but it could be that "changing the language base" just means that deviating away from the English language would provide no benefit towards exploiting the methods used or the plaintext. I am pretty convinced that it is digital (substitution/transposition) at the surface and analog (code talk) at the center. That would make the most sense in my opinion.

What would also make sense to me would be to combine the first two keys to create a new key (possible the one with SBILITY in it?) and then to decrypt (Vigenere) k4 using this new key and either the inner or outer tableau provided in the sculpture.
After that would come transposition.
Then the code talk.

Also, I think someone can have an "absence of mathematical ability" and have amazing propositional logic skills at the same time.

Welcome, Sean.

To your questions ...

1. There are all kinds of peeps and all kinds of approaches here. You'll
find subjective viewpoints and hardcore cryptanalysis and everything in
between. You'll find people who work in small groups and some who work
alone; most do a combination of the two and then check in to report
whatever they've learned to the group--sometimes frequently, sometimes
occasionally. There are various clusters of members who bounce ideas off of
each other to good effect. About every 2 years, on average, everyone in the
group is invited to an in-person brainstorming session, usually with a
couple dozen of us showing up. The next such get-together will likely be
held on or about May 14, 2022, in the D.C. area (details to appear here as
they gel).

2. Since we're a very diverse group, we often disagree about which specific
observations are significant and which are not. And every few weeks or so,
someone will prematurely announce that he or she has solved it. The fact
that we don't yet have the solution to K-4 means that we're obviously
missing the system and/or the keys. But, over the years, we've reached a
loose consensus (sometimes backtracking) about which systems and keys are
likely NOT used. We definitely count that as progress here.

Tell your parents "Semper fi," from a fellow Marine.

Bill Briere

s: Update on (yet another) failed K4 attempt
t:
Regarding the Z-340 solution -- the "night move" transposition was merely a result of that team using the wrong padding. With the correct padding, the message is simply read out vertically down the columns. (This is similar to early incorrect padding on K3 yielding the solution along diagonals.)

As for methods that haven't worked, I can add my latest results here. K4 was NOT encrypted by:

1. Quagmire III using KRYPTOS-keyed mixed alphabet and a keyword found in an ordinary (100,000+ word) dictionary

followed by

2a. Incomplete columnar transposition of any permutation of 9 columns or less (414,152 permutations)
Or
2b. Incomplete columnar transposition keyed by any 10-15-letter keyword found in the above dictionary

The same search was tried using the regular alphabet instead of the KRYPTOS-keyed alphabet in the substitution step. The "highest scoring" permutation (where scoring was with LOG tetragraphs of the first 25 letters of candidate plaintext) was:

1. Kryptos mixed alphabet
2. Quagmire keyword: LITURGIES
3. 8-column transposition with column order 65871423 (can be keyed by MOONCALF)

The intermediate ciphertext following columnar transposition decryption was:

"WKGFBOWVAWKBSBTQTGUNOKQQJDHYLRSPKKUPIUJRLZAVFOQNUXUTBXSGDTETBOSKIJKMWGESACCZFHKSWDAFLUZOIIRPRLZTN"

The first 25 letters of plaintext are then:  SECLAMBERSETEALONATTRONAR

Doesn't mean that K4 ~wasn't~ encrypted with Quagmire III followed by columnar transposition. Jim could have used a different mixed alphabet, or a keyword not found in my dictionary, or 10 or more columns in the transposition but not keyed by a word in my dictionary.  --Rob

Hello,

I would like to propose the following key schedule applied to the last 97 characters.  DESPARATLYUNDERGRUUNDIQLUSION.  If repeated throughout the cipher, it matches up perfectly with the letters.  DESPARATLY begins and ends the key schedule.

DESPARATLY = 40 letters in the key schedule.
UNDERGRUUND = 11 LETTERS = 33 letters in the key schedule.
IQLUSION = 24 letters in key schedule.

33+40+24 = 97

However, I think this only gets us half-way to the solution.  I believe the second part requires transposition of the original K4 letters into a position that, when used in combination with the key schedule, gets a solution.

The transposed letters that would give us "EASTNORTHEAST" and "BERLINCLOCK" are the following:

KRWZZQSWXVGCE and CMOBLHYRJDG, respectively.

I have attempted a lot of variations of transpositions including what was used to solve K3 and wrapping the letters around each other (Sanborn did say that the puzzle will unravel itself at one point).  These attempts have all been failures.

I've added a photo album titled "Key Schedule" of what it looks like plus the transposed letters of the cipher for the already given hints.

Why I like this:

1) It fits
2) I remember Sanborn saying that we had to use the other sections to figure out K4.  Here, we use elements of the previous sections - in this case, the three misspelled words found in the previous sections - as the key schedule.
3) Sanborn gave a clue where the 27th letter of the solution needs to be Q.  When this happens and the letter "I" is used as the key in the substitution process, we end up with an "O".  This is the "O" in the NORTHEAST.
4) The pattern formed by the three words repeated throughout the section is similar to the pattern of the Kryptos alphabet we see on the right-hand side of the sculpture.

Best,

ZF

s: Berlin Clock or World Clock, Berlin?
t:
I have been thinking more about the Berlin Clock plaintext in k4 and realized that “World Clock Berlin” would also fit if it was meant to be read from right to left. It could even be “World Clock, Berlin, Germany”. I don’t think the relation between the set theory clock (Berlin Clock) and the sculpture has been verified (based on the quote about there being “many interesting clocks” in Berlin), so there is a slight chance.
Also, I have been thinking about the first part of K2: “it was totally invisible. how’s that possible?” If you replace “it” with “the force”, the sentence seems less mysterious. As far as I know, magnets and light don’t interact, so it is not easy to explain how you can use the Earth’s magnetic field to make something invisible. Unless... you have coordinates that lead somewhere else depending on what state the Earth’s magnetic field is in. Then I guess you could say it was invisible? The whole k2 section is very confusing, so if anyone has any idea as to what is being discussed in those first few sentences, I would greatly appreciate a lesson on that.

s: Breaking K4 – Exploring Concepts and Clues
t:
K 4 Grid – First two letters of K4 form the first row, the rest of the rows are 10 columns. The final row is situated to the extreme right of the grid.

K4 Clues
1.    This method creates a pair of virtual pyramids with a single row of letters between them. These are the BROK and BROQ pyramids. Both contain variants on IQLU.
2.    These pyramids contain twin information - one is the Morse of “T IS” and the other is a Caesar shifting alphabet run of “Tutank”.
3.    The space between – KSVT – is a running Caesar shift of BJ-MK. These are the CT letters from the IQLUSION and UNDERGRUUND segments of Kryptos.
4.    NYPVTT is a phonemic play of Nefertiti and a number/letter play of Tutankhamun
5.    The Nefertiti Bust is in Berlin. The King’s Wishing Cup (water cock)  is in Istanbul.
6.    The Duplicate Letters numeric values match up to the shifts in NYPVTT and MZFPK.

Context – from K3 to K4.
In K3 we’re given a famous Howard Carter quote, and the story stops at the point where Carter raises a candle to see inside the whole they’ve made. What does he see? Wondrous things. The very first thing he sees is the King’s Wishing Cup, what’s known as a clepsydra or water clock.

Concept - Now, visualize the letters between the two pyramids in K4 as a void of darkness and tilt your K4 a quarter turn to the left so that it's a diamond instead of a square. At the end of the void is the end of BERLIN, and the start of the CLOCK in MZFPK. Coincindence? Doesn’t seem likely. A clue, but how to get to it is not as clear. I do believe from what I’ve uncovered that Jim likes his Caesar Shifts. They’re cheesy but easy, and good for puzzle-making.

There’s something I placed on the backburner awhile back, when analyzing the Master Anagrammed Acrostic that surrounds the Kryptos 24-column grid, and that was the acrostic on K4.  I didn’t like the fact that it was misspelled at the time, but it makes a little more sense now – BUST KWOTE. Bust makes perfect sense, but there is no quote associated with the Nefertiti Bust that I know of.

The steganography of K4 seems to involve the visualizations here, but I’m at a bit of a loss on what else can be “seen” here.

Any thoughts?

Over 30 years and no one outside the CIA has a confirmed solution to the final section.  Perhaps that final section was intended for, and only solvable by CIA employees (not agents).  The puzzle was created for the CIA, located on the grounds of the CIA.  A twist would be if K4 is a OTP for a CIA in-house-only cipher.  The PT is a secret for CIA Ops as it resides in the confides of Langley.  If the CIA Op were to disclose of the PT it may be grounds for Treason as the Op would be publicly announcing a secret to the entire World.
On another note- Jim Sanborn did make something that was invisible, visible.  The invisible CT for the coordinates pointing to Langley.
Just some rambling thoughts,

First of all, welcome to the group! It is wonderful that a young person such as yourself is interested in a challenging cipher puzzle such as Kryptos!

All of your comments and ideas make sense. After all, no one in over 30 years (more than twice your lifetime!!) has been able to solve this puzzle, so we have to consider every new idea that we possibly can!

The comments along the lines of Sanborn is an artist, he would naturally gravitate toward a mechanically minded, physical code, I agree completely, this idea makes perfect sense. You are not the only person or the first person to suggest such ideas, but it is always good to bring up worthwhile ideas and express them in new ways, as you have done here.

The only caveat (cautionary comment) that I have to make about your ideas, is that Jim Sanborn has claimed that there is enough information on the model mini-Kryptos sculptures that he made, so that anyone could use only that model mini-sculpture and the information on it, to solve and decipher the fourth and final message of Kryptos. Therefore, the solution should not require special particular knowledge about the angle of the sun as it shines on the exact location of the Kryptos sculpture itself, or other such physical details that depend on the sculpture location itself. Any physical property that is relevant to the solution, should also be apparent on the model mini-sculpture of Kryptos that Sanborn made, which can be placed in any location.

However, certain physical and mechanical properties that you mention are indeed replicated and preserved on the model mini-sculptures of Kryptos as well, as far as I can recall. For example, the S-curve shape of the entire sculpture, and the letters that are punched out instead of engraved, as you mention.

In fact, thinking through these ideas and looking at photos of the actual sculpture and the model mini-sculpture again, has led me to notice a curious significant difference between the original and the model:

In the actual sculpture, the ciphertext of the four messages of Kryptos (the left side or the two left panels of the sculpture) is curved in a *convex* way, that is, curved outward toward the viewer, while the Vigenere tableau (the right side or the two right panels of the sculpture) is curved in a *concave* way, that is, curved inward away from the viewer. The Vigenere tableau, from this viewpoint, is written backward or in a mirror image -- that is, to view the tableau written in the normal forward direction, one would have to walk around to the other side of the sculpture and look at it from that direction, where it would appear to be curved in a convex way, outward toward the viewer, and also it would be on the viewer's left side from that perspective.

But in the model sculpture, the ciphertext of the four messages of Kryptos, while still on the left side, is curved in a *concave* way, inward away from the viewer -- and moreover, from this viewpoint, it is written backward or in a mirror image! Whereas the Vigenere tableau, while still on the right side, is curved in a *convex* way, outward toward the viewer -- and appears in the normal forward direction! In viewing the model sculpture, in order to view the ciphertext of the four messages of Kryptos in the normal forward direction, one would have to walk around to the other side of the model (or simply turn the model around), where it would appear to be curved convexly, outward toward the viewer, but it would now be on the viewer's right side!

I do not know if this curious physical difference in the curvature direction of the left and right sides of the actual sculpture and the mini-sculpture has any relevance to the solution of the fourth message of Kryptos, but it certainly seems to be an interesting detail for us to take note of!

Geoffrey

An alphabet key refers to a way of decimating an alphabet.
In the case of Kryptos sections k1 and k2, he used two keys.

First he decimates the Latin alphabet with the key Kryptos.
To do this he removed the letters KRYPTOS
ABCDEFGHIJLMNQUVWXZ

Then move the letters of the key in front
The 'Kryptos Alphabet' becomes
KRYPTOSABCDEFGHIJLMNQUVWXZ

Using just one alphabet You could exchange the letter 'A' for 'K'
ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ
KRYPTOSABCDEFGHIJLMNQUVWXZ

Adding a second key you get something called a poly alphabetic cipher
Jim used the key PALIMPSEST in section k1

So the key then shifts the alphabet
You get
PTOSABCDEFGHIJLMNQUVWXZKRY
For the first letter of palimpsest
And the first letter of k1 is B

KRYPTOSABCDEFGHIJLMNQUVWXZ
PTOSABCDEFGHIJLMNQUVWXZKRY

'E' replaces the letter 'B' in the cipher text and so on
You'll notice every line of the tableau in The Kryptos scroll shifts the alphabet by one.
So you can look at that and decode k1 and k2 by going through each letter of the key and the cipher.

This is known as a Vigenere Cipher.

At this point, it’s starting to look like the biggest misdirection Sanborn may have pulled was to con people into believing that K4 is a cipher rather than a puzzle that depends on the understanding of ciphers in order to use them as clues.

There are recurring patterns in the Caesar shifts that are almost Gematria-like cipher (Letters and names with numeric values, minus the spiritual overtones. But they also present as far too …. Free-form?

Examine the transition for the partial NYPVTT (Nefertiti phoneme) from plaintext to ciphertext.
R L I N C L O  to  P V T T M Z F

Each transition has two possible Caesar Shifts, depending on the direction of the alphabet.
R to P, for example, is a Caesar shift of +24/-2.  The absolute letter value of each is X/B.
In terms of the pattern ,it appears that we can choose any one of those four values.

I chose these:
Two-Ten-K-T-Ten-N-K   -  Tutenk, Tutenk
O R T H E A S to Q P R N G K shows the same concept at play.
(AKA) Two-Two –Two-T-Two-Ten –  AKA TuTuTuT / Tuten

Any ideas or thoughts? While the clues are great, the idea of tracking 97 letters for variations on Tut’s name is infuriating.

t:
Hello All,
Some prodding from interested parties has caused me to consider revealing some steps necessary in travelling the route to the final solution of K4. I have done all the work that I reveal in the file I just uploaded with the exception of the keyword ABSCISS, which was provided by a Kryptos Group member who does not wish to be named (but, THANK YOU to him). So, I hope I somehow get credit for what little I've come up with.

By now, a lot of you know that K4 isn't going to be solved via simply performing a demasking and then a decryption. Actually, it involves far more than that. In my opinion, it is a great work. As far as I can tell, there are no mistakes and anything appearing as a mistake is either a clue or is being misread by the solver.
I have not provided a lot of my thinking in moving through this. One consideration was why the K in K4 CT corresponds to the K in CLOCK. It all became clear when I determined that Z goes before OBKR. All ya gotta do is repad K4 CT to seven columns. You can see the K repeated in the 5th column. This is a clue!!! All this time we've heard about THE BERLIN CLOCK. It fits as a keyword. You just start with CLOCK. CLOCKTHEBERLIN. It doesn't apply right away... that's too obvious, but what's obvious is it's a keyword. I don't believe Sanborn said that BERLINCLOCK was plaintext appearing in the final solution. He just said it was plaintext, just not how.
So, anyway, my latest upload to files takes you quite a way along the route towards the solution (which I have not reached!!!), but you will have before you a demonstration that what I have to that point is correct. There are a lot of clues in Kryptos, as I've said before. I certainly have missed some of them. Also, I recognize some of them, but I don't understand how to use them. These bug me to death, but I persevere.
I may not make it to the final solution to K4. I'm now 77 and moving forward in this trek is getting very difficult. I hope what I've provided in the file today will bring some of you to recognize what the overall design of K4 is like and allow you to press forward.
All the best,
PaulK

For example the Agent in the field could have received these communications before arriving on site. The reason this is of interest to me is because I recently read in a post here that at a meeting Sanborn said K2 is intended to sound like an interrupted communication. But when I started writing out K0 I came across "T is your position" Which I have seen considered and I believe confirmed that it is cut off but is WHAT. This immediately made me think about the coordinates in K2. Hi,

Perhaps the "Q" in "iqlusion" is a hint for us to see "QKELUSION," a
cryptonym which used to signify the West German Social Democratic Party.
This might fit nicely with the "Berlin" plaintext in K4.

https://www.archives.gov/files/iwg/declassified-records/rg-263-cia-records/second-release-lexicon.pdf

What makes this the most compelling to me is the ELUSION. Elusion is "the
act of hiding". When someone is hiding, they are being elusive. KRYPTOS or
the prefix "CRYPTO" means "hidden". The "QK" has a less straightforward
meaning though.

https://www.maryferrell.org/php/cryptdb.php?bigram=QK

Also if we stick with this theme, the other misspelled "U" in "undergruund"
could be a hint for us to see "GRU" which is like "KGB". Also fitting. I've
seen this mentioned before on the forum, but never "QKELUSION".

I haven't been able to uncover anything else in the puzzle with this yet,
but found it interesting as a theory.

PS - QKWAVER means egypt, but i haven't been able to find a K3 reference to
QKWAVER. Nor have I been able to tie the spelling mistakes in "DESPARATLY"
to the above cryptonym dictionary.

Peace

Jamie

There are 97 characters in K4 and so I think that there should be 97! ways to arrange the letters.  In other words, the first letter could use any of the 97, then the second could use any of 96, then the third 95...  97 x 96 x 95... is a huge number of combinations that I am not sure that you can do anything with.

For K1 and K2 you just use two keys each (PALIMPSEST/KRYPTOS and ABSCISSA/KRYPTOS) with the included Vigenere tableau.  For K3, You just rotate a rectangle, resize, and rotate again.

s: A thought about YAR and the mispellings
t:
Hey everybody, I wanted to share an idea with you that has been roaming my mind lately, and it concerns the superscripted letters YAR and the mispellings along the decoded text.

We have three superscrpted letters - Y, A, R
We have three mispellings along the decoded text - Q in IQLUSION, U in UNDERGRUUND, and the missing E in DESPARATLY.

Since Sanborn had stated that the mispellings were intentional, I thought about the section of the K4 that decodes MZFPK into CLOCK. The fact that the letter K decrypts into itself, I remembered that no other coding system does this except for German Enigma. Now, we know that Sanborn used more than one coding method to encrypt K4 which means that the letters MZFPK probably will not be in this position when they finaly give out CLOCK, but it gave me an idea - What if these six particular letters - three superscripted and three mispelled are used to in some way set the two cylinders that exist on every Enigma machine, and in this way serve as one of the coding methods for K4.

It seems that the story Kryptos tells about cryptography would be empty without the most famous coding device in the history of cryptography.

Anyways, I would like to hear your opinion about this.

s: A thought about YAR and the mispellings
t:
The K in MZFPK matching with K in CLOCK is a clue. If you take K4 CT and add the Z in front, as I have already indicated and shown to be part of solving Kryptos, you will now have 98 characters in K4 CT.
Repad K4 CT into seven columns:
Z O B K R U OX O G H U L BS O L I F B BW F L R V Q QP R N G K S SO T W T Q S JQ S S E K Z Z
W A T J K L U
D I A W I N FB N Y P V T TM Z F P K W GD K Z X T J CD I G K U H UA U E K C A R
You will see that there are four Ks in column five. //BTW, five is a significant number in Kryptos!// Repad K4 CT again, only in columns of fourteen:
Z O B K R U O X O G H U L BS O L I F B B W F L R V Q QP R N G K S S O T W T Q S JQ S S E K Z Z W A T J K L U
D I A W I N F B N Y P V T TM Z F P K W G D K Z X T J CD I G K U H U A U E K C A R
You now see that there are still three Ks in column five and one K in column 12. Before I go further, let me point out that the K in column 12 is the first letter in KLU, which constitutes a clue about something else. But, returning to the Ks in column five now:
These Ks in column five are separated by multiples of fourteen. It comes to one's mind that that is how KEYWORDS are arranged corresponding to the text they are used against. So, let's suppose that these Ks are clues about a keyword. It immediately occurs to us that if this is true, then BERLINCLOCK is part of a keyword because Sanborn said that BERLINCLOCK is plaintext that lies in those positions in the K4 CT. As it turns out, BERLINCLOCK is part of a fourteen character keyword THEBERLINCLOCK. Now, since the Ks are in the positions that they are in, the keyword must be shifted five characters to the right and so it begins withCLOCK. So the keyword is used against the K4 CT beginning as CLOCKTHERBERLIN:
C L O C K T H E B E R L I NC L O C K T H E B E R L I N

I've been down this path as far as Enigma is concerned - it never went anywhere, and it was pretty much established to me that a letter cannot encrypt to itself i.e. K. I think that's the part you're remembering?  I don't recall whether that was due to the math or to the rotors.

I do agree that the mispellings are intentional clues - in particular to the intended K4 Array.

In the Files menu on the left you can find the FIELD MANUAL NO 34-40-2 Basic Cryptoanalysis.  It is my belief that the answer can be found in it.  Sanborn had mentioned that the given Vigenere tableau was to be used for the top, and so I am not certain that a Vigenere is going to be part of the K4 solution.  Looking at the solutions for K1 and K2, they both used the keyword KRYPTOS (as part of the Vigenere).  If you just rotate and resize K3 then you do not use KRYPTOS, but others have solved K3 using a keyed columnar transposition with KRYPTOS as the keyword.  This may or may not mean that KRYPTOS could be one key for K4.

If we could somehow build a list of possible combinations and then try attacking them one by one then maybe we will find the right key for the lock.  I do not think that it can be just substitution or just transposition and so I think that we can rule out a single cipher.  Even just two ciphers is going to result in a lot of possible combinations.  Hopefully, three or more were not used.  You can also double or triple encrypt using the same keys.  Hill ciphers could have A=0 or A=1, and maybe the padding goes at the start and maybe it goes at the end.  One-time-pads could use any of the ciphertext, plaintext, or tableau.

What language are you using for development, and have you built yourself some decent crypto tools yet?

Thanks,

1: I'm interested in how hard K4 was supposed to be.

2: There are too types of "hard". The first is something like the Zodiac 340 where it's cryptographically nearly impossible to crack (no wonder it took 50 years; two methods were combined...maybe K4 mixed two cryptographic methods as well).

3: The second type of "hard" is very hard to quantify because some idiot like me could dream it up after brainstorming for a while and looking at Sanborn's other work and getting a sense for his artistic sensibilities.

4: So when Sanborn says that he expected K4 to be cracked within 10 years or whatever, that's very confusing. He's not saying that it WOULD TAKE TEN YEARS to crack it, right? Rather, he's saying: within a range of time of 10 years, I expect someone during that timespan will come along and make the 5-minute insight needed to crack it. Big distinction there as to what he's saying.

5: Psychologically, it should be pretty easy to gauge things from his response. If you show him something and he IMMEDIATELY says "No" then that gives you a sense that you're not even in the right mode of thinking or the right ballpark or the right approach. It doesn't make sense for him to carefully look over something and then think about it and say "No" if the solution is to stack grids or do something "outside the box".

6: Look at his piece here: http://jimsanborn.net/hires_lite/gw9L.jpg. If we could get dimensions (HOW?) then we could put text in multiple grids. And then we punch holes (somehow) in each layer. So it's a multi-level "grille". 4 layers (or just 2?) with each layer with holes punched in it somehow. Now what, though? Just look at THIS: http://jimsanborn.net/hires_lite/gw9R.jpg.

7: The two parameters are: it can't be too insanely hard, and I'm too uneducated on cryptography to know how difficult it would be to work a multi-layer message into this GIVEN THAT the K1/K2/K3 plaintexts read like organic text. Do the K1/K2/K3 plaintexts look like they're been tortured/massaged/contrived in order to hide a message? No, right? They read pretty normally...so I don't know if that makes it very unlikely that it all fits together.

I am talking out of my @ss here a bit as I did not do any research.  I thought Sanborn said that you just need the ciphertext and tableau to solve it, like the small copies he made can be solved without barcodes in the grass.

I believe that this is a statement that is technically correct, but a misdirection. With any puzzle, there is often an easier way and a harder way to solve it, and in this case that "harder" way involves 30 years of speculation.

Looking at the people involved in trying to solve Kryptos, a lot of bright and probably brilliant mathematical minds oriented on cryptography, it seems to me that Sanborn might have outfoxed even himself with his misdirection(s). People assume that because K1-K3 was a cipher, K4 will be as well, and I don't believe that's the case at all. It's a puzzle in the more traditional sense of the word, and crypto-graphically oriented cryptANALYSIS will note the clues.

Because he has in fact acknowledged there are clues within Kryptos, and simply ignoring the earlier puzzles is a mistake that leads down the harder path.

To note, the Department of Historical Intelligence and the basis of the "Crying Lady" story was discussed a bit in Jim Sanborn's personal Oral History, provided by Elonka. Control-F in the document to find it, it's pretty long with a lot of neat bits.

https://www.aaa.si.edu/collections/interviews/oral-history-interview-jim-sanborn-15700#transcript

To the point: That's actually a really GOOD observation when it comes to reading the Kryptos solutions in a manner beyond the obvious, such as double-speak.

In context of Sanborn, HI's last message was: ""The Department of Historical Intelligence cannot accept responsibility for this artwork. Figure out another way." WW was indicated to have been William Webster, who helped it go forward.

WW KNOWS as a path to go forward seems to be pretty clearly indicated to me - the string is not only found in the K2 plaintext, but appears in the K3 ciphertext, and appears to be in the K1 BENBEN mispelled word puzzle-text and hinted at in K4.

The rest is pretty cool backstory that you wouldn't be expected to know while solving Kryptos. Useful, maybe, but prone to red herrings, pink herrings and misdirection.

My comment to point (4).

Yeah, where does that dangling "?" belong? This probably can't be settled until Kryptos is solved.
One known alternative way of solving K3 is by modular transposition: take every 192:nd character modulo 337; and this solution method in fact requires the length to be 337 (a prime number). The well-established row-column solution on the other hand requires length 336.

I like to think that K3 was designed to be solvable with both these solution methods. I like the modular solution better because it is so straightforward and beautifully simple; but it seems this was not the way JS encrypted it, nor is it likely to be his preferred method given that he is more of a visual person and not a mathematical person.

Regardless, I also like the thought that K3 is length 337 and K4 is length 97, both prime. For a long time I have thought that K4 should also involve a modtrans as one part of its solution, hinted by interpreting the K3 encryption method as demonstrating an example of "layer two" for K4. Modtrans would pretty much require a prime length, i.e. 97. On the other hand, if K4 involves a K3 style row-column transposition, then it is better to include the "?" with K4 and have 98 characters to work with, as 98=14*7. If it is really beautifully constructed, then both methods will work for K4 just as both methods work for K3.
Thanks this is so interesting.

Hi Nick and welcome!

1. The best source for JS's actual words for the K4 clues will be the New York Times articles where the clues were announced.

2. I have often wondered if the omission of the letter in the final line of K2 was really a deliberate decision by JS. It does seem like quite an unlikely coincidence that the "accidentally" omitted letter just happened to be precisely the one letter that still produced a readable English plaintext when omitted! As has been par for the course with Kryptos, I think it would fall within the realm of "fair game" if JS's comments about this omission could be interpreted in multiple ways.

Also, since you mention the palindromic or symmetrical K1+K2 CT row lengths, I would like to point out that my current main working hypothesis about the possible encryption method of K4 involves the K3+K4 CT row lengths, which are "jagged" and not neatly patterned like K1+K2, as a key basis for the input of the so-called "masking step" before the final encryption step. You can read the details of my ideas in the thread titled "masking step idea using K1-K2 CT and K3-K4 line lengths" in the "Techniques" subgroup of this message board, which you can request to join if you ask the moderator. The link to the thread is <https://kryptos.groups.io/g/Techniques/topic/81337368> ; the most important details are described in these messages: <https://kryptos.groups.io/g/Techniques/message/34>, <https://kryptos.groups.io/g/Techniques/message/41>, and <https://kryptos.groups.io/g/Techniques/message/46>.

3. Based on the encryption method of K3, whichever letters are in the places of YAHR (I always include the D in DYAHR in this letter string) will have the same pattern in the PT. But yes, I agree that the omission of a letter in DESPARATLY may well have been done specifically in order to make those particular letters occur in that particular place and order very near the beginning of the first line of the K3 CT. Again I note that DYAHR is the keyword of the final encryption step according to my hypothesis referenced above.

Yes, the occurrence of Q to represent the ? at the end of the K3 PT, followed by ? itself before or at the beginning of the K4 CT, is certainly striking and grabs one's attention. As for Q, it is fair game in cryptography to add less frequently used English letters to a PT message. Also, in the case of the K3 CT, JS may simply not have wanted a ? in the middle of the CT in this message. For example, if someone had correctly guessed that the question comes at the end of the message, the ? in the middle of the K3 CT could have been too much of a clue to make the decryption of the double transposition of K3 too easy. Whereas with the letter Q, if anything, the first instinct is to expect it to occur immediately before a U and thus *not* occur as the final letter of a message.

4. I observe that the ? before or at the beginning of the K4 CT is *included* in the files of the 4th clue (EAST before NORTHEAST) that JS sent out to Sukhwant Singh and others in the spring and summer of 2020. The ? is labeled as position "0", so that the letters of K4 are still numbered from 1 to 97, but the ? is included, so this implies that it is somehow part of the K4 CT message. Again, my own hypothesis, with a Playfair cipher as the final encryption step, requires an even number of letters, so I take ? as the first such character, making a total of 98.

Regards
Geoffrey

I wonder how plausible it is that Kryptos is a representation of a set of three different ways of encrypting something: digital, digital + analog and just analog. The first one at the entrance would be all digital. The sculpture would be digital + analog. The stone slabs with no morse on them would be completely analog. But whatever invisible message is contained within the last set of stone slabs is, it must have some extra component(s). Maybe it’s features and location are the most important and maybe it’s message is based on logic. Maybe the logic is defined in the extra component. For instance, plaintext of K1-K4 could be one extra component, which would contain the logic necessary to interpret the features of the stone slabs with no morse.  The stone slabs with morse on them could also be a component. Each one containing subtle information. Not sure what that information could be, but it is worth thinking about since Kryptos starts at the entrance and becomes more difficult to decrypt as you move forward, meaning that the chances of a third set of messages being hidden in the stone slabs that come after the sculpture are highly likely. That’s fascinating though. I mean they are just stone slabs. Does that narrow the length of the message down? Surely, you couldn’t store an entire book in just those stone slabs, could you? Even if the entire thing was a system and all three sets of messages summed up to another message, it couldn’t be that long of a message could it? Either way, there is definitely a human (analog) component to solving K4 (and probably “K5”) and that is most likely why it has not been cracked yet.

Yeah, where does that dangling "?" belong? This probably can't be settled until Kryptos is solved.
One known alternative way of solving K3 is by modular transposition: take every 192:nd character modulo 337; and this solution method in fact requires the length to be 337 (a prime number). The well-established row-column solution on the other hand requires length 336.

I like to think that K3 was designed to be solvable with both these solution methods. I like the modular solution better because it is so straightforward and beautifully simple; but it seems this was not the way JS encrypted it, nor is it likely to be his preferred method given that he is more of a visual person and not a mathematical person.

Regardless, I also like the thought that K3 is length 337 and K4 is length 97, both prime. For a long time I have thought that K4 should also involve a modtrans as one part of its solution, hinted by interpreting the K3 encryption method as demonstrating an example of "layer two" for K4. Modtrans would pretty much require a prime length, i.e. 97. On the other hand, if K4 involves a K3 style row-column transposition, then it is better to include the "?" with K4 and have 98 characters to work with, as 98=14*7. If it is really beautifully constructed, then both methods will work for K4 just as both methods work for K3.

s: A Potential Lead for the Last Kryptos Passage
t:
I was looking at the DMS coordinates on 8/8/2021 in the solution for passage 2 when I got an idea: What if there was a secret about passage 4 hidden within the coordinates?

Well, I may have been right...

Coordinates within Coordinates
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
I had a feeling that there was something interesting about the coordinates, so I pretty much did random mathematics through trial and error, and in about an hour I found a lead:

If you take the DMS Lat and Long within passage 2, and convert it to decimal (38.951806, -77.145556), you can do this:
lat =  38.951806+(38.951806/-77.145556) = 38.44689
lng = -77.145556-(-77.145556/38.951806) = -75.16501
Then you convert the new lats and longs you got, break the decimals into parts corresponding to DMS notation (38°44′68.9″N, 75°16′50.1″W), and then finally convert it back to Decimal, you get the coordinates: 38.327083, -75.280583.

When I looked it up on google maps, what popped up was a path of forest, with the closest town having a name which I knew couldn't have been a coincidence: Berlin, Maryland.

Dots Adding Up
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
I immediately began doing extensive research into Berlin MD and Jim Sanborn. Within an hour, things began to add up. Here is everything I connected:

1. Berlin is in Southeastern Maryland, and Jim Sanborn lives in the same region of Maryland.

2. Berlin has a clock on a pole at coordinates extremely close to the latitudinal part of the coordinates I calculated.Clock was one of the clues, and Jim further said "You'd better delve into that particular clock".

3. In the solution of passage 2 the keyword was Abscissa, which means Horizontal (X is also mentioned multiple times in the plaintext, which is the axis which abscissa means). I decided to intersect the longitudinal of the clock pole with the latitudinal coordinates I got from the equation. The location was exactly on the house "10 Powellton Ave, Berlin, MD".

4. Berlin, MD is also in the Northeastern United States.

Conclusion
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
So, the 2 potential coordinates of interest I found were "38.327083, -75.280583" (It is a forest near Berlin along Cedar Lane Road), and the address "10 Powellton Ave, Berlin, MD". This potential lead still doesn't account for the "EAST" clue, but this may be better than any other potential clue found so far.
    - BRBos

Anders, I was also interested in the diagonal alignment of YAHR, and I figured out what Nick means as follows:

Write the K3 PT in 8 rows of 42 letters each. If you keep track of the location of each letter in the K3 CT, now the "Y" in YAHR is the 7th letter from the end of the 8th and final row. The "A" in YAHR is the 9th letter from the end of the 6th row; the "H" is the 11th letter from the end of the 4th row; and the "R" is the 13th letter from the end of the 2nd row. Thus these letters are aligned on a diagonal of the 8x42 array, starting with the Y and going up and to the left, with YAHR appearing as every other letter in this diagonal: YTAAHMRA.

This is not some mysterious property belonging only to the YAHR sequence, but a natural consequence of the double columnar transposition method of the K3 encryption. For example, the first three letters of the K3 CT, END (this is the D of DYAHR), also appear as alternating letters in a diagonal in this array: E is the 2nd letter from the end of the 6th row, N is the 4th letter from the end of the 4th row, and D is the 6th letter from the end of the 2nd row.

I also note that the first K3 CT letter E, as the 2nd letter from the end of the 6th row, is thus the 14th letter of the array if one begins with the last column and reads each column from top to bottom. This is related to the 24x14 array of the second step of the double columnar transposition K3 encryption method: When this 8x42 array is rotated 90 degrees clockwise and then re-written out in 24 rows of 14 letters each, this "E" will appear as the 1st letter of the 24th and final row. Indeed if one continues reading each column of the 8x42 array from top to bottom, starting with the last column and moving from right to left, N is the 28th letter, D is the 42nd letter, Y is the 56th letter, A is the 70th letter, H is the 84th letter, and R is the 98th letter. (Oh look, that number 98 again!!) Thus, in the re-written 24x14 array, these letters are the 1st letters of the final 7 rows of the array. When this 24x14 array is also rotated 90 degrees clockwise, ENDYAHR then becomes the first 7 letters of the final K3 CT.

The alternating diagonal letter pattern is a natural mathematical consequence of taking every 14th letter while counting by columns of 8 letters each. For any letter not in the top 2 rows of the 8x42 array, the following 14th letter will appear 2 columns to the left and 2 rows higher, creating the appearance of an alternating diagonal letter pattern for any sequence such as END, YAHR, etc.

Geoffrey

I perceive the first sentence of K2 as being a statement made by someone who knows a message is totally invisible and wants to know how someone else could have possibly read the message. So, from their viewpoint, they know what the message says and expect that no one else ever will because it is not visible. Now, with that assumption in mind, let’s consider the first set of messages at the front entrance (morse code and strata). There is a compass engraved on one of the stone slabs with the needle pointing to a lodestone and some of the morse code appears to be covered up. We know that an analog compass uses the Earth’s magnetic field when it isn’t being influenced by another magnetic field (like a lodestone). Does a lodestone use the Earth’s magnetic field? I don’t think so. Knowing those two things and then considering the second sentence in K2, one might be quick to dismiss the idea that lodestones have something to do with this “invisible” message since the Earth’s magnetic field was allegedly used to retrieve it. But it could actually still have been used. Let’s assume that the “it” referred to in the first sentence of K2 is a message and that it is stored in the stone slabs with no morse code on them. How could it be stored? Maybe by hiding the morse code underneath the top layer? Or maybe by hiding lodestones under and near the stone slabs in specific places that, when observed with an analog compass positioned in the right spot, could be combined with the Earth’s magnetic field to form a message. One way would be to observe how many degrees off of North a lodestone is (assuming you are facing the right direction and have the compass positioned in the right spot) and to then tie that number to a letter or even morse code (a number above a threshold could be a dot and below it could be a dash and vice versa). That would require actually being there with an analog compass in order to solve the last part (if there is one). When thinking about it the way I described though, the compass engraved on the stone pointing to the lodestone doesn’t seem so mysterious. If the last part (stones with no morse) was encrypted the way I just described, then would that technically make the encryption of the message analog since it would require using an analog compass? How does this relate to K4? I don’t think it does, but I think that K4 might relate to it. Meaning that the other pieces around the sculpture can’t be used to solve K4, but K4 could be used to solve the message that comes after it on the stone slabs with no morse (or hidden morse).

The washing machine idea is as decoding is taking place, you rotate the grid 90degrees left, then normal, then right, then normal, etc... Has anyone come up with a way of going from the K4 ciphertext, not to a plaintext, but any kind of mash of 97 letters that: (a) Have the statistical properties of English (b) Have at least the potential of all of the simultaneous words EASTNORTHEAST BERLIN CLOCK? What substitution techniques were used? Vigenère with KRYPTOSABC alphabet. Standard ABCDEFG alphabet for (b) has been invalidated with the most recent 2020 EAST clue.

What were the resultant groups of 97 letters that had the statistical properties of English, including the known cribs? K4 involves the reconstruction of an intermediate key prior to the final decode. KRYPTOS was designed in analog without the need of IC. Hi Robert,
I asked Jim Sanborn about the pulped documents when I interviewed him. I'm
pasting the relevant section below. It doesn't seem like he used them in
Kryptos.

Sanborn: So [the CIA] basically bought a big hammer mill for making paper
pulp. And so everything went into the hammer mill and got pounded and then
dumped into big dumpsters, this sort of wet oatmeal colored stuff.
I made a deal where I asked them for, you know, a bunch of this stuff. And,
I rented a warehouse building and it was actually in a winter, which was
unfortunate. And, I rented a big warehouse building, 6,000 square foot or
8,000 square feet, and then turned the gas heaters all the way up. So it
was like 100 degrees in there. And I took bag after bag of

pulp and put it on the floor and dried it because if I didn't dry, it would
just turn to mold and just, it just melts into a liquid. So I needed the
pieces to be visible. So I dried it over about a month. It cost me a lot of
money in gas, I'll tell you that.

I brought it back to my studio in bags and started making art out of it.

AJ: And I can see those statues that you used the pulping?

Jim: Yeah, they're on my website.

Hello!

This is A.J. Jacobs, the author writing a book about puzzles, with a
section on Kryptos. This is my report from my recent visit to Kryptos
(sorry for the delay. And thanks again to everyone who made suggestions of
what to look for).

Overall, it was fascinating. I don’t think I made any monumental
breakthroughs, but I’m sharing with you everything I observed just in case.

I was not allowed to take photos. However, a network TV crew was following
me for a segment to air when my book comes out in April of 2022. So maybe
we can see some interesting visuals then.

I’m happy to answer any further questions I can. If you want to reach me
privately, my email is [courriel]

1) THE MAIN STATUE

It’s smaller than I expected. In my mind, I had somehow built it up to
rival the Great Wall of China. But it’s also prettier than I expected, the
sculpture’s undulating shape is lovely, and the copper’s oxidized green
tinge makes it seem somehow more stately.

To get there, you have to walk through the CIA halls itself, which are
interesting. There is a red telephone booth which was a gift from “your
friends in Britain,” and paintings of famous moments in CIA history (e.g.
the rescue in Iran that spawned the movie *Argo*).

2) MY TOUR GUIDE

My guide was CIA historian Randy Burkett, who was very nice. He told me
that there are copies of the Kryptos solution in two places

a) A safety deposit box that only Sanborn knows the location of

b) A safe at the CIA headquarters itself.

Question for the community: Is this new information? I have read that the
solution is in a safe on the East Coast. But I don’t remember reading that
it’s at the CIA HQ.

3) COMPASS

One member asked me to bring a compass and look for any unusual activity.

I didn’t notice anything – until we got to the sculpture of the compass and
the lodestone in front of the CIA. There, my compass went crazy. So the
lodestone in the sculpture is a true lodestone. It’s about the size of a
bowling ball. Randy had told me previously that he didn’t think it was a
true lodestone. But I can assure you it is.

4) THE COORDINATES

Randy led me to the spot mentioned in the coordinates in K2.

At least according to him. He said he used Google maps. I know there’s some
debate over where the exact coordinates are.

Anyway, the patch of grass is about 150 feet from the main Kryptos
sculpture (that’s an estimate) in the same courtyard.

The spot is near are two things

a) A dome-shaped drain.

b) A metal rectangular plate in the grass that is supposedly a utility box
cover.

As Randy pointed out, it’s an unusual utility box cover:  “It's not like a
normal access port where you just kind of take it off. Instead you actually
have a plate that’s screwed into the ground. Most utilities will have a
latch or a lift. [But with this], you would have to come out here and
unscrew this to get in there.”

5) SHADOWS AND GRASS

Despite requests, I was unable to see any interesting shadows because it
was overcast.

Also, I didn’t notice any patterns in the grass. And Randy pointed out the
grass has been replanted several times since 1989.

By the way, the pond near the slabs of granite in the courtyard had a bunch
of koi in it.

6) THE SLABS

One community member asked me to look inside the holes in the slabs of
granite in the courtyard.

I did, but only saw discarded plastic.

7) OTHER PATTERNS

One person asked me to look for unusual marks at the bottom of K4. I didn’t
notice any.

I did notice that the screws/bolts that run horizontally through the middle
of the sculpture have slots that are pointed in different directions. There
are about a dozen bolts, and some have a slit that is pointed north/south.
Others are east/west. And others are in between.

It probably means nothing, but I will draw up my findings and post them to
my folder.

Speaking of finding patterns in noise, I kept listening to the sound of the
whirlpool to see if there was any pattern there. I didn’t hear any. I think
I’m starting to suffer from apophenia.

Finally, the TV correspondent pointed out that if you look at the
silhouette inside the letters, there are some interesting shapes. Such as
the letter “A” where the crossbar only reaches partway.

That’s all I can think of. Let me know any questions. Thanks!

--
A.J. Jacobs

Author of, most recently, "Thanks a Thousand: A Gratitude Journey

What I have been working on with de-masking:
I extracted the plaintext at all four corners of each separating “X” in K2 and K3: “HRNTDSOSOWHTOMNHR”.
It starts and ends with “HR” and has “SOS” in the middle of it. Two of the X’s share “SO”, so I removed one of them. I then treated the extracted characters like a key and removed the extra “HR”. Try decrypting K4 using the same tableau and method used to decrypt K1-K2 and key “HRNTDSOWHTOMN”. The resulting plaintext has a column of all E’s that stands out.

Bruteforce

I’ve been screwing around with brute forcing K4 for a while, some people know, others call me crazy… so anyway, you can basically hit certain areas of k4 from the passphrase position, it took some time to identify area, etc, and what letter place holders I needed to manipulate output  text. I’ve also played with the solved sections to see how I could possibly hit on any identifiable

An example would be K1, first line @ NSH - a key of “IIIIIMIIIIIIIIIIPIIIIIIIIIIMP” will place THE at this position - it’s easy because I know what the output is, but the method is to observe its pattern, so following “IIIIIMIIIIIIIIIIPIIIIIIIIIIMPSESTPALIMPSEST” …and you see what I’m looking at.. it’s giving some of the pattern but in a very obscure way. Kryptos k4 however, is uniquely a forest of sheer insanity - always slipping from your reach, checking paths, returning, forgetting, but also observing any flow for pattens or uniqueness. After finding that a passphrase of “WINNIRR” will hit partially for “ABERLINCL” - but of course out of position! Bummer.. but nothing is wasted in this. So my brute forcing methods evolved -

My example is this section:

OBKR
UOXOGHULBSOLIFBBWFLRVQQPRNGKSSO

First four positions and last four positions of K4 - Vigenere is my method because I enjoy using Elonka’s rumkin tool to brute force. But, I find it neat that JIKUSJIKUS repeates twice and produces readable English.. if you play around with it, BORN appears, and the cipher will actually start to be a key or two ahead of what I plan to key in….. also with different JIKUS passes used in conjunction with “WINNIRR” you’ll notice that it places “ABERLINCLUEZ” … “LAST” “TEST” curious? I'm sad to report that Denny McDaniels, an important member of our Kryptos
family, has passed.  He was on that first NSA team in 1992 that solved the
first parts of Kryptos. He was also with us at Jim Sanborn's studio for the
filming of the Great Big Story / CNN piece.

In the CNN video, there's a good pic of Denny at the 4m00s mark.
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CwdUwevayRU

He was mentioned in this Baltimore Sun article, 2000
https://www.baltimoresun.com/news/bs-xpm-2000-03-17-0003180448-story.html

And a Wired article that mentions him, 2013
https://www.wired.co.uk/article/nsa-solved-kryptos

I was corresponding with Denny last year to ensure that the details about
the NSA's early Kryptos work were correct in my new book, "Codebreaking: A
Practical Guide". In some informal email chats, Denny told me that when the
sculpture first came out, it was a topic for lunchtime talk and
speculation, but nothing serious. His boss had a friend at Langley who
eventually arranged a trip for about 15 of them, so they could look at
Kryptos and the other things that Sanborn had placed around the courtyard.
Then when Director Mike McConnell decided to take it seriously, he
contacted the "chief/cryptanalysis organization, who contacted chief/manual
systems". Denny didn't know exactly why he and the other two were chosen
for the Kryptos team. They didn't work together, but they did know each
other and had "LOTS" of experience in manual systems. He said he had
continued to stay in touch with the other two, but that they wished to stay

Just a brief comment about the references to Sanborn's "mistakes" or "screw ups" in K1-K3 and the idea that such may be in K4 as well:

I think the suggestions of Sanborn's "mistakes" are quite overblown. The omission of a letter in DESPARATLY was clearly intentional, and it makes everything fit neatly in the double columnar transposition encryption method employed for K3. The fact that the misspelling also occurs in the same word strongly suggests intentionality in that decision as well. If the two "mistakes" were random, it's unlikely they would have occurred in the very same word.

Likewise, the misspellings in K1 and K2 appear to be intentional rather than accidental as well. They do not occur in random places, but rather in double-letter combinations LL>QL (IQLUSION) and OU>UU (UNDERGRUUND). Moreover, it can be argued that IQLUSION may be intended to sound like the word "occlusion", which can have the meaning of "darkness" or "absence of light" in one definition. (Already in K1, "subtle shading" is a possible definition of "nuance", as has appeared in crossword puzzle clues in the New York Times and elsewhere.)

Finally, the supposed "mistake" in omitting an "S" from near the end of the K2 ciphertext, transforming the decryption from XLAYERTWO to IDBYROWS, is evidence of great skill rather than a lack of skill. Think about how difficult it is to get the same eight ciphertext letters to decrypt to intelligible English words when the letters of the Vigenere keyword are all shifted by one!! If such a thing is done by mistake or accident, it will produce nonsensical letter sequences 99.9999% of the time. On the contrary, it requires a high level of artistic and cryptographic skill to arrange a text in such a way that such a transformation is even possible at all by omitting one ciphertext letter.

Geoffrey

Hello Elonka,

Perhaps it would be best to provide a simpler comparable to have a conceptual understanding of approaching K4. There is also another non-cryptographic circumvention available, but it would require time, money, and to live in the Washington DC area. That method should only be used for the purposes of verification.

To work through KRYPTOS in an analog pencil and paper manner heavily relies on the recovery of keys/hints for K1 through K4. The hints are not the actual words or phrases per se, but bits of information that simplify the process. It could be anything from a single value, phrase or shape. In terms of substitution, the alphabet and/or keylength may be given and for transposition, it will involve a component of the algorithm. While it make take some time to follow the logic, it is there in KRYPTOS. Take for example Mr. Ed Scheidt's driveway address code. With the only clue of Mayan in base 60, there was now sufficient evidence to decode the two parts to 1048 (3990-2942) and 22101 (2,2,-49+150). KRYPTOS was also expertly crafted in similar fashion by Mr. Scheidt but I digress.

As requested for a test case, the simplest way is to look at the K1 repeating key of:
PALIMPSEST PALIMPSEST PALIMPSEST PALIMPSEST PALIMPSEST PALIMPSEST PALIMPCEST PAL (the *C* or IQLUSION is intentionally part of the key recovery)

then sort in alphabetical order
AAAAAAAACE EEEEEEIIII IIILLLLLLL LMMMMMMMPP PPPPPPPPPP PPPSSSSSSS SSSSSSTTTT TTT

First we can examine potential for English language statistics for kappa-plaintext IC of 0.067 (1.73/26). Whilst both provide a kappa of 0.1229 (3.1956 normalized), one could come to the conclusion that the string of characters is clearly NOT English! Further frequency analysis shows that while the monogram frequencies are identical, the bigrams and trigrams are shockingly different!

Now let's revisit K4 with the same logic as above. Imagine that K4 could also be manipulated to produce a 97 letter string hiding in plain sight. By rearranging the letters, the intermediate key would be applied to K4 using KRYPTOS or standard alphabet substitution. If that were the case, then the unigram frequencies are required for EASTNORTHEAST and BERLINCLOCK:
1. KRYPTOSABC alphabet - RDUMRIYWOYNKY ELOIECBAQK [3 Y's @ 28, 31, 34]
2. ABCDEFG standard alphabet- BLZCDCYYGCKAZ MUYKLGKORNA [3 Y's @ 28, 29, 66]

*prior to 2020 EAST clue*
With transposition alone, the number of Y's available to decode K4 into NORTHEAST BERLINCLOCK are insufficient as there is only one at 65Y. The only other possible method would logically be another substitution (masking) layer that is either done monoalphabetically or polyalphabetically. If done polyalphabetically, then some sort of key should have been deployed and for monoalphabetic (masking) substitution, there is only 25 possibilities after eliminating the zero shift. Currently there is no known polyalphabetic key deployed so monoalphabetic masking is pursued. By frequency counting each position and arranging in the respective alphabet, one could perform the monoalphabetic shifts and see if the adjusted letter frequencies would be valid. To elaborate, simply write out the alphabets and mark the K4 positions for each letter akin to unigram charting. Next, perform a Caesar shift for each of the 25 monoalphabetic possibilities. For the KRYPTOS alphabet, the best candidates prior to the 2020 EAST clue were encoding by 7 and 11 and for standard alphabet the matches were encoding by 5, 6, 7, and 9. After analyzing the monoalphabetic candidates, the encoding by 7 was most promising and to my surprise also matched the secrets deployed in the K1! That is, betweeN subtlE shadinG anD theE abscencE oF lighT lieS thE nuancE oF iqlusioN or NEGDEEFTSEEFN (-7 or negative seven). The iQlusion or palimpCest misspelling refers to a monoalphabetic shift hint for K4. While the encode/decode was unclear, it was evident that encoding by 19 was not possible so the syntax is decode by -7 or encode by 7 shifts in the alphabets.

*after 2020 EAST clue*
The new 2020 EAST clue resulting in a 4 letter key of RDUM and BLDC for the KRYPTOS and standard alphabet respectively. A third C was required for standard alphabet after monoalphabetic shifting 7 characters from V to C. Evidently there are only 2 C's available at positions 25V & 67V already required for nOrthEast. As with the KRYTPOS alphabet, the additional letters RDUM were readily available to produce EAST at positions 22-25. In light of the EAST plaintext news, pure standard alphabet can eliminated by contradiction.

In summary, a three layer mask+transposition public key recovery followed by a substitution decryption supports the 1:1 ciphertext to plaintext relationship and addresses Mr. Scheidt's Moscow Billboard analogy. K4 is ultimately a KRYPTOS alphabet substitution, but the 97 (probably 98 with a null) character key must be reconstructed. Simply put, K4 is a cheeky code that can be decoded from itself! Of course the too complicated and didn't even attempt degrees of freedom excuse is readily available, but let's leave it at that for now and discuss the other steganography hints later.

s: different rectangular arrays for Kryptos ciphertext panel letters for "flipping and turning"
t:
Sanborn's comments about having to do a lot of "flipping and turning" in the K4 encryption process naturally suggest the idea of some kind of rotation or reflection of the arrays of letters on the panels of Kryptos. But it is an interesting and challenging question, which arrays of letters did he use as the basis for such a process?

Of course he could have simply kept all the letters in the same rows and places as they appear on the sculpture. The difficulty is, the rows contain different numbers of letters/characters, which presents a problem when one is "flipping and turning" such a jagged irregular array. It is much neater to flip and turn an exactly rectangular array of letters and characters. Indeed, for the K3 double transposition encryption process, Sanborn rearranged the K3 text into an 8x42 rectangular array and then into a 24x14 rectangular array in order to perform the transposition encryption.

The most obvious rectangular array for each panel is 14 rows of 31 characters each. The characters of K3+K4 fit exactly into such a 14x31 array. However, with the K1+K2 panel there is a stubborn extra character sticking out somewhere from such a 14x31 array, and the missing letter at the end of K2 would only create a second extra character if it were added. Deleting the three question marks doesn't solve this problem, as this can yield 432 or 433 letters, but not 14x31 = 434.

Another problematic issue is that at the time of performing the K4 encryption process, the K4 ciphertext did not exist yet! So as part of the K4 encryption process, Sanborn could have used all of the K1+K2 ciphertext panel, but only the K3 ciphertext portion of the K3+K4 panel. Thus, one panel had 432-436 characters, while the other panel only had the 336 letters of K3. I think it's interesting to consider how Sanborn could have designed rectangular arrays of rows and columns that could have possibly suited both amounts of letters/characters.

I find it striking that if one deletes the three question marks from K2, the K1+K2 panel has 432 letters. This would allow neat rectangular arrays such as 18x24 or even 9x48.

And the K3 text of 336 letters can be arranged into an array of 14x24, as we know from the actual K3 encryption process, or also into a 7x48 array.

This simply adds to the challenge and difficulty of considering all possible K4 encryption processes, as the basis for some key step could have been generated by "flipping and turning" any one of these possible rectangular arrays of the K1+K2 and/or K3 ciphertext.

Geoffrey

s: different rectangular arrays for Kryptos ciphertext panel letters for "flipping and turning"
t:
You are completely right about the degrees of freedom apparent in choosing an array to work with. The most obvious is as you say - a rectangular array (by height, not width), employing the flattening that the K3-K4 section on the sculpture hints at, and the neatness of of the K3 numbers can be considered a clue. For a whole lot of reasons I won't go into here, I chose 14x24.

We COULD limit it to the the 336 of K3. But then K1-K3 loses that aesthetic of a singular work. It becomes an uneven block on top of a really nicely aligned big one.

A step further. Are we looking at the CT or the PT? We KNOW that Jim manipulated the PT and can do things with that - K1 and K2 are his personal invention and K3 is an altered copy of a known script. Why did he alter K3?

I'd say that PT is the place to look, on an array of 14x24 applied to the entire Kryptos sculpture.

Full disclosure, this is not speculation and this does achieve results that I believe are necessary for K4.

James

Hi.  It’s been a very long time since I posted on this forum, but your title caught my eye.   Where did Sanborn mention “flipping and turning?”

One possibility is that he used the plaintext itself for the “flipping and turning”.
