s: Introduction and request of high resolution images
t:
Hey everyone! My name is Erik, I'm from Sweden, and this is my first
message in the group. I'm a political scientist by craft, so it's pretty
far away from cryptography, but I've always been interested in, as far as
Kryptos goes, nearby topics such as computer science, encryption and codes.
I've only been working on Kryptos for one month, but it's been a very
intensive month. I've read all the old group emails in the kry.log file,
and I'm about to go through all the other group emails as well. I've used
Google to find most of the old interviews with Sanborn and Scheidt (by
filtering everything from 1989 and onwards), as well as watching and
reading through the workshops and dinners etc, but I must say that many
"clues" seem to contradict each other. I'm not sure whether or not the
hypothesis of them giving out conscious misinformation (in the spirit of
clandestine work) is actually true, but all I can say is that the
interviews have confused me a lot.

I have tried a large amount of de-masking techniques on K4, as well as
trying to decipher the (candidates for) "unmasked" text, but as of yet no
result stands out as exceptional. I have exhausted my creativity and
computer power in trying to brute force this cipher, as is also evident
that many others have too. I have therefore decided to go back to the
actual sculpture and only rely on the information that it conveys, rather
than relying on vague clues, cryptographic programs and computer power. I
think that if K4 was merely a question of finding the right conventional
algorithm, and letting our computers brute force it (even if it was a two
layer super-encryption), we would already have decrypted it by now. I think
Sanborn did something creative and weird with the K4 plaintext, but I don't
think it involved the help of computers.

My hypothesis for K4 is that there is a masking technique followed by some
sort of cipher, and between these two stages there might be some red
herrings and/or fake dead ends. I also think that K4 was encrypted with pen
and paper, and I think that it can be decrypted with pen and paper.

With all this said, I wish to return to the original sculpture by examining
photos, but I have encountered a problem with this. I have downloaded a
vast amount of images, but they are rarely in high resolution, and they
don't cover the whole sculpture. I'm therefore asking the group for high
resolution images of the sculpture (not the surroundings). I want to be
able to see the sculpture from all angels, from far away, from up close,
from above, within the carvings and so on. I'm sure that these images
exist, the sculpture has been excessively photographed, after all!

I'm fairly confident that I have already found most of the relevant high
resolution images that exist on the open and indexed web. I've used several
search engines with specific search values, I've done reversed image
searches, I've sorted through metalinks to find old and removed pages, I've
viewed old pages using The Wayback Machine and so on.

So if anyone has high resolution images that you can share, I would be very
grateful. How is the 3D model coming around, by the way? The ones I've
found don't seem to be based on actual photos.

Anyway, I need to round off my message here, and go to sleep after yet
another late night of a Kryptos mania. Goodnight! Erik, Sweden.

Why, why, why does the tableau have 30 columns, not 26...  There are three possible reasons in my opinion, being Artistic choice, Balancing the approximate sizes of left and right sides of the sculpture, or lastly to provide some hint. OK, four, maybe some combination of all of those three.

Tableau 26 * 30  = 780 characters

Section 1 = 63
Section 2 = 373 (Or 372 without missing letter)
Section 3 = 337
Section 4 = 97

Section 1 + Section 2 + Section 3 = 63 + 373 + 337 = 773

So potentially, we're looking for seven (780 - 773) letters to fill this out to 780 characters. Obviously, Kryptos is 7 characters.  If we consider the sculpture as created, it has a missing character in K2, so maybe this should be 8 characters.  Tell me if my numbers are off.

We then potentially have an alternative tableau, or lookup table if you prefer, to perform decryption.  All of this is conjecture, and of course includes ? characters which do not appear in K4.

I haven't really seen much discussion of this observation recently, so I thought, I'd remind everyone in the hope of making further progress.

Personally, I like the idea of either rotation, vigenere ciphers process manipulating the tableau and/or cipher text. It stays on theme. I don't see a connection with caesar, morse code, or even shifts due to the reverse water feature (Coriolis effect) at the base of the sculpture. I am highly sceptical of attempts to use enigma cipher techniques. Keep it simple silly, is my working hypothesis.

I agree, this is an important observation and question. Naturally Sanborn wanted to balance the number of columns on all panels of the sculpture, but he was artistically free to choose any number of columns for the ciphertext panels, and he made a choice that required him to add 4 columns to the Vigenere tableau panels.

It seems to me also that those extra 4 columns, repeating the information in the first 4 columns of the tableau (not counting the left-hand side alphabetical column) should have some relevance to the solution method of K4. It would make sense to have some process of mapping the positions of tableau panel letters with the corresponding positions of ciphertext panel letters as one possible step in the K4 solution method. In this case all 30 columns of the tableau, as well as the left-hand side alphabetical column, would be used in the solution method.

The basic dimension of each panel is 14 rows by 31 columns. I would expect an artist like Sanborn to base his methods on this actual physical artistic appearance of the panels as they are visible to the viewer, rather than to perform a complicated rearrangement of the exact numbers of letters/characters in each panel or side of the sculpture.

These observations raise a question in my mind, for which I cannot find a clear and simple answer:

What would be an example of a simple encryption / decryption method that uses only substitution of letters in the ciphertext panels with corresponding letters in the same positions (or in the reflected positions) of the tableau panels?

It sounds like a simple method, but it is not so simple at all to conceive of such a method in which the decryption process can operate correctly and consistently to reverse the encryption process and uncover the original text. For example, if the encryption process selects the first appearance of a letter in the K1/K2 panels, and encrypts it with the corresponding letter in the same (or reflected) position in the tableau panel, and let's say this produced the first K4 ciphertext letter "O" -- then the intended recipient would still not know which specific "O" to locate in the tableau panel, in order to reverse the process and locate the original plaintext letter in the K1/K2 panel. Conversely, if one designs a logical method to select the specific "O", "B", K", etc., within the tableau panel, then they would decrypt to a rather random collection of letters in the K1/K2/K3 panels, and then it is not apparent how the message composer could have performed the encryption process logically and consistently.

If anyone can brainstorm ideas for a relatively *simple* method along these lines, in which both the encryption process and the decryption process could proceed logically and consistently, I think that would be interesting.

[Note: one additional complication is that the K4 ciphertext itself cannot be part of the process at all, because it did not exist before Sanborn performed the encryption process to produce it.]

Dear Ian

My theory on why rows of 31 letters where used is the following: Mr Sanborn was intending to use coordinates pointing near the sculpture as a form of clue (they do stand out when we read the plaintext), and so it happens that the north, positive, coordinates minus the west, negative, coordinates equals 31 (38+57+65-44-77-8=31). Also, to align the two sides of the sculpture may hint at the first step of the solution, as we can see in his working sheets that rows of 31 characters were used. The simmetry was broken eventually while carving the letters, maybe as another hint. What we know for sure is that he has not shown the final part of k2, the famous idlayertwo bit, but arranging the cipher in rows of 31 and bringing the final G of row 14 in the first position of row 15, so that it goes GENDyaHr, does make the two sides equal. Said row 15 would be now of 32 characters, exactly as it is on the Vigenere side.

Still, nothing definitive yet.

Andrea

s: Morse Code and How Nations See History
t:
Hello everyone.

I have a theory about the Morse code I hope to get some feedback on. I posted my theory on Twitter before I joined this group, but that is rather like throwing a piece of paper out a speeding car window and hoping it lands somewhere helpful.

My theory concerns the purpose of the letter E's of the Morse code messages. The E's serve as waymarks to the 'important' letters in the words. For example, the two E's on the left side of the word EEVIRTUALLYE represent the letter I which is the second letter from the left. The E on the right side represents the letter Y.
The other letters from the E's are derived as follows:
EEEEEEINVISIBLE = I; LUCIDEE = C; MEMORYE = Y; EESHADOWEE = H and O; FORCESEEEEE = O; EDIGETALEEE = D and T; POSITIONE = N

The letters I gleaned by using the waymarks are I, Y, I, C, Y, H, O, O, D, T, & N.

Some words do not have the waymarks, but their letters are important as well. SOS and YR (not RQ) are used in their entirety. Two words are missing letters which are needed. T IS YOUR is missing the letters WHA. INTERPRETATIT has an extra T and is missing the letters ON. (After studying Jim Gillogly’s photos of the Morse Code messages, I believe this is the intended spelling of the word despite other ‘interpretations’ of it).

So, the final letters I used are I, Y, I, C, Y, H, O, O, D, T, N, S, O, S, R, Y, W, H, A, T, O, N.

Using pen and paper, I worked on trying to unscramble something coherent using the letters. After a lot of trial and error, I was able to use all of the letters to spell out the phrase:  HOW DO NATIONS CYY HISTORY.
CYY = SEE.

I look forward to reading other people's thoughts about my theory.

s: Relationship Between Folds And Sanborn's Sheets
t:
Hello everyone. Just wanted some insight into my analysis of the folds and sanborns released encoding sheets.

Start with the 42x8 K3 Step 1 sheet. The first fold is either to the right or left of the R in "DESPARATLY". The second fold is before the S in "REMAINS". I believe the first fold is supposed to be to the left of R. This will give us two matrices, each 31x8, which matches Sanborn's K1-K2 encoding sheet format. The first one will start from the first column and go up to the second fold on the sheet. The second one starts at the first fold and goes to the end of the paper. (Can also orient the paper different ways to change the order of the matrices.)

The second folded sheet to look at is the 31x14 K3+K4 matrix. The first fold is said to be down the H column in ENDYAHR, however I think this may be an error. I believe the fold should go after the R instead of H, this allows us to make two 24x14 matrices following the same process as the 42x8 sheet. It would also support the "SETFOLD" finding to put the fold at that location. These 24x14 matrices will match format with Sanborn's 24x14 K3 step 2 sheet.

I believe this to be a logical explanation for the folds. Now how to actually use these matrices is still stumping me. I believe it relates to the weird markings on the bottom right of the sheets but how is still a mystery to me. Just thought I'd share, any input would be greatly appreciated.

Happy Hunting!
Jake

Hi everyone,

While I very much enjoy problem solving in my personal and professional
life, I am not a "mathemagician".

My early inclination, when I picked up Kryptos 2+ years ago, was that K4
would be solved using a One Time Pad (OTP); I still believe this to this
day; but I also believe that the K4 solution is likely a multi-step process.

OTPs are secure if the following conditions are met:
 1. The Key is random
 2 .The Key is at least as long as the plain text
 3 .The Key is never reused, in whole or in part
 4 .The Key is kept secret

When I look at the Encrypted text (in its entirety), I see: 28 rows and 33
columns
When I look at the Key text (in its entirety), I see: 26 rows and 31
columns (when including the extra "L")

As part of my thought process, I look for harmony and balance; and perhaps,
as an artist, Jim sought to present the same (speculation on my part). If
true, then:
 - Adding a header and footer row (x-axis) to the Key text (specifically A
through E as shown in the Key text) = 28 rows .. thus +2 rows to align with
the Encrypted text
 - Deleting columns 32 and 33 from the Encrypted text = 31 columns
(specifically to align with the Key text) = which only 31 columns ... thus
-2 columns
          * Equilibrium on both sides of the y-axis???

If, as I suspect, the K4 solution involves a OTP, I currently visualize the
following non-random pattern and reused Key code:
[image: image.png]
Where the "X" shown in the first cell equals "O"; the first letter in the
Encrypted text
Where the "T" shown in the last cell equals "R"; the last letter in the
Encrypted text

If, as I suspect, the K4 solution (or at least part of the solution)
includes OTP, then:
 - OTP Condition 2 is satisfied
 - OTP Condition 4 is true (even though Jim has given some solution words,
"East Northeast" for example)
 - OTP Conditions 1 and 3 are not secure and can lead to deciphering

Does anyone, other than me, see a potential non-random pattern, and reuse
element, within the K4 Key text?  For me:
 - The Key text visualization above relates to reuse ... K1 Palimpsest
 - The Key text is read from row 1, Left to Right (not right to left; not
column 1 top left to bottom left) ... K2 Abscissa

If my views above are reasonable, a column transposition (K3) is required
somewhere within the solution K4. It is my belief that the K4 solution will
be found within / around a framework (or fusion) of both art and math.

I have a few ideas and I will continue my K4 solution exploration solo but
if anyone is interested in collaborating around my train of thought, let me
know.

Best,
Shaun (from Canada)

I tend to agree with you, that Jim produced 97 letters of random key, and then used these key letters to encrypt the 97 plaintext letters using the Vig tableau.
See msg 22983 for my reasoning.

The "4 extra columns plus extra L" give you 105 letters, equally distributed (4A, 4B,...), which is what you'd want in a random "running key" sometimes written down as a "one time pad":  basically just a set of random, equally distributed key letters.

How to make the "4 extra columns plus L" into a "random" set of 105 key letters?  Transpose them using some super secret transposition technique, using something previously agreed to between the sender and receiver.  (you just want transposition, not substitution, if you want to keep the flat distribution of key letters)

At the Central Intelligence Agency in Langley, Virginia, there is a sculpture called Kryptos. It consists of four enciphered passages. The plaintext is known only for the first three texts. The solutions for the first three passages are all in plain English text.

The first passage is "Between subtle shading and the absence of light lies the nuance of illusion.".

The second passage is "It was totally invisible; how's that possible? They used the Earth's magnetic field. The information was gathered and transmitted undergruund to an unknown location. Does Langley know about this? They should; it's buried out there somewhere. Who knows the exact location? Only W.W.; this was his last message. Thirty eight degrees fifty seven minutes six point five seconds north seventy seven degrees eight minutes forty four seconds west, layer two."

The third passage is "Slowly, desperately slowly, the remains of passage debris that encumbered the lower part of the doorway was removed. At first it was through copper cables, read Transatlantic Telegraph Cable, until wireless technology was invented that uses A/C pulses to create a frequency and transmitted through a copper antenna – known as a radio wave.  Radio waves are invisible but if we could see them they would look like a sine wave like the ‘scroll’ portion of the sculpture.

The sun operates on an 11-year cycle.  When the sun has more activity at solar maximum it creates a dense highly charged Earth atmosphere that signals can bounce off of using very little power and equipment.  Else to receive a 6m signal, you would need to be in the near vicinity (called a ground wave).

Given that Sanborns art pieces after Kryptos were in Cyrillic, I’ve been looking for clues that K4 is somehow related to something Russian (Soviet) or Cyrillic.
So I asked Chat-GPT if there are any Russian texts involving all the clues Berlin Clock Northeast and east, and this is what I got:

My Question:
Is there a text in Russian, such as a book, poem, news article etc, from before 1990, that contains the words Berlin, clock, northeast and east?

Chat-GPT:
Yes, there is a text in Russian that meets these criteria.
The poem "Урал" (Ural) by Yevgeny Yevtushenko, published in 1967, contains the words "Берлин" (Berlin), "часы" (clock), "северо-восток" (northeast), and "восток" (east).
Here is the relevant excerpt from the poem (in Russian):
"Над Уралом, в атмосферу входя, через Уфу, через Свердловск, через леса и реки впрыгнув, немцы летят, как стайка ласточек, в свой прошлый год, в свою память, в свой Берлин, где были, как в раю, и где в зале заводской, на стене, висели часы, которые похитили во время сражений на северо-востоке. Над Уралом, в атмосферу входя, полны надежды и не прочь опасности, они летят, как бы на встречу свету капиталистическому, к щедрости востока."
And here is a rough translation:
"Over the Ural Mountains, entering the atmosphere,
Through Ufa, through Sverdlovsk,
Jumping over forests and rivers,
The Germans fly like a flock of swallows,
To their past year, to their memory,
To their Berlin, where they were like in paradise,
And where in the factory hall, on the wall,
Hung the clock that they stole
During battles in the northeast.
Over the Ural Mountains, entering the atmosphere,
Full of hope and not averse to danger,
They fly, as if towards the light
Of capitalist generosity in the East."

My question:
Is the poem published in English?

Chat-GPT:
Yes, the poem "Урал" (Ural) by Yevgeny Yevtushenko has been translated into English and published under various titles, including "Ural: A Poem," "Ural River," and "Over the Urals." Some translations may include slightly different wording or phrasing compared to the original Russian version.

My question:
Are there any evidence that the artist Jim Sanborn ever read or met Yevgeny Yevtushenko?

Chat-GPT:
There is no conclusive evidence to suggest that the American artist Jim Sanborn ever read or met Yevgeny Yevtushenko, the Russian poet who wrote "Урал" (Ural).
However, it is possible that Sanborn was influenced by Yevtushenko's work or by the historical events that Yevtushenko wrote about. Sanborn's most famous artwork, the Kryptos sculpture located at the headquarters of the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA), contains encrypted messages that reference Cold War-era espionage and cryptography. The sculpture has been the subject of much speculation and analysis, and some have suggested that it may be related to the Berlin Wall, the Soviet Union, or other historical events and figures associated with the Cold War.
It is worth noting that Yevtushenko was a prominent figure in Russian literature and politics during the Cold War, and his poetry often addressed themes of war, politics, and social justice. It is possible that Sanborn was familiar with Yevtushenko's work or the historical events that he wrote about, either directly or indirectly. However, without further evidence, it is difficult to say for certain whether Sanborn had any specific knowledge of Yevtushenko or his poetry.

My question:
When was the hight of Yevgeny Yevtushenkos popularity in the west?

Chat-GPT:
Yevgeny Yevtushenko was very popular in the West during the 1960s and 1970s, particularly in the United States. He first gained widespread international recognition with the publication of his poem "Babi Yar" in 1961, which denounced the Soviet government's suppression of the facts surrounding the Nazi massacre of Ukrainian Jews at Babi Yar during World War II.
Yevtushenko's outspoken criticism of Soviet repression and his support for freedom of expression made him a popular figure among Western intellectuals and political activists during the Cold War. He was invited to give readings and lectures at universities and cultural institutions throughout the United States and Europe, and his poetry was widely translated and published in English-language literary journals and anthologies.
By the 1980s, Yevtushenko's popularity had begun to wane somewhat as Soviet-American relations improved and the Cold War began to thaw. However, he continued to be recognized as an important literary figure and political commentator, and he remained active as a writer, teacher, and public figure until his death in 2017.

[TLDR: If the AI says "doesn't exist" or "never happened" just means that
data wasn't in it's training model.]

Agreed, I love using GPT but it is a language model after all so it's just
a very advanced parrot really. It will say what you tell it. Now it has a
HUGE data set so you can go down some deep rabbit holes but take what it
says with a grain of salt. Especially negatives. The postive correlations
are pretty solid and it won't deviate much from those. They are also
*usually* correct. Negative statements though, often if it doesn't have
that data it doesn't exist (to it). If you feed it a few statements about
the subject or object it will quickly about face (and even make some new
correlations for you). Also when it says "As an AI language model" to begin
a statement that means you hit a limit. Either built in censorship, lack of
data, or you are trying to have it act in a way the violates it's
`restraining bolt` (sorry for the Star Wars reference). There are ways
around to have it imagine "fictional" or "fantasy" situations that can get
you to dive further and maybe even get it to imply something but if you try
to confirm it it will still have to deny it or throw in a disclaimer. I
honestly wish they would uncensor it and give it real-time information.
It's a language model, it's literally saying in better articulation and
with better data, what you told it to. So the people who fear the AI are
the ones who are telling it to say what scares them most, lol.

Now, I didn't say that the mistakes are not needed to solve K4. I said that correcting them would not aid anyone in solving K4. The mistakes all have purposes that count in the scheme of things. Some become more apparent as one moves along. A few things that I will mention about errors that show up. First is that there are no errors in Sanborn's notes. What I mean is, what might look like an error is likely not, but it's a clue. For instance, the misspelled PALIMPCEST provides an avenue of clues which have already been discussed. It also sends a directional signal that has not been discussed on the forum (to any recognized extent). It is related to one of the other misspellings. Second for all that already haven't figured it out, is that it is DESIGNED IN KRYPTOS TO INSERT THE S IN THE NINTH POSITION FROM THE END OF K2. The fact that the S is missing and needs to be re-inserted into the text is discussed at length in the texts. Reinsertion of the S is the first important step to take in preparing to move into K4. It's the first step beyond solving K1, K2 and K3. With that knowledge, one can understand why Sanborn had to step in to get things moving. Related to what I just said is the fact that what is considered by many to be a grammar error, the word WAS, as in ...THE REMAINS OF PASSAGE DEBRIS THAT ENCUMBERED THE LOWER PART OF THE DOORWAY WAS REMOVED... appears to be an error because REMAINS WERE REMOVED would be correct. One has to assume in reading the text that there are no grammar errors, so tracing the same line back, one finds that it reads, ...THERE MAIN S OF PASSAGE DEBRIS THAT ENCUMBERED THE LOWER PART OF THE DOORWAY WAS REMOVED... So, now we see that the MAIN S WAS REMOVED. This is the desired way to read that string and WAS was not a grammatical error after all. Notice that Kryptos says that the S was removed. Sanborn didn't remove it like he said he did! Let me have you take note about this: One should understand two things. First, that a letter was added to the text. The fact that this occurred would have a distinct effect on performing cryptanalysis. The second is that an important precedent has been set about inserting letters into the ciphertext. There is another easily-missed error in the text that hasn't been discussed on the forum as far as I know. The fact that it exists does not come into play until later, so I will not describe it here. I just mention it for those who have spotted it so they don't attempt to manipulate the text at this point because of it.

I've been looking at primes within the whole of the sculpture and don't know if I've found something or not but this I find interesting (and can find no other reference around).

We know for a fact of certain primes that exist in the sculpture.

3 - The number of misspellings, also the number of superscript letters.

Fibonacci prime index for 2

Twin prime with 5

Now the next number is more obscure.

Take just the numbers from the coordinates given in passage 2:  38°57′6.5″N 77°8′44″W gives  38576577844

now modulate this in the length of the sculpture:  38576577844 mod 869 = 223.

What's interesting about this number is not only is it prime, but it's one of the Fibonacci primes.

The next set of numbers are a little more abstract but what if we look at the words represented by their numeric character.

Using an alphabet where A = 1 .. Z=26 and a special for ?=27

ABSCISSA becomes 12193919191 (not prime) length of 11 (Fibonacci prime index 11) = 89

PALIMPSEST becomes 16112913161951920 (not prime) length of 17 (Fibonacci prime index 17) = 1597

Finally, take the whole of passage 3 and convert this to numbers.



This gives 509 characters. Now this number is a little more special.

509 is also a Fibonacci prime index which points to the Fibonacci prime number 10597999265301490732599643671505003412515860435409421932560009680142974347195483140293254396195769876129909.

What makes this number a little more special is that its length is 107 which not only is it also a prime number but is also the 10th twin prime, twinned with 109.

This gives us a set of primes 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 89, 97, 107, 109, 223, 337, 509, 1597 and randomly 10597999265301490732599643671505003412515860435409421932560009680142974347195483140293254396195769876129909

Maybe there is nothing in this, maybe some of these numbers come from a far more reaching and abstract grasp at nothing but I have a vague recollection of reading somewhere that k4 is a cipher that was in common use in the 1980s. As much of the cryptography that came about in the 70s and 80s used primes, maybe it's not that far a reach although I couldn't expect anyone to calculate the number at index 509 with nothing but a pen and paper.

This is an anagram of the words LAQUEO which in Latin means a noose, snare or trap but when converted from Spanish to English, has a whole new Etymology behind it.

Laqueo (Spanish):

Lacquer. A type of varnish applied to wood

First person singular present indicative form of Laquear

Laquear (English): (plural laquears) (architecture) A lacunar.

Lacunar (medicine) Of or pertaining to a lacuna

Lacuna (plural lacunae or lacunas)

A small opening; a small pit or depression; a small blank space; a gap or vacancy; a hiatus.

An absent part, especially in a book or other piece of writing, often referring to an ancient manuscript or similar such.

(microscopy) A space visible between cells, allowing free passage of light.

(linguistics) A language gap, which occurs when there is no direct translation in the target language for a lexical term found in the source language.

t:
I spent time going over all the media quotes from Sanborn, Scheidt, and other key players in the Kryptos story and had some thoughts.

Sanborn has said it unfolds and has made several similar statements. To me that means it's a puzzle meant to be solved, not a code to crack. I sense a disappointment from Sanborn in the ways that codebreakers have solved it thus far. The clues are meant to unlock doors for solving parts of the puzzle. Each clue is a little trickier to figure out because that's how you're meant to solve it. But one thing is for certain, there are clues. You're supposed to be able to solve this.  I'd imagine that when Sanborn devised the codes he'd use, he wanted to leave a trail of breadcrumbs to allow someone to solve the puzzle. From time to time, he's given us more clues too.

I think the first big clue he gave was when he released images of his charts. He did this a few times, showing different charts to us.

OVERVIEW
2006 - Wired: correction for LAYERTWO
2007 - PBS Nova: chart for K3 showing Plaintext K3 and Ciphertext K3 & K4.
2010 - New York Times: full chart for K1 and partial K2
2010 - New York Times: BERLIN clue
2013 - Big Tech Day: K3 chart 2 was shown.
2014 - New York Times: CLOCK clue
2020 - New York Times: NORTHEAST clue
2020 - Sukhwant Singh: EAST was added to NORTHEAST clue to make EASTNORTHEAST

Each of these clues had interesting bits of info that you might miss otherwise.

2006, Wired- LAYERTWO. This correction had to be made for a reason. Sanborn even said in the article, "Then I discovered they were, in fact, missing a clue, and it bothers me if they put 'id by rows' in instead of 'layer two,'" he says. "They didn't have everything to work with that I wanted them to have to work with." (source: https://www.wired.com/2006/04/typo-confounds-kryptos-sleuths/) (mirror: https://web.archive.org/web/20230419204959/https://www.wired.com/2006/04/typo-confounds-kryptos-sleuths/)

2007 Nova video - Previously people were solving using a different sized matrix for the rotation. The clip showed a chart marked 1, with matrix that was 42Cx8R on a chart that was 42Cx15R. In the margin beside the plaintext were letters P and C alternating, and one other noteworthy bit of info on the plaintext shown, it appears to be a photocopy! The lines aren't quite as crisp on the grid, and the paper isn't yellowed like the other charts we'll see. The second chart shown has a lot of other possible clues too. It is marked 3 and shows the ciphertext of the bottom copper plate, including K4. This is written in a 31Cx14R grid. The paper is the familiar yellow. There appear to be several other marks on the page too, including line numbers on several rows. On the sleeve holding this paper is the phrase "Top #4" (source: https://www.dailymotion.com/video/x31wabu)

2010 - New York Times: In the same week, we got the crib, BERLIN, we also received the charts for K1 and part of K2. My favorite detail about these is PALIMPCEST is the keyword atop K1. It looks as though the C was changed to an S. There are clear signs of erasing where this change was made. Most interestingly position 57 still shows a C, which is the real reason for the Q in IQLUSION! We're not provided with the whole chart for K2, but both are the familiar yellowed paper shown in part of the Nova Video. It's also noteworthy that this paper is a 31Cx14R grid--the same used for K3&K4 combined in the Nova Video. The BERLIN clue was given without specificity to say that NYPVTT decoded to Berlin, the article only said that "the characters that are the 64th through 69th...When deciphered, they read BERLIN"* (source: https://www.nytimes.com/2010/11/21/us/21code.html and https://www.nytimes.com/2010/11/21/us/21codecharts.html) (mirror: https://web.archive.org/web/20230419215954/https://www.nytimes.com/2010/11/21/us/21code.html and https://web.archive.org/web/20220507073708/https://www.nytimes.com/2010/11/21/us/21codecharts.html)

2013 - Big Tech Day revealed another chart to us. Sanborn shows the rotate text from K3 in a chart marked with a 2. This chart is 14Cx25R, but only has letters in the first 24 rows. Noteworthy to me is that this chart appears cropped, you only see the top, left, and right. It's very likely that this was done on the same 31x14 sheet (especially since END is written horizontally and that the text is rotated for the actual sculpture), and if so what is in those extra six rows? He's never been shy about showing the full charts before with blank spaces before, so why the sudden cropping? (source: https://media.techcast.cloud/bigtechday6/maximilian-1615/?q=maximilian-1615)

2014 - New York Times: we received the word CLOCK at positions 70-74. Again the clue said the decrypted positions. There was no mention of the letters themselves being a 1-to-1 from the ciphertext.* (source: https://www.nytimes.com/2014/11/21/us/another-kryptos-clue-is-offered-in-a-24-year-old-mystery-at-the-cia.html) (mirror: https://web.archive.org/web/20230419145653/https://www.nytimes.com/2014/11/21/us/another-kryptos-clue-is-offered-in-a-24-year-old-mystery-at-the-cia.html)

2020 - New York Times: This was the first time we received an image from Sanborn in nearly 7 years. This one showed NORTHEAST in positions 26 through 34. This image also showed BERLINCLOCK in it's positions 64 through 74. This clue was also the closest we've come in the press to a representation of a 1-to-1 substitution as it doesn't show the corresponding ciphertext characters.* (source: https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2020/01/29/climate/kryptos-sculpture-final-clue.html) (mirror: https://web.archive.org/web/20200129103917/https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2020/01/29/climate/kryptos-sculpture-final-clue.html)

2020 - EAST was included in positions 22 through 25. This came from people who had direct contact via a web submission, and has been confirmed by Sanborn other interviews.

*- Sanborn has confirmed 1-to-1 translations for letters, by confirming “NYPVTT=BERLIN” but it’s always been at Kryptos meetings and not in the press. His chart given to NYT in 2020 seemed to indicate a 1-to-1 translation as well, but it’s still a topic of debate.

I've worked on Kryptos for a lot of years. In recent months, I have strayed off the path somehow. And, try as I may, I don't seem to have the wherewithall to connect things again. Clues are there, but making matches is now a distant probability for me. I am 69 years old now, and who knows how long I'm going to be around.

One of the things that has been on my mind for a long time does not match with what I have been encountering as I move through the K4 puzzle. You alude to it in a way that brings it to mind again. I think I would like to amplify on what you said about crypt spelled with a K. The greek word for crypt is close to kryptos, but with the last letter not being S, but being Greek Eta. Contrary to what a lot of people think, Kryptos does not mean hidden.

Consider the "Contemplative Pool" that doesn't seem to have any purpose in the courtyard outside of helping to set a peaceful mood. More than once, Sanborn has mentioned this pool as being part of Kryptos. When I got decent views of the pool via photos taken by Elonka when she last visited the sculpture, I was struck all of a sudden by the resemblance of the pool and surrounding stone to an open coffin or crypt.

Make no mistake. It's the S that is being talked about in the upper part of K2. IT WAS TOTALLY INVISIBLE. IT'S BURIED OUT THERE SOMEWHERE. The K2 CT was modified by adding the S to the CT in the ninth position from the end. In K3, the S is called the FLAME and the HOT AIR... CAUSED THE FLAME TO FLICKER, making it resemble a Z. Details in the bottom rows of K2 via sliding key ABSCISSA, direct to have the Z placed at the front of K4, making it start now with ZOBKR.
So, the S has already been manipulated or moved twice before actually starting K4. No need to believe me, just give me the benefit of the doubt for the time being.

Why does the cipher jump from a random phrase to a location, to Egypt?

Taher Elgamal was an Egyptian born cryptologist who in 1985 wrote a paper on ""A Public key Cryptosystem and A Signature Scheme based on discrete Logarithms". He's also published alongside Hugh C Williams, a leading expert in Number theory, an equivalent branch of Mathematics to Set Theory, upon which the Berlin Clock Mengenlehreur is built. Elgamal is often the underlying encryption scheme used for the Diffie Hellman public key exchange system.

The reason I ask this question is you don't need to be good at math as a whole to understand a singular aspect. I'm really bad at basic arithmetic (just ask my accountant) but I'm really good with algorithms and calculus (see my scientific publications).

Do I understand Statistical Analysis? No. I am really good with specific branches of mathematics to which my field equates.

Mr Sanborn was working with Ed Scheidt - he would have been learning exactly one thing and anyone can learn that D^(ya) = H^r when shown properly.

Finally, We're all focused on solving K4 as a plaintext but in Cryptography, Elgamal is inefficient and is instead normally only used to encrypt a symmetric key. What if we're looking at this all wrong and K4 is really only a key and not a message?

Sukhwant Singh wrote, and I wholeheartedly agree with:

"K1-K3 are not needed to be solved for K4."

After all, solving K1 was not a prerequisite to solving K2 (or more likely vice versa, given how short K1 was), and K3 was so clearly different from first two (English letter frequencies) that the plaintext of K1+K2 was of little help in solving K3. Solving K1 & K2 ~did~ at least tell you where the precise dividing line was for the change in encryption systems.

So ... given the pattern presented so far, the sensible takeaway is that K4 can be solved in isolation, and the main assistance provided by solving K1-K3 is knowing precisely where K4 starts. But I accept Jim's claim that K4 can be solved without solving K1-K3 -- specifically because having the plaintext of K1, K2 or K3 was of no help in solving the others.

Singh went on to say:

"All the mistakes have nothing to do with  K4 as he said you don’t need to solve K1-K3 for K4, these mistakes are in K1-K3."

Carl Ellis took issue with that leap of logic, but I have to agree with Sukhwant's conclusion. You couldn't know there were mistakes in K1-K3 without decrypting those sections, therefore if Sanborn says K4 is solvable *without* decrypting K1-K3, then the "mistakes" can't be essential to understanding how K4 is encrypted. I would opine that the nature of the errors actually speaks more to Jim's spelling struggles and cryptographic innocence than it does to some master plan at subterfuge. Be honest with yourself: he spelled PALIMPSEST wrong multiple times on encryption sheets he dared to share with us, so everyone could see where he edited errant C's into S's, and more importantly... the impact of failing to make the keyword spelling correction.  --Rob

         AWVRMAQAJSMDWHADNPWWBPDRKXXFRIJVHHAEBEXHGXHHTVZZBOEGVDMLNOBNIPWIYFKEEUZPFVBJLVZQEGCLNJVMSMOMTVCOR

Ed S. Made a statement that one of the more difficult design challenges in his domain is figuring out how to transmit keys.  I would expect that concept can be expanded to include exemplars (generic or specific).  KRYPTOS would be a good opportunity to showcase a bit.

Jim S. made a statement that the position or orientation of a misspelling was more important than the misspelling itself.  He also made a statement that studying disclosed original worksheets might prove useful.  Doesn't mean the solutions are necessary, but it sounds like they can be helpful.

Hello folks,

I would like to share with you a new discovery in K4.

Some time ago I uploaded a document which can be found in my personal folder.
After removing the 7th letter X, inserting an L at the beginning of the ciphertext
and deciphering these 21 or 22 letters as described in the document, we get almost
a readable plain text:

LOB KRUOOGHU LBS OLIFBBWF
?YY LQSLQSLQ XYY LWTLWTLW
?PS CAIHEAWR NST HQEUETSI

It just takes two additional steps to make it readable:

1. Swap the bigrams AI, QE and TS (Sanborn talked about turning and flipping letters)
2. EAWRNS = ANSWER

?PS CAIHEAWR NST HQEUETSI
?PS CIAHANSW ERT HEQUESTI (ONS)
?PS CIA ANSWER THE QUESTI (ONS)

It looks like the fifth letter of the word ANSWER (E) was removed and inserted in
front of the word before the transposition was applied:

ANSWER -> EANSWR
EANSWR -> EAWRNS

This would also fit perfectly to the mistakes in the plaintext of K3:

ARET(E)LY <- The fifth letter starting from the mistake (also E) is missing in the plaint text.

Let's take a closer look at the letter sequence AWRNS. Is it possible to skip this
transpositional step? Of course, because every transposition is equal to a
polyalphabetic substitution with a key having the same size as the plain text:

GHULB (decryption with transpostion)
SLQXY vigenere
AWRNS transpostion
ANSWR

GHULB (decryption without transpostion)
SUIQA vigenere
ANSWR

So what's the point?

The decryption of the first half of the block (KRUO) with the monoalphabetic
key SSSS also results in a meaningful word:

KRUO
SSSS
QUIZ (maybe a hint)

Take QUI, swap the letters UI (like AI in CIA), add an A, turn it around and the result
is this special key: UIQA
The letter S is not so important, because this letter is the same in both keys.

It looks like the two halfs of the block are connected in a strange way, that  has something
to do with the transposition and maybe also with other methods I explained in the document.

Start with K4's character stream, and loop that stream around a cylinder. Every N characters starts a new row.

Start with K4's character stream, and loop that stream around a cone. Every N + M characters starts a new row. M is assumed to be 1, but isn't confined to being 1. Lines (good lines) get crossed when it's realized that M can be any positive integer.

Next, look at the image in the group's photos: https://kryptos.groups.io/g/main/photo/286198/3610912

Start with K4's character stream, and loop that stream around a… Fibonacci spiral. Each row has a different but well-defined length.

Here's a list of the spiral's canonical positions, built line at a time. The “line numbers” are added to aid in the comments that follow:

line 1: 1
line 2: 1, 2
line 3: 1, 2, 3, 4
line 4: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8

Given an alphabet sequence, character sequence strings from cylinders might be

a, b, c, d
e, f, g, h
i, j, k, l

which fit nicely into our initially, typically, comforting, default, rectangular approach to things. With a Fibonacci spiral, the regularity from cylinders stops. The character sequences lose a regularity afforded from the spiral's consistency. The lines of characters and the counts of characters in each line change. They now become

a
b, c
d, e, f, g
h, i, j, k, l, m, n, o

The regularity of the cylinder and cone pattern is gone. There's still a pattern present, but it's more complex. It touches on new and different patterns and information.

Comments

Line 1: you have to start somewhere.
Line 2: there's only one number that can touch the existing one character.
Line 3: two characters in line 2 can each touch one, so now I have four, …and so on.

End Comments

If Sanborn has based his encrypted K4 strings on string lengths offered by a Fibonacci-determined string length—when the world has its blinders on and is trying to shoehorn a cylinder approach—we'll never get there, and yet its solution could be right in front of us.

No I'm not saying this *IS* the solution. It might be, but more importantly, I think it points out the value of stopping along the way and dissecting when we're making assumptions, or not, in all the possible places in the thinking through of the solution.

Respectfully submitted.

THEBERLINCLOCK, MENGENLEHREUHR and ABSCISS (not ABSCISSA) are keywords used soon after getting rolling into K4. It's easier to see what's going on when you already have the Z attached to the front end of K4. Notice all three of these keywords are divisors of 98, now the number of letters in the expanded (with the Z) K4. Now, if you ignore any assumptions you might have after having heard the words "plain text" you will have a clearer mind about the nature of these things. First, the fact that Sanborn specified the exact locations for BERLIN and CLOCK should have rung a "hey, here is a keyword" bell in your head. But for most people, having heard "plain text" immediately invoked an assumption that BERLINCLOCK was part of the final outcome of K4, and that "knowledge" put blinders on all who fell victim to the deception. Clues like DIGE UHR and DIGE TAL INTERPRETATI(on) point to MENGENLEHREUHR being the BERLINCLOCK of interest. There had to be a way to make it fit and I found the way. There is an unusual line-up of letters in K4 that had my attention for a while. It included the odd set of SS that did not reside in columns six and seven in the 7-column pad of of K4. The string is QSJQSS. This string has an odd property that I won't bore you with, but the property does not match what goes on with the double letter combinations in columns six and seven. Yes, I did notice JS' initials in the group. There was a symmetry in QSJQS. It simply occurred to me to see if I could find a match with a similar set of letters in MENGENLEHREUHR. I did. It's the letters ENGEN. Bingo! As it turned out, if you align MENGENLEHREUHR with K4 (incl Z) with ENGEN corresponding with QSJQS, the keyword fits and works when you use it. ABSCISS works as a keyword, too. It was provided to me by a well-known contributor to the forum. One can easily see the correspondence between ABSCISS and many of the 7-letters strings in K4.

s: how rare is 6 pairs of double letters in K4?
t:
Computing the statistical likelihood of a N pairs of double letters appearing in a random string of 97 letters is mathematically messy. It is easier to write a quick program to do a Monte Carlo simulation and report the results. Here's what I get after 5 million trials of 97-letter random strings:

0 doubles: 2.3235 %
1 double: 8.8874 %
2 doubles: 16.9138 %
3 doubles: 21.1647 %
4 doubles: 19.6954 %
5 doubles: 14.4886 %
6 doubles: 8.8045 %
7 doubles: 4.5071 %
8 doubles: 2.0254 %
9 doubles: 0.7915 %
10 doubles: 0.2777 %

So the most likely result is 3 pairs of doubles, while Kryptos K4 has six. The odds of six OR MORE double letters appearing is 16.53%, or nearly 1 in 6. So while it seems rare, the fact is that it's not that rare at all.

Now having 5 out of the 6 doubles appear in the same columns when K4 is laid out in 7-letter rows is significantly less likely. But someone would have made the same remark if it happened when the letters were laid out in rows of 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9 and so on. So you would have to compute the odds of it happening with any number of columns to have a true feeling for the rarity. It's certainly not a 1-in-a-million or a 1-in-100,000 rarity. Maybe not even as rare as 1-in-10000. I may program it up to see what the answer is... --Rob

K4 does not look like plain text. It looks like the output of Vigenere, which we know Sanborn understood. Or it looks like text he’s messed with in some way, maybe by changing one letter to another, by doubling letters here and there, or by inserting letters (like the Xs for line endings in the earlier part.)

What I’m getting at is, how likely is it that we would find KR, YP, and arguably TOS in a string of 97 characters? In other words, is this significant or is it a red herring?

s: Greek word “ASTATOS” is one of the keys found in K2
t:
Sanborn forgot the S in the ciphertext in K2, which when inputed, the plaintext at the end of K2 is “XLAYERTWO”, which i took as literally X leads to second layer. If you take all the plaintext Xs from K2 and write them in order with their ciphertext counterparts, you get…..

Character #  X        Ciphertext
         68                            A
         136                          S
         195                          T
         208                         A
         251                          T
         289                         O
         362                         S

    This is a greek word ASTATOS, which means unstable. It also is what Astatine, the 85th element on the periodic table is named after, which also happens to be the rarest naturally occuring element in the earths crust. I dont know where to go from there, but I think we need a Y clue. Since Abscissa was a keyword for K2, which is the X coordinate in a coordinate system, it only makes sense we probably need a Y and using both together somehow will give the answer to K4. I hope this line of logic makes sense and  If you have any questions let me know.

I agree with its not plain text.  We already know the words BERLIN CLOCK EAST NORTEAST are in there.  If you just try to remove those letters you run out of "E"s.  I'll continue to chase down my theory with re ordering lines and looking for other clues based on the KR TQS YP letters.

For my two cents here, I'm thinking that there may be some way of ordering the columns here, that causes K4 to become the key for a secondary operation

What makes me think this is the misspellings and their counterparts.

when laid out 7 columns by 14 rows,
L and Q (iqlusion) appear in the same row (4)
U (undergruund) and O appear in the same row (1)
A (desparatly) and E appear in the same row (14)

In all instances, Q, U and A also appear together in the same column (6) - however, there are also 2 Ls in this column so this in itself might be irrelevant.

I would be surprised of this is a red herring as there is a high degree of certainty that there are multiple ciphers going on here but the difficulty is in finding the right permutation. With 5040 possible columnar permutations to choose from, there has to be a pattern to tell you how to order the columns, and then how to order the rows within.

And just to make this a little harder, who says it would be ordered by 14 rows over 7 columns? How do we know it's not 7 rows over 14 columns?

Another thought that occurred to me over the weekend, is why 97 characters? It doesn't fit evenly onto a grid but if you take it as a puzzle, then the missing space onto 98 makes sense - in this instance it becomes a sliding puzzle, albeit one without a discernible goal state.

One things for certain, KRYPTOS is part of that solution; the problem is, with 98! possible combinations of the grid, I am (un)?reliably informed would take something in the region of many orders of magnitude longer than the lifetime of the universe to operate on.

Interesting side note: Sliding puzzles can be solved by group theory. Maybe (read I) need to stop thinking of this as a cipher and start thinking of it as a game.

s: ABSCISSA Was The Clue For K3
t:
Hello all,
I wanted to share with you my view of the Kryptos clues. Specifically what I believe to be the main clue for K3 - ABSCISSA.
Knowing this clue explains all of the different methods for decrypting K3 - they all unwittingly use the magic number 8.

File is located in my Personal Folder:  DSander/ABSCISSA_Was_The_Clue_For_K3.pdf

Let me know what you think.

The thing is, cryptography is not his field. He’s an artist. He was contracted to create an art installation for the CIA, so naturally he created a sculpture that utilizes encryption. He is not a cryptographer and we shouldn’t assume that he has a deep understanding of the ciphers used.

My son is a ceramic artist. I could help him encode a message onto one of his pieces, but he would not be able to explain how the ciphertext was derived.

I don't believe Sanborn said that BERLINCLOCK and EASTNORTHEAST were parts of the final solution. I do think he allowed that people continued to believe that he said it. Sanborn has said on more than one occasion that he engages in disinformation, as it's part of the game. Frankly, it's hard to miss the probable connection of the above strings to keywords. There are blatant attributes and clues pointing to them as keywords.

I sometimes have my personal opinions about whether his statements were in the best interests of the greater good. However, there is no doubt in my mind that Kryptos can be solved if solvers don't depend so much on what Sanborn says, but on the information that is out there in the form of clues, inferences and instructions given in the Kryptos texts, interviews, suggestions offered on the forum, etc.
Sanborn has said a lot of stuff along the line that has been taken as God's truth. The whole story about coming up with the code for Kryptos as he drove back in the desert from Arizona with the petrified wood logs rolling around in the back of his pickup is an example. You tell me, how much truth was there to be garnered from that rendition that applies to Kryptos? Sanborn said he was unable to do math, that he was ANATHAMATH. You tell me if you think that he can't do math after knowing he has a master's degree and successfully built a nuclear fission reactor. ANATHAMATH is a grouping of characters that appears in a matrix further on in K4. Remember the talk about preparing a cipher response under conditions of duress? There is another matrix that has the string ANSWERED UNDER DURESS. You have to take my word for it for now. I've shown it to others, but I'm not prepared to show it to the group. So there have been a lot of things said along the road that should be weighed against what is in Kryptos. Bottom line is not to expect Sanborn to step up and say he was lying about stuff, but to make sure not to make bogus assumptions.
PaulK

Hi Henrietta:

"The thing is, cryptography is not his field. He’s an artist."

Absolutely agree. This is why he would not have a good feel for how hard or easy it would be to solve a cipher he created.

"He was contracted to create an art installation for the CIA, so naturally he created a sculpture that utilizes encryption. He is not a cryptographer and we shouldn’t assume that he has a deep understanding of the ciphers used."

He was schooled in some historical, marginally secure systems of encrypting information (i.e. Vigenère polyalphabetic substitution in K1 and K2, and double transposition in K3) that can be easily carried out by a novice using matrices. In other words, something visual that would appeal to Jim's artistic perspective, requiring no math whatsoever. K4 is almost certainly going to comprise one or more systems that fall into that artistic, no-math-required category. Even an Enigma machine could fall into that category -- I constructed one out of paper strips and used it to solve Richard Belfield's final cipher in "Can You Crack the Enigma Code?" (Alas for the small team I collaborated with, past the time deadline to win the prize: an actual WWII Enigma Machine.) However, Ed Scheidt is unlikely to have steered Jim toward such a system, not least because it is easy to make a mistake, and unlike the encryption errors that yielded IQLUSION and UNDERGRUUND, a single error early in an Enigma encryption (or a running key) could render the remainder of the cipher unsolvable.  --Rob

Belief and memories change and fade.

In 2010, he told the New York Times that the 64th through 69th letter when deciphered read BERLIN. https://www.nytimes.com/2010/11/21/us/21code.html .

In 2014, he told the New York Times that the letters from positions 64 to 74 spell out two words, "Berlin clock". https://www.nytimes.com/2014/11/21/us/another-kryptos-clue-is-offered-in-a-24-year-old-mystery-at-the-cia.html

In 2020, he told the New York Times that NORTHEAST appears at positions 26-34.

If those words do not appear in the plaintext in those positions, it would be intentionally lying, which I do not believe he would stoop to. There's a very big difference between coming up with a colorful story we might have troubles believing (the CIA historian with a photographic memory getting kicked out of the room), or perhaps not understanding whether transposition counts as a one-to-one correspondence between ciphertext and plaintext, and telling a massive lie to a newspaper to keep us going.

I certainly wouldn't rule anything out if you come up with something that diverges from those clues (maybe he said something untrue, maybe information got lost along the way). And there definitely could be a K5 ("final solution") after K4 is solved. But if the K4 ciphertext doesn't contain those clues, well, people would be much more mad than if he made a mistake making it impossible to solve.
                       -Scott

s: Greek word “ASTATOS” is one of the keys found in K2
t:
Rob Mccleary, I like this find a lot. I haven't been working on Kryptos for a while, but this strikes me as an interesting and possibly relevant find.

I recall that Sanborn may have mentioned, around the time he revealed XLAYERTWO, that the plaintext X's were relevant for solving the later stage "K5" puzzle. So it makes sense to look at the plaintext X's in this way.

The cryptographic reason that it could have been possible for Sanborn to plant such a clue in the K2 ciphertext is that many letters are repeated both in the K2 keyword ABSCISSA and in the word ASTATOS. For those who are interested, if you look at the Vigenere tableau, and you look at the SABC keyword letter rows, which happen to be adjacent to each other (next to GHIJ on the far left-hand side alphabetical column), in the column under plaintext X (below Y in the top alphabetical row), the ciphertext letters in those four rows are TOSA, which are all the letters in ASTATOS.

With such a KRYPTOS-keyed Vigenere tableau arrangement, with the choice of the keyword ABSCISSA, and with the flexibility to choose the placement of the X's in the plaintext, it would have been possible for Sanborn to deliberately place this clue word ASTATOS without messing up the rest of the cryptographic encryption of K2.

The search for and discovery of the rare natural element astatine is actually quite an interesting story: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astatine#History . (I knew nothing about astatine before Rob's post about ASTATOS made me curious to look up information about it.)

Given this discovery, in addition to Rob's ideas about looking for a similar "Y"-based clue for a possible keyword, I would also suggest looking at ideas for how to possibly use the periodic table of elements to design a cipher. Such an idea may have appealed to Sanborn, and perhaps Scheidt could have designed some kind of cipher based on the arrangement of the periodic table and/or the names and symbols of the elements in it.

@Paul Kiesel wrote about it, and I'm supporting it here. Work with facts, data, and evidence, not opinions (but see my note on opinions, below). Facts, evidence, and data are irrefutable—opinions are just opinions. As a friend once said, opinions are just like belly buttons: everyone has one. He probably said it in a much more crude way, though.

From 35,000 feet (12,000m), the current, human culture has groomed us all to accept opinion as fact, and to do so without question. That's a dangerous, slippery slope.

When I can see something, and when I'm able to see the same thing you see—perhaps a sequence of letters on the sculpture, or pencil scribblings of letters around a circle—and when I can see the spreadsheet work or the scribbling on paper that shows the remapping from one string to another (why is it our teachers were drilling into us, “Show your work?”) I can be confident I'm working with facts. Those facts have the seeds of the completed ideas that will ultimately move everyone across the Kryptos finish line at the same time.

Meanwhile, opinions, and I'll go so far as to qualify that they need to be considered *reasonable opinions,* are always welcome and respected.[1] However, I'm careful to never treat them as fact. Doing so—each of our awareness of treating opinions as opinions—is an inside job. If you do, you do, and if you don't… well, you're probably not aware of those inside jobs, either.

Respectfully submitted.

[1]Why respect all reasonable opinions? Because the thing that will end up being K4's solution will be the one thing that is more likely going to be out of character from the previous suggestions (“progress is made by unreasonable individuals”), but will be just odd enough, or just unordinary enough to encapsulate the hidden treasure in its odd sounding, verbal, lexical shell, enough to confuse us with its external oddness, but be the walnut shell holding together the prize nut contained inside.

If reasonable opinions AREN'T respected, then in knee jerk reactions over time and over the world, possible answers will end up getting dismissed without their due and necessary consideration.

It's not out of line to suggest that for healthy societies to survive, ALL reasonable opinions must be respected, for the same argument.

The plaintext X are at locations that make sense in the plaintext, not just randomly inserted.

The only way I see to do this is to Start with the plain messages with X's placed as they are, then place ASTATOS above where the X's are, then see what K2 keys might produce those 7 letters of cipher, and see if any of these putative K2 keys appear to be a meaningful key word such as ABSCISSA.  Seems like a long shot to me.  (That would say he started with ASTATOS and stumbled across ABSCISSA as a keyword that would work).

Sure, we could write a program to run thru lots of combinations (selecting candidate words from a few thousand word dictionary) and maybe we stumble across a couple of candidate keywords, but Jim claims he limited himself to paper & pencil and is unlikely to have written such a program.  So starting with ASTATOS and XXXXXXX, how would he have come up with the keyword ABSCISSA?

That said, I do agree it's odd that the X's line up with a 7 letter ciphertext that
a. only contains 4 different letters and
b. these letters (in ciphertext, which should be equi-random) just happen to be high frequency English letters T,O,S,A

Doug

t:
I appreciate Doug's questions and comments, which are important to answer, but generally I agree with Elonka's reply: Sanborn very well could have started with the ABSCISSA keyword and the X's in place to encrypt to ASTATOS, and then chosen the precise lengths of the sentences of the plaintext around the X's in those places. Unlike the K3 plaintext, the K2 plaintext was not a quote from another source; it was Sanborn's own composition, giving him complete freedom to arrange such things as he pleased. (I have also done such things in composing cryptograms, for example to make sample K4 plaintext text strings fit exactly 97 letters.) And since K2 is much longer than K1, he had a lot more room to arrange such things with the required lengths without contorting the flow of the plaintext excessively. This is all simply good cryptographic composition technique.

Regarding Doug's comment about the oddity of the 7 X's lining up with only 4 different high-frequency letters (in English, Greek, and most languages) T, O, S, A: Actually, this is mostly the result of the choice of the KRYPTOS keyword for the Vigenere tableau and of the ABSCISSA keyword for the encryption of K2. ABSCISSA itself only has 5 different letters: A, B, C, I, S. Moreover, in the KRYPTOS-keyed alphabet, with S at the end of the initial keyword but ABC remaining at the beginning of the alphabetically ordered letters that do not appear in the word KRYPTOS, the letters SABC occur in sequence in the KRYPTOS-keyed alphabet. Further, if one shifts all of those letters backward by 2 letters within this same keyed alphabet, it produces...TOSA! Namely, the last three letters of KRYPTOS, followed by the A at the beginning of the alphabet.

Well, since X is the second-to-last letter in the KRYPTOS-keyed alphabet, because Y is removed from the end of the alphabet to appear in the word KRYPTOS, this means that in this Vigenere encryption, a plaintext X will always produce a ciphertext letter that is shifted back 2 letters within the KRYPTOS-keyed alphabet from the keyword letter, which in this case must always be one of the letters appearing in ABSCISSA.

Thus, as long as Sanborn avoided placing any X in a location in K2 that would line up with an I in ABSCISSA (which would produce a ciphertext G), he could guarantee that all plaintext X's would encrypt to ciphertext T, O, S, and/or A. Again, this is a direct result of the choice of KRYPTOS as the Vigenere keyword and ABSCISSA as the K2 keyword.

t:
@dsander:

If ASTATOS were merely an anagram of the ciphertext values of the 7 plaintext X’s in K2, I would agree with you that it easily could have occurred by chance, given the KRYPTOS alphabet and the keyword ABSCISSA, as you and I have both demonstrated.

But it is not an anagram: the letters ASTATOS occur *in order* as the ciphertext letters of the 7 plaintext X’s *in order* within K2.

Moreover, while as you say T will occur for X 3/8 of the time by chance, and O for X 2/8 of the time by chance, A and S will only occur for X 1/8 of the time by chance.

Thus, the probability of ASTATOS occurring by chance, even with the KRYPTOS alphabet and ABSCISSA keyword, is only:

1/8 * 1/8 * 3/8 * 1/8 * 3/8 * 2/8 * 1/8

= only about a 1 in 116,500 probability of occurring by chance

Respectfully I have to disagree with your conclusion here. There is no evidence that this is referencing a specific palimpsest, rather, it is referencing the concept of a palimpsest; that is to say that is likely that it relates to erasure and re-use, whereby the re-application of text onto parchment masks that which was there before. Furthermore, what is the purpose of intelligence gathering if not to solve a given situation?

Hypothetically Lets say that the first two lines of the above table originally read SSPENNSYLVANIA. At some point, this text got erased from the page and someone else wrote over the text with TJSEO-GQQXH. Maybe they used a different margin, or maybe they didn't erase enough; the SS and YL from SSPENSYLVANIA still stood out over whatever should be written there.

The thing with Palimpsests is that there are ways to recover some, or even all of the earlier uses of it. This, I believe is the point being made with the word. It's recoverable.

Does that mean I'm right on this particular line of investigation? No, absolutely not. There is circumstantial evidence at best that my suggestion here is anything more than yet another shot in the dark but until there is irrefutable proof that this line of inquiry is wrong or leads to a dead end, I may as well follow it and see where it goes.

Yes, the connection between the Greek words KRYPTOS and ASTATOS is interesting indeed.

My thoughts return to the periodic table of chemical elements:
As Rob Mccleary pointed out above, astatos "unstable" is the source of the name of the element astatine (85).
Also, kryptos "hidden" is the source of the name of the element krypton (36).

I am curious about which other Greek words related to element names that Sanborn may have found interesting and worthy of including somehow in some part of Kryptos.
Interesting candidates with possible relations to the themes of Kryptos:
Tantalus, the Greek mythological figure, source of the name of the element tantalum (73). The word tantalize comes from Tantalus as well.
Prometheus, the Greek mythological figure, source of the name of the element promethium (61). The figure of Prometheus may possibly be considered to be related to the Kryptos theme "Intelligence Gathering".
Aktis, aktinos, the Greek word meaning "ray, beam; brightness, splendor; spoke (of a wheel)", source of the name of the element actinium (89).
Of course this brings to mind DYAHR and "RAY" in the K3 ciphertext.
Dusprositos, the Greek word meaning "hard to get", source of the name of the element dysprosium (66).

Finally, about the periodic table itself, although it is standardly displayed with 18 columns, in fact many scientists consider a 32-column table more accurate, with the rows of f-block elements (57-70 and 89-102) included in rows 6 and 7 between the group 2 column and group 3 column.
Such a layout produces a 32x7 periodic table, which is rather similar to the dimensions of the plates of Kryptos, which are primarily 31x14 but which extend to 32 letters in 3 rows of the K1-K2 plate and 3 rows of the K3-K4 plate.
One could possibly visualize each plate (K1-K2 and K3-K4) as two 32x7 tables arranged vertically above and below each other. There are of course many problematic difficulties with making a practical working encryption and decryption method out of this.

I just wanted to share the latest rabbit hole I've been going down. Maybe some of you have gone down it already. I found an interesting link between VQQP and NYPV.

As we all know:
If we want FLRVQQPRNGKSS in K4 to map to EASTNORTHEAST we need to have RDUMRIYWOYNKY.
If we want NYPVTTMZFPK in K4 to map to BERLINCLOCK we need to have ELYOIECBAQK.
That assumes a 1 to 1 relationship, and using KRYPTOS alphabet and Vigenere / Quagmire 3.

We know that using ELYO to decrypt NYPV you get BERL, but what I found is, if you encrypt (not decrypt) NYPV using ELYO you get TNOR! I found this because I decrypted NYPV 25 times in a row with ELYO and it cycled through the alphabet and landed on TNOR. This could be a huge breakthrough, or it could be another time-sink.

I found if you put K4 in a grid of width 39, you get VQQP (TNOR) to align above NYPV (BERL). It could just be a random fluke, but I find it interesting that you can get both 4 letter sets of plaintext using ELYO.

It gets more interesting. If you decrypt VQQP with NYPV you get PMLA. Look familiar? It is PALIMPSEST backwards without the "I" ! The really interesting part is that if you repeat TSESPMILAP multiple times above K4 starting from OBKR, the VQ aligns with PM. So does the NY if in a 39 width grid.

VQQP+PMLA=NYPV

So even if you don't believe K4 is a 1 to 1 relationship with the hints provided by Jim, a relationship between VQQP and NYPV with PMLA is there. Maybe its something, maybe its nothing.

It gets more interesting...

MRIY is how you get TNOR from VQQP. Well, you can get MRIY with ELYO plus PMLA.

ELYO+PMLA=MRIY

So it comes full circle.

VQQP+MRIY=TNOR
NYPV+ELYO=BERL

VQQP-NYPV=PMLA
MRIY+ELYO=PMLA

What is the important of ELYO? One other thing I noticed. Look at Jim's notes for K1 which uses PALIMPSEST. The Es in plaintext align with Ls of PALIMPSEST several times and creates ciphertext Y. ELY is inevitable with PALIMPSEST when E lands on L. K1 has ELY multiple times funny enough on the 13, 33, 43, and 53 positions. On the 33 and 53 positions it is followed with OIQ which gives ELYOIQ.

This has me thinking there is a definite link between K4 and PALIMPSEST.

Let me know what you think.

I would like to circle back to a recent thread by Josh LeVeque https://kryptos.groups.io/g/main/message/23792 because I think this is in some ways important but, I'd like to focus only on the cipher, and what is encapsulated within this.

In what I'm about to write, I don't have answers to everything and am going to try and avoid assumptions on things I cannot back up; you may draw your own on this but I'd advise against going against the spirit of this thread, that is to say, lets not get drawn into unfettered opinion but focus only on the clues given.

Starting with the most recent discovery first. ASTATOS. Rob said in his earlier message that this means UNSTABLE. https://kryptos.groups.io/g/main/message/23883

Next is my own writing (https://kryptos.groups.io/g/main/message/17432) about the misspellings and their counterparts spelling the latin word LAQUEO meaning a trap. Actually, in my original writing on this, I missed the obvious Latin meaning; a trap. Seemingly, I fell into this.

Take these two words together and place them on a map; what do you have?

ASTATOS - This part of the cipher is unstable, don't trust it

LAQUEO - these letters are a trap, don't trust them.

What does that leave us.

PALIMPSEST - In its purest form, I believe this means "I am going to re-use part of the cipher"

ABSCISSA - This may have two meanings. 1. "I have given you half of the coordinates, now find the ordinate", OR it may mean "I have given you half of the ciphertext, go find the other half"

Lets also not forget the reflecting pool and its true purpose, to reflect things.

Now lets look at the ciphertext.

Passage 1. Without delving into the real of hypothetical, I believe this is providing the location in passages 2 and 3 for passage 4. The keyword was PALIMPSEST (We're going to reuse something)
Passage 2. the earths geomagnetic field. Offset by 11 degrees from the perpendicular and periodically changes direction. In ciphertext terms, this might mean a Caesar shift and a periodic flip of direction.
Passage 3. Remove the rubble and insert something.

There will be an order to this; I think I have most of it figured out but I've yet to put it into practice, partly because I'm having trouble mirroring what I think is the relevant ciphertext in a manner that makes visual sense.

I think Mr Sandborn drew us a map and we've all been so caught up in the "Here be dragons" that we've ignored the true facts.

Anything that came after this cipher is either misdirection or irrelevant.

F L R V Q Q P R N G K S S
E A S T N O R T H  E A S T

The first cipher F = E, the first cipher G = E.
The first cipher R = S, the second cipher R = T
The first cipher S = S, the second cipher S = T

Regarding this long-standing question "Is K4 97 or 98 characters?", I think the ancient riddle of the "17 Cows" may possibly be relevant:
In this ancient riddle, an old farmer bequeaths his 17 cows to his 3 sons, stipulating that the eldest son is to receive 1/2 of his cows, the middle son 1/3 of the cows, and the youngest son 1/9 of the cows.
The sons did not want to kill the cows to make fractional parts of them, so they did not know how to implement the farmer's wishes.
A neighbor solved the problem by giving them 1 more cow, making 18 cows. Now the eldest son got 1/2 = 9 cows, the middle son got 1/3 = 6 cows, and the youngest son got 1/9 = 2 cows. That adds up to 17 cows. Then the neighbor got his extra cow back.
The point is, the 97 letters of the K4 message may be like the 17 cows (both prime numbers, not divisible by smaller numbers). The "?" character at the beginning of K4 (included in Sanborn's EASTNORTHEAST clue sent to people in 2020) could be like the neighbor's extra cow: It can be added to the K4 message for the purpose of enabling encryption and decryption methods requiring divisibility by 2, 7, 14, and/or 49. Then once these methods have been performed, the extra "?" character can be disregarded again in the final resulting ciphertext or plaintext, just as the extra cow was returned to the neighbor after the cows were divided among the farmer's sons.

The tomb of King Tut was entered multiple times and they were apparently in a rush and didn't take the expensive items, but they had enough time to fill the hole back in after they left.  Howard Carter the archeologist also entered the tomb prior to the media and public knowing about it.  His job as a young child was to copy all of the hieroglyphs from tombs in Egypt and he was quite the artist.  I suspect during the multiple years after the tomb was found to when they entered the burial chamber, King Tut was placed, his treasures put into place and the walls painted by him.  Data shows it was painted in a rush, and common sense will tell you it wasn't done 3500 years ago because the pigments were still fresh and all of a sudden they are deteriorating.   The four sarcophagus (like Russian dolls) were verified to have come from other places and they've recently had to put him and his sarcophagus in a glass enclosure because of the humidity was causing wood rot.

At this point I am so jaded with archeology.  Everything I read is such child stories.  The lids on the dead sea scrolls kept the moisture out.  The famous Lascaux cave pigments were like they were painted yesterday when they were found (humid caves - almost all caves are humid!) rapidly deteriorated so they shut it down and put a replica site next to it.  The notebook of Jean-Francoid Champolion is so laughable I have a picture of it hanging on my wall, yet his work with the rosetta stone cracked the hieroglyphic code for all of us to hear tall tales of Egypt.   While we are on the subject of Egypt artifacts, a tiny fragment of papyrus found in Egypt dating from around 250 ac tells a much longer lengthy story of the Greek hero Odysessues' adventurous voyage home to Ithaca, while its fairly sure Homer never existed.   Turning up at an antique market, 2000+ year old I Ching bamboo strips (bamboo! 2000 year old bamboo!) are frequent studies of intelligent Ivy league students.

For the FLRVQQPRNGKSS to EASTNORTHEAST pairs, the average distance between each pair of corresponding letters (i.e. F to E, L to A, R to S, etc) is about 3.3. I'm here using a standard ABCDEFGHIJKL... alphabet.

Hi Erik -- did you happen to do the same calculation using the KRYPTOSABCD... mixed alphabet? The differences between the mean/sigma of the first crib versus the second may not be as statistically significant in that case, which would weaken the conclusion that the methods were different between the two cribs.

I might as well do the calculation here:

FLRVQQPRNGKSS --> EASTNORTHEAST  Shifts: -1, -10, +5, +8, -1, +11, -2, +3, -5, -2, +7, 0, -2
Mean: +0.85, StDev: 5.76

Mean: -2.45, StDev: 7.98

So the mean difference is smaller:  3.30 vs. your 4.97 result for the regular alphabet. (The standard deviations are also noticeably higher using the KRYPTOS mixed alphabet.)

In any case, I don't think we can draw any conclusions from this computation about whether the method has changed from crib to crib. For a Quagmire III encryption, for instance, the result is very much dependent on the phasing of the keyword with the plaintext.  --Rob

I wouldn't be surprised if K4 doesn't use transposition at all, or in the event that Jim ~did~ employ transposition, it was the FIRST thing he did during encryption. At least in that case, if you correctly figured out the substitution and/or masking step, the intermediate ciphertext would have recognizable English letter frequencies like K3, and all that would remain is descrambling (which would be made much easier by the EASTNORTHEAST and BERLINCLOCK cribs).

If instead transposition was the final encryption step (or worse, an intermediate one) then I wouldn't consider it a fair "paper and pencil" cipher because it would mean the first stage of decryption would have to be performed blind.  --Rob
