I do believe Scheidt provided him with a plan with a very clever, novel, and difficult, but fair, encryption method. For example, some novel "masking step" based on a clever use of some features of the Kryptos sculpture text, followed by a classical encryption method. That is already extremely difficult to crack with fewer than 100 letters of text, but perhaps it can be solved. The difficult question is whether, and how much, Sanborn added extra layers of encryption on his own, perhaps overestimating the possible powers of cryptanalysis and cryptanalysts. Adding a third step on top of a novel masking step and a classical encryption method could be virtually impossible to solve. Adding a fourth step (or more) could make it completely impossible to solve.

As an amateur, I continue to learn what it is that's going on in the group's attempts to break Kryptos' clues.

Are we figuring out the order of two (or three, or N) conversion steps Sanborn chose long ago, trying to guess which ones and in which order, and simultaneously running through and exhausting all their permutations—in multiple dimensions, I might add—until one of them spits out something that appears to be something that's somehow, nearly, “English-looking?”

If my words-to-graphic efforts are productive here, then maybe it'll help someone toss together the Excel spreadsheets or the python programming to do just that. I'm sure in the history of cryptography, it's also, already, been done. I'm pretty late to the game. (-;

Good morning, friends.

Recently, I was playing around with K4 and discovered a possible new insight. It didn’t make sense to me at first, but as I have thought about it more it is growing on me as a real possibility.

If one assumes Vigenere substitution with a long, mixed-text key as the cipher method in play in K4, then there is a possible partial repeat in the key - the first twenty characters and the last twenty characters have a barely perceptible repitition at positions 9 and 11:

OBKRU OXOGH ULBSO LIFBB
KZXTJ CDIGK UHUAU EKCAR

I don’t know if it is clear in all fonts, but the pairing is GHU / GKU.

As one example - not well tested on my end - this might come from enciphering “SPI” and “SIO” with the same key (in this case, a key of “AES” which is consistent with a key made up of scrambled English text).

If true, what are the implications?
* The overall key is 77 letters
* There is a 57 letter “desert” between the repeated-key segments which cannot be solved directly. The key does not repeat in this section, so it is effectively a one-time pad until and unless some method can be discerned to recreate the key.
* Helpfully, we already know 24 letters in this desert.

Why am I warming to this as a possible productive insight?
* 57 and 77 are familiar numbers already. Both appear in the plaintext of K3, and 57 is also the letter position of the errant “Q” in K1.
* The 20-57-20 shape of this proposed solution may fit nicely with K1’s plaintext. Subtly shaded ends with an “absence of light” in the middle.
* I continue to strongly feel that K4 is tied to Howard Carter’s journal entry on 28 Oct 1925, the day he first opened Tutankhamun’s coffin. Specifically, the passage “The pins removed…symbolizing Osiris”, which is 154 characters long. Some system of halving or pairing this text might lead to a 77-letter key.

Admittedly, this is a very odd placement for a repeat. One might normally expect to see either a full repeat, or no repeat at all.

I welcome any and all to help try to see what sense can be made of the 20-letter ends of K4.

As a started, and quite possibly wrong (but fun!) - if OBKR = FROM, then KZXT = AMPU.

Hi Dennis. Another thing I've been considering regarding the clues we were given is the location of the clues. The K in CLOCK is 24 characters from the end of the text. The S in the first EAST is 24 characters from the start of the text. Writing the ct forwards and backwards underneath it will lead to "STNORTHEAST" lining up with "KCOLCNILREB". You can argue that there are a couple clues that could be interpreted as having to write the ct backwards first. Basically, I wouldn't be too surprised if "RVQQPRNGKSS" = "KCOLCNILREB".

Observation: This forward/backward comparison fits the pattern for the T's, too.

Like, the "T" in the first EAST lines up with the second "C" in CLOCK.  The ciphertext for the Cs in CLOCK is just shifted by their positional difference:

BERLINCLOCK
NYPVTTMZFPK

Those Cs are three positions apart, and their corresponding ciphertext (M and P) are also three characters apart in the ABCDEFG alphabet. (This is an old/well-known analysis by now)

When we look at the T that corresponds to the C in the reversed overlay, it's four positions away from another T.

RVQQPRNGKSS
STNORTHEAST
KCOLCNILREB
KPFZMTTVPYN

The T's ciphertext (V and R) are also four characters apart in the ABCDEFG alphabet.  So the seems to be a coincidence in the encoding rules for these corresponding forward/backward positions, at least, which is exciting because I've always viewed the two halves as having a different set of rules from one another.

This kind of works for the third T, too...  it's 5 positions away from the second T, but its ciphertext is "S", which is a difference of +1 from the second T's ciphertext ("R").

However, we can get "R" - 5 to equal "S" if we break the alphabet into a 6-character chunk (i.e., a modulo-type operation):

     1 2345
VUTSRQ VUTSRQ VUTSRQ
or
WVUTSR WVUTSR WVUTSR
       12345

Sadly, this doesn't seem to work through the rest of the cipher because one of the two Ts in NYPVTT would need to decode to a "T", but we know that they decode to "IN".

Hi all,

I've gone and surprised myself - was trying another bunch of techniques and found one with legs that seems novel. Doesn't appear in any of the public code books nor the cracking chapters released from the NSA by William Friedman, or I may have missed it....

Not sure, might be fooling myself, hence why I am reaching out. CryptoCrack also has no idea of what to make of it.

Say I wanted to encode "ABCDEFG". For this scheme we'll use A=0, B=1, C=2...

I'll calc the diffs between the current letter and its immediate predecessor, starting at the second letter, in this case "B".

So B-A=1 which is equivalent to the letter "B"
C-B=1 --> "B"
D-C=1 --> "B"
etc

So we would publish the initial PT letter "A" unchanged as it keys the remaining letters and then just add "BBBBB" as the subsequence letter diffs --> CT="ABBBBB"

To recover the PT:
A (stays as is)
A + B/1 --> B
B + B/1 --> C
C + B/1 --> D
etc

It is kind of bigram'ish in usage but doesn't double the length of the CT. It does however reduce the length of the CT by one letter - perhaps the "S" that is Kryptos itself (out of the MIST/"missed") is added as per my padding below...

s: Differential Encoding: Is it a known system?
t:
Mike,

Your method is a form of an autokey cipher with a single-letter "primer" key, S. The other slight twist is that your method effectively reverses the typical standard direction of encryption and decryption using a standard tabula recta. But it is still essentially an autokey cipher.

For example, take your first ciphertext letter B and your "primer" letter S as the first key letter. Using a standard tabula recta, find B in the left-hand column and S on the top row (S in the left column and B on the top row works the same). This row and column cross at "T" in the tabula recta, which is the first plaintext letter (not including the "primer" letter S).

Now take the second ct letter O and the first pt letter T that was just found, and repeat the process: the O and T row and column cross at "H" in the tabula recta, which is the second plaintext letter.

Next, take the third ct letter X and the just found second pt letter H, and perform the process again: the X and H row and column cross at "E" in the tabula recta, the third plaintext letter.

In a standard autokey cipher, the process I have described for decryption would be performed for encryption instead. This is why CryptoCrack may not be able to solve it as an autokey cipher with key "S", without special programming to reverse the encryption and decryption processes.

Andrea, thank you for writing. You may not know it, but I get very few non-negative responses to my notes to the forum. I think the reason for this is that most readers have not developed the method of the puzzle. Ed Scheidt once said you have to first figure out the method, then go after the puzzle. The method is there is no method. Namely, you have to look for clues and find the ways they apply.

Without intending to be disrespectful, I will remind you that I have often cautioned (actually warned) about making assumptions about what is happening in Kryptos. All the obvious "mistakes" found in Kryptos have their own purposes. Three of them have positioning involved, however, but they are unrelated. The DESPARATLY "mistake" will be read SEPARATED LIE or LIES SEPARATED. Shortly, it is talking about the S that lies separated between the double-Ls in K3 CT. Another is the missing dit in the Morse slabs, causing DIGITAL to appear as DIGE TAL. The meaning here is not lost; it is DIGITAL INTERPRETATION. In the 7-column pad of K4 CT one finds near the bottom DIGE and UHR. This is a short way of saying DIGITAL CLOCK in German. Put them together and you have MENGENLEHREUHR, THE BERLIN CLOCK. The remaining one is the UNDERGRUUND "misspelling".
The UNDERGRUUND misspelling had me puzzled the longest. When I read John Wilson's guess as to what it meant, it then occurred to me what the C in PALIMPCEST (in Sanborn's handwritten notes) was doing. I had already determined in previous steps working through Kryptos, that Russian language was now involved. Until that point, I had always thought of the C in PALIMPCEST as being a C, but then the LIGHTbulb went on. I then saw it as it was meant to be seen, as the letter S in cyrillic. There are a couple of connotations to be gathered here.
1. There was discussion early on about deriving the K2 keyword ABSCISSA directly from words in K1 PT. There was a question in some minds about how the C could be derived from "the speed of light", whereas the other letters could be attributed to words or parts of words in the K1 PT. ...ABSENCE OF THE SPEED OF LIGHT... just didn't make sense. My paper the other day filled in the gap, providing the needed LIGHT (CBET in Russian), which was previously ABSENT.

2. Back to PALIMPCEST. There is a suggestion here (actually an implied statement) that it will now be possible to combine cyrillic letters with latin letters in a Kryptos plaintext passage resulting in a modification of what is there, rendering it no longer English, but something else! Notice, this PALIMPCEST thing is not part of Kryptos, but was a clue given by Sanborn in his hand-written notes.

KRYPTO SITE AM EAST / ROOND EAST NORTH EAST / I FORCES / DYNAMO WAVE ROUND GROUP / TE /  BERLIN CLOCK / CHURCH TUNNEL / UK GCHQ CODE (R).

The Church Turing thesis is a famous conjecture about computable functions and it strikes me that in 1990 Turing may not have been as well known as he is now hence the reason why the plain text might need to be explicit.

The other quote I posted before was this one. As far as I can tell, the manuscript he is talking about is the "Mappae Clavicula" (12th century) where some words about alcohol distillation are enciphered with a Caesar cipher with shift 1.

This was solved by Berthelot in 1893. In the 12th century in Europe, there were no polyalphabetic ciphers or complex transpositions.

Scheidt has also contributed to cracking codes in the academic world. He helped break a Middle Age manuscript that illustrated an alcohol distilling process by guiding the translator to what he thought was the methodology that provided the key.

“Not too exciting today, but in the 13th century, how to make alcohol would have been a secret and not shared with the masses,” Scheidt said.

I agree with Elonka -- Jim has waffled a bit on the whole 1-to-1 CT to PT decryption, and doesn't appear to fully appreciate the ramifications of a correct yes/no response to that question. If he decisively said yes -- that it's one-to-one -- then that would rule out a large number of cryptosystems (to include transpositions of the type used in K3). It would also rule out fractionated ciphers like Playfair.

Now, even if in Jim's system the N at position 64 decrypts to B using no other ciphertext letters (and so on for YPVTTMZFPK --> ERLINCLOCK), then transposition could *still* be involved in the system. For instance, if it's one of the Vigenere variants, the KEY could be transposed. And in fact the key could be transposed in such a way that it is non-repeating over the entire 97-character length of K4, foiling polyalphabetic incidence of coincidence tests.  --Rob

A long hiatus has me picking back up where I last left off . . . .

I once spent a great deal of time on the mini Kryptos-like sculpture that Ed """"accidentally"""" left out as his house back in 2019.

That sculpture sure had some oddities.... A keyed Tableau not used for decryption (GIRASOL), a permuted keyword (GRU -> RUG), misspelled words (INTU & WHTHOUT), a letter removed from the ciphertext (T[H]E) and even once re-inserted some un-readable plaintext at the very end (EWJ).

My focus has always been on the last three letters of the plaintext that have yet to be recovered.

The plaintext that was encrypted was either (you'll have to fixed-width font this yourself):

THEKEYETRANSEWJ
UGRUGRUGRUGRUGR
---------------
NNVEKPYZIUTJYCA

or:

THEKEYETRANSPOS
UGRUGRUGRUGRUGR
---------------
NNVEKPYZIUTJJUJ

Let me back up one thought. I feel like the proper ending to this plaintext should be "ETRANSPOS" with the "E" in "TRANSPOSE" being permuted to the front of the word. This is in line with the theme of "GRU" being permuted to "RUG" for the key. I suppose this assumption could be wrong and some other 3 letter fragment is actually what was tucked at the end of this plaintext, but I'm going to run with this assumption again for now.

So, either the last three letters in "ETRANSPOS" were masked in some way to arrive at EWJ, or the encryption was carried out as normal and the "POS" was encrypted with "UGR" (a continuation of the key) and "JUJ" was masked in some way to arrive at YCA. This is a bit of the entire dilemma with K4, which operation would have been carried out first.

Regardless, I've yet to produce a logical method to do either transformation with the non-keyed (ABC) or keyed (GIRASOL) alphabets. I'm re-posting this to perhaps drudge up some interest from the group. My thought is that so much of this practice sculpture looks and feels like Kryptos that perhaps this contains the masking element and Ed left it out on purpose for us to have a working example to discover it.

Jim

This is precisely the garbage you get from a home-brewed cipher system. You're at the mercy of the guy with the pen and paper and whatever his brain is dreaming up.

Now, give that guy some leeway to throw a whimsical transposition your way and you're pretty much sunk. This is the general fear I have for letting Sanborn have any personal say in how the system played out. He seems to really like transposition and has called our attention to how individualistic those systems can be. That's the scary part.

It was very cool to see how this system worked and I'm glad someone made some leaps and figured it out!

Some time ago, I left this message to the group.

https://kryptos.groups.io/g/main/message/21979

I still believe it's the best summary we have to date, from Ed, on why K4 looks like it does and on top of that, acknowledges (potentially) how it was done.

To summarize . . .

It's a multi-stage encryption; there's a masking technique - the impact of some kind of math function on the underlying English language statistics; added to that there's the math of the cryptography (substitution and/or transposition); which leads to our first step not being cryptanalysis of the ciphertext, but instead our job is to recreate, without prior knowledge, the system that was put in place to obfuscate the English language statistics.

That's . . . a lot. It also got me thinking (again), about which order these things would have been applied and how would we know what to look for?

Let's consider some options:

1. Ed gave Jim a simple system for masking the plaintext (substitution) and Jim put it through his washing machine of transposition(s)

In this scenario, there are two ways this can play out. Here's the first. Jim first uses the masking system, then transposes.

You may have to put the ciphertext that is K4 in the correct order to be able to work backwards through the math. What I mean by this is if there is some kind of function you're stepping through, the state of the n-th or n-th+1, etc. step of the masking function may be crucial to arriving back at the original plaintext. Think of a cipher wheel (my favorite example), where you are rotating the wheel some amount after every substitution to create a flattened distribution. This creates a dynamic result with an IC in that 3.8 range. However, if that text is then transposed in some way, the "math of the cryptography" then disperses the order in which you'd need to work back through that math. In it's simplest application each letter will have been moved in the alphabet anywhere from +0 to +25, but is no longer in order (First letter +1, Second letter +2, Third letter +3, and so on).

Consider the math of K3 (modular addition or what some people call skip counting and wrapping back around). The first three letters of the ciphertext (ENDYA) are at positions 251, 165, 79, 330 and 244 of the plaintext. So in my hypothetical example where we have a cipher wheel and we simply increment it one step each time the math is that the E was modified by +/- 17 positions it he alphabet depending which way you turn the cipher wheel, the N was modified by +/- 9 positions, the D +/- 1, the Y +/- 18 and the A +/- 10 positions.

In order to decrypt the cryptogram, we'd have to make this assumption about the transposition (double transposition that yields +192 mod 336 math) remove the masking math (the +/- 17/9/1/18/10) and check for plaintext. You'd also have to consider the cipher wheel could have started in any one of the 26 starting positions.

Now, let's contrast that against the second scenario where Jim does his transposition(s) and then uses Ed's masking system to cover his tracks.

In this scenario each letter of the ciphertext has been modified pseudo-randomly with the same cipher wheel concept I described before. However this time, in the base scenario, it's easier because you just pull off the +/- based on the current position of the ciphertext because it was applied last. What's left is monoalphabetic (IC ~6.8) in nature, but is out of order (just like K3). Now your job is the same as K3 where you need to consider Jim's beautiful mind and what artistic transposition technique he used to get the text in that order.

This becomes more difficult if the math function for using the cipher wheel is more than +1 mod 26. Let's say you increment the wheel +1 each time until you've done that 5 times, but the 6th time you increment it +7 and repeat that process. The options here are pretty much limitless as you can create a pretty complex function with just turning the wheel forward and/or backwards according to any algorithm you wish to create.

I actually favor the "transpose then mask" scenario for creating a fair puzzle, because it better meshes with what Ed stated is the desired outcome for this challenge. That you're unable to begin with the English language statistics, that you're in the posture of recreating without prior knowledge and that you'd need to solve that technique first and then go for the puzzle. In the "mask then transpose" scenario you're actually just guessing, unless that transposition key is given to you.

Now, think about how simple this encryption technique is yet how difficult it is to unwind and remember that there' no classical substitution layered on top! Think if I added that? Zero chance you'd ever solve it.

Jim

Back before he said that "DYAHR" and the out of alignment letters has nothing to do with K4, I would have bet on that railfence having been used in part on K4, but he has seemed to strongly indicate that has nothing to do with anything. It's too bad he won't just confirm what it was if it has nothing to do with K4.

One of the problems I have with the masking in general, is that unless it's
extremely basic, it essentially is a substitution cipher.  And if it takes
plain text with a normal english IC and basically squashes it so it's near
random text, I would argue it's not a simple substitution, but a complex
one (at least in terms of mangling everything).  Which means we now have
substitution on top of transposition, which hardly any clues to either.

I'm ok if it's that, but then why continue to refer to it as a 'mask', and
not some type of cipher?   Ed doesn't say K1 or K2 is masked, he talks
about them being encoded.  And yet in K4 he continues to bring up the idea
of masking.

So to me there are two possibilities:

1) The mask is something simple, but the job is to distort the plain text
such decoding in step 2 would produce something that wouldn't immediately
be recognized as english text.  Something simple like dropping all Es, and
advancing every letter forward by a few spaces would accomplish this. It
would likely have a minimal effect on IC but would obscure the plain text
if and when you stumble upon it.
2) Would be some encoding scheme that would drastically compress the IC.
Depending on what it is, #1 may help obscure the ability to decrypt it
since even if you figured out the puzzle, you may not see anything legible
during decryption.

Possiblity two is

1) The mask is something more complicated that compresses the IC
drastically. To me it's difficult to do without some type of complex
substitution cipher.  It certainly could be this, but then why call it a
mask, and not an encoding or cipher?
2) The actual encoding scheme here could be far simpler, since #1 obscured
the language.  It could even be a transposition without any additional
substitution.

I like the idea of a cipher wheel as well, because it's easy to implement,
and using Jim's gorilla math, could represent a washing machine type of
cipher.

--
Duane

https://kryptos.groups.io/g/main/message/23926

Basically, I alternated shifting the letters of K4 between the Kryptos (K) alphabet and the unmodified ABC alphabet (A). It resulted in a lot of gibberish until the letters UAUEKC in positions 90-94 in the ciphertext. With an alphabet pattern of A-K-A-K-A-K and a - 2 shift, the resulting text is SOS CIA.

Then, I tried transposing the ciphertext by splitting K4 in two sections. The first one used the first 49 letters in a 7 x 7 grid using KRYPTOS as the keyword. The other used the remaining 48 letters in a 6 x 8 grid using SOS CIA as the keyword.

The results look like this:

K R Y P T O S

O F S O T O R

The "OF SOTOR" from the KRYPTOS block and the "HTRY PI" from the SOS CIA block, I believe, refers to the words "history" and "Ptolemy I of Sotor" who was the founder of the Ptolemaic dynasty in Egypt. Also, the name Ptolemy was the first word gleaned from the hieroglyphs on the Rosetta Stone.

Of course, this could all be a coincidence that the letters end up in those spots and I'm just seeing shapes in clouds because the plaintext of K4 is still a mystery.

As far as I can see it, „1-2-3“ could be interpreted in any number of ways. It would be interesting to hear from the people present at the meeting whether there was more context to the answer, like „it was clear that he was referring to K1-K2-K3, so it’s settled once and for all that the raised letters might have anything to do with K4“, or „obviously, he was referring to the Billy Wilder movie (which takes place in Berlin)“, or (and that’s my personal guess) „it was totally unclear what he meant by that comment“.

I think the idea of a Vigenere cipher that alternates between using the Kryptos-keyed alphabet (as in K1 and K2) and using the plain alphabetical top row and left column of the tableau is a legitimate and logical idea worth considering and pursuing. But I think that the appearance of SOS CIA, OF SOTOR, and HTRY PI are probably just a coincidence.

"You have been put into the posture of re-creating without having prior knowledge" and "he other intent was well is there a way to make the challenge so that the first step is not that and now that gets to be hard, and that's what you all are facing"

I mean, if and when this is solved, I'll likely look back and this will seem obvious.  But now, I struggle to understand how anybody can solve a problem of this nature without having any idea of what they are solving.  Even with Jim and Ed hand-holding  most people for several decades, people aren't any closer to solving K4.  Imagine sitting down in front of Kryptos in the late 90s with a pen and paper.  How would anyone have any idea how to approach K4 without Ed even hinting it had some masking step?   To be a fair challenge, I would argue there *has to be* something on the sculpture itself that leads someone towards a solution, but with K4, I don't feel like we have anything left.   It sounds like Ed doesn't seem to believe using a statistical/mathematical approach will work on K4, which means the way forward has to be some other way.  Once again, I argue it has to be something logical that stems from the sculpture itself. If it's just guessing, I don't think it's a fair challenge.

"And finally, back to my commentary. If there are no clues on the sculpture as to what Ed gave Jim for obfuscating the ciphertext/plaintext it has to be something that's mechanically simple and within the realm of someone guessing at."

But then, how do you know you've removed the mask?  I don't think using IC works, nor do I think asking someone sitting in front of kryptos to calculate an IC for every attempt at solving K4 would be realistic.  It's laborious enough with a computer.  I have produced enough high ICs in my day with random programs I've written to know that even if the IC is high, you still don't know if you've made progress.

So if it's fair, and IC isn't in play (people can disagree with me on this, but I don't believe that's a realistic way forward), then how do you know you've made progress?  To me, it would mean there is some obvious indicator that the mask has been removed. It may something as simple as OBKR literally turning into the word MASK when it's removed - I obviously don't think that is what it is, but that would be something along the lines of what I'm thinking.  Then lets say the real puzzle is a transposition cipher, harder than K3, those MASK characters might be redistributed all over the place, and potentially could be nulls.  I'm just saying, I think for this to be fair, there have to be breadcrumbs to follow at some point in the process.  Guessing isn't a fair challenge, and that's what I feel we are left with.

My interpretation of their comment, quoted by Jim above, is that the raised position of the letters Y-A-R is not relevant to the encryption/decryption of K4, but that they are relevant, as "1-2-3", to the later stage puzzle "K5" that can only be solved after K4 is solved.

In the past, I have thought of one possible meaning of this: If DYAHR is the keyword of a 5x5 Polybius square in some step of the K4 encryption/decryption process, then the letters D, Y, A, H, R would be the top row of this square, each at the top of a column. Then in some step of the later "K5" puzzle, "Y-A-R" = "1-2-3" could refer to a rearrangement of those columns of this Polybius square, such that the resulting order is then Y, A, R, D, H. It seems to me that such a process may possibly also be related to the clue "ID BY ROWS" at the end of K2. But of course there are many possible "rows" that this clue could be referring to.

Of course my idea is pure speculation at this stage. It is just an example of one possible meaning of the "1-2-3" comment in reference to the raised letters Y-A-R.

s: The role of K1 and other recent thoughts
t:
Hi all,

I haven't had time to look at Kryptos in quite awhile, but I've recently thought of a few ideas:

1. Perhaps K1 needs to be overlaid onto other sections of the code (i.e., K2, K3, and/or K4) before any other cryptographic methods can be used. Note how in the New York Times' images of Sanborn's original work, he has clearly cut K1 from K2. That made me think: Why would he do so? One plausible response is that he needed to be able to move K1 to put it on top of the other sections of code, perhaps rotating it ninety degrees or something before doing so. This would be consistent with ABSCISSA, which would have been a clue to cut off K1. This also would have been consistent with creating layers of writing alluded to with PALIMPSEST. Sanborn was an artist, so such a method would seem like something that he would do, rather than a highly technical cryptographic approach. I think that Sanborn once said in an interview that he was surprised that nobody had reverse engineered what he had done once images of his documents were released, so there should be important clues in there. Of course, there is the small matter of how K1 could interact with the other sections of code once layered, and I do not know the answer to that. Perhaps close attention to some of the strange symbols on Sanborn's original documents could provide some insight into that matter.

2. The Berlin Clock is undoubtedly important, but perhaps it has been a bit of a red herring. Clues from one section should support the solution of subsequent sections, but the Berlin Clock clue is from K4 itself. Maybe the clock is therefore more relevant to what has to be done after K4.

3. I don't get time to read many emails that I receive from this group, but when I do, I sometimes see what appear to be very complex mathematical methods suggested. I do not think that is what Sanborn would have done. Again, as an artist, I suspect that he layered the sections of code, causing them to interact in some way. He then probably applied one of the cryptographic methods that had been suggested to him to the resultant palimpsest. At that point, the method would not necessarily have to be something overly complex, nor would I think that he would gravitate towards a highly technical system.

I apologize if I'm repeating points that have been previously made--like I said before, I have not been able to keep up with the conversations in here. Let me know what you think of the above points!

t:
"2. The Berlin Clock is undoubtedly important, but perhaps it has been a bit of a red herring. Clues from one section should support the solution of subsequent sections, but the Berlin Clock clue is from K4 itself. Maybe the clock is therefore more relevant to what has to be done after K4."

Whenever I see the 'Berlin Clock' mentioned, it's almost always in reference to 'Mengenlehreuhr', the Berlin Set Theory clock.  To me, this is the least likely clock for Jim to be interested in, since he's gone on record repeatedly and said that math isn't his thing.  So why would a clock built around set theory excite him?  I personally just don't see it.

What is far my likely in my mind, is the 'Urania World Clock', the World Time Clock in Alexanderplatz square.  Jim has mentioned that a big event before Kryptos was unveiled was the fall of the Berlin wall.  Not many people remember how significant it was, be the re-uniting of East and West Germany and the later collapse of the Soviet Union were some of the important geo-political events in the last 100 years.

The World Time Clock and Alexanderplatz square were important meeting places for several of the marches that preceded the collapse of the Berlin wall.   The 'Alexanderplatz demonstration' on the 4th of November, 1989 was one of the largest demonstrations in German history.  Five days later, the Berlin wall fell.

So it wouldn't surprise me in the least, and I'm willing to put a nice beer on the line as a wager, that when K4 is finally revealed, it's a reference to a meeting near the Berlin Clock sometime around this date, right before the Berlin Wall fell.  It's in a similar vein to K3, where Sanborn talks about the moment immediately before opening Tut's tomb.  But this time it's a reference to a moment right before the Berlin Wall fell, and East and West Germany were finally reunited.    East-Northeast, one of the cribs he's released, could be a reference to the compass rose under the World Clock, and a hypothetical meeting place prior to a march.

One of the expressions that came out of this event was 'We are one people'...  It wouldn't surprise me at all if K4 finishes on that, since it was the promise of that moment and what it meant for the future.

Just my 0.02 about the Berlin Wall.  But I don't think it's the set theory clock at all - that doesn't jive with Jim as an artist or Kryptos as a statement.

I mean, if someone said to look at the great pyramid in Egypt, and without knowing how they did it, devise a method to do it. Many people could. But none of us would know it’s “the” method. Hi All,

I made a post a couple of months ago about a K4 solve that reads:

KRYPTO SITE AM EAST / ROUND EAST NORTH EAST / I-FORCES / DYNAMO WAVE ROUND GROUP / TE / BERLIN CLOCK / CHURCH TUNNEL UK / GCHQ CODE (R) where the final R is unmapped.

I've tried to convey the framework that generates this result a number of times both here and on the Facebook Group, but I thought it might be worth stepping back to the very beginning of the process to examine the most important result.  The whole framework is predicated on the existence of 6 (3x32) matrices that exist in the cipher text.  Put the cipher text on a 32x28 grid and use a pencil to shade all instances or the letters RE as they occur together both horizontally and vertically.  You'll immediately find two instances where there is a repeating group of RE with an F and V offset by one character to the left above and below the letters RE (this initial observation was originally pointed out to me by James Churchill).  If you left shift row 1 by 13 characters you'll create the exact same pattern in rows 1-3.
If you examine the entire cipher text you'll only find these 3 instances for where RE is in the horizontal plane.
If you repeat the process for the RE groupings that are in the vertical plane then you'll find there are only 3 in which F and V occur with a separation of 6 characters either above or below the rows with the letters RE.  Again, exhaustive examination shows that there are only 3 of these vertical markers.
If you now examine the plain text for rows 12-14 and left shift row 14 so that the word TWO is aligned under the start of the words SIX and SEVEN then you will have extracted what I believe is Jim's 'original matrix'.  There is a cross of 5 letters formed composed of the letters that make up the word THREE and if you look further out you'll see the word EIGHT.  This is important as the number of distinct row combinations of a 3x32 matrix is 32768.  If you now right shift the middle row by 7 letters then you'll find that the presence of these numbers in the 3x32 matrix has remained invariant.  There is still a 5 letter cross of the letters making up the word THREE and the word SEVEN has shifted to the position where the previous one was sited prior to the row shift.
Jim's decoding charts show 6 or 7 matrices that are of the order 3x31, so maybe this was a big hint!!!  I've derived some intellectually satisfying results by pursuing the path that these observations lead down and that has eventually culminated in the full 97 letter string given above.  You may disagree with the rest of the solution steps, but there is definitely something anomalous going on with 3x32 matrices, so if this isn't already on your radar, then I hope it gives you a nudge in a novel direction.

All the best,
Matt

Once again, you’re doing a wonderful job stating exactly what Ed described as the challenge. You no longer have that thread to pull on, to be able to see the plaintext. That’s frustrating and also the stated challenge.

You’re also doing a great job stating my frustration from 4 years ago. If there’s nothing on the sculpture to tell you anything about either 1) how to unmask it 2) that you’ve done that correctly; then why would anyone want to participate?

I’m all for trying random stuff on an unknown, one-off system if the clues are there to guide you. Even if they are obtuse or metaphorical. But if they don’t exist, that’s assinine.

That being said, I’m still going to do some experimenting with a couple ideas to mask the ciphertext after transposing it and see how many false positives I get with IC based confirmations.

This is similar to a method I've been toying with recently. Perhaps the first panel (in this case, the end of K2) is used as a lookup table for the Vigenère tableau in the following manner:

1. Take a letter from K4 and find its matching letter from the end of K2, i.e. the letter it would overlap if the two texts were layered over each other. (For example, let's use the last letters, R and G respectively.)
2. Do the same for the K2 letter and the Vigenère tableau. (In this case, the letter I.)
3. In the column the Vigenère letter belongs to (column D), find the K2 letter.
4. Using the plain alphabetical row at top, find the K4 letter. Look in the row the K2 letter belongs to (row K) and find whatever letter is in this position (which also happens to be R). This is the unmasked ciphertext letter.

I find this method satisfying since it incorporates many of the clues we have been given (layer two, abscissa, palimpsest, the extended Vigenère tableau with an unused plain alphabetical row). Of course, there's a few factors that might complicate things:

1. Do we keep the text in rows of 31 or do we put it into rows of 30 to match the row markings?
2. On the actual statue, the tableau and ciphertext actually read backwards relative to each other. Should this also be taken into account?

Has anyone here ever suggested something similar?

I certainly don't want to dissuade anyone from trying or moving the needle
forward.  I'm still here, despite being frustrated.

But let's say you're going to do an unmasking attempt - what IC is your
threshold for thinking you've succeeded?  If you take a perfectly random
distribution and colour it with a non-random (i.e. organized one), you're
going to raise the IC (because you've made something unorganized slightly
more organized).  So pretty much anything you do to K4 will raise its IC.

As a reminder, the IOC for the first two vigneres that were cracked are:

K1 - 0.03789
K2 - 0.04547

So conceivably anything in that range can be a Vingnere-like cipher.

K4's IC is, as you pointed out before,  0.03608. So not that much different
than K1 (of course, K1 is probably a bit low due to lack of characters in
general, but let's ignore that).

Let's say I wake up one day and have a brilliant idea about how to unmask
it - I read LAYERTWO and think we are meant to put K4 on top of K2, i.e.
align the two Kryptos left-hand panels, and use the bottom text of K2 as
the demasking key for K4.

So I grab this text from the bottom of K2 (basically the equivalent text of
K4 if we were to overlay them):

EDFQELZZVRRGKFFVOEEXBDMVPNFQXEZLGREDNQFMPNZGLFLPMRJQYALMGNUVPDXVKPDQUMEBEDMHDAFMJGZNUPLGEWJLLAETG

and plug it into a Vignere decoder as the key using a Kryptos alphabet
and the text of K4 as the cipher text:
OBKRUOXOGHULBSOLIFBBWFLRVQQPRNGKSSOTWTQSJQSSEKZZWATJKLUDIAWINFBNYPVTTMZFPKWGDKZXTJCDIGKUHUAUEKCAR

And I end up with this:
QXHADHZSLGQTBQNUDRWDIYZONRBCPBHCNOQQTDBHGRANQHBVOSHVXDTMYHYNJYDWYKFDCKHTMJOZKNGSHPDLQDCBPXLTQNXPH

That has an IOC of 0.04553.  It's as "Vignere" as K2 is according to
the IOC, and well beyond according to K1s IOC.  Should I proceed
assuming I've removed the mask?  I argue not.

All I've really done is take a mostly random distribution and
colour/modify it using an organized one.  I've produced a lot of false
positives like this with various attempts I've made.

Unless we're looking at pure english after de-masking (i.e. pure
transposition), which has an IOC of close to 0.0667, then I don't
believe IC will be useful in determining if you're making progress,
sadly.

--
Duane

Hi Duane/All,

Duane asked: "But let's say you're going to do an unmasking attempt - what IC is your threshold for thinking you've succeeded?  If you take a perfectly random distribution and colour it with a non-random (i.e. organized one), you're going to raise the IC (because you've made something unorganized slightly more organized).  So pretty much anything you do to K4 will raise its IC."

You won't always raise the IoC, even if the coloring is highly organized. Take the simplest case of the coloring being to just add a string of 97 E's atop K4 (i.e. shift every letter by 5). The IoC won't change. But yes, most types of masking steps when applied to K4 are going to increase its IoC ... but that's largely because K4's IoC is actually lower than that of random text (0.03847). So the most likely outcome of any operation applied to K4 is that it's going to bring it closer to random text.

   That's true, but we have a bit more to work with than that. We can compute the polyalphabetic IC of both K1 and K2, and see immediately that they are likely polyalphabetic substitution:

At period 5, K1 has an IoC of 0.079; at period 10 it's 0.0914. (Now, the statistical significance of high polyalphabetic IoC's is not that great when you have so few samples in each alphabet (only 6-7 in the case of K1 with its 10-letter keyword).

The statistical significance of the poly IoC of K2 is far greater since we have much more ciphertext to work with:

At period 8, the IoC is 0.0680, which is robust since we have 46-47 letters in each alphabet. The incorrect periods from 2-10 yield IoC's of less than 0.05, with the exception of period 4 (harmonic of 8) at 0.0553.

     Correct. I'd be unimpressed by any demasking result that yields an IoC of less than 6%. For instance, at period 5, the IoC of your string is 0.0598. This is problematic with a short cipher like K4 since there are plenty of perfectly normal English sentences that have anomalously low IoC's of under 5.5%. So if Jim's K4 plaintext is one of them, IoC alone may steer us away from the correct demasking step. Side note: the IoC of the 24 letters of plaintext we DO have is only 0.0471! In other words, I unfortunately agree with Duane's ending statement:

 --Rob

Yeah, I’m looking for plaintext. I’m not looking for another layer of substitution. If that’s what he did, I’ll pass. There’s no chance you’re guessing the masking technique and then guessing at another substitution encryption after that. That’s some bonkers stuff.

My working hypothesis will be that transposition happened and those tracks were covered with the masking technique.

I’m in the process of writing some code, but I’ll report back what I’m looking at when I’m done.

Like Duane, not here to dissuade any ideas, I’m just doing a proof of concept on some ideas of my own.

I'm glad that Adam Gallina's comment referred back to my solution of the last 3 letters of Pre-K. (See my message about that in 2021 at this link: https://kryptos.groups.io/g/main/message/22534 )

In short:

P encrypts to Y on the B key row of the GIRASOL tableau.
O encrypts to C on the A key row of the GIRASOL tableau.
S encrypts to A on the Z key row of the GIRASOL tableau.

Here is the relevant portion of the GIRASOL-keyed Vigenere tableau with the critical letters highlighted by asterisks:

GIRA*S**O*LBCDEFHJKMN*P*QTUVWXYZ
IRASOLBCDEFHJKMNPQTUVWXYZG
RASOLBCDEFHJKMNPQTUVWXYZGI
*A*SOLB*C*DEFHJKMNPQTUVWXYZGIR
SOLBCDEFHJKMNPQTUVWXYZGIRA
OLBCDEFHJKMNPQTUVWXYZGIRAS
LBCDEFHJKMNPQTUVWXYZGIRASO
*B*CDEFHJKMNPQTUVWX*Y*ZGIRASOL
...
*Z*GIR*A*SOLBCDEFHJKMNPQTUVWXY

Thus, the "key phrase" is simply the backward alphabet, ending at ...BA and then wrapping around to start at Z again.

I played with some methods like that a few years ago, back when the YAR raised letters were still in play. I realized that while the K4 frequency distribution has certainly been flattened, it’s not flat. I also realized that a lot of the most frequently used letters in English, for example E, T, A, O, all have lower frequency letters next to them in at least one spot. So if you took an English text, and simply wobbled it forward and back (E becomes D or F, etc), you would pretty effectively smear the distribution. I think I had tried simple things like DOWN UP UP DOWN UP and the results were inline with the resulting distribution in terms of flatness.  You could do this using both alphabets on the tableau too, Kryptos and regular. Ie for some positions you could find the alphabet in the regular text, and wobble it in a direction. You could also find the letter in the Kryptos alphabet and wobble it on that one. Given that there are a higher frequency of K, S, R and O I think, it may be possible that alphabet does come in play.

But let us know what you find.

s: standard orders of letters in Morse Code?
t:
We know that Morse Code is relevant to Kryptos, and Morse Code is a good candidate for the "different language base" that Ed Scheidt says he used in the masking step: "a language that was really only used in the world for about 100 years" and "when it was used as the mask it was current, in 2020 secret". (Indeed, the usage of Morse Code in official communications globally has steadily been discontinued between 1990 and today.)

But it is very difficult to design workable ciphers with Morse Code, because more frequent English plaintext letters are represented by 1, 2, or 3 dots/dashes, while less frequent English plaintext letters are represented by 4 dots/dashes. Also, spacing between each letter is essential to avoid ambiguity in Morse Code. These features make it difficult to use Morse Code dots and dashes as the basis of a cipher that could have been the masking step.

One idea for a cipher or masking step based on Morse Code that could be workable would be to use an order of the alphabet based on Morse Code. However, I cannot find one official standard for such an order. Instead, I find a variety of popular orders for learning groups of letters in Morse Code. The Radio Society of Great Britain published a chart with a "Code Order" of letters in Morse Code as follows:

EISHAUVWJRLFP  TMONGZQDBKCYX  (The first set begin with a dot, the second set begin with a dash)

Some people recall learning the simplest group of Morse Code letters as "ETIMSOH" or "EISH TMO". (These letters consist of only dots or only dashes.) However, after this group, I find a broad variety of orders of learning the rest of the letters. Some popular examples include:

E I S H - T M O - A N W G - D U V J B - R K L F - P X Z C Y Q

E T I M S O H - A W U J V F - C G K Q F Z - R Y L B X D N

EISH  TMO  AN  DU  WG  BV  PX ...

EISH  TMO  AWJ  NDB ...

It would be "fair game" for the K4 masking step to use some such order of the alphabet related to Morse Code. For example, it could be the basis of a Vigenere or other substitution cipher. But is there any way for us to guess which particular Morse-related order of letters that Scheidt and Sanborn may have chosen?

I do not know if the following anomaly in the K4 ciphertext letter distribution has been observed or examined before, but I think it's worth noting:

Due to the relatively high frequency of the letters K, S, T, U, O, W in the K4 ciphertext, there are 49 letters in the K4 ct whose Morse Code form has an odd number (1 or 3) of dots/dashes, vs. 48 letters in the K4 ct whose Morse Code form has an even number (2 or 4) of dots/dashes.

This is unexpected, because on average truly random text is expected to have only about 38.5% of letters with an odd number of dots/dashes in Morse Code (10 out of 26 letters). So we would expect only 37 such letters in the K4 ct, vs. an expected 60 letters with an even number of dots/dashes.

English plaintext, on the other hand, typically has about 53.5% of letters with an odd number of dots/dashes in Morse Code, due to the high frequency of E, T, O, S, R (and D). (The other such letters are U, W, G, K.) In 97 letters of English plaintext, we would expect 52 such letters, vs. 45 letters with an even number of dots/dashes.

Thus, in this particular respect related to Morse Code, the K4 ciphertext (50.5% "odd" Morse letters) is actually much more similar to English plaintext (53.5% "odd" Morse letters) than it is to random text (38.5% "odd" Morse letters).

I do not wish to bombard or overwhelm the group with excessively long or numerous posts about my Morse Code cipher ideas, but I would just like to provide a brief summary of my idea here, which I expound on at greater length and in more detail in my recent post in the Techniques sub-group for readers who may be interested to take a look at it.

I created an altered form of Morse Code where every letter has 3 or 4 dots/dashes (much easier to mask letter frequencies in a cipher based on it). Most letters are the same as in Morse Code, but a logical set of changes is applied to certain letters:

E = ... (= EEE)
T = --- (= TTT)
A = .-.- (= AA / ä)
M = ---- (= MM)
N = -.-. (= NN)
I/H = .... (= II, and cf. "DECHPHER WHTHOUT" in the pre-Kryptos mini-sculpture message)
K/C = -.- (shared as in the Knock Code)
O = ---. (= ö)
S = ..._ (opposite signs of O)
V = ..-- (= ü)

Now it is possible to design a workable masking cipher, with the only restriction being the necessity to preserve the total number of letters with 3 dots/dashes and with 4 dots/dashes in the plaintext and in the resulting ciphertext. This way, pt and ct have the same number of letters. The preservation of a slightly elevated combined frequency of the group of 3-dot/dash letters ("TRUCK WEDG") is a slight weakness of the cipher, but it would be very hard to detect in a 100-letter message without knowing how the cipher works. My sample encryption of K1 produced a masked text with an IC of 3.89, virtually identical to random text.

On this basis, one may perform substitution and transposition steps on the string of dots and dashes in this altered Morse Code, and one may transpose the sequence of letter lengths (3's and 4's) as desired.

For the record, the K4 ct does have the elevated combined frequency of the group of 3-dot/dash letters TRUCK WEDG that would be the only readily apparent indication of the use of this masking cipher.

I've spent a pile of time lately thinking about masking English language statistics and how to do so in a way that there's still a fair challenge that remains.

As we all know, there are infinite things Ed Scheidt could have done to mask the plaintext. None of what I'm going to describe is being purported to be "how it was done". I'm solely musing on the solution space that's left for a would-be codebreaker to check. What's feasible? What can be left for you to find to create the problem that Ed said he intended to give us.

As a refresher, Ed said he wanted to take away frequency counting and our "tools" as the first step to make this problem more difficult. That we're in the posture of re-creating without prior knowledge.

I've been stating that I believe it's feasible that Jim Sanborn solely applied a transposition(s) and then used Ed's masking technique to cover it's tracks. For instance, we could use K3 as an example.

JIBHCFIVKUFNKZAMMRYJUSAESZYBYKPHKIOSVYKTBWVZOQDRGF
UTNXHFLMEHEAESNFMSCOVPPTEWLTRMBCQHDHBXPSFQLXPFVGLR
OBHCCTIXWVZGBHJDPYTGKEFGCFSHCBNIRTDPCHZZBAROVIUMDP
WQWTWPLEXOQVIVUHZBNGKRHRMQUJAWGFSTIDQGOHNZEHYXLWPY
HZUWDJNTCTANWMRXRHFNFJXYAXCMIAQJPAYSRMDIJCDSSQTCIR
TUZQVFAMANSXFVAWSPOWBYTEWOJRMOMJLTJOZPXLTYSSJAEDUY
BSCVKIIAQJPAYJYDLEHMUTKVMDKQGHARMUQQ

So there we go, I've masked the K3 plaintext, and now you have to find it. I'm not asking you to find it, but using it as an illustrative example.

In order to find the plaintext, you'll need to make some assumptions. How did I do it? Well, as you know, I'm fascinated by cipher wheels. So I used that. Just an inner and outer alphabet and I used an agitation cycle.

Is there something left over that tells you what I did? Probably not. But here's what's important - the potential solution space to check.

As I said, there are two alphabets. They probably can't be randomized because that creates some crazy 26! to the n-th power thing that no one will ever solve. So maybe they are given to us. Maybe it's just ABC...XYZ or maybe it's KRYPTOSABC...WXZ. Maybe it's one of each. Those are the types of things we can handle checking for. Maybe one of them is backwards, maybe the both are. No bother, totally fine, we can handle all those small combinations. They don't add a great deal of difficulty to the problem space.

So what does? Well, how about where you start the two wheels? Nope, those just create monoalphabetic substitutions of one another. An IoC check will find these to be the same.

How about the length of the pattern? Let's say I just click the wheel ahead by a single number each time. Wonderful. Just don't pick a factor of 26 (13 or 2) and we're all good. That will sufficiently create enough alphabets to mask the plaintext. Now, that leaves only 24 permutations to check. Probably too easy. What if I can shift forward or backward on the wheel? Well, that doesn't matter in the pick one number scenario as any number of clicks forward can also be represented by the complimentary number backward (6 forward is the same as 20 backward, etc).

So how about 2 numbers in the pattern? I could click forward by 2 and backward by 3 and carry that on for the entirety of the plaintext and I will have sufficiently masked it. But again, how difficult is the problem? If I search through the entire solution space will I get any false positives? Depends how far I open the net. When I set the bar at .06 for the Index of Coincidence - I don't get many and the ones I do get I can quickly throw out with frequency ananlysis. And at length 336, I probably shouldn't. That should be damn near 0.067. I can find the unmasked solution in 5k to 10k trial decryptions.

So let's bump it up to 3 numbers in the pattern. I'm not entirely sure of the full math of the solution space, but it's somewhere in the neighborhood of 48^3 / 2. So I go and check 50k random patterns and I find the solution with 2 false positives that I can throw away with frequency analysis.

How about 4? 48^4 / 2? Okay, so I'll check a million trial decryptions and I find the solution along with a couple of false positives that I can again throw out due to frequency analysis.

If I take the problem much above this, it gets to the point where I don't consider it feasible. I'm going to have to check a couple hundred million. That's getting to be a bridge too far for me, though I can easily find the solution with my computer.

The takeaway here is this... What's left over, even if I transpose first, is still findable/recognizable so long as my base assumptions are correct. I ran simulations where I used the wrong alphabets. There are no false positives. Or if there are, they are about 1 per billion and can quickly be discarded with frequency analysis.

For fun, and to prove a point, I just randomized the first 97 characters of K3.

EUSRTTEPRNAAYHIEBLLIPSOAWTLLSAFCPOEITSMESGOBREEWOSWYTERFTOWHMRDLYROLAEDTEHWEDHMENAOEOSYVEDDWSAARR

From there, I masked it using my cipher wheel.

DINAITUUPHAVKXOJNMXDWILMQSTNSPHKNAPVGRRBYONULNZSTWAXZZMUIZGGXMDAKBEWMEJUFTZVRQOFRPWYMEWCXFMKYZOEL

IoC of 0.0339

I can run trial decryptions and quickly find the plaintext even though it's transposed, with only 3 false positives that are clearly not transposed plaintext.

The moral of my story and the result of my research on this one kind of system is that you can put a ceiling on the difficulty. You can also pick a system that will yield minimal or zero false positives until you hit the correct permutation. This will then leave you where you started with K3. Overall, I'm happy with the research and glad I was able to prove out the concepts of limiting a solution space and creating a fair challenge.

Sanborn has stated several times that he is an “anathemath” – having a self-proclaimed fear of mathematics; that he has no math skills. He also said, when questioned why K4 hasn’t been solved by cryptanalysts yet, that it’s probably because they don’t think like him (an artist). Therefore, it stands to reason that K4 was not designed using math. That’s not to say it can’t be solved mathematically, but approaching it as such may prove to be a very circuitous and ultimately unsuccessful route to the solution.

Jim Melichar recently called my attention back to the idea of ternary encoding of letters: A = 111, B = 112, C = 113, D = 121, etc. Such an encoding is used in the Trifid cipher, which has been mentioned a number of times in relation to Kryptos, since it is typically described as having three "Layers" of 3x3 squares, so the phrase "LAYER TWO" relates naturally to it. Trifid typically uses a keyed alphabet, for example K = 111, R = 112, Y = 113, P = 121, etc.

Jim M. also pointed out in this group, years ago, that the Four-square cipher, with an obvious visual connection to the panels of the Kryptos sculpture, is really a special form of a Bifid cipher, or a CM Bifid (different grids for plaintext input and ciphertext output), encrypting with a simple period of groups of 2 letters at a time.

It's notable to me that Four-square was often included among typical military field ciphers (such as in the US Army Field Manual) while Bifid was not. Perhaps this was due to a desire to avoid the risk of mistakes and confusion with long strings of numbers. One may possibly make a comparison with Sanborn's stated aversion to mathematical methods.

So, just as the Bifid cipher can be re-designed as the Four-square cipher, I have thought of a way to re-design the Trifid cipher in a geometric form that avoids the necessity to use long strings of numbers: an Eight-cube cipher comprising a 2x2x2 3-D array of eight 3x3x3 Trifid cubes.

One can visualize the eight cubes in NW, NE, SW, and SE position, with an Upper cube and a Lower cube in each position. Each cube is 3x3x3 containing the alphabet (either plain or keyed) plus one extra symbol (perhaps "?" for K4).

In this cipher method, one encrypts groups of 4 letters at a time. The plaintext input comes from the NW-Upper, SE-Upper, NE-Lower, and SW-Lower cubes, while the ciphertext output comes from the NE-Upper, SW-Upper, NW-Lower, and SE-Lower cubes. (For comparison, the four Upper cubes work like the Four-square cipher, where pt is in NW and SE position, ct is in NE and SW position.)

If one followed the typical Four-square design, the plaintext cubes would be filled with letters in plain alphabetical order, while each ciphertext cube would have its own keyword and keyed alphabet order.

The rules for encryption would proceed as follows. Take a group of 4 plaintext letters and locate them in the NW-Upper, SE-Upper, NE-Lower, and SW-Lower cubes respectively. Then identify the 4 resulting ciphertext letters in this way:

1st ct letter in NE-Upper cube: Take the same Row as the NW-Upper cube pt letter (as in Four-square), the same Column as the SE-Upper cube pt letter (also as in Four-square), and the same Layer as the NE-Lower cube pt letter.

2nd ct letter in SW-Upper cube: Take the same Row as the SE-Upper cube pt letter (as in Four-square), the same Column as the NW-Upper cube pt letter (also as in Four-square), and the same Layer as the SW-Lower cube pt letter.

3rd ct letter in NW-Lower cube: Take the same Row as the NE-Lower cube pt letter, the same Column as the SW-Lower cube pt letter, and the same Layer as the NW-Upper cube pt letter.

4th ct letter in SE-Lower cube: Take the same Row as the SW-Lower cube pt letter, the same Column as the NE-Lower cube pt letter, and the same Layer as the SE-Upper cube pt letter.

Very interesting discussion here. Of course I also like the idea of a Morse Code-based cipher, since I tried to invent one recently, but I equally well acknowledge the problems involved with it. Fractionated Morse and many other possible ways to use Morse Code in a cipher will tend to change the number of letters between the plaintext message and the ciphertext message. This is actually not uncommon in cryptography, as null letters or other forms of extra ciphertext letters arise in many cipher methods. However, if there's one fact about K4 that Jim Sanborn has made very clear, it is that the K4 plaintext message, the correct "solution", has 97 or 98 letters, just like the K4 ciphertext does. There might be one extra letter or one missing letter, as in K2 and as in Ed's Pre-K message, but it won't be a large difference like a plaintext with only 77 letters or something like that. So we really need to preserve the same number of letters in the plaintext and the ciphertext with any cipher method that we use.

Morse Code itself is problematic for ciphers because the most frequent letters have fewer symbols in their representation and the less frequent letters have more symbols. Most methods that disguise this identifying information about the most frequent letters will also tend to change the number of letters in the pt and ct of the message. It's very hard to get around this problem.

I made a massive effort to get around these problems in my recent Morse Code-based masking cipher method. But I had to convert all the 1-symbol and 2-symbol letters into 3 or 4 symbols (dots/dashes) to do it. That displaced the representations of some other letters, which I had to assign new representations for. I had to make a 24-letter altered Morse Code alphabet, so two pairs of English letters had to share the same code form. I made it all make logical sense in a certain way. BUT -- I admit that it is asking a lot to believe that I have somehow re-invented the exact same modification of Morse Code that Ed Scheidt invented 35 years ago and Jim Sanborn used in the encryption of K4 !  I am not so delusional that I believe that is very likely at all.

So these are the massive problems we run into when we try to incorporate Morse Code into an encryption / decryption method for K4.

It would be a good choice for Ed Scheidt's "language that was only used for about 100 years and is dead now". But unfortunately, it has all the same problems that standard Morse Code has, in terms of different lengths of the code forms of more frequent and less frequent letters, etc., etc., that make it very difficult to use for a cipher that preserves the same number of letters in the plaintext and ciphertext.

If you change the language base, as has been detailed here with binary stuff over the years, you run into the whole problem of how to translate it back into English characters, which is what we see in K4.

This _does_ fit with the comments of "I've masked the framework". If you encode your plaintext as "something else" then do "other operations" on the "something else", whatever you have left has then presumably been mapped back to English characters and I've yet to see a non-haphazard-rule-creation based way of doing that.

In theory, base-3 is the closest thing you've got, but even then, why change it to base 3 unless you're going to operate upon the digits. And once you operate on the digits, either via transposition or some kind of substitution, you're eventually going to have to deal with the 27th character in the same problematic way that you have to deal with the 27th through 32nd characters in the binary problem.

As a thought exercise, I suppose I could code up something that uses all the 000, 001, 002 through 220, 221, 222 base-3 substitutions and encode a message, do some transposition and see what falls out. Worst case scenario is you have a few mispellings when you either hit 000 or 222, whichever one you don't have mapping to an actual English character and you just pick something.

Man, I hate the haphazardness of that kind of stuff.

Something to keep in mind about all of Ed Scheidt's comments in the AJ Jacobs interview: It seems to me that they are pitched toward a general audience that knows little or nothing about classical cryptography. So he explains what substitution is, then he explains what transposition is, and he talks about "changing the language base", "masking the framework", "masking the letter frequencies", etc. For a general audience, it is possible that these phrases might simply represent Ed's idea of elementary descriptions of the cryptographic properties of digraphic / polygraphic systems such as Playfair, Four-square, Bifid, Trifid, etc.

I observe that in Lanaki's classical cryptography course, he discusses polyalphabetic substitution systems first (Vigenere etc.) up through Lesson 13, transposition systems next in Lesson 16, and finally Playfair, Four-square, Fractionation, Bifid, and Trifid ciphers in Lesson 17. This lesson appears to represent the apex or culmination of Lanaki's presentation of classical cryptographic systems.

On Jim M.'s points about the 27th character in base-3 (3x3x3 = 27) representations of the alphabet, such as the Trifid cipher or my new "Eight-cube" cipher:

As Jim M. notes, a misspelling or two could be employed to hide one or two occurrences of the 27th character in the ciphertext. A combination of these options might be enough to remove all occurrences of the 27th character, especially if the cipher were designed to tend to make its representation (000 or 222 or the equivalent in a visual geometric system) occur less frequently than other ciphertext combinations.

Also, I note that Lanaki's description and analysis of the Trifid cipher in his course lesson suggests that the 27th character can be hidden by designating, for example, "ZA" to designate the 27th character and "ZB" to designate actual Z. However, this probably does not help us much with K4, since it would effectively add an extra null letter in the ciphertext for each occurrence of the 27th character as well as of one other letter. Again, this goes against Sanborn's repeated insistence that the K4 plaintext is essentially the same length as the K4 ciphertext.

s: K4 letter spacing in Sanborn's EASTNORTHEAST clue layout
t:
We are well familiar by now with Sanborn's EASTNORTHEAST clue, revealed in 2020 and made public by our own Sukhwant Singh. Sanborn revealed this clue by sending a file to Singh and others with a layout of the entire K4 ciphertext, in the same format as it appears on the sculpture, with the plaintext clue letters EASTNORTHEAST and BERLINCLOCK included in their respective positions.

I have just now noticed that, in this K4 layout by Sanborn, the letter spacing of ?OBKR at the beginning of the K4 ciphertext is quite different from the letter spacing in the other 3 complete rows of K4.

The 3 complete rows are lined up almost exactly with each other, so that 31 "columns" of 3 letters each are lined up as well as possible, despite the varying widths of different letters (e.g., W is wide, I is narrow).

However, the letters ?OBKR at the top do not follow the same letter spacing width as the rows below them at all. There is much less spacing between them, so that they do not line up with the "columns" of letters in the rows below them. Thus, the first letter O is fourth from the right in the top row, but it lines up closer to the column of letters that are only third from the right in the rows below. The letters BK in the top row do not line up with the columns of letters in the rows below them at all.

I only noticed this because I am investigating an encryption method idea that Scheidt and Sanborn may have used the sets of 3 letters lined up in columns in the 3 complete rows of K4 as encryption blocks. Using such trigraphs, for example in a perhaps modified form of a Trifid cipher, would effectively produce a period-31 seriation of the text. This would foil the standard cryptanalysis of a Trifid cipher, which relies heavily on identifying typical repeated sequences of plaintext such as "THE" and other known repeated words. Seriation is a known technique with Playfair, but not with Trifid as far as I am aware.

The letter spacing of the K4 layout in Sanborn's final clue may point to the use of the "columns" of 3 letters in the 3 complete rows of K4 as encryption blocks, but ?OBKR may not follow the same method and may have been encrypted in some other way.

My latest idea about a modified form of Trifid, which is much simpler than my "Eight-cube" method that I posted about recently, is to use trigraphs as encryption blocks. One may think of the method as a sort of "Trifid Playfair", which could be performed in a visual geometric way without the need to use Trifid numbers 1,2,3 or 0,1,2 at all. It only requires a single 3x3x3 Trifid array, for example:

K R Y   B C D   L M N
P T O   E F G   Q U V
S ? A    H I  J    W X Z

Encrypt groups of 3 letters at a time in the following way:

KFZ -->
M (Row of K, Column of F, Layer of Z)
O (Row of F, Column of Z, Layer of K)
H (Row of Z, Column of K, Layer of F)

There is no requirement for special rules for letters in the same row or column, as there is in Playfair, because the shift of the Layer will mask 2/3 of such occurrences rather than pass them through as transparencies.

Also, this idea can elegantly be complicated by reflecting (“flipping”) and rotating (“turning”) individual Layer squares of the Trifid array between each group of 3 letters to be encrypted. This would comport with Sanborn’s “flipping and turning” comment and with Scheidt’s “It’s reflective” comment.

One more observation about how to hide the 27th character in a base-3 or Trifid type cipher encryption:

At the end of K3, Sanborn uses the letter "Q" to represent the question mark at the end of the question "Can you see anything?" It seems fairly clear now that the "?" character, at the end of K3 / beginning of K4, belongs to K4 rather than K3. So within K3, it is the final "Q" that signifies the question mark.

I mentioned above in this thread (message #24308) that Lanaki's cryptography course gives an example of a Trifid where "ZA" designates the 27th character while "ZB" designates actual (ciphertext) Z.

Following the idea of Q = ?, what if Sanborn used "Q" in the manner that Lanaki used "Z" : Followed by a certain letter it designates the 27th character, and followed by a certain other letter it designates actual (ciphertext) Q.

Well, I observe that in the K4 ciphertext, "Q" occurs 4 times: the first 2 times as the double letter QQ, and the next 2 times Q is followed by S both times.

It would be entirely in line with Lanaki's method, if "QQ" represented the 27th character and "QS" represented actual ciphertext Q, or alternatively if "QS" represented the 27th character and "QQ" represented actual ciphertext Q.

I readily admit that there are a few things not to like about this idea: It destroys any idea of a 1-to-1 correspondence between plaintext and ciphertext, and in particular it calls into question "QQPRNGKSS = NORTHEAST". But on its own, it makes sense, it is consistent with a known method, and it is thematic for Kryptos in accordance with the "Q = ?" at the end of K3.

Since myself and others have recently been discussing the idea of a ternary or trinary base-3 system (whether based on a Trifid cipher or otherwise) to encode the K4 message, I noticed the following curiosity:

Sanborn's BERLIN clue, his first clue revealing a word of the K4 plaintext message, was published in The New York Times on November 20, 2010, or 11-20-2010. Since this numerical date contains only the digits 0, 1, and 2, it is a ternary or base-3 number.

I would be curious to know if John Schwartz could possibly tell us whether Jim Sanborn had any control over the date of publication of this clue in the Times. For the record, the next clue CLOCK was also published on November 20, but of course the year 2014 contained a non-ternary digit 4. The NORTHEAST clue was published on January 29, 2020, a date with one non-ternary digit 9.

The NPR online article documenting the segment about the BERLIN clue on its All Things Considered program is dated November 22, 2010, or 11-22-2010.

But what is truly bizarre is the following: Looking through the Notes section of the Wikipedia article about Kryptos, I find a strikingly large proportion of the sources listed there are cited as "Retrieved" on dates with all ternary digits 0, 1, and 2. Of course one would logically expect this must be a coincidence, unless Sanborn or Scheidt somehow had control, overt or covert, over the cited retrieval dates of sources listed in the Kryptos article on Wikipedia. But for the record, as of the current version of the article (which I have saved as a screenshot, just in case the retrieval dates are changed later), one finds the following:

Note 2: "Retrieved 2011-11-12."
Note 8: "Retrieved December 11, 2011." (12-11-2011)
Note 10: "Retrieved December 11, 2011." (12-11-2011)
Note 13: "Retrieved December 11, 2011." (12-11-2011)
Note 16: "Retrieved 2011-11-12."
Note 18: "Retrieved 2011-11-12."
Note 22: "Retrieved 2021-11-11."
Note 23: "Retrieved 2011-11-12."
Note 24: "Retrieved 2011-11-12."
(Notes 23 and 24 cite the NY Times and NPR sources for the BERLIN clue.)
Note 34: "Retrieved December 11, 2011." (12-11-2011)

I understand that it is standard for an article editor to retrieve a large batch of sources on the same date. I am simply observing that the two dates of the large multiple-source retrievals were 2011-11-12 (November 12) and December 11, 2011 (12-11-2011). It is most likely a pure coincidence.

s: A New Perspective from K1 to K4
t:
While we're aware that K1 has been deciphered, its true significance still eludes us. Could the key to unlocking this enigma actually reside within the phrase itself, specifically, "ORDO AB CHAO"?

Dan Brown touched upon this phrase in his novel, "The Lost Symbol."  This term, associated with the Freemasons, serves as the motto of the 33rd Degree of the Scottish Rite.

Examining K1 through the lens of Freemasonry's philosophy, we find that "THE ABSENCE OF LIGHT" represents ignorance and obscurity, while "ILLUSION" signifies a state where the boundaries between dreams and reality blur. These striking contrasts between light and darkness, order and chaos, truth and misperception might symbolize the evolution of human knowledge.

K1 serves as a prelude to the entire Kryptos puzzle, leading us to wonder if its clues extend into K2 through K4. For instance, consider the sentence "ONLY WW" in K2, which, when rotated, could be interpreted as "only the 33rd degree." In K3, the word "Scott" in "Scottish Rite" is said to derive from the Egyptian Pharaoh's queen, Scota. Is it possible that "ORDO AB CHAO" is projected onto K4 as well?

I want to stress that I'm not an expert, but sometimes fresh perspectives can ignite breakthroughs in cryptanalysis.
