s: "BERLIN" split between "East" and "West" sides of K4
t:
I periodically study maps of Berlin in my K4 research, looking for clues related to "BERLIN CLOCK" and "EASTNORTHEAST", among other things in order to generate candidate words and phrases to test as possible K4 plaintext, especially in positions 35-63 between the two known plaintext segments.

It occurs to me that if one envisions the layout of K4 on the sculpture in very general terms as a "map of Berlin", then it is interesting to observe that the word "BERLIN" itself is located half in the "East" side of K4 (BER in positions 64-66) and half in the "West" side of K4 (LIN in positions 67-69).

One of my current working hypotheses is that Sanborn used two different Trifid cube arrays for the encryption of K4, one for the left half (the columns from positions 5-36-67 to 19-50-81) and one for the right half (the columns from positions 21-52-83 to 35-66-97). It now occurs to me that one may conceive of this division as "West Berlin" and "East Berlin". Perhaps the middle column, positions 20-51-82, may have a special status within K4, and may be visualized as the "Berlin Wall" or "Brandenburg Gate" or the like. (It is possible that this "Wall" section may extend to encompass the middle three or five columns rather than just the one middle column.)

Another historical feature of Berlin, still current when Sanborn was designing Kryptos, before the reunification of Berlin and Germany, were the so-called "ghost stations" on certain U-Bahn and S-Bahn train lines that ran through East Berlin territory (the Mitte historic city center borough) between the West Berlin areas on both sides. The stops within East Berlin on these lines were the "ghost stations" where the trains never stopped. It seems to me that such places may have appealed to Sanborn. One of these "ghost stations" was Alexanderplatz, the location of the "World Clock" ("Weltzeituhr") in Berlin.

The oldest technique in cryptanalysis and the first one taught to aspiring code breakers is frequency analysis. Ed Scheidt would surely have covered this with Jim Sanborn.

The crib “EASTNORTHEAST” contains most of the letters most commonly used in English, and a few of those letters are repeats. About 53% of English text used the letters AEHNORST.

What if, after so many years of failed guesses, Sanborn was trying to send us as clear a hint as he could make it? I don’t feel like the choice of these letters was accidental.

Yes, this is a noticeable feature of the word EASTNORTHEAST indeed.

I think the message that it sends is simply that Sanborn is not doing anything "weird" with the plaintext, such as misspelling or omitting a large number of frequent letters to hide their frequency, etc. Of course one or two letters may be misspelled or omitted, as in K1, K2, and K3, but not a large proportion of the K4 text.

It is the K4 encryption method that masks the letter frequencies of the plaintext, not an alteration of the plaintext itself.

BERLINCLOCK had slightly unusual English letter frequencies: 2 C's, a K, a B. Even 2 L's is a bit unusual since L is not quite as frequent in English as Wheel Of Fortune may have led some people to believe. (L is far less frequent than T, N, S, R.) But EASTNORTHEAST underlines the point that we can expect the K4 plaintext to be almost entirely normal English text.

My analysis of my current working hypothesis for the K4 encryption method involves many complicated technical details that I do not want to bother the group with on a regular basis, but from time to time I like to share possibly interesting observations that other group members may be able to brainstorm some interesting ideas about.

My current focus is on the 14 columns on the right side of K4, not including ?OBKR for now. This means positions 22-35, 53-66, and 84-97. However, I suspect there may be a missing letter removed (as in K2) before position 84, which would shift the true position of all following letters one position to the right, so what we see on the sculpture as pos. 83-96 are the actual pos. 84-97.

We know EASTNORTHEAST is the plaintext in pos. 22-34, and we know BER is the plaintext in pos. 64-66.

My current best guess, based on analysis of the method I am investigating, for pos. 53-63 is ATION ? WHICH. This implies that there is a question ending in a word that ends with -ATION, followed by what appears to be another question that begins with WHICH BERLIN CLOCK ...?

I am now applying a similar analysis to pos. 84-97, which as noted above may extend to include pos. 83, shifted one position to the right when a missing letter is reinserted into K4. First of all, according to my method, it is possible that the very last character of K4 is a question mark "?". I consider that this would be quite thematic for Kryptos and for Sanborn.

At the end of K4 before this final "?", the best phrase that I have been able to find, which is consistent with the quite strict restrictions imposed by the encryption method I am analyzing, is BOTH WAYS.

This would produce a question at the end of K4 of the form "WHICH BERLIN CLOCK + 14/15 letters + BOTH WAYS ?" (15 letters in the middle if there is a missing letter to be reinserted as I believe there may well be.) Unfortunately, many natural words before BOTH WAYS are not consistent with my method: For example, the preceding letter cannot be S, ruling out many natural singular forms of verbs here. Words that are possible before BOTH WAYS, according to my method, include HEAD, HELD, DYAD, DEAD, and BEAD. Unfortunately, before HEAD, the word YOU is not consistent with my method. Of course, if I take the liberty to allow a single misspelled letter, then I can shoehorn in LEAD or READ in place of HEAD. I am extremely reluctant to take such a liberty unless it is absolutely necessary, but it's fair to expect at least one such intentional misspelling somewhere in K4. Curiously, since YOU HEAD is not possible, the most natural possible readings suggest that HEAD is a plural verb form. Does this mean that the letter in position 75 is S, producing "WHICH BERLIN CLOCKS ..." ? This would be sneaky, but Sanborn never stated that CLOCK cannot be part of CLOCKS in this position.

Also, if BOTH WAYS is correct, it makes me wonder, could there possibly be a second compass direction in the first part of K4, along with EASTNORTHEAST ? In this case, BOTH WAYS could be a reference to ENE and to the other direction, whichever one that may be.

Hi all,

My name is Dan Ungureanu.
I considered K4 on and off for a few years now.

My current idea for the encryption process for K4 is the following:
Each letter of the alphabet has associated either a wheel (like in the Jefferson cipher or M-94) or a strip (similar to M-138-A).
However all the alphabets used are just the normal, in-order alphabet, and not scrambled.
At the start, each letter of the alphabet has an associated encoded starting letter selected on its wheel or strip (based on a certain unknown configuration, maybe derived from a secret keyword)

Then, for each of the 97 plaintext letters, the following two step process is applied:

1. Based on the current configuration, the letter from the plaintext is mapped to its corresponding letter on its disk or strip (for the first one this will be O - the first letter of the cipher text).
2. The configuration is updated as follows: for each letter of the alphabet, the disk (or the strip) shifts exactly one spot, either in one direction or the other.
It may be that part of the disks shift in one direction, and the others in the opposite direction.
The exact determination of which letters shift in which direction can vary at each iteration of this step.

 Arguments in favor of this:
a) The L at position 67 maps to V, the L at position 71 maps to Z. It matches to the algorithm indicating that the encoding for L always increases in this range (67 - V, 68 - W, 69 - X, 70 - Y, 71 - Z)
b) The C at 70 maps to M, the C at 73 maps to P -  matches also with  always increasing, 71 - N and 72 - O
c) The T at 25 maps to V, the T at 29 maps to R - matches with always decreasing, 26 - U, 27 - T, 28 - S
d) The T at 29 maps to R, the T at 34 maps to S - matches to two decreases and three increases
e) This means that if the same plaintext letter appears in two different positions, the parity of the difference in their positions must match the parity of the difference between the
 two corresponding cipher letters.
All the known examples of a plaintext letter occurring multiple times verify this:
E maps to F at position 22, to G at position 31 (position difference 9, cipher letter difference 1)
E maps to G at position 31 and to Y at position 65 (position difference 34, cipher letter difference -8)
A: L at 23, K at 32 (PD 9, CD -1)
S: R at 24, S at 33 (PD 9, CD 1)
N: Q at 26, T at 69 (PD 43, CD 3)
O: Q at 27, F at 72 (PD 45, CD -11)
R: P at 28, P at 66 (PD 38, CD 0)

I would love to hear feedback, or to provide inspiration to others.
Happy deciphering!

 - OTPs work if the key is random (thus never repeating)
 - As I have, using a OTP method, shifted EASTNORTHEAST and BERLIN CLOCK,
each letter has its own shift amount (left or right, different values)
 - This make sense if K4 is in fact a OTP

Then I got to thinking: as K4 has 97 characters and as 97 is a prime, could
the key's shift also be a prime number?

I have played around with a few primes and came up with something
interesting:
 - If 53 is used (meaning: the first 53 characters of K4 comprised the key
in its entirety), thus will partially repeat through the rest of the K4
characters
 - So, I assigned each letter in the encrypted text #1-53, then started
again with #1 at the 54th K4 character (which is letter L) ... also
interesting that the letter "L" is the only letter in the Tableau in column
31 (hmmm)

Using the KRYPTOS alphabet, which is still 26 characters long, and dividing
it at the 13th letter (between F and G) ... as would be done using an
old-school OTP (paper strips and board) ... I shifted EASTNORTHEAST and
BERLINCLOCK to align with the centre line (between F and G) and made note
of the shift quantity (e.g., -4 on the x-axis for E; +1 on the x-axis for
A, etc) ... this aligned the decrypted letters in a north-south direction

starting at #1 from the K4 54th letter ... as such, BERLINCLOCK becomes new
#s 11 through 21

key facilitating decypering, I find it interesting that when using the
prime number 53 as the key length, the left-right shift for the
deciphered letters / words BERLINCLOCK (placement #11-21) fits in nicely

s: Some reasons why K4 is not a OTP
t:
Hi Shaun/Jared/All: in my opinion, a one time pad is ruled out by Sanborn and Scheidt's various statements over the years. As Jared pointed out, a *true* OTP is, of course, ruled out unless the key is provided on the sculpture (and does not involve *deciphered* text from K1-K3). My recollection is that either Jim or Ed said that (at least?) four different encryption methods were used with Kryptos. We know two of them (Quagmire III used twice in K1 and K2, and transposition via double rotation used on K3). If we exclude the Morse code found elsewhere on the C.I.A. grounds (which isn't really an encryption method), and we further assume having two different keys for K1 and K2 doesn't count as two separate encryption methods, then K4 must involve at least two processes that haven't previously been used. One of those would seem to be the so-called "masking step" that foils the usual methods of attack (frequency counting, incidence of coincidence, Kasiski examination, etc.) A masking step would be quite unnecessary (and unfair) if an OTP was used on K4.

I personally think the masking step (if it truly is a separate step, and not part of an integrated method) is likely to be something visual that would appeal to the artist in Jim. Something very simple to carry out, yet very effective (apparently!) in disguising the presence of some other more classical encryption such as straight Vigenere.  --Rob

An excellent observation. Whether he said those words or not, they are true. Someone once observed to the forum:

"...The final few words in section 2... ID by rows. It would be interesting to give thought to the coordinate system from clue 2, and if this translates in any way to the lines used in 3 but thats just a curiosity."

Words in K3:
"...THERE MAIN S OF PASSAGE DEBRIS THAT ENCUMBERED THE LOWER PART OF THE DOORWAY WAS REMOVED".

So, the MAIN S had been removed causing the doorway (the bottom 120 characters of K2) to be incomplete. The implication is to reinsert the S. Doing this will complete the doorway. We insert the missing S into the 9th position from the bottom corner of the doorway:

T G P U A E C N U V P D
J M Q C L Q U M U N E D
F Q E L Z Z V R R G K F
F V O E E X B D M V P N
F Q X E Z L G R E D N Q
F M P N Z G L F L P M R
J Q Y A L M G N U V P D
X V K P D Q U M E B E D
M H D A F M J G Z N U P
L G E S W J L L A E T G

Notice all the symmetry in this matrix. It describes a doorway. With S now inserted, the doorway is complete. Before the S was inserted, the last letters were shifted one position to the left, leaving the last two rows to appear as:

M H D A F M J G Z N U P
L G E W J L L A E T G

When you apply the Quagmire Vigenere routine using ABSCISSA as keyword, the last two rows appear as:

F O U R S E C O N D S W
E S T I D B Y R O W S

After inserting the S, you get:

F O U R S E C O N D S W
E S T X L A Y E R T W O

When Monet (Nicole Friedrich) tried shifting the keyword one position to be BSCISSAA and applied it to the matrix with the S still not inserted, she got:

C Z T R O E B A J T I W
D S P L A Y E R T W O

When Sanborn acted and indicated that an X should appear in the 9th position from the end of K2 PT, it should have been obvious to immediately suspect that a keyword shift had occurred causing LAYERTWO to appear shifted over one position to the left in Monet's matrix. But, nobody picked up on it immediately. After too long a time mostly because I was utterly untrained in cryptography, I determined to try running the whole doorway matrix using all shifts of ABSCISSA. Long story short, I found that the bottom two rows of the doorway matrix when run against all shifts of ABSCISSA when compared with the K3 narrative, revealed that the S ultimately became a Z (via PT X). Keyword SAABSCIS has:

E S T X W F D S M E I Q
Y A 0 Z J B E B M O X S

Notice that ESTX now appears above YAOZ, with the X above the Z. And the Z is going to be inserted at the beginning of K4. Notice that the doorway matrix, when run against keyword AABSCISS renders the bottom two rows as:

D B R M S F C S L G F H
E A T Z I D B Y R O W S

So, IDBYROWS has not gone away and the S has been changed into a Z by virtue of HEAT. Hot air caused the flame to flicker.

TREMBLING HANDS caused the OUX arrangement of letters in K4 to become UOX as the candle was inserted into the upper left hand corner. Keyword CISSAABS gives:

F B P K T F A X N G H V
C A Y L L D D D Z O U X

Now K4 has had the first action on it, the insertion of the Z before OBKR.

Now, I have not been able to complete the puzzle, but my interpretation of the results I've gotten so far indicates that K4 is not just a masked single cipher. Ed Scheidt once said you have to first figure out what's going on. This isn't the first time I've laid this stuff out. There will be some dyed-in-the-wool cryptographers who still will not accept all of this because K1 through K3 are, on the surface, just simple ciphers, which they are, and they will continue to assume that K4 is similar but with a mask applied.

So, I have to agree with Carl that it's almost surely the case that you have to understand and follow the indicators in K1, K2 and K3 (as well as discover and follow many clues, where-ever they may appear) in order to find success in engaging K4. But, I say "almost" because I have not come to the Kryptos solution, so I'm not taking any large bets. :)

I'm likely in the minority in this opinion, but I think the K2 "IDBYROWS" alternate decryption (due to Sanborn deleting a letter) is just random happenstance. Certainly Jim himself had NO expertise in engineering such an "under duress" outcome. Ed could have engineered such a remarkable thing (though not without significant effort), but it would have been completely impossible for Ed to do so without knowing the plaintext and keyword Jim wanted to use. And frankly, there's no chance in hell Jim could have made this happen deliberately on his own -- no disrespect to Jim.

So anyone drawing significance from "ID by rows" is -- again in my opinion -- wasting their time going down an irrelevant rabbit hole. Jim seemed as surprised as anyone that an intelligible outcome could result from a one-letter shift at the end of K2. It took him months to realize that the first folks to solve K2 had incorrectly decrypted the final eight letters of K2 -- again evidence that he had no idea there was an ambiguity there introduced by his mistake.  --Rob

Hi Duane:

You and I are on the same wavelength as far as the arguments against K4 being OTP. I would extend that logic to exclude Enigma or other rotor-based encryption schemes since you wouldn't need multi-step encryption if you used either OTP or anything Enigma-like.

I truly believe K4 is going to be only incrementally more difficult than the ciphers that preceded it, as opposed to orders of magnitude harder. It's going to be something "fair" but perhaps with a unique artistic twist that has so far successfully foiled classical attack strategies (including computer attack). I have thought of lots of simple artistic twists that Jim could have employed that would prevent such a blind computer attack. (I know, because I have programmed such attacks exploring the premise that various non-linear visual adjustments were made to either the ciphertext or plaintext.) That's the nature of the problem: until you hit on a very close analogue to what Jim ~actually~ did to trip-up frequency analysis and Kasiski, a blind computer attack will surely fail.

Naturally it's tempting to use and/or interpret the plaintext of the prior solved sections as clues as to how to proceed with K4. But based on the balance of Jim and Ed's comments over the years (specifically, the claimed solvability of K4 without previously having solved K1-K3), I think that's a dead end. We have other evidence to support that takeaway. Nothing in K1 or K2 was helpful in solving K3. And had K3 been solved first, it would have been useless as far as solving K1 or K2.

Now arguably, once either K1 or K2 was figured out, the solver would have had the ~method~ that would work for the other -- just with a different keyword. But there was nothing in the PT of K1 -- or its keyword -- that would help you solve K2, and vice versa. So we have six examples of opportunities for prior solved sections to lend a hand in solving other solved sections. Not once did Jim exploit the opportunity, so I think it's a curious leap for cryptanalysts to assume he did differently with respect to K4.  --Rob

t:
I've taken a close look, and wrote a program in C to reproduce the results of column "AZ" ("HOUSTON EE HAQE..."). I did not factor in the other columns (which would result in "HOUSTON EE HAVE..."). I figured that "HOUSTON EE HAQE" is close enough to valid plaintext, with less possibility for "forcing" the plaintext than if I looked at the other columns as well.

From my analysis, it looks like the plaintext letters were hand-picked from a large group of possibilities. In other words, not what I would consider statistically significant.

Basically, for all 97 positions, we can pick from 4 rows (column AM: 1, 2, 26, or 27), 4 columns (column AN: 1, 2, 30, or 31), and 2 secondary rows (column AR: 1 or 2) to generate a possible plaintext character. That's 32 positions you can look at for characters; minus duplicates that becomes about 11-23 different characters to pick from for each position.

Let's look at the ciphertext letter "O" at the beginning of K4 (OBKR...). There are 20 different characters to choose from: ABCDEFGHIJLMOPQRSTXY.

You couldn't force the plaintext NEWYORK as the first 7 characters ("N" isn't one of those 20 possibilities for the first position). You could, however, easily get mis-spelled plaintext like ATLAGTA or SENBORN, or a limited number of correctly spelled words like FT WORTH. If you see something you like, you can continue on, and can get (for example) "FTWORTH IS BEYOND THE PEG EASTNORTHEAZT OF LANGLLY...".

So if I were going to investigate this further, I would try to see if there was some pattern to the numbers in columns AM, AN, and AR, and if there was some sort of algorithm to generate those numbers. With no such algorith, I would see no reason to think that the plaintext begins with HOUSTON as opposed to the FTWORTH in my example. But if there is such an algorithm, I would consider this a very likely solution.
                         -Scott

Sukhwant,
Let me address each of your points, please.
Mengenlehreuhr is the Berlin Clock. There are multiple clues in Kryptos pointing to this clock. The first one occurs in the Morse code text: DIGE TAL INTERPRETATI(ON).

You make an assumption that cannot be backed, that Mengenlehreuhr "requires maths". Why would it require maths when it comes to Kryptos? You can't dismiss a fact because you don't know the answer. Why does JS talk about Carter's opening of Tutankhamun's tomb in K3 when he hasn't in K1 or K2?
Chance has nothing to do with it. The probability of someone taking the right approach is the point to be taken.

I don't think JS would tell someone directly if they were close to a solution. However, if someone believes they know how Kryptos works and can demonstrate that by showing their work, they might have already disclosed this to the Group somehow.
I have submitted thoughts to JS several times along with my 50 bucks. In each and every case, he has answered in a negative way. This is his way of doing things, which is not to indicate progress of the solver.

As a postscript to the above, let me reiterate about MENGENLEHREUHR, THEBERLINCLOCK and NORTHEAST, that they are certainly keywords. The primary clue that BERLIN is part of a keyword is that JS
indicated its exact position. Same thing with NORTHEAST. By adding CLOCK, he provided more evidence of this and more evidence was added when he revealed the addition of EAST to the front of NORTHEAST. Now, JS keeps indicating that BERLINCLOCK and EASTNORTHEAST are parts of the final solution of 97 characters. I have trouble believing this for two reasons: 1. I have already worked out that they are either keywords or parts of keywords and 2. BERLINCLOCK plus EASTNORTHEAST add up to 24 letters which is almost 25 percent of the length of K4 and, while it can't be shown that they are not part of the solution, it also can't be shown, to this point in time, that they are helpful in solving K4. So then, why give away BERLINCLOCK and EASTNORTHEAST? I answered that in the beginning sentences of this paragraph.
PaulK

Tool for complete decryption of K4 from start to finish and beyond. Instructions to follow.

Hi All,

You should see a file upload made in the last 24 hours called KryptosMatrixSolutionsV6.zip.  Once unzipped this will give you an HTML page that can be used as a tool to verify the solution that will gradually be imparted over the next couple of weeks.

I outlined the general method in the paper, 'Eris and Harmonia', which was published here back in March 2021, but its taken another two and a half years to fully identify the short comings in that paper and show why the general approach was so effective in generating all known plain text in the correct positions using a consistent technique derived from first principles.

That original paper was perhaps too dense for some, so I'm going to try a new approach, which is to present one piece of evidence at a time in order to allow people time to recreate the results using the tool provided.  I'm completely aware that some of you won't be invested in the solution given here for all manner of reasons, but for those falling into that camp I would be extremely happy for you to play the role of team red and call out any flaws in the logic presented.

I'll start in reverse order this time round and say that I did send the following proposed 97 letter string for K4 to Jim back in mid August 2023:
KRYPTO SITE AM EAST. ROUND EAST NORTH EAST. I FORCES. DYNAMO WAVE ROUND GROUP. TE. BERLIN CLOCK. CHURCH TUNNEL. UK GCHQ CODE(R).
Note.  This solution only produces 96 letters so the final (R) of K4 is unmapped and taken as is by appending to the previous 96.

Jim's response was as follows:

Hi Matt thanks again, I have stated previously that K4 says something (like the clues I have given) its prose, not a jumble of letters, hope this helps, all the best, jim

I should point out that I presented the result above to him as a collection of 12 discrete 8 letter solves without spaces, but even so, make of that response what you will.  I'm confident that the first 36 letters are correct for reasons that will become apparent later, but it may be that some of the later cryptograms have been interpreted wrongly, in which case I'm open to sharing the credit if you can spot any flaw in the logic and can correct any particular solve.

There have been three big changes to the methodology previously put forward.  The first is the order in which the six 3x32 matrices are processed and the second and third are the imposition of additional constraint conditions that were not apparent or obvious two years ago, despite already being present in some of the results.

I'll show the clues and reasoning along the way, but at the very least I hope you enjoy the journey and find it as fascinating as I did.

I appreciate this has been a lengthy post, so I'll cut it short there and start gradually stepping you through the solution in subsequent posts.

Matt

Note: The HTML page is not designed to be used on mobile phone, but it should be fine on a laptop or tablet.  I've not tried it on a MAC as yet, so let me know if anything weird happens in the Safari browser.

on a right path for solving K4.

s: New Old Member - Paper and Pencil solution
t:
Just an observation.  For K1/K2 we have a 26x26 square with the 26 shifts of the Kryptos alphabet.
To encrypt, find your plaintext letter in the 1st row, and the key letter in the 1st column, and read the ciphertext at the intersection.

The tableau is a 27x27 square, with a standard alphabet as row (an col) 1, and Kryptos alphabet in row 2.  You've used columns 1,2 in your approach.
That suggests an encryption strategy of having a 2 bit selector associated with each of the 97 letters:
00:  find plaintext in row 0, and key letter in column 0 (both standard AZ alphabets)
01:  find plaintext in row 0, and key letter in column 1 (Kryptos alphabet)
10:  find plaintext in row 1, and key letter in column 0.
11:  find plaintext in row 1 and key letter in col 1 (both plain and key located in Kryptos alphabets).
That gives 4 possible ciphertext letters for each plaintext, depending on the 2 bit selector.

If the encryption scenario is Control TO Agent, Control could broadcast something that conveys the sequence of 2 bit numbers for the Agent to use in decrypting a cipher message.  A "Numbers Station" could transmit Morse coded phrases, which are made up or dit/dots:  the Morse on the Kryptos status has approximately 200 dit/dots, enough to convey 100 2 bit selectors for a 97 character message.

In addition, the tableau also has 4 "extra" columns for a 27x31 square.  (You've used columns 30,31 in your approach).  A 4 bit selector could somehow be used in conjunction with these 4 columns, picking one of these columns for each letter encryption.

If you want to get really crazy, assume OBKR is a "message indicator" and shift the 4 "extra" columns such that OBKR is in row 1.

At one point I considered that the 4 extra columns could be transposed to generate a "one time pad" containing 104 equally distributed key letters:  4 of each in the 104 letter block.  But K4 doesn't seem random enough to suggest a one time pad.

There are just too many possibilities for what Jim "might have done" to produce K4.

The problem with these "unknown selector" approaches is that you generate lots of plausible strings, as you have freedom to choose words that seem to make sense.  Further, when your system doesn't work, you can just attribute the anomaly to a supposed "spelling error".  That gives you a lot of freedom in forcing a solution, almost to the point where you can force any message (that you're free to rephrase as necessary to "fit" the solution).

What you seem to have is a scheme to generate 16 letter strings for each of the 97 cipher letters, then see if you can find a path through these strings (pick a letter from string 1, then a letter from string 2, etc.) that forms a plausible message.  And where you're blocked, just attribute it to a "spelling error".  That's consistent with a forced solution as others have pointed out.

I'd start with the 2 known cribs EASTNORTHEAST and BERLINCLOCK and assume no misspellings, and see if you can come up a sequence of 2 or 4 bit selectors that use row/col 1,2 or cols 28,29,30,31 somehow.

Your method doesn't start with L, but starts with key letter K to encrypt H to intermediate L, and then encrypts that to get ciphertext O.

I did like your presumed plaintext, Houston we have a problem (or the more accurate Houston we've had a problem), in the context of the CIA Berlin tunnel project being compromised (which seemed to be the context of K3 when the Russians "discovered" the vault with the telephone taps).

But to be credible to me as a solution, you'd need to show a viable keyword beginning K that can be used to generate the intermediate letters that then produce the given ciphertext.  If we had that, then we could look for an algorithm that generates the 97 selector values.

Step 1.  Breaking The Seal

One of the outstanding questions that continues to come up is whether or not K4 is part of a larger puzzle or a novel cipher type that is susceptible to discovery through cryptanalysis.  The answer is that it's both.  Whilst the K4 cipher will be seen to be a discrete and logical entity in its own right, it would of course be entirely unfair not to provide clues within either the cipher or plain text of parts K1-3.  The best analogy I can give on this front is the MIT mystery hunt.  By solving lots of small seemingly disconnected puzzles, the solver is taken further towards the eventual goal of revealing the nature and mechanism of the K4 encipherment method.  As Jim said himself in those early interviews, you go through one set of doors into a room only to find another set of doors leading you ever deeper into other rooms (I'm paraphrasing of course, but that was the general gist).

There have been many observations that appeared to offer potential breaks over the years, but for the purpose of these emails I'm going to step through a subset of those clues in a very specific order to show how the case is gradually made apparent for the framework upon which the proposed K4 solve is predicated.  I should point out that this is not the order in which the clues were discovered, but instead a rationalization of what the perfect order of discovery would have been in order to solve the puzzle as part of a process rather than a series of haphazard discoveries made over a longer timescale.

The solution framework on the front page of the tool provided (see previous upload notification for KryptosMatrixzSolutionsV6.zip) is a hard-wired presentation of the framework needed to solve K4 that will naturally drop out of the steps in the proceeding emails.  To verify the observations that lead to this specific subset of the sculpture rows you will need to follow along initially with the freeform tools that are accessible via the green colored 'Raw' button in the right hand margin.

After pressing this, you'll be presented with a view of the cipher text and plain text side by side laid out on a 28x32 grid that uses a fixed width font.  You will noticed that the T in A in row 23 have been omitted from the cipher and plain text respectively in order to achieve this bounding requirement.  The need for a 28x32 grid is important as it allows us to represent the cipher and plain text as two closed cylinders whose rows can move about the center independently of each other much like a Jefferson cylinder.

For the purposes of this first step we are going to use the palette functionality, which is the strip of 11 colors in the top left corner of the screen.  Click on a color of your choice and then click on any letter in the grid.  It will now be highlighted in the color you selected.  Click it again to unassign the color.  We'll use this feature to mark our initial entry point into solving K4.

To give this clue some context, we should remember that an early form of concealment, was mirror writing.  This rather simple technique was famously employed by Leonardo Da Vinci to guard the contents of his notebooks, but for the purposes of this first clue we're going to use the palette tool to highlight some letters left for us to find in the plain and cipher text. In column 23 of row 15, find the letter T and then highlight the next 5 letters beneath it, which will give TUYANI.  Now do the same thing in the same location of the cipher text to highlight the letters BSBEHE.
Now highlight the 6 letters to the left of that B in the cipher text to show 7 letters that will read CPTEOIB.  Repeat the same operation in the plain text to highlight the string in row 15 that reads SLOWLYT. The previous instructions have sketched out half of a 7X6 square, so now complete the remaining 2 sides and you will notice that the inner 6 letters of the plain text square are ORWDSI.  We can now re-arrange these letters to give the string ID ROWS.  This appears to be significant, so lets re-arrange TUYANI to give AN(Y)UIT and CPTEOIB to give COEPTI(B).  Annuit Coeptis is of course the wording on the Great Seal Of The United States, but most interestingly the misspellings give BY, which fits neatly between ID ROWS to show that ID BY ROWS was always the intended string that would lead to the proceeding steps that we'll explore next.

The description of each subsequent step will probably be around this general length and can be followed along with by using the tool provided.  Hopefully, that will be easier to digest than an overly long document.

Until the next instalment,
Matt

Step 3.  Find the repeating pattern

We saw in step 2 that mirroring our actions in both the plain text (pt) and cipher text (ct) leads to the uncovering of the phrase ANNUIT COEPTIS and ID (BY) ROWS, both of which have been cryptically hidden.  If you have followed the last step correctly then you should have two squares highlighted.  The pt square contains the 6 letters ORW and DSI and the cipher text square contains NEL and EUD.  Given that we have found a cryptically hidden string from the pt of K2 in the first 6 rows of the pt of K3 it follows that there may well also be a reciprocal relationship linking the pt of K3 back to the pt of K2.

This idea is most easily explored geometrically by using the highlight tool to mirror the squares that we have just discovered along the dividing line between rows 14 and 15.  If we highlight the letters in row 14 between columns 17 and 23 then we'll capture the string NDSWEST.  Highlight the 5 letters above the last T in column 23 to capture TESSIS.  Fill in the remaining two sides and you will have successfully mirrored the plain text square below.  Repeat this operation for the cipher as we are still mirroring every operation performed on the pt.

You will notice that the six letters in the new pt square that resides in K2 now contains the letters GRE and FIV.  Remember from step 2 that we need to consider the pt and ct simultaneously, so if you now look at the ct view in columns 29-31 on row 12 you will find the letters GRE, which you can highlight.  Now look directly above in row 1 and you will see the letters FIV sitting above it, which you can also highlight.

This second clue is designed to draw our attention to something important in relation to repeating letter groups. Highlight the F and the V above and below the GRE string in the ct (at cols 29-31, row 12).  Now de-select the G.  This will leave you with F, RE and V highlighted across 3 rows of the ct.

Now look at rows 7, 8 and 9 in the ct directly above and you will notice the exact same letter groupings directly above.

It was mentioned earlier that the grid pattern is presented as a 32x28 cylinder, which means we can rotate any individual row of the ct and pt simultaneously about the cylinder's axis.  Make sure the box below the red buttons in the top left shows the number 1 for row 1 and then hit the left hand red button 13 times to shift row 1 13 places to the left.

You can now highlight F, RE and V across rows 1-3 in the ct starting with the F that now resides in column 16 of row 1.  You will also notice that an I and a G sits above and below the R, giving us a direct link back to the original FIV GRE clue in the pt square.

A further consequence of applying the left hand shift has been in the pt.  If you now look at column 2 of the pt you will see the string HOT is written downwards crossed with the string EOF.  Looking at column 22 it can be seen that we now have TOH crossed by EOF.  This should be noted as it will become important later, but are three more of these repeating groups of F, RE and V still to be mined from the ct.

Unfortunately that will have to wait until the next instalment, but I'll finish up this step with a couple of notes.  Firstly, the repeating letter groups in rows 7-9 and 11-13 were first brought to my attention by a graphic designer called James Churchill and it wasn't until a couple of days later that I realized the previous papers I'd published here since 2013 all included a left shift of 13 in row 1, which completed the pattern we've arrived at above by an alternate path.
The second thing to note for anyone that may not have seen it in the 2021 Eris and Harmonia paper is that a ROT13 operation on ER,I and S gives RE, V, and F.  Given that Eris is the Greek goddess of discord, I found it fitting to implicate her in the role of protecting the secrets of Kryptos when writing up that paper.

Until the next step,
Matt

Step 4.  Find the next 3 repeats of F, RE, and V.

In the last step we saw how our attention was drawn towards the discovery of 3 repeating instances of F, RE and V that occur over 3 rows of the cipher text.  The next step will require some sleuthing to verify the veracity of the claim, but the tool provided will offer the assistance necessary in this respect.
If you use the free form text box beneath the blue search button in the right hand margin and type in the letters FREV then the Raw view will automatically highlight all of the individual letters in that string in different colors after pressing 'Search'.
Your job is to find all instances of the 2 letter string RE that occur in the vertical plane of the CT, rather than the horizontal as we saw for the previous 3 repeats.  Pay particular attention to the pair that straddle rows 14 and 15 and as they are easy to miss due to the gap in the rendering between rows.
Once you have identified all the potential candidates look in the rows above and below to find instances of the letters F and V.
It will soon become obvious that there are 3 instances where this requirement is satisfied, with the additional constraint of there being a six character gap between the F and V identified.
I'll leave that to yourselves to verify at your leisure, but ultimately you will find the vertical repeats starting at column 1 in rows 24-26, column 7 in rows 15-13 and column 28 in rows 5-3.  Once you have found them you can also use the row shift tools to line them all up to see where they sit with respect to each other, but this isn't necessary for the deciphering process itself.

So to recap, we have found 6 repeats of the letter group F, RE and V across the ct, of which 3 have a horizontal
orientation and 3 have a vertical one.  The three rows that each of these repeating groups straddle represent a unique 3x32 matrix that includes both letters and spaces.

At a basic level these are the raw 3x32 matrices that you see on the front page of the tool when the tool first loads up, but there are some additional steps to go through before the nature of the cipher method becomes apparent.  Perhaps the most obvious question is, 'if these 6 3x32 matrices are of interest, then what order should we approach them in'?  Kryptos does not give up its secrets easily, so to answer that question we will have to solve an entire 'puzzle within the puzzle' before we can proceed any further.

Again, we are not without help in finding a place to start.  If we look to the left of the pt square that was previously highlighted containing GRE and FIV then we can create a new 7x6 sqaure identical to the last one by using the sides YFOURSE on row 14 and EEPGWE going upwards from the E.  Once you have filled in the other two sides you'll find the strings TYE and SSI in the middle, just like the previous clues.  If you can't see it yet, then once re-ordered, this clue reads, 'YES ITS'.  For those that haven't read the original Carter diary the original entry reads, 'Can you see anything?' 'Yes, it is wonderful…'.

Using this clue, along with everything else we have learned so far will lead us directly to the prescribed order in which the 6 matrices should be addressed.

Until then,
Matt

I found a similar clue in K4 but it starts from positions. 1,3,5,9 and 12

Step 5.  Can you see anything? Yes, it is wonderful...

This clue is perhaps the most important one to document and to verify for yourself.  The method of concealment is ingenious and was only found after exhaustive scanning of the plain and cipher text simultaneously to see if any relation existed between the rows containing F, RE and V in the ct and the letters in the pt.  I should confess that this relationship dropped out of rigorous analysis first and it was only in retrospect that the 6 anagrammed letters in the plaintext square highlighted in step 4 yesterday were found.  Note: For the purposes of making things easier to read, I'm going to refer to any set of three rows containing F, RE and V as matrices from herein as both the horizontal and vertical forms both sit across a 3x32 matrix.

To partake in this mini puzzle and check the results for yourself, you'll need to spend some time curating the results given to you by the search tool.  The string you want to search for is YESIT.  We do not need to include the second S in the search string itself, but we will want to look at all 28 rows of the pt and eliminate any row that doesn't contain all the letters of YES ITS.  To be clear, the row must contain 2 S's to be considered.  De-select any letters in rows that do not fulfill this criteria.

De-select any letters highlighted in the ct and instead select letters on the left hand side of the ct across the rows that contain matrices.  That will mean the rows of interest are 1-5, 7-9, 11-15 and 24-26.
The purpose of highlighting the rows in the ct is purely to help identify rows of interest in the pt.

If a YES ITS row in the pt falls outside of any of the matrix rows, then discount it and de-select the letters.  (Only rows 10 and 27 fall into this category btw).

Once you've completed this step you should have 7 rows of interest highlighted in the pt.  Row 11 and 13 are unique as they fall across the first and last row of a single matrix.  All the other matrix rows are only touched once by a YES ITS relationship and are therefore easily linked to the corresponding YES ITS row in the pt.

Despite having the advantage of software, the true nature of the concealment was elusive for some time until the penny finally dropped and it became clear that the frequency distribution of the letter E in the YES ITS rows was actually being used as a numeric marker.  This is successfully obscured by two misdirects.  The first is that the distribution of E's for the matrix in rows 11-13 is taken from the row between the 2 YES ITS rows due to its unique double association.
The second method of obscuring the marker pattern is vaguely fiendish as we need to put the two missing E's back into the word DESPERATELY in row 15.

Once we do that, it will become apparent that each matrix is labelled as followed by the corresponding distribution of E's.

Matrix 1 Rows 1-3
Matrix 2 Rows 7-9
Matrix 3 Rows 24-26
Matrix 4 Rows 11-13
Matrix 5 Rows 13-15
Matrix 6 Rows 3-5

Now that we have the id of the matrix rows we can move one step closer to understanding the nature of the K4 cipher itself.  In the next post we'll explore an additional clues that will give us an idea of where to start.

Until then,
Matt

Step 6.  It was totally invisible..

The next step is a whole meal in itself that could easily fill an additional paper on the subject, but we shall skip across it in a single step as we only need to extract the information that is pertinent to progressing towards the eventual K4 solve.  That said, it will hopefully fill you with a sense of awe at just how adept the puzzle creators have been in displaying their craft.

The previous clues in the pt squares that we have mirrored in the ct have so far read, ID ROWS, GRE FIV and YES ITS.  Curiosity alone is enough to make us realize that there is a potential 4th square missing in this arrangement.  Using symmetry as your guide you should easily be able to highlight this missing fourth square, which when done correctly will contain the letters, RTO and MBL.  We can re-arrange as per the previous clues to give TOMB LR.  It took a while to understand the relevance of LR, but it soon transpired that it meant Lower Right.  If you do a search for the string TOMB using the tool then you will notice an odd phenomena.

There are only two places in the pt where the letters of TOMB form a 3 letter diagonal, with the 4th letter of the word directly appended.  If your having trouble seeing it, then highlight the first one in row, col coordinates: M(18,10);T(17,11);O(17,12);B(16,12) and the second at
coordinates: B(25,29);M(24,29;O(24,28);T(23,27), which is indeed in the lower right with respect to the first instance.

On the 3 letter diagonal of each of those two structures continue the diagonal patter until the two lines converge on the letter I in the word POINT.  The fact that the two lines converge to form a closed triangle is not quite as remarkable as the fact that counting from the B in the lower right shows that we have 13 steps until reaching the 'I' at the top of the pyramid.  It appears that we have come full circle in relation to the first clue that gave us ANNUIT COEPTIS as all of these elements are present on the one dollar bill.

If we draw the same structure mirrored in the ct rows then we start to see some further relationships of interest.  The first and most important for progressing to the next step is that the center line of the triangle (or pyramid!) terminates in row one on the D of USD.  This is of interest for reasons that will be explained in later steps, but in relation to the information above it is also extremely likely that we are being told the string USD is important!

It will be seen that the center line in the pt has the string ANIT in rows 1-4 and this occurs again in the center line of the ct on rows 21-18.  The center of each pyramid also contains the same string AET in the ct and ATE in the pt.

If anyone is still wishing to write this off as coincidence then I'll direct your attention to the moniker WW on row 10 of the pt.  This is mirrored on the diagonal in the ct in row 4 with the string MM at column 18.  If we do the same thing as we did with the initial ANNUIT COEPTIS clue and use these 2 positions to sketch out a square then we find a 7x7 square about the pyramids center line.  In the pt this is composed of the sides SEDTHEE, ETDSDKW, WSIHTWW and WRYOTNS.  There is something remarkable about this 7x7 square other than being centered on the pyramids central axis.  It contains a signature.

Highlight the following within the 7x7 square: E(9,14);W(9,16);D(7,16);R(5,16);A(5,18).  You should see a beautifully artistic rendition of the name EDWARD embedded within the 7x7 square.  I can imagine that this may not be enough evidence for the more skeptical of readers, so in that instance highlight the letters DTHE on the top side of the square.  Add the SI letters directly above the letters HE.  Now repeat on the bottom side of the square for the letters THIS and then add the letters DE below the IS.  We have 2 symmetrical anagrams of SCHEIDT adorning the name EDWARD in the center of the square.

If there are any die hard skeptics still wanting to write this off as coincidence then that is their prerogative, but before dismissing this entire step you might want to look at the 7X7 box that is mirrored in the ct.  At its center you'll find 3 letters, SJH.  This community refers to 'Jim' so often that I suspect we've forgotten his full name, which is 'Herbert James Sanborn'.

In the next step, we'll see that the string USD offers us our first tangible glimpse of the actual K4 cipher.

Until then,
Matt

Step 7.  A pointer to USD via another clue.

Back in 2011 I noticed that the wording of K1 was similar to that used in cryptic crossword clues.  I know that this observation has also been discovered by others like Mark Brady who have in fact taken the analysis much further than myself.  The clue relies on some cryptic word play around the sentence: BETWEEN SUBTLE SHADING AND THE ABSENCE OF LIGHT

When comparing between the two parts of that sentence [SUBTLE SHADING] and [ABSCENCE OF (light) by writing one over the other we get:

SUBTLE SHADING
ABSENCE OF

If we now remove the letters that make up LIGHT from SUBTLE SHADING then we get:
SUBESADN
ABSENCEOF

If we now remove all the common letters in each word we are left with:
USD
CEOF

These are both 3 and 4 letter strings in the ct and pt respectively (rows 1 and 2), so once again our attention is being drawn towards the fact that USD is somehow relevant.  I had sat on this clue for years not realizing that USD and CEOF was actually an anagram of FOCUSED, which I had never twigged until Mark pointed it out in his own research.

For my part, I spent a lot of my early years on Kryptos writing programs to recreate the results of parts 1-3 for myself.  The way I had written the implementation of the Vigenère tool allowed me to both encrypt and decrypt a letter for a given keyword at the same time.  It was due to this layout that I first noticed that the first letter of K4, which is the O encrypts to a K when using U as the key.  I was curious whether USD was a pointer to a start position and whether there might be a discernable pattern that could be extracted from K1.  You can use the tool to highlight the U of USD and then count along another 10 letters in K1 to find the N.  If you now count along another 9 letters then you'll drop to the second line and land on the Y.  Count another 10 letters from here and you'll land on another Y.

Encrypting OBKR using a string of UNYY as the key gives an output of KRYP.

The next observation was that if row 1 was left shifted 13 places (which we have already used as the step to discover the F, RE, V string in a previous step for matrix 1) then the UN and the YY sit on top of one another.  Right shifting row 3 by 13 places actually puts the K and C in the ct directly beneath the YY.  An encryption of UNYYCK with OBKRUO gives KRYPTO, so this was obviously an intriguing result that I continued to wrestle with through multiple papers going all the way back to 2013.

It wasn't until sometime around November 2019 that I finally realized what I had missed, which was a critical step.  The left shift of 13 in row 1 was correct and created the UNYY block of four that would encrypt to create KRYP, but what I hadn't seen was that a left shift in row 2 of 10 places led to the preservation of that same UNYY block.  You can test this for yourselves in the tool, but the crucial outcome of this operation was that it now exposes another four letter block starting in row 3 and terminating in row 2 that can be read as either CKBF or CKBD.  Either outcome when joined with UNYY would give KRYPTOSL or KRYPTOSI as an output when used as a key to encrypt the first 8 letters of K4.  It should also be noted that we previously identified this same 3x32 matrix in which the result occurs as number 1 of 6 in the previous steps.

It's such an intriguing result that you may be forgiven for thinking that we could jump straight into a description of the K4 cipher method immediately, but there are in fact another 2 or 3 steps to take into consideration before we start that process.  Each one of these additional observations starts to create something of a visual crib of how we should proceed beyond this point.  There are still 2 ingenious clues to relate that were left for us to find, but they will have to wait for the next installment.

Until then,
Matt

Step 8.  Additional observations on row shifts applied to the first matrix

When I first wrote about the phenomena being described here in 2021's Eris & Harmonia paper I was still short of a few key observations and described the cipher type as one which uses 'Invariance under transformation' to identify 8 letters in the ct for each matrix that can be used to encrypt against the letters of K4.  I still think that 'Invariance under transformation' isn't a bad classification for the cipher, but over the past couple of years I've realized that its more nuanced than that and should really be termed a 'cymatic cipher' as it scaffolds itself on the coincidental digram statistics that occur in all four views under consideration.

When I say the 4 views, I should clarify that these are for any given 3x32 matrix of the 6 identified:
1) the matrix under examination in the ct (this is the one in the top left in the tool btw)
2) the symmetric counterpart in the ct at the other end of the cylinder (for example, rows 1,2 and 3 have rows 28,27 and 26 as their symmetric counterparts)
3) the mirror of the matrix under examination in the pt
4) the symmetric counterpart of the pt matrix in 3), which is also the mirror in the pt of 2)

We have seen in the previous steps that the four boxes provided as clues were already hinting at four different view points being considered simultaneously, so the collision of digram statistics to combine something akin to standing wave patterns when certain row shifts are performed should not be too great a conceptual leap.

It will however need some supporting evidence, which we can provide via the tool in the raw view mode.  If you start afresh and left shift row 1 by 13 places as per the previous steps you will notice that the tool automatically 'right shifts' row 28 by the same number of places.  If you now left shift row 2 by 10 places it will also 'right shift' row 27 by 10 places.  These operations are 'counter symmetric' and are always performed on the symmetrical row at the other end of the cylinder.

After you've performed this operation take a look at the bottom right hand corner and you'll notice a 4 letter block that reads  DI written over DI.

As we saw in the last step this same transformation has shifted the rows in the matrix 1 position to the configuration needed to extract either UNYY CKBF or UNYY CKBD as four letter blocks, which encrypts with OBKR UOXO to give either KRYPTOS L or KRYPTOS I.  On closer inspection we can also see the letters A(8,1);N(9,2);L(10,3) in the top half of the pt and the letters
A(6,28);N(7,27);L(8,26) in the lower half of the pt.

If we use the highlighting tool to draw along the diagonal of both of those ANL relationships then the lines cross at an interesting point in the sculpture layout.  You will see that the lines cross in the block EE WE in rows 13 and 14, but directly beneath we find the letters WL.

These letters are part of a remarkable visual clue that will lead us one step further towards determining the basic rules of the cipher, but first we need to observe the clue we are being directed towards.  One of the morse decoding's from the Kryptos courtyard installation reads SHADOW FORCES.  If we look at the block of four letters above and below the letters WL in column 4 of row 15 then they are SEFO and ASOW, which are missing RC and HD respectively, but have at least drawn attention to the letters WL.

There is something else about the letters WL that is also of interest.  In the ct they are the first two raised letters that give the YA in YAR.  The letter separation between the letters WL that the ALN lines framed is 16 spaces, which means that on a cylinder of width 32 we can simply swap places, which again seems like a nod towards the concept of 'invariance under transformation'.  You can try this out for yourself using the tool by left or right shifting row 15 16 spaces either way.  On a cylinder this is geometrically equivalent to a 180 degree rotation each time.

This observation will turn out to be crucial in making sense of the cipher method when we extend it in the next step, but for the time being have a play around with rows 1-3 and 26-28 to see if you can spot anything else of interest going on.

Before the next instalment we have in fact covered just enough ground for you to take a look at Cryptogram 1 on the start page (this is the first one that loads up btw).  If you use the red button to left shift row 1 13 spaces and the green button to left shift row 2 10 places then you will be able to hit the blue 'set' button.  This will create a copy of the current row shifts in the view below.  If you now shift the middle row in the lower view 'right' by 10 places then you will be in the start position in which the two crosses of HOT and EOF occur (seen in an earlier step).

The relevance of all this will be explained (including the ABC striping in green) as we progress through the next steps, but right now, this is your first view of the actual K4 cipher in action.  If you hit the red select button and highlight the UNYY CKBD letters in order before pressing the green encrypt button then you will also see the first plain text result (note: because the C and B in the ct view you're selecting from are highlighted in green, you'll need to hit them twice in order to see them in the encrypt selection).

If you have any problems using the tool then simply hit the page refresh and that will simply start things over again.

Until next time,
Matt

Step 9.  Superposition

This next step is fundamental to the proposed solve framework, but I'll declare up front that it may be difficult to follow, but that in itself is not to be unexpected as we will now gradually start make a segue from interesting observations to some probing questions around combinatorics, so I'm hoping that any cryptographers, mathematicians or gifted generalists can start to engage with questions/flaws/improvements to the proposed solution framework as we start defining the subsequent cryptogram solves.

I've just realized that I've jumped straight into using the word 'cryptogram' to describe each matrix without giving the proper background.  The proposition is that there are 12 solves each of which extract 8 characters from the ct within the 6 matrix positions (that would imply the ct letters are a palimpsest overwritten by the rest of the ct btw).  You will immediately notice that we only have 6 defined matrix positions, so the foreknowledge that we were looking for a result in the order of 97 characters implied that we needed to extract 2 distinct cryptogram solves from each matrix position.

It was seen in the last step that some very specific patterns were seen in the ct and pt when we counter-rotated the opposite rows on the cylinder.  One of the only degrees of freedom left for us to exploit in order to derive 2 different results across the 4 views from the same matrix is to perform a symmetric rotation of the reciprocal rows whereby if we move left for example then we move the reciprocal rows at the opposite end of the cylinder left as well.  On the right hand margin of the tool, you will see two buttons that say CS and SS.  CS stands for counter symmetric and is used as we have already seen on all odd numbered solves.  The other button is SS and stands for simple symmetric.  Having access to these two different behavior's will help you verify the observations that follow.

We know from the observations already made on cryptogram 1 that the cipher framework is exploiting patterns that naturally arise from digram statistics.  During the early period of lockdown in 2020 it became apparent that there was an additional degree of freedom available in each matrix position in order to alter these statistics for any given matrix position.  Other then the extraneous L on the tableau as inspiration for this next step I can only relate that it was hours, days and weeks of tinkering that firmed up the following observation, which rather luckily was then verified in retrospect by an astonishing supporting clue.

The breakthrough was to shift all letters in both the ct and the pt right by one position in the KRYPTOS alphabet.  The key thing to consider here is that moving through the KRYPTOS alphabet is not the same as moving through the conventional Alphabet, so the effect of a right shift is that it scrambles the previous positions digram statistics to a subtle degree.  In the raw view you can use the green left and right buttons to explore the effect that this has on the pt and ct.  The value you see in the box below is the 'Kryptos Right Shift' or KRS.

Rather than approach cryptogram 2 using the framework provided on the front page we'll instead walk through the remarkable clue that was found in retrospect back in 2020.  This clue is a visual crib that extends the finding in the last step whereby we found the two intersecting lines that extend from the letters ALN in the diagonal after the left shifts of 13 and 10 have been applied to rows 1 and 2 respectively (with the counter rotation in the reciprocal rows).

Remember that the WL framed by these lines was interchangeable with the WL that corresponded to the raised letters YA in row 15.  If we take the raised letters YA and R as a clue that we need to extend a ray between them, then we can frame this instance of WL as well.  The idea of two focal points for two different sets of 'rays' conjures up a range of different metaphors, but the one idea that continued to persist back in March 2020 was that if WL was metaphoric of some kind of polarization filter (the absence of light!) and ANL was going down one path then could the other path contain the letters CDE in order to correspond to the total light given by a CANDLE.  Whilst CDE didn't jump out at any point in that period of time the letters CDI did, which phonetically would still give CANDIL.

In order to recreate this clue you'll have to use the highlighting tool in the raw view to frame both instances of WL on line 15 in the pt.  Without any row shifts applied that will highlight the following letters in rows 28, 27 and 26. F(6,28);Q(7,27);L(8,26) and I(19,28);K(18,27);W(17,26).  Now use the green right hand button to shift the all ct and pt text forward one place in the Kryptos alphabet.

Once you've done this, select the SS option button in the right hand margin (this will put the row shifts in the reciprocal rows into simple symmetric mode).  Now shift row 1 two plaaces to the right, which will also move row 28 2 places to the right.  Left shift row 2 10 places.  Right shift row 3 11 places.  You should now have NLA in place of FQL and DCI in place of IKW.

So now we have the letters of CANDIL in the path of the rays that we are projecting.  If we examine rows 1-3 in the first matrix then we can also see that there is a letter grouping of LWFR PRRG which when encrypted against the next 8 letters of K4 gives TEAM EAST.  Once again these blocks of 4 letters occur above each other at postions: P(15,1);R(20,1);R(15,2);G(20,2) and L(10,2);W(32,2);F(10,3);R(32,3)  Note also that in the reciprocal matrix we have the letters CAB striped across rows 28-26 in column 27 (this will become important later when we summarize the cipher method).

Remember that in cryptogram 1 a left shift of 10 places in row 2 showed an invariance of the letters UNYY.  By an equal token, if you now right shift row 2 by 11 places you'll find a complete invariance under transformation with the letters PRRG now occurring at P(26,3);R(31,3);R(26,2);G(31,2) and LRFW now occurring as a block of four at positions L(19,1)R(20,1)F(19,2)W(20,2).  It was this relationship that was discovered prior to the visual CANDIL clue, but it would appear given the steps above that we are also led here by virtue of a stunning piece of kinetic art in action.

I will summarize all the steps we have taken so far before we lay down the rest of the rules for the K4 cipher, but before detailing each solve (which I know many of you are waiting patiently for) there is one final clue to digest that wasn't known about until earlier this year, but which allowed me to finally arrive at a decrypt for K4 that felt self consistent enough to lay before you all in these steps.

That will have to wait until the next instalment as I appreciate this one has most likely been the heaviest yet and may have been too confusing for some, but persevere and it should make sense.  I hope I've given enough detail here to recreate the solve for cryptogram 2, but the rationale and two additional constraints not known of in 2021 should start to make sense of this after the next step.  In the meantime continue to play with the tool provided and please feel free to re-use the source code if you want to run any of your own experiments.

Until next time,
Matt

Step 10.  Somewhere in the right ballpark

In the previous steps we've followed a number of clues that have led to two candidate solves for cryptograms 1 and 2.  The framework starting to emerge would appear to be based on 6 3x32 matrices in the ct that interacts with reciprocal rows at the other end of the cylinder that are mirrored in the pt leading to 4 simultaneous views at any one time.  The first cryptogram displayed some partial invariance under transformation whereas the second showed complete invariance under transformation. The second variation of the first matrix was discovered by using a simple symmetry scheme rather than counter symmetry and all ct and pt text was shifted one place right in the Kryptos alphabet.  Both of those solves required only a single operation on the middle row in order to achieve the invariant relationship.  Both solves led to the appearance of the letters ABC striped across either the matrix itself or its reciprocal rows.  Other artefacts were also present in the first solve that we will explore later, but for the time being we have the general form of a potential cipher scheme starting to take shape.

Let's ponder a question.  What if Ed and Jim had passed away in December 1990 just after the unveiling of the sculpture.  What if no plain text clues were ever released to the general public.  How would we ever know if we were on the right track?  A lot of what has been put forward in the previous posts is no doubt of interest to some, but everyone always asks the same question, what does Jim think about this?

If you look at Jim's previous comments on record, he was once quoted as being amazed that nobody had ever retrieved the 'original matrix'.  The layout of the original decoding charts do indeed look similar to the matrices that have already been described in the previous steps, but on closer examination these appear to be 3x31 matrices and not 3x32, so I suspect the 'original matrix' he was referring to was something sitting in plain sight.

To uncover that original matrix and check it out for yourself, you need a simple piece of math to unlock it, which has at its heart a simple question that is at the very core of the previous steps.  The question is this.  If you have 3 rows of 32 characters, then in how many different ways is it possible to arrange them, or more simply how many different combinations are possible in a 3x32 matrix?
The answer is pretty simple. It's 32x32x32, which is equal to 32,768 different combinations.

So here's another question, do those numbers THREE, TWO, SEVEN, SIX and EIGHT occur anywhere in the pt?

Yes they do.  In rows 12, 13 and 14 all fitting within a perfect 3x32 matrix.  That's a pretty intriguing find, but the best part is that it's our first direct evidence that we're in the right ball park in determining the nature of the underlying K4 cipher.  There is one final observation that we can make when examining this matrix that will unlock the rest of the path ahead of us and leave us free to start deciphering all of the remaining cryptograms.  This result is so important that I've added it to the tool as 'cryptogram #0' accessible via the green button to the left of cryptogram #1.

In order to see this framed in the best way possible, select Cryptogram #0 in the tool and shift rows 1 and 2 to the left by 3 places so the pt rows in rows 1 and 2 will now start with MINUTE and SEVEN respectively.  If you now right shift row 3 10 places to the right then row 3 will now start with TXLAYER.  This is where it gets interesting.  SIX, SEVEN and TWO now sit above each other in the pt in rows 1, 2 and 3, so highlight them as well as the word EIGHT in the middle row.  At the end of row 2 you will find RTH with the letters E and E above the T forming a cross that spells THREE.  We now have the numbers 32,768 written directly in front of us contained within a 3x32 matrix.  Now shift row 2 7 places to the right.  You will find that this simple action has preserved the numbers SIX SEVEN and TWO in the same location and that the cross forming the word THREE has now moved to being one place to the left of the word SEVEN.  As an additional bonus you will also find the letters F, RE and V forming a T across columns 16 and 17 in this transformed position.

So to recap, we've just used the exact same method we used to extract the plain text from cryptograms 1 and 2 whereby we found a start and end position before shifting between them only using the middle row.

In light of this result, we're now ready to use the tool to re-appraise cryptograms 1 and 2 and start deciphering the remaining 10.

Until then,
Matt

The Christmas party season starts with a vengeance in the next couple of days, so these posts may not be so regular until the week between Christmas and New Year, but I have had some thoughts on how we can best organize ourselves as we lay out the proposed solves for all 12 cryptograms.

We have been using the 'KRYPTOS From Start to Finish' title for all the posts so far, so instead I'll switch the headings on the next posts to 'Cymatic Cipher Cryptogram #1' etc ...for each solve.  If people have specific questions or perhaps even better solutions for a given matrix then we can converse in the context of the cryptogram number, so that all relevant discussion remains in context.

The rules of the cipher should be starting to become clearer now, but I'll declare them again here in order to recap everything we covered in the previous steps.  We can also begin to make some sense of the general rules as well as there were still too many degrees of freedom in the solves presented in 2021's Eris and Harmonia paper.  We also have the advantage of now knowing the order in which the matrices should be processes in this time round.
A fundamental change to the previous paper is that we can cull any row shifts that don't create an ABC relationship in one of the 4 matrix views.  This is a huge advance as it cuts the 32,768 possible row shifts that we would have had to have checked down to a manageable number for each cryptogram that can be checked by hand.
In the previous paper we looked for two repeating trigrams in the vertical plane in order to fix our start position, but it will become obvious that cryptograms 1-6 rely specifically on the presence of trigrams that must contain A, B and C.  This start position that locks in the ABC relationship is the one from which we extract the 8 letters each time, but it is the transformation position that reveals which 8 letters are invariant in each case.  To recap, that transformation position is always discovered by moving row 2 in the matrix to a position that will turn out to have its own set of associated rules.
Not all cryptograms are perfectly invariant, but as we shall see in the case of cryptogram #1 there are some interesting rules that appear to come into play under such circumstances.

So what we shall see in the course of the next 12 solves is that in all cases:

1) There are 2 solves per matrix position.
2) Odd numbered solves use counter symmetric rotations and even ones use symmetric ones
3) The row shift positions are initially fixed by identifying candidates that contain trigrams of ABC for cryptograms 1-6 and XYZ for cryptograms 7,8,11 and 12. (Cryptograms 9 and 10 are exceptional for reasons that will be explained).
4) Transformed positions that expose the invariant 8 letters are always achieved by moving row 2.
5) After each cryptogram is solved all ct and pt is right shifted one place in the KRYPTOS alphabet.
6) The 8 invariant letters identified are then used as the key to 'encrypt' 8 letters of K4 at a time.

There are some other really interesting features of the cipher, especially for those cryptograms that don't display complete invariance, but these 6 fundamental rules stay consistent throughout and drive out all the known plain text in the correct positions.

I appreciate that this has been a lot of information to take in over the last week or so, but I'm happy to report that we're finally ready to begin!

Until then,
Matt

Looking at k4 ..again.. I noticed something I find interesting.
On any given alphabet the first letter of the alphabet will be equal to zero.
for instance in the 'kryptos' alphabet ie: KRYPTOSABCDEFGHIJLMNQUVWXZ corresponds to the values 0,1,2,3,4..so on
so any plain text letter that encrypts to itself in a modN alphabet will be encrypted with the letter K. example: P=3 + K=0 = P=3 && K=0+K=0 = K=0
The inverse also must be true for K encrypted by any letter of the alphabet. K=0 + P=3 = P=3 && K=0+K=0 = K=0
Since this rule must hold true and looking at the K4 encryption I realized that two letters encrypt to themselves the K of berlinclocK
and the S of eastnortheaSt.

Provided
1) Sanborn was honest about the plain text given as clues
2) The characters of the cipher text are in order
3) My thinking is not flawed

That would mean that either the S or the K must represent the first letter of the alphabet (or technique) used for encryption.
This caused me to shift my attention not to what alphabet was used but rather what key could produce that result.
It seemed to me that the key would be something in Sanborn fashion similar to palimpsest and abscissa.
The problem is that there isn't one at least not that I can find. After programming up a few simple lines of code
I exhausted all the words(English mostly) at my disposal and didn't find anything that looked like it might be something Jim would use.

So what conclusions should be drawn?
Are the letter maybe not in order?
Two part encryption? (or more)
Long running key?

Can anyone give concrete reasons why any of these can be ruled out given what we know about cryptos.

Well I think thats all the info I have so far. Hope everyone is doing well for the holidays.

t:
If a one-time pad were used, then the S and K would be against the first letter of the alphabet for that position.  In terms of the ABC alphabet, this just means that there's an "A" in the pad text being used to encipher the "S" or "K" character, so no substitution takes place.

Example:

EASTNORTHEAST PT
BLZCDCYYGCKAZ Pad (ABCDEFG..., A=0)
FLRVQQPRNGKSS CT

Interestingly, having this first alphabet character in the plaintext also means that the pad character in that position will be used verbatim (e.g., the "A" in "EAST" preserves the pad's character).

- I to R: 12

- H to G: 25
- T to H: 10
