s: Probable encryption system used for K4
t:
Hello everyone,

My name is Joackim, I am a cybersecurity engineer, and I am French. First of all, I want to apologize for my mediocre English, but I hope my message will still be understandable.

Lately, I've been particularly interested in the last part of the encrypted code (K4), and I must say that one aspect seems particularly intriguing to me, especially in light of the various clues provided by Jim Sanborn. I've been following the discussions closely, and it seems to me that no one has raised this point yet (I could be mistaken, and if so, I apologize). I want to clarify that the observation I'm about to share may not be entirely reliable considering all the clues, but I find it interesting enough to discuss here. I will focus solely on the "NORTHEAST" index, which should be encrypted as "QQPRNGKSS".

Here, we can observe that consecutive letters in the alphabet are encoded with the same letter (QQ = NO, SS = ST). This should be taken with caution because according to new clues, FLRV, which translates to EAST (RV = ST), invalidates our previous hypothesis that consecutive letters in the alphabet are encrypted with the same letter. However, this observation remains valid only if this code fragment (FLRV) is encoded differently from the index (QQPRNGKSS). Nevertheless, I have conducted research to discover a encryption system that could cause this type of anomaly (QQ=NO, SS=ST) in an encrypted text, and I have found only one which encrypts consecutive letters in the alphabet (in reverse order). This is the Wheatstone cryptograph. You can find more information in the publication: "Riverbank Publications No. 20 Several Machine-Ciphers and Methods for Their Solution." https://incoherency.co.uk/interest/several-machine-ciphers.pdf

You'll notice my remarks when analyzing the example given on page 9. So, you might say that "QQPRNGKSSS," which decrypts to "NORTHEAST," is in the right order, but what about "TSaehtrON"? If we assume the keyword "KRYPTOS" to create the alphabet, then the alphabet can be constructed as follows:

KRYPTOS
ABCDEFG
HIJLMNQ
UVWXZ

That is: KahurbivycjwpdlxtemzSGQ

I tried to reconstruct an alphabet from the NORTHEAST index (TSEAEHTRON), and something caught my attention. (Make sure you understand the methodology of this Wheatstone cryptograph algorithm beforehand.):

QQPRNGKSS
TSAEHTRON

TS: TUVWXYZ+ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRS = 26 (Q)
SA: STUVWXYZ+A = 9 (P)
AE: ABCDE = 4 (R)
EH: EFGH = 3 (N)
HT: HIJKLMNOPQRST = 12 (G)
TR: TUVWXYZ+ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQR = 25 (K)
RO: RSTUVWXYZ+ABCDEFGHIJKLMNO = 24 (S)
ON: OPQRSTUVWXYZ+ABCDEFGHIJKLMN : 26 (S)

+ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ
N--------SQKG------P---R--

Here, we notice the letters SQKG, which strongly resemble the "SGKQ" portion of the alphabet created from the KRYPTOS key above. This is a thin clue, I admit, however, Jim Sanborn could have modified this algorithm, or the algorithm could be similar to a clock cipher. Or the keyword could simply be something else. I also encourage you to explore the works of Sir Charles Wheatstone regarding the telegraph. Additionally, I want to add that from memory, some Berlin clocks are involved in telegraph use, and the Earth's magnetic field has a certain history with such primitive technology.

Furthermore, I absolutely do not believe in a multilayer encryption for K4. Jim proposes a challenge here that seems achievable manually, which is perceptible. Under no circumstances would he propose an indecipherable challenge, as the main objective of this sculpture is to convey an artistic message, not to provide a lifelong challenge.

If you're interested in this initial evidence, please share your discoveries here, as simple letters replaced by dashes for you could reveal a keyword for others. Good luck, personally I'm stopping here for now because this little discovery has made me crazy enough to doubt and share it with you here. :)

The WW-II Japanese PURPLE system divided the plaintext alphabet into 2 pieces (initially vowels AEIOUY and consonants) and encrypted the 6 vowels using a different algorithm than the 20 consonants.
I wonder if we have something similar going on here.  Consider the following, as an encryption method:
1.  Take the 4 "extra" columns at the right end of the tableau and slide/rotate them according to some 4 letter keyword.
2.  Encrypt K4 as a normal Vig cipher:  for each plaintext character, using a repeating keyword, select the alphabet row.  Locate the plaintext letter in the top row, and run down that column to the selected row to locate the ciphertext letter as we did with K1.
3.  However, if the plaintext letter is one of the 4 letters in the top row of the extended tableau, use that column instead.  Run down that column to the selected row and locate the ciphertext letter.
4.  Steps 3/4 provide 2 alternate encrypton alphabets:  one for the 4 letters in the extended tableau, and another for the remaining 22 letters using the main tableau.
5.  Decryption is done in a similar fashion.  Uisng the Vig keyword, select the alphabet.  Run across the selected row to find the ciphrtext letter, and read the plaintext letter from the top row.  If the ciphertext letter appears in the extended tableau, use the plaintext from the extended tableau.
6.  The four letter keyword for the extended tableau can be by prior agreement between the parties, or can be sent as a "message indicator" as part of the ciphertext message.
It's a workable encryption scheme.  My question is, if such a system was used, how would we be able to confirm this by examination of the ciphertext message?

The Berlin clock essentially uses banks of lights to represent time.
For hours, there are 2 banks.
The top is a bank of 4 red lights representing 5 hours each.
Below a bank of 4 red lights representing 1 hour each

Below is a bank of 11 orange minute lights representing 5 minute blocks, coloured for 15 minute intervals.

The general principle for the separate banks is that every 4 units, the light one cell up is lit.

Hi all!
I'm new to this forum. My name is Martijn, I'm a programmer from the Netherlands and I love solving puzzles like Kryptos.

- Theory -
Well, it's not really a theory, and maybe other people have posted similar things. But I got thinking about the Mengenlehreuhr (Berlin Clock) and each time can be represented by 4 numbers. 01:30 will translate to [0, 1, 6, 0], 15:46 translates to [3, 0, 9, 1]. So I'm basically counting the turned on lights in each row, starting at the top.
Just like a keyword in Vigenere, a time could represent a 'keyword', where each number would tell you how much to shift in the alphabet. So "BERLINCLOCK" encrypted with 15:46 [3, 0, 9, 1] would lead to "EEAMLNLMRCT" in a standard alphabet.
In this system, the shifts are limited from 0 to 4 in three of the four rows, and from 0 to 11 in one of the four rows.
If something similar would be happening in one of the steps to solve K4, this could explain some observations of relatively small shifts in letters.
This is for example observed in Table 3 of the Cryptodiagnosis of “Kryptos K4” paper by Richard Bean where we see that most letters (7 out of 9) stay within the 0-4 range and some (2 out of 9) stay within the 0-11 range.
It's not very strong, I know, but maybe this will give someone else a creative idea :-)

- Funfact -
In the Netherlands we have a puzzle competition each year organised by the AIVD (the Dutch CIA) with a series of very complicated puzzles and encryptions. It's called "AIVD kerstpuzzel". There's normally 20-30 puzzles and they try to make them in such a way that each puzzle is solved by at least one person and nobody solves all the puzzles. Most years they succeed in doing that. Anyway, that's how I got into cryptography and I've seen quite some new and creative ways to encrypt messages in the puzzles from that competition.

Sukhwant,
I have to step in to argue with you about the "mistakes" in Kryptos. All the apparent "mistakes" in the ciphers are clues. Wending one's way through Kryptos requires identifying clues and implications and then acting on them. I am puzzled by your claim that K4 has a mistake. I wonder what mistake that is. There are clues in K4, yes. One of them is marked KLU and points to DIAWINFBN. This clue is related to the part of the K3 PT passage that says ...PRESENTLYDETAILSOFTHEROOMWITHINEMERGED... So, you can see that the odd language used in parts of the PT suggest there are meanings other than the obvious. The most important one is the passage
THEREMAINSOFPASSAGEDEBRISTHATENCUMBEREDTHELOWERPARTOFTHEDOORWAYWASREMOVED. Many see this as sayingTHE REMAINS OF PASSAGE DEBRIS THAT ENCUMBERED THE LOWER PART OF THE DOORWAY WAS REMOVED. Of course, if read like this, it is obvious that the verb WAS should be WERE and, hence, WAS is a mistake. On the other hand, there is another way to read the passage, it isTHERE MAIN S OF PASSAGE DEBRIS THAT ENCUMBERED THE LOWER PART OF THE DOORWAY WAS REMOVED. Here we see that the verb WAS is used correctly and modifies the MAIN S. Extremely important note here: The major implication is to replace the S into the same place that it came from.

So, it makes sense to assume that apparent mistakes in Kryptos are not mistakes, but are clues or implications or might have to be read in a different, more correct, way.
I might comment further that I have never found an error in Kryptos. At this point, I believe there are none.
PaulK

I think some folks here are reading WAY too much into Jim's reply to Sukhwant's attempted decryption. I thought Jim's reply was clear: your solution is wrong. That's all he really needs to say. He's certainly not going to tell you something like "Well, you got 4 or 5 words right, but the rest is wrong." When Jim says it's all or nothing, the simplest interpretation is that he means the decryption technique will reveal the entire plaintext, not bits and pieces of it. In other words, it'll unfold as it did for K1, K2 and K3 (with the hiccup at the end of K2 probably due to Jim not appreciating the negative impact of a missing ciphertext letter).

For those who disagree, I would challenge you to draft any pleasant reply that Jim could send that you couldn't (or wouldn't) attempt to twist into a deliberate clue. I say "pleasant reply" because I think Sukhwant would have been more upset if Jim had written something extremely curt like "Your solution is wrong. Jim" (Would be pretty hard to read anything into that.) Jim is polite because he knows how much time people have invested in trying to solve his puzzle, so I don't think it's fair (or healthy) to read into it more than a straightforward, common sense interpretation.

Whoever ultimately figures out the decryption and plaintext of K4 will not need to ask Jim if it's correct, any more than those who first solved K1-K3.

--Rob

I've tried to understand your method for a while now without success, but think I got further this time.  To [hopefully] add clarity for others:

When you refer to "satisfies the Vigenere Matrix", you mean to use the outside ABC alphabet of the tableau as a lookup to the inside KRYPTOS alphabet.  (Perhaps this can be referred to as a Layer 2 lookup).

So, in your example of LVL: row L and column L intercept at V.

One of these Ls would be considered the plaintext, and the V would be the cipher text (when he was encrypting).  Therefore, the source of the other L is the puzzle (and this is what your method tries to explain).

Do you suggest that this comes from another adjacent ciphertext in K4?  Or, does it come from elsewhere in K1-K3?  This is the part I'm still a little fuzzy on.

This method can probably be reduced to a one-time pad with the pad somehow coming from the sculpture in some systematic way.

A Vigenere tableau is simply an addition table.  If you assign values to each letter in the alphabet (starting with zero), then a cipher character is just the sum of the plaintext and key character values (modulo 26).

Example:
Alphabet K=0, R=1, Y=2, P=3, T=4, O=5, S=6, A=7 ... X=24, Z=25

(An example from K1)

B+P=E  -->  08 + 03 = 11

E+A=M  -->  11 + 07 = 18

T+L=U  -->  04 + 17 = 21

W+I=F  -->  23 + 15 = 12

E+M=P  -->  11 + 18 = 03

E+P=H  -->  11 + 03 = 14

N+S=Z  -->  19 + 06 = 25

What complicates things about using the ABC alphabet to look into the KRYPTOS alphabet is that there's a mapping required.  Perhaps this serves as the infamous mask.

(An example from K4 crib. I reverse-engineered the key letters by looking
them up in the Vigenere Tableau using the "Layer 2" method, but these
would be what Sukhwant Singh's method tries to explain their source)

N+H=Q  -->  13 + 07 = K[20]

O+G=Q  -->  14 + 06 = K[20]

R+M=P  -->  17 + 12 = K[03]

T+I=R  -->  19 + 08 = K[01]

H+M=N  -->  07 + 12 = K[19]

s: Why can't we decode Kryptos K4?
t:
The questionmarks apply only to the apparent plaintext you get after deciphering K2 and K3. After that they don't appear (at least to the point where I am working on the puzzle). Actually, I can't envision any reasonable way to re-introduce punctuation marks into Kryptos after beginning to work on K4. The questionmarks need to be ignored when working on Kryptos ciphers.
No monkey wrench has been thrown into the works. I have found no unintentional errors so far. There are intentional errors, however. Example: The misspelled PALIMPCEST that appears in Sanborn's notes does two things. When you consider the C as being in English, it results in the Q appearing in IQLUSION. But if you consider it to be an S in cyrillic, the word is spelled correctly. This is a clue and is related to the UNDERGRUUND misspelling which reveals a misspelled CBET the CT meaning LIGHT in Russian. As I have shown to the group, the meaning of K1 PT refers to the ABSENCE OF LIGHT. Just like the implied need to replace the S in K2 CT, we get the implication to attach C in front of BETWEEN..., forming CBET, LIGHT. The clue QJNCE at the end of row 1 of K2 CT hints to changing the J in FIVJ (VJYQT twice) so that it forms the word FIVE. Doing this, causes K1 PT to now read as BETWEEN SUBTLE SHADING AND THE ABSENT EOF (END OF FILE) LIGHT LIES THE NUANT EOF IQLUSION. One of the interpretations of IQLUSION is that it should be INCLUSION. So, this clue talks about including the something to the end of the line. Note, by doing this the keyword ABSCISSA now becomes complete because we are not now talking about C being the speed of light not fitting, but now we have light. K1 PT was a clue in the first place!
Forgive me for going on like that, but I think I have made my point.

Now, having not yet arrived at the final Kryptos matrix, I do not know this. HOWEVER, the fact that those strings were assigned to specific places turned on a red light in my mind that they were keywords. By analyzing what I had in front of me, I determined that three keywords must exist. The fact that the K in MZFPK corresponded to the K in CLOCK, is a clue. Analysis of the bottom lines of K2 PT using the shifts of ABSCISSA revealed that Z is attached to the front of K4, which now begins ZOBKR. I have mentioned this many times. So, now what was the K4 matrix with 97 characters is now a matrix that has 98 characters. Because 98 has factors of 7 and 14, I tried padding the matrix to 7 columns. Now, appearing in column 5 are three Ks that appear in multiples of 14 skips. Further checking shows that, in fact, we have a keyword THEBERLINCLOCK, which has 14 characters in it. From the several clues that pointed to it, it was easy to determine that MENGENLEHREUHR, the name of the Berlin clock that is read via DIGITAL INTERPRETATION, was another possible keyword. How it fit was determined later. Another keyword, ABSCISS, can easily be imagined as applying to the several rows of K4 text that now ended in double letters. I successfully used all three of these keywords in the first steps of solving K4. This can all be seen in my Side-by-Side file, which I have pointed to many times.
Now, my memory may not serve me now about this, but I do not recall Sanborn saying that BERLINCLOCK and EASTNORTHEAST are present and can be read letter-for-letter the same way in the final solution. I do recall that they were assigned specific positions and that they were represented as plaintext.In his recent message to me and also in a prior message he mentioned including the clues given. He did not specify what the clues were, but most people would assume they are BERLINCLOCK and EASTNORTHEAST. I remain convinced that BERLIN and NORTHEAST somehow come into the picture, however. And I am, beyond a doubt, sure that the final has 97 characters.

To address your clarification question, your observation about what is left after the dust settles is quite valid. This implies that there are AT LEAST two forms of manipulation, but in the CT at first, with the addition of Z to the front of OBKR. In the steps following this, the results of ciphers are commonly called plaintext, but in the case of Kryptos, one can hardly call these results plaintext. Rather, they are matrices that use clues to determine the next steps.

In my line of work, reverse engineering, it is vital to try and understand every decision that was made by the previous engineer(s). This is why I set out to fully understand K3 in every way possible. K1 and K2 share the same technique with one small change. Perhaps K3 and K4 share something as well.

The first three ciphers are straight-forward with K3 having multiple correct ways to decrypt it. There is some value in seeing how ciphers are structured, but we must move on and stop loitering.

Once these three ciphers are decrypted, we soon discover some clues in them. We go after solving what they mean and then act on them instead of dwelling on the methods of solving a simple cipher.
The small change you mention is not small in the large picture. You are speaking about the S needing to be inserted into the ninth position before the end of K2 CT. When you negotiate your way through the puzzle, you soon recognize the importance of this. In fact, inserting this S is crucial to moving forward. Do you now sense that wrestling with the methods of solving K3 rank low as compared to discovering the clues that exist? I mean, after all, having followed the clues and solved for insertion of the S, you must now realize that this must be only the first clue to be discovered. You must also realize that Kryptos is not just ciphers, but also must be manipulated, when called for, outside the realm of ciphers. In fact, solving Kryptos involves finding clues and acting on them, not concentrating on the various ways to solve a cipher. Believe me, you will get a lot of practice doing both, but finding ways to solve each cipher will become as natural as looking at the back of your hand.
So far in my trek, I have used vigenere, rotation, caesar, repad, flip horizontally, flip vertically, exchange columns, playfair, scytale and other forms of skip. All done successfully. Some of it was easy, but most was not. It gets harder and more complex as one moves along.
By the way, I'm responding to a number of postings to the group lately as a way to relax. Right now, the path through Kryptos for me is full of unseen obstacles and rabbit holes. I keep looking back to the last valid matrix that I came up with and trying again.

s: Ed's time and role in Athens
t:
Hi All,

Apologies for the lack of communication since my 'start to finish' series of posts just before Christmas, but my time was focused on reaching the deadline for the submission of an academic paper that pretty much wrapped everything I'd already disclosed in those posts. The paper was eventually rejected due to a lack of academic discipline, so I'm looking at an alternate route to disclosure this summer that skips the need to publish in a formally recognised journal.  When I say disclosure, that's still the same 97 letter string as I've been hawking around for the last year or so, which reads, 'KRYPTO SITE AM EAST. ROUND EAST NORTH EAST. I-FORCES. DYNAMO WAVE ROUND GROUP. TE. BERLIN CLOCK. CHURCH TUNNEL UK GCHQ CODE(R)'. There may well be some alterations required to this string, but my confidence in the first 32 letters is extremely high. The fact that BERLIN CLOCK also drops out in the right location from the same method further strengthens my conviction that the K4 cipher is cymatic in nature. Cymatics deals with the patterns made by wave interference and K4 would appear to be a fantastic exposition of such a phenomenon. I think I may have lost many of you on the way to this point previously, so I'm not going to muddy the waters as most of the method is available in my previous long form write ups such as 'Eris and Harmonia'
For this post though I am asking for general group knowledge about Ed's time in Athens. Do we know what his role was there? Most importantly, what was he working on? Did he devise a new type of classical cipher in that period? Any group knowledge on this beyond what is available in a general Google search would be much appreciated as it seems to be the missing link between the cymatic cipher method and the stepwise evidence I presented before Christmas.

Many thanks,
Matt
p.s. I'll put the rejected paper in my personal folder later today in case it's useful to anyone.

I have a file entitled "Ivan's Find" wherein I show a second way to insert Z in front of OBKR. In the file, you see where YAR does play a role. For those who haven't seen it, it has a notable other feature. It has the decryption using the standard alphabet at the side of the tableau, and the "extra L" row of the tableau at the top, which demonstrates one of the instances that they are there for a reason. And your notion about the Cyrillic connection of YAR is correct. You show the string SSKGNR which has NGKSS in reverse. This string is in its NUANCE OF ILLUSION configuration. It's normal configuration is NSKGS, whose occupation in the 10-shift of K4+Z has strong importance (begins JYLUB).

PaulK

There are two places where running all shifts are called for in the early stages of Kryptos. The first one is to run all shifts of ABSCISSA on the last 120 characters of K2 CT (with the S included). The other one is to run all Caesar shifts of K4 (with Z attached to the front).

Kasiski works fine for Vigenere with repeated ciphertext (e.g., VJYQT in K1) where the ciphertext maintains the positional order with the plaintext (the 1:1 we kept asking about).

But if you follow a Vigenere substitution with a transposition, you lose that correspondence and mask the repeats and can't use Kasiski directly.  That takes away the repeating ciphertext strings.

You can't attack the substitution without first solving the transposition, and you can't attack the transposition without first solving the substitution.

Hi Doug -- I can't think of any tests that could conclusively tell that plaintext had undergone substitution followed by transposition. As for how I would go about solving such a beast, I think I would have to brute force it: try a candidate transposition and then test the resulting intermediate CT for high polyalphabetic incidence of coincidence and/or Kasiski hits. Unfortunately, with such a small amount of ciphertext, the false alarm rate on poly IC will be high if the period of the polyalphabetic substitution (i.e. the keyword length) is greater than about 7. And of course there is no guarantee that the plaintext has repeated trigraphs (or longer) separated by some multiple of the keyword length. (The exception with K4 would be if Jim chose a keyword with 9 letters, then Kasiski would certainly ping on EASTNORTHEAST.)

Many years ago, I tried brute-forcing thousands of different transpositions/rotations (single and double) and then scoring the intermediate ciphertext. (I think I restricted my scoring to poly IC's with periods of 12 or less). I don't recall if I did Kasiski testing as well -- I'll have to check my software. My recollection is that I found many instances of poly IC's exceeding 7% for longer keyword lengths, so if Jim chose a keyword with 8 letters or more, the correct transposition will be hard to recognize just from its IC vs. the many false positives that score even higher.  --Rob

You can actually use the cribs to rule out a lot more periods IF (and only if) you assume the polyalphabetic substitution is a standard Vigenere or a Quag III (like K1 and K2).  I know you know this stuff Rob, but for everyone else, here is how:

Let's say you number each letter 0-25, with K=0, R=1, Y=2...Z=25 and so on.  We know that in a Vigenere or a Quag III cipher, the following relationship will hold:  CT(x) - PT(x) = KL (x), where CT is value of the Ciphertext letter, PT is the Plaintext, KL is the Key Letter and x is the "xth" position in the cipher.  Therefore, another way to derive the implied ELYOIE keyword from the original BERLIN crib is do do the following (with mod 26):   [19,2,3,22,4,4] - [8,11,1,17,15,19] = [11,17,2,5,15,11] or in English [NYPVTT] - [BERLIN] = [ELYOIE].

If we want to test Rob's comment above that the cipher is polyalphabetic with a period of 19, we can offset the two cribs by a multiple of 19 like this:

E    A    S    T    N    O    R    T    H    E    A    S    T
                B    E    R    L    I    N    C    L    O    C    K

We can do the same for the ciphertext:
F    L    R    V    Q    Q    P    R    N    G    K    S    S
                N    Y    P    V    T    T    M    Z    F    P    K

Since we hypothesize that letters in the same column are enciphered using the same key letter, we can begin to build a table of relationships that will ultimately help us derive the alphabet used in the cipher.  There are 9 overlaps above, and therefore there are 9 relationships we know, which are:

pos(q)-pos(n)=pos(n)-pos(b)
pos(q)-pos(o)=pos(y)-pos(e)
pos(p)-pos(r)=pos(p)-pos(r)
pos(r)-pos(t)=pos(v)-pos(l)
pos(n)-pos(h)-pos(t)-pos(i)
pos(g)-pos(e)=pos(t)-pos(n)
pos(k)-pos(a)=pos(m)-pos(c)
pos(s)-pos(s)=pos(z)-pos(l)
pos(s)-pos(t)=pos(f)-pos(o)

Where pos(x) is the position of the letter x in the ciphertext alphabet.  Note that we don't know the absolute position of any letter, only the relative position.  That said, one can still use relative position and algebra to find logical inconsistencies. In this case there is a really obvious inconsistency second to the bottom in the table (s-s cannot equal z-l).   Therefore, we know this isn't a quag III or Vigenere with a period of 19.   Which leads to my final thought:

How do we better use the cribs to test a large number of possible techniques or answers quickly?

Been thinking about how one might do this for a few days.  I don't know a conclusive generalized test for ALL transposition methods, but you can make some observations about this specific situation.  For example:

1) Any transposition method similar to K3 will leave a telltale repeating "period".  As an example, K3's period occurs every 192 characters.  That pattern is an artifact of the encryption method (in the case of K3, double transposition). Obviously, more exotic transpositions (spirals, diagonals, etc.) will not leave behind this sort of artifact. Assuming this isn't something exotic, you could create an "untransposed" set of intermediate ciphertexts for all 97 possible "periods"
2) From there, you can check the Poly IC for each one to see if any of the intermediate cipher texts exhibit any periodic properties.
3) If you get a hit on one, then you can check for conflicts.   For this, you use the cribs.  As an example, let's say you think the intermediate ciphertext is periodic at 7.  Let's further say that you observe that "S" decrypts to "E" in one position, but 14 letters later "S" encrypts to "N".   This is impossible, and therefore your "hit" is a false positive and can be discarded.
4) if something passes items 2 and 3 above, you can attempt to solve.

All of this can be done in a spreadsheet.

As an aside, my personal bias is that Sanborn didn't do a Vigenere/quagmire combined with a transposition.  Why? The big reason is the implied keyletters that you get from the cribs don't look much like English, and that's trying multiple different grid/tableaus (see below).  The astute reader will note that Sanborn could have simply used a different keyed alphabet besides the Kryptos alphabet.  If that's what Sanborn did, then I think there is a real possibility that we could have the entire plaintext and still not be able to deduce the method.

Sorry, but your statistics are mistaken.   What you have identified is most likely random variance.

Here is why.  Random text is what statisticians would call a "uniform distribution."  All letters are equally likely.  Such a population will have a mean of 12.5 and a standard deviation of 7.21 (assuming letters are given the values 0-25).   So... if you want to test to see if your sample of 24 is somehow unusual, you just look at the confidence interval.  In this case, that is given by:  12.5 ± ((7.21/√24) x 2.064) = 9.46 to 15.53.

Said another way, a sample of 24 letters is NOT 99% likely to be 12.5.   Rather it's 95% likely to be between ~9.5 and ~15.5.

I know this is an old thread, but I want to revisit it because its super relevant.  In the thread, Jim Melichar (who I wish was still around) threw out a cipher challenge.

JAAUL MBOQE QNACF FGJHM SMQTJ HFGOL XDDFW OPIKA DYEJQ VIWYC IQVWZ JYFSZ VOKRK YZPKH ENXTF PXWFD VXWIC YPNHJ RHFZG LYYGE QUKDJ TNBRQ KBVQM KJXCZ XVXHVLPNLA CDSRR MTXBL HXBLT OAPZJ TVIWJ WCLOO QQDJA KHDUE GEOJE OAEHH ZABOJ VEWGG QZEGA YBJWI

I know this is not a forum for cipher challenges, but there is a point here.  First, it represents something that Sanborn might have done.   Second, it gives us a roadmap on how to attack a two stage cipher, which is probably what k4 is.   Why is it something Sanborn may have done?  Well... the plaintext was first masked (in Jim M’s challenge, we know that 3 of every 5 letters were altered), then it was enciphered using the same method as K1 and K2, but with a different key.   The periodicity of the second step is destroyed by the masking step.  If you have been here a while, this should sound VERY familiar.

Unfortunately, with Kryptos we don't know the method, but we do have a rather long crib.  So, if k4 is indeed a two step process, then the algorithm for solving is:  1) speculate what step two might be; 2) TEST IT (emphasis added) and look for statistics that indicate you are on the right track.  Incidence of coincidence, and Kasiski are examples; 3) use the crib to forcibly unwind the masking step and see if that results in readable plaintext; and 4) rinse and repeat.

That's basically the roadmap to solving the challenge above: 1) run a dictionary attack and look for output that is periodic (in this case at period 5).  2) once you identify an intermediate ciphertext with the appropriate Poly IC (and it should be obvious once you do), then you "unmask" to arrive at the final plaintext.  This is difficult to break, but as Jim contended, it IS doable.  It took a few hours with a spreadsheet.
I think you should look and report back

s: Some Handy Spreadsheet Tools for Everyone
t:
For those of you who like to fiddle with K4-type ciphers in a spreadsheet, I have written some User Defined Formulas which will make your life MUCH easier. If you aren't familiar with UDFs, google it.  They are super handy.   I'm attaching three such formulas here as follows:

1) Vigenere_Decode:  this UDF will decode a Vigenere cipher given: a) the ciphertext; b) the keyword and c) the keyed alphabet.  All must be strings, but they can simply be text strings in an excel sheet.  The keyed alphabet can be anything.  It could be ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ for a normal vigenere cipher or KRYPTOSABCDEFGHIJLMNQUVWXZ for the kryptos K1 and K2 ciphers.  Tested and confirmed accurate on K1 and K2.

2) EveryXthLetter:  this will return every Xth letter of a text string.  The inputs are: a) the text string, b) the starting point; and c) the interval of X.  This is extremely useful for transposition ciphers and for testing for periodic properties, especially in combination with #3 below.

3) IncidenceOfCoincidence:  this will return the incidence of coincidence of a text string.  The only input is the text string.    For the uninitiated, an IC value near .067 signals English-like frequencies.  Random text has an IC of .038.

Function Vigenere_Decode(ciphertext As String, keyword As String, alphabet As String) As String
    Dim i As Integer
    Dim keywordIndex As Integer
    Dim decodedCharIndex As Integer
    Dim decodedChar As String
    Dim result As String

    ' Convert ciphertext and keyword to uppercase
    ciphertext = UCase(ciphertext)
    keyword = UCase(keyword)
    alphabet = UCase(alphabet)

    For i = 1 To Len(ciphertext)
        ' Get the index of the current keyword character
        keywordIndex = (i - 1) Mod Len(keyword) + 1

        ' Get the index of the current ciphertext character in the alphabet
        decodedCharIndex = (InStr(1, alphabet, Mid(ciphertext, i, 1)) - 1) - (InStr(1, alphabet, Mid(keyword, keywordIndex, 1)) - 1)

        ' Handle negative indexes
        If decodedCharIndex < 0 Then
            decodedCharIndex = decodedCharIndex + Len(alphabet)
        End If

        ' Get the decoded character
        decodedChar = Mid(alphabet, decodedCharIndex + 1, 1)

        ' Append the decoded character to the result
        result = result & decodedChar
    Next i

    Vigenere_Decode = result
End Function

Function EveryXthLetter(text As String, startingPoint As Integer, stepSize As Integer) As String
    Dim result As String
    Dim i As Integer

    If Len(text) < startingPoint Then
        EveryXthLetter = "Starting point exceeds the length of the text."
        Exit Function
    End If

    For i = startingPoint To Len(text) Step stepSize
        result = result & Mid(text, i, 1)
    Next i

    EveryXthLetter = result
End Function

Function IncidenceOfCoincidence(text As String) As Double
    Dim totalLetters As Integer
    Dim frequencies(0 To 25) As Integer
    Dim i As Integer

    ' Initialize frequencies array to 0
    For i = 0 To 25
        frequencies(i) = 0
    Next i

    ' Count occurrences of each letter
    totalLetters = 0
    For i = 1 To Len(text)
        Dim c As String
        c = Mid(text, i, 1)
        If c Like "[A-Za-z]" Then
            Dim index As Integer
            If Asc(UCase(c)) >= 65 And Asc(UCase(c)) <= 90 Then
                index = Asc(UCase(c)) - 65
            Else
                index = Asc(UCase(c)) - 97
            End If
            frequencies(index) = frequencies(index) + 1
            totalLetters = totalLetters + 1
        End If
    Next i

    ' Calculate incidence of coincidence
    Dim sum As Double
    sum = 0
    For i = 0 To 25
        sum = sum + (frequencies(i) * (frequencies(i) - 1))
    Next i

    If totalLetters > 1 Then
        IncidenceOfCoincidence = sum / (totalLetters * (totalLetters - 1))
    Else
        IncidenceOfCoincidence = 0
    End If
End Function

Hi Bob:

Re: "I wonder... can anyone else here solve this?   I'm not holding my breath, but I would love to be wrong."

I gather you mean besides me? 😉  (I did post here that I had solved Jim's challenge cipher a few weeks after he posted it in early November 2015). Looking back at my filed email, I see you also solved it back in November 2015, as did Andrew Jones. I think Doug Price might have also -- he was certainly on the right track.  --Rob

Extra Extra!

I had another look at a way to apply the last letters of the K1-K3 passages words and needed a way to strip down those 13-75-75 words groups into something more K4's 50-47 characters.

What I found was that splitting all of the odd numbers letters and even numbered letters into two groups that they retained the same the sinusoidal property!

The suggests that Sanborn went to great lengths to:
(1) decide on a 75 word passage length for K2 and again the same word length 75 for K3
(2) fill in the offsets required based on some sinusoidal-like scheme
(3) fill in a selection of word endings that were close to the offset required, and of course, ensuring at the same time "L" wasn't used
(4) then, work backwards to fill in passages that spoke of the method (or blind alleys) that are meant for K4...

I do not know how humanly feasible that lot is, i certainly couldn't do it even with a couple of years up my sleeve, maybe!

There is still a question of how to apply some many letters into K4 as intended, if indeed it is meant to be solved this way...

The other thing I experimented with was this:

If we had to recreate the same sinusoidal pattern we see, how would we do it?

I started with a simple saw-tooth pattern and applied those offsets to the letter "L" ("A"=0, modular-26) and then also plotted the behaviour against the CT to be masked e.g. all letters between A and Z, also Modular-26.

Doing this was sufficient to recreate the dynamic range using  the same 24-element moving average method.

The range itself being approx. 7 through 18. (Out of interest, the CT for the min position was "P" and the max position "Y")

BUT, the magic bit is that the saw-tooth values needed to range between 0 and 16. The centred "L" offset + the 24-element window working hand in hand via addition and modular-26 to recreate something close to what we need.

Still a ways to go yet though ...

I've shared pictures of the spreadsheet results so you don't need to hunt - The spreadsheets are already uploaded but very much a WIP.

Cheers, Mike

Funny thing:  In the first draft of my earlier note, I had written "(except Rob)" but then removed the parenthetical.  Guess I should have left it in.   😉

Also funny: I re-solved this last weekend before I realized that I had solved it 9 years prior.  These things blend together after a while, and the discussion of the solution is in a different thread, which is why I missed it.  Strangely, I have no idea HOW I did it before, but I'd bet money it was a different method.   How did you do it?

This is why I'm asking.  Let's speculate for a moment that k4 is a very simple "mask" followed by a Vigenere, much like the challenge cipher.   What are the techniques that we could employ to go about solving such a thing?  I know what I have tried, but what would others do?  That's why I'm so curious.

Here is thing: the K4 solution space is massive... so massive that the puzzle may be, in fact, impossible on a practical level.  On the other hand, Jim M's puzzle can be solved with tried and true crypto techniques that rely mainly on statistics (at least that's how I did it) - but only because we had a pretty good idea what Jim M did.   If you expand the solution space a la K4, the statistics start generating false positives - lots of them.  For me anyway, I feel like I've never made good use of the cribs other than to check to see if my technique is correct, which is frankly a feeble use of what should be a powerful tool.  Can the cribs be used to reduce the false positives, but in an automated way?

As an aside (and sorry for the long note), when Turing and Welchman broke the Enigma, they essentially used cribs (plus automation) to rule out logically impossible solutions until they were left with the correct answer.  We can do that with K4, but only to a point, and only if we make some specific assumptions on the cipher type.   For example, as you already observed Rob, K4 cannot be a single step Vigenere (or one if its variants) with a period of 7.  The cribs make that logically impossible.  We don't even need to test it.  Where my small brain is struggling is how to use cribs effectively when combined with a mask and a Vigenere at the same time.

Final thought:  It's easy to create a 97 character cipher that is impossible, even using simple techniques.  It's much harder to create a cipher that is challenging but solvable.  I'm not convinced Jim Sanborn knew the difference.

I also coded up and attempt at solving this automatically using the know constraints.

The process is a following:
1) try a dictionary word and decode with Vig. using the KRYPTOS alphabet
2) walk down each of the 5 columns and perform an IOC on them
3) score the IOC's, select the best two and if both of those are above a threshold then ...
4) cycle a offsets against the original letters 1-26,1-26 and 1-26 for the remainder of the low IOC columns
5) perform a bigram scoring across the lot and store the best
6) kick myself for not learning how to do this in a couple of hours with a spreadsheet manually!!!

Step 4 concerns me: Surely the modified/masked columns are just another standard alphabet for that exact position? This means that me adding a standard offset to the same spot is no different from some random keyword that does the same job for the same repeat position...

Of course the program is just doing really basic scoring, nothing extra special that 101 eyeballing/cracking could do better.

It does hint that the offsets are progressively modified deeper into the length of the code such that the same position never gets the same offset e.g. masked letter at position 4 gets 4 added/subtract to it, and so on...

Cheers,
Mike

Let's assume that the key size is 11 and K4 uses a Viginere with the Kryptos alphabet.  Based on the known plaintext, we should be able to derive most of the key.  Even if we were only able to determine 3 letters in the key then I could easily brute force the rest.

Using the same idea, it would be easy to test other key sizes assuming they were not extremely large.  But even if the key was large, NORTHEAST is big enough that that it could likely allow a person to eyeball more of the key.  For instance, if NORTHEAST translated to part of a key such as **********ARTOFTHEK****** (part of the key) then we could guess that P comes before ART and EY follows the K.  ChatGPT or a dictionary could assist with this sort of attack.

It is an interesting idea since this method could be applied to other polyalphabetic substitutions.

My guess is that if you try a key size of 11 using the Kryptos alphabet and reverse engineer the key according to the known plaintext then you will end up with gibberish.  If it turns out to not look like gibberish and you need help with the brute force then let me know and I can assist.  My belief is that if K4 utilized a Viginere with the Kryptos alphabet then it would have been solved a long time ago.

If it used a Viginere with something other than the Kryptos alphabet then that is a lot more difficult, and my best guess for cracking it would be to use a dictionary attack since there are far too many combinations (26 factorial) to brute force the alphabet.

t:
Jim, Bob, Rob,

OK, so what did we learn from this exercise.

1.  Blocking the text into columns (of 5 in example) and independently prewhitening each column by a simple substitution prior to the Vig encryption leaves statistical evidence.  Using a simple distance metric d between two distributions shows that 2 of 5 columns (in the example problem) match English, and the remaining 3 columns don't match English.  But, when you sort the distributions, the sorted distribution for each of the 3 columns matches the sorted distribution of English.  That's how I determined which 2 columns were English (using guessed keywords from a dictionary), and how I derived the prewhitening substitution for the remaining 3.

2.  I used a very simple distance metric for comparing two frequency distributions of letters: d = abs(freq1[A]-freq2[A]) + abs(freq1[B] - freq2[B]) .....

3.  Then given some distribution of letters, comparing that dist to a Uniform dist shows how random the dist is.  Comparing to dist of English shows how close to English it is (including transpositions, since that doesn't change the frequencies). Comparing the sorted distribution to the sorted English distribution shows how close it is to English if the letters were "masked" using simple substitution.  If the masking converts E to Z, sorting aligns the frequency of E to frequency of Z.

4.  I've started to look at K4.  The overall distance of the 97 letters to Uniform is large, indicating that K4 is not random:  that says that things like running key, etc. are not likely, since they would yield a "more random" result than we're seeing with K4.  I then looked to see if it was blocked into columns, each of which was prewhitened with some substitution prior to Vig encryption.  I would have expected 4 columns, corresponding to the 4 extra columns on the tableau.  But the best result I get is blocking into 3 columns, where there's a very strong correlation (low distance d) between the sorted frequencies of column 3 and a sorted English distribution.  The other 2 columns show a good match as well, just not as strong.

5.  The distance to the sorted English for the 97 letters as a whole doesn't correlate well, but the 3 individual columns do, implying that 3 different simple substitutions may have been used.

6.  Note that transposition doesn't affect letter frequencies.  So he may have transposed first, then blocked into 3 columns and applied a simple substitution to each.  This is a work in progress.

7.  When Jim Melichar issued his challenge way back, I just took it on faith that it would show how simple things could mess up our standard analysis methods.  But then when I went back and actually solved the challenge, I gained some insight into what was going on with simple substitution prewhitening.
Very instructive -- thanks Jim!

Yes, the video is very interesting and very well-produced and well-researched.

I do have a couple of quibbles with a couple of details in the video:

1. I think the focus on "how could a solver of K1 and K2 have found the keywords PALIMPSEST and ABSCISSA on their own?" is not nearly as significant as the video implies that it is.

The standard pencil and paper methods to solve such Vigenere ciphers, which the video also describes, do NOT include, entail, or require figuring out the keywords themselves. It is only after solving the cipher by other analytical methods that the keywords become apparent in retrospect. "Guess or deduce the keyword or keywords" is NOT a standard method of cryptanalysis to solve ciphers. This segment of the video may create the misleading impression that guessing or figuring out a keyword is supposed to be a critical step to solve a cipher such as K1 or K2.

It is true that brute force dictionary attacks may indeed uncover such keywords. But a brute force search of a dictionary of hundreds of thousands of words is not at all the same as guessing or figuring out the keyword in the way that the video suggests.

I have in mind in particular the segment of the video where it speculates about the letter string ALLYINVI which appears in both the Morse Code sculpture and the K2 plaintext, and shows how this letter string could be used with the K2 ciphertext to reveal the keyword ABSCISSA. The problem with this idea as a supposed possible method to solve K2 is that there is no way a solver would know in advance that this particular letter string would have significance for K2, as opposed to all the other possible strings of letters among the words in the Morse Code sculpture messages and elsewhere. It is only in retrospect, after K2 has already been solved, that one can see the matching ALLYINVI letter strings and think of this idea to reveal the K2 keyword.

2. The video asserts that the appearance of ID BY ROWS at the end of the original decipherment of K2 was a complete coincidence, an entirely accidental fluke not intended by Sanborn at all. I find this quite difficult to believe. Also, I seem to recall Sanborn once implying that "ID BY ROWS" was intended to appear in a later step of the "puzzle within a puzzle" after all parts of the Kryptos plaintext have been solved. This would also suggest that the appearance of ID BY ROWS was intentional, not an accidental fluke.

Once again, these are small quibbles. Overall the video is excellent, well-produced and well-researched.

Hi all,

I was looking at the masking technique as per the K1K3 steg offset stuff I've recently found + those K4[1 thru 50] & K4[51 thru 97] offset patterns and came to the following conclusions:

1) The offset pattern in K1K3 steg could be considered sinusoidal or pyramidal as it's neither one not the other. The fact that it swings negative (or at least below 11/the middle letter "L") leans more towards sinusoidal.
2) I am of the opinion that a couple of spies out int he fields might share a easily obtainable maths book but would probably be better off using the values/digits of PI as a one time pad, rather than calc sin/cos offsets, so that leans more towards a pyramid shape.
3) I did try out a saw tooth patterns initially as was able to get the letter "T" as the first offset + a ramp of 1 thru 17 as the best combo to reduce the difference between the two K4 section offsets, but that just happened to be something I was already looking at.
4) I've dismissed saw-tooth offset and sinusoidal offsets for the above reasons + saw-tooth offsets still retain a recoverable period...
5) The pyramidal offset hides the recovery period via statistics, Freidman, Kasiski etc methods nicely.

Example:

Say we start with a absurdly simply CT to demonstrate:

CT: A,B,C,A,B,C,A,B,C,A,B,C

A statistical analysis (+ 101 eyeballing) will reveal that the period is 3.

If we were to use a simple ramp/saw-tooth offset, we simply shift the repeats out to the newer period, in this case 6.

Offset: 1,2,3,4,5,6,1,2,3,4,5,6,....
CT: A,B,C,A,B,C,...
New BiGram Disrupted CT: B,D,F,E,G,I,B,D,F,E,G,I,B,D,F

To be able to hide the underlying period, we need something that is (1) easy to remember in the field (2) not complex to implement and (3) inherently aperiodic. Perhaps something like the following:

New Offsets (visually showing the aperiodic spread):
___3________3________3
_2__2_____2__2_____2
1____1____1____1____1
______4_4______4_4
_______5________5
Offset: 1,2,3,2,1,4,5,4,1,2,3,....
New BiGram Disrupted CT:  B,D,F,C,C,G,F,F,D,C,E,E,B,F,I

Due to the distance between the various offsets, we've embedded multi-period offsets into CT to mask it's own inherent statistics.

To demonstrate the reoccurrence distance of the CT-->NewCT mapping, refer to the following:
A-->B @ 12 steps further away,B-->D @ 18 steps further away,C-->F @ 24 steps further away,A-->C @ 6 steps further away,B-->C @ 12 steps further away,C-->G @ 18 steps further away,A-->F @ 24 steps further away,B-->F @ 6 steps further away,C-->D @ 12 steps further away,...

The underlying factors from analysing the above are: 3,4,6,8,12,24 and, of course, none of them work :)

I'll stop the with the analysis there but it other interesting properties if you wish to explore yourself.

Note that a sinusoidal wave would do much the same with more complex aperiodic behaviour depending on resolution...

So what's new with the above? Probably not much and it is possibly mentioned in one of Friedman's texts or Army manual - I've yet to look properly.

But, Why is it of interest?

If it wasn't for the obvious pyramidal shape in the last letter's of the words in the K1-K3 passages, I'd dismiss it as having no relevance whatsoever.

Scheidt's comment regarding "evening out the 1's and 0's" weigh's against it as a single layer of the K4 CT masking technique...

However! I've discovered most of the original offset framework which dictates what letters need to go where during the steg phase. It seems to run in groups of seven ranging from 9 to 19 within K1~K2. It restarts at 12 for K3 onwards but I've still some work to recover the tail as it is out...

Still, I'm strongly considering it a the masking steps applied to he 50 character K4 lengths and will give it a go. Obviously the K1K3 steg is much longer the K4 so the groups of 7 below will need to be reduced down...

Anyway, just reporting in the findings :)

Cheers, Mike

t:
ding ding ding.  Congrats.  Well done!  That's roughly how I did it too.   So Doug asked earlier what did we learn from this.  For me its the following:

1) The fact we had direction on the encipherment method made this puzzle much easier.  Absent direction, it would have taken much much longer to solve (if ever).
2) having 200 characters vs. 97 characters helped a great deal.  I tried to solve the 97 character version and failed.  "Frequency" wasn't the top option (though it was on the list) and Kasiski was not useful.

If you have items 1 and 2 above, the puzzle is fairly easy for someone with a computer and decent crypto skill.   If you know either 1 or 2, I submit the puzzle is very very difficult, but probably solvable with enough time and effort.   If you don't know 1 and you only have 97 characters, the puzzle is VERY difficult, to the point of not being a fair challenge.  The other lesson learned is the two techniques involved here are trivial, but when combined create a pretty difficult nut to crack.  It's conjecture, but that's probably what Sanborn did with K4... combine two easy things to make a hard thing.

Perhaps it's fatalist, but I'm back to the point of thinking K4 may be inadvertently unsolvable.  If Sanborn wanted this solved, he could give an actual clue as to the method or release a much longer example of the cipher text.  I bet if we had, say, a 1,000 character example, K4 would fall within days or weeks.

t:
Nice job!

OK, so we had 200 letters masked with one of two whimsically simple substitutions.  That gave us enough to work with.

If K4 is similar to the sample problem, we have 97 letters with (perhaps) 4 substitutions, with approx 25 letters in each of 4 substitutions.

Looking at the tableau, we have 4 alphabets on the far right which could be the masking substitutions.

If the plaintext was masked in columns of 4, then at position 20 (starting at 0) we have -EAS TNOR THEA STxx
and at 60 we have ---B ERLI NCLO CK--

The two T's in col 0 must map to the same masked letter, and the two  L's in col 3 must map to their same masked letter.

I used that as a test, and ran a dictionary attack decrypting the 97 letter ciphertext into a 97 letter masked intermediate text.
Not that only 1 in 26 squared  (676) keywords will pass this test.

One passing keyword is DECIPHERMENTS which seems promising.

Now I'm speculating:  the actual plaintext is 93 letters.  The encrypting party chooses a four letter masking keyword, uses it to mask the 4 columns getting a 93 letter masked text, and forms a 97 letter message by appending the 93 letters to the masking keyword.
The 97 letters are then Vig encrypted and transmitted.

What I'm suggesting is the OBKR is the Vig encrypted masking keyword.

More speculation:  the 4 columns on the right of the tableau are shifted to match the 4 letter masking keyword.  That gives us the 4 "shifted Kryptos" alphabets to use for masking.

There are a couple of variations on this theme:
use a standard A-Z to look up the plaintext letter, and select the corresponding letter from the per-column alphabet.
use a Kryptos alphabet, such as leftmost column of the tableau to lookup the plaintext letter
mask by row vs mask by column

I've started to run experiments.

Doug

s: Notes from Kryptos Workshop and Dinner, 10/24/15
t:
Hi Henrietta,

Ciphertext is often shown as 5 letter groups because that's how it was transmitted via telegram.  The telegram services typically charged by the "word" and the question arose as to what to charge for enciphered messages.  The sender would like to treat a 1,000 letter ciphertext as one big word;  the service would like to charge for 1,000 one letter words.  A compromise was worked out to charge 5 letter groups as a word.

It's also convenient to break ciphertext into 5 letter groups when writing it down.

But I don't necessarily see it being helpful with masking.  I can envision Jim writing the original plaintext in a 3,4,or 5 row matrix and then performing the masking, substitution, rotation/transposition, etc. operations on that matrix.  I lean to 4 rows or columns which would match the 4 extra columns on the tableau, which might play a role in masking.

An argument can be made for 5 rows of 21 (with padding at the end) which would place the cribs at the beginning of rows 2 and 4;  maybe that's why he chose those cribs to give us.  He could have masked 4 of the 5 rows using the extra columns, but I would have expected him to mask all 5 rows and not leave one unmasked.  I also played around with masking the 5 vowels separately from the 21 consonants, but didn't get very far with that.

He could have done a lot of different things;  sooner or later we may stumble across what he did.  10,000 of us Kryptos monkeys banging away at a keyboard just might come up with a readable message!

Cheers, Doug

Hi KRYPTOS.groups.io,

I wondered how I could change the 6 letters A, E, I, O, U, Y that represent the vowels into a 97.
So I Wrote down the numbers for each of these 6 letters from our Alphabet in the U. S. O. A.
So the letter A=1, E=5, I=9, O=15, U=21, Y=25.
Then I counted the letters A+E=15, and the letters I+U=30 or Two 15, 15, and the letter O=15.
Then I went back and picked up the 3 numbers BETWEEN each of the 4 #15 for a total of 12.
So the A, E, I, O, U add up to 4#15 or 60 plus the 4 #3's=12 for a total of 72 and add the Y=25 for a total of 97.
I thought this might help with the part 4 of KRYPTOS solution.

William C. Papke

--

s: Reverse of Cribs for Partial Solve
t:
For those interested, I include below a Vigenère cipher key that can result in the plain text cribs provided by Jim.  It assumes the continued use of the Kryptos alphabet 'kryptosabcdefghijlmnquvwxz', as taken from the tableau and used already in K1 and K2.  Personally, I don't think its worth much, as the key appears unrelated to anything I can see in the CT or PT of Kryptos.

'---------------------RDUMRIYWOYNKY-----------------------------ELYOIECBAQK--'

The hyphen character is simply 'some wild card character' that won't alter the plain text of the cribs.  For instance,  swapping the hyphen character for 'X' produces the following plain text.

'ADYPWAKAIJWNDBANLHDDZEASTNORTHEASTASZSVBMVBBGYRRZCSMYNWFLCZLUHDBERLINCLOCKZIFYRKSMEFLIYWJWCWGYECP'

So whilst you can read the eastnortheast and berlinclock in their correct locations, as we don't have the rest of the key, the remaining content is meaningless rubbish.

The shortest key, with length 27 characters, I could find to create the eastnortheast and berlinclock plaintext is 'YWOYNKY--ELYOIECBAQK-RDUMRI', but this is also clearly wrong.  It produces something (also rubbish) like 'PEUZYOV..PTIPLQBAOHB.EASTNORTHEAST..FGMRRCWXTSZ.VWCXZYNGDOTIL..BERLINCLOCK.FKOAWIHFOGQKN..VTCUQVM'.

Like others, I've stared at DYAHR for far too long, trying to figure out its meaning.

As an anagram, HYDRA could refer to the Naval Enigma Machine.  Using an Enigma code seems way too complicated for Kryptos, but there does seem to be some behavior that mimics the concept of the rotors advancing after each character (i.e., the QQ and SS in NORTHEAST decrypting to sequential letters of the ABC alphabet)

As a misspelled anagram, KRYHA jumps out to me.  This polyalphabetic cipher requires a key of numbers to represent the shift after each character.  We certainly have a string of numbers (from K2).  But, nothing that I was able to make sense of.

As an artistic representation, it sort of looks like a palimpsest with the raised characters being the original text that the regular text covers up.  Perhaps a visual nod from JS to acknowledge Carter's Diary?

THE REMAINS OF PASSAGE DEBRIS THAT ENCUMBERED THE LOWER PART OF THE DOORWAY WERE REMOVED

EN.DyaHr.OH
...DEBRIS       <-- Debris? With the H being a partially erased R.

I also note that there are "EN" (N) and "OH" (O) surrounding DYAHR.  So, perhaps the cipher alphabet is something like ABCDEFJKMN LIGHT OPQRSUVWXYZ?

To me, this is the big mystery.  The orientation of these letters is clearly not an accident, and therefore it must have some purpose.   For me, I'm not a believer in the anagram idea, primarily because Sanborn would have had to be exactingly clever to do a transposition that produced an anagram of hydra (or any other word for that matter) by design.  Plus, he used a known plaintext, not something he wrote himself.

I feel (without evidence, of course) that its more likely that misaligned letters have nothing at all to do with the letters themselves (e.g. the letters DYAHR are irrelevant), but rather the position of the letters.

Also, note that it's not just "raised" letter, although the vertical alignment is the most obvious.  The N appears to be shifted left toward the E.  The D appears to be shifted right, as does the O.  Maybe its for aesthetic reasons to make the DYAHR stand out, maybe its meaningful, I don't really have a view on that.

Unfortunately, k4 is not an enigma cipher.   The enigma machine was not able to encipher a letter to itself (e.g. an "e" could not encipher to an "E").  This was the primary weakness that allowed it to be broken.

Using the cribs, there are two instances where a plaintext letter enciphers to the same ciphertext letter (the "K" in clock and the "S" in the second east).   Therefore, its impossible for k4 to be an enigma cipher.

Yes, this cipher was not produced using a real Enigma machine, but there is strong evidence that it has something to do with the Enigma. It is possibly a "pencil-and-paper" version of an Enigma machine that can encypher a plain text letter to itself. We found a short phrase at the beginning of K4 that also hints to the topic of the Enigma.

s: K1-K3 Plaintext Cannot Help Solve K4
t:
I think it's a mistake to assume that knowing the plaintext solutions to the first 3 parts of Kryptos will give you special insight or critical clues in deciphering the final 97 characters. I've pointed this out before: the plaintext of K1 was of no help in solving K2 or K3. The *method* behind the solution of K1 was of course quite helpful for solving K2, but not the plaintext, nor the keyword.

Likewise, the plaintext of K2 was worthless for solving K3, and if per chance K2 had been solved prior to K1, its plaintext and keyword wouldn't have helped you one iota in solving K1. Only knowing K2's cipher system would have helped you in solving K1.

Finally, had someone solved K3 first, neither the method nor the plaintext would have told you ANYTHING about how to solve K1 or K2.

So I don't understand how people think that Jim would break from this (sensible) compartmentalization of the individual systems with K1/K2/K3 when crafting K4. Furthermore, Jim has said you wouldn't have needed to solve K1-K3 in order to solve K4. (I don't have the exact quote, but I'm confident one of the veterans still here can provide it).

We have one advantage with K4 that we didn't have with K1, K2 or K3: we know where the ciphertext begins (the leading question mark notwithstanding), and we know where it ends. I'm treating it as a standalone cipher that involves substitution, but is not just Quagmire 3 (or 1 or 2) alone, and may not involve a Quagmire system at all.  --Rob

Rob, I strongly disagree.  e.g., say you've solved K1, with the "error" at #57.  Presently it may occur to you that the "error" is not just the Q, but also the I just before it, at #56, the actual PT to be encrypted being ALLUSION.  In trying to make something of this, eventually we try multiplying 56 by 57 (it's not so much what they are as where), and we get 3,192.  We may not immediately understand what this is telling us, but if we got this far by idly kicking things around, we should eventually realize that for Section 3 we use a skip interval of 192, and we no longer need the rotated matrices.  And Ed will be happy because we solved it the way we were meant to.

How might we know the error is at 57 if we haven't broken K1?  Possible mnemonic device - the 3 letters of KRYPTOS consecutive in the standard alphabet add to 57.  But to know that 56 is to be used we would still have to have the PT to experiment on.

There is stuff like this all through the thing; the coordinates of 'his last message' are a regular gold mine.  No way there is no help for K4 in K1-K3.

Carl Ellis

s: K1-K3 Plaintext Cannot Help Solve K4
t:
Hi Adam,

I think it's easy to "Monday morning quarterback" and retroactively convince yourself that there were clues in earlier sections (e.g. Morse code for K1) that could help you solve later sections. But NOBODY solved it that way. The ones who solved it first used standard cryptographic techniques. So if they were deliberate clues, they were crappy ones. In particular, you would never find PALIMPSEST in the way you've outlined: 10 different words in scrambled order, with variable kerning. Just getting the words in the right order is a 1-in-3,628,800 prospect (10 factorial) -- that's just not actionable. (Actually, the odds are slightly better than that -- 1 in 907,200 -- since the order of the Morse words used to create the two P's and two S's doesn't matter.) Nevertheless, there are probably hundreds if not thousands of words that could be created in this fashion from those words in various orders, so how would you know which was the right one? At best it's an Easter Egg.

The ABSCISSA clue within K1 may well have been deliberate, but again you only spot it *after* you've already solved K2 by conventional means.

Finally, you suggested "What is clear is that brute force deciphering has not worked for 30 years, and so perhaps logic and intelligence gathering needs to be applied in new and creative ways!" I would say that brute force works perfectly fine for K1-K3, once you know the cryptographic method. Brute force and intelligence can also tell you a lot of things that K4 isn't. The security of K4 is not in its choice of a keyword or keywords; it's that the method hasn't been found. There are hundreds of different simple methods that Jim could have used that would make it virtually unsolvable. So I agree with you that you have to do some intelligence gathering: think like Jim would think, and focus on the sorts of methods that would appeal to an artist.  --Rob

I find these debates about which solutions are deemed to be allowed or not vaguely fascinating as they are reminiscent of the arguments that have always raged amongst even the most learned of people.  We have a search feature available in the forum here, but all that will ever output is raw information.  It will never be able to give an accurate weighting to the result until such time as the solution is actually known.

There are a few sites, including this forum that have logged in varying degrees of detail the comments Ed and Jim have made over the years in print and TV/Radio and on top of that there are almost certainly numerous other anecdotal snippets from personal correspondence and fleeting dinner conversations that float around here in the realms of institutional memory.
If you distil the information gathered from posts to this forum alone, then ultimately all you are left with is a map that is a binary branching tree representing a chained series of assumptions that create further branches at each step of the tree.
Various members have made their way to multiple points in this tree over the years and along with others will have a preference for which branches they favour in terms of likely solution paths.

Due to a lack of commonly agreed nomenclature, no member really knows where they are standing on that map relative to anyone else, so unless anyone can suggest a way to classify the various approaches in a coherent format that can be adhered to by all contributors, then there will always be an omnipresent danger of babies being thrown out with the bath water, especially when people go on something of a spring clean to invalidate entire areas of that as yet undefined map.

That statement obviously comes with a few caveats.  The first is that there is some map culling that can easily be performed by cryptanalysis, but that would only appear to apply to the situation where K4 is a vanilla example of those same systems.  Any mixing or n step processes would appear to be enough to rule back in some of the systems that were initially ruled out, so let's also take Ed at his word and assume that all advantages for 'standard' cryptanalysis have been removed.

The second caveat is that Jim in all of his interviews to date seems to have actively tried to help cull areas of the map that won't bear any fruit.  Back in 2013 for example, I uploaded a paper called Valkyrie to my personal folders, which showed how Berlin could be found at positions 63-70 in the stego coordinate scheme that I've outlined in other papers and videos to date such as the Machine R1 paper (also available in my personal files).  I subsequently found a quote by Jim saying that you didn't need the plain text in order to solve K4.  That one piece of information allowed me to cull the particular area of the map I was standing on and move back up a couple of assumptions before attempting a different path of ascent.

A theory that doesn't generate the known plaintext in the right positions may obviously lie in a culling region of the map that needs to be pruned, but we need to keep an awareness that a lot of the information gathered here to date may have a part to play in a longer process of unravelling K4's underlying mechanics.  An analogy might be that of finding a ball of Christmas lights that are tangled and spotting a bulb that isn't working.  Do you try and replace the bulb or simply cut it out and sever the wires?  The order and connectivity of information would appear to play a role.  Didn't Jim say that the piece is supposed to unravel slowly over time?  That doesn't sound like a standalone crypto system in which the plain text can be safely ignored.

If we take the cymatic theory I currently have on the table as an example, then the proposed K4 solve can be presented without any need to have the plaintext to hand, as all values come from the cipher text in one of the 6 matrix positions outlined.
Here's the rub though. Without the plaintext, the actual mechanics of the cipher fall apart as the theory requires the row shifts to create what is effectively an interference pattern between bigrams in both the cipher and plain text matrices.  The statement that, "you don't need the plaintext to decrypt K4" would hold for the theory currently before you all, but would not hold for the very similar statement, "you don't need the plaintext to prove the solution to K4".

I think all 'eye rolling' will be reserved for the students of tomorrow who will have the benefit of hindsight and massive compute power.  I suspect their interest won't be in K4 itself however, but will be in examining the human psychology of group interactions and how the competing ideas around K4 were aired, critiqued and evolved.  If anyone is interested in such things then I'd definitely recommend reading up on the life of Hermann Grassmann.

Will look forward to meeting some of you in person for the first time at Histocrypt later this month.  Safe travels!
Matt

t:
Bold move suggesting that knowing plaintext is worthless in solving the final 97 characters, but I strongly disagree with that premise.  For those attempting brute force and/or dictionary attacks, it allows them to weed out billions or trillions of combinations as opposed to having to visually inspect each making feasible which would otherwise be infeasible.  This is because if the plaintext does not exist in the result then it can be ignored, and if it does exist then it can then be visually inspected which saves enormous amounts of time.  A person just needs to think up a method and then try every combination to prove it right or wrong in a reasonable amount of time.

The problem is that we do not know how the plaintext is enciphered.  The clues are obscure enough that to this day the method used is still unknown, and part of the reason is that k4 is short.  Not even AI has been smart enough to figure it out.  We are left guessing.

For me, saving my time makes it not "worthless" to have known plaintext, and so this is why I disagree.  I suppose in the right context it is worthless.  For instance, even if we knew the entire plaintext then we may still be unable to figure out the method used to create the ciphertext.  At this time, it is computationally infeasible to try every possible combination. - especially if more than one method was used to encipher the text.

With a lot of people trying, there is a chance that maybe someone will get lucky enough to find the solution.  Or maybe quantum computers, some advanced AI, or some other technology can narrow it down for us.  If that happens, then maybe we will know for sure if knowing the plaintext was worthless or not.
