Recently "Government Attic" published the "Tales of the Krypt" newsletters of the NSA KRYPTOS Society from 1994-2003, somewhat redacted.

The original FOI request was in 2010!

By far the most useful section of the 813 pages, for the purposes of this group, was this part on diagnosis (pages 776 to 779, very little redaction).

Context: The KRYPTOS Society was established in 1981 to promote cryptanalysis and excellence in the cryptologic community.  [I don't think there's any connection to the CIA sculpture name.]

----

(U) Principles of Diagnosis

(U//FOUO) These principles of cryptanalytic diagnosis were gathered by R. Dale Shipp, a Distinguished Member of the KRYPTOS Society (1999). Except for the first, they are not in order of importance. Where known, the originator or popularizer of the principle is credited.

(U//FOUO) A short bio for Dale may be found in the November 1999 issue of Tales of the KRYPT.

1. (U) Look at the data.
(U//FOUO) Corollary: It might be plaintext.
(U//FOUO) Too often in this modern world, we rely on programs to analyze data and extract preprogrammed features. The human eye and brain are powerful tools that see things that have not been programmed for. Examples exist where direct visualization were [sic] of direct importance in successful diagnosis.

2. (U) Let the data tell you what to do. (A Jim Bates saying.)
(U//FOUO) When you see an effect in the data that is statistically significant, listen to it. It needs to be explained or expanded.

3. (U) Remember that diagnosticians do not know what they are doing.
(U//FOUO) When doing attack development, you usually have a complete model and can evaluate exactly what the scores are telling you. Since you know what the correct answer should look like, you can aford [sic] to reach deep into the noise to pull it out using elaborate secondary tests. You can afford to ignore other high random scores which do not fit the known model.
(U//FOUO) When doing diagnosis, you have only models that you have invented based upon incomplete knowledge or even speculation. There may well be effects caused by things you do not know. When designing attacks, you should consider statistics that do not depend too deeply on the specifics of your model. I call these "robust statistics." You must be prepared to observe and examine interesting scores that are different from exactly what you were testing for. You cannot often afford to spend significant resources digging deep into the noise. Your time and energy are better spent designing new models and attacks against them.

4. (U) Use all of the data you can afford.
(U//FOUO) This is related to the point above. When doing attack development, you can usually evaluate the amount of data needed to produce the desired result. The use of more data often carries a cost of processing and may well not add significantly to the chances of success. In any case, because you know what you are doing, you can evaluate both the cost of using the additional data and the gain in success arising from doing so.
(U//FOUO) Since the diagnostician does not know the underlying truth, she cannot normally evaluate with certainty the gain in success arising from the use of additional data, nor the loss resulting from not using it. Often the curve of success versus data size has a sharp knee. Depending on where one is on that curve, a doubling of the data size may increase chances of success by a minuscule amount (e.g. from nil to almost never, or from .99 to .999) or by a significant amount (e.g. from .1 to .8). We cannot afford to take the chance on being on the wrong side of the later [sic] possibility.

5. (U) Do not worry that you will not understand the meaning of a result from a diagnostic run. Do worry about being able to determine the significance of an answer.
(U//FOUO) The best example of this principle comes from a historical antedote [sic]. Once when proposing ... [redacted]
(U//FOUO) We do tests that have been successful at uncovering statistically interesting and relevant phenomena in the past. So long as the current knowledge of the system does not imply failure of the tests, it may well make sense to apply them -- even if we do not immediately understand what the results would mean.
(U//FOUO) The type of tests that are of more dubious value are those for which we are unable to decide whether a result is statistically interesting or not. If we are unable to make this evaluation by either mathematical analysis or simulation modeling, then the value of the test is highly suspect.

6. (U) Data quality is important.
(U//FOUO) This is more true for diagnosticians than for those who are doing exploitation, but true for both. When the goal is to turn cipher into plain on a know [sic] system, garbles can often be tolerated and compensated for. Many diagnostic attacks have combinatorial aspects to them that can be devasted [sic] by garbles. Even more common is that many times diagnosticians have had to first diagnose things that we ourselves had done to the cipher at some stage in its processing.

7. (U) Know the quality of your data.
(U//FOUO) Knowledge of the quality of the data is perhaps as important as the quality itself. By understanding the various processing steps and knowing what could have gone wrong, you are better prepared to understand the results of your tests, and the limitations of them.

8. (U) Believe in yourself and have confidence that you can succeed.
(U) If you do not believe that anything will work, then nothing you devise will work and you are only going through the motions. You need to have an inner sense that the answer is there, and that you will be able to find it and to recognize its signs. Persistence and imagination have overcome difficult odds.

9. (U) Put yourself in a position to be lucky. (Another Jim Bates saying.)
(U) Even when you have little hope for success, keep something going. If you ... [redacted]
Be prepared to capitalize on good fortune when it comes your way -- but do not sit around waiting for it either.

10. (U) Cooperate and share data and information and ideas.
(U) This has got to be one of the most important principles and values. Very few successes come as the result of sole individual effort.
(U) No one person nor organization owns the data. Chances for success are enhanced when the data is made available to those who can work on it and contribute, and when all relevant information about the data is shared.
(U) The creative process thrives on diaglog [sic]. By sharing results and ideas, even the half-baked ones, we spark ideas in others and lead to more progress on our problem and on other problems.

11. (U) Document and publish.
(U) Too often, those who have been successful at diagnosis have not published how they achieved that success and only the fact of the success and the result are published. This robs the more junior analysts of a chance for growth. Those who were primarily observers in a successful important diagnosis can contribute to the lore by writing a history of what they saw so that others can see and know the paths that led to success.

Thanks for sharing the NSA KRYPTOS Society "Principles of Diagnosis" bullet points. Some of these are quite relevant to the analysis of test results I've generated over the last couple months on Kryptos K4. Last fall, I came up with a candidate encryption layer idea that would appeal to Jim Sanborn, then wrote code to apply it to the K4 ciphertext. This technique has three parameters, but those parameters take on a manageable number of discrete values, so it's easy to have the computer run through all the combinations (hundreds, not thousands). The result of each combination is 97 letters of intermediate ciphertext which can be evaluated by standard statistical means (e.g. primarily polyalphabetic incidence of coincidence and Kasiski).

If Jim first encrypted with polyalphabetic substitution (as he did in K1 and K2), and then followed it up with the candidate masking technique I've proposed, then it will reveal itself as an IoC spike at a period matching the length of the repeating keyword. The question is: if a spike (or multiple spikes) turn up, how to distinguish a real signal from a false positive? This is where point #2 comes in:

2. (U) Let the data tell you what to do. (A Jim Bates saying.)
(U//FOUO) When you see an effect in the data that is statistically significant, listen to it. It needs to be explained or expanded.

The key here is identifying what is "statistically significant". This can partially be answered by looking at the mean and standard deviation of all the IoC scores of all the variants that were run (which I did as a function of polyalphabetic period). My sample size is several hundred values at each period, which is good but not great. I have found a couple outliers at the 4-sigma level, which at first glance sounds quite promising. But to be statistically robust at 4-sigma, I would need tens of thousands of samples, not just hundreds. This point is hammered home in NSA KRYPTOS Society's 3rd point:

3. (U) Remember that diagnosticians do not know what they are doing.
(U//FOUO) When doing attack development, you usually have a complete model and can evaluate exactly what the scores are telling you. Since you know what the correct answer should look like, you can aford [sic] to reach deep into the noise to pull it out using elaborate secondary tests. You can afford to ignore other high random scores which do not fit the known model.
(U//FOUO) When doing diagnosis, you have only models that you have invented based upon incomplete knowledge or even speculation. There may well be effects caused by things you do not know. When designing attacks, you should consider statistics that do not depend too deeply on the specifics of your model. I call these "robust statistics." You must be prepared to observe and examine interesting scores that are different from exactly what you were testing for.

So my next step is to run this same statistical analysis against a million or so randomly generated 97-letter strings to see how often high scores are generated by pure chance. And then as a second statistical experiment, I'll try a million different random shufflings of K4's letters. That should tell me whether the spikes I found are significant. This sort of "null hypothesis" testing addresses NSA's point #5:

5. (U) Do not worry that you will not understand the meaning of a result from a diagnostic run. Do worry about being able to determine the significance of an answer. ...

I'll report back when I've got the results of these random-string tests. --Rob

Hi All -- discovered I had already computed (a couple years ago) Incidence of Coincidence histogram stats for random strings of 97 letters. For each polyalphabetic period from 2 to 10, I ran a million cases. Here were the results, where the value in the first IoC column corresponds to a less than 1 in 10,000 chance of exceeding that IoC, and the second IoC column is a less than 1 in 1,000 chance:

Period IoC 1  IoC 2
------ -----  -----
   2    5.8%   5.4%
   3   6.25%   5.7%
   4    6.6%   6.0%
   5    6.9%  6.25%
   6    7.2%   6.5%
   7    7.5%   6.7%
   8   7.75%   6.9%
   9    8.0%  7.15%
  10    8.3%  7.35%

So for example, suppose Jim first encrypted the K4 plaintext with polyalphabetic substitution using a 9-letter keyword. (Could be straight Vigenere, Quagmire III as in K1 and K2, or whatever.) Suppose he then applied some masking trick on the resulting intermediate ciphertext. What the statistics above tell you is that if you guess incorrectly and apply the wrong unmasking technique, there is a 1-in-10,000 chance that you’ll generate an intermediate ciphertext with an IoC at period 9 of greater than 8% (i.e. a false positive).

Returning back to my theory about what Jim’s masking technique was, one of my permutations generated an IoC of 6.83% at period 7. From the table above, you can see that there was a less than 1 in 1,000 chance of that happening. But since I ran 360 different permutations to get that result, it’s not that much of a surprise. (A little less than a 1-in-3 chance that could happen by dumb luck.) So that is not a robust statistical result.

However, I had another case of a high IoC at period 9: 8.31%. That is a bit more statistically significant – about a 1-in-16,000 chance of happening randomly, or a 1 in 44 chance of finding such a result after 360 permutations.  --Rob

Rob,

This is pretty cool stuff.  It sorta confirms that: 1) you run to huge false positive issues if you try to use statistics to test masking techniques and 2) those problems get worse the longer the cipher period.

Have you tried incorporating the known cribs?  In some cases it should be able to materially reduce false positives.  The most obvious example is at period 9.  The two EASTs from “eastnortheast” overlap at exactly that period, and so the intermediate cipher text you generate from your unmasking must generate the same letters in those positions.

Said another way, if your intermediate ciphertext at that position is YZQRxxxxxYZQR, that’s a potential hit.  If it’s YZQRxxxxxLLRP, it’s inconsistent and can be immediately discarded.

Period 9 is an extreme case… the odds of those letters lining up by chance is 1 in 457,000.   Even having one overlapping letter can reduce false positives by 26x, which is surely useful.  I’ve been trying to do this very thing as well.

Again, thanks for the numbers.  Super helpful.

TWO - Scheidt did say that he "masked the English Language" to make frequency analysis impossible for K4. However, he never said that all types of statistical analysis are useless. That would be impossible. Even ciphertext with a uniform distribution of monograms and bigrams can be analyzed statistically to rule out encryption algorithms that don't generate ciphertext with a uniform distribution of letters.

What Rob is doing is analyzing the Index of Coincidence (IoC) at periods from 2-10 for random strings of length 97 characters. The period is the length of the keyword used for a polyalphabetic substitution cipher (e.g. Vigenère, Quagmire III, etc.). The idea is that if you apply the correct unmasking technique, then you could immediately suspect that your results are significant based on the intermediate ciphertext's anomalous IoC at some period.

Rob - this is really good work. Thank you for sharing. However, there is one big assumption being made - this technique assumes that an incorrect unmasking attempt will generate a random string. Since the ciphertext of K4 is itself not a random string to begin with (See "Cryptodiagnosis of Kryptos K4" by Richard Bean), this assumption is very dubious. In practice, the statistical properties of the string generated from the unmasking attempt may resemble the ciphertext of K4 more closely than a random string. Of course, this would depend on the details of the unmasking algorithm.

Rob, Nice work.

You postulate a Vig encryption followed by a Transposition / Permutation.

One approach is to guess the Vig cipher, and then determine the following Transposition.  I tried using a dictionary of potential keywords for the former, but failed to come up with a solution for K4.  If Vig is used, he could have used a keyword not in a dictionary (such as a name or a location).

Another approach is to guess the permutation, invert it to get intermediate text, and solve the Vig cipher.  Since Jim was taught by Ed a method for doing skip transpositions by blocking text into matrices and rotating/copying to other matrices, I tried guessing the transposition and the seeing if there was a viable Vig decryption that satisfied the crib letters.

IF this is what Jim did for K4, there are 41 possible invertable skip transpositions for a 98 element matrix in which the 98th element is a pad which doesn't change (it's a permutation of the first 97 letters, using a mod 98 skip cipher with 3 parameters:  start position, skip offset, and modulus).  Since you refer to 360 permutations in your testing, I assume many of these are general permutations, not limited to skip transpositions using the method that Jim was taught.

What Ed said is that he "did something" that "masked the frequencies of English letters" that we were able to use to solve K1 thru K3.  One possibility is that he did simple substitutions of pieces of K4 before encrypting.  So I looked at "masking" by doing simple substitutions of rows or columns of a blocked plaintext;  e.g., block the 97 letter plaintext as 4 rows of 25,  or 4 columns or 25, and apply a separate substitution to each row or column.  I've tried 2 to 5 rows and columns of masking, followed by transposition or by Vig encryption, and using the crib letters to rule out potential methods.

Since none of these worked, my next step will be to assume Vig encryption followed by transposition.  A combination of Vig and Transposition makes sense, if you view K1..K3 as training exercises in the the techniques used for K4.

Note that any transposition violates his claim of 1:1, that CT NYPVTTMZFPK decrypts letter for letter to PT BERLINCLOCK.  I suppose he could have used a Transpose/Vig/Inverse_transpose construct which would be 1:1, and also allow the message to be padded to some number greater than 97 (e.g., 105 = 5 rows of 21), which after the TVT process ends up with scrambled pad characters at the end of the 105 letter message;  these can be discarded and the receiver can still decode the message.

Another point is that we don't know the length of the plaintext or where it starts.  We know that the K4 ciphertext is 97 letters, and that CT position 63 (starting with 0) holds NYPVTTMZFPK which decrypts to BERLINCLOCK.  But I'm not sure Ed or Jim ever said, specifically, that BERLINCLOCK occurs at plaintext location 63.  For example, the first few letters of K4 could be some kind of message indicator, followed by the encrypted message.  You might have a 4 letter MI followed by 93 letters of encrypted message.  Then NYPVTTMZFPK would be at CT position 63, but BERLINCLOCK would occur at 59 within a 93 letter plaintext.  If we take these variants into account, we have yet more transpositions to guess (93, 95, 96, 97, 98, 100, 105 etc. letter transpositions) which could be used to generate our 97 letter challenge problem.

My head hurts!

s: K4 Running Key Cipher from The Tomb of Tutankhamun
t:
The key letters associated with the cribs could be part of a long running key.  The sequence of implied key for the cribs don't appear to be English text, but might be derived from a longer stream of English (take each nth letter, etc.)

If the running key was random, you'd have essentially a one time pad.

I had thought about using the 104 (or 105 if you include the extra L) letters from the extra 4 columns as the basis for a running key (e.g., transpose the 104 letters to form a running key with flat distribution, since each letter appears 4 times).
That uses all 26 of the shifted alphabets in a Vig tableau, using each about 4 times for a message length of 97.

But K4 doesn't appear random enough to account for a "flat distribution" running key.

Your approach of using an English passage from a book as the running key would use all 26 alphabets of the Vig tableau, but not with a flat distribution:  each of the 26 alphabets would get chosen according to the natural frequency of the letter (if "E" occurs 1/8 of the time in the book passage, then the corresponding "E" row of the Vig shifted alphabets will be used 1/8 of the time).  I haven't checked, but I suspect that would still result in a somewhat random K4 (more random than the actual K4).

Others have postulated a GROMARK style algorithm (GRONsfeld with Mixed Alphabet and Running Key).
That typically uses a random running key of base 5 or base 10 digits, such that you'd use only 5 (or 10) of the Vig tableau alphabets.

Classic GROMARK uses a matrix transposition to generate the alphabet which then is used to produce the shifted alphabets in the Vig tableau, and uses some "random number generator" to generate a sequence of one digit numbers which select the tableau row to use for each letter as you encrypt.

So all you need to figure out is how many shifted alphabets are used (e.g. 5 or 10 or...), what the specific alphabet is, what the random number generator is, and what the initial seed for that generator is.

Doug

Hi Doug -- there is a closed-form expression for this sort of problem. It's easy to compute the odds of a single double occurring in

a string of 97 letters:  (25/26)^95 * (1/26) * 96 combinations = 8.895%. Even two doubles isn't much harder: (25/26)^94 * (1/26)^2 * 4560

combinations = 16.900%.

While it's easy to see what's happening with the first two terms of the equation, the number of combinations -- C(N, R) -- in each case is less obvious. The formula for the number of combos is C(N,R) = N! / [R! * (N-R)!]. In our case, N is 96 (96 possible pairs in a string of 97 letters) and R is 6 (if we're interested in the odds of pairs happening exactly 6 times in 96 opportunities). C(96,6) is a rather large number:  96! / (6! * 90!) = 927,048,304.

So: odds of exactly 6 pairs in a string of 97 is:  (25/26)^90 * (1/26)^6 * 927,048,304 = 8.795524%.

However, I took the easy way out a year or two ago, coded it up to run Monte Carlo style, and ran 10 million cases. 😉  --Rob

I agree with your questions.  My working assumptions are that K4 is either a Substitution followed by a Transposition, or it is a substitution using a Running Key.

Rereading Richard Bean's paper Cryptodiagnosis of Kryptos K4, there seems to be evidence in support of the Running Key theory.
He postulated a GROMARK structure, which uses a Running Key from a numerical random number generator, which doesn't match what we assume about Jim's encryption process (I can't see Jim calculating a stream of random numbers using a PRNG).

But I could assume some sort of "random letter generator", with these letters used as the Running Key.

What I reported is that the CT seems to be drawn from a Reversed Kryptos alphabet arranged in a Vigenere Square analogous to the tableau on the statue.  And that the rows are not selected in "random" fashion or in a "repeated keyword" fashion, but that there is a probability distribution to the Running Key.  In particular, row 7 of the Vig Square (containing the reversed Kryptos alphabet shifted left 6 times) seems to be used 1/7 of the time, but not with a periodic repeating key.  Since 1/7 is close to the frequency of 'E' in English, I'm thinking the Running Key may be an English text of some sort.

I looked at the extra 4 columns of the tableau, with a transposition of the 104 (or 105 if you include the extra L) which would give a flat distribution of key.  That's not consistent with the "row 7" alphabet being used 1/7 of the time.

Also, you could rotate the 4 extra columns right to give 4 rows of Reversed Kryptos alphabets.  Jim did provide a comment early on that you needed to "try all shifts" of something, but as always he was vague.

I think what I'm seeing is consistent with Richard Bean's analysis with regard to "close distances" between CT and PT for the cribs.

What might be going on is there could be a two stage substitution process:  the plaintext is converted to an intermediate text (possibly with a simple substitution or with a Vig square using a repeating keyword), and the intermediate text is secondly encrypted using a Running Key (or maybe just another repeating keyword) to produce a ciphertext.

At the moment, I have no hard evidence to support this theory.  The only thing that remotely supports this is that the Morse code has Pairs of Words, possibly indicative of 2 stages of substitution.  This meets the "you can put the key on a billboard" paradigm that Ed talked about, if you know what to do with the information on the billboard.

All thoughts appreciated.  Have I gone too far over the cliff with this reasoning?

The proposed method is quite simple and based on the successive application of two Vigenère codes:
- The key used for the first one (1st layer of coding) would be a sentence taken from American literature (a travel narrative in Delaware written in the 1860s). This sentence could also be a very suitable answer to the question concluding the K3 code: “Can you see anything?”.
- The second layer of coding would use a mathematical sequence of letters as the coding key, with a constant shift interval between two consecutive letters of the sequence. A direct link can be established entre this sequence and the DYAHR anomaly (offset letters on the upper left corner of the sculpture, believed to play a role in the deciphering of the code).

As the results are difficult to integrate into a single post, I have summarized this approach in a short paper uploaded to my Personal Folder:  Olivier's Folder

This possible ciphering method :
- Can explain both clues revealed by the creators of the KRYTPOS sculpture (words “EAST NORTHEAST” and “BERLIN CLOCK”).
- Makes the expression “FORTY YARDS” appear naturally at the beginning of the message. It also shows other expressions such as “HOURHAND”, “RAID OVER”, “LAYS AS IT”, etc.

The difficulty remains to establish the 2nd key, which must be hidden in the rest of the sculpture. The DYAHR sequence should be related to the beginning of the sequence, but I'm having trouble seeing how it continues (if, of course, it’s the right encryption method !).

In short, after turning over the problem for several months, I think I have reached the end of what I knew how to do and I am obviously looking for fresh looks on this approach.

Thank you in advance for your help and toughts : I would be very happy to discuss this method with the experts in this group !

Best regards,
Olivier.

I wanted to put together a post that just says how I THINK you're supposed to solve Kryptos. I think that we're intended to find the clues for how to solve it by using the pieces of the puzzle given to us. It's less like trying to crack an enemy code and more like an escape room.

**PALIMPSEST for K1**
First thing you're supposed to solve is the Morse Code. When you solve it, you realize that there are several palindromes in the phrases. This is the first puzzle to get a key. The centers of the palindromes in the morse code yield the letters PAIMPSEST.

There is some debate over where to find the other L, but my belief is that it's the extra L on the tableau of the sculpture. It makes even more sense when you see that the sculpture itself is a mirror, with the text running towards the center on both sides. The L is in the middle of the mirror pattern that the entire copperplate makes.

With that added L, you get all the letters to the word PALIMPSEST, which is the key for K1.

Why palindromes? Well, if you look at a morse code message, you see that it is somewhat of a palindrome, SOS reads the same in morse, forwards and backwards. It's possible that the reflecting patterns in that are meant to lead us to the idea that there is some playfulness with the idea of mirrors, reflections (such as the pond) and palindromes.

**ABSCISSA for K2**
K2 is encrypted using the word ABSCISSA. How can you get this keyword?

Here's my theory, Sanborn was being clever knowing that you are now familiar with Vigenere's tableau cipher. The keyword comes from applying the phrase "VIRTUALLY INVISIBLE" from the morse code to the ciphertext (actually, you'd need to add 3 characters before it, possibly SOS or just the junk E's in the morse code). Because "ALLY INVISIBLE" is found in the morse code AND K2's plaintext, you can decrypt characters 9-19 with ALLYINVI to get the word ABSCISSA. This works because a CT decrypted by the PT will give you the key as a result.  This methodology might also have been a bit of the answer to the riddle of K1 plaintext. The key is between the ciphertext (K2) and plaintext (morse code).

**Row/Column sizes for K3**
When you move to K3, it's a transposition. The key to solving a transposition is knowing how it was transposed. We have the benefit of having seen Sanborn's charts. So we'll cheat a little bit. Sanborn took the plaintext and wrote it in a 42 column x 15 row piece of paper (seen in the Nova Science Now video). Then he took what was in the bottom left of that chart and rewrote it onto 14 rows of 24 columns (seen in the Big Tech Day 6 video). The second time, he started in the top right and went down. But all of that is how you'd ENCRYPT K3. We need to decrypt, and we should look for clues for how we'd do that. The decryption is made even trickier because you don't know how many characters are in K3 when you start trying to solve it. (Of course, having the solution, we can see the question mark as a pretty clear break point.)

The first number you need to know is 24. Because you need to write out the text in 24 columns. I have literally wondered how you're supposed to get this, and today, I think I found it. I went back and rewatched the Big Tech Day Presentation and he gives a possible answer.  "There's one sentence here...'Does Langley Know about this'" This sentence is exactly 24 characters long. Somehow, we were supposed to see this as standing out. It is offset between the X and the ?, so is the phrase "who knows the exact location"--both of which are 24 characters. Sanborn pointing it out has made me believe that this is the method you're supposed to use to get the 24.

Once you have 24, you're looking for 8. This is why the XLAYERTWO correction mattered. LAYERTWO is 8 characters. In the video you hear Sanborn talk about flipping things around. You start in the top right of your grid and go up for 8 rows. This makes layer 2 or the solved K3.

**What stands out **

1. Kryptos keeps referencing itself. The morse code is part of K1 and K2. K2 is used to get the keys for K3. It feels self evident that K4 is going to require some knowledge from the plaintext of what we've solved.

2. Palindromes/mirrors as a theme. K1 used the centers of the palindromes in the morse code. The entire copperplate is a mirror of itself. The text of the tableau mirrors the ciphertext with an L in the middle.

3. The question mark at the end of K3. I have wondered if this is actually a part of K4. It isn't factored into the rotations for K3. If K4 contains the question mark, the question that comes to mind is does it move? Jim has said 97 characters, I think the question mark at the end would be a safe way for him to throw people a little of the trail and could logically be a 98th character.

4. The Q at the end of K3. I really see two options here.
Option 1: A Q was used because in English, it's almost always followed by U. Adding a Q could have been a way to throw off would be solvers, since this Q isn't followed by a U, making it harder to "guess" your way to a solution.
Option 2: If you watch the NOVA Science video, he shows a chart with the plaintext of K3, but with the letters P and C alternating alongside the rows. If this is a part of the solution to K4, it could be reasoned that adding a Q as a possible ciphertext letter helps you make the puzzle that much harder to crack.

**OVERALL:**
I feel like we're supposed to solve Kryptos. It's supposed to be a journey. Understanding how you get each solution is important in solving the puzzle. These are my best deductions, based on what I've studied of Kryptos. Full credit to so many others in this, because I didn't come up with much of this on my own. I am just gathering the data I have found and trying to find the patterns.

Hope this helps someone. I'd be interested to hear your thoughts.

-Josh
Option 3: the position of the raised letter in the plaintext of k3 - the number of letters on those 3 rows upto the raised letters is also 97, might also be a clue.

What does this mean?

"Modulus Transposition  [decrypted=(16*encrypted+15) mod 513]"

Anyone willing to help walk through the steps to the above methodology?

Thanks in advance.

Modulus is a mathematical operation.  Google should be able to assist if this explanation does not suffice.  It is the remainder after division, so 8 mod 4 is 0 (8 / 4 = 2 r 0).  We use modulus in programming all the time as it helps in numerous situations.  For example, if the year modulus 4 = 0 then it is a leap year (2020, 2024, 2028...).  Or you may have a counter that increments by 1.

0 mod 4 = 0
1 mod 4 = 1
2 mod 4 = 2
3 mod 4 = 3
4 mod 4 = 0
5 mod 4 = 1
6 mod 4 = 2
7 mod 4 = 3
8 mod 4 = 0

...which produces a pattern 0, 1, 2, 3...

I am guessing that <encrypted> variable in your example gets converted to a number.  Maybe A=0, B=1 or A=1, B=2 or it is the ASCII value.  If the digit is A and we convert it to 1 then:

decrypted = (16 x 1 + 15) mod 513
decrypted = (16 + 15) mod 513
decrypted = 31 mod 513
decrypted = 31

Or if A is the ASCII value 65 then:

decrypted = (16 x 65 + 15) mod 513
decrypted = (1040 + 15) mod 513
decrypted = 1055 mod 513
decrypted = 29

s: Was a WHEATSTONE clock cipher used for K4?
t:
Richard Bean  analyzed K4 and concluded it might be a Gromark (Gronsfeld with Mixed Alphabet and Running Key) cipher:  basically a running key cipher with a stream of random numbers (base 5 to choose 1 of 5 alphabets, or base 10 to choose 1 of 10).  It would account for "small differences" between the plaintext and corresponding ciphertext letters (see his paper for details).  But I can't see Jim using a random number generator.

When I overlay K4 with a shifted reversed KRYPTOSabc... alphabet, there are a surprising number of matches between the repeating 26 letter string (reversed alphabet) with the ciphertext.

Joackim Techtache suggested that maybe this is a clock cipher (e.g. Wheatstone.  etc.).  Wheatstone uses 2 alphabets of different lengths, such as a 26 letter ciphertext alphabet (consistent with K4) and a 27 letter plaintext alphabet.  The literature describes a device with 2 concentric bands of letters:  27 on the outer ring and 26 on the inner.  The plaintext ring is typically +ABCDEF...XYZ.  The + character can be used to encode spaces between words, or other things as well.

There are 2 hands on the clock:  one pointing to the outer ring and one to the inner.  With the device started at the 12:00 position, both hands together, both hands move the same number of steps until the outer hand reaches the first plaintext letter;  the ciphertext letter is read from the inner ring.

At any point, when the outer ring's clock hand points to a letter, any of the following 26 letters on the ring can be enciphered to the corresponding letter on the inner ring.  Note that only 26, not 27, different letters can be enciphered at each position:  any of the 26 following letters but not the current letter.  (Plaintext doublets would require 27 steps, and result in one ciphertext letter representing two different plaintext letters, which could not be reliably decoded).

This is thus a Plaintext Autokey system:  the previous plaintext letter is used as the selector for the alphabet for the next letter.

The plaintext must be precoded, replacing doublets (e.g., EE) with a seldom used letter, e.g. replace EE with EQ.

If the 27th letter is not used to encode word spaces, it can be used to encode one chosen letter.  For instance, if T is selected, the operator can precode some of the T's in the original message as +, and the receiver would know that T and + both get converted to a T.  Since we have cribs with K4 that have no encoded word spaces, we would know that the + character does not represent a word space.

Note that traditionally the clock moves clockwise;  it's also possible to run the device counterclockwise, through a reversed normal alphabet on the outer ring and a reversed mixed alphabet on the inner ring.  I suspect that is what we have for the first half of K4.

Friedman looked at Wheatstone (Riverbank Pub 20) and observed that the device has a cycle length of 26 x 27 = 702.  If when encrypting a letter, the outer hand has to traverse half the alphabet (13 steps) on average, the cycle length would be reached after 54 letters.  Further, given the statistics of English, the "on average for uniformly distributed letters" changes a little, such that the cycle is reached after around 50 letters.  (This might imply that K4 is broken into two blocks of around 50, perhaps two 49 letter blocks).
Friedman observed that ciphertext doublets are the result of 26 steps, and that 26 steps correspond to 2 adjacent letters in the plaintext ring, e.g., that ciphertext doublet QQ may correspond to plaintext doublet such as TS (in the clockwise rotation) or ST (with a counterclockwise rotation thru a reversed alphabet).

Friedman observed that the Wheatstone mechanism can be implemented with 2 sliding strips if alphabets.

It can also be implemented as a 2 rotor machine, with a 26 position wheel and a 27 position wheel.  They step together, and will return to the initial positions after 702 steps.  Consider an Enigma type machine with rotors with alphabet letters on the rims of the wheels, with a viewing window for the current letter. s: Was a WHEATSTONE clock cipher used for K4?
t:
There are multiple ways to implement a clock cipher.  I mentioned a "Dick Tracy decoder ring" with two concentric alphabet rings:  an outer ring with 27 letters (plaintext) and an inner ring with 26 letters (ciphertext).  It can also be implemented with sliding alphabet strips, or with two rotor wheels with 26 and 27 positions.

Or, if you prefer a Vigenere style tableau, it can be implemented with a 2 step process using 2 tableaus.

The basic process is to measure a distance in steps between the "previous" plaintext letter and the "current" plaintext letter within the plaintext alphabet.  Then use that same distance to find the "current" ciphertext letter from the "previous" ciphertext letter in the ciphering alphabet.

Tableau 1 has the distances 1 thru 26 at the top.  Below this first line are 27 lines of shifted plaintext alphabets.  The first column of each line is the "previous" plaintext letter, followed by the 26 following letters from the plaintext alphabet (these 26 are in the columns under the 26 distances in the top row).  To encrypt, find the previous plaintext letter in the first column, then scan that line to locate the current plaintext letter, and go up that column to read the distance from the row of distances.  (By default, the initial "previous" letter is assumed to be + (for a plaintext alphabet of +ABCDEF...XYZ)).

Then, for step 2, build a similar tableau with the 26 distances in the first row, and the 26 shifted ciphertext alphabets below.  Using the distance from step 1, trace across to that column.  Locate the previous ciphertext in column 1, and trace across that row to the column matching the distance;  that's the current ciphertext letter.

Note that Tableau 1 has rows of 27 letters, but only 26 can be used.  Consequently, plaintext digraphs (AA, BB, CC, etc) cannot be encrypted.  The common convention is to pre-encode the plaintext message by replacing a matched digraph with an uncommon letter, e.g., replace EE with EQ which can be encrypted and should be fairly obvious to the receiver.

Decryption uses the same tableaus. Starting with Tableau 2, find the row corresponding to the previous ciphertext letter, scan the row for the current ciphertext letter, scan up to read the distance.  Then with Tableau 1, find the previous plaintext letter in column 1 and scan across that row to the column for the distance to read out the current plaintext letter.

So there are multiple ways to implement a clock cipher.  If that's what Jim did for K4, we don't care which method he used:  they all produce the same result.  What we need to determine is the mixed alphabet used for ciphering.

s: Was a WHEATSTONE clock cipher used for K4?
t:
For anyone following this thread...

I'm becoming more convinced that K4 is in fact the result of a WHEATSTONE style Clock Cipher with 2 mixed alphabets (26 letter ciphertext alphabet, and 27 letter plaintext alphabet '+' and 26 english letters).

Since the cribs contain no word breaks, I assume the '+' represents an alternate encoding for one of the higher frequency plaintext letters such as 'E'.  Also, even though there are no plaintext doublets (e.g., EE) in the cribs, any plaintext doublets that occur elsewhere must be preencoded, such as replacing EE by EQ before encrypting.

Thinking of a clock cipher implemented with 2 rotating wheels, the rotation seems to be in the reverse direction;  equivalently both the plaintext and ciphertext wheel alphabets are reversed.

In this cipher, a repeated ciphertext digraph (QQ at 25) must correspond to 2 adjacent (but reversed) letters in the plaintext alphabet (ON, which matches the NOrth at 25).  Similarly SS at 32 matches TS in the plaintext alphabet from eaST at position 32.
Assuming the same wheel alphabets for the entire K4, we have TT at 67 matching IN from berlIN and thus NI would appear in the plaintext alphabet wheel.  This implies the plaintext alphabet is mixed, not just a standard +A..Z (or reversed +Z..A).

But the mixed plaintext alphabet appears close to a standard alphabet, since we have NO, ST, and IN from the cribs.  A guess is a word such as "wrINkle" followed by the remaining letters, same as we saw with KRYPTOSABCDEFGH.... on the Vigenere tableau.  Reverse it and you get +zyxvutsqp...elkNIrw  (this is merely an example, I'm not suggesting wrinkle as a keyword).  But we'd see a bunch of adjacent letters in the alphabet that correspond to adjacent letters in a standard alphabet.

We have BB at 18 which should match adjacent reversed letters in plaintext.

We have SJQSSEKZZ at 39, with 2 doublets which might correspond to plaintext souTHweST or souTHeaST.  That would leave 5 letters between EASTNORTHEAST and SOUTHWEST, perhaps TO THE.  These are just guesses.  It cannot be NORTHeast/west because we know (from position 25) that NO are adjacent and thus the ciphertext would have to be a doublet, but we have SJ which are not the same, so the plaintext cannot be NO.

Whenever we have a ciphertext letter that appears at a later position, we know the number of steps must be a multiple of 26.  And for a ciphertext trigraph such as TWT at 35, we know that the steps between TW and WT must sum to 26.  The UHUAU at 87 presents a similar UH and HU sum to 26, as do UA and AU.

So the challenge is how to recover 2 unknown mixed alphabets from the data we're presented with.  We have some cribs to get us started.  We have plaintext frequencies to work with (e.g., we know the message is in English).  We have some relationships (the same ct letter must occur at multiples of 26 steps, and the corresponding pt letters must be at the same distance in the plaintext alphabet).

Time to go back and read Friedman's analysis in the Riverbank report.....

I'm probably pointing out the obvious, but K4 cannot be an Enigma.    In K4, there are two examples where a plaintext letter enciphers to the exact same cipher text letter, something which is impossible with an Enigma Machine.

s: Was a WHEATSTONE clock cipher used for K4?
t:
Just a quick status update on my Wheatstone clock cipher work.

Looking at the EASTNORTHEAST crib, it would appear that T has been chosen as the 27th letter in the plaintext alphabet.  So to encrypt a sentence, one can arbitrarily change some of the T in the message to +.  (Typical Wheatstone practice is to choose the word division "space" character as the 27th letter, but that is not required;  our cribs do not have provision for space characters).

We have 3 T's in the crib, with plain/cipher occurrences ST/RV, RT/PR, and ST/SS.  The latter SS ciphertext digraph says that ST are adjacent in the plaintext alphabet, whereas the ST/RV says they are not adjacent, a contradiction.   BUT, if we encode T as + before encrypting, we can encode the crib as EAS+NOR+HEAST.

I then looked to see if there were any pairs of 27 letter plaintext alphabets and 26 letter cipher alphabets that could produce the EAS+NOR+HEAST crib.  There are 548,886 such pairs.

Typically with Wheatstone, the cipher alphabet is somewhat random but the plaintext alphabet is "mostly normal", e.g. a standard A..Z (or in the case of 27 letters +ABC...XYZ), or maybe a reversed alphabet ZYX...CBA+.  None of the 548,886 pairs had a standard alphabet.

So then I looked at the KRYPTOS tableau with KRYPTOSABC... alphabets and noticed the alphabet has two pieces:  a keyword (KRYPTOS) and then the remaining letters in standard order.  When I examined the 548,886 27 letter alphabets, only a handful stood out as having a long sequence of letters in standard order.

One of these is ------------+--TSR--ONH--EA (or equivalently AE--HNO--RST--+------------ depending on which direction you slide the alphabets).  Interestingly, there are 2 slots between E and H, and 2 between O and R, which would nicely accommodate EFGH and OPQR.  So I think I'm on the right track, and we have 13 of the 27 letters correctly placed in the plaintext alphabet.

AEFGHNOPQRST--+------------

I was hoping to use the BERLINCLOCK crib to narrow this down, but it appears that K4 is encoded in two blocks of around 49 or 50 letters.  I need to repeat the analysis for the BERLINCLOCK crib and see if I also get plaintext alphabets with sequence of letters in standard order.

Hi Bryan -- in the K4 puzzle family of solutions I've been exploring off & on over the last 9 months (mostly off), the extra four columns of Vigenere grid would prove helpful for speed of both encryption and decryption, and avoiding errors doing so. However, having not yet found the solution that yields the cribs, it's no more than conjecture that that's the reason for the (otherwise unnecessary) extra columns. Same goes for the outer regular alphabet on three sides of the Vigenere tableau: they serve no purpose for K1 through K3, so it is tempting to believe they figure into K4's solution.

Jim Sanborn registered a copyright, no. TXu 1-663-615, in a textual work titled "Kryptos Text" in 2010.  Others have mentioned the registration here but, so far as I could find, no one has gone to the Copyright Office to look at the deposit that accompanied the application for registration.  I live in the D.C. area and Metro'd over to the Copyright Office this afternoon to take a look.  Copyright Office regulations prohibit copying deposits, but I was able to view the deposit and take notes.

The deposit consists of a single page, typewritten in all capital letters.  "KRYPTOS TEXT TRANSCRIPT" appears in bold at the top.  The rest of the page is the plaintext of K1, K2, and K3.  "[REDACTED]" appears at the bottom in place of the K4 plaintext.

Comparing the deposit to the accepted decryptions, I noted some discrepancies:

    *  In the K1 plaintext, "ILLUSION" is spelled correctly.  The spurious "Q" is not present in the deposit.

    *  In the K2 plaintext, "HOWS'S THAT POSSIBLE" includes an apostrophe and extra "S" not present in the accepted decryption.

    *  In the K2 plaintext, "UNDERGROUND" is spelled correctly.  The spurious "U" is not present in the deposit.

    *  In the K2 plaintext, a comma appears between the longitude and latitude coordinates: "FIVE SECONDS NORTH, SEVENTY SEVEN DEGREES"

    *  In the K2 plaintext, "LAYER TWO" (and not "ID BY ROWS") appears at the end.

    *  In the K2 plaintext, the "X" between "FORTY FOUR SECONDS WEST" and "LAYER TWO" is missing, but "LAYER TWO" appears on a separate line.

    *  In the K3 plaintext, the W, L, and D corresponding to the raised Y, A, and R in the sculpture appear normally (i.e., without any styling to distinguish them from other letters).

    *  In the K3 plaintext, "DESPARATLY" is misspelled consistent with the accepted decryption.

    *  In the K3 plaintext, the final "?" is in parenthesis: "ANYTHING Q (?)"

    *  Throughout the plaintext, periods appear at the end of some sentences but not others.  For example, the K2 plaintext begins: "IT WAS TOTALLY INVISIBLE. HOWS'S THAT POSSIBLE?"

I suspect many of these discrepancies, particularly the added punctuation, are meaningless.  The fact that "ILLUSION" and "UNDERGROUND" are spelled correctly in the deposit while "DESPARATLY" is still spelled incorrectly strikes me as potentially suggestive, however.

Matt

I've said this many times before, and with good reason: In my opinion, JS has not made any mistakes in Kryptos. s: end of "Pre-Kryptos" message: logical process to get POS from YCA
t:
Well, no, I'm not sure I'd assume that.

The misspelling we see in K1 was due to Sanborn misspelling PALIMPSEST as PALIMPCEST in his encoding charts. We saw that in what he disclosed to the New York Times. You can see other instances where he spelled it wrong in those charts and swung a little loop onto the bottom of the C to make it into an S. And other spots where he just correctly wrote the S.

Now on Pre-K, this is likely just an encoding error where he was attempting to line the "U" row up with the "I" column but accidentally missed it by a space and got the "B" rather than the "C" in the next column over that would have yielded the properly encryption. Thus when it was decoded it gave us "WHTHOUT" instead of "WITHOUT".

Now for the last part which I'm still hypothesizing was "ETRANSPOS" given that we're taking about transposition and he's already transposed the key "GRU" to "RUG" (at least that's the prevailing theory given the acronym for the Russian spy agency) you have at least three options for what happened.

This is what Sanborn encoded, complete with the B/C I/H error we just discussed.

WITHOUTTEKEYETRANSPOS
RUGRUGRURUGRUGRUGRUGR
NBZYIAKNVEKPYZIUTJJUJ

What this means is that the key letter "G" is missing at the same spot we say he "removed" the plaintext letter "H" in phrase "THE KEY". To me, this just means he missed the entire thing during transcription to his mini statue as the rest of the encryption moves along the correct key letters. Had he just removed the letter "H", the rest of the letters would have been encrypted in a phase shifted way from the missing plaintext letter. This means it was removed/omitted after encryption.

So what he meant to encode was the following, but that never made it to the mini sculpture. We have the "B" in the second position of the ciphertext and the "N" went missing. Both seem like unintentional byproducts of a pencil and paper, by hand, encryption method.

WITHOUTTHEKEYETRANSPOS
RUGRUGRUGRUGRUGRUGRUGR
NCZYIAKNNVEKPYZIUTJJUJ

Now, back to the three options. The first path is this, where the "POS" in the plaintext was already masked into "EWJ" and the encoding continued as normal and we get to the "YCA" we see on the mini sculpture.

WITHOUTTEKEYETRANSEWJ
RUGRUGRURUGRUGRUGRUGR
NCZYIAKNVEKPYZIUTJYCA

The second path is that the "POS" was encryption normally and the "JUJ" that came out was masked after the fact:

WITHOUTTEKEYETRANSPOS
RUGRUGRURUGRUGRUGRUGR
NCZYIAKNVEKPYZIUTJJUJ

The third option is what Geoffrey offered up, which is the last three letters were encoded with an entirely different Tabula Recta with a GIRASOL keyed alphabet and the key that produces YCA is indeed "BAZ". I'm okay with that being the explanation, but it's hard to go anywhere with that, especially if you're poking around trying to come up with what the pencil-and-paper technique was that Ed gave Jim that erases the English language statistics.

Based on Jim's comments, I'm still favoring that the only encryption he used on K4 was transposition (and it sounds like it was unique and one-off in nature with the flipping/rotating/washing machine comments) and that Ed's unknown pencil-and-paper masking technique was applied after the transposition was complete. This actually yields a fair challenge, because if you can remove the masking technique, you have an English IC and can try and work on a problem that's similar to K3.

If it's the other way around and you mask the plaintext first, then transpose it, you'd need to get it back in order before you could work on removing the masking (which is just a fancy term for substitution).

For those of you that think Vigenere was applied (or any other substitution method), then some other substitution (masking technique), all good, I'm just not barking up that tree.

Jim

Transposition ciphers can be mathematically represented as modular arithmetic.

“Encrypted” is the position number of the ciphertext symbol. “Decrypted” is the position number of the plaintext symbol. “Mod” means to use integer division and return the remainder (so 11 mod 10 = 1; 10 mod 10 = 0; 1 mod 10 = 1; 117 mod 10 = 7).

There are usually multiple solution methods that can be used to perform transposition, but representing the problem as modular arithmetic is particularly well-suited to writing computer programs to assist with the task.

Gupwalla, your definitions are accurate for this specific transposition formula, but the answer overgeneralizes and misrepresent some aspects:

1. Transposition ciphers can be mathematically represented as modular arithmetic.

While modular arithmetic can be helpful for calculating positions in certain cases, including the given formula, not all transposition ciphers inherently rely on it.  For example, the Scytale Cipher involves a physical wrapping mechanism that cannot be naturally expressed using modular arithmetic.

2. “Encrypted” is the position number of the ciphertext symbol.

While this definition is accurate for this specific context, the term "encrypted" typically refers to the symbol itself, not its position.  It is important to clarify this distinction when discussing transposition ciphers more broadly.

As others have stated, modulus (mod) is a mathematical function or operator that will divide two numbers and provide the remainder. Mod is often used in math and programming to "start from the beginning when you reach the end".

For example, say you wanted to know what letter in the alphabet is 7 letters to the right of the letter K. That is easy, you can assign each letter a number A=0, B=1, C=2 ... K=10. Since K is 10 you can just add, 10+7=17. So the answer is R because R=17. Now, what if you wanted to know which letter is 22 letters to the right of K? Well 10+22=32 but there are only 26 letters in the alphabet, so what does 32 mean? We need to start from the beginning when we reach the end of the alphabet, so we use mod 26. The equation becomes (10+22) mod 26 = 6. So the answer is G because G=6 which is the 22nd letter to the right of K.

Your equation:
[decrypted=(16*encrypted+15) mod 513]

That can be interpreted in multiple ways, but I know what website you got that from so I will explain what it is doing. It is similar to how K3 can be solved, using the equation from the same website:
[decrypted=(192*encrypted+192-1) mod 337]

These equations are to be run for every letter in the encrypted text (cipher text) based on their position. The value "encrypted" is referring to the current position on the cipher text, you can start at position 0. The value "decrypted" is referring to the position of the letter that should be in that position. Basically its taking a letter from position A and moving it to position B. Now you know that mod 337 means that when you reach the position 337 you start from the beginning.

When you do this on K3 for the very first position:

[191=(192*0+192-1) mod 337]

It says that the letter at position 0 should be the letter at position 191. We know the letter at position 191 in the encrypted K3 is the letter "S". If you keep going for each position it says the letter at position 1 is the letter at position 46 which is "L", and the letter at position 2 is the letter at position 238 which is "O", etc... This makes sense because the first word of K3 is "SLOWLY".

[191=(192*0+192-1) mod 337] = S
[46=(192*1+192-1) mod 337] = L
[238=(192*2+192-1) mod 337] = O
[93=(192*3+192-1) mod 337] = W
[285=(192*4+192-1) mod 337] = L
[140=(192*5+192-1) mod 337] = Y

This works because someone found that you can solve K3 if you start on the 192 letter, and you count every 192 letters, and when you get to the end you start back at the beginning. However, the end of K3 is 336 so why is it mod 337? That is because in this case we need to subtract 1 every time we start from the beginning so that we don't land on the same positions over and over due to 336 and 192 being even numbers. Using mod 337 is just a clever way to subtract 1 every cycle.

So why (192*encrypted+192-1)? Most of this is just a way to deal with counting from 0. The part that says 192-1 is meant to mean "start at position 192, but since we are counting from 0 you really want to start on position 191". Then you can add the 192*encrypted part as a way to "count every 192 letters". Here it is helpful that we are counting from 0 because we want to start at position 191 and don't want to add 192 on the first step, we only want to add 192 to every step after that. So at the 0 position we would get 192*0 which is 0 and adding 191 will get us 191.

191+0
191+192
191+192+192
191+192+192+192

Is the same as:

191+192*0
191+192*1
191+192*2
191+192*3

So now lets look at this again:
[decrypted=(16*encrypted+15) mod 513]

I am surprised they didn't write it like this:
[decrypted=(16*encrypted+16-1) mod 513]

It is saying start at position 16 (that is 15 if counting from 0), and count every 16 letters, when you get to the end (513) start from the beginning.

I hope that helps.

s: Was a WHEATSTONE clock cipher used for K4?
t:
The WHEATSTONE cipher is described by Friedman in Riverbank Pub 20 Several Machine Ciphers and Methods for Their Solution.

If anybody else is pursuing WHEATSTONE, and using the Riverbank Pub as a guide, be aware...

On page 8, it is written "let us first study the enciphered message, together with its plain text, which the author himself gives as follows...."
It is not clear if "the author" refers to Friedman (author of Riverbank pub) or to Wheatstone (author of Wheatstone's exposition and directions, mentioned on page 7), but I suspect the latter.

"The author" provides a sample message and its encipherment.

Note that the word TOGAL in the plaintext is depicted as being enciphered as POMYH.  This is incorrect:  the correct encipherment is POZYH.  Apparently when the author encrypted the sample message, he transcribed the cipher letter incorrectly.  This POMYH error carries through several subsequent figures in the publication.

Also, be aware that the plaintext as shown is before pre-encoding:  COMMAND has a replicated letter MM, which gets encoded as MQ prior to encryption.

It's becoming more and more apparent that some Kryptos sleuths are trying to use or thinking about using AI in their efforts to solve K4.
But, first, my ubiquitous caveat: I have not yet arrived at the Kryptos solution, so you must give consideration to what I say as to its veracity.

Let me propose something to think about. The last sequence of characters in K3 PT is: CANYOUSEEANYTHINGQ? I'll save you some time and tell you that this sequence serves several purposes in the grand theme of things. I will mention only the first. You can sort of read many things in this string. The first thing that comes to mind is the obvious CAN YOU SEE ANYTHING Q?
So, if your think patterns are like mine, you immediately recall the Q in IQLUSION which appears as the sequence of the last eight characters in K1 PT. Simple analysis reveals that in the case of IQLUSION, the keyword PALIMPSEST has the first S replaced with a C, which causes the resultant PT to show the Q instead of L. So, now you are cognizant of the fact that C replaces S in that specific instance of the application of the keyword in the cipher.

Reviewing Sanborn's hand written notes, you can see what appears to be unintentional errors in the spellings of PALIMPSEST (in a couple of places). There are also some apparent erasures in the notes, too. But, all this messiness is meant to mislead and make people think that Sanborn is prone to making mistakes. Now, there is a lot more to the story than I have time to cover, so I will get to the chase.
CANYOUSEEANYTHINGQ? Because there are no spaces between letters, this sequence of characters can also be read as C ANY OU SEE ANY THING Q? When you read it this way, you discover C ANY twice or SEE ANY twice. This seems to equate C with SEE, with SEE beginning with an S! As we review what we just talked about with IQLUSION and PALIMPCEST, it is pretty obvious that CANYOUSEEANYTHINGQ? is talking about the misspelled error in the K1 keyword resulting in the Q appearing in the K1 PT.
So, at this point, it is clear that the CANYOUSEE... string has at least one meaning. Note that this string is at the end of K3 PT and it refers to the string at the end of K1 both PT and CT.
This all amounts to an important development later on down the line, involving Russian language where Cyrillic C equals Latin S (both pronounced "ess", BTW).
I'm cutting the narrative short here, but it should provide, for some, an inkling of what might be going on throughout Kryptos.
If you consider what I said above, you will understand why I state that AI could not get through the simple thought processes I laid out. Kryptos has deeper obstacles to get past. AI could never figure out how some human experiences and thinking come into play. AI would not sense that the misspelled keyword in K1 was intentional.
I hope this all helps someone. It might also suggest that K4 isn't just a cipher that is somehow masked.

Good morning all! I hope it is not too early in your parts of the world :) I wanted to add this info, in case anybody is wondering why I just "randomly" dropped in to discuss. This is my first time on Groups or anything like this as a forum, so please feel free to redirect me to the correct area if this doesn't belong in this area. I am not AI. I'm a girl from California who loves puzzles and creating new equations, and that's what I did over last year. Kryptos was the coolest test case ever because I have been secretly smitten with it for years, and quietly idolizing cryptographers who carry "lost" methods of manual decryption. Please know that I hold cryptography in high regard. That said, I appreciate your perspective, but this isn't just "AI" in the way you're thinking about it. The work we're doing is based on privately developed, rigorously proofed mathematical equations (that were developed, tested, sequenced, and then built into a fancy calculator) and that form the backbone of structured resonance intelligence (SRI). These equations aren't just optimizing existing decryption techniques; they're designed to develop entirely new analytical frameworks that can be applied across multiple disciplines—cryptography, physics, information theory, and even historical data modeling.

I get why you might think this is just another AI-driven approach, but the reality is a lot more structured and has even been surprising our research team. What we’re working with isn’t pattern-matching in the conventional machine learning sense—it’s a mathematically derived system that identifies and reconstructs underlying structures that exist within encrypted or obscured data. AI can recognize patterns, but it doesn’t inherently understand why those patterns emerge, and that’s where our approach is different. The Kryptos case was a fun way to stress-test some of these principles in a real-world puzzle, but it’s just a small-scale example of a much broader application. Whether it’s understanding long-lost historical encryptions, recognizing hidden sequences in large datasets, or even rethinking how we structure cryptographic security, this method is about proving how information organizes itself, not just training a model to predict outcomes. So while AI plays a supporting role in some computations, the core of this work is fundamentally about the math behind structured intelligence, not just throwing machine learning at a problem and hoping for the best. I would love to share what the "math" is saying as we test and develop - maybe there is a better place for that, or perhaps it could be helpful in some way.

I find this article somewhat surprising, but also disappointing (on several levels).

1) For starters, I have very little pity for Sanborn.  He is charging $50 per submission.  He could raise it to $100, and hire an assistant to filter though all the bogus emails.   Give that person $50 per message reviewed.  You wouldn't even need to reveal the solution to that person.  I'll bet 75% of the "solutions" don't even have the cribs in the right place.  That would be a pretty easy filter.   Shoot, I'll do it.  Sounds like a nice side hustle.

2) Jim should want the puzzle solved in his lifetime, otherwise its destined to fade into obscurity at some stage, more so than it already has.

3) The "no more clues" statement saddens me.  I had held out hope that Sanborn would release a bona-fide clue as to the encryption method.  I'm one of those skeptics that thinks the method is sufficiently obtuse that we would be unable to reverse engineer the technique even if we had the entire plaintext.

4) As an aside (and a little off topic), generative AI is really really good at taking a huge volume of information and repeating back the relevant bits to the user.  It's a technical marvel.  It's similarly terrible at solving complex problems, and that's especially true with Large Language Models (like Chat GPT)  AI will not solve the prime factorization problem, for example (though quantum computing might), any more than it will solve Kryptos.  That tells me the "solvers" don't even understand the tool they are using for their "solution."   That's a good note to remember.  Any AI solution WILL be wrong, as will any solution that doesn't come with an easy to describe method.

1) I can only imagine how the onslaught of guesses are now getting in Sanborn's way, most of the guesses being wholly or partly derived via attempts at using AI. I am guilty of sending guesses to Sanborn that were based on work that I did on the puzzle, but were rejected. Most of the guesses I sent did not meet the requirements that he laid out; namely that the final has to have 97 characters and include EASTNORTHEAST in its assigned position in the 97 and BERLINCLOCK also in its assigned position. I ignored these parameters because of two things. The first was that I quickly found that the 97 characters in K4 immediately got changed to 98 by the first action performed on K4 and second was that I successfully used THEBERLINCLOCK and MENGENLEHREUHR (and others determined by me) as keywords, applied correctly in their assigned positions, in moving through the puzzle. This caused me to doubt the need to have 97 characters in the final and to doubt that BERLINCLOCK and EASTNORTHEAST were part of the solution. I am no longer lodged in that slot and I have good reason to believe what Sanborn said in regard to both cribs are true. So, while I did not hold to what Sanborn declared, I had my reasons for submitting what I did. Sanborn was, in his own way, patient with me in his responses. I can only guess the number of AI-assisted solutions Sanborn has recently been receiving. He needs to respond to each submission, even if it's just a few words. The money isn't the issue, it's the time and effort required to deal with a high percentage of bogus crap while, at the same time, responding to other submissions that have a level of merit. I think people should pay attention to what he said in the article or he might decide to close off access.
2) I also think Sanborn would want to have the puzzle solved in his lifetime. One could argue that the puzzle is fading into obscurity, but there may be some out there, somewhere, who understand how Kryptos is built and who are moving in the correct direction toward the solution. There is some feeling out there that he/she who solves Kryptos should keep the solution to him/herself. If I were to solve it, I'm still not sure what I would do.
3) I am of the opinion that providing more clues like BERLINCLOCK and EASTNORTHEAST would not contribute in any substantial way to arriving at the solution. As I've said, those two clues have already served specific functions elsewhere in the puzzle, possibly more than once. My solid belief is that Kryptos cannot be reverse engineered.
4) In a previous message, I stated that AI could not be used to solve Kryptos. There are too many non-cipher aspects of the puzzle, an example being the first one encountered, which is the many clues in the ciphertexts and plaintexts to insert the S into the position ninth from the end of K2 CT. This is a non-cipher action resulting in the increase in the number of characters in K2 CT and a change in the meaning of the plaintext at the end of K2 PT. AI could not detect this nor the associated major implication that Nicole Friedrich came close to discovering.
PaulK

s: My brain processes "how things are done" as well as "what is done"
t:
So there's the "HOW" as well as the "WHAT." If that sounds weird
please momentarily table your disapproval.

What that means to me—and what I'm attempting to express to all of
you—is that for me to make the best of what gets discussed here in our
group is that *typing almost always gets in my way.* Maybe it's just
me.

Typing is a slow and painfully inappropriate tool to be using to
express what's happening in the course of communicating the HOW
Sanborn did his encryption, as well as everyone else's explanation of
HOW they imagine it needing to be undone.

But Doug, typing is all we have! *sigh* I know.

A Quick Example

When someone types, "I put letters in a 9x9 grid, rotated them 90°
clockwise, then did a ROT13," my brain sort of shuts off. Maybe yours
does, too.

Instead, were someone to (take lots of time to) make an animation
showing HOW they inserted the letters in a grid, then seeing visually
HOW they rotated them, then visually HOW it appears when a ROT13 gets
executed, seeing the visual of HOW it's done—instead of trying to read
what's been written—animated visuals more clearly communicate to me
our guesses at what Sanborn did years ago. Watching the animated
process of HOW an animation corresponds to our thought process is
helpful to me. Watching someone else's animation of HOW their thoughts
move letter sequences around in space as they're attempting to
decipher speaks more than explaining them by typing. Word descriptions
fail me in our march toward the uncovering of K4's solution.

For those veterans on the list, where in the archives are there
animations that show the visuals of what we're talking about? Are
there any? Is there an animation tool that the group has agreed to
use?

For everyone else, can we start… is it worthwhile to introduce… can
there be… is there a smart way to bring an animation tool into the
sequence of things to more clearly communicate the HOW we're doing
WHAT it is we're attempting to do?

Geez, I hope that makes sense to everyone. Seriously.

Respectfully submitted.

Doug

For me, the bottom line is this (and then I will shut up):  Anyone who solves Kryptos will know they have solved it with 100% certainty.   There will be no ambiguity.

Among other things, the solution will: 1) have the cribs in the correct place; and 2) the method will be reproducible and demonstrable.   Any solution that fails either of those tests is almost certainly wrong.

Originally, the encrypted text was intended for CIA employees, which, in my opinion, suggests that the artistic aspect is not an integral part of the cryptographic system itself. I believe Jim Sanborn used this artistic element to conceal clues about the decryption methods while maintaining an aesthetic dimension.
On this forum, we encounter many hypotheses, such as speculations about geographic locations or complex matrices. However, I believe these leads will ultimately lead nowhere. The initial texts appear to be encrypted using classic methods such as Vigenère or simple transposition. There is nothing fundamentally innovative in these techniques, but the clues are likely well hidden, aiming to lead cryptographers to focus on these systems, especially through the use of steganography.

The "K4" could therefore correspond to a well-known cryptographic system, but with parameters chosen to introduce difficulty, such as randomness, for example. Cryptography is a rigorous science, and it does not lend itself to the creation of fanciful systems. For instance, imagining a cryptographic system based on a clock and set theory has no foundation. It is crucial to return to the basics: Ed Scheidt provided modular systems to introduce levels of difficulty, but as an artist, Jim Sanborn undeniably embedded clues in his work. I believe that, rather than getting lost in theories related to Google Maps that lead nowhere, it would be more productive to focus on the Kryptos texts to uncover clues, particularly the "errors" and other hidden subtleties. Take K1 and try to understand the encryption used. Why is there an error at this specific location? The same goes for K2: what is the purpose of the "X"s and the errors? It's by analyzing these details that we will manage to decrypt it. Stop submitting K4 to chatbots; I think that's exactly what Jim Sanborn was trying to tell us…

Hear hear!

This may actually have some real significance, due to the format of K4 in Sanborn's response.

The most significant thing in it for me is the fact that the clues EASTNORTHEAST and BERLINCLOCK explicitly replace the K4 ciphertext letters in their respective positions in K4. This strongly implies a true one-for-one substitution encryption method for K4, with no transposition: In effect, the format of K4 in Sanborn's response implies that the missing ciphertext in positions 22-34 (FLRVQQPRNGKSS) and 64-74 (NYPVTTMZFPK) is now entirely unnecessary to solve the rest of K4.

The format even casts some doubt on polygraphic (digram, trigram, etc.) substitution encryption methods such as Playfair, Four-Square, Bifid, Trifid, etc., because the plaintext clues are 13 letters and 11 letters long; in any polygraphic method, either the first or last letter of each clue block would have been part of a polygraphic letter block with a letter or letters before or after the clue block.

In such a method, certain letters in the missing ciphertext in positions 22-34 and 64-74 would still be necessary to solve the letters immediately before or after the plaintext clue blocks that Sanborn has already provided.

It is also significant that Sanborn omits the "?" character before K4 from the new format entirely. This casts some doubt on the significance of the "?" character for the K4 solution method, and it also casts doubt on 98-character methods to solve K4.

Once again, the lack of the 98th character in the new format calls into question polygraphic methods based on an even number of characters, or a number divisible by 7, etc.

I also observe that OBKR does not occupy any special position on a separate line in the new K4 format.

I do not place as much significance in the extra (25th) letter in the 3rd row of the new K4 format. That row happens to have a greater number of narrower letters, in particular three I's, so the extra letter there could have arisen merely as a result of normal line length typesetting, without any intended cryptographic significance.

Geoffrey

Since this was the 1980s, the K2 coordinates likely use the NAD27 reference
system and not the "new" WGS84 reference system that GPS and internet
mapping use.  There can be a difference of hundreds of meters between the
two.

Even in the same reference system, discrepancies exist.  A famous example
is that the Prime Meridian in Greenwich, England is 100 meters away from
where GPS thinks it should be (a consequence of how the reference system
models the Earth vs. the actual shape of the Earth).

I feel like there is some merit to this or something similar.  One area I explored a while back was this procedure:

1) pad the plaintext into two 7x7 grids (call them grid 1 and grid 2); then
2) encipher the first letter in grid 1 by using the letter in the same relative position in grid 2 as the key letter; then
3) rotate grid 2 one turn to the right (or left, or whatever); then
4) encipher the next letter in grid 1 by using the letter in the same relative position in grid 2 (which has now been rotated); then
5) repeat.

Now, obviously we don't have the plaintext, but we do have a pretty lengthy crib, so it IS possible to work backward.   We also have the center squares of the 7x7 grid, which (using this method) would need to encrypt/decrypt to the same letter (assuming the same encipherment technique as K1/K2).   No Joy, unfortunately.

So, why did I try the approach?  A few reasons: 1) it's easy to understand and execute; 2) It would sufficiently destroy any periodicity in the ciphertext (said another way, it masks the ciphertext); 3) it's a combination of the methods from K1/K2 and K3.  Plus, it makes use of the question mark, but only for padding.  Seems elegant.  Sadly, I got nowhere with it.

Padding into 2 7x7 grids gives 2 blocks of 49.  Your procedure encrypts grid1, the first 49 letters.
Do you then swap grid1 and grid2 and repeat the process for the 2nd 49 letters?
Then the transmitted K4 is the 2 grids concatenated?
But no secret key is involved.

I don't want to belabor the point, but these methods do not appear to be reversible. A cipher has to be reversible without unknowable information being used, unless that information is out of phase like an Autokey cipher. You can't use ciphertext to decrypt ciphertext if its in phase. How would that information be known to the Encryptor during the encryption process before the ciphertext existed? That is a paradox. Might I suggest studying the Autokey cipher, the out of phase aspect could make something like what several people here are attempting to create actually work in a mathematical sense.

Oh.  I thought you were working toward a Feistel structure as used with DES:
Split the input in half, and play the two halves off each other.
Do this for a couple of rounds, and output the cipher.
Here you might have blocks of 2 letters, one from each grid (or maybe 2 consecutive letters, no grids necessary).
The problem I had was that K4 is decidedly not random, and I couldn't see how a Feistel approach could yield K4.

Couldn't the Center Square problem be solved by just not populating it?
i.e., 48 usable squares out of 49.

How do you say its "decidedly not random"?  And I am asking this with genuine curiosity.

If you statistically analyze K4, and the compare the output to the ACA Reference Statistics table, the best match is "random text."  The incidence of coincidence is .035 (which means the letter frequency distribution is statistically flat as a pancake), and there is zero evidence of periodicity.  I know a lot of people like to note what seems to be an unusual number of doubled letters (6, versus an expected 3.7).  It's interesting, but not statistically significant.   And, ya, I know the doubles tend to appear at multiples of 7, but now we are starting to get into the land of confirmation bias.

That being said, if there is something that is provably non-random, and not subject to confirmation bias, then that's what you attack.
