Wow, that's a neatly put together website! Welcome Colin.

I don't know if you're aware of the call of duty video games. Those contain ciphers, and there's a community of interested people there. A number of ciphers there went unsolved for years; and were suddenly all solved at once by "randomizer". Their approach was automation of the solving process, but in that case essentially guessing the keys to be common but the process to be random. Basically, they discovered that there used to be a website where you could paste your plaintext and key and press a Random button that would replace your plaintext with an encrypted version of it. And the way those ciphers had been created was to press the random button over and over!

This has interested me, because it's the only example I know of multilayer problems being solved. Now, some of the layers are trivial: reverse the string, rot 6, rot13, ascii to octal, ascii to hex, and so on; but those layers form an important staging post, because the stricture that appears in the cipher (eg only 9 character types for octal strings) is a signature that both affirms the previous layer and also determines the next layer.

With K4, there certainly are features that give clues to kinds of processes that might have been used. We have a similar scenario that it was put together by hand, by a non-expert with an expert's advice. And there are left-over clues from the other parts of the puzzle. For me, the fact that JS won't certify solutions to those parts, only plaintext, implies that all it is necessary to solve all those parts in order to decode K4. And for me that means for example that LAYERTWO is necessarily a key for K4. Also RQ. And dYAhRo. Just as the compass must contain clues to duress codes and so on.

So my own view is that it's much more likely that we can guess the set of keys and systems that were used and discover the solution through search of the space of reversal of those than it is we can bruteforce an unknown key to an unknown method.

The archives here have been more valuable than the discussion here of late. In particular, there are first hand accounts by Elonka and others of meetings with Jim and his comments on things. There are patterns in those comments beyond not wanting to answer questions: the story of digging and concreting while being supervised and xrayed, forming the original matrix, the orientation of the letters is important (also whats the point). You can find that the clue "in many different directions" was given before EASTNORTHEAST, for example.

Best,
colski

Colski,

  Thank you for this, the Call of Duty analogy is one of the best frameworks I've encountered for thinking about multi-layer problems. The key insight isn't the specific
  methods (rot13, hex, etc.) but that each layer leaves a detectable signature that both confirms you've peeled the previous layer correctly and points you toward the next.
  That maps directly to Sanborn's "designed to unveil itself... pull up one layer, come to the next."

  We've actually been pursuing something in this spirit computationally. A digram frequency test on K4's carved text produces a signature that's consistent with substitution
   as the outermost layer, meaning whatever you encounter first when working inward is a substitution cipher, with something else underneath. That's exactly the kind of
  staging post you're describing.

  Your point about LAYERTWO, RQ, and DYAHRO as extracted parameters rather than decoration resonates strongly. The sculpture gives you the keys; the challenge is knowing
  which locks they fit and in what order. Scheidt's "novelty is in the combination" supports this, the individual components are probably textbook, but the assembly is
  bespoke.

  On the archives being more valuable than discussion, completely agree. One observation from digging through the Antipodes material that I haven't seen discussed
  elsewhere: the KGB memo that Sanborn chose for the Cyrillic side (August 31, 1982, Fedorchuk, from the Nancy Drysdale Gallery files) contains the phrase "a counterbalance
  to the declaration of 97 Nobel Prize laureates." K4 is exactly 97 characters. Sanborn had the full KGB archive to choose from and selected the document containing that
  number. Given his precision with every other detail in the installation, I don't think that's coincidental.

  The "in many different directions" predating EASTNORTHEAST is a great catch, do you have a source for the chronology on that? I'd like to add it to our reference
  collection.

  Best,
________________________________

Greetings all, and thanks for the warm welcome. I wanted to share the primary line of investigation I’ve been pursuing regarding Kryptos K4, which centers on what I call the 73-character hypothesis.
Jim Sanborn’s yellow legal pad contains several boxed notes: “14 Lines,” “342,” “8 lines,” and “73.” On the sculpture, K4 is the final four lines and contains 97 ciphertext characters. If 73 represents the true plaintext length, that implies 24 null characters embedded in the text. The number 24 appears repeatedly in ways that may not be coincidental: 97 − 73 = 24 nulls; EASTNORTHEAST (13) + BERLINCLOCK (11) = 24 known plaintext characters; and the Berliner Weltzeituhr referenced in K3 has 24 facets.

This interpretation also aligns with comments from Ed Scheidt, the CIA cryptographer who consulted on Kryptos. In Wired he stated, “I used a bit of stego when designing the fourth part” and that “the masking technique may not be a known technique.” A null mask (embedding a real message inside padding) would qualify as a straightforward form of steganography. There is also a historical detail that may be relevant: during Scheidt’s CIA tenure, IBM punch cards were still widely used, where columns 1–72 contained data and 73–80 were reserved for sequence numbers or metadata. If intentional, the appearance of 73 in Sanborn’s notes may not be arbitrary. K2 ends with a stray X separator; K3 ends with a trailing Q. If K4 follows the same pattern, the real message is 72 characters plus a delimiter (72 + 1 = 73) and 72 = 8×9, matching Sanborn's "8 lines" note perfectly. (73 is prime, so no clean grid without a delimiter.)

After evaluating 668+ billion configurations across more than 600 attack scripts, the strongest result so far is a configuration consisting of a null mask at positions 0,1,2,5,8,12,14,20,36,38,39,40,52,55,58,59,74,75,78,84,85,88,94,96; a columnar transposition of width 7; and an Autokey Beaufort substitution using the keyword DEFECTOR with a standard A–Z alphabet. This produces a score of 15 out of 24 crib matches (ENE = 7/13, BERLINCLOCK = 8/11).

This configuration appears to be a hard local maximum. A neighborhood search involving 223 million evaluations produced no improvement. DEFECTOR is uniquely the only keyword reaching 15/24, while 18 other keyword or variant combinations plateau at 14. Notably, four of the five W positions in K4 appear as consensus nulls across every mask that reaches this score, which supports the hypothesis that W may function as a delimiter, the additional of the dots on Antipodes being the clue, (treat W's as periods) The ceiling suggests the configuration may be close but not fully correct, or that an additional transformation remains undiscovered, but the thematic relevance of DEFECTOR and its statistical uniqueness make it difficult to dismiss.

If anyone wants to experiment with this configuration directly, I built an interactive cipher workbench that runs entirely in the browser: https://www.kryptosbot.com/workbench/ . It includes 14 cipher methods, six transposition types, a clickable null-mask grid mapped to the sculpture layout, and live crib scoring. Selecting “DEFECTOR 15/24” loads the current best configuration so you can experiment with variations. If you hit 23/24 with one stubborn miss, check what letter is at that position — it might be the K4 equivalent of K3's trailing "Q".

Happy hunting.

s: The long & the short of it
t:
More just-for-the-fun-of-it...

The two longest lines on the two sides of the sculpture are 33 letters (front, 23rd line [K3]) and 32 letters (back, 15th line NGH...IJL), which add to 65.

The "shortest line" would be the 27 characters of line 25 on the front, ending with the query, just before K4 starts with OBKR.

This is only 92 so far, so we'll grab DYAHR for 5.

65 + 27 + 5 = 97 -- Now we use that as an additive, or a vig key, transpose it a bit first if we like, whatever.

To find ourselves a confirmation, we go to the Coördinates from K2. The 6.5 draws our attention because of the point. Then we encounter 77, which we will think of as two sevens, short anamathist's notation, 27; then reversing direction (Jim said he did a lot of flipping & rotating) we return to the 5. And we again have 65 + 27 + 5 = 97, thus supporting our conjecture, QED. ;)

When two layers of the onion appear to point to each other, how do you know which is the outer and which the inner? Or are they pointing elsewhere entirely? Or are they Ed's rabbit holes? (Rabbit holes in an onion?)

Carl

Firstly welcome to the new members.

Secondly, I should have called the topic Sanborn's Sabotage!

I've done spectral FFT analysis of the signal after I realised that the K4 stream of characters could represent AM/FM modulation like transforms using a simple sinusoidal offset in different ways with letters. (just passed my HAM advanced cert yesterday btw :)

On looking at the spectrum I found a very strong stream of 33 letters in K4 with an alternating +4/-4 offset applied. I have removed these and am hence forth referring to the residual as K4 minus one (as in minus one layer).

It seems that the area has some important properties which we need to explore that give away the method as to what/how K4 minus two can be reconstituted.

This hold so far with a lot of what Scheidt and Sanborn have been hinting with "if we hide frequency analysis" & "take you tools away" - classical cryptographical attack methodologies will not work (if they did it extremely well) BUT they would've had to have left a path and clear signatures as to how to recover the original text. That is what we're dealing with.

So what caused Sanborn to panic last minute? Did he feel it would be cracked too soon? Did he know enough about spectral signatures from Scheidt to realises that the +4/-4 could be detected and removed? Or did he just want to be infamous and never have it resolved and essentially just scribbled over an important section??? Who knows? - only WW apparently lol

You will also notice in the below that I have divided K4 into and upper and lower 48 characters centred around that middle W (it is an S now) as I have a strong conviction that my "mirror offset pattern around a rising 'L'" is not random. Kryptos K4 - A Vectorial Reading
A Compass + Clock Framework on a KRYPTOS-keyed Polybius Grid

Author: Benoit Desnos <[courriel]>
Paper (PDF): […]
Date: May 2026

1. The problem

Kryptos is a cryptographic sculpture installed in 1990 in the inner courtyard of CIA Headquarters at Langley. Its first three passages (K1, K2, K3) were solved in the late 1990s. The fourth passage, K4 (97 characters), has resisted public cryptanalysis for over three decades. Between November 2010 and August 2020, the artist Jim Sanborn released 24 (position, plaintext) pairs serving as anchors: EAST NORTHEAST at positions 22 to 34, and BERLIN CLOCK at positions 64 to 74.

In September 2025, journalists Jarett Kobek and Richard Byrne discovered the complete K4 plaintext in the Smithsonian archives. The documents are sealed until 2075, and the encryption method has never been published. The cryptanalytic problem remains open.

2. Approach

The paper proposes a vectorial reading of K4 on a KRYPTOS-keyed Polybius 5x5 grid (POLYBIUS_STD), with a "shortest mod 5" arithmetic on both axes. Each anchor produces a vector v(p) = coord(cipher) - coord(plain), classified as ID, TOUR (axial), FOU (diagonal), or CAV (knight's L-jump).

A decomposition hypothesis v(p) = b(p) + h(p) is formulated, where b is a compass component (knight vector) and h is a clock component (rook or bishop vector).

3. Principal findings

(a) The xp_W to vectorial class rule (V1 and R1). Under a KRYPTOS-cycle convention with reset on each W letter of the ciphertext, the parity xp_W correctly predicts the vectorial class of 21 (V1) to 22 (R1) out of the 24 anchors. Monte Carlo p = 0.0033%. Cross-Kn gap relative to max(K1, K2, K3) is +38 points.

(b) The A/B multiset frequency symmetry (Lethuillier 2025, reproduced and formalised). The 5 W letters split K4 into 6 alternating segments. The two interleaved blocks A and B (46 characters each) exhibit identical letter-count multisets. Monte Carlo p = 0.45% under random partitioning.

(c) A reflexion-symmetric trio around the median W3 (position 49). Anchors at positions 25, 69, 73 share exactly the same pair of span vectors ((-2, -2), (0, -2)), with Monte Carlo p < 0.0001.

4. Physical motivation

Three elements placed by Sanborn on the sculpture motivate the compass + clock framework:
- An engraved compass rose on a granite slab, with a needle pointing West-South-West.
- A magnetite (raw lodestone) aligned along that axis, a few centimetres from the slab.
- The Weltzeituhr (World Clock) at Alexanderplatz in Berlin, confirmed by Sanborn in November 2025 as the referent of the BERLINCLOCK anchor.

5. Epistemic status

The proposed framework constrains the 24 confirmed anchors without predictively generating the 73 unknown positions. This non-predictivity is explicit and assumed. The paper offers a reading grid compatible with the physical clues and the observed algebraic constraints, not a decryption algorithm.

All scripts, conventions, and Monte Carlo seeds are public and reproducible.

6. Falsifiability

Three scenarios would invalidate the contribution:
- Publication of the Smithsonian plaintext revealing a method that does not use POLYBIUS_STD or does not admit the v = b + h decomposition.
- A concurrent alternative method that reproduces the 24 anchors at equal or higher score without Polybius or compass + clock.
- Reproducible discrepancy on any published

CAD/3D modelling from reference images is how most modeling is done actually, I've done CAD and 3D modelling for decades with reference image techniques.

s: Interest in a small tool i've written
t:
Hello All,
20 years ago I wrote a couple of small Kryptos related tools in Visual Basic and did share them around at the time.  Individually they did mostly small operations like produce the Vigenère lookup table on screen then perform an encrypt/decrypt.  Their purpose wasn't to auto solve but to do the 'pen and paper' processes for me quickly so I could burn through a bunch of Krpytos solve ideas.

Recently I've started mucking about with C# .net and decided to take all of my little tools and bring them together into 1 program.  The program does:

  *
Vigenère Encrypt/Decrypt
  *
Solves a Vigenère for a keyword
  *
Ceaser Shifting
  *
Transform text into a table and perform rotations
  *
Provide a cipher text and plaintext at a known location, output the Vigenère keyword required.
  *
Has buttons with K1 to K4 presets on many screens.

The program does not use any form of AI. It does not write data anywhere except in memory while the program is open.  The program is pretty simple overall and only takes up 1.3mb in size in its zip file.

(I will upload the file soon.)

Kind Regards,
Ross Edwards

Some more details for Andrew (and anyone else curious):

* Submissions are private even from us. We only see email addresses and
whether the submission was correct or incorrect.
* We don't log a plaintext version of each submitted candidate or
methodology anywhere.
* We do log a encrypted copy of each submitted candidate and methodology.
It is encrypted using a Google Cloud KMS key. But I should disclose that we
can theoretically decrypt those logs through a certain manual process, and
that we do email the candidate and methodology in plaintext back to the
submitter for their own convenience (and email is not a secure medium). We
generally are less fanatical about submission security than we are about K4
plaintext security.

As for transcription errors, we had Jim enter the plaintext twice, with the
second submission verified directly against the HMAC stored on the server.
His entry of the plaintext also confirmed that the known clues
(EASTNORTHEAST and BERLINCLOCK) were in the correct place. It's never
possible to completely eliminate the risk of error, but we took every
precaution we could. We do have the K4 plaintext in an offsite vault.

Derek—we do have the K5 ciphertext and expect to release it in the future.
Won't say any more than that for now.

One more thing I could mention is that we had Jim record private video
messages for the solvers of K4 and K5... in case anyone needs any more
motivation!

Best,
Dan

s: K4 architecture paper: body XORed against tableau
t:
Hello,

I've been refining my latest K4 work from a few months ago and I uploaded a draft paper to the files area, it's here at "Personal Folders/DU Folder"
https://kryptos.groups.io/g/main/files/Personal%20Folders/DU%20Folder/k4_xor399_architecture.pdf

To state the most important part upfront, it's not a K4 decryption. It's statistical work that (good news) is reproducible and shows a pattern that's likely not chance, but (bad news) does not provide any obvious decryption hints. Or less obvious ones I should have spotted after bashing my head against it.

The core of the working theory (detailed in that paper) is this: K4 can be split into a "body" and "flanks" - head and tail. The "body" is from position 25 (start of NORTHEAST) and runs until position 85, then "KUHU..." ciphertext is the tail. The body has an interesting property: take the running KRYPTOS key from the tableau side. At position 25, where the body starts, align the "ABCD..." part of tableau row M (or, align the F of row L, offset 399, with the start of K4, which is how this was actually done). Either way, this key stream continues for the duration of the body, and it's taken from the tableau, row headers included and the "extra" L on row N included as well. Then, XOR the ciphertext ("body" part, to position 85) with the key. Letters alphabet-indexed (A=1, Z=26) and out-of-range values pass through unchanged.

The result is a big IoC spike to over 0.08 over the body. It's a notable spike even across the entire K4, to 0.0573. Random shuffles have a median of 0.0485, and of 1000 random shuffles less than in 1 in 300 have such an IoC spike, at any tableau key offset. The paper lays this out in more detail but the summary is, the alignment is significant at p=0.003. The body part's de-XORed stream is then:

{PSSVKALSZ}ASWTQSGQBFSKBZWSMZKCFEKBSLHAJ{GSPYTTGVKPZ}BQSSZSFSSPFT

with the bracketed parts being NORTHEAST and BERLINCLOCK.  Under this scheme, the de-XORed stream is the next layer of encryption (but I had no success there), and meanwhile the flanks remain very distinct from the body statistically. If so, there's probably different masking methods used for the body stream and for the flanks.

I do like that this incorporates the DYAHR observation made by Michael Hörenberg. DYAHR letters can be interpreted as M, and in this case you start doing the XOR at row M's start-of-alphabet.

Any and all thoughts are certainly welcome - I did my best to treat the investigation rigorously and the pattern is certainly there,  but I remain unsure as to what to make of it. When I first saw the XOR pattern, I definitely hoped it would also reveal some clues about the next layer but I've come up short.

In one of the pictures Paradigm shared, there appears to be a document from 5 May, 1874, signed by Ulysses S. Grant. It uses the same template as presidential pardons from that era. The document references China and Mr. Avery (presumably Benjamin Parke Avery), who would have been Chief of Mision at that point. The rest of the document isn't visible.

Does anyone have any ideas as to why that document would have been included?

A much better outcome than if I had won the auction!

Second, for those that missed it, we now have several new "confirmations" (I won't call them clues, since they verify what many people have believed).

It confirms that the plaintext is indeed exactly 97 characters long. That eliminates shorthand that some people have attempted (e.g. if a decryption method results in plaintext of "SMRTPSN", you cannot expand that into "SMART PERSON").

It also confirms that the cribs appear exactly where Jim Sanborn said they did: some people did not believe that was necessarily true. The solution submission page makes it pretty clear that the plaintext is not something like "Move the clock from the east of berlin to the northeast...".

Interesting... So it seems like the IDbyrows was deliberate? He knew about
it but acted like it was just a mistake

Yes, and it caused a lot of people (almost everybody) to believe he made a mistake, when all the clues in K1, K2 and K3 pointed to the missing X due to the missing S. I think his error in judgement by saying he made an error by removing the S misled people into thinking he made mistakes in Kryptos, which he didn't.

In my opinion the removal of the S/X was intentional, this claim is supported by the text "could take out" seen in the images, but the spelling of "ID by rows" instead of resulting in gibberish was accidental.
And the intended spelling is "Layer two", probably as a hint that the second layer of K4 is transposition.

The final design of Kryptos was to have it noticed that the X was missing after WEST in K2 which amounted to an implication to make the correction. One might think it possible that ID BY ROW S is a strong clue to solve this problem.
In my latest message, I indicated that clues exist in K1, K2 and K3 to insert the S into the 9th position from the end of K2 CT. There is a clue also in K0, the Morse code. It says (text hidden by stone)T IS YOUR POSITION. Sanborn mentioned that Morse text continues under the stone. I suggest that the first T is the last letter of the word WEST.

I've always said that there were no mistakes in the sculpture.  That is to say, nothing was carved there that was not supposed to be, and nothing was left out that was supposed to be left in.  You can always claim it was a "mistake" in that what you decided to do gave away too much info, or might better have been done elsewhere, or was insufficiently aesthetic, &c, &c., but it was never an execution mistake.

If we didn't think so on our own, when the ambiguity was revealed Ed Scheidt presently said (approximately) "Jim chose to announce it as a mistake", which seems a fairly broad hint at "the hell it is".

There are several numerical things this "error" does.  Depending whether you approach K2 as sculpted or as supplemented with the S/x, it is 369 or 370 letters long.  You need it to be 369 so that when it is divided by 3, you get 123, to go with the 21 from K1 and the 112 from K3.  You need it to be 370 so that it is expressible as 17^2 plus 9^2 and also as 19^2 plus 3^2.  Jim's into hidden forces, yes?  Hidden forces, hidden powers, whatever. The whole thing has 1,732 letters; if you yank the 3 (YAR) that appear sort of half-yanked already you get 1,729, which, as Ramanujan mentioned to Hardy (dYAhR), is expressible as 10^3 plus 9^3 and also as 12^3 plus 1^3.  Thereby hang various tales which may be pertinent or may be some of Ed Scheidt's Red-herring-Rabbit-holes, but in either case the sculpture needed a device to make us notice both things.  Thus a final 8 letters that say 2 coherent things depending on the shift of the key.

I may have missed a mention of it somewhere, but I don't recall seeing anyone reading that area as "ID by rows end" or "layer two end".  I realize that is a mixture of PT & CT, from 2 different sections, but I can't quite see that propinquity as a coincidence either.

Also, has anyone noticed an arguable near-echo at the end of the first line of K3?  Let's do a little Cyrillicization on YAhR, viz: Y is the 25th letter of the Roman alphabet, SH ditto in the Cyrillic, Roman R looks like a reversed Cyrillic YA, let's make our YAhR into Shanya.  At the far end of the same row, just after a BY divided by an ID, is ciphertext SHNAIA.  "N" in the wrong place, but close enough to make one wonder if it is intended to mean something.

Carl

s: K4 architecture paper: body XORed against tableau
t:
Not sure how many people are still studying K4 cryptanalytically but update anyway - I spent some time refining this and de-XORed interior stream remains mathematically notable under many tests. With some pushing and prodding, I got to a nice consistent model where the interior is a poly substitution with numbers assigned to plain text letters, and then I sent some serious effort on statistical computation to try and obtain more text. The hypothetical encryption mechanism here is simple enough (I made worksheets, totally feasible) and it has statistical support but, unfortunately, it's also a dead end - way too many possible readings. My computations only give a few letters across K4 with high probability, and that's not enough to get at the actual text. Even with some word guesses that seem reasonable and further extending the search around those, nothing entirely convincing shows up and, worst of all, there's nothing falsifiable so chances are that even my the best intermediate calculations were just words that happen to align crossword-style.

If I'm right about the XOR pattern and the key, it now seems to me a proper decryption isn't possible, too many degrees of freedom. And if I'm wrong about the pattern's significance (not about it being there, it's definitely there) then I don't have even a remote guess as to how else it could appear in the ciphertext.

Jamie,

Hi Steven,

I've been trying to use the Q and direction of each of the letters around
that singular Q as an emitter.  I.e. D equals a North emitter, Y as a West
emitter, A as a South, H as an East and R as a NorthEast emitter.  Combined
with this, I used K3 as the emission source.  For example, on FLRVQQPRNGKSS
= EASTNORTHEAST, find an F in the K3 CT and look in the direction of the
emitter. This worked for many letters (most were 1 square away), but it
fell apart on the Qs and the K to A mapping.  This might have been wishful
thinking because the letter density of K3 is very high and finding emission
letters from that density could render almost any phrase.  Or, it's
possible that Sanborn used a different emission source.

The doublets of Q and S in the FLRVQQPRNGKSS string and the corresponding
Q={N,O} and S={S,T} are a big clue here.  We just have to figure out how
the DYAHR ring around the Q factors into this.

Pat

An anomaly I noticed about 15 years ago and I forgot to write up. Using a standard Vigenère grille (not the KRYPTOS
keyed one) the following is true: MZFPKW + ERLINB = QQQXXX.

If you're mathematically inclined, you can think of + as addition modulo
26, using alphabet numbers where A=0, B=1, etc.). If you're not then "+"
means "use the Vigenère tableau".

pos   ct  val    key  val    sum   mod 26   letter
 ----------------------------------------------------
  69    M   12  +   E    4   =  16   =  16   ->  Q
  70    Z   25  +   R   17   =  42   =  16   ->  Q
  71    F    5  +   L   11   =  16   =  16   ->  Q
  72    P   15  +   I    8   =  23   =  23   ->  X
  73    K   10  +   N   13   =  23   =  23   ->  X
  74    W   22  +   B    1   =  23   =  23   ->  X

And the jump from Q to X is 7 letters (standard alphabet). And 7 seems
important. At the time it struck me as really surprising that a apparent
rotation of BERLIN immediately after where BERLIN appears in the plaintext
would result in QQQXXX.

However, I've been unable to extend this further.

Here are some observations when exploring K4, this is not a solution but some parts may be candidates.

Method: Quag3/Vigenere switching alphabets between Kryptos (K) keyed alphabet and Regular (R) A-Z.

CT:    OBKRUOXOGHUL
KEY:   QUXXLATUTEMF
MASK:  KKKKKKKRRRRR
PT:    EGYPTXQUNDIG

"EGYPT X Q UNDIG .."

QUXXLA: This was found from anomalies in order: iQlusion, undergrUund, POINT as X, Xlayertwo, L extra on tableau, despAratly.
TUTEMF: Initial letters in first answer "They used the earth's magnetic field."
OWWTWH: Initial letters of third answer "Only W.W. this was his last message."

Each key is capped at 6 letters. Alphabet switches are runs of 7+ letters. This switches at position 8 where UNDIG shows, a fairly rare word.

OWWTWH extends the output into EGYPTXQUNDIGNWSSMY or "NW SS MY", with much lower confidence.
The second answer was skipped because it did not seem to fit anywhere, TSIBOTS: "They should it's buried out there somewhere."

Nothing too interesting shows up for the known plaintext of BERLINCLOCK and EASTNORTHEAST on the immediate decryption.

    - Carvings on the petrified tree which form shadows generally align with lines: 4,8,10,25.

"When asked about the solutions that have been sent to him (Jim Sanborn), and whether any of them were close, Jim said he got one from Germany about a year ago that was "kind of scary", that the first part had started to look right, but then the rest didn't."

In his work he is using a message key of CIAX; it breaks apart in his examples, but I wanted to share something that I found a while ago, it's an interesting Vigenere key, but on an encode (not a decode)

Problems: It will produce EAST (in wrong location) and then BERLEN in the correct positions, missing the I for E. (LEN(ONE) LIN(OIE)

Key for the encode is: XUAIC (*reversed: CIAUX*)
Standard Kryptos alphabet K-Z

PPAJ
TPNFYWNFIUHIDNWLUAXJOMIDJYEUGUH
YMECIHIGUQXQSFJYEASTBDHFXLAIBER
LENRWADISEOAHAYEJZXEUYPTOJMIMOV

I thought it was odd that CIAX appeared in his work and on a different simpler Vigenere encode, of CIA (U)X reversed, XUAIC, it actually produced clue words.
